core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Irrigation and Regenerative Agriculture for Climate-Resilient Food Systems of Kayumbu watershed in Rwanda
core_fields.description: The project addresses climate vulnerability and food insecurity affecting 500 smallholder farmers in Kayumbu Watershed caused by rain-fed farming and land degradation. It deploys solar-powered irrigation, regenerative land management, and nutrition-sensitive agriculture to enable year-round production on 5 hectares. Expected outputs include 20-40% yield increases and restored soils. The project will improve nutrition, raise incomes by 20%, and benefit 10,000+ community members, especially women and youth.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Kayumbu Watershed, IN Rwanda Southern Province, Kamonyi District, rely on rainfall, making them highly vulnerable to drought, soil erosion, and declining food production. This innovation introduces a solar-powered irrigation and regenerative agriculture model that enables continuous production of nutritious crops while restoring degraded landscapes. The solution integrates renewable energy for water pumping, efficient irrigation technologies, climate-smart farming practices, and watershed rehabilitation. This approach simultaneously increases food availability, improves dietary diversity, reduces environmental degradation, and enhances household livelihoods. Unlike traditional irrigation systems that rely unpredictable rainfall, this model uses solar energy, making it affordable, sustainable, and resilient to climate change. The scientific and technical foundation includes solar photovoltaic pumping, soil-water conservation engineering, agroforestry systems, and nutrition-sensitive crop diversification. Regenerative practices, mulching, terracing, composting, and contour bunds, restore soil fertility, sequester carbon, and improve water retention, keeping food systems within planetary boundaries. Immediate benefits include reliable water access, higher yields, reduced hunger months, and improved income for farmers. Sustainable long-term benefits include restored ecosystems, reduced food loss during drought, affordable nutritious foods in local markets, empowered women and youth, and greater resilience to climate shocks. The innovation directly benefits farmers, households, schools, cooperatives, consumers, and the wider environment, offering a scalable model for Rwanda and similar countries like Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, DRC, and Burundi.

core_fields.title: Wajanajae Kaliwirinae Project: Framework Plan for the Socio-Economic Development of the Indigenous Reserves.
core_fields.description: The Project strengthens the socio-economic development of Indigenous Reserves in the Colombian Altillanura through the Framework Plan, a long-term, identity-based partnership co-created with the communities. By integrating Indigenous Reserves into Agropecuaria Aliar S.A. s sustainable agroindustrial value chain through the collective production of maize and soy, the project improves food security, generates fair income, restores soils, and reinforces cultural autonomy. Reinvested income resources expand education, livelihoods, and environmental initiatives, ensuring long-term community well-being and territorial resilience
core_fields.abstract: The Wajanajae Kaliwirinae Project is a transformational cultivation model that integrates agroindustrial technology with Indigenous cosmovision to regenerate soils, strengthen cultural identity, and enable fair economic participation. Co-created over 13 years with the Indigenous Reserves of Wacoyo, La Victoria, and Umapo, the project implements precision soil restoration, bio-input fertilization, adaptive seed selection, and regenerative field rotation through community-led protocols grounded in ancestral ecological knowledge. This demonstrates that Altillanura soils long considered unproductive can be rehabilitated at scale and sustainably cultivated. The innovation is agronomic and systemic. It bridges Indigenous economies and formal value chains by positioning the Reserves as primary suppliers of maize and soy. Since 2013, more than USD 25 million have been invested, generating USD 2.1 million in community income and enabling 2,783 hectares of sustainable production an unprecedented, culturally aligned inclusion of Indigenous territories into a formal, traceable supply chain. Instead of extractive market dynamics, the model uses a community-designed revenue structure: 71% of earnings return directly to families and collective funds, 28% is reinvested in long-term project sustainability, and 1% supports social and cultural initiatives. Benefits are immediate and enduring. Restored soils remain productive even without external investment. Families improve food security through diversified systems such as gardens, fish farming, and poultry, reducing dependency. Youth find dignified livelihoods within their territory, mitigating migration and cultural loss. Through Fundaci n Pervivir and Fundaci n Pa s de Ra z, reinvested resources strengthen governance, leadership, conflict resolution, and environmental stewardship. More than 4,000 people benefit annually, consolidating long-term community autonomy, resilience, and well-being.

core_fields.description: This project establishes a climate-smart poultry layer farm in Zonkwa, Kaduna South to produce affordable, high-quality eggs while recycling poultry dung into organic manure for local farmers. It improves soil health, boosts food nutrition, creates jobs, and trains youths and women in sustainable agriculture. The initiative strengthens food security, promotes best farming practices, and supports environmentally friendly, income-generating agribusiness.
core_fields.abstract: The Climate Smart Sustainable Poultry Project introduces an innovative approach to egg production by integrating poultry farming with organic waste recycling. The core idea is to use poultry dung as a valuable input for organic manure production, which improves soil fertility, reduces the cost of farming, and decreases dependency on chemical fertilizers. This combined model solves two key problems: the rising cost of high-quality protein foods and declining soil fertility due to unsustainable agricultural practices. The relevance of this innovation lies in its ability to address food security, youth unemployment, and environmental degradation simultaneously. Egg prices continue to rise, and many farmers face reduced yields caused by degraded soils. This project provides consistent egg supply while helping farmers improve crop productivity through nutrient-rich organic fertilizer. The solution is grounded in scientific insights on nutrient cycling, soil microbiology, and sustainable waste-to-resource systems. Poultry manure is scientifically proven to enhance soil structure, increase nitrogen content, and support long-term soil health. By collecting, drying, and processing dung into organic fertilizer, the farm closes the loop between animal production and crop farming. Immediate benefits include access to affordable eggs for households, schools, and vendors; job creation for youths and women; and improved farm productivity for local producers. Long-term benefits include healthier soils, reduced environmental pollution, improved nutrition across communities, and a sustainable agribusiness model that generates ongoing income. The project strengthens climate resilience and empowers farmers with best practices that enhance yields while protecting the environment.

core_fields.title: Bagong Siklo: Integrated Solar Aqua Cycle for Renewable and Biodiverse Model for Climate-Resilient Farming
core_fields.description: Bagong Siklo: Integrated Solar Aqua Cycle for Renewable and Biodiverse Model for Climate-Resilient Farming enhances existing Department of Agriculture solar-powered irrigation systems by integrating aquaculture and a circular water cycle. Fish waste-enriched water is reused as natural fertilizer for crops, while native frogs and clams improve soil health and reduce pests in rice fields. Using treated bamboo for aquaponics, the system promotes biodiversity, sustainable farming, dual-income opportunities for farmers, and low-cost, eco-friendly, climate-resilient agriculture.
core_fields.abstract: Many solar-powered irrigation systems remain underutilized, limiting their potential to enhance productivity and sustainability in farming. Bagong Siklo addresses this by integrating circular aquaculture ponds with these existing systems, creating a closed-loop, nutrient-rich water cycle. Fish waste and aquaculture water are reused as natural fertilizer, reducing the need for synthetic inputs and lowering production costs. Bamboo-based aquaponics replaces PVC pipes, using renewable, eco-friendly materials for food production. To enhance biodiversity and provide additional income, native edible frogs are introduced into rice fields. These frogs naturally control pests, improve soil aeration, and can be harvested as an additional food source, generating dual-income opportunities for vulnerable farmers. Clams are also added for food production and nutrient cycling, further enriching soil and water health. The innovation draws on scientific insights from aquaponics, nutrient cycling, and biodiversity-based pest management, combined with locally available renewable materials and solar energy. By leveraging underutilized infrastructure, Bagong Siklo enhances water efficiency, soil fertility, and climate resilience while promoting eco-balanced farming practices. Immediate benefits include higher yields, diversified income, and reduced chemical use. Sustainable benefits extend to enhanced biodiversity, healthier soils and water, community adoption of renewable technologies, and resilience in disaster-prone areas. Consumers gain access to sustainably produced food, while communities benefit from strengthened livelihoods and scalable, climate-adaptive agriculture.

core_fields.title: Institutionalised Regenerative Integrated Soil Fertility Management Model for Sustainable Smallholder Food Production (i-Regen ISFM)
core_fields.description: Our project empowers smallholder farmers to transform farm and household waste into high-quality organic fertilizers, improving soil fertility and reducing costs. The innovation lies in institutionalizing this circular model through farmer cooperatives, which coordinate training, soil testing, and guaranteed compost off-take. Working through these existing structures enables efficient scaling, consistent quality, and the production of premium organic, biofertilizers, and customized organo-mineral blends that build resilient, nutrition-focused food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Kenya are struggling with declining soil fertility, rising fertilizer prices, and reduced crop productivity. At the same time, large quantities of farm and household organic waste are discarded, contributing to pollution, poor sanitation, and avoidable methane emissions. The i-Regen Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM) model directly connects these challenges by transforming organic waste into a valuable, affordable soil solution. Our model empowers farmers to convert their own biodegradable waste into high-quality vermicompost using red wigglers and Black Soldier Fly systems. Through a tripartite partnership with farmer cooperatives and agricultural training centres, farmers receive hands-on training, soil testing, and a guaranteed market for the compost they produce. Mzuri Organics then processes this compost through a proprietary blend of BSFL frass, vermicompost, and beneficial microbial inoculants, creating biofertilizers and customized organo-mineral fertilizers tailored to each farmer s soil needs. Scientific insights on organo-mineral blends and microbe-rich fertilizers show that they restore soil structure, enhance nutrient cycling, improve water retention, and significantly boost crop yields. The benefits are immediate and lasting: Farmers reduce input costs, regenerate their soils, increase yields, and earn income from compost sales. Households and communities gain access to safer, more nutritious, chemical-free food. Communities grow vegetables using their own waste. The environment benefits through reduced waste pollution, lower methane emissions, and improved soil carbon storage. The i-Regen ISFM model creates a circular, climate-resilient food system rooted in collaborative solutions, local resources and farmer-led innovation.

core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Cold Storage Hubs for Resilient Food Systems in Somalia
core_fields.description: We will expand a recently installed solar hybrid mini-grid into a community-owned service hub by adding cold storage and desalination. The facility will allow dairy producers and farmers to safely store milk and produce, reducing spoilage and enabling year-round sales that can triple incomes. By integrating renewable energy with essential food-system services, the project demonstrates a scalable model for improving nutrition, livelihoods, and climate resilience in rural Somalia.
core_fields.abstract: Alley-Badey is a small border town between Ethiopia and Somalia with strong potential to become a trading hub for dairy producers and farmers. However, without cold chain infrastructure, producers cannot store milk or their harvest safely. Dairy farmers can only sell milk 2-3 days a week when a distribution truck arrives to take goods to Hargeisa, the regional capital. Milk produced on other days spoils, limiting income. Farmers also lose a significant share of their harvest to heat and spoilage before it reaches market. Our innovation leverages a solar hybrid mini-grid we recently installed by adding a community-owned cold storage and desalination facility. By co-locating renewable energy, cooling, and water services, we create a food-energy hub that directly addresses the town s infrastructure gaps. The approach leverages a key technical insight: solar mini-grids generate surplus daytime power that can be used for productive loads such as refrigeration and water treatment, improving both energy-system economics and food-system resilience. The project delivers immediate benefits. Dairy producers can chill milk daily, reduce spoilage, and increase sales year-round. Farmers can store fruits and vegetables safely, improving market timing and income. Households gain affordable, clean water. Because all services operate within a community-owned business structure, revenues stay local, strengthening long-term sustainability. Environmentally, the project reduces food waste, cuts emissions, and avoids diesel-powered cooling with solar energy. The model can be replicated across rural Somalia to build more resilient, equitable, and low-carbon food systems.

core_fields.title: BIKI Point: End-to-End Food Rescue Point in Fruit and Vegetable Packing House
core_fields.description: BIKI will establish 5 BIKI Points, which are food rescue points in packing houses that belong to farmer groups across Sumatra, Indonesia. BIKI Point is partnerships with packing houses belonging to farmer groups by promoting GHP Standards, implementing Edible Coating Technology, and incorporating Digital Traceability. We involve the women for the post harvest process to support gender equality and has been designated as one of the national best practices in preventing food loss in Indonesia.
core_fields.abstract: Indonesia s agrifood sector faces urgent challenges, such as: food loss and waste, climate vulnerability, and the socioeconomic hardships of farmers. Fruits and vegetables, which make up a significant portion of food loss (more than 50%), account for 5.7 million tons wasted annually, costing over $320 million, produce carbon emission and methane gas that cause climate change, and depriving millions of Indonesians of essential nutrition. Additionally, nearly 70% of farmers live below the poverty line, and inefficiencies across the supply chain contribute to resource waste, habitat degradation, and biodiversity loss. To address these issues, we provide solutions designed to build resilience in agrifood systems and prevent food loss and waste especially in the post harvest stages. Our main solution is the BIKI Point, a community-based agri hub hosted in farmer group packing houses. Each BIKI Point delivers 4 integrated services: 1. Chitasil, a natural edible coating applied post-harvest that and has been tested for efficacy in extends shelf life up to 2x of more than 20 fruit and vegetable commodities. 2. GHP standards training to ensure safe and efficient crop handling. 3. Digital traceability, providing buyers visibility into freshness and origin in the retail market. 4. Market facilitation, linking farmers to retail, online, and export channels. With its operation so far, BIKI has directly benefited various stakeholders. We empower 500 farmers with increased income and 150 women to support gender equality and increasing the sustainability and climate mitigation awareness of more than 10,000 consumers in the BIKI Ecosystem.

core_fields.title: Women-Led Climate Nutrition & Resilient Grain System (W-CNGRS) in North Bihar (India).
core_fields.description: North Bihar face chronic food insecurity driven by climate variability, declining soil fertility, limited nutritious food access, and high post-harvest losses. GPSVS proposes a hybrid innovation Women-Led Climate Nutrition Gardens and Community Digital Grain Banks to build a regenerative, nutrition-focused local food ecosystem. The model integrates climate-resilient gardens, smart grain storage with mobile grain-credit access, and women-led governance through SHGs and KMM groups, enabling equitable, affordable, year-round nutrition while reducing food loss and strengthening climate resilience.
core_fields.abstract: GPSVS introduces a breakthrough hybrid food system model that integrates climate-resilient food production, smart grain preservation, and equitable community-led food access all powered by women's leadership. This innovation responds to chronic food insecurity, malnutrition, and recurring floods in North Bihar, where smallholder households lack diverse nutritious foods, face high post-harvest losses, and depend on unstable markets. 1. Climate-Resilient Nutrition Gardens (CRNGs) CRNGs are homestead or community micro-farms designed for flood-prone environments using raised beds, vertical gardens, biochar-amended soils, composting, micro-irrigation, mulching, and greywater recycling. Women cultivate climate-resilient vegetables, herbs, and medicinal plants while operating indigenous seed banks that preserve local, adaptive varieties. Scientific foundation: regenerative soil biology, water-efficient micro-irrigation, and biochar for carbon sequestration and soil health. Benefits: year-round access to safe and nutritious foods, improved dietary diversity, reduced input costs, and enhanced climate resilience. 2. Digital Community Grain Banks (DCGBs) DCGBs combine community-owned grain reserves with modern technology. Hermetic storage units reduce moisture, mold, and pests; IoT sensors track grain quality; and a mobile-based grain-credit system enables families to withdraw grain during floods or lean seasons. A digital ledger, managed by women's groups, ensures transparency and equitable access. Benefits: reduced post-harvest losses, stable supply during climate shocks, and decreased reliance on exploitative traders. 3. Women's Climate Leadership Circles (W-CLCs) Women's SHGs and KMM groups lead food planning, climate-risk mapping, nutrition awareness, and market linkages, ensuring collective ownership. Benefits: women's empowerment, inclusive governance, better household nutrition, and a sustainable, community-led local food ecosystem.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Moringa Innovations for Climate-Smart Nutrition and Zero-Waste Food Systems

core_fields.abstract: Super Moringa Supplies introduces a regenerative, zero-waste moringa innovation that transforms how communities grow, process, and use nutrient-dense crops. The problem we address is twofold: declining soil health from unsustainable farming and significant food loss across rural value chains. These challenges limit farmer incomes, weaken community nutrition, and push food systems beyond planetary boundaries. This innovation is guided by agricultural research demonstrating moringa s capacity to improve soil fertility, increase biodiversity, and provide complete proteins and micronutrients. Local processing technologies and solar-powered drying ensure minimal spoilage while preserving nutrients. Immediate benefits include higher farmer incomes, reduced crop losses, improved food security, and affordable nutrient-rich products for consumers, schools, and communities. Sustainable benefits include restored soils, reduced pressure on land and water, resilient rural livelihoods, and circular value chains that minimize waste and emissions. By combining regenerative agriculture with zero-waste bioprocessing, the innovation delivers environmental, social, and economic impact while helping food systems operate within planetary boundaries.

core_fields.title: Shifting Power to Farmers Through a Fair, Traceable, and Nutritious Food System
core_fields.description: Agronomy is building a producer-first food distribution model that directly connects farmers with consumers to improve nutrition, reduce waste, and restore fair livelihoods. By shortening supply chains through transparent pricing, real-time traceability, and efficient cold-chain delivery, the project increases access to fresh, trustworthy food while reducing emissions and food loss. Piloted in Finland, Agronomy demonstrates a scalable pathway toward more resilient, equitable, and sustainable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Agronomy addresses a structural failure in modern food systems: small and medium-scale farmers receive a shrinking share of food value, while consumers face limited access to fresh, trustworthy, and affordable food. Long, opaque supply chains increase food loss, emissions, and nutritional degradation, while disconnecting producers from end consumers. The innovation is a producer-first, traceable food distribution model that directly connects farmers with consumers through short, transparent supply chains. Agronomy combines transparent pricing, real-time traceability, and coordinated cold-chain logistics to ensure farmers are paid fairly and consumers receive fresh, nutritionally intact food. By removing unnecessary intermediaries, the system reduces waste, shortens transport distances, and improves economic outcomes for producers. The solution is informed by the insight that food system inefficiencies are not only logistical, but economic and informational. Farmers lack access to fair markets and real-time demand signals, while consumers lack visibility into how food is produced, priced, and transported. Agronomy integrates these functions into one model that aligns incentives across the value chain. Immediate benefits include improved farmer incomes, reduced food loss, lower emissions, and increased access to fresh, trusted food for communities. Sustainable benefits include strengthened regional food security, support for environmentally responsible farming practices, and a scalable model for equitable food distribution. Piloted in Finland, the innovation is designed to be replicated across regions facing similar structural food system challenges.

core_fields.title: NutriGrow: A Community-Based Food Innovation for Child Nutrition and Farmer Empowerment in Klaten
core_fields.description: NutriGrow is a community-driven nutrition initiative that provides locally sourced complementary foods, delivers intensive nutrition education for pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, and trains local farmers to produce healthier crops. Targeting 50 children at risk of stunting, 50 mothers, and 50 farmers in Klaten, the program integrates social intervention and a scalable sociopreneur model. NutriGrow strengthens community food security, reduces stunting risk, and offers a flexible, replicable model for wider impact.
core_fields.abstract: NutriGrow is a community-based nutrition innovation that integrates local food processing, nutrition education, and farmer empowerment to address the persistent problem of child stunting in rural Indonesia. Despite abundant local crops such as cassava, communities still rely on non-local or low-nutrient foods, while farmers face low product value and post-harvest losses. This disconnect between agriculture and nutrition results in limited access to affordable, nutrient-dense foods for young children and mothers. NutriGrow introduces a zero-waste, small-scale cassava processing model that transforms locally grown cassava into nutritious PMT (Supplementary Feeding) products for children. The solution is built on three core components: (1) regenerative and standardized post-harvest handling by farmers, (2) modular and low-cost processing techniques such as drying, fermenting, and fortifying cassava to increase nutrient bioavailability, and (3) community-based nutrition education for pregnant and breastfeeding mothers. These elements are supported by insights from food science on cassava fermentation, improved digestibility, and micronutrient enrichment, enabling the creation of affordable, culturally acceptable, and nutrient-rich PMT formulations. The innovation benefits multiple stakeholders. Children gain access to safer and more nutritious locally produced foods. Mothers receive practical nutrition knowledge that improves household feeding practices. Farmers increase income through value-added processing and reduced wastage. Schools and Posyandu obtain a reliable supply of affordable PMT. Communities and the environment benefit from a circular model that upcycles cassava peels into animal feed and compost, reducing waste and improving soil health. NutriGrow offers an immediately implementable, scalable, and sustainable model that strengthens food systems from farm to community nutrition.

core_fields.title: AI-Powered Personalized Meal Solutions to Improve Urban Nutrition and Reduce Food Waste
core_fields.description: Our project uses AI-powered personalization to deliver healthy, nutrient-balanced meals tailored to individual needs, helping urban Rwandans improve their diets and reduce the risk of non-communicable diseases. We reduce food waste, and make affordable, trusted nutritious food more accessible by integrating data-driven meal planning, local farmer sourcing, and sustainable packaging. This innovation strengthens urban nutrition, supports local agriculture, and promotes healthier, more sustainable food systems
core_fields.abstract: Urban populations in Rwanda face rapidly rising nutrition challenges. According to the WHO, 22% of adults are overweight, and 44% of annual deaths in Rwanda are linked to non-communicable diseases, many of which are diet-related. Young professionals often rely on fast, ultra-processed foods due to time constraints, while 20 30% of locally grown fruits and vegetables are lost postharvest, mainly because of poor demand forecasting and limited access to consistent buyers. This mismatch between nutritional needs, food availability, and consumption habits makes the problem urgent and relevant. Our innovation uses AI-powered personalized meal planning combined with nutrition science to deliver healthy meals tailored to individual health goals, dietary needs, and budgets. Users provide preferences (e.g., weight loss, diabetes support, plant-based, allergies), and our system generates customized plans using caloric algorithms and nutrient-density scoring. This ensures that every meal meets recommended dietary guidelines while remaining affordable and culturally relevant. We integrate data-driven demand forecasting and weekly subscriptions to significantly reduce food waste which is one of the biggest contributors to greenhouse emissions globally (food waste accounts for 8 10% of global GHG emissions). By sourcing directly from local farmers, we create predictable demand, increase farmer income stability, and reduce postharvest losses. Immediate benefits include convenient access to nutritious meals, reduced time preparing food, individualized health support, increased farmer income, and improved workplace productivity through corporate meal programs. Sustainable benefits include reduced NCD risk, minimization of food waste, strengthened local agricultural systems, and a lower environmental footprint through eco-friendly packaging and regenerative sourcing.

core_fields.title: TRANSFORMATION OF LAKE TANGANYIKA FISH WITH PRECISION FISHING USING AI AND IOT
core_fields.description: Our project involves processing fish from Lake Tanganyika using our solar photovoltaic dryers and precision fishing techniques, deploying fishing drones and IoT sensors in the water to address the problems of overfishing, the use of illegal nets, and the effects of climate change on Lake Tanganyika. This lake contributes to the animal protein needs of one million people in the region, but unfortunately, the malnutrition rate continues to rise.
core_fields.abstract: Traditionally, fishing in lakes like Lake Tanganyika relies on intuition and experience, leading to overfishing, inefficiencies, and pressure on ecosystems. Indeed, according to ANAPI (the National Agency for Investment Promotion) of the DRC, Lake Tanganyika has a production capacity of between 300,000 and 1 million tons of fish. Unfortunately, the local population suffers from food insecurity because much of the catch ends up being thrown away due to a lack of roads to transport it to major cities, the absence of modern preservation methods, and the use of unsustainable and environmentally unfriendly fishing practices. To address this problem, we have developed a solution that significantly improves the situation by combining real-time satellite observations (chlorophyll, water temperature, turbidity) with high-resolution monitoring based on drones and IoT sensors deployed in the water. These data streams are analyzed using AI models to generate "predictive maps of fish hotspots" and to send direct SMS messages and app alerts to fishers, guiding them to sustainable fishing areas while warning them when they enter restricted zones. After being caught, some of these fish are dried in our solar dryers, and others are canned for export to major cities. This allows cooperatives, communities, and producers to benefit from a scalable service to increase their income by reaching new markets, and provides consumers with access to nutritious, affordable, and reliable food. Finally, this approach directly addresses pressing environmental challenges, including declining fish stocks and biodiversity loss, by reducing overfishing and enabling adaptive management of aquatic resources.

core_fields.title: Feasibility of implementation and efficacy of the use of farmXP to strengthen food systems.
core_fields.description: FarmXP (farm expert) uses simple WhatsApp conversations to turn everyday farming decisions into better diets and healthier habits. The system guides smallholders toward diverse, nutrient-rich crops, safer production practices, and smarter post-harvest handling that protects family nutrition. At the same time, it nudges farmers to adopt regenerative practices like mulching, composting, crop rotation, and reduced burning. These signals build a living picture of soil health and resilience that external partners can use to target support.
core_fields.abstract: In Malawi, many smallholder farmers face challenges, including declining soil health, limited crop diversity, and inadequate access to agronomic advice. These challenges lower yields and force families to rely on diets that lack essential nutrients. Extension services rarely reach remote areas, and most farmers rely on basic phones and informal knowledge that may not be accurate. FarmXP transforms WhatsApp into a straightforward companion that guides farmers toward healthier diets and regenerative farming practices. By sending short messages about crops, soil, pests, or harvest plans, farmers receive advice tailored to their location, conditions, and season. The system encourages nutrient-rich crops such as legumes and vegetables, supports safer food handling, and helps reduce post-harvest losses. It also promotes practices that rebuild soil, such as mulching, composting, rotation, and reduced burning, and it tracks how these behaviors change over time. A key part of the approach is understanding who is engaging and how. FarmXP can identify patterns across men and women, notice where participation drops, and adjust the guidance to better reach groups who are often overlooked. This approach makes interventions more gender-responsive, inclusive, and likely to be sustainable over time. The insight behind FarmXP is that advice delivered through a tool farmers already trust leads to faster and lasting change. Without installing new apps or learning new systems, farmers receive practical steps they can act on immediately. The Malawi pilot will test how this approach improves nutrition, strengthens soil health, reduces waste, and helps farming households build resilience in a changing climate.

core_fields.title: Seeds for the Desert: A Horticulture Initiative to end Chronic Malnutrition in Afar Communities
core_fields.description: The Afar Region in Ethiopia faces extreme food insecurity due to climate change, drought, market exclusion, and the collapse of pastoral livelihoods, resulting in high chronic malnutrition. SONNE-International and the Afar Pastoralist Development Association (APDA) launched a horticulture program (2022) that reached over 140,000 people, to grow and market vegetables and fruits, improving nutrition and livelihoods. The Growth Phase will reach out to more communities, expand cultivation methods and food processing, and improve market accessibility.
core_fields.abstract: The project addresses Afar s escalating food insecurity. Recurrent droughts, degraded grassland and shrinking herds have left pastoralist families without access to diversified, nutritious food. Milk, once the dietary backbone, is now scarce for up to seven months a year, driving chronic malnutrition and high stunting rates. The solution: equipping pastoralist families to become horticultural producers, introducing sustainable local food production and processing into a traditionally livestock-based society. Through our culturally rooted, mobile community structures, a central horticultural training and demonstration centre trains pastoralists in crop production, irrigation, nutrition, food processing and cooperative marketing. Practical learning is combined with behaviour change on dietary diversity and household nutrition. Women make up 80% of the targeted trainees, recognising their role as key drivers of improved nutrition. By passing on knowledge and leading this major livelihood shift, traditional gender roles get challenged and women emerge as acknowledged experts within their communities. The novelty: While small household gardens exist in Afar, no comparable initiative has systematically combined training, seedling production, food processing and market access into one coherent model tailored to the Afar semi-nomadic pastoralist context. Our center is the first to integrate all these elements in one place - with the perspective of evolving into a self-sustaining social enterprise within 5 6 years. Immediate / lasting benefits: Reduced malnutrition, diversified nutrition, improved climate resilience, transformed gender roles. Communities gain both food security and agency, laying the foundation for sustainable, self-driven development in one of Ethiopia s most climate-affected regions.

core_fields.title: Eco-Smart Aquaculture and Agri-Production for Community Food Security
core_fields.description: This project establishes a sustainable, technology-supported tilapia and rabbit production system to increase local food supply, create youth employment, and reduce dependence on imported protein. Using eco-friendly methods such as solar-powered systems, efficient tank culture, and organic feed integration, the project will produce affordable fish and rabbit meat for households, markets, and restaurants. The initiative strengthens food security, empowers rural communities, and builds a scalable agribusiness model for long-term economic growth.
core_fields.abstract: The project introduces a sustainable, technology-assisted system for producing tilapia and rabbits in rural Cameroon, addressing the country s persistent shortage of affordable animal protein. Cameroon imports more than half of its fish supply, making local prices high and access unreliable for households, schools, and low-income communities. At the same time, youth unemployment remains widespread, and many small farmers lack the skills or tools to enter profitable agribusiness. The solution combines innovative tank-based fish farming, solar-powered aeration systems, mobile monitoring tools, and eco-friendly feed and herbal health boosters (such as moringa, neem, bitter-leaf, garlic). These techniques significantly reduce production costs, improve survival rates, and allow fish to be raised efficiently even in small land areas. Rabbit production complements the system by providing a fast-growing, low-input protein source whose manure enriches crop farms creating a circular economy model. Scientifically, the approach relies on proven aquaculture principles such as controlled water quality, recirculatory systems, and density-optimized tank culture, which deliver higher yields than traditional ponds. The use of local plant-based additives supports fish and rabbit health naturally, reducing dependence on expensive imported medications. Immediate benefits include steady supply of affordable protein, income generation for young farmers, and better nutrition for families and schools. Long-term benefits include reduced reliance on imports, stronger rural economies, new agri-tech skills for youth, and a cleaner environment due to low-waste, solar-powered operations and organic farming practices. This integrated system offers a scalable, replicable model for strengthening food security and empowering communities sustainably.

core_fields.title: Healthy schools, food sovereignty and adolescent empowerment in Raqaypampa, Tin Tin and San Vicente, Bolivia
core_fields.description: This project transforms three rural schools in Raqaypampa, Tin Tin and San Vicente into healthy school food systems with agroecological gardens, laying-hen units and semi-industrial kitchens improving adolescent nutrition, learning and empowerment. Gender-balanced youth brigades co-lead food production, menu design and hygiene monitoring while building life skills. The model strengthens food sovereignty, reduces malnutrition and enhances retention through hands-on training and community participation. Local production ensures sustainability, benefiting 600 students and 1,800 community members.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation transforms three rural secondary schools and boarding facilities into integrated school food systems where adolescents are central protagonists, guaranteeing daily access to safe, nutritious and culturally rooted diets. Agroecological gardens and small laying-hen units supply fresh vegetables, native crops and eggs, while semi-industrial Healthy School Kitchens transform these ingredients into diverse, balanced meals that meet adolescents' micronutrient needs. Youth nutrition brigades, led mainly by girls, co-design menus, monitor food quality using simple checklists, promote hygiene and safe food-handling practices, and advocate for health-promoting food environments. This model directly addresses high anemia prevalence, undernutrition and poor dietary diversity among rural Andean adolescents, especially those living away from home in boarding facilities. This innovation directly benefits 600 students (at least 50% girls), 41 boarding students, 36 teachers, 60 mothers/caregivers and school cooks, and 120 local promoters and health/education personnel. Indirectly, it reaches more than 1,800 parents, siblings and community members who experience improved food environments and knowledge transfer. Scientifically, the model integrates evidence from adolescent nutrition, agroecology, behavior change, small-scale poultry systems, and home-grown school feeding. By improving dietary diversity and micronutrient intake while building practical food-system skills and youth leadership, it enhances health, learning outcomes, school retention and girls' empowerment offering a replicable, cost-efficient, climate-resilient pathway for Andean rural schools.

core_fields.title: Adapting Additive Manufacturing Elements to the Realization of Agricultural Components in Nigeria
core_fields.description: This initiative investigates the viability of addtive manufacturing (AM) technologies for bolstering the production of agricultural components in the Nigeria. This is aimed at enhancing the efficiency and efficacy of agricultural operations in the region. Our strategy reviews and selects AM technologies, local Nigerian materials and case studies in manner which promotes suitainable development goals 1, 2, 3, 8 and 10 via adaptation of essential manufacturing parameters in Nigeria and eventually into other regional market.
core_fields.abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) has greatly revolutionalize the design and manufacture of mechanical components. Its ability to consolidate parts within an assembly has greatly minimized the number of manufacturing steps required to realize novel mechanical components. This has profound implications for agricultural machineries within Nigeria which is currently experiencing relatively low manufacturing index, a situation compromising initiatives aimed at reducing poverty. While AM has the potential to ameliorate the devastating effects of Nigeria's manufacturing deficit, The country is yet to be fully engage it. This pilot project develops a potent strategy which adapt what is usually known as the four "ms" of AM, (manpower, machine, materials, and metrology) to manufacturing realities within NIgeria. It reviews the vast number of technologies within the AM family to ascertain which offer the greatest opportunity for Nigeria as revealed by local agricultural materials, cost of AM machinery and ease of manpower training. Secondly, via acquisition of a relatively cheap AM technology, the project demonstrates the viability of AM for a critical Agricultural component. This includes an study which evaluates the most viability agricultural components for AM which is further manufactured with the acquired machinery. The initiative investigate the capacities of regional waste materials to be used as AM feed material to sustainably promote adoption of AM technology. Our strategy will bolster avaibility of local agricultural component, in a manner which reduce environmental waste, promote local manufacturing opportunities and reduce the need to fly agricultural machinery and its components into Nigeria and neighbouring nations.

core_fields.title: In vitro and in silico evaluation of entomopathogenic fungi for the weevil borers.
core_fields.description: Biological control has established itself as a viable alternative worldwide, but its application in the field still has limitations. Therefore, the aim is to evaluate new encapsulated formulations that protect the infectious units of entomopathogenic fungi and improve their effectiveness against the black weevil, which represents one of the main threats to Musa cultivation in Colombia and to the food security of the population
core_fields.abstract: This project addresses the limitations of biological control using entomopathogenic fungi, which, although a sustainable alternative, have reduced effectiveness in the field due to environmental factors such as UV radiation, temperature, and humidity. The research focuses on controlling the black weevil (Cosmopolites sordidus), one of the main pests affecting Musa crops not only in Colombia but also in neighboring countries such as Ecuador, Brazil, and Uganda, causing productivity losses, increased use of chemical insecticides, and risks to food security. The proposed solution consists of the development and evaluation of encapsulated formulations of entomopathogenic fungi with new biomaterials, designed to protect the spores, improve their stability, and prolong their biological activity. This innovation integrates in vitro and in silico approaches, combining experimental bioassays with mathematical modeling and computational simulations that allow the behavior of the formulations to be predicted, their performance to be optimized, and development times and costs to be reduced. From a scientific and technical perspective, encapsulation emerges as an effective strategy to overcome environmental barriers and improve biocontrol efficiency, while in silico modeling strengthens data-driven decision-making. Immediate benefits include greater effectiveness in controlling the black weevil and reduced use of agrochemicals, In the long term, innovation contributes to agricultural sustainability, environmental protection, and the health and food security of Musa farmers.

core_fields.title: Hybrid Intelligent Solar Dryer for Sustainable Food Preservation
core_fields.description: Our project develops a Hybrid Intelligent Solar Dryer that helps farmers and small processors preserve food safely and efficiently. It combines solar energy with a backup heating source, forced-convection airflow, and sensor-based controls to dry fruits, vegetables, meat, grains and fish faster, cleaner, and with better quality. The solution reduces post-harvest losses, improves food safety, and offers an affordable, low-carbon technology adapted to rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: In many parts of Africa, farmers lose large shares of their harvest because they cannot dry and preserve food properly. Traditional sun-drying exposes products to dust, insects, animals, unpredictable weather, and long drying times that damage quality. Electric dryers are expensive to run, and most rural communities face unstable power supply. These challenges lead to avoidable losses, lower income for farmers, and limited access to safe, nutritious dried foods. Our Hybrid Intelligent Solar Dryer solves this by combining solar thermal energy with a small backup heating source, a forced-convection airflow system, and an intelligent digital controller. Sensors measure temperature, humidity, and airflow inside the drying chamber, while the controller automatically adjusts the heat and ventilation to maintain ideal conditions for each product. This makes drying faster, safer, and more consistent, even when sunlight fluctuates. The idea came from our engineering work in energy-limited communities and our understanding that food preservation cannot rely on a single energy source. By hybridizing solar energy with a controlled auxiliary system and embedding automation, we can deliver industrial-level drying performance at a cost accessible to smallholder farmers. The immediate benefits include cleaner, safer, and more nutritious dried products; reduced post-harvest losses; higher income for producers; and more reliable food supplies for consumers. Long-term benefits include stronger local food systems, reduced dependence on grid electricity, lower carbon emissions, and a technology that can be replicated and maintained locally. The dryer supports farmers, cooperatives, schools, women s groups, small processors, and rural communities seeking affordable, climate-friendly food preservation.

core_fields.title: AI-enhanced thermal energy storage for resilient agricultural cold chains in West Africa.
core_fields.description: The Seeding the Future Prize will support Gyre Energy to expand its existing agricultural cold storage pilots in West Africa. The project deploys offline-capable, low-data AI refrigeration control with thermal energy storage to improve reliability, reduce diesel use, and prevent food spoilage. Building on live pilots in Nigeria and Ghana, this phase bridges technical feasibility to commercially viable cold storage models that strengthen agricultural supply chains and access to safe, nutritious food.
core_fields.abstract: PROBLEM & SOLUTION In West Africa, and more broadly emerging economies, cold storage facilities serving agricultural value chains are constrained by unreliable grid electricity and heavy dependence on diesel generation. This drives high operating costs and leads to food spoilage (up to 40% post-harvest losses) due to temperature breaches during outages, particularly for perishable foods such as fish, fruit, and vegetables. Gyre Energy addresses this by integrating physics-based AI models with Thermal Energy Storage (TES). The AI optimises cooling to occur when energy is available or cheap, storing it in TES. This project continues this work by developing an offline AI controller that allows systems to optimise autonomously during internet or power outages. INSIGHT Cooling can be treated as a dynamic energy resource. While electricity batteries are often cost-prohibitive in cold room settings, Thermal Energy Storage is approximately 10x cheaper per kWh, making it viable for storing cold energy. AI is often considered unsuitable for rural contexts, this project focuses on low-data models that run on offline edge controllers to ensure operations continue reliably in low-connectivity environments. BENEFITS For cold storage operators, TES and AI controls reduce operating costs by lowering diesel reliance and optimising renewable electricity use. For agricultural producers, reliable cold chains reduce post-harvest food loss and increase sellable volumes. Environmentally, the solution reduces emissions and local pollution by displacing diesel generation. The project also develops local technical capacity through upskilling local installers.

core_fields.title: Novel circular economy in palm plantations: insect-based waste management for sustainable diets and livelihood creation
core_fields.description: Our technology redirects palm plantation waste from burning to the production of insect-derived oil, protein, and fertilisers for sustainable agriculture . After proving feasibility with experimental-scale trials in West Africa, we will now integrate the full process at larger scale with partners in South Asia, from waste collection to insect production and locally beneficial outputs. This demonstration will validate financial, environmental, and social benefits for smallholders and position the technology for replication across palm-growing regions.
core_fields.abstract: Palm agriculture spans an area larger than Germany and generates vast volumes of fibrous waste. Across producing regions, this waste is commonly burned, releasing harmful smog and substantial greenhouse gases that threaten human health, biodiversity, and accelerate climate change. Yet oil palm remains a critical global crop: it supplies more than 40% of the world s vegetable oil from only 8% of farmland, supports millions of livelihoods, and is essential for food security. The challenge is not to replace palm with more harmful alternatives, but to transform its sustainability. Rhynco s innovation uses specialised insects to convert palm waste into three valuable products: nutrient-rich insect protein, insect oil, and frass fertiliser. Our proprietary process - developed through five years of research with Imperial College London - is the only insect-based system capable of breaking down tough palm biomass at scale. This technology addresses multiple urgent needs. The insect protein and oil provide affordable, sustainable nutrition for human foods or livestock feeds in regions where healthy diets remain inaccessible. The frass, returned to plantation soils, improves soil fertility and acts as an antifungal agent, helping combat devastating fungal diseases currently threatening global palm production. By replacing open burning and unmanaged waste with a circular, value-creating system, our approach cuts thousands of tonnes of emissions, improves plantation soil health, and enables smallholders to achieve lucrative sustainability certification whilst creating new income streams. The result is a scalable, science-driven solution that strengthens food security, supports smallholder livelihoods, and reduces environmental harm across the tropics.

core_fields.title: Zambia s Circular Food Solution: Youth-Led Urban Farming for Climate-Resilient Communities
core_fields.description: The Urban Farming & Permaculture Learning Space in Kafue, Zambia turns food waste and idle land into compost, nutritious food, and eco-friendly products. By training youth and women in composting, climate-smart gardening, and biofabrication, the project improves household food security, reduces waste, builds income opportunities, and strengthens climate resilience through a practical, community-led circular food system.
core_fields.abstract: The Urban Farming & Permaculture Learning Space introduces an innovative, community-driven model that transforms food waste, idle land, and untapped youth potential into sustainable food systems, income opportunities, and climate resilience. The innovation combines three elements rarely integrated in low-resource urban settings: 1. Food-waste rescue and composting, 2. Compost-based polyculture gardening, and, 3. Biofabrication using banana fiber to produce eco-friendly products. This model addresses several urgent problems: rising food insecurity, high urban waste generation, unemployment among youth and women, and limited climate-adaptive skills in urban communities. By turning organic waste into compost and empowering households to grow nutritious food, the program reduces household expenditure, improves diets, and promotes circular, climate-smart practices. Early results demonstrate strong feasibility: 108 youth trained, 38 home gardens established, 1,762 kg of food waste rescued, 4,169 kg of compost produced, and 335 kg of vegetables harvested, directly improving nutrition for nearly 350 children daily. These outcomes show that the approach is practical, replicable, and enthusiastically adopted by end users. In 2026, the innovation will scale to reach an additional 100 youth through a structured garden club model and 90 women, mothers and guardians of the youth, through 3-month-training cohorts. Production capacity will expand through herbs and cultivation of seedlings, while an electric bike will enable larger-scale food-scrap recovery across local markets and informal settlements in Kafue. By combining hands-on training, environmental stewardship, and income generation, this innovation is uniquely relevant for building food-secure, climate-resilient households, while empowering youth and women as leaders in sustainable change.

core_fields.title: Scaling Drought Resilience for Smallholder Farmers: A WaterBank Pilot in Bukanga, Isingiro District, Uganda
core_fields.description: Our project uses locally available fruit waste to create organic moisture-retention granules called Waterbank, which help smallholder farmers reduce irrigation needs by up to 60% and protect crops during dry spells. While improving soil moisture for up to three months, Waterbank strengthens food security, reduces waste pollution, and enables farmers in drought-prone regions to maintain yields despite climate-induced water stress. This project will pilot Waterbank with smallholder farmers and generate evidence for scalable impact.
core_fields.abstract: Climate-induced water stress is one of the most urgent threats facing smallholder farmers in Africa. In Uganda alone, over 70% of farmers rely solely on rainfall, yet droughts and erratic weather now cause yield losses of 30-60% annually. At the same time, cities generate millions of tons of organic waste each year, much of which decomposes in landfills and releases methane. Our company bridges these two challenges through a simple, homegrown innovation: an organic, food-waste-derived moisture-retention granule designed specifically for smallholder farmers who lack irrigation. When applied to soil, Waterbank absorbs and stores water during rains and gradually releases it to crop roots over several weeks, significantly extending soil moisture availability and reducing the need for frequent watering. This solution emerged from on-farm observations that farmers cultivate in hilly loose soils and cannot afford irrigation and its infrastructure, thus a need to retain the little moisture available. By refining fruit waste into a stable granular absorbent, Afrotym created a product that is low-cost, biodegradable, and easy for farmers to apply by hand or with basic tools. The benefits are immediate and sustainable. Farmers gain greater crop survival during dry spells, more predictable yields, and reduced dependence on expensive or inaccessible irrigation. Communities benefit from improved food security and a reduction in organic waste pollution. Environmentally, Waterbank lowers methane emissions by diverting fruit waste from landfills and enhances soil health through increased microbial activity and water efficiency.

core_fields.title: Transforming Rice Husk and Mexican Tea into Sustainable Natural Protectant for Grain Storage in Tanzania
core_fields.description: This project is designed to transform rice husk waste and locally available Mexican tea (CHENOPODIUM AMBROSIOIDES) into natural food safe grain storage protectant. The project intends to develop an insecticide product prototype based on laboratory validation and participatory farmer field trials in Morogoro. The product will help to reduce postharvest food losses and promote sustainable pest control as well as strengthening food security among smallholder farmers.
core_fields.abstract: Cereals including maize, experience postharvest loss of 10 to 20%, most of it caused by storage insect pests leading to income, food and nutrition insecurity. Improved storage facilities and technologies are not accessible and affordable to majority of smallholder farmers. Individually, rice husk waste and Mexican tea (CHENOPODIUM AMBROSIOIDES)) have demonstrated pest control potential (Rohan et al., 2015: Charles et al., 2016). The syntactic effect of these products has not been tested against insect storage pest including SITOPHILUS ZEAMAIS. The proposed project seeks to transform rice husk and Mexican tea into biogenic silica and botanical powders, respectively, to make one natural grain protectant. The product will provide affordable alternative grain protectant for addressing food safety and availability, environmental sustainability and creating employment for youth and women. The project is novel because it transforms large amounts of rice husk waste into food safe amorphous silica combined with botanical powder as natural protectant for grain, something never produced or tested.

core_fields.title: Formalizing Indigenous Knowledge: Building Regulatory Infrastructure for Traditional African Beer Homebrewers
core_fields.description: Kwela Brews restores dignity to Traditional African Beer, a R5.5B sector where 1M+ African women hold centuries-old fermentation knowledge yet remain economically excluded. Our Slow Food-funded Re-member Project proved market demand (160+ consumers) and cultural resonance. Now we're building the missing bridge: scientific validation honoring traditional methods, certification pathways navigating regulatory complexity, quality systems preserving authenticity. We're creating replicable infrastructure letting Indigenous knowledge participate in formal without erasure.
core_fields.abstract: Over 1M African women homebrewers steward Traditional African Beer (TAB) knowledge spanning grain ecology, microbiology, and nutritional science. Yet colonial stigmatization and regulatory exclusion trap their expertise in informal economies. Simultaneously, harmful high-alcohol variants emerged from economic desperation creating legitimate safety concerns that policymakers now apply to all traditional brewing, conflating authentic practice with dangerous imposters. Our Approach: We're building the first systematic formalization pathway for traditional fermented beverages, not by industrializing production, but by creating infrastructure that validates Indigenous knowledge as legitimate food science. Using modern food technology tools and traditional brewing expertise, we're developing authentication protocols distinguishing safe ancestral methods from harmful variants. The Innovation: This isn't beverage commercialization, it's infrastructure creation. We combine pH analysis, microbiological testing, and fermentation science to document why traditional methods are inherently safe, then translate findings into accessible certification pathways homebrewers can navigate. Technical Foundation: Traditional TAB's wild yeast fermentation naturally limits alcohol to 2-4% while producing beneficial probiotics and enhanced nutrient bioavailability. The challenge isn't the method it's formalizing validation systems respecting cultural protocols while meeting food safety requirements. Immediate Impact: Homebrewers gain legal market access, consumers access nutritious fermented foods, municipalities acquire tools distinguishing safe practices from harmful variants, policymakers receive replicable models for informal food sector formalization. Short term impact: Increased income for homebrewers, good quality beer for consumers, celebrated heritage of homebrewers and TAB Long term impact: Improved livelihoods for homebrewers; Positive attitudes towards TAB and Challenged policies and practices to centre and celebrate homebrewers in the TAB industry

core_fields.title: EcoHeat Nutrition Pack: Climate-Smart Self-Warming Meals for Food-Insecure Communities
core_fields.description: Our project introduces the EcoHeat Nutrition Pack, a safe, natural self-warming food pouch designed for communities with limited access to fuel, clean water, or electricity. Using a plant-based HeatCell Bio-Chamber , the pouch warms meals within seconds through a gentle, non-metallic reaction. The packaging is fully recyclable or biodegradable, enabling climate-smart nutrition for emergency zones, low-income regions, and high-need populations. This innovation delivers safe, convenient, environmentally sustainable meals anywhere.
core_fields.abstract: Access to warm, safe, and nutritious food remains a major challenge for millions of people living in crisis zones, low-income communities, schools without infrastructure, and regions affected by climate change. Many households and humanitarian settings lack fuel, clean water, or electricity, making it difficult to safely heat meals. Existing self-heating solutions rely on metallic reactions, require added water, generate high heat, and are unsafe or environmentally harmful. The EcoHeat Nutrition Pack introduces a completely new, sustainable approach: a plant-based self-warming food pouch that heats meals gently within seconds using a natural, non-metallic HeatCell Bio-Chamber . This chamber contains food-grade salts and botanical activators separated by a pull-tab barrier. When the user pulls the tab, the barrier opens and a mild, controlled reaction releases safe heat inside an insulated micro-chamber that never touches the food. The entire pouch is made from recyclable or biodegradable bio-laminate materials, ensuring minimal environmental impact. This innovation emerged from insights in food chemistry, passive thermal reactions, and bio-based material science, proving that safe low-temperature exothermic reactions can be achieved without metals, without added water, and without risk. Immediate benefits include: Safe, hot meals anywhere no stove, fuel, or electricity Reduced reliance on charcoal, wood, or unsafe heating methods Protection against foodborne illness by enabling warm consumption Fast deployment for emergencies, refugee camps, and school feeding programs Environmentally friendly materials that reduce waste and carbon footprint The EcoHeat Nutrition Pack provides a practical, scalable, climate-smart nutrition solution that strengthens food security for vulnerable populations

core_fields.title: Scaling Women-Led Climate Resilient Farming
core_fields.description: The Women-led Climate Resilient Farming (WCRF) model addresses declining soil health, climate vulnerability, poor nutrition, and limited recognition of women farmers. Developed by Swayam Shikshan Prayog, it places women at the center of regenerative, chemical-free agriculture using indigenous seeds, crop diversification, and water-smart practices. Combining agroecological science with traditional knowledge, the model reduces input costs, improves food security and nutrition, strengthens women s leadership, and builds resilient, sustainable local food systems.
core_fields.abstract: The Women-led Climate Resilient Farming (WCRF) model developed by Swayam Shikshan Prayog addresses a critical challenge in India s food system: smallholder farming households, particularly women, face declining soil fertility, increasing climate shocks, rising input costs, poor dietary diversity, and limited decision-making power. Conventional agriculture has intensified chemical dependence, weakened indigenous seed systems, and reduced farm resilience, while women s agricultural knowledge and leadership have remained undervalued. The WCRF model places women farmers at the center of regenerative and nutrition-sensitive agriculture. Developed and refined over more than a decade, the model integrates chemical-free farming, soil and water conservation, indigenous seed preservation and exchange, diversified cropping systems, and agri-allied livelihoods. Women are organized into collectives and leadership networks that promote peer learning, experimentation, and collaboration with local governments to access public programs and resources. The approach is informed by agroecological science, climate risk analysis, and participatory learning methods. Scientific insights on soil health, biodiversity, and water efficiency are combined with traditional knowledge of local seeds, cropping patterns, and food practices. Demonstration farms allow women farmers to test, adapt, and refine practices suited to local agro-climatic conditions. Immediate benefits include reduced production costs, improved food security, better nutrition, and increased incomes through diversified crops and value-added products. Over time, the model restores soil health and biodiversity, strengthens seed sovereignty, builds climate resilience, and transforms women from laborers into farmers and decision-makers. Communities benefit from more sustainable food production, healthier diets, and stronger local institutions capable of responding to climate and market risks.

core_fields.abstract: The proposed innovation integrates climate-smart agro-ecological practices with affordable, nutrient-rich food production to ensure safe, sustainable, and equitable diets for vulnerable households in Bangladesh s coastal areas. Bangladesh, with estimated 36 million coastal people severely impacted. Salinity intrusion has reduced agricultural productivity and increasing poverty, forced livelihoods change, economic losses, food insecurity, market price, desertification and health issues. The solution works by enabling households and producers to grow their own safe, appealing, and trusted food while strengthening local food systems. Functional linkages with markets, service providers, and community groups ensure equitable access, especially for small farmers, Climate affected society and low-income families. Immediate benefits include reliable access to fresh vegetables, dairy and meat products, reduced production costs, improved dietary diversity, and enhanced knowledge of climate-resilient practices. Sustainable benefits include stronger household resilience, improved soil and water conservation, reduced environmental impact, and long-term adoption of regenerative, circular food system practices. Overall, this innovation empowers consumers and producers alike by ensuring affordable, accessible, and sustainable food for all.

core_fields.title: Community-Owned Food System Hubs: Youth-Led Regenerative Agriculture and Climate Resilience in South Africa
core_fields.description: ForAfrika establishes six integrated Food System Hubs across Gauteng, Mpumalanga, and Limpopo each functioning as production center, processing facility, training academy and youth-led cooperative. Using proven agroecological practices, circular waste systems, and climate-smart technologies, hubs produce nutritious food year-round while training 180 youth and women as farmer-entrepreneurs. Produce supplies 6,000+ people through ForAfrika's 150 ECD centres and local markets, demonstrating economically viable, climate-resilient, community-owned food systems ready for government replication across South Africa's underserved municipalities.
core_fields.abstract: Problem Addressed: South Africa's food systems face converging crises: 40% household food insecurity in underserved communities, climate variability threatening production, degraded soils, water scarcity, and 50%+ youth unemployment. Existing interventions typically address single aspects production OR processing OR training creating dependency without genuine community ownership or economic sustainability. Our Innovation Solution: ForAfrika's breakthrough is the Six-Function Integrated Hub Model a community-owned platform simultaneously addressing: 1. Nutritious Food Production: Agroecological methods (raised beds, intercropping, indigenous seeds, zero chemicals, compost-based fertility) 2. Post-Harvest Processing: Solar dehydrators reducing 30-40% food loss to 10%, enabling year-round storage and income 3. Circular Economy: Converting 30 tonnes/week organic waste into compost, closing nutrient loops 4. Climate-Smart Infrastructure: Drip irrigation, rainwater harvesting (10,000L tanks), solar pumps reducing water use 30% 5. Youth Enterprise: Not training-only but cooperative business ownership with assets and income generation 6. Environmental Monitoring: Tracking soil health, water use, biodiversity, creating evidence for policy Why Integration is Innovation: Synergies impossible with siloed programs emerge: Processing waste becomes production compost. Solar dehydration extends shelf-life, enabling income. Cooperative ownership ensures post-project sustainability. Youth aren't beneficiaries they're entrepreneurs with productive assets. Scientific Basis: Agroecology increases soil organic matter 25% (demonstrated in ForAfrika's Northern Cape site), reducing water needs 30%. The model leverages BASICS extensive work with national and state rural livelihood missions and will generate a scalable framework for state-wide adoption.
core_fields.abstract: Bundelkhand region of Uttar Pradesh has long been recognized as a nutrition-deficient region with: Prevalence of stunting, underweight children, and anemia among women Low dietary diversity and excessive dependence on cereals Seasonal hunger is due to erratic rainfall and low agricultural productivity. There is limited integration between nutrition programmes and smallholder agriculture. While India promotes fortified foods, millets, and diversified production, districts lack a structured mechanism to translate these goals into actionable, convergent food system plans. The Food Systems Transition Planning Unit (FSTU) is a consulting-led innovation designed to close this structural gap. Led by BASICS leveraging a decade of experience with National and State Rural Livelihood Missions, and supporting women Producer Groups and Women FPCs the FSTU will create a district-level systems intelligence and planning architecture. The innovation includes: 1. Food System Diagnostics 2. District Food System Transition Plan linking nutrition priorities, indigenous crops, and institutional procurement. 3. Nutri-Basket Procurement Pathways connecting SHG/CLF/FPC producers to schools, Anganwadi s, and hospitals. 4. Digital Food Systems Dashboard for tracking production, procurement, and dietary diversity. 5. Institutional Convergence Framework for SRLM, Agriculture, Horticulture, MDM, and ICDS. The model is novel because it does not implement activities directly it builds district capacity through planning, protocols, analytics, procurement design, and advisory behavior-change. The benefits include improved local availability of nutritious foods, strengthened women-led production systems, and district adoption of evidence-driven procurement and consumption pathways. Long term, the model creates a replicable state-wide architecture for transforming rural food systems.

core_fields.title: Promoting Neglected and Underutilized Species for Nutrition, Livelihoods, and Climate Resilience in Baringo County
core_fields.description: The proposed project is designed to enhance nutrition, food security, and climate resilience in Baringo County, an ASAL region facing drought and low productivity. By promoting resilient and nutrient-rich Neglected and Underutilized Species (NUS), the project will conduct surveys, establish community seed banks, and train farmers especially women and youth on value addition and nutrition. Seed fairs, enterprise incubation, market linkages, and policy advocacy will strengthen NUS value chains, improve livelihoods, and secure long-term government support
core_fields.abstract: The proposed project introduces an innovative approach that promotes Neglected and Underutilized (NUS) especially sorghum, millet and cowpeas using agro-ecological practices as a practical solution to food insecurity, malnutrition, and climate vulnerability in Baringo s arid and semi-arid (ASALS) environment. The main problem being underutilisation of traditional nutrient rich crops species that are resilience and well adapted to the changing climate. This challenge is highly relevant today as communities continue to experience recurrent malnutrition, rising food prices, and declining crop diversity. The innovation solves this problem by combining traditional knowledge with modern community-led systems: Mapping existing NUS crops, establishing seed banks for conservation, building farmer skills in value addition, and creating incubation programs for women and youth led NUS enterprises. This intergrated model transforms sorghum, millet and cowpeas from forgotten crops into nutritious foods and viable economic products. The solution is guided by scientific and local insights showing that many NUS such as sorghum, millets and indigenous vegetables are naturally drought torelant, require fewer inputs, and contains higher nutritional value than most staple crops. Strengthening their seed systems and market provides an environmentally sustainable alternative for ASAL communities. immediate benefits include improved access to diverse seeds, better household nutrition from newly developed recipes and increased income from value added NUS products. In long term, communities and producers gain resilient food systems, stronger local markets, youth and women employment and improved biodiversity conservation all contributing to healthier environment and more food secure society.

core_fields.description: The Green Scholars project improves nutrition and education in Ethiopia by establishing organic school and household gardens. core_fields.abstract: Rising food prices, poor dietary diversity, and limited practical learning opportunities are creating urgent nutrition and education gaps for children and adolescents in Ethiopia. core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Mobile Cold Chain Innovation to Reduce Food Loss and Waste
core_fields.description: AkoFresh provides modular solar-powered cold storage, mobile refrigerated transport, market linkage and training to reduce post-harvest losses for smallholder farmers and women traders in Ghana. Our solution extends crop shelf-life by up to 21 days, stabilize food supply, boosts farmer incomes, and reduces emissions from food waste. This project will expand modular cold rooms, solar-powered refrigerated tricycles, and farmer training across new regions, strengthening food security and climate resilience for thousands of rural farmers.
core_fields.abstract: Up to 45% of fruits and vegetables grown by smallholder farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa spoil before reaching consumers due to rising temperatures, weak cold-chain systems, and unreliable market access. This waste reduces farmer income, accelerates food insecurity, and contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions. AkoFresh addresses this urgent climate and food systems challenge through an integrated, solar-powered cold-chain and distribution solution built for rural communities. Our innovation includes solar-powered cold storage hubs, solar refrigerated tricycles for last-mile cooling transport, and a digital marketplace that connects farmers directly to buyers. The system is strengthen in proven scientific and technical principles, temperature and humidity optimization for perishables, renewable energy engineering, and community-led service design. Farmers pay only for the services they use, removing the barrier of high capital investment. By extending crop shelf life up to 21 days, AkoFresh reduces post-harvest losses by up to 50%, improves produce safety and quality, and enables farmers to sell at better prices. Women traders and youth gain access to reliable distribution and new economic opportunities. Communities benefit from increased availability of nutritious food, lower spoilage-driven price volatility, and reduced emissions from wasted produce. Complementing the technology, AkoFresh trains farmers and traders in post-harvest handling, climate-smart practices, and storage management. Our youth-led team co-designs every project with farmer groups to ensure solutions fit local realities, leading to strong adoption and trust. AkoFresh creates immediate economic gains while building long-term climate resilience and transforming food systems from a cycle of loss to one of opportunity.
