core_fields.abstract: Mtaah Farm is an integrated digital farm-to-market innovation designed to address high post-harvest losses, low farmer incomes, food safety risks, and inefficient, carbon-intensive food distribution systems. Smallholder farmers often lose 30 40% of their harvest due to poor market access, inadequate storage, and fragmented logistics, while consumers face high prices, inconsistent quality, and limited trust in food safety. The innovation combines five core components into a single, connected food system. First, AI-powered advisory tools provide farmers with localized guidance on climate-smart production, pest and disease management, and post-harvest handling. Second, a digital marketplace links farmers directly to households, schools, retailers, and institutions, reducing reliance on intermediaries and improving price transparency. Third, decentralized aggregation and solar-supported cold storage reduce spoilage and preserve nutritional quality. Fourth, QR-based traceability enables tracking of produce from farm to consumer, improving food safety and trust. Finally, low-carbon last-mile delivery using electric motorbikes reduces logistics costs and emissions while creating youth employment. This solution is informed by agronomic research on post-harvest loss reduction, data-driven advisory systems, and sustainable logistics models adapted to low-resource contexts. Immediate benefits include reduced food loss, higher and more predictable farmer incomes, improved access to safe and affordable food, and lower delivery emissions. Long-term benefits include more resilient local food systems, increased adoption of regenerative practices, reduced environmental impact, and stronger food security for communities and institutions such as schools.

core_fields.abstract: In Uganda, 72% of farmland is smallholder-operated, 70% of the population works in agriculture, and farmers lose up to 40% of potential profit due to post-harvest losses. Rural farmers face multiple challenges: limited access to energy, post-harvest processing, markets, training, and nutritious foods. Smart Agri-Centres (SACs) are community-based agricultural hubs designed to address these barriers, providing energy, value-addition services, and training for off-grid communities to reduce losses, increase income, and improve nutrition. Market access support helps farmers reach local, national, and international buyers, while training builds knowledge of sustainable and nutritious farming practices. The SAC design is informed by seven years of research affiliated with Oxford and Cambridge Universities, which revealed why many development projects fail and identified the effectiveness of integrated, community-led approaches. Smart Villages developed a holistic model combining technology, governance, and business solutions, ensuring sustainability and enabling communities to scale independently. This project will scale SACs through market implementation at current sites and completion of a toolkit for replication. Immediate benefits include increased incomes (from $800 to $3,100 in one year at our pilot SAC site), improved crop utilisation, enhanced nutrition, and skills development. Sustainable benefits include long-term livelihood improvements, equitable access for women and youth, strengthened community capacity, and environmentally regenerative farming practices. SACs provide a holistic, evidence-based solution to transform rural agricultural systems for farmers, communities, and the wider food system

core_fields.title: Enhancing the Functionality of Dark Chocolates through the Incorporation of Baobab Powder
core_fields.description: This project seeks to replace the sugar in dark chocolate by substituting it with baobab powder and studying the effect of the baobab on the quality characteristics of the product. The production of the baobab dark chocolate would be carried out using the melanger as an alternative chocolate production technique. The project is expected to diversify the utilization of baobab and enhance the nutritional and health-promoting properties of dark chocolate for enhanced well-being of consumers.
core_fields.abstract: Chocolate is the most popular cocoa-derived product, and it is highly valued by consumers all over the world. Its popularity stems largely from the sensory pleasure and pleasant emotions it evokes due to its distinct aroma, taste, and structure. In addition, dark chocolate is considered a functional food due to its beneficial effects on cardiovascular health. This is due to the presence of bioactive compounds (primarily polyphenols, flavanols, and theobromines) in dark chocolate. There is therefore a dynamic change in the chocolate industry, with a drive towards high cocoa content in chocolates. However, the high cost of cocoa beans on the international markets significantly adds to the cost of chocolates with high cocoa content. Again, despite the numerous health benefits of dark chocolate consumption, some negative effects of chocolate consumption have been reported, as chocolate is high in sugar (which can account for up to 50% of the ingredients). This limits dark chocolate's use as a functional food product. To address this issue and improve the health benefits of dark chocolate consumption, there is a need to find an economical food ingredient that eliminates, if not completely, most of the added sugar content. Baobab (Adansonia digitata L.) is receiving increased recognition as a health-promoting food due to the presence of essential components such as vitamins, minerals, polyphenols, and fibre, and provides an opportunity for the development of functional foods. Incorporating baobab into dark chocolate will enhance its health-promoting properties and contribute to consumers' good health and well-being.

core_fields.title: Strengthening Farmer Resilience through Soil Testing and Integrated Pest Management
core_fields.description: This project delivers a bundled service that improves soil health, reduces pest losses, and strengthens market access for smallholder farmers. Building on successful partnerships that enabled soil testing for over 600 farmers and CS-IPM training for over 30,000 farmers, we aim to scale an integrated package combining soil testing and advisory, climate-smart pest management, and structured market linkages. The project empowers farmers to increase productivity, improve resilience, and secure fair prices for their produce.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Ghana face interconnected challenges that limit productivity and resilience. Declining soil fertility, frequent pest outbreaks such as Fall Armyworm and whiteflies, and dependence on unpredictable markets reduce yields and farmer incomes. Farmers also lack timely pest and climate information, rely heavily on chemical pesticides that damage soil and the environment, and have limited adoption of integrated pest management (IPM). Early warning systems for pest and climate risks remain inadequate or inaccessible. This project introduces a bundled solution that integrates soil management advisory, climate-smart IPM, and structured market access into one accessible service package. The innovation builds on insights from collaborations with the University of Passau, University of Ghana, Sesi Technologies, IITA, and CSIR-INSTI. Through these partnerships, we tested soils for 600+ farmers and trained more than 30,000 farmers in CS-IPM for maize and tomatoes. These experiences confirmed that farmers who understand their soil, receive timely pest alerts, and follow IPM practices experience fewer losses and higher productivity. Using WamiAgro's digital platform, the project delivers real-time pest monitoring, early warning systems, climate updates, and tailored soil-based recommendations. Coupled with guaranteed market linkages, farmers gain improved production and stable income. Immediate benefits include reduced pest losses, healthier soils, increased yields, and reliable markets. Long-term benefits include climate resilience, reduced chemical misuse, improved incomes, stronger food systems, and better environmental health.

core_fields.title: Climate Smart Agriculture as the Foundation for National Innovation in Sustainable Food Systems in Malawi
core_fields.description: The project will empower 2,750 smallholder farmers to sustainably boost crop yields (up to 125%), restore degraded soils, and improve access to safe, nutritious diets. This is done through facilitated learning sessions in the Climate Smart Agricultural method of Deep Bed Farming (DBF), a low-cost, regenerative approach to sustainable, affordable and nutritious farming. The project will also run demonstration plots and Field Day events across Malawi which facilitate engagement at the policy level.
core_fields.abstract: Malawi faces severe land degradation, with 15% of arable land lost, over 40% of soils nutrient-poor, and 75% degraded. Recent cyclones destroyed more than 220,000 farmers fields, worsening food insecurity, low yields, and poverty, particularly for subsistence farmers on fragile land. Our innovation scales Tiyeni s Deep Bed Farming (DBF), a climate-smart, low-cost regenerative method that breaks compacted soil and creates raised, contour-aligned planting beds. DBF reduces erosion, improves water retention, and enhances aeration, supporting stronger plant growth and resilience to extreme weather. Intercropping up to five legume species restores soil fertility through biological nitrogen fixation while enhancing household micronutrient intake. Unlike intensive alternatives, DBF uses simple hand tools, requires less labor, and relies on organic fertilizers, reducing costs for the poorest farmers. Over 18 months, 2,750 farmers will receive training, supported by 3000 participants at national field days. In 2026, 250 lead farmers will further accelerate peer-to-peer knowledge sharing across villages, including areas currently lacking lead farmers. Collaboration with the Mulanje EPA Government Agriculture Office and village leadership ensures sustainability: 30 government agriculture staff will be trained, while local authorities adopt DBF on their own land. Field days will advocate for climate-smart agricultural policies and mobilize donor support. Expected benefits include 70 125% yield increases, up to 150% household income gains, and a 40% improvement in food security. Long-term, DBF restores degraded soils, reduces deforestation and erosion by up to 80%, and strengthens climate resilience for Malawi s most vulnerable farming communities.

core_fields.title: Rolazo

Using collagen-based casings and traditional food-processing technologies, Rolazo protects and enhances food while eliminating plastic waste. It is compatible with existing industrial processes, and supports a scalable circular economy that both improves human nutrition and reduces environmental impact.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation addresses two urgent and connected problems in modern food systems: the widespread use of single-use plastic packaging in prepared foods, and the limited availability of real, nutritious meals in fast, on-the-go formats. Today, consumers are often forced to choose between convenience, health, and environmental responsibility. This solution rethinks food packaging by replacing plastic with an edible collagen-based casing, inspired by how fruits naturally protect themselves with peels. Using well-known food-processing techniques adapted in a novel way, complete home-style meals such as traditional dishes can be safely contained, heated, transported, and eaten directly, without plates, cutlery, or plastic waste. The key insight behind this innovation is viewing packaging not as waste, but as a functional, edible component of the food itself. Collagen casings provide structure, protection, and food safety while also adding nutritional value, allowing traditional slow food to be consumed in a convenient, street-food format.

core_fields.abstract: Our innovation focuses on designing and manufacturing affordable agricultural machines that directly address the productivity gaps facing smallholder farmers in Malawi. Farmers lose up to 40% of their harvest during processing because they rely on slow, manual methods that are physically demanding, especially for women and children. These losses deepen food and nutrition insecurity, limit incomes and weaken community resilience. This challenge is becoming more urgent as climate change reduces yields and increases pressure on already strained food systems. Agrimec s solution combines practical engineering and local manufacturing to create machines that reduce post-harvest losses to below 2%, increase processing speed and provide farmers with reliable, low-cost irrigation through solar-powered technologies. The insight behind this approach came from working directly with farmers and observing that most imported machines are too expensive, difficult to maintain and unsuitable for local crop varieties and field conditions. By manufacturing locally and using readily available materials, we lower costs, simplify repairs and ensure the tools truly match the daily realities of smallholder farmers. The immediate benefits include higher yields reaching the market, reduced labor hours, increased income for rural households through quality produce and safer working conditions for women and children. Over time, these innovations support more resilient food systems by improving storage quality, expanding dry-season farming and creating skilled jobs for young technicians. Communities gain better access to nutritious food, farmers become more competitive and the environment benefits from reduced waste and more efficient resource use. core_fields.title: Zambia Seeds of Resilience Community-Led Agroecology and Food Security Innovation
core_fields.description: This project strengthens food security in climate-vulnerable rural Zambia by scaling community-led agroecology, indigenous seed systems, and diversified green livelihoods. Working with women and youth smallholder farmers in Sinazongwe District, the innovation improves access to safe and nutritious food, promotes regenerative farming within planetary boundaries, and expands equitable access to affordable and trusted food through locally governed seed banks, climate-resilient practices, and inclusive market and policy engagement.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Southern Zambia face recurrent droughts, declining soil fertility, biodiversity loss, and food insecurity driven by climate change and unsustainable agricultural practices. Women and youth who form the backbone of food production are disproportionately affected, yet often excluded from decision-making, access to quality seeds, climate information, and livelihood opportunities. This undermines dietary diversity, farm productivity, and long-term resilience of local food systems. The innovation addresses these challenges through an integrated, community-led agroecological model that combines indigenous drought-resistant seed systems, climate-resilient sustainable agriculture, diversified green livelihoods, and farmer-driven policy engagement. At its core are low-cost community seed banks and farmer field demonstration plots that preserve agrobiodiversity, reduce dependence on external inputs, and ensure consistent access to nutritious crops adapted to local conditions. Simplified weather information, agroecology training, and water-harvesting techniques enable farmers to plan, reduce risk, and regenerate soils while staying within ecological limits. This solution is informed by evidence that agroecology, when paired with local knowledge and social organization, delivers higher resilience, improved nutrition, and lower environmental footprints in rain-fed systems. Immediate benefits include increased availability of diverse, nutritious foods; reduced food losses; improved household incomes through green jobs such as beekeeping and small livestock; and strengthened women- and youth-led farmer groups. Sustainable benefits include restored soils, conserved biodiversity, reduced chemical use, empowered local food governance, and scalable models that communities and local authorities can replicate across Zambia, contributing to equitable, climate-resilient food systems.

core_fields.title: Ka Por Perut : Agroforestry Yerba Mate Production and Atlantic Forest Restoration in Misiones, Argentina.
core_fields.description: Ka Por Perut is a community-led initiative by the Mbya-Guaran of Perut , Misiones, Argentina, that restores the Atlantic Forest while strengthening local economic autonomy through agroecological and agroforestry yerba mate production. This culturally and economically significant traditional infusion supports sustainable incomes, biodiversity conservation, and the preservation of ancestral knowledge. The project integrates cultivation, native species reforestation, and a low-impact community drying facility to improve livelihoods for 280 families while promoting environmental justice and gender equity.
core_fields.abstract: The Ka Por Perut project addresses two interconnected challenges in Misiones Province, Argentina: the degradation of the Atlantic Forest (Selva Paranaense) and the limited economic autonomy of the Mbya-Guaran community of Perut . This Indigenous community comprises approximately 280 families (around 1,500 people), of whom about 40 currently cultivate yerba mate on roughly 50 hectares using traditional, agrochemical-free practices. Women play a central role in production, preserving ancestral knowledge and ensuring quality and sustainability. A structural challenge faced by Mbya-Guaran communities is increasing youth migration to urban centers due to the erosion of communal livelihoods and weakened connections to land and nature. Ka Por Perut responds by strengthening social cohesion, safeguarding traditional knowledge, and generating fair and sustainable employment within the community. The innovation is a locally led agroecological and agroforestry model that integrates ecological restoration, sustainable production, and community-based value addition. The project will integrate more than 2,000 native trees into yerba mate plantations through agroforestry systems, improving soil health, protecting water resources, enhancing biodiversity, and increasing climate resilience in one of South America s most threatened forest ecosystems. The project also includes low-energy drying and storage infrastructure, cooperative strengthening, and the development of a differentiated and environmentally responsible business model. This enables local harvesting, drying, milling, and packaging, reduces reliance on intermediaries, increases product value, and strengthens the long-term economic viability of the community-led initiative.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Freeze-Drying of Indigenous Crops to Reduce Food Loss and Improve Nutrition Access
core_fields.description: The Oleanderlife Project deploys climate-smart freeze-drying, a nutrient-preserving technology rarely used in African food systems, to reduce post-harvest loss and expand access to nutritious foods made from indigenous crops. Unlike conventional dehydration, freeze-drying retains significantly more nutrients while extending shelf life without additives or refrigeration. By converting surplus and seasonal produce into safe, shelf-stable foods using energy-resilient processing, the project strengthens food system resilience, improves year-round nutrition access, and supports smallholder farmers.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation addresses persistent post-harvest food loss, limited access to nutritious foods, and unstable processing conditions in many African food systems. Fruits and herbs often spoil within days due to seasonality, unreliable power, and inadequate preservation methods, resulting in wasted produce, lost farmer income, and reduced nutrition availability for consumers. Conventional dehydration, widely used, degrades nutrients and limits product quality and acceptance. Oleanderlife s innovation applies climate-smart freeze-drying, a technology rarely deployed in African contexts, to preserve indigenous fruits and herbs while retaining significantly more nutrients, flavor, and structure than dehydration. Freeze-drying removes moisture at low temperatures, extending shelf life to over a year without additives or refrigeration. This scientific insight, preserving cellular structure rather than collapsing it, enables safer, more nutritious, and more appealing foods. For consumers, the innovation delivers convenient, ready-to-eat access to nutrient-dense foods that are traditionally seasonal, perishable, or difficult to prepare. For farmers, it creates reliable offtake for surplus and imperfect produce, reducing waste and stabilizing incomes, particularly for smallholder and women farmers. Communities benefit from improved food availability, reduced spoilage, and stronger local value chains. Environmental benefits include reduced food waste, lower emissions from spoilage and diesel-powered processing, and more efficient use of existing agricultural output without land expansion. The solution integrates energy-resilient processing to function in power-constrained environments, making it immediately deployable and sustainably scalable across similar food systems.

core_fields.title: Ethiopia Dairy Farm and Processing Social Enterprise
core_fields.description: Aroma Dairy Farm will establish a modern, sustainable dairy enterprise in Ethiopia that increases access to safe, nutritious, affordable milk. By combining high-yield cattle, improved feed systems, and local processing, the project strengthens food security, supports child nutrition, and creates rural jobs. Environmentally responsible practices, including biogas, regenerative land use, and efficient water systems, ensure long-term resilience and scalable impact.
core_fields.abstract: The Ethiopia Dairy Farm Initiative introduces a modern, high-yield, commercially operated dairy enterprise in the Sidama region an area with strong agricultural potential but limited access to quality milk. The innovation solves a core national problem: demand for dairy far exceeds supply, due to low-yield indigenous cattle, traditional management practices, and weak market infrastructure. This gap contributes to malnutrition, low rural incomes, and inconsistent milk availability in growing urban centers such as Hawassa and Addis Ababa. The project applies proven scientific and technical solutions: high-yield Holstein-Friesian cows, improved feed systems, artificial insemination, veterinary care, pasteurization technology, and automated processing equipment. These practices dramatically increase productivity from 1.5 liters of milk per cow daily (national average) to 20+ liters, creating a reliable, safe, and scalable milk supply. The innovation also integrates value-added processing (yogurt, cheese, butter, ghee), cold-chain systems, and biogas waste-to-energy technology, enabling efficient production with reduced environmental impact. Immediate benefits include: Affordable, safe, high-quality dairy products for consumers. New local jobs across farming, processing, transportation, and marketing. Improved household nutrition, especially for children and women. Training and market access for nearby smallholder farmers. Long-term sustainable benefits include: A resilient regional dairy value chain aligned with Ethiopia s national development goals. Increased rural incomes and economic stability. Reduced import dependence and strengthened food security. Regenerative land use and reduced waste through biogas and compost systems. This model establishes a scalable, environmentally responsible dairy enterprise that strengthens communities while transforming Ethiopia s dairy sector.

core_fields.title: Decentralised food processing in Nano factories
core_fields.description: GUARO FARMS is pioneering decentralized manufacturing in Ethiopia by deploying Nano-factories in 20-foot shipping containers for farm gate post-harvest drying and packing, slashing food loss. We are solving a $200M+ post-harvest loss problem while creating dignified jobs for young rural women. One factory serves more than 500 smallholder farmers within walking distance. Our model flips traditional supply chains instead of raw commodities, leaving villages, where value is captured locally, cutting supply chain emissions.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation tackles post-harvest loss in Ethiopia, where up to 40% of most fruits, herbs and crops are wasted due to poor handling, long transit times, and lack of processing infrastructure near farms. This loss translates to lost income for smallholders, environmental waste (super-pollutant emissions from spoilage), and diminished food quality. Solving this is critical for Ethiopia's food security and economic stability. GUARO FARMS solves this through decentralized manufacturing. We design and deploy 20ft shipping container-based smart Nano factories right at the farm gate, within walking distance of 500 smallholder farmers. Our approach is moving manufacturing closer to the source of production and processing within hours of harvest, and locally is key to preserving the potency and purity of food. Our modular, asset-light nano-factory design and the proprietary Sebseb + ERP software enable distributed manufacturing, a model that flips the traditional, centralized supply chain for greater agility, efficiency, and traceability.

core_fields.title: Scaling Climate Smart Aquaculture for Affordable and Nutritious Fish in East Africa
core_fields.description: This project strengthens East Africa s food system by scaling climate smart aquaculture through digital advisory, quality inputs and efficient logistics. By improving farm productivity, reducing losses and stabilizing supply chains, the project increases the availability and affordability of nutritious fish for low income households. The initiative empowers smallholder farmers, particularly women and youth, to improve their incomes while expanding access to sustainable, locally produced protein across the region.
core_fields.abstract: East Africa faces a growing nutrition gap as fish supply declines due to climate impacts, fragmented value chains, poor quality inputs and limited technical support for smallholder farmers. This reduces the availability and affordability of nutrient dense protein for communities that rely on fish as a primary food source. The innovation solves this problem by digitizing and strengthening the aquaculture value chain through a combination of digital advisory, quality inputs, and efficient logistics. The solution is built on practical scientific and technical insights drawn from aquaculture management, feeding efficiency, water quality control and post harvest handling. Farmers often lose up to 40 percent of potential production due to avoidable factors such as poor feeding practices, unreliable input access, and weak market linkages. By providing a WhatsApp based advisory service, streamlined delivery of certified feeds and fingerlings, the innovation improves survival rates, feed conversion ratios and overall farm productivity. Efficient harvest aggregation and distribution reduce post harvest losses and increase the availability of fresh, nutritious fish in local markets. These combined improvements create immediate benefits for farmers through higher yields, lower losses, and more stable incomes. Consumers and communities benefit from greater access to affordable, locally produced fish that support better nutrition outcomes. The model also reduces environmental pressure on overfished wild stocks and promotes climate smart aquaculture practices that conserve resources and increase resilience across the food system.

core_fields.title: Production of affordable plant-based Ready to use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and Nutritious food paste
core_fields.description: Afrinut Enriched Foods develops affordable, locally sourced, plant-based Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and a nutritious food paste to combat malnutrition in Ethiopia. By producing locally using indigenous ingredients, we reduce costs, ensure quality, and reach vulnerable children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and underserved communities. Our scalable, replicable model strengthens local supply chains, creates jobs for women and youth, and provides sustainable, accessible nutrition solutions while promoting community health and economic empowerment.
core_fields.abstract: Afrinut Enriched Foods addresses the critical challenge of malnutrition in Ethiopia by developing affordable, locally sourced, plant-based Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and a complementary nutritious food paste. Severe malnutrition affects millions of children under five and pregnant or breastfeeding women in Ethiopia, leading to high mortality, stunting, and reduced cognitive development. Imported RUTF is costly and often limited in supply, leaving only one in three children with access. Our innovation lies in local production using predominantly indigenous ingredients, which drastically reduces costs without compromising quality, which will enable us to reach a larger portion of the malnourished community. Leveraging advanced formulation and processing techniques, we will produce RUTF that meets nutritional standards while maintaining taste, texture, and shelf life. our second product, the nutritious food paste retains the appealing flavor and some nutritional value of RUTF but is specifically formulated for healthy consumers, including fitness enthusiasts and health-conscious individuals. This dual-product strategy not only introduces a new revenue stream but also strengthens the sustainability and resilience of our business model. Our solution is designed as a scalable, replicable model: small production units can be established in different regions with minimal investment, supported by comprehensive training programs for local producers. By sourcing raw materials from local farmers, the model strengthens supply chains, creates job opportunities for women and youth, and empowers communities economically. Immediate benefits include improved child health and nutrition, while sustainable benefits encompass economic empowerment, resilient local food systems, and a replicable, long-term solution to combat malnutrition across Ethiopia.

core_fields.title: Regenerating Smallholder Farms in Peru Through Biodiversity-Driven Integrated Trophic Design (ITD)
core_fields.description: Smallholder farmers in Peru face soil degradation, climate stress, and unstable markets (World Bank, 2017). TANIT will deploy Integrated Trophic Design (ITD) a biodiversity-driven, AI-enabled regenerative framework to restore soil health, increase crop diversity and nutrient density, and strengthen livelihoods via site-specific polyculture design, technician-led implementation, and data-verified ecological monitoring. This 250-farmer pilot is catalytic, establishing quantified regenerative benchmarks targeting 10 30% soil organic matter gains, biodiversity increases, and verified nutritional indicators while creating a T-Tier based supply chain for botanicals.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Peru face linked challenges including soil degradation (Kassam et al., 2015), biodiversity loss affecting nutrient-rich and medicinal species (Zimmerer et al., 2020), climate volatility (Vuille et al., 2018), weak value chains (Zimmerer et al., 2020), and persistent rural nutrition gaps (FAO, 2019). Although Peru is globally recognized for its plant biodiversity, most smallholders have over the past decades become increasingly reliant on simplified monocultural systems that reduce ecological resilience and limit participation in high-value markets. TANIT s Integrated Trophic Design (ITD) introduces a novel, science-based framework that designs agriculture using the logic of natural trophic networks. Instead of optimizing a single crop, ITD structures functional interactions among soil microbes, complementary plant guilds, pollinators, and local climate conditions to regenerate ecosystems and increase nutrient density. ITD is innovative in three primary ways: Biodiversity-driven design: Site-specific polyculture planting guides are generated using soil data, microclimate, and altitude aligning with evidence that diversified systems improve productivity and resilience (Vandermeer, 1989). Quantifiable regeneration: TANIT s T-Tier spectrum tracks soil health, biodiversity recovery, water resilience, and crop diversity, addressing the transparency gap common in smallholder systems (GRI, 2021). Integrated market access: Digital traceability links regenerative practices to transparent, premium botanical value chains. While regenerative agriculture exists, ITD is distinct in providing a structured, AI-assisted, and measurable methodology for implementing complex polycultures at a smallholder scale. The ITD platform synthesizes soil parameters, climate data, altitude, and field-level biodiversity observations to generate site-specific polyculture designs and trophic planting guides and continuously refines them through verified monitoring data.

core_fields.title: Food4Life
core_fields.description: Dudu Masters Food4Life project uses insects to transform farm and household waste into affordable protein and organic fertilizer, restoring soil health and strengthening local food systems. By training women groups to manage waste through insect farming and buying back their outputs, we create income, reduce environmental harm, and lower the cost of food production. Food4Life delivers nutrition, improves soil health, boosts crop yields, and dignifies the people at community level.
core_fields.abstract: Food systems across Africa are strained by degraded soils, rising feed and fertilizer costs, and un- managed organic waste. Smallholder farmers, especially women, are disproportionately affected, yet remain central to food production. Food4Life addresses these interconnected challenges through a decentralized insect-based system. Our innovation converts farm and household organic waste into high-value insect protein and organic fertilizer using insect farming. We partner with women groups, train them in waste management and insect rearing, and buy back insect products that feed directly into our production value chain. This ensures quality control, predictable income for communities, and scalable supply for Dudu Masters. What makes Food4Life novel is not the insect technology alone, but the community-embedded circular model: waste is sourced locally, processed locally, income stays local, and outputs directly reduce the cost of food production. Unlike centralized insect farms, our model decentralizes production while centralizing quality and market access. The solution is grounded in entomology, soil science, and circular economy principles, recognizing natures ability to up - cycle waste into nutrient-dense protein (>45% crude protein) and soil-restoring fertilizer. Immediate benefits include reduced waste, improved soil health, lower feed costs, and new income streams for women. Long-term benefits include sustainable local food systems, improved nutrition, reduced environmental degradation, and affordable food access for growing populations.

core_fields.title: NatureLEAD: The Living Supply Chain for Regenerative Agroforestry & Food Security in Madagascar
core_fields.description: NatureLEAD permanently breaks the destructive slash-and-burn (Tavy) cycle by establishing a resilient "Living Supply Chain" for Arachis pintoi, a perennial legume that restores severely degraded land. Our Green Credit Model eliminates the capital barrier by distributing regenerative inputs at zero upfront cost. We transform "dead" land into productive, resilient agroforestry, securing nutritional diversity and generating a triple-stacked income stream (Carbon, Water, Biodiversity) for 1,000 farmers while restoring the entire ecosystem.
core_fields.abstract: The Problem: Millions of Malagasy farmers are currently forced into destructive slash-and-burn because existing farmlands are severely degraded (yielding 0t/ha), and they lack the capital for regenerative inputs. This poverty-driven necessity destroys primary rainforests. The Solution: NatureLEAD introduces a hyper-efficient Living Supply Chain for Arachis pintoi, a perennial legume proven to fix 120kg N/ha/yr of biological nitrogen. Novelty: Our Green Credit Model solves the "propagation bottleneck." Farmers receive "Regeneration Kits" (10kg cuttings) at $0 upfront. They repay 20kg biomass after 6 months, creating a viral, zero-cash loop that guarantees scaling. Scientific Insight: A. pintoi creates a permanent living mulch, increasing soil infiltration by 32% and enabling rotation with rice and high-value agroforestry (Vanilla/Cocoa). We explicitly integrate nutritious intercrops (beans, greens) to combat malnutrition. Benefits: 1) Immediate: Restores food security (2.0t/ha rice). 2) Sustainable: Saves farmers 5 hours/day labor and provides a permanent verified carbon sink we monetize.

core_fields.title: Zukunftshirse: Climate-Smart, Gluten-Free Pearl Millet for Healthy, Sustainable Diets in Germany and Sweden
core_fields.description: Zukunftshirse introduces climate-resilient, gluten-free pearl millet to Germany and Sweden by combining crop adaptation, indigenous fermentation, sensory-guided product development, and nutrition validation. The project delivers cold-tolerant genotypes, shelf-stable flour, and 3 4 consumer-ready prototypes, supported by a controlled human pilot study (n = 20 healthy adults). It strengthens sustainable agriculture, preventive nutrition, and European food system resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Climate change threatens wheat-based food systems across Europe, increasing the need for drought-tolerant, low-input cereals. Pearl millet is highly resilient and nutritionally rich but remains underutilized due to rancidity and lack of adapted processing chains. Zukunftshirse addresses this gap through three integrated innovations: 1. Climate-Adaptive Agriculture Pearl millet accessions are evaluated across Germany and Sweden (SLU) to identify cold-tolerant, photoperiod-adapted, and low-rancidity genotypes. Multi-environment testing strengthens resilience and scalability across temperate and Nordic conditions. 2. Indigenous Fermentation as Low-Energy Stabilization African fermentation and germination practices are scientifically validated using FTIR and metabolomics, extending flour shelf life naturally without additives or energy-intensive processing. 3. Nutrition-Driven Food Innovation Fermented millet ingredients are transformed into 3 4 gluten-free prototypes (porridge, baking mix, beverage base). Sensory evaluation and phytochemical metabolomic profiling guide optimization. A human pilot study (n = 20 healthy adults) evaluates glycemic response and gut microbiome shifts, providing proof-of-concept nutrition evidence.

core_fields.title: Circular dairy byproduct biofertilizer for Maasai Women-Led Gardens

core_fields.abstract: Pastoralist Maasai communities, who are located far from large cities like Arusha, face limited access to affordable, high-quality bio inputs, limiting the production of leafy vegetables and fruits, which are part of TACCEEI s initiatives of promoting household nutrition and climate resilience. The Circular Dairy Waste Biofertilizer innovation addresses both challenges through a local circular solution. The initiative turns whey into high-quality biofertilizer for women-led gardens built as part of the Maasai Women Empowerment and Climate Adaptation initiative. The strategy improves access to sustainable bio-inputs while reducing waste and strengthening local food systems. The solution is grounded in scientific research. During her master's studies, Natosim examined the potential of dairy whey as a biofertilizer, with laboratory and field trials demonstrated the formulation's effectiveness, validating its use as a safe and effective bio input. The project aims to strengthen household nutrition, climate resilience, and women s economic empowerment through sustainable agriculture. Through reduced reliance on external inputs and empowering communities to produce their own bio inputs using locally available resources. By combining local knowledge, scientific data, and circular economy concepts, the innovation provides long-term environmental, social, and economic benefits to farms, schools, communities, and the larger ecosystem.

core_fields.title: Vortex-Driven Thermal Energy Separation for Sustainable Aquaculture Optimization
core_fields.description: This project introduces a vortex tube system, powered by excess energy from solar panels, to generate hot and cold streams from compressed air for sustainable aquaculture. The cold stream optimizes macroalgae growth, while the hot stream stabilizes temperature fluctuations in hatcheries and facilities during winter, rainy seasons, and nighttime, enabling chemical-free pathogen sterilization. It seeks the Welthungerhilfe Seeding Grant for food system innovation.
core_fields.abstract: This innovation introduces a vortex tube system, powered by excess solar panel energy, to generate hot and cold water streams for sustainable aquaculture. The problem addressed is inefficient temperature control in aquaculture facilities, leading to suboptimal macroalgae growth, pathogen proliferation, and high energy costs amid climate variability. This is relevant as global food systems face increasing pressures from environmental changes, with aquaculture providing 50% of seafood but relying on energy-intensive and chemical-dependent methods that harm ecosystems. The solution employs a vortex tube to separate compressed air into hot (for temperature stabilization and sterilization) and cold (for algae optimization) streams, integrated with solar surplus to minimize grid dependency. The insight stems from the vortex tube's thermodynamic principle, where centrifugal forces create temperature differentials without moving parts or refrigerants, enabling efficient, chemical-free thermal management inspired by industrial cooling applications adapted to renewable energy. Immediate benefits include reduced operational costs for farmers through energy savings, higher yields for producers via optimized growth conditions, and safer products for consumers without chemical residues. Sustainable advantages encompass environmental protection by lowering carbon emissions and pollution, enhanced community food security in climate-vulnerable areas, and societal gains through scalable, eco-friendly protein production.

core_fields.title: Seeding Resilience through Women-Led Enset Value Chain for Food Security & Prosperity in Weliso Town
core_fields.description: We scale a proven model/new variety to transform Enset, a native Ethiopian "false banana," from a labor-intensive staple into a profitable, women-led business. By introducing simple processing technologies and business training, we will empower 600 women as entrepreneurs, improve food security, and create a climate-resilient value chain. This project strengthens 1,200 farming households and delivers a sustainable blueprint for replicating women's economic empowerment across East Africa.
core_fields.abstract: In Ethiopia, millions of women rely on processing Enset (false banana), a nutritious, drought-resistant staple, using arduous, days-long manual methods. This limits income, perpetuates poverty, and wastes the crop's potential as a scalable solution for food security and climate resilience. Innovation & Solution: We combine appropriate technology (mechanized scrapers, pulverizers, hygienic fermentation tanks) with a replicable women-led enterprise model. The technical insight comes from successful collaborations with Ethiopian agricultural research institutes (e.g., Areka Research Center), which developed and validated these locally sourced, durable tools. We integrate this hardware with a "hub-and-spoke" business framework: a central training Centre for Enset Business Incubation (CEBI) supports satellite women-owned processing cooperatives. Immediate & Sustainable Benefits: For 600 Women Entrepreneurs: Immediate 80% reduction in processing labor, turning a subsistence chore into a viable business. They gain secure income, business skills, and leadership roles. For 1,200 Smallholder Farmer Households: A reliable, higher-value market for their Enset, increasing and stabilizing their agricultural income. For Consumers & Communities: Increased availability of safe, consistent, and affordable staple food. The model strengthens local economies and promotes gender equity. For Society & Environment: Creates a scalable blueprint for transforming traditional agro-processing across Africa. It promotes a perennial, soil-conserving crop system, enhancing climate adaptation and sustainable land use.

core_fields.title: Earth Observation Systems Architecture for Food Insecurity Reduction in Climate-Vulnerable Regions
core_fields.description: This project uses Earth observation and data analytics to reduce food insecurity in climate-vulnerable regions. By monitoring crops and agricultural assets before and after climate shocks, the system makes food loss visible, supports faster recovery, and improves decision-making for farmers, governments, and humanitarian organisations. The project strengthens climate resilience, supports sustainable agriculture, and enables more effective food security interventions across the Global South.
core_fields.abstract: Climate change, droughts, floods, and extreme weather are causing large amounts of food to be lost before it ever reaches people. In many climate-vulnerable regions, this loss is not measured accurately, which delays disaster response, weakens food security planning, and excludes smallholder farmers from insurance, recovery funding, and climate support. As a result, food insecurity deepens even when resources exist to respond. This innovation addresses that gap by using Earth observation technologies and data analytics to make food loss visible, measurable, and actionable. Satellite data is used to monitor crops and agricultural assets over time, establish baseline conditions, and detect early signs of climate stress. After climate shocks, the system quantifies damage and food loss quickly and objectively, providing decision-ready information for farmers, governments, insurers, and humanitarian organisations. The key insight behind this solution is that food insecurity is often driven not only by production failure, but by the absence of trusted, timely data. Earth observation makes it possible to monitor large areas consistently, even in remote regions where field surveys are slow, costly, or unreliable. Immediate benefits include earlier warning of crop stress, faster recovery planning, and better targeting of food assistance. Sustainable benefits include reduced food loss, stronger climate resilience, improved access to insurance and recovery finance for farmers, and more informed policies that support sustainable and regenerative agriculture. Together, these outcomes strengthen food systems and protect livelihoods in climate-vulnerable regions.

core_fields.title: The Agricultural Recovery Program
core_fields.description: One-third of food is lost or wasted, and more than 735 million people across the globe are facing hunger. Food banks play a key role in ensuring that surplus food is used for human consumption. As food being recovered from the agricultural sector has a significant opportunity to scale, The Global FoodBanking Network (GFN) has launched The Agricultural Recovery Program to support food banks to recover surplus fruits, vegetables and other agricultural products.
core_fields.abstract: Across supply chains, half of global food loss occurs postharvest with the agriculture sector accounting for the highest rates of loss. Smallholder farmers, herders, and fishermen, which produce about 70 percent of the total global food supply, are especially vulnerable to economic and environmental pressures caused by such postharvest loss. To tackle the pressing issue of food insecurity and the significant food loss occurring in the agricultural sector, The Global FoodBanking Network (GFN) has launched an Agricultural Recovery Program with a dedicated Knowledge Center, which will serve as a global resource that equips food banks worldwide with skills and training to advance on-farm and postharvest surplus recovery. With a NorthStar goal of expanding tenfold by 2030, from recovering and distributing 135 million kilograms to 1 billion kilograms, The Agricultural Recovery Program is designed to harness the global reach of food banks, with resources and training targeted at agricultural food recovery efforts where food losses are most prevalent and building capacity at the local level where food loss and food access needs intersect. The program supports food banks in building strong partnerships with smallholder farmers and other stakeholders across the agricultural value chain. By facilitating models such as bartering with farmers, purchasing surplus produce at subsidized prices, and implementing market recovery programs. It enables food banks to redirect food that would otherwise be wasted into local distribution channels like food pantries and kitchens, community-based organizations and school feeding programs.

core_fields.title: Scaling Up The EMSAS (Empowering Communities with Sustainable Agricultural Solutions
core_fields.description: Green Habitat Initiative seeks the $250,000 Grand Prize to scale its EMSAS model by training and equipping 500 farmers in climate-resilient techniques in Kaduna using integrated hydroponic and regenerative-agriculture systems. The project will improve yields by 20 40%, cut water use by up to 90%, restore degraded soils, and reduce input costs for farmers by nearly 50%. An immersive VR tool will catalyse policy uptake and community engagement, strengthening climate-adaptation pathways across northern Nigeria.
core_fields.abstract: Rural communities in Northern Nigeria face entrenched food insecurity driven by degraded soils, erratic rainfall and high input costs that reduce the viability of conventional agriculture. These pressures limit productivity, heighten vulnerability, and restrict year-round food availability. The EMSAS pilot showed that low-cost hydroponics can overcome many of these constraints by enabling soil-less cultivation with up to 90% water savings and significantly higher cropping frequency. The proposed scale-up strengthens this model by adding regenerative-agriculture systems that rebuild soil organic matter, improve nutrient cycling, and increase long-term land productivity. The innovation combines two complementary systems. Hydroponics ensures consistent year-round production even when rainfall fails, while regenerative agriculture restores degraded land, enhances water retention, boosts biodiversity, and reduces dependence on synthetic fertilisers and pesticides by 40 50%. The approach is novel in its dual-system design, its community-embedded structure, and its adaptation to low-resource rural contexts through simplified kits, locally sourced materials and decentralised farmer cooperatives. This creates a pathway for producing more food on less land while rehabilitating the environment. A further innovation is the use of immersive VR for stakeholder engagement. The VR experience visualises climate impacts, demonstrates the benefits of hydroponics and regenerative agriculture, and strengthens policy dialogue. This medium allows policymakers and community leaders to experience scenarios that encourage faster adoption of climate-smart practices. Immediate benefits include increased yields, reduced crop losses, lower input costs and improved food access. Sustainable outcomes include restored soil fertility, strengthened resilience to climate shocks, diversified farmer income and wider community support for climate-adaptive agriculture.

core_fields.title: Bioclimatic agroecology system for indigenous and peasant resilience and welll nutrition in high-mountain regions
core_fields.description: In communities located in high mountain areas above 3800-4000 meters of elevation, where climate constrains food production, our system, based on a lowcost greenhouse shelter and a set of associated agroecological practices for circularity and ecological regeneration at the farm, allows farmers to grow nutritious vegetables and small livestock (guinea pigs) during the whole year, enhancing their diet. This model strengthens food security and sovereignty, reduces the need for external inputs, and increases climate resilience.
core_fields.abstract: In communities settled in high mountain areas above 3800-4800 meters of elevation, frequent frosts, harsh conditions and rain seasonality dramatically constrain production and access to fresh food, provoking poor diets and food insecurity, especially in children. In Per , 50.3 % of rural children (aged 6-35 months) have anemia. This problem worsens with climate change, degradation of grasslands and soils, and hydric scarcity. Additionally, connection with markets is difficult due to distance and deficient or inexistent transport infrastructure, which increases the local costs for external food supplies. Our innovation consists of a circular low-external-inputs agroecological system, especially adapted to this context, centered in a bioclimatic greenhouse that allows to grow nutritious vegetables and breed guinea pigs (recognized for its nutritional and health value) as a source of nutrients and manure in extreme weather conditions, during the entire year. Besides, it integrates a set of agroecological practices focused on the regenerative management of soil, grasslands and water sources, aiming to restore and strengthen their ecosystem services. The system encourages and draws upon indigenous knowledge, summed up with contemporary agroecological practices. Conventional greenhouses already exist, but the proposed model uses more affordable and local materials, traditional knowledge, and lower energy inputs. Immediate benefits include an increase in the availability of fresh vegetables and meat, as well as a reduction in family costs associated to external food and agricultural supplies (food sovereignty). In the midterm, it contributes to reducing child/family anemia and malnutrition, it enhances soil, ecosystems and climatic resilience, and reduces economic vulnerability.

core_fields.title: Genomics-Enabled Deployment of Native Potatoes for Climate-Resilient Food Systems
core_fields.description: This project deploys genomic and multi-environment trial data to transform native potato biodiversity into climate-resilient, nutritious, and adoption-ready solutions for smallholder farmers. Using a genomics-enabled deployment platform, we identify elite native potato varieties with proven performance across environments and pilot their integration into farmer seed systems and local markets. The approach reduces climate risk, strengthens agrobiodiversity conservation through use, and improves access to resilient, nutritious food.
core_fields.abstract: Climate change is increasing yield instability, pest pressure, and production risk in potato-based food systems, while modern potato varieties remain genetically narrow and poorly adapted to emerging stresses. At the same time, native potato varieties possess exceptional genetic diversity for climate resilience and nutrition but are largely excluded from formal seed systems, markets, and food policies, leading to biodiversity loss and missed opportunities for farmers and consumers. This project introduces a genomics-enabled deployment platform that transforms native potato biodiversity into climate-resilient, nutritious, and adoption-ready solutions. The innovation integrates genomic analysis with multi-environment trial data to identify elite native potato varieties that consistently perform across diverse climatic conditions. Rather than focusing on conservation or research alone, the platform converts complex genomic and phenotypic data into clear, actionable selection and deployment decisions. Using this approach, we select a small set of elite native potato varieties and pilot their deployment through farmer-managed trials, seed multiplication pathways, and engagement with local markets. The solution is grounded in scientific insights from population genomics, genotype-by-environment analysis, and applied breeding, combined with practical deployment strategies developed with growers. Immediate benefits include reduced climate risk and yield variability for smallholder farmers, improved access to resilient and nutrient-dense potatoes for consumers, and economic incentives for conserving native biodiversity through use. Over time, the platform strengthens food system resilience, supports agrobiodiversity conservation, and provides a scalable model applicable to other native crops and regions.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Nutrition Systems: Promoting Milk and Local Crops for Sustainable Diets (RNS)
core_fields.description: The project applies a multi-sectoral approach to improve food and nutrition security in the Bara District. Working through the District Milk Producer Cooperative Union, it will strengthen 13 dairy cooperatives to produce safe, hygienic milk and encourage higher milk consumption through behavior change efforts. The project will also promote regenerative dairy practices and integrate neglected and underutilized crops into circular economy models. Successful approaches will scale through the Milky Way initiative, reaching 10,000 families.
core_fields.abstract: Nepal s Madhesh Province (20% of country s population), nation s food basket, ironically has the highest poverty rates (23% monetary, 48% multidimensional) and worst child nutrition: ~31% of children 6 23 months receive a minimum acceptable diet, and >50% of women are anaemic. Rural households eat little animal-source food, rely on unsafe milk, spend >65% of income on food, and face climate risks and post-harvest losses. In Bara district alone, ~40,000 L of daily milk production is sold cheaply outside the district, leaving just ~3,000 L for local families. This project introduces quality-based milk pricing so farmers earn more for safe, high-quality milk while encouraging greater household consumption. It will build regenerative household food systems by integrating climate-smart dairy practices and regenerative home gardens of nutrient-dense Underutilized Crop Species. Regenerative Heros will demonstrate these practices on demo farms and train neighbours. Farm and kitchen waste will be converted into low-cost nature-based agri-inputs using black soldier fly larvae, biochar, and vermicomposting. Implemented through existing Milk Producers Cooperatives and their Union for long-term sustainability, Dairy Learning Centers serve as digital training hubs, milk/NUCS collection points, and venues for promoting nutritious recipes. Nutritional Ambassadors provide family-level nutrition/ food processing education, and schools incorporate nutrition education into curricula and dairy products in midday meals. The government creates enabling policies; the private sector provides lasting market linkages, investment, and technology. Immediate benefits: safer milk, diverse diets, reduced malnutrition. Long-term impacts: resilient low-input systems, higher cooperative incomes, reduced pollution, and stronger local value chains, breaking the vicious malnutrition cycle.

core_fields.title: Re-Harvest Pakistan - Solar Food Hubs
core_fields.description: By creating solar-powered circular food hubs that incorporate solar food dehydrators, cold storage, value-addition processing, residue recycling, this project seeks to drastically lower post-harvest losses and food wastage in Sindh and Punjab. It increases yields, lowers environmental pollution by turning agricultural waste into biofertilizers and biodegradable packaging. The program, which is backed by a digital marketplace (App) and cold-chain transportation, improves farmer market connectivity while promoting ecologically friendly agricultural practices, climate-resilient livelihoods, especially for women.
core_fields.abstract: Pakistan s food system faces persistent inefficiencies, including 20 40% post-harvest losses, residue burning, limited market access, inferior seed quality, rising fertilizer costs, and male-dominated decision-making restricts women s participation (Rehman & Sharif, 2019; Hussain & Saeed, 2019). Sindh s banana belt alone generates approximately 35,000 tons of plant waste annually, while Faisalabad, Punjab, produces over 2.1 million tons of cereal residues, nearly 45% of which are openly burned (Ahmed et al., 2021). Building on our UNDP Italian Government Youth4Climate supported banana-waste bioproducts initiative, this project scales up the proven model into integrated, solar-powered circular food hubs in Tando Allahyar and Faisalabad. First, in five villages, five solar dehydrators and five value-addition units, dry and transform excess produce, reducing post-harvest losses by more than 40%, increasing shelf life, and preserving up to 80% of nutrients, which generate new revenue streams and strengthen farmers' financial stability. The GreenLink digital marketplace (App) facilitates direct connections between farmers and consumers, offers real-time pricing, guarantees access to verified premium seeds, and offers focused instruction in modern, sustainable farming methods. Furthermore, 3000-5000 tons of banana, sugarcane, and cereal waste are converted into biofertilizer and biodegradable packaging/fiber each year by two waste-to-resource facilities in Sindh and two in Punjab, promoting applied research for efficiency. Women and Youth are prioritized across processing, enterprise development, digital operations, and capacity-building initiatives to strengthen income, resilience, and leadership. Through residue diversion, solar-powered processing, and cyclical waste-to-resource interventions, the invention supports regenerative agriculture and lowers 6,000 10,000 tons of CO2 emissions per year.

core_fields.title: Promoting innovative cassava cultivation to increase productivity through the pre-germination method (PICGEM)
core_fields.description: A Kenyan smallholder farmer has developed an innovative cassava planting method, using two node cassava stem cuttings pre-germinated in plastic bags, which are then transplanted on east-west ridges after the roots sprout. This improves survival rates, reduces maturity time by up to three months, boosts yields by 30%, reduces harvest losses, and enables intercropping. Two thousand farmers will be trained through participatory methods to support farmer-led experimentation, adaptation and participation in the cassava value chain.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation is a low input, cost effective solution to cassava propagation. When planted directly, cassava cuttings are at risk of stunted growth or complete crop failure due to increasingly erratic rainfall. Cassava is both a food and cash crop and therefore low production adversely affects both food security and incomes. The innovation involves pre-germinating cassava cuttings in polythene bags filled with a little water. The bags are kept in shade thus creating a micro-climate necessary for the roots to sprout in 3-4 weeks before the cuttings are transplanted in ridges filled with organic manure at the onset of the rains. The cuttings are placed in a way that ensures that the roots, which later develop into tubers, face the same direction. This enables the farmer to know the location of the tuber, making harvesting easier and reducing losses. This method also allows intercropping, especially with indigenous vegetables, beans and other leguminous crops, and cereals. It reduces the risk of crop failure, increases yields, shortens maturity time, encourages crop diversification through intercropping and promotes sustainable ecological management. Soil health is enhanced through the use of organic manure and integrating nitrogen-fixing legumes. Because of the increased productivity per land unit, this method minimizes the need for increasing farm sizes as a prerequisite for increasing food production.

core_fields.title: Empowering Smallholders with Sustainable Food Production Technologies.
core_fields.description: ASEDI Agric Services Ltd, a Ugandan agribusiness established in 2009 and incorporated in 2023, has demonstrated strong growth and alignment with national agricultural development goals, particularly in seed multiplication and input distribution. Based in Soroti district, ASEDI is dedicated to transforming agriculture across the Teso, Lango, Karamoja and Acholi sub-regions by empowering thousands of smallholder farmers through Seed Multiplication, Seed Trade, Advisory Services, and Market Linkages.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Uganda face significant challenges accessing quality certified seeds due to the prevalence of counterfeit seeds, limited investment in staple crop seed production, inadequate infrastructure, and weak coordination between research institutions and seed companies. Women farmers are disproportionately affected, lacking sufficient access to quality seeds, training, and market opportunities. ASEDI addresses these challenges through a vertically integrated, community-based model linking foundation seed suppliers, over 30 farmer cooperatives, and institutional buyers. Currently, the company supports over 2,500 farmers, 65% of whom are women, providing access to quality declared seeds, training, and structured market linkages. The company s mission is to facilitate the adoption of modern agricultural technologies and create sustainable livelihoods for rural communities. Uganda s northern regions, characterized by fertile land and high demand for quality seeds and advisory services, present a substantial growth opportunity. However, smallholder farmers continue to face limited access to certified seeds and formal markets gaps that ASEDI is uniquely positioned to fill. Over the next five years, ASEDI aims to expand seed production, strengthen farmer networks, and scale market access solutions to benefit over 20,000 smallholder farmers.

core_fields.title: AgroNutriHub: Solar-Powered Nutrient Densification for Kenyan Smallholders
core_fields.description: AgroNutriHub deploys affordable solar dryers and nutrient encapsulation tech to transform post-harvest losses into nutrient-dense fortified flours for rural Kenyan schools and markets. core_fields.abstract: In Kenya, 30-40% of maize and vegetables spoil post-harvest due to poor storage, exacerbating malnutrition affecting 26% of children and straining planetary resources. AgroNutriHub solves this via low-cost solar dryers integrated with microbial encapsulation, converting waste into shelf-stable, micronutrient-fortified flours (iron, vitamin A-enriched). The insight stems from TVET research on local fungi for natural encapsulation, bypassing expensive synthetic fortification.​ Farmers dry produce 3x faster, cutting losses and emissions from spoilage transport. Immediate benefits: schools access affordable, appealing porridge (50% cost reduction), improving health outcomes; communities gain income from cooperative sales. Sustainable gains include regenerative soil practices via crop residue recycling, trusted local branding, and scalable tech for 1M smallholders, staying within water/land boundaries

core_fields.title: Young Food Systems Changemakers: Child-Led Nutrition and Food Trust Innovation
core_fields.description: This project empowers children and adolescents to become trusted changemakers in nutrition, food safety, and sustainable diets. Through youth-led digital media and community engagement, the initiative builds nutrition literacy, improves food safety practices, and strengthens trust in local food systems. By positioning children as credible messengers, the project drives lasting behavior change at household and community levels using a scalable, low-cost model.
core_fields.abstract: Children and adolescents strongly influence household food choices, yet they are rarely equipped with accurate, trusted, and culturally relevant information about nutrition, food safety, and sustainable diets. This gap contributes to poor nutrition outcomes, unsafe food practices, low trust in food systems, and declining consumption of nutritious local foods, especially in low-income communities. This innovation establishes a child- and youth-led digital platform that builds nutrition literacy, food safety awareness, and trust in sustainable food systems through participatory media and community engagement. Trained children and adolescents co-create short videos, audio stories, and interactive content that explain safe food handling, nutritious local diets, and climate-smart food choices in child-friendly and locally relevant ways. Content is distributed through schools, community hubs, mobile phones, and social platforms widely used by families. The solution is grounded in behavioral science and evidence that peer-to-peer learning and trusted local voices are more effective than top-down messaging in changing food behaviors. By positioning children as credible messengers, the innovation improves understanding, acceptance, and adoption of nutritious and safe food practices within households and communities. Immediate benefits include increased nutrition knowledge, safer food handling practices, and improved dietary choices among children and caregivers. Sustainable benefits include long-term behavior change, stronger trust in local food systems, increased demand for nutritious and sustainable foods, and community-level shifts toward healthier, climate-resilient diets. The model is low-cost, scalable, and adaptable across diverse food system contexts.

core_fields.title: HarvestPlanner: AI-Driven Post-Harvest Loss Prevention System for West African Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: HarvestPlanner is an integrated digital platform combining satellite imagery, weather data, and AI recommendations to reduce post-harvest losses for smallholder farmers in Nigeria and West Africa. Using web, mobile app, and SMS channels, it provides timely information on harvest timing, storage conditions, and market access, transforming fragmented agricultural information into actionable intelligence that preserves food security and farmer income.
core_fields.abstract: Post-harvest losses in West Africa reach 40-50% of total production, costing farmers billions annually and exacerbating food insecurity. The root problem is information fragmentation: weather data exists but doesn't reach farmers when critical decisions must be made; market intelligence is scattered; and harvest timing recommendations lack localization. HarvestPlanner solves this through an integrated risk assessment system that aggregates multiple data streams sub-hectare satellite imagery via Google Earth Engine, real-time weather APIs, soil moisture sensors, and market price feeds into a unified decision-support platform. Our scientific insight: post-harvest loss is predictable when you combine agronomic modeling with hyperlocal environmental monitoring and behavioral economics. The system operates across three channels (web dashboard, mobile app, SMS) ensuring universal access regardless of digital literacy or connectivity. Starting with our baseline database of 38,000 farmers from World Bank ACReSAL consultation in Kogi State, we've identified critical decision points where timely information prevents losses: optimal harvest windows based on moisture forecasts, storage condition alerts preventing spoilage, and dynamic market connections reducing time-to-sale. Immediate benefits include 30-40% reduction in post-harvest losses, 25% income increase for farmers, improved food availability for communities, and reduced environmental waste. The ground-truthing surveys ensure cultural appropriateness and continuous system improvement, while our multi-channel approach overcomes Nigeria's connectivity challenges where 60% of rural farmers lack smartphone access but can receive SMS alerts.

core_fields.title: Advancing Food Security through Renewable Energy, in Rural Communities.
core_fields.description: This project will construct a hybrid solar-energy facility designed for both drying and cold-preserving diverse produce. Furthermore, we will deliver post-harvest management training to 500 subsistence farmers in five off-grid communities within Sierra Leone. Our primary objective is to help in reducing the current post-harvest loss and waste, which is 25% -30% in Sierra Leone. In establishing this hygienic, sustainable processing solution, we will enhance long-term food security, improve quality, and boost farmers economic resilience.
core_fields.abstract: The facility is a 40x20ft, dual compartment solar-powered drying/refrigeration unit within a repurposed shipping container that will be powered by photovoltaic and battery-powered storage, preserving staple crops (e.g. rice, cocoa) alongside perishables (fish, meat and fresh fruits). Crucially, the program will also train 500 local farmers in post-harvest management, covering safe harvesting, processing, facility operations, and establishing robust market linkages to optimize income. Without proper crop preservation and post-harvest knowledge, 40% of crops in rural villages rot [1]. This is relevant because 55% of Sierra Leoneans rely on agriculture for their income[2]. Last year 20% of Sierra Leoneans suffered acute food insecurity due to low crop yields and inflation lowering the household capital and endangering communities[3]. FAIECY-SL has already built three passive solar-drying huts while training over 1000 farmers across Sierra Leone in post-harvest loss reduction. These pilot initiatives have successfully benefited 500 households by improving their product value and combating malnutrition from food insecurity. Hybrid solar dryers and cooling storage is shown to be more efficient in preserving nutritional value, quality, and quantity of cash crops than conventional methods. Our innovation is novel due to its integration of solar energy off-grid drying and a complementary solar-powered cold storage unit within a single facility. This hybrid design will deliver a comprehensive, climate resilient, and highly efficient preservation solution, effectively reducing food waste across all types of agricultural output.

core_fields.title: Reducing bushmeat hunting pressure through sustainable protein production around Ta National Park, C te d Ivoire.
core_fields.description: Local communities in C te d Ivoire face food insecurity and protein shortages, leading to an increase in illegal wildlife hunting, including the critically endangered western chimpanzee. The proposed project aims therefore to reduce bushmeat hunting pressure by providing sustainable alternative protein resources to local communities around Ta National Park. By promoting rice-frog and mushroom-palm-larvae production, it will strengthen local livelihoods and food security through a scalable business model while supporting long-term wildlife and habitat protection.
core_fields.abstract: Local communities around Ta National Park, one of the last significant remnants of primary rainforest in West Africa, face chronic protein shortages and food insecurity. Limited access to affordable animal protein often leads to wildlife hunting, including the critically endangered western chimpanzee, making sustainable alternative protein solutions essential for both community well-being and biodiversity conservation. This project will introduce locally adapted, sustainable protein production systems that are culturally accepted, environmentally sound, and economically viable, while reducing the risk of potentially fatal diseases associated with bushmeat consumption. The first innovation is a rice-frog production system combining permaculture rice farming with edible frog cultivation. Frogs naturally control pests, reducing production costs and increasing rice yields, while providing a high-quality protein source that is widely consumed but increasingly scarce and expensive due to overharvesting. The second approach involves producing mushroom and palm larvae, fast-growing and nutrient-rich proteins produced from local materials and agricultural by-products. Both are widely consumed but typically harvested opportunistically, making adoption immediate and feasible, even for low-income households. The project will be led by the Wild Chimpanzee Foundation in partnership with the local NGO Grainoth que, a permaculture specialist with experience in similar ecological and socio-economic contexts. Selected community promoters and WCF field officers (agricultural engineers) will receive hands-on training in these production techniques and then provide daily technical support to local farmers, monitoring, data collection, and simplified business planning. Combined with bushmeat awareness-raising, this approach will ensure durable knowledge transfer, improve food security, increase incomes, and reduce pressure on wildlife.
