core_fields.title: Scaling Ethiopia s Indigenous Spirulina for Nutrition, Sustainability & Equitable Access
core_fields.description: alignAfrica proposes scaling production and use of indigenous spirulina a nutrient‑dense, low‑resource microalgae to strengthen food system, improve sustainable production, and expand equitable access to affordable food. We have legal access to native spirulina biodiversity and proven pilots in school feeding and emergency support (COVID‑19 hospital nutrition). With expanded cultivation, fortified products, community enterprise models, and policy engagement, this initiative aims to transform food systems, reduce malnutrition, and create green jobs for youth and women.
core_fields.abstract: Malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and accelerating climate pressures continue to undermine food and nutrition security in Ethiopia. Conventional protein and micronutrient sources are increasingly constrained by high water and land requirements, environmental degradation, and limited affordability. As a result, nutritious foods remain inaccessible to many vulnerable communities. Spirulina globally recognized as a highly nutrient-dense, climate-resilient microalgae offers a powerful solution. alignAfrica holds the first national permit to cultivate and utilize Ethiopia s indigenous spirulina biodiversity, enabling the transformation of a naturally occurring resource into a scalable, locally owned nutrition innovation. This project pioneers transition from extractive food systems to regenerative, low-footprint production models. The innovation integrates multiple components across the food system. These include large-scale spirulina cultivation using water-efficient pond systems, solar-assisted drying and processing, and quality-assured production of spirulina powders, supplements, and fortified foods designed to complement local dietary practices. Distribution is anchored in community-based delivery systems, including women- and youth-led micro-enterprises, ensuring affordability, trust, and equitable access. Spirulina products are integrated into schools, health centers, and emergency responses, with prior deployment supporting frontline facilities like EkaKotebe Hospital during the COVID-19 response. What makes this innovation novel is its fusion of indigenous biodiversity, climate-smart production, public health nutrition, and inclusive economic models. Pilot activities demonstrate strong cultural acceptance, consistent production yields, and early evidence of improved nutritional outcomes. Through evidence generation and policy engagement, the project also supports the integration of spirulina into national nutrition and food security frameworks, positioning Ethiopia as a regional leader in sustainable, nutrition-driven food system transformation.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Solar powered Agriculture for Inclusive Food Security and Community Empowerment in Oromia Region, Ethiopia.
core_fields.description: Green Hope Energy Works PLC integrates solar-powered irrigation and sustainable farming practices to tackle Ethiopia s challenges of energy access and food insecurity. By combining clean energy with nutrition-dense crops like wheat, chickpea, onion, and avocado, the project boosts production, reduces costs, and minimizes environmental impact. Targeting 1,000 households (4,000 people) in Oromia Region , it improves diets for women and children, raises incomes for youth and women-led SMEs, and builds resilient, inclusive, climate-smart food.
core_fields.abstract: Green Hope Energy Works PLC introduces an innovative approach that integrates solar-powered technologies with nutrition-dense agriculture to address Ethiopia s dual challenges of energy access and food insecurity. The problem is that smallholder farmers in Oromia region often lack reliable irrigation and energy, limiting production of fresh, nutritious foods and contributing to poor diets, particularly among women and children. This is highly relevant in Ethiopia, where malnutrition and limited dietary diversity remain pressing public health concerns. The solution leverages solar irrigation, with best agricultural practices such as the use of natural composting system to increase the availability of key nutritious commodities such as wheat, chickpea, onion, & avocado. Scientific and technical insights show that solar water pump provides consistent water and power for agriculture, reduces costs, and minimizes environmental impact. By linking clean energy with food production, the project creates resilient, inclusive local market systems that are both climate-smart and socially empowering. Immediate benefits include improved access to healthy diets, increased incomes for youth and women-led SMEs, and reliable food supplies for 1,000 households (4,000 people). Sustainable benefits extend to stronger community resilience, reduced dependence on fossil fuels, empowerment of women and youth, healthier schools and families, and long-term environmental protection. For society, the innovation demonstrates how renewable energy can catalyze food security, inclusive growth, and climate adaptation.

core_fields.title: Agroforestry in Communities for Restoration and Empowerment (ACRE)
core_fields.description: ACRE Ghana integrates agroforestry and mushroom cultivation to restore degraded farmlands, enhance food security, and improve livelihoods in the Asuogyaman District. Using spent mushroom substrate as organic fertiliser, the project enriches soil fertility and promotes sustainable food production. It empowers smallholder farmers, especially women and youth, to adopt regenerative agriculture, diversify incomes, and reduce reliance on chemical inputs while strengthening community resilience to climate change.
core_fields.abstract: The ACRE Ghana project combines agroforestry and mushroom production to regenerate degraded lands and strengthen local food systems. The innovation transforms agricultural waste and spent mushroom substrate into organic fertiliser that boosts soil fertility, increases crop yields, and minimises dependence on chemical fertilisers. This circular model tackles two major problems: soil degradation from deforestation and unsustainable farming, and limited economic opportunities for women and youth. Integrating trees, crops, and mushrooms restores ecosystem balance, increases carbon sequestration, and ensures year-round food and income streams. Insights from successful pilots in Ghana's Eastern Region show that mushroom-agroforestry integration improves soil organic matter, enhances water retention, and yields higher productivity per hectare. The system's local adaptability, low-cost inputs, and scalability make it highly relevant for smallholder farmers facing climate stress. Immediate benefits include improved soil fertility, higher yields, and diversified diets. Sustainable benefits include restored biodiversity, reduced emissions, women's empowerment, and strengthened rural economies, making ACRE Ghana a replicable model for climate-resilient agriculture across Sub-Saharan Africa.

core_fields.title: HYBRID SOLAR DRYING FOR AFLATOXIN CONTROL: SUSTAINABLE PATHWAY TO SAFER, RESILIENT GLOBAL FOOD SYSTEMS (SOLARSAFE)
core_fields.description: Aflatoxin contamination undermines food safety, nutrition, and market competitiveness across tropical agri-food systems. The innovation is intended to deliver highly efficient and climate-resilient hybrid solar drying technology that delivers safe, uniform moisture levels under high humidity, thus preventing fungal growth and aflatoxin formation at the most critical postharvest node. The project aims to optimize the prototype through scientific validation and community-based demonstration sites to catalyze safer, more affordable, trusted and scalable renewable-energy-powered grain handling systems.
core_fields.abstract: Aflatoxin contamination is a persistent threat to food safety, public health, and market integrity in Kenya and other tropical regions. Warm, humid postharvest conditions allow Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus to infect maize from the field through storage. The current drying practicesâ€”particularly open-air dryingâ€”expose maize to slow, uneven moisture loss, intermittent rainfall, and reabsorption of humidity. These conditions promote fungal growth during stoking, slow drying on the cob, shelling of wet maize, inadequate air-drying of shelled grain, premature bagging, and improper storage. As a result, contaminated maize frequently enters households, schools, and informal markets, contributing to significant health risks and economic losses. This project introduces a next-generation hybrid solar drying system designed to break this contamination cycle at the earliest intervention point: initial drying immediately after harvest. The innovation integrates high-efficiency solar-thermal capture, controlled convection airflow, insulated chambers, and low-power auxiliary heating to ensure fast, uniform drying even under high humidityâ€”conditions that drive 60â€“70% of aflatoxin formation. The system further incorporates IoT sensors and actuators for real-time monitoring and automated adjustments, enabling precision drying previously unavailable to smallholders. Developed using locally available materials, the dryer is portable, climate-conscious, and optimized for small-scale farmers, micro-millers, schools, and community institutions. It prevents aflatoxin buildup before storage, reduces post-harvest losses, improves grain quality, and protects vulnerable consumers such as children in school feeding programs. Environmental benefits include lowering drying-related emissions and supporting climate-resilient production. Community co-design and local manufacturability strengthen adoption and scalability for high impact.

core_fields.title: Real-Time Water Tracker: Improving Water Use for Sustainable Food Production
core_fields.description: We are developing a real-time water tracker within our digital twin of the global food system. This innovation continuously monitors agricultural water availability and use, tracking surface water, soil moisture and groundwater resources, often critically-depleted. The system quantifies unsustainable extraction, traces virtual water embedded in trade, and evaluates water management alternatives. Organizations like WOTR in India can benchmark operations, test alternatives, and provide evidence-based guidance to the farmers they serve, improving water security and livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: Climate change intensifies droughts and floods while groundwater reserves deplete rapidly. Farmers, and organizations that support them, lack the tools to monitor water use in real-time or understand how management decisions impact long-term water security. Local field measurements are time-consuming and difficult to scale, while remote sensing cannot anticipate changing circumstances or evaluate alternative scenarios. Our innovation addresses this gap. Building on the state-of-the-art, we're designing a real-time water tracker that monitors both availability and use for agriculture globally. This applies the latest scientific insights at a resolution (10km spatial, monthly updates expanding to weekly) and accuracy that makes it decision-relevant for organizations managing agricultural programs and providing extension services to farmers. The challenge we're solving is operational: taking the latest climate observations and forecasts, validated environmental models and machine learning techniques, then implementing them to work continuously with real-time data at scales useful for decision-making. Our approach quantifies: (1) current water availability versus extraction rates, (2) sustainable versus unsustainable use, (3) real-time impacts of alternative water management scenarios, and (4) virtual water embedded in crops and trade flows. Benefits for extension and implementation organizations like WOTR: benchmark water use efficiency across their programs, identify high-risk periods for farmer advisories, receive timely warnings about resource depletion, and evaluate alternative water management strategies. Benefits for end users, farmers; accurate information on regional resource availability, forecasts, and management alternatives at relevant timescales. Sustainable benefits: reduced groundwater depletion, improved crop water productivity, better targeting of water-saving investments, enhanced climate resilience.

core_fields.title: The World s First Superfood Rice, Transforming Consumer's Health, Farmers' Lives and the Planet
core_fields.description: We use the World s First Superfood Rice as a tool to transform the food system in 3 key areas, consumers health, farmers livelihood and the planet. This system enables farmers to increase income by up to 14 times through organic and regenerative farming practices that improve soil health and reduce CO2 emission. The superfood rice offers global consumers a nutrient-dense alternative to conventional rice which allows equitable access to affordable food for everyday healthy diet.
core_fields.abstract: Over 40% of the world or 3.5 billion people, rely on rice as a staple food. While rice provides basic energy, it's also one of the biggest causes of diabetes and other metabolic diseases, with high Glycemic Index (GI) and low nutritional value. At the same time, there are more than 140 million rice farmers around the world living in poverty. In Thailand, where this project is based, there are 17 million rice farmers earning $0.40/day. Rice is not friendly on the environment, with significant greenhouse gas emissions, heavy water usage and soil degradation. As one of the biggest commodities in the world, it's bad for consumers health, farmers livelihood and the planet. Our game-changing innovation disrupts everything. We work with a rice scientist who spent more than 12 years developing a new variety of rice through natural cross-breeding. The result? A rice that has 30 times more fiber, twice the protein, 30% lower in GI, good source of vitamins/minerals and is naturally rich in prebiotics which supports gut health. The best part? It s absolutely delicious! We then create a farmer and planet-first system to produce this Superfood rice that is based on organic and regenerative agricultural practices. The result? Our farmers income went from $0.40/day to $5.80/day, an increase of 14 times. This has lifted 2,500 farmers families (12,500 people) we work with out of poverty. At the same time this system has reduced more than 17,600MT of CO2 emission per year. There is no comparable solution globally.

Farmers lose up to 40% of value due to exploitation by middlemen and lack of real-time market data. Our solution, Goho, is a "Phygital" platform . core_fields.title: PURE Uganda: Flexible Solar Financing & Regenerative Production for Farmer Groups
core_fields.description: PURE Uganda enables rural farmer groups to adopt solar irrigation, drying, and milling through crop-aligned financing and enterprise support. By pairing clean-energy loans of about USD 2,000 - 2,700 with training, bookkeeping assistance and regenerative agriculture, groups increase yields by roughly 35% and reduce losses by about 25%. A 30-member group generates around USD 3,600 in new seasonal value, an estimated 50% ROI. PURE will reach 15 groups, strengthening food safety, resilience, and market access
core_fields.abstract: Rural farmer groups in Uganda face persistent barriers to adopting clean, productive-use solar technologies that can improve yields, reduce losses, and enhance food safety. Many groups rely on rainfed production, diesel milling, and open-air drying systems that result in low productivity, contamination risks such as aflatoxin, high post-harvest losses, and volatile input costs. Traditional lenders require collateral that smallholder groups cannot provide and offer rigid monthly repayment schedules that do not match agricultural income cycles, leaving rural communities excluded from clean-energy financing. PURE Uganda introduces a financing and enterprise-strengthening model tailored to the rhythms of agriculture. Rather than fixed instalments, PURE aligns repayments with crop cycles, using equipment value and offtaker agreements as collateral. Loan capital, typically about USD 2,000 - 2,700 per group, supports the acquisition of solar irrigation, drying, and milling technologies supplied through private-sector partners such as Tulima Solar. PURE blends financing with a structured capacity-building package: a practical enterprise bootcamp, digital bookkeeping setup, outsourced accounting support, and regenerative agriculture training. This integrated approach reduces default risk, strengthens governance, and improves technology utilisation. Evidence from existing deployments shows that solar irrigation and regenerative practices increase yields by approximately 35%, while solar drying reduces post-harvest losses by about 25%. Combined, these improvements create roughly 60% additional seasonal value, equivalent to about USD 3,600 for a typical 30-member farmer group, resulting in an estimated 50% return on investment after one production season. PURE offers a scalable, community-rooted approach that strengthens agricultural productivity, food safety, financial inclusion, and climate resilience.

core_fields.abstract: Problem: GOAL s multisectoral behaviour change initiative NIPP achieves remarkable results (89% malnutrition cure rates; 86% purchasing biofortified seeds; 93% households with fuel efficient stove). It creates continuous dialogue between communities, development practitioners, and food system actors, converting conversations into predictive analytics for evidence-based decision-making. Novelty: Unlike existing digital agriculture or mHealth apps that deliver one-way information, ANCHOR uniquely transforms community voice into actionable intelligence through AI-automated analysis. It integrates nutrition, agriculture, and wellbeing holistically rather than in siloed digital solutions. Science: Researchers have published various academic articles on GOAL s NIPP programme benefits. Also knowing the increasing evidence base of successful genAI chatbots for promoting positive behaviour change, GOAL developed ANCHOR for health in Africa during 2025. It is now time to apply this technology to improve food, farming, and diets. Immediate Benefits: Families gain accessible advice for growing nutritious food responsibly, preparing diverse meals. Frontline workers receive insights on who needs more support. Food system actors access real-time community data enabling evidence-based resource allocation and adaptive programming. Communities maintain behaviour changes. Sustainable Benefits: Reduced malnutrition rates, enhanced food security, climate-smart agriculture adoption, strengthened local food systems, and scalable model reaching more households beyond programme graduation.

core_fields.title: Circular Mushroom Farming and Agro-Waste Biofertilizer Innovation for Food Security in Benin
core_fields.description: Our project develops a circular agriculture model that transforms agro-waste into affordable mushrooms and organic biofertilizer, powered by solar energy. We install modular production units and provide digital advisory to farmers, empowering youth and women with income-generating skills. This innovation improves food security, reduces chemical fertilizer use, and strengthens climate resilience while expanding sustainable protein access to rural communities in Benin.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation introduces a circular, low-cost agricultural system that transforms locally abundant agro-waste into two essential products: nutritious mushrooms and organic biofertilizer, powered by solar energy and supported by digital advisory tools. This approach directly addresses food insecurity, soil degradation, youth unemployment, and the high cost of agricultural inputs in Benin. Benin faces persistent protein deficiency, overreliance on imported fertilizers, and poor waste management. Agro-waste is often burned or dumped, contributing to pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, many farmers, especially women and youth, lack affordable inputs and access to modern techniques. Our solution responds to these interconnected challenges with a sustainable, scalable model. Using insights from mycology, agroecology, and renewable energy integration, we designed modular mushroom-growing units that use crop residues as substrate. The remaining biomass is processed into a nutrient-rich biofertilizer that improves soil health and reduces dependence on chemical inputs. Solar power ensures continuous, low-cost operation even in off-grid rural areas. Digital advisory support (SMS/WhatsApp bots) provides step-by-step guidance, troubleshooting, and climate-smart recommendations to producers. Immediate benefits include: Affordable, locally produced protein for households and schools New income-generating opportunities for youth and women Reduced production costs for farmers Lower environmental pollution and improved soil fertility Long-term benefits include: Strengthened climate resilience Scalable circular agriculture practices Reduced dependence on chemical fertilizers A more sustainable and inclusive rural economy This innovation delivers both immediate impact and lasting systemic change.

core_fields.description: In response to rising soybean and fishmeal costs and increasing pressure on natural resources, Act4Community is developing fish, poultry, and livestock feeds without soybean or fishmeal. These feeds are formulated using Black Soldier Fly Larvae (BSFL) meal and Azolla. This sustainable, nutritious, and affordable innovation aims to support local farmers and strengthen the resilience of food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Our project addresses a critical challenge: farmers dependence on soybean and fishmeal, which are costly and environmentally unsustainable. This dependency reduces farm profitability and impacts the long-term sustainability of local agricultural and fisheries resources. The innovation involves producing animal feed without soybean or fishmeal, using Black Soldier Fly Larvae (BSFL) meal and Azolla two local, nutrient-rich and sustainable protein sources. The problem is addressed by converting organic waste (crop residues, food by-products) into BSFL biomass and cultivating Azolla, a fast-growing aquatic fern. These raw materials replace traditional plant and animal proteins that compete with human food and strain ecosystems. This solution is built on principles of animal nutrition, bioconversion, and aquatic agronomy, confirming that BSFL and Azolla offer comparable protein and energy profiles to conventional diets. Immediate benefits include significantly reduced feed costs, increased autonomy for farmers, and the creation of new local value chains. Long-term benefits include reduced pressure on fish stocks, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and improved waste management. BSFL frass also provides a rich biofertilizer that enhances soil fertility for farmers. Overall, this innovation supports a circular and resilient food system.

core_fields.title: Integrated Climate-Resilient Bio-Secure Aquaculture: A Paradigm Shift Through Microbiome Engineering
core_fields.description: A microbially engineered aquaculture treatment (AquacBio), developed at Kagoshima University (by Yukun Zhang s team) , harnesses native bacteria and enzymes to shift pond nitrogen cycling to energy-efficient, carbon-positive anaerobic pathways . This low-cost, antifragile consortium removes ammonia and nitrite via integrated microbiomes and degrades antibiotics in situ , improving fish health. Pilot trials show ~30% nitrogen removal without aeration . The system is tailored for small farms in developing regions (Africa, Asia, Americas).
core_fields.abstract: Conventional aquaculture's energy-intensive aeration generates high N2O emissions, while prophylactic antibiotics pollute water and create antimicrobial resistance. These issues degrade ecosystems, harm fish health, and exclude small-scale farmers who comprise 70% of Asian production supporting 200 million livelihoods from sustainable solutions. Our AqucaBio enzyme consortium rewires pond microbiomes to favor anaerobic ammonium oxidation (Anammox) for nitrogen removal. Pilot trials demonstrated a 50-fold surge in the anammox gene hzsA and 9.4-fold rise in anammox bacteria, achieving up to 70% total nitrogen removal without aeration. The pre-measured sachet formulation simply requires stirring into ponds, where native bacteria self-assemble the treatment no equipment or power needed. A critical discovery reveals that sub-lethal antibiotics prime rather than inhibit this system. Metabolomic studies show low-dose fluoroquinolones upregulate carbon fixation and nitrogen enzymes, enabling concurrent degradation of 36 51% of antibiotic residues. This antifragile response creates a biosecure environment that enriches beneficial Nitrospira bacteria while competitively excluding Vibrio pathogens, yielding healthier fish and safer food. Key Benefits: Smallholder Accessibility: Sachet-based activation in static ponds eliminates infrastructure barriers for resource-poor farmers. Climate Security: Anaerobic nitrification reduces aeration needs by 60%, slashes GHG emissions, and enables carbon crediting. Biosecure Health: Engineered microbiomes degrade antibiotics and prevent ammonia/nitrite toxicity without chemical inputs. Food & Environmental Impact: 70% nitrogen removal produces reusable water, boosting yields while reducing downstream pollution. This Integrated Climate-Resilient Bio-Secure Aquaculture (ICRBE) standard delivers a transformative, antifragile solution that is climate-positive, biosecure, and inherently accessible to smallholder communities.

core_fields.title: Knowledge Hub to Assist Nutrition Action (KHANA)
core_fields.description: Malnutrition persists in vulnerable communities due to limited nutrition knowledge, poor diet diversity, and weak market access. KHANA addresses these gaps using digital technology to combine behavioral change communication, digital vouchers and local vendors. In partnership with Welthungerhilfe Nepal, the pilot will integrate this model into WHH s nutrition-sensitive programme areas, testing how coordinated information and improved access to nutritious foods through local markets can strengthen diet diversity, healthier behavior and equitable access to vulnerable families.
core_fields.abstract: Nepal s malnutrition challenge persists because families have lower understanding and affordability constraint related to nutrition. Existing Social Behavior Change Communication (SBCC) approaches within wider Nutrition Cluster rely heavily on interpersonal communication, frontline workers, which are effective but difficult to harmonize, scale, or monitor across multiple partners and municipalities. Simultaneously, the lack of an integrated platform to capture who is implementing what activities, in which locations, and with what nutrition results hampers coordinated planning and weakens opportunities for adaptive, evidence-driven program adjustments. KHANA addresses these systemic gaps by establishing an integrated, multi-actor Nutrition Knowledge and Monitoring Hub. Beyond serving as a repository of validated, government-aligned SBCC content, the Hub enables actors such as municipalities, NGOs, community structures, and market partners to visualize program footprints, monitor progress against key nutrition indicators, and assess improvements in key indicators. This strengthens alignment with Nepal's Multi Sector Nutrition Plan frameworks and enhances joint accountability across the system. Restricted digital nutrition vouchers operationalize behavior change by linking improved knowledge with the ability to act with incentives to purchase recommended nutritious foods. Local vendors and cooperatives become nutrition enablers, supplying targeted foods, stabilizing local availability, and contributing data that enriches monitoring and forecasting. Aria s existing offline-capable LALI360 infrastructure integrates messaging, vouchers, vendor operations, and indicator dashboards, creating a continuous feedback loop that supports evidence-based decision making. KHANA enables healthier food choices, strengthens local economies, and supports long-term, data-driven nutrition improvement of vulnerable families by integrating nutrition knowledge, targeted restricted vouchers, and market actors,.

core_fields.title: Calcium fortified Anchote Based Bar

core_fields.abstract: The innovation is a calcium-rich snack bar made from anchote (Coccinia abyssinica), an indigenous Ethiopian tuber that is highly nutritious but underutilized in modern food systems. Ethiopia faces a serious public health challenge of calcium deficiency, affecting over 40% of women and contributing to rickets in children and complications during pregnancy. Despite the availability of nutrient-dense local crops, affordable and convenient calcium-rich foods remain limited. This project addresses the problem by transforming anchote into a shelf-stable, affordable, and appealing snack bar. Traditionally, anchote is consumed boiled and has limited shelf life. Using simple food processing techniques, anchote is converted into flour and blended with oats and honey to create a nutritious bar with high calcium content, balanced energy, and good taste. Scientific evidence showing anchote s high calcium levels (450 500 mg per 100 g) guided the crop choice, while formulation trials and sensory evaluations ensured product quality and consumer acceptance. Immediate benefits include improved calcium intake for children, pregnant women, the elderly, and health-conscious consumers. Schools and communities gain access to affordable, locally produced nutritious snacks. Farmers benefit from increased demand and better income for anchote, while youth gain employment in processing and marketing. Environmentally, the project promotes biodiversity, climate-resilient indigenous crops, reduced food loss, and stronger local food systems. Over time, the innovation supports healthier diets, resilient livelihoods, and sustainable food systems rooted in local knowledge.

core_fields.title: FairChain Intelligence: The Transparency Infrastructure For Global Food Systems
core_fields.description: Smallholder farmers lose 40-70% of income to middlemen who control market information. FairChain Intelligence solves this through integrated transparency infrastructure: AI-powered fair price alerts (proven 43% income increase), blockchain supply chain verification (91% consumer trust), IoT food safety testing (zero contamination incidents), and predictive waste reduction (53% decrease). Operational pilot: 2237 farmers, 8 months, Kenya. The Selina Wamucii platform processes $10M+ transactions across 90+ countries.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: Smallholder farmers globally lose $100+ billion annually because middlemen control one critical resource: market information. Farmers don't know fair prices, so they sell at whatever middlemen offer. Consumers can't verify food safety, so trust collapses. Buyers can't predict supply, so produce spoils before sale. This information asymmetry is the root cause of farmer poverty, food waste, and supply chain failures. Solution: FairChain Intelligence is transparency infrastructure for agricultural markets. Selina Wamucii is making pricing, transactions, safety, and demand completely visible through four interdependent components: 1. AI Fair-Price Intelligence: Real-time SMS alerts analyzing 5+ years of global price data (90 countries). Farmers know when offered prices are exploitative. Result: 43% income increase (pilot validated, n=237). 2. Blockchain Supply Chain Verification: Every transaction recorded immutably. Contamination traced in 4 hours vs. 3 weeks traditional systems. QR codes enable farm-to-consumer traceability. Result: 91% consumer trust, zero contamination incidents. 3. IoT Food Safety Testing: Portable NIR devices detect aflatoxins, verify nutrients at source. Farmers prove quality; consumers see verified results. Result: 95% testing accuracy vs. lab verification. 4. Predictive Waste Reduction: AI analyzes weather, historical demand, market signals to match farmer surplus with institutional buyers before spoilage. Result: 53% waste reduction (38% baseline → 18%). Benefits: Farmers earn living wages. Consumers trust verified food. Institutional buyers access reliable supply. Environment benefits from eliminated waste. Platform operational: $10M+ annual transactions, 90+ countries.

core_fields.title: Scaling Solar Food Drying Systems to Strengthen Nutrition, Reduce Waste, and Support Local Farmers
core_fields.description: Ardi Ardak, in partnership with Oxfam, is scaling SunCode, a solar-hybrid food dryer equipped with IoT automation to cut energy use, reduce food losses, and improve food safety. The system enables farmers to process fruits and vegetables efficiently at near-zero operating cost, while ensuring consistent quality. The project also strengthens rural value-addition, increases farmer income, expands access to nutritious dried foods, and enhances climate resilience for vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: Ardi Ardak introduces a solar-hybrid convection dryer SunCode with an integrated IoT monitoring system designed to reduce post-harvest losses, improve food safety, and cut energy consumption for farmers and cooperatives. Lebanon faces extremely high food spoilage rates, unstable electricity, and dependence on costly electric dryers, making traditional drying unsafe, slow, and inconsistent. This innovation replaces energy-intensive processes with a renewable, climate-smart alternative that provides reliable drying at near-zero operational cost. The system combines solar thermal collectors and photovoltaic panels with smart sensors that automatically regulate temperature, humidity, and airflow. IoT alerts allow farmers to monitor drying remotely, reducing the need to visit the station and ensuring continuous, precise control. Scientific studies on hybrid solar dryers demonstrate 37 54% energy reduction and up to 100% CO₂ elimination when operating fully on solar PV. Industrial electric dryers consume approximately 100 kWh per 40 kg batch, equal to 2,500 kWh per ton, generating nearly 1.8 tons of CO₂. SunCode s hybrid system reduces energy consumption to 0 40 kWh per ton, cutting emissions by up to 1.8 tons of CO₂ for every ton of fruit or vegetables dried. The innovation delivers immediate benefits: farmers gain control over quality and market timing, schools and households access safe, nutritious dried foods, and women and youth participate in new value-added jobs. Sustainable benefits include reduced food waste, lower methane emissions from spoilage, improved climate resilience, and strengthened rural economies. Co-implemented by Ardi Ardak and Oxfam, the project integrates community engagement, inclusive outreach, MEAL systems, and policy alignment.

core_fields.title: Scaling Climate-Resilient Enset Foods for Nutrition, Livelihoods and Planetary Health
core_fields.description: Lucy Enset Plc is developing scalable, nutritious, and trusted enset-based foods by modernizing the traditional processing, improving nutritional quality, and reducing post-harvest losses. The project integrates climate-resilient production, regenerative practices, and inclusive market models to deliver affordable, appealing foods while increasing incomes for smallholder farmers and women processors. This innovation transforms an underutilized indigenous crop Enset into a high-impact solution for healthier diets, sustainable food systems, and equitable access
core_fields.abstract: Enset is a climate resilient indigenous crop that sustains over 25 millions in Ethiopia, yet its full potential is limited by labor-intensive traditional processing, inconsistent food quality, post-harvest losses, and weak market integration. Although enset-based foods are culturally important, many are produced under conditions that constrain scalability, consumer trust, and access to diverse, modern food markets particularly for health-conscious and vulnerable populations. Lucy Enset Plc is transforming enset into safe, nutritious, diabetic-friendly, organic, and gluten-free food products through improved processing technologies, controlled fermentation, and standardized quality processing systems. Drawing on our patented technologies, the innovation enhances nutritional balance, digestibility, sensory quality, and shelf stability while maintaining cultural authenticity. These improvements enable enset foods that are suitable for people managing diabetes, gluten intolerance, and other diet-related health concerns. The project integrates regenerative enset production, waste-reducing processing methods, and inclusive sourcing from smallholder farmers, especially women processors. By upgrading traditional practices with appropriate technologies, the solution reduces food loss, improves consistency, and supports organic production systems that stay within planetary boundaries. Immediate benefits include affordable, appealing, and trusted foods for consumers; expanded market access and higher incomes for farmers and processors; and improved food availability for schools and urban communities. Long-term benefits include strengthened climate resilience, reduced environmental impact, and equitable access to healthy diets. By repositioning enset as a modern, market-ready food, Lucy Enset Plc delivers scalable innovations that support healthy diets, environmental sustainability, and inclusive food systems transformation.

core_fields.title: REVOLUTIONIZING UGANDA'S FARMING THROUGH AGROECOLOGY TO STRENGTHEN FOOD SECURITY, BIODIVERSITY, AND SMALLHOLDER FARMER RESILIENCE.
core_fields.description: EverGrow Organics will implement a 15-month, community-driven agroecology project to address soil degradation, biodiversity loss, and climate vulnerability among Uganda's smallholder farmers. The project will establish a functional demonstration and training farm as a learning hub for regenerative practices, farmer experimentation, and peer exchange. Through structured training cycles, 1,500 farmers will adopt organic and climate-resilient practices, restoring 300 acres of farmland, strengthening food security, livelihoods, and ecological resilience in alignment with Uganda's Vision 2040.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Uganda face persistent challenges including soil degradation, declining biodiversity, low productivity, and increasing vulnerability to climate change. Reliance on conventional farming and synthetic inputs has depleted soil health and weakened resilience, threatening household food security and the livelihoods of rural families. To address this, we propose an evidence based agroecology intervention designed to strengthen local food systems through sustainable production, market access, and adaptive capacity building. This 15 month initiative will establish a functional model agroecology farm as a living learning hub where structured training cycles, farmer field schools, and peer exchange sessions are carried out. The model farm will demonstrate regenerative practices such as crop diversification, agroforestry, composting, integrated pest management, and organic soil restoration. These practices are grounded in agroecological science showing that biologically active soils and diversified systems improve nutrient cycling, water retention, and climate resilience. Using a phased approach, we will engage 1,500 smallholder farmers through repeated, experiential training and field mentoring, enabling sustainable adoption of practices. We will restore 300 acres of degraded farmland with organic inputs, closely monitoring soil health indicators and crop performance through seasonal assessments. Farmer groups will receive market facilitation support including value addition training, buyer linkages, and collective marketing coordination to improve incomes. The project's evidence generation, documentation, and farmer led learning pathways ensure adaptive scaling beyond project boundaries. By strengthening local capacity, ecological integrity, and market participation, this initiative promotes resilient food systems, enhances biodiversity, and increases rural economic opportunity.

core_fields.title: A Novel Capillary Irrigation System for Improved Leafy Vegetables Yields and Water Use Efficiency
core_fields.description: The research aims to introduce a capillary irrigation system (CIS) to the smallholder farmers for the cultivation of Amaranthus in Osun State, Nigeria. The CIS uses polyvinyl chloride pipes to irrigate the crop. This method conserves water, increases Amaranth yield by 190%, and reduces soil pollution. The project will select 160 farmers, use demonstration plots, , and analyse adoption and impact, with goals to improve food security, bridge gender gaps, and create local jobs.
core_fields.abstract: Dry season vegetables production in Nigeria involves a lot drudgeries, labour intensive and thus limited production far below demands. The capillary irrigation innovation is a simple device involving the use of PVC pipes. It features a buried PVC pipe (reservoir) connected to capillary tubes, which delivers water directly to plant roots in response to evapotranspiration demand. Water moves from the reservoir (higher potential) to drier soil (lower potential) within the plant rooting zone. A graded sand column inside the capillary tube provides channel for water movement and is driven by the combined effects of evaporation and plant transpiration. Water is only released when needed, making the system efficient and maintenance-free, and suitable for most arable crops. Water will only move from the reservoir through the capillary tubes to replenish water loss at the soil surface and at the root zone. It is simple to install and maintenance free, and it is suitable for most arable crops. Additionally, the system supports fertigation, allowing nutrients to move from the reservoir to the root zone by mass flow and diffusion, which improves fertiliser use and reduces costs. Since fertiliser remains enclosed within the reservoir until required, it prevents soil pollution. The system also reduces the labour involved in irrigation compared to the traditional methods, making it more accessible and user-friendly for women farmers involved in vegetables production.The system also reduces the labour involved in irrigation compared to the traditional methods, making it more accessible and user-friendly for women farmers involved in vegetables production.

core_fields.title: AI-Enabled Advisory for Climate-Resilient Smallholder Farming
core_fields.description: This project deploys an AI-enabled, mobile-based agricultural advisory system to support smallholder farmers with timely, localized, and climate-smart guidance. Implemented in partnership with the Government of Uttar Pradesh, Columbia University, and the Reliance Foundation, the project integrates artificial intelligence with agronomic expertise and public extension systems. Delivered through accessible platforms such as WhatsApp, it improves farmer decision-making, productivity, and resilience while reducing environmental impacts and strengthening inclusive, sustainable food systems in the Global South.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers face persistent information gaps on crop management, pests, inputs, and climate risks. Public agricultural extension systems are often understaffed, slow, and unable to provide timely, localized advice, while private advisory services are frequently costly or biased toward input sales. As climate variability increases, these gaps directly undermine productivity, incomes, and environmental sustainability, making the problem both urgent and highly relevant to global food security. This project addresses this challenge through an AI-enabled, mobile-based agricultural advisory system that delivers timely, localized, and climate-smart guidance directly to farmers via widely used platforms such as WhatsApp. The system combines artificial intelligence with validated agronomic knowledge, local crop calendars, weather data, and insights from public extension services. Farmers can ask questions in natural language and receive practical, context-specific recommendations aligned with sustainable farming practices. The innovation is grounded in recent advances in artificial intelligence and natural language processing, combined with field-based insights from development economics and agricultural extension research. Rather than replacing public institutions, the system is designed to complement and strengthen them by scaling expert knowledge efficiently and consistently. Immediate benefits to farmers include faster access to reliable advice, improved decision-making, reduced crop losses, and lower input misuse. Over time, the solution supports higher productivity, increased resilience to climate shocks, reduced environmental impacts, and stronger rural livelihoods. At the system level, it enhances the reach and effectiveness of public extension services, contributing to more inclusive and sustainable food systems.

core_fields.title: Vertically Integrated Sustainable Coffee Value Chains at Origin
core_fields.description: EXIM connects Cameroonian smallholder coffee farmers directly to international markets through vertically integrated processing and fair trade. With milling at origin and distribution via Switzerland, the project improves farmer incomes, ensures traceability, creates rural jobs, and valorizes coffee waste into fertilizers and bio-products. The model is proven, scalable, and sustainability-driven across economic, social, and environmental pillars.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder coffee farmers in Cameroon remain trapped in poverty due to fragmented value chains, weak bargaining power, and lack of access to processing and export markets. Most value is captured by intermediaries, while farmers face income instability, limited infrastructure, and environmental degradation from unmanaged waste. EXIM addresses these systemic challenges by redesigning the coffee value chain around farmer inclusion and local value creation. The innovation lies in full vertical integration at origin: EXIM directly purchases coffee from farmers at cooperative-defined prices, processes and mills locally, and exports through its Swiss entity to international buyers. This structure guarantees transparency, quality control, and fairer income distribution. Technical expertise in post-harvest processing preserves quality and enables specialty market access, while circular-economy principles guide the transformation of coffee waste into fertilizer pellets, charcoal, and cosmetic inputs. These innovations reduce environmental impact while generating additional income streams for rural communities. Immediate benefits include higher and more stable farmer incomes, employment for women and youth, and improved market access. Long-term benefits include strengthened rural economies, reduced migration pressure, climate change mitigation, healthier soils, and increased consumer trust through traceable, ethically produced coffee.

core_fields.abstract: Engage rural-communities to envision solutions to their health-concerns, through their produce. Rural communities of KONKAN burdened by health-issues linked to poor dietary patterns will be cohorts for this study. Millets, rich in proteins, minerals, fibre and phytochemicals help in lowering oxidative and metabolic stress. They use C4-pathway, a specialized photosynthesis, making them super-efficient in hot, dry climates, semi-arid environments and thrive with less water and fertilizer. However, millets contain antinutrients reducing the absorption of proteins and minerals3. Unless suitably processed they don t release their complete nutritional potential. Simple processing methods like soaking, germination, or roasting can reduce these antinutrients, improve protein digestibility and increase bio-availability4. Combining millets with pulses complements their amino-acid profiles: millets supply certain sulphur‐containing amino acids (methionine, cysteine), while pulses supply lysine and other amino acids that millets lack5. Addition of oilseed for enhanced essential fatty acid profile brings in dietary diversity and most importantly, the combination enhances the flavour and overall sensory acceptance. This Millet-Pulse-Oilseeds and Right Processing boosts intake of high-quality protein; essential minerals, micronutrients, supporting immunity, energy, growth, and general health; promotes steady energy, better digestion, stable blood sugar and metabolic health. Processing and cooking of combinations, its health-benefits, decrease in complications linked to NCDs (diabetes) will be demonstrated in communities encouraging them to gradually adopt and include this millet-pulse-oilseed combination in their diet instead of the current single-staple, rice. Not an academic study, the approach here is to partner with communities at their doorstep and help them visualise the knowledge highly needed.

core_fields.title: Change Sierra Leone through a Resilient Food Systems for a Healthier Population
core_fields.description: Sierra Leone s population of 8.46 million (2023) is projected to reach nearly 13 million by 2050, intensifying challenges in food security, water access, and gender equity. Over half rely on unsafe water, driving waterborne diseases that cause 20% of deaths. This proposal advances food system transformation through water harvesting, school feeding programs, and women s empowerment. By aligning with SDGs 2, 3, 5, and 6, it delivers measurable impact in nutrition, sustainability, health, and equity.
core_fields.abstract: This innovation tackles Sierra Leone s interconnected challenges of unsafe water, poor nutrition, and gender inequity issues that perpetuate disease, poverty, and limited opportunities. More than half the population relies on contaminated water sources, driving waterborne illnesses that account for 20% of deaths. Children miss school due to illness and hunger, while women and girls bear disproportionate burdens of water collection and food insecurity. The solution integrates three proven approaches: water harvesting and safe access, school feeding programs, and women and girls empowerment initiatives. Rainwater harvesting systems and borehole rehabilitation provide reliable, clean water, reducing disease and freeing women from long collection journeys. School gardens and local food procurement supply daily nutritious meals, improving attendance, reducing stunting, and strengthening local food chains. Training, micro-grants, and mentorship empower women and girls to lead in agro-processing, budgeting, and food enterprises, shifting gender dynamics and building resilience. This approach is grounded in public health and food systems science: safe water reduces disease burden, nutrition interventions improve cognitive and physical development, and gender equity enhances community leadership and sustainability. Immediate benefits include reduced illness, improved school attendance, and new income opportunities for women. Sustainable benefits include community-owned water systems, resilient local food supply chains, and empowered female leadership driving equitable development. Together, these innovations deliver measurable impact for consumers, farmers, schools, and communities, while advancing environmental sustainability and aligning with SDGs 2, 3, 5, and 6.

core_fields.title: Compostable Food Packaging from Naturally Stranded Seaweed Biomass
core_fields.description: This project develops compostable food packaging made from stranded seaweed biomass, addressing plastic pollution and unmanaged coastal biomass simultaneously. The solution has been validated at laboratory scale and targets horticultural food packaging applications. The project will focus on food-contact safety certification, technical validation, and a semi-industrial pilot with a food producer. By valorizing seaweed before decomposition, the project supports circular food systems, reduces environmental impact, and advances sustainable alternatives to fossil-based packaging.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation consists of developing compostable food packaging made from stranded seaweed biomass, addressing two interconnected challenges within food systems: dependence on single-use plastic packaging and the accumulation of unmanaged seaweed on coastlines. Food packaging is essential for food safety and distribution, yet current solutions rely largely on fossil-based plastics that generate persistent pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, large quantities of seaweed wash ashore in coastal regions worldwide. When left unmanaged, this biomass decomposes, releasing CO₂ and methane and causing environmental and economic impacts on coastal communities. The proposed solution transforms stranded seaweed biomass into compostable packaging materials for horticultural food applications. Unlike other bio-based approaches, the innovation uses the entire seaweed biomass rather than extracting specific compounds, enabling a simpler, more adaptable and resource-efficient process. While current development focuses on Rugulopteryx okamurae, the technology is species-agnostic and transferable to other regions facing similar challenges. The solution has been validated at laboratory scale, demonstrating technical feasibility. The next phase focuses on food-contact safety certification, technical optimization and a semi-industrial pilot. Immediate benefits include reduced plastic use, valorization of an environmental residue and avoided emissions from biomass decomposition. In the longer term, the innovation supports circular food systems, sustainable packaging alternatives for producers, healthier coastal ecosystems and reduced environmental impact for society.

core_fields.title: Supporting Timor Farmers Through Small-Scale Avocado Oil Production to Increase Income and Reduce Post-Harvest Loss

core_fields.abstract: We aim to improve the livelihood in Timor Tengah Selatan (TTS) District, where communities face unfair pricing for local avocado varieties. During the harvest season, supply far exceeds local demand, resulting in significant post-harvest loss as many avocados rot. Middlemen often pressure communities to sell at extremely low prices, citing high transportation costs. Avocados in the area are typically priced at IDR 1,000 per kilogram, yet the same fruit can sell for IDR 30,000 - 60,000 per kilogram in urban markets. As communities currently have no knowledge access to any avocado-based value-added products, there is limited ability to increase their potential income from avocados. To address this gap, we propose the introduction of simple, locally manageable, and scalable tools and processes to produce avocado oil. Avocado oil is slowly gaining popularity in major cities in Indonesia as a healthier alternative oil, high in nutritional value and unsaturated fatty acids. Avocado oil commands a premium price, reaching up to IDR 900,000 per liter. This presents a huge potential for communities to increase their livelihood through the selling of avocado oil. The local avocado variety contains 12-16% of oil, making it suitable for avocado oil production. We draw inspiration from existing small-scale coconut oil production technologies that we adapt to the unique characteristics of avocado oil. Careful considerations are applied to increase the ease of use by the communities, in formulating the workflow for producing avocado oil for household use, and in commercial sales to support sustained community income.

core_fields.title: Reducing Post-Harvest Losses Through Pre-Harvest Market Access for Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: This project pilots a farmer-first, logistics-enabled platform that connects smallholder farmers to verified buyers before harvest. By combining pre-harvest buyer matching, aggregation, safe storage, and coordinated delivery, the project reduces post-harvest losses, improves income predictability, and strengthens food system efficiency. In 2026, the pilot will support 200 smallholder farmers in Ghana, creating a scalable model for equitable, low-waste food systems in the Global South.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Ghana and across the Global South lose up to 30% of their produce after harvest due to lack of guaranteed buyers, poor storage, price uncertainty, and inefficient logistics. These challenges reduce farmer incomes, increase food waste, and limit access to affordable, nutritious food. This innovation addresses these challenges through a farmer-first, logistics-enabled platform that connects farmers to verified buyers before harvest. Farmers list expected crops and harvest timelines in advance, enabling buyers, such as retailers, aggregators, and processors, to commit early. The platform coordinates aggregation, provides access to short-term storage through a shared warehouse, and links produce to verified transport partners for timely delivery. The solution is informed by a key insight from field engagement: post-harvest losses are primarily a coordination and market-access problem, not a production problem. By securing demand earlier and aligning storage and logistics around confirmed sales, food loss is prevented before it occurs. During the 2026 pilot, the project is expected to support 200 smallholder farmers, reduce post-harvest losses by an estimated 15 20%, and improve farmer income predictability by 10 25% through better pricing and reduced distress sales. For buyers, the model improves supply reliability and reduces sourcing inefficiencies. Over time, this approach contributes to more sustainable food systems by reducing food waste, improving resource efficiency, strengthening rural livelihoods, and expanding equitable access to affordable, trusted food.

core_fields.abstract: This innovation addresses the urgent problem of food loss and waste by focusing on underutilized fermented foods along Sino Southeast Asian migration corridors. Globally, over 930 million tons of food are wasted annually, undermining food security, straining water resources, and accelerating climate change. Fermentation offers a natural solution: it extends shelf life, transforms surplus produce, and recycles nutrients, while also enhancing digestion, immunity, and nutrient bioavailability. Yet, many traditional fermented foods in South China and Southeast Asia remain overlooked, understudied, and underutilized. The project solves this problem by combining ethnographic research (documenting cultural, medicinal, and economic values) with advanced scientific analysis (DNA sequencing, chromatography, and metabolomics) to uncover the microbial, nutritional, and safety profiles of these foods. Insights from Indigenous knowledge and modern science converge to identify enablers and barriers to adoption, guided by Diffusion of Innovation theory. Immediate benefits include empowering communities to preserve food culture, reduce waste, and improve nutrition. Farmers and producers gain new opportunities to valorize surplus crops through fermentation, while schools and households benefit from healthier, affordable foods. Sustainable benefits extend to society and the environment: reduced greenhouse gas emissions from food waste, strengthened food security, and new entrepreneurial pathways in local food industries. By linking traditional practices with modern science, this innovation not only safeguards cultural heritage but also contributes to global goals on hunger, health, responsible consumption, and climate action.

core_fields.title: Go Green: Grower Consumer Partnership in the Netrakona District of Bangladesh
core_fields.description: This project establishes a village-based green marketing system in Netrokona, Bangladesh, enabling indigenous and marginalized households to sell small surpluses of eggs, vegetables, and fish directly to urban consumers. The system uses local vendors, traceable safe-food tags, and efficient distribution to ensure fair prices, reduce food waste, and provide safe, locally sourced food, strengthening rural livelihoods and consumer trust.
core_fields.abstract: This project will establish a village-based green marketing system to collect surplus vegetables, eggs, and fish from indigenous and poor households in the Durgapur and Kalmakanda sub-districts. These communities face persistent challenges in accessing markets due to high transportation costs, long distances, dependence on middlemen, and low farm-gate prices. As a result, small surpluses often go unsold, leading to food waste, lost income, and continued poverty particularly for women farmers. To address these barriers, ARBAN will deploy trained local vendors, known as safe food collectors, who will operate mobile collection points across villages. Two mobile vans per union will visit pre-set collection points in each village, allowing farmers especially women to sell their produce conveniently at fair and transparent prices. The collected products will be aggregated and transported to ARBAN Green Display Shops in nearby district towns such as Netrokona and Mymensingh, ensuring efficient market access. Each product will carry a safe-food tag displaying the farmer s name and contact information, ensuring full traceability, accountability, and consumer confidence in food safety. Beyond physical market linkage, the project will create and strengthen market demand through awareness campaigns and community networking that promote fresh, safe, and locally sourced food.

core_fields.title: Collection and Characterization of Native Tanzanian Unique Sesame Germplasm for Climate-Resilient Variety Development and Deployment
core_fields.description: This project will collect and characterize a representative set of Tanzanian sesame germplasm from threatening agro-biodiversity to generate the first structured diversity dataset for this crop. By collecting atleast 50 unique accessions, conducting basic morphological and seed-quality characterization, and analyzing key traits, the project will identify trait-specific promising lines and knowledge gaps. The results will provide a scientific foundation for future sesame breeding, conservation, and scaling efforts that can later be supported by larger funds.
core_fields.abstract: Tanzania possesses a rich genetic diversity of sesame, but existing germplasm collections are incomplete and under-characterized. This limits national breeding efforts, germplasm conservation planning, and smallholder access to improved, climate-resilient varieties. The project addresses this germplasm gap by implementing a focused, early-stage pilot to collect and characterize diverse and unique sesame germplasm from key production regions. The innovation lies in translating scattered and largely undocumented diversity into a structured, analyzable dataset for an underutilized but economically and nutritionally important oilseed crop. The project will collect at least 50 sesame germplasm accessions, document their passport data, and conduct basic morphological, agronomic and seed-quality characterization under representative growing conditions. This will generate the first systematic trait matrix for Tanzanian sesame, highlighting variability in yield-related traits, maturity, biotic and abiotic stress tolerance indicators and seed quality characteristics such as diverse proteins, healthy oils and various bioactive compounds. While no specific varieties will be released within this Seed Grant, the work creates a critical evidence and germplasm base for future breeding, participatory testing and seed system investments. Immediate benefits accrue to researchers, breeders and national genebank managers, who will be able to understand the genetic diversity base, prioritize trait-specific augmentation of germplasm accessions and design more targeted sesame improvement strategies. In the longer term, this foundational work will enable more resilient, higher-yielding and nutritious sesame varieties to reach farmers, supporting income generation, nutrition, transform sesame value chains, open investment opportunities for public-private partnerships, boost exports, and climate adaptation.

core_fields.title: Indigenous Food Innovation in Senegal from Farm to School
core_fields.description: We spent seven years co-creating Indigenous food products with Senegalese farmers, establishing market opportunities for Indigenous plants to incentivize wild forest preservation, and diversifying local income and dietary sources. Working with the African Development Bank and the World Food Program, we will pilot the Indigenous Food to School Initiative in Senegal and establish a digital Indigenous Food Innovation Library, creating gateways for the food industry and academic professionals to contribute to global Indigenous food sovereignty.
core_fields.abstract: Indigenous peoples account for just 6% of the global population but make up 19% of the extreme poor, while their lands host at least 47% of threatened mammalian species. Under the economic stress, West Africa undergoes the world s fastest deforestation, losing the area of nearly two soccer fields per second. We used to harvest from the Acacia forest next door to make couscous for children. Now the forest has been burnt down for cropping, we ride horse carts for four hours to get imported foods, shared by our Senegalese partnering farmers. This is why we focus on Indigenous food innovation with smallholder farmers, incentivizing wild forest preservation by entrepreneurship opportunities, while sustaining Indigenous food access. Through seven years of working with women farmers in Kaolack, Senegal, we co-developed Indigenous food products using Indigenous plants such as Baobab, acacia gum, and sorghum, which led to the building of the community s first food processing plant by the African Development Bank. We have recently established a partnership with their World Food Programme to pilot the developed Indigenous food products in their school feeding program. This grant will support planning, launching, and evaluating the Indigenous Food to School initiative, and establishing an Indigenous Food Innovation Library for global farming communities. Piloting the Initiative will help the World Food Program gauge opportunities to connect its current global school feeding work with agroecological system management. Establishing the digital Library will empower global farming communities and academics to collaborate on Indigenous food innovation that advances food sovereignty.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Nutrition-Sensitive Homestead Food System Approach to Improve Nutrition in Rural Bangladesh
core_fields.description: This project strengthens the DAE-EFNHUP initiative by introducing a nutrition-sensitive food systems approach to address gaps in post-harvest preservation, food-waste utilization, and market access. It integrates climate-smart production, home-based food processing and preservation, nutritious use of household food waste, and women-led cooperative marketing to improve diet quality, resilience, and income. The project targets climate-vulnerable farm households, especially women with young and school-aged children.
core_fields.abstract: Establishment of Family Nutrition Garden in Homestead and Uncultivated Fallow Land (EFNHUP) project, has improved household-level production and nutrition awareness, critical gaps persist in post-harvest preservation, household food-waste utilization, and organized market access. These constraints limit the sustainability of dietary improvements and livelihood gains. Moreover, while international evidence demonstrates that climate-smart agriculture, food preservation technologies, and cooperative models can enhance resilience, nutrition, and income, context-specific evidence from Bangladesh remains limited. This initiative addresses these gaps by applying a nutrition-sensitive food systems approach that builds directly on the DAE-EFNHUP platform, strengthening and extending existing extension services. The proposed innovation adopts a nutrition-sensitive food systems approach and builds directly on the DAE-EFNHUP platform by layering additional food-system functions onto existing extension services. The innovation integrates four complementary components: (i) climate-smart production technologies, including salinity- and drought-tolerant crops, sack gardening, and composting from household food waste to enhance resilience and year-round production; (ii) home-based food processing, preservation, and storage technologies such as solar drying, fermentation, germination, and pickling to reduce post-harvest losses, retain nutrients, and create value-added products; (iii) improved household food-waste utilization through nutrient-dense recipes to diversify diets; and (iv) cooperative-based processing and marketing of value-added products to strengthen women-led entrepreneurship, income generation, and empowerment. The target population comprises men and women farmers with under-five children (0-5 years) and school-aged children (6-10 years), with a particular focus on women in climate-vulnerable households.

core_fields.title: "Seeds of Sustainability: Enhancing Local Food Systems with Regenerative Practices in Zambia"
core_fields.description: The "Seeds of Sustainability" project enhances local food systems in Zambia's Southern and Northern provinces by promoting regenerative farming practices. It improves soil health, diversifies crops, and supports smallholder farmers to grow nutrient-rich foods. This leads to healthier diets, better nutrition, increased food security, and greater resilience to climate change, while fostering environmental sustainability and strengthening community livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: The "Seeds of Sustainability" project addresses the critical problem of food insecurity, poor nutrition, and environmental degradation in Zambia's Southern and Northern provinces. Smallholder farmers often face depleted soils, limited crop diversity, and vulnerability to climate change, resulting in low agricultural productivity and insufficient access to nutritious foods. These challenges affect the health and livelihoods of local communities, making the problem highly relevant for social and environmental well-being. The project solves this problem by introducing regenerative farming practices such as crop diversification, soil restoration techniques, and sustainable land management that restore soil fertility and improve ecosystem health. By combining traditional knowledge with modern agricultural insights, this approach enables farmers to cultivate nutrient-rich crops that support healthy diets and improve nutrition among community members. Scientific and technical insights underpinning this solution include understanding soil microbiology, nutrient cycling, and climate-resilient crop varieties. These inform practices like cover cropping, composting, and agroecology, which enhance long-term soil productivity and reduce dependence on chemical inputs. Immediate benefits to farmers include increased crop yields, diversified food sources, and improved income opportunities. Communities benefit from better nutrition and strengthened food security. Schools and households gain access to healthier diets, while the environment experiences restored biodiversity and reduced degradation. Over time, these sustainable practices build resilience against climate change, empower local farmers, and promote ecological balance, resulting in lasting socio-economic and environmental improvements for society.

core_fields.title: LibreAgro: AI-Powered Production Assistant for Agroecological Food Systems and Ecosystem Restoration
core_fields.description: LibreAgro deploys an AI-Powered Production Assistant across 18 family farming organizations in C rdoba, Argentina: improving 8 poultry operations (LibreIncu) and establishing 10 horticultural nurseries with global scalability potential. We transform nurseries strategic agricultural bottleneck into agroecological hubs with digital traceability, implementing blockchain. Combining validated open-source hardware with participatory methodology, we achieve impact: thousands of certified seedlings and improved poultry production. Our proven approach demonstrates transferability between chains, partnering with provincial forestry programs for ecosystem restoration.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: Nurseries are agriculture's most strategic yet vulnerable control point, where family producers abandon in-house production due to excessive manual labor, creating dependency on commercial suppliers selling industrial genetics. This concentrates genetic control and demands agrochemical inputs for production. Existing production systems lack integrated tools connecting IoT data with business management and agroecological certification. Solution: LibreAgro provides an Integrated Production Assistant combining IoT automation, ERP management (Odoo), and non-conversational AI serving both existing poultry operations and new horticultural nurseries. The Assistant consolidates sensor data (temperature, humidity, soil pH, EC) with management data (purchases, inventory, sales...) generating early problem detection, historical analysis, predictive recommendations, and actionable insights. Each seedling batch receives digital certification documenting complete traceability of monitored processes and agroecological practices, connecting directly with consumer. Innovation: Three integrated innovations: (1) Participatory R&D methodology where end-users co-develop technology proven with 86% hatch rate vs 79% commercial in poultry incubators deployed across 8 organizations over 12+ months; (2) Complete open-source stack enabling global replication (hardware designs, firmware, ML pipelines); (3) Cross-chain transferability the same Assistant serves poultry, horticulture, and forestry through strategic alliance with C rdoba Ministry's Gen Nativo program (100,000 native trees/year reforestation mandate, Provincial Law 10,467). Benefits: 18 organizations (8 poultry + 10 horticultural) in this phase produce with digital traceability and participatory agroecological certification. Organizations access specific markets; consumers obtain verifiable agroecological food; provincial forestry programs optimize production. Complete manufacturing in rural FabLab ensures technological sovereignty at USD 1,000/unit vs USD 3,000+ commercial alternatives without equivalent capabilities. Global scalability potential using same methodology.

core_fields.title: CarBIO: A waste-to-energy emissions reduction project for African dairy farmers.
core_fields.description: With approximately 1.3 million dairy farmers in the country contributing to GHG emissions through composting, CarBIO aims to reduce their carbon footprint while improving their waste management practices. Most of these farming households also use biomass fuelled cookstoves, contributing further to GHG emissions and related health effects. With CarBIO, farmers access an enhanced waste management experience, renewable energy, and organic fertilizer, and benefit from the generated carbon credits.
core_fields.abstract: Every day, dairy farmers tend to their cows and clean up after them. They compost over 2 tonnes of waste per animal annually, which releases tonnes of GHG emissions. Furthermore, over 80% of rural households use biomass-based cookstoves, exposing their families to indoor pollution. CarBIO channels carbon financing to address both challenges. Using our waste-to-energy solution, farmers convert animal waste to biogas and bioslurry, reducing GHG emissions and generating carbon credits. CarBIO biogas digesters offer improved thermal efficiency to enhance biogas production. Enabling farmers in cold-climate regions to produce biogas all year round, and even farms with just 2 cows to produce enough biogas for the household energy needs. There are two main competitors in the East African region: Sistema.bio and HomeBiogas. During our market research, to validate our solution, we discovered that a majority of small-holder dairy farmers lacked access to biogas technology, and those who had access complained of decreasing efficiency. For instance, farmers with constructed dome-biogas digesters experienced technical difficulties that reduced biogas production over time, despite the high acquisition costs. With CarBIO, farmers gain access to reliable biogas digesters and renewable energy to cook, light, and power their agricultural products, improving their farm productivity. Access to clean cooking energy further improves household sanitation standards and promotes good health (improved eye and respiratory health). Women and children regain time spent sourcing cooking fuel for work and leisure. Farmers can also access bioslurry to regenerate degraded soil, increase crop yields, and enhance climate resilience.

core_fields.title: Development of a sustainable fish value chain through solar and agro-ecological innovations
core_fields.description: The project consists of setting up an integrated fish production and processing activity in order to improve the availability of quality fish and increase the income of local stakeholders. It covers on the one hand the breeding of fish in controlled and environmentally friendly conditions using a self-cleaning solar aquarium, and on the other hand the processing and conservation of part of the production using petro-solar ovens. This approach makes it possible to limit post-harvest
core_fields.abstract: To respond to the constraints linked to water management and the sustainability of fish farming, Mr. Eug ne ROUAMBA has developed a major agro-ecological innovation: a self-cleaning solar aquarium. This ingenious system incorporates a two-step water recycling process. First, mechanical filtration by brushes retains the solid waste resulting from fish activity, then biological purification by oxygenation allows the digestion of the homogeneous biomass. More than 80% of used water is thus treated and reinjected into the basin, considerably reducing water consumption and operating costs. In a circular economy logic, the raw residues from filtration (fish excrement) are used as compost for the benefit of women doing market gardening, strengthening agriculture-livestock integration. The results of the pilot phases demonstrated a notable improvement in the quality of fish produced and more sustainable management of resources. Currently the promoter has 6 10m3 tanks for 1000 fry which he wishes to deploy on a large scale to satisfy customers. Building on these successes, the project leader now aims to expand the value chain by integrating the fish processing and conservation component, through the use of petroleum-solar ovens. This complementary innovation will reduce post-harvest losses, increase the added value of fishery products and promote local, clean and resilient solutions.
