core_fields.title: Crops To Corner Stores: Transforming Food Access
core_fields.description: Saba Grocers Initiative uproots systemic barriers faced by small corner store owners to bring nutritious produce into urban neighborhoods without a grocery store. These retailers want to feed and nourish their communities instead of selling cigarettes, alcohol and junk food. Saba helps shift corner-store inventory to healthy foods, through wrap-around programming including low volume produce at wholesale price, free delivery and refrigeration. Our goal is to serve 50 corner stores in the next 5 years.
core_fields.abstract: Saba transforms persistent food deserts by changing the systemic conditions that create food access inequality and drive community food insecurity. Our innovation focuses on an overlooked, powerful lever for change: neighborhood corner stores. In Oakland one of the most diverse yet deeply segregated cities in the U.S. racial and economic inequities mean many residents live far from supermarkets and face higher instances of diet-related illness. In West and East Oakland, 30% and 24% of residents, respectively, live below the Federal Poverty Line. The USDA Food Access Atlas indicates many of these households live a half mile to more than a mile from the nearest grocery store. It is projected that half of Oakland s Black and Latinx children will develop diabetes in their lifetime. Corporate consolidation has pushed corner stores out of the supply chain. Pallet-sized order minimums and high transport costs make wholesale produce inaccessible to corner stores, which lack storage, loading docks, or purchasing power. These stores instead rely on shelf-stable, low-nutrition products alcohol, tobacco, and junk food despite community demand for healthier options. Supermarkets avoid these neighborhoods altogether. Saba fills this critical gap, rebuilding an equitable, community-centered food system. We partner with corner stores based on proximity to schools, low-income housing, acceptance of federal nutrition benefits, and distance from supermarkets. Our programming collective produce purchasing, local produce distribution, store transformation, and nutrition incentives immediately benefits consumers, small businesses, and farmers. By restoring affordable, appealing, and trusted access to fresh food, we build long-term resilience in communities historically excluded from the food system.

core_fields.title: Seeding the Future: Tatua Conical School Farms for Nutritious, Sustainable and Equitable Food Systems
core_fields.description: Tatua Conical Farms (Tatua meaning Solve in Swahili) is a school-based innovation that addresses food insecurity, sustainability, and equity in semi-urban communities. The project installs multistorey vertical conical farms in schools to produce nutritious vegetables using minimal land and up to 90% less water. By integrating food production into school feeding and learning, Tatua Conical Farms solve nutrition gaps while building climate-smart, regenerative, and inclusive food systems for the future.
core_fields.abstract: Tatua Conical Farms (Tatua meaning Solve in Swahili) is a school-based food production innovation designed to solve nutrition, land, and water challenges in semi-urban communities. Many schools struggle to provide fresh, nutritious food due to limited land, high food costs, water scarcity, and unreliable supply chains. At the same time, children lack practical exposure to sustainable food systems. Tatua Conical Farms solve this problem by installing multistorey vertical conical farming structures within school compounds. The cone-shaped design allows crops to be grown vertically, producing significantly more food on a small footprint while using up to 90% less water than traditional gardens. The farms are built using locally available, recyclable materials and organic growing media, making them affordable, low-tech, and easy to maintain by teachers and students. This solution is informed by insights from vertical farming, plant spacing efficiency, gravity-fed irrigation, and regenerative soil management. By increasing surface area for planting and reducing water loss, the conical design maximizes yield while staying within planetary boundaries. The immediate benefits include a steady supply of fresh, nutrient-dense vegetables for school meals, reduced food costs, and improved dietary diversity for children. Sustainable benefits include hands-on climate and nutrition education, reduced pressure on land and water resources, lower food miles, and empowered school communities that actively participate in local food systems. Tatua Conical Farms transform schools from food consumers into resilient food producers, benefiting learners, communities, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Jun Chwinqlal, Jun Twitz Tx otx : Maya Midwifery Led Food Systems for Healthy Pregnancy and Resilient Futures
core_fields.description: This project empowers Indigenous Maya midwives to lead community-based food systems that improve pregnancy nutrition and maternal health in rural Guatemala. By reviving ancestral foraging, seed saving, and regenerative food cultivation, midwives provide pregnant women with culturally trusted, nutrient-rich foods that prevent low birth weight and chronic malnutrition. Integrating ancestral Maya knowledge with evidence-based nutrition, the project strengthens food sovereignty, supports healthy pregnancies, and builds resilient, sustainable food systems rooted in Indigenous leadership and community.
core_fields.abstract: This innovation addresses the persistent crisis of maternal malnutrition, low birth weight, and chronic child undernutrition in Indigenous Maya communities in Guatemala. Pregnant women often lack access to affordable, nutritious, and culturally appropriate foods, while ancestral food knowledge and sustainable farming practices have been disrupted by poverty, climate change, and exclusion from formal health and food systems. These challenges directly affect maternal health, infant development, and long-term community well-being. The project solves this problem by positioning Indigenous Maya midwives trusted community health leaders as drivers of localized, regenerative food systems. Midwives are trained to integrate evidence-based maternal nutrition science with ancestral Maya knowledge of foraging, seed saving, food cultivation, and preparation. They lead community food gardens, revive nutrient-dense Indigenous crops, and provide pregnancy-specific nutrition guidance alongside clinical midwifery care through birth centers and mobile clinics. The solution is grounded in scientific evidence showing that maternal dietary diversity and adequate micronutrient intake during pregnancy reduce low birth weight and improve lifelong health outcomes. It is further informed by agroecological science demonstrating that Indigenous polyculture systems increase biodiversity, climate resilience, and soil health. Social science and public health research confirm that culturally trusted providers significantly improve adoption and sustainability of health interventions. Immediate benefits include improved maternal nutrition, healthier birth weights, reduced anemia, and increased access to affordable, nutritious foods. Long-term benefits include strengthened food sovereignty, restored biodiversity, reduced dependence on ultra-processed foods, empowered women leaders, and resilient community food systems that protect both human and planetary health.

core_fields.title: Ending malnutrition for 100 million people by ensuring every meal contains lifesaving nutrients.
core_fields.description: Full bellies aren't enough; everyone needs essential nutrients to grow and stay healthy. Yet, every day around 8,000 children die from micronutrient deficiencies. Sanku tackles this by empowering local millers to sustainably fortify flour equipping them with IoT-enabled Dosifier, which precisely adds critical nutrients into each bag of flour, the nutrient premix needed for fortification as well as ongoing training and maintenance of the Dosifier to guarantee that every meal supports healthy growth and development.
core_fields.abstract: Micronutrient deficiency, also known as hidden hunger, affects one in five Africans, particularly in low-income regions, where diets rely heavily on calorie-dense but nutrient-poor staples such as maize and wheat flour. This deficiency leads to preventable health issues, including impaired cognitive development in children, weakened immunity, increased maternal mortality, and reduced economic productivity. With over 280 million undernourished people in Africa 57 million more since the COVID-19 pandemic micronutrient deficiency is an escalating public health crisis. Food fortification is one of the most effective, safe, and cost-efficient interventions for addressing malnutrition, with nearly a century of proven success. A 2020 review of 50 studies found that fortifying staple foods like maize and wheat flour reduced anemia rates by 34%, neural tube defects by 41%, and vitamin A deficiency for three million children in one year, significantly lowering mortality. However, typical initiatives in Africa often fail to reach the most vulnerable populations and rural poor, who lack access to centrally processed foods. Sanku s innovation addresses this gap by partnering with and empowering small and medium-scale millers in hard-to-reach communities across Eastern Africa. We provide these millers with our IoT-enabled Dosifiers, high-quality nutrient premix that we locally blend in our Nutrient Premix Blending Factory in Tanzania, and offer ongoing training, technical and maintenance support, so that they are able to sustainably and accurately fortify staple flour consumed daily by families. Currently, Sanku is partnering with over 1,500 millers in Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia and reaching 32 million people with nutritious flour daily.

core_fields.title: Heat resilient confectionary fats for chocolate stability in hot climate supply chains
core_fields.description: Our innovation is a plant-based heat-resistant cocoa butter designed to withstand tropical storage and transport conditions of chocolates while remaining affordable. Using Brazil as a model, we will validate thermal stability under realistic logistics scenarios and model cost-efficiency at pilot and early industrial scales. This approach eliminate risk for the buyer in Global South markets. Opening up new source of revenue and reduce chocolate wastage due to melting and access to healthy and sustainable chocolates.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: Traditional cocoa butter melts at moderate temperatures, limiting its use in tropical regions with weak cold-chain infrastructure. High costs and supply chain vulnerabilities prevent equitable access to quality chocolate and fat-based products. Solution: We developed a heat-resistant cocoa butter from locally available and sustainable vegetable oils that maintains texture, melting behavior, and taste under temperatures up to 40 C. Our approach relies on structured lipids without trans-fats or allergens, offering a scalable alternative to conventional cocoa butter. Novelty & Insight: No commercially available fat combines thermal stability, performance, and cost-efficiency for tropical markets. The solution leverages patent-pending lipid structuring-rebuilding the cocoa fat at molecular level, validated in lab-scale trials, with strong evidence from sensory analysis and public blind testing. Benefits: Immediate: Manufacturers can produce chocolate and bakery fillings suitable for hot climates without cold-chain reliance. Sustainable: Reduces dependence on imported or environmentally costly fats. Our fat is 90% less carbon footprint compared to cocoa butter (LCA) Consumer & Community Impact: Affordable, high-quality chocolate and fats increase equitable access in tropical regions. Environmental: Supports climate-resilient supply chains and reduces energy use from refrigeration.

core_fields.description: This project will design, implement, and evaluate participatory models to improve healthy school food environments in rural Argentina. Through a pilot in four rural schools in Misiones province combining one anchor school with three additional schools it will co-design solutions with school communities and local family farmers to integrate fresh, minimally processed local foods into school meals, strengthen nutrition and environmental education, and generate actionable evidence on implementation barriers and facilitators in rural contexts.
core_fields.abstract: Across rural regions in Argentina, school feeding programs continue to rely heavily on ultra-processed foods, despite national policy frameworks that promote healthy school food environments. In recent years, economic and governance changes have weakened public support for food education, local procurement, and family farming, widening the gap between policy commitments and everyday school food practices particularly in rural contexts. This project addresses that gap by testing and refining a participatory, operational model for healthy school food environments in rural settings. Through a pilot in four rural schools in Misiones province, the initiative combines an intensive intervention in one anchor school with comparative learning across three additional schools. Structured co-design processes engage school authorities, educators, families, and local family farmers to integrate fresh, minimally processed local foods into school meals, align menu planning with local production, and incorporate nutrition and environmental education into daily school life. The innovation lies not in creating new policies, but in translating existing food and nutrition policy principles particularly Argentina s Healthy Eating Promotion Law into feasible, context-adapted operational practices. Unlike isolated or short-term interventions, the model integrates food procurement, education, and sustainability practices, such as the valorization of native foods and responsible organic waste management, within routine school operations. Simple monitoring and documentation tools are embedded throughout the pilot to capture costs, barriers, and enabling conditions. This evidence-driven approach generates practical learning on what works, under which conditions, and at what cost, creating a solid foundation for future replication and scale-up in other rural territories.

core_fields.title: AfriScout: Better Grazing for More Resilient Food Systems and a Healthier Planet
core_fields.description: AfriScout is transforming pastoralism in East Africa and driving restoration of 1.3 million hectares of Ethiopian rangeland by blending technology with time-honored Indigenous knowledge and adaptive grazing practices. Across 70 communities, 44,000+ households with a collective herd of over 1.1M animals are participating in the AfriScout Regen Carbon Project, using AfriScout to collectively migrate their livestock in ways that improve herd condition and regenerate the grasslands that are critical to Africa s economy and food security.
core_fields.abstract: Intensive animal agriculture accounts for 14.5% of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, consumes nearly a third of the world s crop calories, and drives deforestation and biodiversity loss at an unprecedented scale, costing the world nearly $1 trillion each year in health, environmental, and social damages. Meanwhile, Africa s vast grasslands vital ecosystems for more sustainable, climate-smart, extensive livestock production are in crisis: 70% are degraded, releasing carbon into the atmosphere, eroding biodiversity, and threatening the livelihoods and food security of hundreds of millions of people. AfriScout s patented platform digitizes Indigenous knowledge in community-defined, remote-sensing derived grazing maps to power Adaptive Multi-Paddock (AMP) grazing, a proven regenerative practice that restores rangelands and can sequester between 1 5 metric tons of CO₂ per hectare annually. AfriScout s digital ecosystem integrating AI, remote sensing, and behavioral nudges optimizes collaborative community grazing plans to help pastoralists manage pasture, grow grass, sequester carbon, and verify outcomes at scale. Participating pastoralists gain real-time pasture intelligence, reducing herd losses, conflict, and costs. A two-year evaluation found 98% adoption of grazing plans, 83% increase in improved pasture, and 57% higher herd value than control groups. AfriScout connects the project to the Voluntary Carbon Market and, as a non-profit social enterprise, returns the majority share of revenue from sale of carbon credits to participating communities then reinvests to scale its impact. AfriScout is a scalable, market-driven innovation delivering measurable environmental, social, and economic returns. This model strengthens food systems, boosts resilience, and positions pastoralists as leaders in the fight against climate change.

core_fields.title: Scaling the World's First Climate-Resilient Tropical Almond Industry in Ghana
core_fields.description: Talmond is pioneering a climate-resilient tropical almond value chain in Ghana, planting 100,000 trees with smallholder farmers across diverse regions. The project produces nutritious, plant-based foods, kernels, flour, and milk, with high protein and alternative protein potential, while promoting sustainable, rain-fed agroforestry that restores soil, protects biodiversity, and saves 13.5 M m of water. By integrating farmer training, industrial processing, and market-ready products, Talmond generates livelihoods, jobs, and scalable, environmentally sustainable impact locally and globally.
core_fields.abstract: Talmond addresses the fragility of the global food system, where only 15 crops provide 90% of human diets, and 60% comes from rice, maize, and wheat. Climate change, land degradation, and water scarcity threaten yields, while Africa s smallholder potential remains largely untapped. The almond industry exemplifies this vulnerability: global production reached 1.7M t in 2024, yet conventional almonds require ~12L of water per kernel and face drought, pollination risks, regulatory pressure, and market volatility. Our innovation revives the underutilised, climate-resilient tropical almond in Ghana. Our scientific R&D evaluated 116 trees and identified 24 elite varieties based on kernel, morphological and sensory traits, the first systematic effort to develop high-yielding tropical almond strains. Nucleus farm trials demonstrated >95% survival under rain-fed conditions, and smallholder outgrowers have planted 51,900 trees across four regions, with pilot school plantings in arid northern Ghana achieving 87% survival. Dynamic agroforestry systems restore soil, protect biodiversity, and diversify income. Sensory studies and application testing ensure consumer acceptability of kernels, flour (54% protein), and oil (palm-oil replacement/cocoa butter enhancer). Industrial cracking solutions enable scalable processing. Immediate benefits include stable incomes for >2,000 farmers, 200 jobs, nutritious plant-based foods with alternative protein potential, and climate adaptation. Sustainable benefits include water savings, soil regeneration, biodiversity protection, and scalable tropical almond production, diversifying the foods we eat, strengthening food-system resilience, and empowering local communities.

core_fields.title: Nutrition Early Warning System (NEWS) for Predictive Food and Health Supply Chains
core_fields.description: The Nutrition Early Warning System (NEWS) develops technical specifications for predicting nutrition supply disruptions 2-4 weeks before they occur in humanitarian settings. NEWS integrates logistics, climate, and health data into offline-capable alert systems, enabling health facilities in crisis-affected regions to prevent stockouts of therapeutic foods. The validated framework guides governments in implementing predictive supply management across low-connectivity environments
core_fields.abstract: The Nutrition Early Warning System (NEWS) develops technical specifications for predicting stockouts of therapeutic and supplementary foods 2-4 weeks before they occur. IFRAD's 2024 needs assessment and 2025 baseline study revealed that ten surveyed health facilities in Uganda experienced stockouts in the preceding 12 months, with facilities in refugee-hosting and underserved regions experiencing the longest disruption durations due to data delays, poor storage, and fragmented digital systems. These disruptions cause prolonged shortages that undermine nutrition outcomes for malnourished children and vulnerable populations. NEWS provides a validated framework for integrating climate forecasting with health supply chain data to enable early warning systems. The technical breakthrough defines how to combine environmental data (seasonal flooding, impassable roads, drought patterns) with logistics tracking from e-LMIS, e-AFYA and health utilization patterns from DHIS2. Unlike commercial predictive logistics systems that rely on consistent connectivity and stable infrastructure, NEWS is designed for offline-first operation and volatile contexts. The framework establishes specifications for prediction mechanisms eg how to forecast that heavy rains in two weeks will make roads impassable, enabling pre-positioning of nutrition commodities. Built on Elrha/FCDO-funded research, the NEWS framework specifies ensemble forecasting approaches (XGBoost for stockout probability, Prophet for seasonal patterns), offline-first architecture requirements, and human validation protocols. These specifications ensure future systems maintain local control over automated predictions, adapting to unpredictable conditions. Immediately, NEWS provides governments and humanitarian actors with validated technical blueprints for designing and implementing predictive alert systems. Long-term benefits include improved supply, reduced wastage from expired commodities, strengthened equity in nutrition access.

core_fields.title: Women-Led Circular Food Solutions for Healthier Communities
core_fields.description: This project will reduce food waste and improve nutrition in Musanze District by turning unsold market produce into affordable, nutritious foods and organic compost. Women and youth groups will manage small processing centers that dry and mill surplus fruits and vegetables into safe, low-cost products for schools and households. The remaining waste will be used for animal feed and compost, creating green jobs, cleaner markets, and better diets through a sustainable circular food system.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation turns daily food waste from Musanze markets into affordable, nutritious foods and compost through a simple, community-led circular model. Every day, traders discard kilos of unsold vegetables and fruits, even though many families nearby cannot afford a balanced diet. The problem comes from poor storage, lack of processing knowledge, and limited market access for fresh produce. According to the Musanze District Nutrition Review (2023), nearly 38% of households experience moderate food insecurity, while over 25% of market produce is wasted weekly. Our solution introduces women-managed mini processing and compost hubs that sort, dry, and process surplus food into vegetable flours, soup mixes, and dried fruit snacks for schools and households. The remaining peelings and scraps are turned into animal feed and organic compost for local farmers. This idea grew from RUYA s youth programs promoting zero waste and nutrition awareness. It combines traditional food preservation (sun drying and milling) with small-scale solar drying and hygienic packaging. The approach reduces waste, creates jobs, and increases access to nutritious, affordable foods. In the long run, it builds a circular local food economy where nothing is wasted and every actor from farmer to consumer benefits.

core_fields.title: Project Aladinn
core_fields.description: Project Aladinn is a digital platform that connects smallholder farmers to buyers, storage facilities, and transport services, helping them reduce post-harvest losses and earn fair prices. Using a network of local youth agents and data-driven tools, the platform aggregates produce, matches supply with demand, and ensures traceability from farm to market. By digitizing rural food trade, Project Aladinn strengthens food security, creates jobs, and builds a more efficient, inclusive, and sustainable food system across Africa.
core_fields.abstract: Across Africa, up to 40% of food produced by smallholder farmers never reaches the market due to poor storage, limited market access, and inefficient logistics. This not only increases food insecurity but also reduces farmer income and contributes to greenhouse gas emissions from wasted produce. Project Aladinn is a digital innovation that tackles this challenge by connecting smallholder farmers to buyers, storage, and transportation through a single, user-friendly platform. Using mobile technology and a network of trained local youth agents, the platform aggregates farm produce, enables real-time price visibility, and links farmers directly to verified markets. The insight behind this innovation came from observing how decentralized digital systems in other sectors. like ride-hailing and delivery, improved efficiency and transparency. We applied this model to agriculture, integrating logistics, market intelligence, and payment systems to streamline the movement of food from farms to consumers. Through this approach, farmers earn better prices, buyers access quality produce, and food waste is significantly reduced. The platform also collects data to inform production planning and demand forecasting, further strengthening local food systems. Immediate benefits include increased farmer income, job creation for rural youth, and reduced post-harvest losses. Sustainable benefits include improved food security, lower carbon emissions from waste reduction, and a more resilient and inclusive food supply chain. Project Aladinn demonstrates how technology and community-driven innovation can build a future where no harvest is lost, and every farmer thrives.

core_fields.title: Program to safeguard animal genetic resorces of endemic cattle breeds of the Galapagos Islands
core_fields.description: For nearly four centuries, Cimarr n cattle have survived in the Gal pagos, adapting to extreme dryness, saltwater consumption, and parasites. This project seeks to preserve their unique genetics, confirming their endemic heritage and contributing to climate resilience and food security. Supported by AGROCALIDAD and FAO, the initiative will domesticate and study feral calves, compares genetics with local herds, and develops a gene bank to strengthen Ecuador s sustainable livestock systems and protect its exceptional animal genetic diversity.
core_fields.abstract: Gal pagos Islands face a food security crisis. According to the Plan Galapagos 2023, the islands receive 64% of their food supply from mainland. During the summer of 2023, the food supply dropped by 60% due to disrupted cargo shipments. Unsustainable tourism and demographic pressure led to exorbitant food prices, and price speculation, making produce unaffordable for locals. This project emphasizes local livestock production and consumption, offering socially, environmentally, and economically viable strategies. Diversifying the economy away from tourism is essential for the archipelago s resilience. The Cimarron cattle possess a unique genetic profile, adapted to arid environments, with global potential for livestock conservation and sustainable breeding practices. Currently, we have research results that demonstrate the high capacity of its adaptability to Galapagos environmental conditions. We found that their physiological constants and hematological values have not varied from the constants of the species for the most part. But we have observed that creatinine and alkaline phosphatase levels do differ from their congeners from other islands. Establishing a new gene bank aims to grant national cattle ranches access to this invaluable genetic material, enhancing livestock breeds with adaptable traits for arid regions. This groundbreaking research has far-reaching implications for global livestock conservation. By prioritising local livestock production, this initiative aims to secure a sustainable food supply for the Galapagos Islands, preserving their unique ecosystem and benefiting communities. Promoting local cattle products offers a solution to the food security crisis, reducing dependency on imports, and fostering a self-sustaining economy.

core_fields.title: Sustainable Cooking Education for Food Security and Climate Action
core_fields.description: The project Sustainable Cooking Education for Food Security and Climate Action creates a community-based learning space in Santo Domingo, Ecuador. It teaches families, especially women, to prepare nutritious, affordable, and local meals using sustainable practices that reduce food waste and environmental impact. Through hands-on training and communication campaigns, it strengthens food security, empowers vulnerable groups, and promotes a culture of sustainable and regenerative cooking.
core_fields.abstract: Ecuador faces increasing food insecurity currently the third country in Latin America most affected by hunger as families struggle with high food prices, limited access to healthy meals, and the loss of traditional culinary knowledge. At the same time, large amounts of food are wasted daily, contributing to environmental degradation and greenhouse gas emissions. The Sustainable Cooking Education for Food Security and Climate Action project introduces an innovative, community-based educational model called Green School , where participants learn practical, science-based methods to prepare nutritious, affordable, and climate-friendly meals using local ingredients. The innovation lies in connecting nutrition education, circular economy, and environmental awareness through participatory cooking sessions that transform kitchens into learning spaces for sustainable behavior. By integrating knowledge from nutrition science, environmental education, and community empowerment, the project demonstrates that simple changes in how food is selected, prepared, and reused can significantly reduce waste, improve nutrition, and generate local income. Immediate benefits include improved family nutrition, reduced household food waste, and empowerment of women as agents of change. In the long term, the initiative will contribute to healthier diets, stronger local food systems, and reduced environmental impact fostering a replicable model that connects food security with climate action and social inclusion in Ecuador and beyond.

core_fields.title: Samoa Regenerative Farming Project
core_fields.description: Over 70% of Samoa's population is overweight, and nearly half are obese. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) cause about 80% of deaths and could cost 8.5% of GDP by 2040. Diets have shifted from traditional foods to processed imports. Mercy Ships Australia's regenerative farming project in remote Samoa aims to tackle obesity and NCDs by promoting sustainable farming and healthier diets through collaboration with government agencies and the UNDP, addressing both public health and environmental challenges.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation aims to address two major challenges in Samoa the rising burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) caused by poor dietary habits and the heavy reliance on chemical fertilizers and pesticides in farming. The project introduces a digital platform and mobile app that will train and support local farmers in smart regenerative farming practices, providing them with real-time weather updates, soil data through sensors, and practical guidance on crop diversification, pest management, and sustainable techniques. This platform will also include educational materials to help Samoan communities make healthier dietary choices, reconnecting them with traditional, nutrient-rich foods and reducing dependence on imported processed foods. Currently, there are no locally tailored digital solutions to support these goals. Scientific and health studies including the 2021 Food Systems Summit Dialogue and WHO reports highlight that over 70% of Samoa's population is overweight, with NCDs causing around 80% of deaths. This innovation directly addresses those health and environmental risks by linking sustainable regenerative farming to nutrition awareness. Immediate benefits include improved farmer knowledge, increased access to healthy local foods, and a stronger local food economy. Long-term benefits include reduced healthcare costs, greater food security, and environmental sustainability. The project will also promote gender inclusion by supporting women-led farming groups and contribute to climate resilience through the introduction of climate-smart crops. Ultimately, this innovation empowers Samoan farmers and families with the knowledge, tools, and technology needed to create a healthier and more sustainable future.

core_fields.title: Sustainable Value Addition and Market Linkages for Tanzanian Spices and Dried Fruits
core_fields.description: This project empowers smallholder farmers in Morogoro, Tanga, and Pwani to produce high-quality spices and dried fruits through regenerative farming, improved post-harvest handling, and value addition. By establishing solar-powered processing hubs, certification systems, and export linkages, the project reduces waste, increases incomes, and promotes sustainable livelihoods for women and youth, positioning Tanzania as a trusted source of premium natural ingredients for local and international markets.
core_fields.abstract: Tanzania's spice and fruit farmers face high post-harvest losses, low market prices, and limited access to value-adding technologies. Much of their produce is sold raw, while profits are captured by exporters and processors abroad. This project introduces an innovative, regenerative sourcing and processing model that integrates solar-biomass hybrid drying, traceability, and circular waste utilization to transform how farmers grow, process, and market their products. The innovation combines clean-energy drying systems with local aggregation hubs and a digital traceability platform that ensures quality and transparency from farm to market. Farmers are trained in regenerative agriculture using composting, intercropping, and organic pest management to improve soil health, increase yields, and enhance climate resilience. By-products such as pineapple peels and spice residues are converted into animal feed, biogas, or essential oils, minimizing waste and adding new income streams. Scientifically, the approach is based on combining renewable energy technologies with circular economy principles and agroecological practices. Technically, the solar-biomass hybrid dryers ensure consistent product quality while cutting post-harvest losses by up to 40%. Immediate benefits include higher farm-gate prices, reduced losses, better product quality, and new local jobs, especially for women and youth in processing and packaging. Long-term benefits include improved soil fertility, lower carbon emissions, diversified rural economies, and stronger competitiveness of Tanzanian spices and fruits in global markets. This integrated innovation turns smallholder farmers into key actors in a sustainable, inclusive, and climate-smart food system.

core_fields.title: TRANSFORMING EDIBLE WEEDS INTO SUSTAINABLE SOLUTIONS FOR FOOD AND NUTRITION SECURITY-WEEDIBLE PROJECT
core_fields.description: Project WEEDIBLE transforms underutilized edible weeds into sustainable, nutritious, and market-ready foods and feeds, enhancing food and nutrition security in vulnerable communities along the Lake Victoria Basin. WEEDIBLE will scale production, processing, and community adoption and uptake, combining traditional knowledge with innovative techniques. By promoting regenerative agriculture, inclusive supply chains, and value-added products, the project delivers affordable, safe, nutrient-dense foods while creating economic opportunities and climate-smart, replicable solutions for resilient and equitable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Communities along the Lake Victoria Basin suffer from undernutrition and hidden hunger brought by climate related crop and livestock losses leading to lack of dietary diversification and consumption of poor-quality diets (Korir et al., 2022). The vulnerable groups include pregnant and lactating mothers, infants, old and the adolescents from low-income households. Anaemia prevalence stands at 45.5% among children under five and above 50% in pregnant and lactating women, with iron deficiency as the leading cause. This has led to poor maternal outcomes; low birth weight and heightened risk of eclampsia, while in children it has been associated with delayed cognitive and motor development, impaired growth, and increased infection risk. At the same time, smallholder farmers, youth and women, face limited economic opportunities, high production costs, and insufficient access to markets coupled with effects of climate change, while underutilized nutrient-rich edible weeds, traditionally used as food, are often destroyed or ignored, representing a lost resource for food, feed, and income. Project WEEDIBLE proposes transforming edible weeds into safe, market-ready food and feed products using modern processing technologies. Species such as Amaranth, Blackjack, Purslane, Basella alba, and Corchorus olitorius are rich in vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, and phytonutrients, supporting dietary diversification and reducing micronutrient deficiencies. Their fast growth, minimal input needs, and soil protection benefits make them suitable for regenerative, climate-smart farming. By engaging youth, women, and smallholder farmers, the initiative will expand income opportunities, improve community health outcomes, reduce waste through circular production, and contribute to resilient, inclusive, and sustainable food systems.

core_fields.title: Climate Smart Agriculture and Early Warning Innovation for Resilient Food System in Northern Zambia.
core_fields.description: This project scales SEPA s Climate-Smart Agriculture and Early Warning Network (CSAEWN), which integrates solar-powered irrigation, organic farming, and mobile weather advisory services for smallholder women farmers in Northwestern Zambia. It addresses recurring droughts, soil degradation, and low yields that threaten food security. By improving access to water, timely climate information, and resilient farming practices, the innovation enables year-round production of safe, nutritious food while restoring ecosystems and increasing incomes for rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: Save Environment and People Agency (SEPA) have developed the Climate-Smart Agriculture and Early Warning Network (CSAEWN), an integrated solution that empowers smallholder farmers, especially women, to adapt to climate change and achieve year-round food security. Rural farmers in Northwestern Zambia face erratic rainfall, prolonged dry seasons, and degraded soils that limit crop productivity. Most rely on rain-fed farming and lack access to timely weather information or irrigation technologies, leading to frequent crop losses, hunger, and unstable incomes. The CSAEWN innovation combines solar-powered irrigation, regenerative organic farming, and a mobile-based early warning system. Solar irrigation enables continuous food production using renewable energy. Regenerative practices such as composting, crop rotation, and agroforestry restore soil fertility and biodiversity while reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers. The mobile system delivers localized weather forecasts, pest alerts, and market prices through SMS and WhatsApp in local languages, allowing farmers to make informed decisions. The innovation is guided by scientific and technical insights that integrate clean energy, local meteorological data, and indigenous knowledge to create a practical, low-cost, and inclusive approach. This innovation delivers immediate benefits by improving crop yields, food availability, and household incomes. Sustainable benefits include increased resilience to climate shocks, enhanced nutrition, empowerment of women farmers, and reduced environmental degradation. Communities become more self-reliant and capable of sustaining healthy ecosystems while ensuring equitable access to nutritious food and clean energy.

core_fields.title: Egg4Life: Promoting Local Egg Recipes for Nutrition and Market Sustainability
core_fields.description: This project encourages the consumption of eggs in local African diets by creating and delivering the culturally appropriate egg recipes that not only enrich household nutrition but also prevent the occurrence of egg market gluts. The project will give women and youth the freedom to start egg-based consumption and businesses which will raises dietary diversity, lessens the post-production waste, and consumers for a sustainable food system
core_fields.abstract: The project unfolds a culturally grounded food innovation that addresses protein malnutrition and the unstable egg market in African communities. Eggs are one of the most affordable and nutrient-dense foods, yet their consumption is very low due to the limited recipe diversity, cultural eating habits, and lack of awareness of their nutritional value. Meanwhile, poultry farmers are faced with egg gluts that result in waste and losses of income during oversupply periods. These gaps are closed by facilitating the consumption of eggs in the local diets through the joint creation and recording of both traditional and modern egg recipes that are not only in line with the local tastes but also with the cooking practices. The innovation uses knowledge from food science and community nutrition that increasing cultural relevance and culinary variety of healthy foods results in sustained dietary adoption. It also uses behavioral change research that advocates practical, hands-on training as more effective in changing eating long term cultural food habit. Women, youth, and community caterers get training through which they acquire the skills of preparing, marketing, and selling affordable egg-based dishes. This strategy co-exists with the nutrition enhancement aspect and the creation of local enterprises that stabilize poultry markets and reduce food waste is another aspect of it. This project will offers immediate advantages through better diets and livelihoods, and its long-term sustainability is ensured by the formation of a culture of egg-based nutrition and the attendant transformation of the food system.

core_fields.title: NDALO AGRIHUB SMART FARMER MODEL
core_fields.description: This project strengthens nutrition, incomes, soil health, and climate resilience in rural Western Kenya by supporting 2,000+ smallholder farmers to grow nutrient-dense, climate-smart, culturally accepted rotational crops and linking them to local processing. Building on our proof of concept, we improve the accessibility, availability, and affordability of nutritious products for school-going children and adult women facing heightened micronutrient needs. Activities include training farmers in regenerative organic farming, food-to-food fortification, and commercialization for sustainable impact.
core_fields.abstract: Siaya County faces a severe nutrition and health crisis: one in four children is stunted, under-five mortality is nearly three times the national average, and 29% of women suffer from iron-deficiency anaemia. Many children arrive at school hungry and depend on a single daily meal of low-nutrient maize porridge. At the same time, climate shocks and soil degradation reduce food quality and farmer incomes, disproportionately affecting women, who make up 66% of smallholder farmers. This makes the problem urgent and highly relevant. Our innovation solves this by linking regenerative organic agriculture, food-to-food fortification, and a circular local food economy. Guided by the principle Feed the Soil to Feed the Future, farmers restore soil fertility using composting, mulching, legumes, and biochar. Nutrient-dense crops are then processed locally into affordable fortified foods, ensuring that nutrients are retained, accessible, and culturally accepted. The solution is informed by our scientific insights showing that beta-carotene and organic acids in indigenous plant foods (our regenerative rotational crops) enhance mineral bioaccessibility by keeping iron and zinc in soluble forms. Proof-of-concept trials using in vitro mineral dialysability assays showed that fortifying sorghum porridge with these plant foods increased bioaccessible iron by up to 469% and zinc by over 80%, meeting CODEX effectiveness standards. Immediate benefits include improved nutrition for children and women, affordable fortified foods for schools and households, and higher incomes for farmers. Long-term benefits include healthier soils, greater climate resilience, stronger local food systems, and sustained reductions in micronutrient malnutrition benefiting communities, producers, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Proving efficacy for autonomous disease detection in aquaculture
core_fields.description: Our project pilots an autonomous biosensor with Pacific Seafood and Blue Ocean Mariculture to detect viral diseases in aquaculture before outbreaks occur. The system performs real-time DNA analysis directly in the water, eliminating lab delays and human sampling. These pilots will validate the technology s accuracy, optimize sampling rates, and generate data to refine a Beta version for commercialization advancing early pathogen detection, biosecurity, and sustainability in aquaculture.
core_fields.abstract: Aquaculture producers face costly and frequent losses from viral and microbial disease outbreaks that spread rapidly through water. Current monitoring relies on manual sampling and lab testing, which can take days or weeks too late to prevent major stock losses. Nucleic Sensing Systems (NS2) has developed an autonomous biosensor that detects and quantifies environmental DNA and RNA directly in the water. This innovation combines droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) and advanced microfluidics to perform precise genetic analysis on-site, without human intervention or lab processing. The system continuously scans water for pathogen genetic material and transmits results in real time, enabling farmers and aquaculture managers to identify emerging threats before fish or shellfish show symptoms. The solution emerged from NS2 s breakthroughs in real-time molecular detection and aerosol biosecurity monitoring, adapted for aquatic environments. By miniaturizing and automating PCR chemistry, the system brings laboratory-grade diagnostics directly to the field or farm. Immediate benefits include early disease detection, reduced stock mortality, and fewer emergency chemical or antibiotic treatments. Sustainable impacts extend to improved food security, environmental health, and resilience across aquaculture and agriculture systems. For producers like Pacific Seafood and Blue Ocean Mariculture, this technology provides continuous, data-driven biosecurity and helps ensure a stable, sustainable seafood supply.

core_fields.title: Towards Healthier Diets with Orange Fleshed Sweet Potatoes (OFSP) in Kilifi County, Kenya
core_fields.description: Vitamin A deficiency remains a significant public health challenge, particularly affecting children under five and pregnant and lactating women in Kenya. This deficiency contributes to impaired vision, weakened immunity, increased risk of illnesses and mortality rate. ChildFund Kenya has promoted the cultivation and consumption of Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) in Kenya. OFSP is a proven, cost-effective food-based solution to address micronutrient deficiencies.
core_fields.abstract: OFSP solution is mainly addressing two main problems. One is micronutrient deficiency (hidden hunger) in form of Vitamin A deficiency. Vitamin A deficiency is affecting 17.4% of all children in Kenya. Kilifi County has the highest number of stunted children in Kenya, with one in every three children affected, and with one in five under-5 children being underweight. Of the 1550 ECDE centers in the county, only 110 have a feeding program. This issue is relevant because it leads to preventable illness and deaths, poor child development, and weakened productivity in society. The second problem OFSP is addressing is poor dietary diversity among vulnerable populations. Diets in many arid areas are often monotonous and heavily reliant on staple grains with limited nutritional value. Kilifi county has low food diversity score with 66% of children not having access to least 4 food groups. The solution works by increasing access to OFSP planting materials, training farmers in improved agronomic practices, and teaching households how to prepare nutritious OFSP-based foods. Its success is grounded in scientific understanding that biofortified crops significantly improve micronutrient intake without changing eating habits or increasing food costs. Promoting cultivation and utilization of orange fleshed sweet potatoes has improved household nutrition, especially for mothers and children, enhanced food security for households and communities, contributed to income generation for farmers by selling surplus produce, access to nutrient rich additions to school meals for schools, increased gender equality by support women to participate in the value chain and environmentally friendly production.

core_fields.title: Scaling Solar-Powered Agri-Hubs to Eliminate Post-Harvest Loss and Strengthen Food Security in East Africa.
core_fields.description: Global South builds solar-powered Agri-Hubs that eliminate post-harvest losses, increase smallholder farmers incomes fourfold, and ensure year-round access to safe, nutritious potatoes for institutional buyers. By combining regenerative agriculture, decentralized cold storage, and guaranteed off-take agreements, the model strengthens food security, stabilizes prices, and reduces emissions. The Grand Prize will accelerate the construction of two Agri-Hubs in Kenya, enabling rapid scale-up to 550 farmers and a climate-positive, resilient food system.
core_fields.abstract: Africa loses 30 40% of its harvested food because smallholder farmers lack proper storage, quality seed, and reliable markets. In Kenya s potato sector - an essential staple for millions - yields remain at 7 10 t/ha despite a potential of 30 40 t/ha, and annual supply shortages exceed 900,000 tons. These structural challenges fuel food insecurity, unstable prices, and rural poverty, making the problem urgent and highly relevant. Global South addresses this through an integrated model combining solar-powered cold storage, regenerative agriculture, and guaranteed market access. Decentralized Agri-Hubs near farms reduce post-harvest losses from ~40% to below 5% while operating entirely on renewable energy. Farmers receive certified seed, input credit, regenerative training, and agronomist support, significantly boosting yields and climate resilience. Guaranteed off-take agreements stabilize incomes and ensure processors receive consistent, high-quality supply year-round. The approach is novel because, while cold storage or outgrower programs exist independently in East Africa, no solution integrates renewable-energy cold storage, regenerative production, digital monitoring, and long-term buyer contracts into a single, affordable system tailored for smallholders. Scientific insights inform the model: controlled-temperature storage preserves nutritional quality for months; soil science shows regenerative practices improve productivity and water retention; IoT sensors optimize storage conditions; and drone imaging enhances field-level precision. Immediate benefits include 4 higher farmer incomes, reduced food loss, and more reliable, safer food for consumers and schools. Long-term benefits include lower emissions, healthier soils, reduced chemical inputs, improved rural livelihoods, and a scalable, climate-positive food system capable of transforming regional supply chains.

core_fields.title: SafeMarketMap (SMM App)
core_fields.description: SafeMarketMap target youth and women to form cooperatives or groups that supply informal markets with traceable, lab-verified safe produce. The project fills the knowledge gaps in primary production of safe fresh food and drive demand through massive consumer awareness campaign on health and environmental implications related to chemical overuse. It reduces post-harvest losses through aggregation hubs and builds consumer trust through verified market points, making safe and nutritious food affordable and available for communities.
core_fields.abstract: SafeMarketMap addresses the critical gap in food safety, traceability and hygiene assurance in Africa s informal fresh-food markets, where most households and schools source food daily without knowing whether it is chemically safe or free from contamination. Studies show that informal markets handle over 80% of fresh produce in Sub-Saharan Africa and often contain pesticide residues exceeding recommended Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) (FAO & WHO, 2019; Okonya & Kroschel, 2016). Produce rejected from export chains due to high residues frequently enters domestic markets, increasing food-borne disease risks, chronic chemical exposure and post-harvest losses (Hollinger & Staatz, 2015). These challenges disproportionately affect women and children, weakening public health, market trust and farmer incomes (Grace, 2015). SafeMarketMap responds by organizing youth- and women-led cooperatives that aggregate and supply traceable, lab-verified produce and its AI platform uses geospatial machine learning to map market access points, scores markets and vendor hygiene through structured field inspections and tracks produce batches via offline-first QR codes. Consumers can verify origin and laboratory MRL results through smartphone scans. This approach is supported by evidence that food safety improves when agronomic data, storage conditions and hygiene indicators are combined with digital traceability and periodic lab testing (Akatwijuka et al., 2020; Kibret & Abera, 2012). Benefits include safer food for households and schools, reduced spoilage from decentralized cold-chain storage and stronger market access. Long-term benefits include increased cooperative incomes, youth agribusiness employment, reduced chemical exposure, lower food waste and strengthened trust in informal market systems, supporting healthier communities and ecosystems (HLPE,2020)

core_fields.title: Towards Aflatoxin-Free Foods In Refugees: Validating Sodium Metabisulphite Sheets in Storage to Eliminate Aflatoxins (Afla-SHIELD)
core_fields.description: Afla-SHIELD builds on our recent breakthrough (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodcont.2025.111797 showing that sodium metabisulphite sheets reduces aflatoxins in stored cassava to undetectable levels. Afla-SHIELD will validate the technology in maize and peanut-high-risk staples largely consumed by 90% of Refugees in Nakivale Settlement, and examine any sensory changes after treatment. We will run small household trials in 111 homes across the three administrative units assessing fungal and toxin reduction, sensory quality, and acceptability through See-and-Do Farmer Field Schools approach.
core_fields.abstract: Aflatoxins are among the most dangerous foodborne toxins globally, responsible for up to 40% of liver cancer cases in high-exposure regions (WHO, 2018) and strongly linked to childhood stunting, immune suppression, and impaired development. In Uganda, the Uganda Cancer Institute reports 34,008 new cancer cases annually, with an estimated 40% associated with contaminated foods, particularly peanuts and maize (UCI, 2024). Recent work shows up to 76% of maize and peanut samples exceeding the East African limit of 10 g/kg (Murokore et al., 2024). Refugees depend heavily on WFP food aid and local purchases, receiving maize flour as a core ration and often buying groundnuts as their main protein source. In Nakivale Refugee Settlement-one of Uganda's oldest and largest, hosting over 170,000 refugees-families rely daily on these staples, yet store them in hot, humid, poorly ventilated shelters that favour Aspergillus growth that produces aflatoxins. Conventional controls (drying, sorting, hermetic storage) often fail under labour-intensive, resource-limited conditions. Our recent breakthrough (Oyesigye et al., 2025) showed that sodium metabisulphite sheets (NaMBS) can reduce aflatoxins in cassava to undetectable levels. The sheets release a safe, food-grade sulphur dioxide vapour that suppresses fungal growth and blocks toxin formation, requiring no electricity, equipment, or extra labour-ideal for humanitarian settings. Afla-SHIELD will adapt and validate this innovation to highly aflatoxin prone food crops (maize and peanuts) through real-life trials in 112 households. This project will deliver a community-validated, scalable, low-cost solution that safeguards food, reduces disease burden, strengthens nutrition, with a strong potential for economic scale-up.

core_fields.title: Solar AI Powered Pest Detection and Climate Smart Crop Monitoring for Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: AgroGuard is an AI driven crop protection and farm monitoring platform that helps smallholder farmers detect pests early, prevent losses, and improve yields by monitoring soil nutrient, water level fire out . It uses image based diagnostics, weather insights, and simple actionable alerts delivered through mobile devices. By combining local data with machine learning, AgroGuard reduces crop damage, boosts food production, and strengthens climate resilience for farmers who currently rely on guesswork or delayed manual
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers lose up to 40% of their crops each year due to pests, diseases, and unpredictable weather. Most lack access to agronomists, reliable diagnostics, or timely information that could help them act early. This leads to lower yields, wasted resources, and increased vulnerability to climate change. AgroGuard addresses this by using AI and mobile-based farm monitoring to deliver fast, accurate pest detection and clear action steps. Farmers take a photo of affected crops, and the system analyzes symptoms using a trained machine-learning model built on local datasets. The platform also integrates weather forecasts, soil conditions, and crop-specific risk alerts, helping farmers understand what is happening on their farms and what to do next. The solution grew from field research showing that farmers recognize symptoms late, rely on costly pesticides, and often over-apply chemicals due to uncertainty. AgroGuard reduces this guesswork by providing simple, data backed guidance in local languages. Immediate benefits include reduced crop losses, lower chemical use, and improved decision-making. Sustainable benefits include increased productivity, higher incomes, and better resilience to climate change. Communities benefit from safer food, reduced environmental impact, and improved livelihoods. The platform supports farmers, cooperatives, schools with gardens, producer groups, and rural extension workers.

core_fields.title: Rematriating Indigenous Seeds and Foods in Lenapehoking and Lumbeeland
core_fields.description: Indigenous communities of Delaware/Lenapehoking (the Nanticoke) and southeastern North Carolina (the Lumbee) are challenging corporatized U.S. food systems that have made fresh, healthy, local ingredients inaccessible. The seeds saved by our ancestors are resilient, sustainable, culturally relevant, and highly productive. But to reclaim our food system, we have to know we are growing the right seeds. Our partnership creates a method to recover our communities' ancestral crops and restore our food sovereignty.
core_fields.abstract: Seeds are nature's innovation, ancient technologies that repair harms of an extractive, destructive food system. Access to ancestral seeds, cultivated and adapted over generations by Indigenous communities, supports healthier ecosystems and people. "The seed knows this area and knows what it needs to do," says team member, farmer, and researcher Millard Locklear (Lumbee). He reminds us that seeds are locally specific, regionally adapted technologies, wise beings and tools, foundational to resilient and culturally grounded foodways. Our team has already identified ancestral seeds from our communities. We are growing them, saving them, and sharing seeds and harvests with our people. The results are transformative. Reconnecting with culturally meaningful crops in stories like the Three Sisters has brought us together in gardens and around tables. We belong to and actively collaborate with the Nanticoke Indian Tribe of Delaware and the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina. Bringing our two communities together, despite distance and difference, is an innovation: learning from each other and leveraging our work. The partnership's strength is its reciprocal structure, modeled on ancestral seeds designed to strengthen each other. In that spirit, each Tribal partner enhances the knowledge and reach of the others through shared research, seeds, and community practices. Seedkeeping offers a pathway for BIPOC communities to reconnect with foods that carry cultural memory and place-based knowledge. This work supports physical, mental, and spiritual wellbeing while transforming food systems. By bringing ancestral crops back, seedkeeping reduces hunger, restores land relationships, and creates meaningful economic opportunities for growers and farmers.

core_fields.title: Maendeleo Arusha: African Regenerative Farming
core_fields.description: Maendeleo Arusha: African Regenerative Farming is a 30-month intervention implemented by AKF and Beegreen in Arusha, Tanzania. The project aligns with AKF s broader Maendeleo program, an initiative that promotes regenerative farming for smallholder farmers (SHFs). Building on this, AKF and Beegreen will train stingless beekeeper SHFs on regenerative farming and pollinator management. The project will also expand SHFs access to markets and promote their products, strengthening climate-resilient livelihoods, biodiversity, and sustainable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: In Arusha, 39% of the population is facing food insecurity, with 36% of children under five experiencing stunting because of severe undernutrition (Molina et al., 2020; Kejo et al., 2018). Key drivers of this include climate change, crop pests, and disease, which have resulted in over USD 200 million per year in national agricultural losses (Farm Africa, 2024). Conventional farming, particularly the use of synthetic pesticides, is also degrading soils, harming beneficial insects, and reducing agrobiodiversity (Munishi et al., 2021; Santaliestra, 2021). The combination of regenerative farming and stingless beekeeping (meliponiculture) emerge as an innovative solution to these challenges, restoring soil health, enhancing crop quality, and strengthening biodiversity. Meliponiculture also serves as a sustainable pollination solution since it is limits ecological risk and has lower management demands than apiculture. However, meliponiculture remains underutilized in agricultural systems because it is primarily seen as a forest-based practice in northern Tanzania. Likewise, limited access to practical guidance on regenerative farming continues to act as a barrier to its adoption by SHFs. Maendeleo: Arusha addresses these gaps by delivering regenerative farming training in a simplified, accessible format, while integrating meliponiculture into farming systems to promote poverty reduction, ecosystem restoration, and food system transformation. The project strengthens value chains for nutrient-rich crops (including indigenous vegetables, coffee, mangoes, passionfruit, and beans), enhances market access for SHFs, and expands consumer awareness of sustainably produced foods. Together, these interventions will increase the availability of nutritious, affordable foods, improve livelihoods, and support long-term ecological and economic resilience across Arusha.

core_fields.title: Eco-Harvest: Scaling Regenerative Practices to Ensure Equitable Access to Nutrient-Rich Foods
core_fields.description: Eco-Harvest will prototype a decentralized, community-owned system utilizing regenerative practices, and renewable resilient energy system low-cost smart cold storage. We aim to validate that this integrated model can simultaneously restore soil health, drastically cut post-harvest food loss, and ensure equitable access to high-quality, nutrient-rich foods. This project builds the critical proof-of-concept needed for scaling a truly resilient and sustainable local food economy.
core_fields.abstract: The Problem: Global smallholder communities face a devastating synergy of issues: conventional farming degrades soil and climate resilience, while inefficient, distant supply chains cause high levels of post-harvest loss and inflated food costs. This prevents vulnerable populations from accessing affordable, nutrient-rich foods that improve their health . The Solution (Eco-Harvest Prototype): Our innovation is the Community-Owned Regenerative Hub (CORH) model a novel, integrated socio-technical solution. The core scientific insight is combining microbial soil ecology (through tailored regenerative practices) to maximize crop nutrition and resilience, with smart, decentralized renewable energy cold storage technology to halt spoilage immediately at the source. This creates a hyper-local, short-loop system . Benefits (Seed Grant Validation Focus): The Seed Grant funds are critical to prototype and test this integration in a real-world setting. We will demonstrate that the CORH model can achieve three simultaneous benefits: 1) Restore soil health and enhance climate adaptation (Sustainability), 2) Dramatically reduce post-harvest waste (Waste Reduction), and 3) Provide a validated, low-cost platform to ensure equitable access to high-quality food, laying the groundwork for a scalable, self-sustaining model that benefits farmers, communities and producers.

core_fields.title: Upcycling Agro-Industrial Byproducts into Low-Cost Nutrients for Sustainable Protein Production
core_fields.description: The fungus Trichoderma reesei is a well-established model for agro-industrial waste valorization. We validated upcycling of lupin by-products as a low-cost carbon source for recombinant protein production in P. pastoris. Pilot-scale upcycled fermentations produced key proteins for cultivated meat, including myoglobin and growth factors. Next, we will scale T. reesei cultures, perform life cycle assessment, and validate the full supply demand chain for sustainable implementation to enable industrial scalability, economic feasibility, and measurable environmental impact.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation addresses a major bottleneck for the industrialization of cultivated-meat: the high cost and limited sustainability of growth media components, especially carbon sources and recombinant growth factors. These inputs account for a significant share of production expenses and environmental impacts, limiting the scalability and affordability of new protein solutions. We propose a biotechnological route that upcycles agro-industrial lupin by-products into low-cost nutrients using Trichoderma reesei, a well-established cellulolytic microorganism. Through this process, residues that are often underused or discarded are converted into a fermentable nutrient source capable of supporting high-density Pichia pastoris cultures. This yeast is widely used to produce recombinant proteins, and we have validated this method to produce growth-factor variants for cell-culture media in the cultivated-meat sector. The scientific insight enabling this solution lies in combining two validated strengths: (1) the ability of T. reesei to efficiently valorize lignocellulosic materials, and (2) the robustness of P. pastoris as a recombinant protein producer. Pilot-scale experiments confirmed that lupin residues can sustain productive fermentations, reducing reliance on expensive refined sugars and imported inputs. Additionally, we are validating the supply demand chain to ensure that lupin by-products can be consistently sourced, enhancing regional bioeconomy resilience. This innovation provides immediate benefits to producers, lowering media costs and enabling local, circular supply chains, and long-term benefits to farmers and communities by creating new value streams from existing crops. For consumers and society, it supports more sustainable, affordable alternative proteins with reduced environmental footprints, contributing to healthier diets and more resilient food systems.

core_fields.title: Healthy Farmers, Thriving Cooperatives, Strong Supply Chains
core_fields.description: Elucid will partner with Ghanaian Fairtrade cocoa cooperatives to provide comprehensive health coverage for 1,000 farming households (~5,000 people). We enroll families in NHIS and add gap-filling coverage for essential, maternal, and emergency care reducing catastrophic spending that drives distress sales, child labor, and productivity loss. Year 1 is grant-funded; Year 2 transitions to Fairtrade Premium + buyer co-financing, creating a scalable cooperative-led model.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: In Ghana, the world's second-largest cocoa producer, farmers face numerous challenges. High healthcare costs push 250,000+ Ghanaians into extreme poverty annually. Though Ghana's National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) exists, most rural farmers lack active membership due to enrollment barriers and coverage gaps. When families face health crises, catastrophic expenses force impossible choices: treatment or food, care or harvest. This destabilizes cooperatives, weakens supply chains, and drives households toward child labor and environmental degradation. Scientific evidence is clear: illness reduces household productivity by up to 20%, healthcare costs decrease farm investment by up to 40%. Sustainable supply chains depend on healthy, financially stable farmers. Solution: Elucid provides a managed healthcare package that includes: End-to-end NHIS enrollment and renewal; Additional coverage that fills key gaps in essential, emergency and maternal care; Targeted health facility upgrades; Data collection to support supply chain due diligence. Innovation: Instead of treating healthcare as a one-off project, the model converts the Fairtrade Premium from short-term capital expenditures into a recurring social protection entitlement. Year 1 grant funding de-risks adoption. From Year 2 onward, costs transition to a blended model where corporate buyers and Fairtrade cooperatives co-finance the program. Cooperatives allocate a portion of their Fairtrade Premiums - collectively governed funds - while buyers contribute the remaining share. This is not a temporary subsidy. It is a governance-approved, recurring benefit tied to cooperative membership, backed by verified data. The result is lasting health coverage that reduces farmer risk, strengthens cooperative stability, and delivers more resilient supply chains.

core_fields.title: DATA-DRIVEN FOOD SAFETY IN RWANDA
core_fields.description: Aflakiosk will close Rwanda s critical data gap on aflatoxin contamination by developing an interactive dashboard that maps contamination hotspots and exposure risks across the maize value chain. Combining large-scale testing with environmental and health data, it will deliver actionable insights for policymakers, development partners, and industry. This will enable targeted interventions, reduce contamination, expand market access, and improve food safety. Over 12 months, the project will design, develop, and validate a scalable, commercially sustainable dashboard.
core_fields.abstract: Aflatoxin contamination invisible to the naked eye - presents a major food safety challenge in Rwanda; In 2021, Aflakiosk conducted a study that revealed 65% of maize grain - the most consumed staple - exceeded safe aflatoxin levels and was unsafe for consumption. The challenge is compounded by the lack of reliable data on aflatoxin contamination and exposure risks in the country, leading to inconsistent, ineffective solutions. Acting without reliable data, government, development agencies, and the private sector have invested millions of dollars to tackle aflatoxin contamination in Rwanda but with limited effect on food safety, trade and health outcomes. Aflakiosk will address this gap through the provision of actionable data on aflatoxin contamination and exposure risks. Utilizing our ISO certified laboratory, we will conduct regular, large scale aflatoxin testing and generate real-time dashboards tracking aflatoxin contamination and exposure risks across place, time, and different stages of the maize value chain. These unique, data-driven outputs will be provided to governments, development agencies and private-sector clients, equipping them with the accurate, actionable evidence they need to design more targeted policies and smarter investments that directly and effectively reduce aflatoxin contamination and exposure in Rwanda. This will support the integration of farmers, traders and food processors into regulated, formal markets and increase economic returns, as well as the production and distribution of safer food products. This will reduce consumers exposure to aflatoxin carcinogens and in turn improve nutrition, lower rates of stunting, and decrease incidence of liver cancer and related deaths.

core_fields.title: Urban Garden of HOPE
core_fields.description: Hope Clubhouse s Urban Garden is a vital therapeutic space where adults living with mental illness plant, harvest, and maintain over 60 varieties of fruits and vegetables. Grown organically in the parking lot medians surrounding our building, this creative use of space yields fresh produce for our Culinary Unit, which prepares hot, nutritious meals for members, often their only meal of the day.
core_fields.abstract: Uniquely grown in the medians of our parking lot, our Urban Garden allows us to use limited green space in a sustainable and innovative way. These unconventional beds maximize otherwise unused areas and demonstrate our commitment to creativity and resourcefulness. By transforming small, overlooked spaces into productive growing areas, we provide fresh, organic produce for our members while promoting environmental stewardship and community pride. This initiative directly addresses a significant problem faced by many Hope Clubhouse members: limited access to affordable, healthy food. Adults living with mental illness experience higher rates of food insecurity due to low income, limited transportation, and challenges maintaining employment. The Urban Garden helps relieve this burden by supplying reliable, organic produce and creating a structured, therapeutic activity that supports wellness, confidence, and practical skills. In addition, the garden offers specific and sustainable benefits that strengthen our long-term impact. Organic growing methods reduce chemical exposure and support soil health, while the use of raised beds and drip irrigation conserves water and improves growing efficiency. Producing food onsite lowers the environmental footprint associated with transportation and packaging. The garden also models sustainable urban agriculture practices that members can learn and apply at home or in future employment. To sustain and expand this resource, we rely on funding for essential materials including organic compost, non-GMO seeds, efficient irrigation, tools, and raised beds.

core_fields.title: BioNBiochar: Nitrogen Enriched Biochar for Maize Productivity and Pest Resilience
core_fields.description: BioNBiochar is affordable, locally produced nitrogen-enriched biochar from farm residues, using black soldier fly larvae to address nitrogen deficiency and boost soil fertility sustainably. It boosts maize soil fertility, improves nitrogen retention, and helps suppress fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) damage. Already validated: presented at MITA 2025 (CORAF) and registered in the EU innovation database. With US$25,000, we will pilot production hubs, train ~150 farmers, run field trials, and build a cooperative business model to scale.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder maize farmers in Cameroon face two interrelated constraints: soils severely depleted of nitrogen and persistent damage from the invasive fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda). Farmers are increasingly aware of biochar as a soil amendment made from crop residues, and some have tried using it because it improves soil structure and water retention. However, conventional biochar is nitrogen-deficient, so its benefits are limited without costly synthetic fertilizers. As a result, many farmers discontinue its use despite recognizing its potential. BioNBiochar introduces an innovative, locally appropriate solution by enriching biochar with nitrogen from black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) frass, a nutrient-dense organic by-product from insect rearing. Through controlled pyrolysis and biological activation, nitrogen and other essential nutrients are integrated into the carbon-rich biochar matrix, creating a dual-function soil amendment: a slow-release nitrogen fertilizer and soil health enhancer. Scientific evidence supports this approach. Nitrogen-enriched biochar increases nitrogen retention, boosts maize yields, improves soil organic carbon, and enhances nitrogen use efficiency compared to fertilizer alone. Biochar has also been shown to reduce fall armyworm herbivory, improving crop tolerance to pest attack and reducing reliance on pesticides. BioNBiochar therefore addresses multiple farmer priorities: restores nitrogen fertility, improves maize yield and resilience to S. frugiperda damage, reduces dependence on external inputs and production costs, promotes circular bio-economy by upcycling residues and BSFL waste, and strengthens cooperative businesses. With these combined agronomic, economic, and environmental benefits, BioNBiochar provides a sustainable pathway for farmers to enhance food security, regenerate soils, and build resilient livelihoods.
