core_fields.title: Establishment of an Experiential Learning Center for Resilience and Sustainable Production
core_fields.description: This project seeks to establish an integrated agriculture demo center for smallholder farmers in Malawi, focusing on regenerative practices. Through hands-on learning, farmers will adopt circular systems such as crop-livestock integration, irrigation, manure recycling, and diversified incomes to boost soil health, productivity, and resilience. The center fosters a savings culture, aiming to improve food security, household wellbeing, and community prosperity.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Malawi face significant challenges including low productivity, reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited technical knowledge, and poor financial resilience which lead to unpredictable incomes, food insecurity, and degraded soils. To address these issues, our project proposes an integrated agriculture demonstration center, practical and operational farm showcasing regenerative practices. Through this integrated agriculture demonstration center, rural smallholder farmers will engage in hands-on learning, adopting circular systems that combine crop-livestock production, fish farming, solar irrigation, and renewable energy. Waste is going to be recycled: livestock manure and crop residue will be used to fertilize maize fields, while nutrient-rich fishpond wastewater will be used to irrigate vegetables. This practice will bring multiple benefits: ensure efficient resource utilization and minimize waste discharge into the environment. The solar-powered pumps will ensure efficient water use. Alongside, a Village Income Bank is going to foster savings habits and collective investment in farm maintenance. Informed by regenerative agriculture and smallholder livelihood studies, the approach proposed in this project boosts soil fertility, increases yields, and strengthens climate resilience. Immediate benefits for participating farmers include enhanced crop yields, diversified production (eggs, fish, maize, vegetables), improved nutrition, and practical skills. In the long-term, the model offers a replicable path to food security, soil restoration, water efficiency, and reduced environmental degradation for not only surrounding communities but also more other rural smallholder farmers from across Malawi. This initiative aims to empower farmers, improve livelihoods, and drive sustainable change.

core_fields.title: Sustainable food production and improved nutrition in Northern province of Rwanda_Musanze District (Nyange Sector)
core_fields.description: This project aims to strengthen sustainable food production and improve nutrition for 150 smallholder farmers in Sustainable food production and improved nutrition in Northern province of Rwanda_Musanze District (Nyange Sector), Northern Province of Rwanda. Through climate-smart agriculture, market access support, and nutrition-sensitive interventions, the project will increase maize and bean yields, enhance household nutrition, and reduce food insecurity and stunting. By building farmer capacity and promoting gender equality, the project will improve community resilience.
core_fields.abstract: The proposed innovation introduces an integrated model that combines climate-smart agriculture, nutrition-sensitive practices, and market-led solutions to address persistent food insecurity and malnutrition among smallholder farmers in Rwanda. Despite Rwanda s strong agricultural base, farmers-especially in rural districts like Musanze-continue to experience low crop productivity, limited access to markets, and inadequate nutrition knowledge, resulting in high levels of food insecurity and stunting. This innovation solves these challenges by merging three evidence-based approaches into one coherent system: Climate-smart agriculture (CSA): Farmers adopt sustainable land management, improved seed varieties, water harvesting technologies, and agroforestry. These techniques increase yields while restoring soil health and building resilience to climate shocks. Nutrition-sensitive agriculture: Kitchen gardens, agri-nutrition training, and gender-transformative dialogues empower households to consume diverse, nutrient-rich foods and create equitable decision-making within families. Market access and value chain strengthening: Post-harvest handling training, business skills, and cooperative development enable farmers to reduce losses, access reliable markets, and increase income. The scientific and technical foundation of this innovation draws from proven CSA methodologies, behavioral change communication (BCC) models in nutrition, and market system development (MSD) approaches used successfully in Rwanda and across East Africa. The immediate benefits include increased crop yields, improved household diets, reduced food losses, and higher incomes. Long-term benefits include strengthened farmer resilience to climate change, reduced stunting, enhanced gender equity, sustainable land restoration, and empowered community-led food systems. This integrated model ensures that both productivity and nutrition outcomes are achieved sustainably, making it highly relevant and scalable.

core_fields.title: SIMBA - Sustainable Innovations for Market-linked Bio-Agroforestry
core_fields.description: FttF works in semi-arid and drought-prone Makueni county, Kenya, on the transition of 700 smallholder farmers to a highly productive syntropic agroforestry system and short food chains for healthy, organic food to nearby urban areas. The project will provide farmers with innovative, but simple and affordable field water harvesting solutions (Zainer, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMtKUcEkq6Y), smart irrigation (Sprayer, https://youtu.be/ZQucPBkuCTg), crop suitability and irrigation advice (Croptimal, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VznztauUv-w) and innovative blended training (SkillEd, https://platform.skill-ed.org/organisations/skilled/videos/skilled.mp4) to boost the farmers climate-resilient production.
core_fields.abstract: Prolonged droughts and unreliable rainfall in Makueni County, Kenya, severely undermine food production and food security for rural households and nearby urban consumers. Smallholder farmers remain highly dependent on rain-fed agriculture, making them vulnerable to climate variability and unable to produce during the dry season. While Feedback to the Future promotes syntropic agroforestry to improve soil health, water retention, and resilience without synthetic agrochemicals, establishing these systems is difficult under persistent drought conditions. This innovation introduces an integrated package of climate-smart technologies to enable successful and scalable agroforestry. It combines mechanized Za planting to improve rainwater capture and soil fertility, low-pressure pivot irrigation (Sprayer), and the innovative Croptimal irrigation advisory tool, which provides daily irrigation and seasonal crop selection advice based on weather, soil, and satellite data. Together, these tools initiate a positive feedback loop of improved water availability, soil regeneration, and resilient production systems. The solution is grounded in proven scientific and technical insights. Za planting has long demonstrated yield increases in drought-prone regions, while farmer-driven innovation led to the mechanization of Za and the development of affordable low-pressure irrigation. Croptimal emerged from R&D showing that data-driven irrigation advice is largely inaccessible to smallholders despite its high potential impact. Immediate benefits include higher and more stable yields, reduced crop failure, improved incomes, and access to dry-season production. Long-term benefits include improved soil health, water efficiency, biodiversity, climate resilience, and increased access to affordable and healthy food for consumers, while contributing to ecosystem restoration and climate change mitigation.

core_fields.title: SMART START for Fortified Futures: Building a Fortified Complementary Food Ecosystem in Cambodian School Environments
core_fields.description: Children in Cambodia face high rates of undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and overnutrition, with limited access to fortified complementary foods. SMART START aims to scale fortified products and build a replicable SME ecosystem producing culturally acceptable complementary foods. Our project strengthens schools and surrounding market systems, aligns with national regulatory and laboratory standards, and fosters consumer trust, advancing sustainable nutrition, scaling production capacity, and improving child health outcomes through coordinated partnerships and market-based solutions.
core_fields.abstract: Rapid social and economic development in Cambodia has increased access to ultra-processed, high-fat, high-sugar, and high-salt foods, especially in school zones where low-nutrient snacks dominate and regulatory enforcement is limited, creating urgent nutrition challenges. SMART START (School-Market Access for Resilient Food System Transformation, through SME strengthening, Technical capacity, Alliance/Association, Regulatory support, and Transforming child nutrition) addresses these gaps by integrating fortified foods into schools and surrounding markets while strengthening consumer trust. Our innovation combines fortified porridges (targeting ages 6-36 months) for nurseries, and micronutrient-dense snacks (for school-aged children, 23 months and older) in primary schools, with a scalable school-market delivery model and circular-economy inputs. This innovation will be co-facilitated by Helen Keller and aligns with Cambodia s developing Complementary Food Products for Children (CPCF) standards and WHO/Codex frameworks. SMART START scales fortified foods through schools and vendors, ensuring safe, nutritious options while supporting enforcement of restrictions on unhealthy foods. Unlike fragmented school feeding programs or small pilots, SMART START integrates four reinforcing components: fortified product innovation, SME upgrading, regulatory strengthening, and institutionalization through the Fortified Foods Association of Cambodia (FFAC). Existing fortified products are not consistently designed for children, locally produced, affordable, or widely available. SMART START fills this imbalance using sensory trials, fortification research, and market analyses. It provides children with daily access to safe, nutrient-dense foods, offers caregivers affordable options, and helps SMEs improve compliance and efficiency. Over time, SMART START sets national standards, reduces food loss, and establishes a sustainable, market-driven, nutritious, fortified foods advancing Cambodia s nutrition goals.

core_fields.title: Fueling Bright Futures: Growing Healthy, Local School Meals at Scale
core_fields.description: Fueling Bright Futures strengthens the Department of Education s (DepEd) Integrated School Nutrition Model (ISNM) by linking agroecological school gardens, healthier canteen menus, and engaging nutrition education to replace ultra-processed foods with diverse, locally sourced meals. Using WFP s School Meal Planner PLUS and vetted local suppliers, six model schools will design affordable, culturally relevant menus that improve diets, support smallholder farmers, and build a more resilient, equitable school food system with potential for national scale-up.
core_fields.abstract: Fueling Bright Futures addresses the issue of poor dietary diversity and reliance on processed foods in Cavite s school canteens, a problem that is prevalent across the Philippines and highlighted in recent reviews of school meal quality and child nutrition. It links school gardens, improved canteen menus, and nutrition education to a scalable Integrated School Nutrition Model (ISNM), enhanced with the WFP School Meal Planner PLUS to design healthy, affordable, culturally appropriate meals using local ingredients. A core feature is fully integrating school gardens into school meals, so children regularly eat what they help grow, reinforcing that food comes from soils and gardens rather than packets and shelves. This hands-on experience deepens children s connection to land and local food systems, fostering the idea that the health of the earth underpins the health of children, people and their communities. This innovation is novel in the Philippines context because it systematically combines science-based menu planning, garden-to-canteen supply, participatory nutrition education, and transparent local procurement on a single platform for public schools. While similar models exist globally, their integration within DepEd s ISNM schools is an innovation fostering scaling. Immediate benefits include healthier, more appealing meals, stronger food literacy, reliable demand and better prices for local farmers, and greater school community cohesion. Over time, the model supports a resilient, equitable local food system that nourishes children while promoting environmental stewardship and sustainable local livelihoods. As one canteen staff shared, Initially, they thought vegetables were just weeds. Now they ve discovered that these can be cooked and eaten.

core_fields.title: Scaling Affordable Bio-Organic Fertilizers for Smallholder Farmers in Rural Zambia
core_fields.description: This project expands smallholder access to affordable bio-organic fertilizers through last-mile Agrodealers distribution, on-farm training, and demonstration plots. Led by Xenia Investment Limited, the initiative will deliver 15,000L of bio-fertilizer, train Agrodealers, and support 2,000 farmers, especially women and youth, to improve soil health, crop yields, and climate-smart farming practices across rural Zambia.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Zambia face declining soil fertility and unaffordable chemical fertilizers, limiting yields, such as soybeans averaging 1.8 MT/ha despite potential yields of 3 MT/ha. The innovation introduces a cost-effective, bio-organic fertilizer system combining a Microbial Soil Enhancer with an Organic NPK blend. This solution restores soil microbiology, enhances nutrient uptake, improves water retention, and strengthens long-term soil productivity. The scientific basis lies in microbial soil enhancement: beneficial microorganisms rejuvenate the soil microbiome, improve nutrient cycling, and stimulate plant growth. Humic compounds improve soil structure and moisture retention, allowing crops to thrive even in nutrient-depleted or drought-prone soils. Xenia s bio-organic combo costs only US$108 per hectare, 67% cheaper than the US$330 per hectare required for chemical fertilizers. Its lightweight 15L pack is far easier to transport than 400kg of chemical fertilizer, solving both affordability and logistical barriers for rural farmers. The project also integrates farmer training, demo plots, and last-mile distribution via local Agrodealers such as Kashikoi Investment Limited. This ensures practical, sustained adoption of bio-fertilizers and climate-smart agronomy practices. End-users benefit immediately from improved yields, reduced input costs, and better soil health, while long-term environmental benefits include reduced chemical runoff, increased biodiversity, and restored soil fertility across rural farming communities.

core_fields.title: Trichoprotectant-and-Trichostimulant: Sustainable Crop Protection and Yield Improvement
core_fields.description: The "Trichoprotectant-and-Trichostimulant" project is based on the use of Trichoderma fungi for enhancing crop protection and yield of essential crops relevant in global agriculture. The project will provide an affordable, easy-to-use bioproduct made from the fungi, which farmers everywhere, no matter their gender or location, can use. In the long-term, the project will promote sustainable farming by reducing the need for agrochemicals, supporting eco-friendly farming practices, and strengthening food security to help the global economy.
core_fields.abstract: Trichoprotectant-and-Trichostimulant is a nature-based biological solution that uses beneficial Trichoderma fungi to protect plants and stimulate healthier, more resilient growth/yield. The project innovation addresses two major challenges facing farmers today: 1) crop losses from soil-borne diseases, and 2) declining soil fertility caused by farmland-and-agrochemical overuse. This problem is relevant as food systems struggle with rising production costs, high demand for safe food products, climate-stress, and the need for sustainable alternatives to synthetic pesticides and fertilizers. Additionally, the innovation works by enriching plants with selected Trichoderma strains with excellent bioprotecting properties (soil adaptation, root colonization, forming natural-shield, out-competing pathogens, producing antifungal compounds that block infections) and biostimulant properties (root development, nutrient-uptake by releasing growth-promoting enzymes and hormones, degrade organic matter). Together, they improve plant vigor while reducing dependence on synthetic inputs. Furthermore, the scientific insight behind this innovation lies in understanding Trichoderma s strong rhizosphere competence, biocontrol efficacy, production of melatonin, volatile-organic-compounds, and indole-3-acetic acid, and phosphorus solubilization; these inspired integrated bioprotective biostimulant development. Benefits provided by the innovation are outlined as follows: 1. Farmers: Higher yields, reduced crop losses, lower input costs, improved soil and crop health. 2. Consumers: Safer food with fewer/no chemical residues. 3. Communities and Schools: Accessible, eco-friendly tools for sustainable gardening and education. 4. Producers: Reliable, renewable bio-based inputs that improve production efficiency. 5. Environment: Reduced agrochemical pollution, restored soil biodiversity, and improved climate-resilience. Overall, the innovation delivers an eco-friendly, cost-effective, and scientifically proven approach to crop protection and yield improvement, supporting both sustainable agriculture and better livelihoods.

core_fields.title: Prevalence and antimicrobial resistance of salmonella in chicken and beef in Phnom Penh, Cambodia
core_fields.description: This project investigates the prevalence and antimicrobial resistance of Salmonella in raw chicken and beef sold in three major markets in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. By collecting and testing meat samples, the study identifies contamination levels and resistance patterns to commonly used antibiotics. The findings will support improved food safety practices, guide public health actions, and contribute to the One Health approach.
core_fields.abstract: Foodborne Salmonella infection is an increasing public health concern in Cambodia, but data on contamination levels in raw chicken and beef sold in local markets and their antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles remain limited. This issue is particularly important in Phnom Penh, where most households purchase meat from traditional markets, and AMR is rising due to misuse of antibiotics in animals. This project establishes an innovative, market-focused surveillance system, collecting chicken and beef samples from three major Phnom Penh markets. Using standardized microbial culture, antibiotic susceptibility testing, MARDI-TOF Biotyper, and Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS), the study identifies Salmonella presence, genetic characteristics, and AMR patterns. The findings are then translated into practical guidance for vendors, consumers, and policymakers to improve food handling, hygiene, and responsible antimicrobial use. One Health research demonstrates that contaminated meat is a major pathway for transferring drug-resistant Salmonella from animals to humans. Understanding contamination at the market level, where consumers directly interact with food, offers a clear, actionable point for intervention. Microbiological testing and AMR profiling provide accurate, science-based tools to detect risks early. This approach benefits multiple stakeholders: consumers gain safer meat and fewer foodborne infections; vendors and producers receive practical feedback to enhance hygiene and reduce antibiotic misuse; farmers gain evidence to adopt safer, more sustainable practices; communities and schools can lower disease burden and medical costs; and society and the environment benefit from slower AMR spread, stronger public health protection, and improved national food safety systems.

core_fields.title: Community-Managed Climate-Resilient Seed Systems for Nutritious, Affordable Food
core_fields.description: This project advances a community-managed, climate-resilient seed system to improve access to nutritious, affordable food for smallholder farmers. Through Quality Declared Seed (QDS) production of beans, sunflower, and sesame by trained hub farmers, the innovation decentralizes seed supply, strengthens climate resilience, and reduces costs. Cooperative-led distribution ensures trusted access, while improved seed availability increases yields, dietary diversity, and incomes, enabling scalable, sustainable food system transformation.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in the Global South Including Tanzania face persistent barriers to accessing affordable, high-quality seed, resulting in low productivity, poor nutrition outcomes, and vulnerability to climate shocks. Centralized seed systems are costly, poorly adapted to local agro-ecologies, and often fail to reach remote communities, limiting the availability of nutritious and climate-resilient crops. This innovation introduces a community-managed, climate-resilient seed system that decentralizes Quality Declared Seed (QDS) production and distribution for common beans, sunflower, and sesame. Trained hub farmers, selected in collaboration with Local Government Authorities and certified by the Tanzania Official Seed Certification Institute (TOSCI), multiply locally adapted improved varieties. Seeds are distributed through cooperative-managed input systems, ensuring affordability, trust, and timely access. The approach is grounded in seed system science showing that locally produced, quality-assured seed performs better under local conditions, increases adoption, and strengthens resilience to climate variability. Integrating nutrition-dense crops and climate-adapted varieties directly links seed systems to healthy diets and sustainable food production, while the Community Agribusiness (CAB) model ensures economic viability and scalability. Immediate benefits include reduced seed costs, increased yields, and improved access to nutritious food for farming households. Sustainable benefits include resilient local seed markets, increased farmer incomes, reduced environmental footprint through localized production, and stronger community ownership of food systems. At scale, the innovation strengthens equitable access to safe, affordable, and trusted food while supporting climate-resilient and sustainable agricultural systems.

core_fields.title: Shambany : Digitizing food safety compliance in our Farms.
core_fields.description: Shambany is Arbarne s flagship solution leading Africa s farm transformation (2026 2030). It tackles widespread pesticide and fungicide misuse by enabling preventive, data-driven farming. By monitoring critical weather elements like temperature and humidity which are key drivers of pests and diseases, Shambany helps farmers make timely decisions, reduce chemical reliance, and protect both their health and consumers. The system promotes safer production, higher-quality food, and a shift from reactive to proactive farm management.
core_fields.abstract: The development of Shambany is rooted in a key scientific insight: pest and disease outbreaks are strongly driven by microclimate conditions, particularly temperature and relative humidity. Research across horticultural systems shows that when these variables rise or fall within certain thresholds, fungal attacks and insect populations multiply rapidly. In Kenya, most farmers cannot observe these microclimate shifts in real time, leading them to apply fungicides and pesticides blindly or only after severe damage. This creates health risks, raises production costs, and contaminates food systems. Shambany was designed to transform this reactive pattern. By integrating affordable sensors, local climate models, and an intuitive decision-support system, Shambany provides continuous monitoring, early warnings, and simple recommendations. This technical approach allows farmers to anticipate risks rather than respond to them. The solution also incorporates remote monitoring capabilities, making it viable for smallholders, schools and youth farmers with limited on farm presence. The immediate benefits include reduced chemical misuse, lower production costs, and fewer crop losses. Farmers gain confidence in their practices, consumers access safer food, schools or community farms adopt better plant health management. The system promotes transparency and traceability, improving trust across the food-system. Long-term, Shambany contributes to sustainable, regenerative farming systems. It minimizes environmental contamination, protects soil and water resources, and lowers greenhouse gas emissions linked to unnecessary chemical use. It builds healthier communities, strengthens food security, and supports a new generation of climate-smart producers. Ultimately, Shambany delivers social, health, economic, and environmental benefits while driving Africa s transition toward preventive, knowledge-driven agriculture.

core_fields.title: HEROIC: "Halamang Gamot" Evaluation R&D through Optimized Irradiation for Industry Standards and Collaboration
core_fields.description: HEROIC aims to establish validated irradiation dose ranges that ensure the microbial safety and preserve the phytochemical quality of DOH-endorsed Philippine herbal medicines. By assessing microbial reduction and chemical stability through TLC, FTIR, and extractive analyses, the project will generate scientific evidence to develop national irradiation-based safety standards. The results will support regulatory agencies, strengthen the herbal industry, and promote safer, high-quality herbal products in the Philippines.
core_fields.abstract: The project introduces a novel, evidence-based framework for establishing irradiation dose standards for medicinal herbs by integrating nuclear technology, chemical fingerprinting, and advanced data analytics. While gamma irradiation is globally recognized as a safe and effective method for microbial decontamination, existing dose recommendations for herbal materials are often generalized and lack plant-specific quality thresholds. The innovation goes beyond conventional pass fail microbial testing by systematically linking irradiation dose, microbial reduction, and chemical integrity. FTIR spectroscopy and TLC profiling are used to generate comprehensive chemical fingerprints of irradiated samples across multiple dose levels. A key novel element is the application of unsupervised machine learning techniques such as clustering and pattern recognition to these fingerprints to objectively detect irradiation-induced chemical changes that may not be evident through visual inspection or single-marker analysis. These data-driven patterns serve as quantitative indicators of quality deterioration. By identifying dose-dependent chemical deviations while confirming microbial safety, the project establishes a scientifically defensible maximum irradiation dose that balances safety and therapeutic quality. This approach shifts dose determination from subjective interpretation toward reproducible, algorithm-supported decision-making. Importantly, the framework is scalable and adaptable to other medicinal plants and food materials. The innovation provides regulators, producers, and researchers with a robust tool for quality assurance that reduces reliance on chemical preservatives, minimizes product losses, and strengthens consumer trust. By combining irradiation science with machine learning, the project demonstrates a forward-looking model for smart, sustainable, and trusted food and herbal product processing.

core_fields.title: Great Green Farmers
core_fields.description: In 2022, we came to Senegal and realized that farmers earn roughly $1.000 per year. Their lands are also degrading, and climatic conditions are threatening crop productivity. At that moment, one thought came to mind: These challenges are reversible . With that, we created the GGF initiative. We are transforming dry cropland into thriving agroforests combined with mid-tech greenhouses. The greenhouse serves as an economic engine to improve the farmer s income by up to eighteenfold.
core_fields.abstract: In Senegal, agriculture is essential for rural livelihoods, employing 60% of the population and contributing 15% of the country s GDP. But rural communities are turning away from agriculture, as revenues are no longer enough to survive in the modern economy. Smallholder farmers only cultivate during the three-month rainy season, and climate change is making conditions increasingly difficult. Heat waves and droughts are becoming more frequent, severely decreasing yields. The Great Green Farmers Initiative brings hope back to rural communities by using reforestation as a tool for economic empowerment. F ro s innovative model combines agroforestry with bamboo-based greenhouses, strengthening food systems while restoring degraded land. The system is designed with our expertise in engineering, biodiversity, and social sciences, along with the support of Delphy, a horticultural knowledge expert. The bamboo greenhouse integrates a solar mid-tech system that regulates light, temperature, CO₂, and humidity. This enables year-round high production of vegetables like tomatoes and peppers. A multilayer agroforest surrounds each greenhouse, including legumes, cereals and trees like mangoes and papayas, that complements greenhouse vegetable production. The immediate benefits of the project include yield increases of 4-20 times compared to conventional outdoor farming in Senegal. For a 1-hectare farm, F ro's greenhouse harvests can boost revenues from the current $1,000 to over $34,000 per year. And we do this by reforesting over 80% of their farmland through the planting of the agroforest.

core_fields.title: Empowering Smallholder Farmers through Sustainable Poultry Production and Market Access in Malawi
core_fields.description: The project will empower 1,200 smallholder farmers in Malawi by improving indigenous and dual-purpose poultry production using BSFL-based feed supplemented with Moringa and pawpaw. It will integrate climate-smart practices, health management, and market linkages to increase productivity, nutrition, and income. The BSFL feed facility will provide sustainable, affordable feed, while farmer training and community engagement will promote adoption. The initiative will deliver nutritious poultry products, economic empowerment, and environmentally sustainable livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: The indigenous poultry sector in Malawi faces critical challenges that limit its potential to improve rural livelihoods. Smallholder farmers, who are the backbone of this sector, struggle with limited technical knowledge, inadequate access to quality inputs, high feed costs, disease-related losses, and weak market linkages. Conventional feed is expensive, forcing reliance on scavenging systems that slow growth, with indigenous chickens taking 6 8 months to reach market weight. Disease mortality is high, averaging 40 50%, while smallholders earn only 30 40% of the final consumer price due to limited market access. Climate change further exacerbates these issues by reducing feed availability and stressing poultry populations, disproportionately affecting women and youth farmers. Our innovation addresses these interconnected problems through an integrated solution: improved poultry genetics combined with vaccination and health management, sustainable and locally adapted feed solutions, targeted capacity building for farmers, development of market linkages, and climate adaptation strategies. This approach is informed by field research showing the critical bottlenecks in feed, health, and market access, and leverages technical insights in poultry breeding, nutrition, and community-based extension. Immediate benefits include higher survival rates, faster growth, and increased incomes for smallholder farmers. Sustainable impacts include improved food security, enhanced nutrition for families and schools, economic empowerment for women and youth, and strengthened rural resilience to climate change. In trying to transform the productivity and profitability of indigenous poultry, the project directly contributes to more resilient communities, a stronger local economy, and a sustainable, inclusive poultry sector in Malawi.

core_fields.title: Bread Upcycling Project: A collaborative and circular game-changer.
core_fields.description: Our project will establish a high-volume resource recovery and processing pilot plant converting surplus supermarket and industrial bakeries bread into food-grade Rescued Bread Flour , a viable alternative to virgin flour. The model will be replicated through a standardised processing design, SOPs, and partnerships with food rescue organisations, governments, manufacturers, supermarkets, and licensees, enabling deployment in new regions without redesign. This project enables the shift from pilot-scale success to scalable, globally transferable upcycled bread flour production.
core_fields.abstract: Bread is one of the most wasted food products globally, estimated to be 18.5 million tonnes yearly. Our innovation to upcycle surplus supermarket and industrial bakeries bread into food-grade Rescued Bread Flour offers a proven, scalable, replicable, and economically sustainable solution to prevent it from being wasted. Since 2021 we have been committed to research in food science, technology, processing infrastructure, circular economy principles and action to demonstrate that upcycled food and ingredients can be integrated into existing food systems to deliver impact and opportunity. Problem Solved and Relevance: By diverting bread up the food waste hierarchy, the project reduces greenhouse gas and methane emissions, reduces pressure on natural resources, and supports affordable, accessible food for communities. It responds to the urgent global challenge of food waste and aligns with circular economy goals. How the Problem is Solved: Surplus bread is collected, processed, and transformed into high-quality, versatile Rescued Bread Flour . This approach combines technological innovation, efficient processing, and systemic redesign of food supply chains and food, enabling both immediate and long-term waste reduction. Immediate and Sustainable Benefits: - Lower greenhouse gas and methane emissions. - Economic growth via new upcycled food markets, products, jobs, technology, and intellectual property. - Improved food security, affordability, and accessibility. - Enhanced community engagement and awareness of sustainable consumption. - Educational participation and opportunities, from primary schools to universities. - Contribution to national and global frameworks, including UN SDGs 2, 9, 11, 12, 13, 17. - Circular redesign to prevent future food waste.

core_fields.title: AgriCarbon: Turning Captured CO₂ Into High-Productivity Climate-Smart Greenhouses
core_fields.description: AgriCarbon captures CO₂ from industrial areas and deploys it into advanced greenhouses to enhance plant growth, boost food production, and generate biomass that is later converted into biochar fertilizers. The project creates a circular carbon system that increases yields, strengthens soil health, and provides farmers with low-cost, high-impact fertilizers. This solution reduces emissions, improves food security, and delivers sustainable income opportunities for rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: AgriCarbon addresses two major challenges in Africa: rising CO₂ emissions from industry and low agricultural productivity caused by poor soils and climate stress. Our innovation captures CO₂ from small industrial emitters and redirects it into controlled-environment greenhouses where elevated CO₂ accelerates plant growth, increases yield, and generates more biomass. This biomass is then processed into biochar-based fertilizers that improve soil quality, water retention, and long-term carbon storage. The scientific foundation of AgriCarbon is based on proven principles: plants grow faster under optimized CO₂ concentrations, biochar enhances soil fertility, and greenhouse environments ensure consistent production even under climate variability. By integrating these components into one circular system, AgriCarbon transforms a waste pollutant into a valuable agricultural resource. End users benefit immediately through higher crop yields, improved fertilizer access, and increased income from selling biomass waste. Communities gain from reduced emissions, more resilient food systems, and new green jobs. Nationally, the system contributes to climate action, sustainable production, and stronger agricultural value chains. AgriCarbon provides a scalable, low-cost model tailored to African conditions delivering environmental restoration, economic empowerment, and improved food security while building Africa s first circular carbon agriculture ecosystem.

core_fields.title: Enhancing sorghum landraces' growth and yield through arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi variable application methods, Insiza, Zimbabwe
core_fields.description: Project aims to develop prototypes of AMF-inoculated and coated sorghum landraces to enhance crop performance in the drought-prone Insiza District. Combining local seed diversity with beneficial soil fungi, the innovation seeks to improve nutrient uptake, water-use efficiency, and yields. The improved local sorghum varieties will undergo testing with local farmers, creating a scalable, climate-smart solution that promotes food security. This approach integrates the genetic resources of local seeds with advancements in soil fungal technology
core_fields.abstract: Sorghum Bicolor is recognized for its drought resistance yet faces declining yields in Zimbabwe due to prolonged droughts, nutrient-deficient soils, and reliance on unimproved seeds. Despite the resilience of local sorghum landraces, biological enhancements are necessary for successful cultivation in increasingly challenging climates. The project introduces a novel method for developing sorghum varieties that tolerate climate change in semi-arid Zimbabwe, utilizing a combination of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) inoculation and seed coating. AMF improve plant phosphorous uptake, enhance soil quality, and promote effective water use, essential for dryland farming (Sene et al 2021). Although AMF technology is available, utilizing indigenous landraces and the dual inoculation and coating method is still nascent in Zimbabwe. This approach offers a cost-effective, environmentally friendly alternative to synthetic fertilizers, backed by evidence that AMF-enhanced plants yield greater biomass even under stress. Insiza District, within Agro Ecological Regions IV and V, experiences low, uneven rainfall, often below 650mm, jeopardizing maize-based farming and leading to persistent crop failures, hunger, and poverty (The Herald 2025). Communities and researchers are collaborating to establish sustainable farming systems focused on traditional grains. The prototype offers immediate benefits: improved germination rates, enhanced drought resistance, reduced fertiliser requirements, and more abundant harvests. This initiative appeals to both conventional and conservation farmers, addressing tillage challenges faced by subsistence agricultural practitioners. Beneficiaries include small-scale farmers, local communities, seed cooperatives, and extension services. Notable advantages include improved food security, decreased environmental degradation, farmer-driven seed innovation, and the potential for replicable dryland farming models in similar regions.

core_fields.title: Integrated Digital and Regenerative Agriculture Solutions for Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: AgreeNect is an integrated digital and regenerative agriculture solution that helps smallholder farmers restore degraded soils, improve food production, and build climate resilience. The project combines a low-cost mobile platform, AI-powered crop and soil diagnostics, localized training, early warning alerts, and a demonstration farm. Tested with 500 farmers in Zambia, the solution has shown strong usability and willingness to pay, positioning it for scalable food system impact.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in the Global South face declining soil fertility, climate variability, limited access to extension services, and fragmented markets, all of which undermine food security, nutrition, and rural livelihoods. Traditional agricultural support systems are often costly, inaccessible, or focused on short-term productivity rather than long-term sustainability. This project introduces an integrated digital and regenerative agriculture ecosystem designed specifically for smallholder farmers. The innovation combines a low-cost mobile platform accessible via smartphone app, USSD, and SMS with AI-powered crop and soil diagnostics, localized regenerative agriculture training in local languages, early warning alerts for weather and crop diseases, and a physical demonstration farm for hands-on learning. By unifying these components, the solution overcomes the fragmentation that limits adoption of sustainable practices. The approach is grounded in scientific evidence that regenerative agriculture such as soil cover, crop diversification, and organic matter restoration improves soil health, water retention, and climate resilience, leading to more stable and nutritious food production. Insights from conservation biology, agronomy, and farmer-centered design informed the development of the platform, ensuring that advanced technologies are adapted to local contexts and low-literacy environments. Immediate benefits to farmers include improved agronomic decision-making, reduced crop losses, lower input costs, and access to markets and finance. Over time, the innovation delivers sustainable benefits by restoring degraded land, increasing resilience to climate shocks, improving household food security and incomes, and contributing to healthier ecosystems and more resilient local food systems.

core_fields.title: Climate Resilient Vertical Farming for Urban Nutrition Security
core_fields.description: This project pilots a solar powered vertical farming system to deliver affordable, safe, and nutritious vegetables to urban communities in Uganda. Using controlled lighting, conditioned soils, and modular vertical racks, it enables year-round production independent of erratic rainfall. The solution reduces food loss, transport emissions, and pesticide use while stabilizing vegetable prices and strengthening urban food security under climate change.
core_fields.abstract: Uganda s food system is highly vulnerable to climate change because most vegetables are produced through rain fed, open field farming. Erratic rainfall, prolonged droughts, floods, pest outbreaks, and declining soil fertility are causing frequent crop failures, food losses, unstable supply, and rapidly rising vegetable prices in urban centers. These shocks directly undermine food access, nutrition, and incomes for low income households, vendors, and farmers. This project addresses this challenge through controlled environment vertical farming using solar powered LED lighting, conditioned soils, and modular vertical racks. Crops are grown inside fully enclosed structures where light, water, and nutrients are precisely regulated. This eliminates dependence on rainfall, reduces pest and disease pressure, minimizes pesticide use, and allows year round vegetable production within compact urban spaces such as garages and warehouses. The solution is guided by agronomic and plant physiology principles showing that optimized light spectra, moisture, and nutrient control accelerate germination, growth, and yield. Early feasibility trials conducted under this project demonstrated faster bean germination and stronger early foliage under LED controlled conditions compared to outdoor farms, confirming technical viability. Immediate and sustained benefits include affordable access to fresh vegetables for urban consumers, stable supply for vendors, reduced post-harvest losses, lower transportation emissions, and improved food safety due to reduced chemical residues. The system also creates urban green jobs, strengthens community food resilience, protects degraded soils, and contributes to long term climate adaptive, low carbon food systems.

core_fields.title: Enabling dry-season farming in Ghana and Senegal to increase food security
core_fields.description: The dry season in Ghana and Senegal significantly disrupts the productivity and livelihoods of smallholder farmers who mostly rely on rain-fed agriculture to produce; it also impacts consumers' ability to access healthy and affordable foods. Our project seeks to establish greenhouse nurseries and efficient block farming irrigation systems to create opportunities for dry-season farming and increase productivity, and deliver crucial agricultural extension services to support farmers in the adoption of improved farming practices.
core_fields.abstract: FLUID's innovation combines an inclusive financing system designed to bridge the gap in agricultural lending to smallholder farmers with improved farming solutions to enable dry season production. 95% of African farmers depend on rain-fed agriculture for food production. In northern Ghana and Senegal, decreasing annual rainfall and less predictable climate patterns are adversely impacting smallholder farmers who are often ill‑equipped to cope. During the dry season, farming activities cease due to water scarcity causing declines in incomes and yields, with only a limited number of farmers having access to the necessary infrastructure to sustain production. This gap in production often creates instability in food supply and prices, affecting local consumers ability to purchase locally produced foods. To address this problem and meet the rising demand for affordable and nutritious foods, farmers cannot rely on rain-fed agriculture alone. Dry-season farming is a largely untapped opportunity to boost farmers incomes, stabilize agricultural markets, diversify consumers diets in cereal-heavy regions, and contribute to strengthening African food systems. FLUID's solution delivers improved farming methods and leverages data and innovative technologies such as greenhouse environmental control systems to enable a more stable and efficient year-round production. This model is novel because it integrates financing, infrastructure access, technology, and high-quality inputs into a single, accessible package for smallholders. Unlike existing solutions that tackle only one of these elements at a time, FLUID provides a comprehensive package that addresses the full spectrum of constraints encountered by farmers, specifically tackling production gaps during the dry season.

core_fields.title: Digitally Connecting Surplus Food to People, Farmers, and Clean Energy Solutions
core_fields.description: SAtillsoogood is an digital-powered circular food system that rescues surplus food and transforms unavoidable waste into community value. Our platform connects food businesses with consumers, community kitchens, and biodigester operators redistributing edible surplus to improve nutrition and converting inedible waste into biogas, compost, and biochar.
core_fields.abstract: Across Africa, one of the biggest paradoxes is that food is wasted while people remain hungry. Restaurants, farms, and food processors generate large volumes of surplus food and organic waste due to poor forecasting, limited storage, and weak redistribution systems. This waste ends up in landfills, contributing to greenhouse gas emissions, soil degradation, and economic losses, while communities struggle to access nutritious, affordable food. We solve this challenge by creating an AI-powered circular food system that transforms food waste into economic, social, and environmental value. Our digital platform uses AI, geo-location, and nutrient profiling to match surplus food from businesses with nearby consumers, community kitchens, schools, and NGOs. Edible surplus is safely redistributed at low or no cost to improve nutrition. Inedible or spoiled waste is routed to biodigester operators and compost producers to generate biogas, compost, and biochar supporting clean energy and regenerative agriculture. The innovation is rooted in insights from food systems research: data-driven matching drastically reduces food loss; organic waste retains high energy and nutrient value; and localized circular systems reduce emissions and strengthen community resilience. Immediate benefits include: Affordable access to nutritious food for households and schools. New income for restaurants, farmers, waste collectors, and biodigester operators. Reduced waste disposal costs for businesses. Sustainable long-term benefits include: Lower greenhouse gas emissions and improved soil health through compost and biochar. Clean energy from biogas for households and institutions. Strengthened local food security and resilient circular economies.

core_fields.title: Scaling agroecological urban farming and street food safety towards food systems transformation in Kenya
core_fields.description: We scale a proven two-pronged innovation agroecological urban farming and experiential street food safety capacity strengthening to transform access to safe, nutritious, and affordable food in Nairobi s low-income settlements. Piloted successfully through our Food Systems Lab, the model uses regenerative farming and on-site vendor mentorship to overcome space and safety barriers, empowering households and vendors while strengthening sustainable, resilient urban food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Low-income urban settlements have fragile, unsustainable food systems, contributing to hunger and food insecurity. Street food vending is a major source of food in these settings, with pronounced food safety challenges. As part of actualizing our 2050 food systems vision to address these issues, we seek to roll out our piloted two-pronged innovation package. This dual approach is innovative because it combines regenerative, space-efficient food production systems with behaviour-change based, on-site food safety capacity building an integration rarely implemented together in urban informal settings. The first prong promotes food justice, supporting own-food production through innovative agroecological urban farming, to enable the urban poor to feed themselves in dignity. Our model utilizes established partnerships with community-organized groups as custodians of community learning and resource centers, champions and technical support infrastructure for penetration of kitchen gardens and edible landscaping in communities. The approaches are nature-based and regenerative, employing vertical gardening techniques; hydroponics, aquaponics; and snail, insect, and small livestock farming. Circular bioeconomy, including recycling of organic waste into organic manure and its use to enhance soil fertility, is supported. The second prong promotes street food safety through engagement of food vendors in low-income settlements in Nairobi. This involves on-site and experiential capacity strengthening of street food vendors by public health officers, guided by Street Food Vendors Manual, developed during the pilot phase. Both solutions contribute to the eradication of hunger, better nutrition, health, and wellbeing; resilience; environmental conservation and sustainability.

core_fields.title: Empowering Smallholder Farmers with Household Organic Fertilizer Production (E-SHOP).
core_fields.description: This 14-month project scales up the validated Earth Nourish Blends research by training 500 smallholder farmers (50% women, 30% youth) in Kiryandongo District, Uganda, to independently produce specific, affordable, and effective organic fertilizer blends using local plant and animal wastes. Key activities include establishing community-based training farms, developing instructional materials, and creating a quality assurance system. The goal is to sustainably increase farmer profits, enhance soil health and biodiversity, and secure food and economic resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Problem Solved and Relevance: Smallholder farmers in Uganda face critically declining soil fertility and reduced crop yields. This is compounded by the high cost and frequent counterfeiting of inorganic fertilizers, increasing production costs and threatening household food security. The innovation is relevant because it addresses the critical gap in accessible, decentralized production and adoption of soil amendments. Solution and Insight: The problem is solved by empowering farmers to become self-reliant in fertilizer production. The project utilizes scientific insight from research confirming the benefits of appropriate organic fertilizer blends that meet the specific nutrient requirements of crops like cereals and legumes. The solution is to train smallholders to produce tailored, good-quality organic blends from locally sourced, disease-free plant and animal wastes. Benefits: Immediate and sustainable benefits include substituting expensive inorganic fertilizers, leading to stable farmer incomes and cost-effective operations. The blends provide essential crop nutrients, enhancing the capacity to attain good, stable crop yields. Sustained benefits include enhanced soil health and biodiversity, resilience to climate shocks, reduced environmental impact by mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and water pollution, and strengthened livelihoods for the farming community.

core_fields.title: CuTruFoR - Truffle Cultivation and Forest Landscape Restoration for community resilience.

This project supports local communities and small businesses to implement truffle-oak plantations and to manage truffle-making forests as a sustainable component of the vanishing "rural mosaic" landscape. They can act a "steamer" for the survival of whole mountain agro-system and its biodiversity and represent and effective and replicable contrast to climate change cause the can act as wildfire natural barriers.
core_fields.abstract: In this framework, truffle cultivation (which has a significant tradition and a growing market in this area) and natural carefully management forests can represent a key strategy to: 1) provide local farmers with a relevant income which can also support other kind of less remunerative food productions, prevent the abandoning and and keep the rural landscape alive a vibrant; 2) make the oak plantations and the thinned natural forests play the role of actively managed firebreak barriers, contrasting the climate change effects; 3) maintain an open-forest structure where a specific biodiversity and other non-wood food produce can grow. Truffle plantation are part of the "rural patchwork which is the more effective landscape-shape to contrast wildfires, caused by the abandonment of the agricultural system. In partnership with University of L'Aquila, we've also tested forest management criteria to improve natural truffle and, at the meantime, reduce the risk of wildfire through forest thinning. The project merges three action lines: 1) to make more profitable the truffle production, establishing a network between local truffle value-chain actors (producers, collectors, processing firms, tree nursery, tourist operators, local shops, restaurants, truffle hunter, dog breeds); 2) to test and develop a protocol for anti-fire truffle-oaks orchards and natural truffle-forest thinning; 3) to support the truffle-farmers/collectors in delivering their truffles and also other every-day produce to local communities and tourists. core_fields.title: Augmented intelligence for agroclimatic risk management supporting sustainable, financially resilient agriculture
core_fields.description: Latin America holds 25% of the world s arable land but produces only 11% of global food, largely due to limited access to tailored credit and insurance for small producers. This project develops an augmented-intelligence (AI+) platform that integrates IoT sensing, ML-based risk forecasting, adaptive GHG valuation, and IoB interaction layers to enable collaborative agro-risk management. The prototype will inform the design of data-driven, climate-smart financial and insurance products for sustainable food-system resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Agriculture in Latin America and the Caribbean faces a structural challenge: despite holding vast arable land, small and medium producers struggle to access credit and insurance because financial intermediaries lack reliable, real-time visibility into how agro-climatic and sanitary risks are managed in the field. This innovation proposes an augmented-intelligence (AI+) platform that integrates IoT sensors, spectral imagery, machine and deep learning models, and an Internet of Beings (IoB) interaction layer to generate prospective risk scenarios and estimate greenhouse-gas (GHG) sequestration potentials based on producers actual management behaviours. Scientifically, the solution builds on advances in spatio-temporal modelling, vegetation indices (NDVI, NDRE, MSAVI, RECI), adaptive technical-financial analysis, and natural interaction via LLMs to transform field narratives into structured risk information. This approach enables a new level of observability and collaborative risk management between producers and financial intermediaries. Its immediate benefits include better decision-making, reduced information asymmetry, and accessible tools for sustainable and climate-resilient production. Long-term, the platform empowers producers to achieve green certifications, strengthens environmental and financial sustainability, and supports the creation of data-driven insurance and financing products aligned with global climate frameworks. For communities, consumers, and the environment, the solution enhances food-system resilience, promotes regenerative practices, and accelerates the transition toward inclusive, transparent, and climate-smart agriculture in the region.

core_fields.title: Circular food system by converting human waste into eco-friendly cooking briquettes and organic fertilizer.
core_fields.description: This project promotes a circular and climate-resilient food system by safely converting human waste (faecal sludge) into eco-friendly cooking briquettes and organic fertilizer. It reduces pressure on forests, improves sanitation, and supports women, children, refugees, and host communities facing energy insecurity. By providing clean fuel for food cooking in refugee camps and host communities and increasing food production through organic fertilizers, the project strengthens livelihoods and environmental resilience in Burundi.
core_fields.abstract: Refugee camps such as Bwagiriza, Nyankanda, Musasa, Kinama, and Kavumu in Burundi face serious challenges: limited clean cooking fuel, poor soil fertility, and unsafe accumulation of human waste (faecal sludge). These conditions harm the environment and threaten the well-being of women, children, refugees, and surrounding host communities. This innovation addresses all three challenges by converting faecal sludge into eco-friendly cooking briquettes and safe, nutrient-rich organic fertilizer using circular and science-based processes. Faecal sludge is first safely collected and treated through dehydration and high-temperature sanitation, eliminating pathogens. For briquettes, the treated material is carbonized and compressed into clean-burning fuel that replaces charcoal and reduces deforestation. For fertilizer, the treated sludge undergoes co-composting with organic plant waste. During this process, microorganisms break down the material, stabilizing nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. The mixture then matures into a high-quality organic fertilizer that improves soil structure, increases water retention, and boosts crop productivity. This technique is widely recognized in environmental engineering as safe and effective. The innovation provides immediate and lasting benefits: -Clean briquettes for food cooking in refugee camps and host communities. -Organic fertilizer that increases food production for farmers, schools, and community gardens. -Improved sanitation and reduced disease risks. -Lower pressure on forests and reduced carbon emissions. -Income opportunities for community groups, especially women and youth. By turning a sanitation challenge into clean energy and regenerative agriculture, this innovation strengthens climate resilience and supports sustainable community development.

core_fields.title: Tusome Chakula: Building Climate-Resilient Community Food Forests for Nutrition and Education
core_fields.description: Tusome Chakula establishes climate-resilient Community Food Forests (CCFFs) in two schools and two community sites in Samburu, integrating drought-tolerant crops, agroforestry, and nutrition education. The project strengthens food system resilience by enhancing local production, reducing hunger-related absenteeism for students, and building climate-smart agricultural capacity among students, teachers, youths and the community. This participatory, systems-based approach creates a replicable, low-cost model for improving nutrition, education outcomes, and community resilience in the ASAL regions.
core_fields.abstract: Tusome Chakula addresses persistent child malnutrition, food insecurity, and low nutrition literacy in the drought-prone ASAL regions of Samburu, where schools and surrounding communities face limited access to nutritious foods, unpredictable rainfall, and weak integration between nutrition and education. The innovation establishes Climate-Resilient Community Food Forests (CCFFs) multi-layered, drought-tolerant agroforestry systems combining vegetables, millet, sorghum, legumes, and fruit trees within schools and community lands. These food forests function as living classrooms, linking nutrition education, literacy development, and hands-on agricultural skills through nutrition-themed reading materials and youth ambassador programs. Tusome Chakula integrates principles from agroforestry, climate-smart agriculture, education, and behavior-change pedagogy, demonstrating that nutrition and education outcomes improve when children, teachers, and communities actively participate in growing, preparing, and consuming food together. By increasing access to nutritious food at school, the model reduces hunger-related absenteeism, supports regular school attendance, and creates enabling conditions for improved academic outcomes. Immediate benefits include improved access to fresh, nutritious foods; enhanced nutrition literacy; strengthened climate-smart farming skills; and improved school attendance. Long-term benefits include resilient local food systems capable of withstanding droughts, empowered communities with sustainable food and nutrition practices, reduced reliance on emergency food aid, and strong potential for replication across other ASAL schools and communities. By integrating nutrition, education, and climate resilience into a single, community-driven model, Tusome Chakula offers a scalable, low-cost, and transformative solution to interconnected food and education challenges in ASAL regions.

core_fields.title: Youth Resilient Food Futures Project
core_fields.description: Chimanimani District faces ongoing climate shocks, fragile food systems, and high youth unemployment. In response, Green Governance Zimbabwe is supporting young people to lead climate-resilient food system transformation through skills development, cultural food heritage revival, and youth-led enterprises. The Youth Resilient Food Futures Project (YRFF) will promote innovations in value addition, food waste reduction, and Agri-FinTech to improve access to affordable, nutritious food. By strengthening youth leadership and sustainable practices, the project enhances resilience and
core_fields.abstract: Chimanimani District in Zimbabwe faces fragile food systems marked by low productivity, high food waste, limited market access, and inadequate access to affordable, nutritious food. These challenges are intensified by recurring climate shocks and the lingering impacts of Cyclone Idai, which weakened agriculture, disrupted markets, and reduced community resilience. Youth and women who form a large share of the population have limited opportunities to participate in or innovate within the food system, making it difficult for communities to consistently access appealing, affordable, and nutritious foods while maintaining environmental sustainability. To address these challenges, the Youth Resilient Food Futures Project introduces youth-led innovations in Chimanimani s Wards 18 and 21, targeting the entire food value chain. These innovations include value addition processes that convert local produce into longer-lasting, nutritious, and market-ready products; food waste and loss reduction interventions such as improved storage, preservation technologies, community collection points, redistribution of edible surplus; and Agri-FinTech tools that expand access to finance, digital payments, climate-smart farming information, and inclusive markets. The design of these solutions draws on climate science, food system analyses identifying key loss points, behavioural insights showing that appealing products increase local consumption, and digital technology trends that enhance youth participation. Indigenous knowledge further strengthens these approaches by highlighting the resilience and nutritional value of heritage foods. These innovations provide immediate and long-term benefits which include access to safer and more diverse foods; farmers reduce losses and increase income; youth gain jobs and market opportunities; communities improve nutrition and reduce waste

core_fields.title: Sustainable Climate-Smart Poultry Project (SCSPP) : A Climate-Smart, Transparent Poultry System for Emerging Markets
core_fields.description: PMCI merges decentralized solar cold-chain infrastructure with a digital trust-based marketplace to create reliable, climate-smart poultry supply chains. Women-led cooperatives operate mini cold rooms, mobile chillers, and verification processes, enabling buyers to access safe, fresh poultry at stable prices. By cutting spoilage, improving handling, and strengthening transparency, PMCI reshapes how poultry is stored, valued, and sold across emerging markets.
core_fields.abstract: The Poultry Markets Cold-Chain Initiative (PMCI) tackles two systemic failures in African poultry markets: high post-harvest losses and persistent market distrust, by combining decentralized solar-powered cold-chain hubs with a digital marketplace that verifies safe handling and enables transparent trade. Women-led cooperatives manage mini cold rooms, mobile chillers, and temperature-logging crates, reducing spoilage from ~35% to under 5% while lowering emissions through renewable energy and food-loss prevention. On the market side, PMCI s platform allows cooperatives to register poultry batches, verify cold-chain compliance, and connect with retailers and restaurants that increasingly demand safe, hygienic products. QR and USSD tools disclose temperature history, cooperative certification, and basic quality information, reducing information asymmetry and stabilizing pricing in traditionally volatile informal markets. PMCI is novel because existing poultry programs focus on production or training, while PMCI redesigns the post-harvest and market architecture itself. Comparable cold-chain solutions in LMICs remain centralized and diesel-dependent; none combine distributed solar chilling, women-led aggregation, and digital verification into an integrated system. Scientific foundations include thermal engineering, food-safety handling standards, renewable-energy systems, and emissions modeling from avoided spoilage. Immediate benefits include safer poultry, lower losses, improved income, and a more reliable supply for consumers. Long-term benefits include strengthened cooperative governance, reduced antimicrobial misuse, and scalable cold-chain ecosystems across Africa.

core_fields.title: Improving Healthy Diets Through AI Coaching and Household Food Production
core_fields.description: HAI Coach is a digital nutrition-education and behavior-change platform that helps low-income families improve diet quality, reduce food expenses, and grow nutritious food at home. Through AI-powered micro-learning, affordable recipes, and step-by-step home-garden guidance, the project strengthens household food security and supports healthier eating patterns. A pilot in Colombia will test adoption, dietary changes, and the feasibility of small home gardens for families facing persistent barriers to nutritious food.
core_fields.abstract: Low-income families face major barriers to healthy eating: limited nutrition knowledge, high food prices, and restricted access to fresh produce. HAI Coach addresses these challenges through an AI-powered platform that delivers personalized nutrition micro-learning, low-cost meal guidance, and practical training for starting home gardens. This combination improves both the demand for healthy diets (behavior and knowledge) and the household supply of fresh foods (production), creating a sustainable pathway to better nutrition. The innovation is based on behavioral science, nutrition education, and simple agronomic practices adapted for small spaces. AI enables personalized content, adaptive coaching, and culturally relevant recipes using affordable local ingredients. Home-garden guidance offers step-by-step instructions on soil preparation, planting, watering, composting, and maintenance, empowering families to grow vegetables and herbs even with minimal space. The solution was inspired by evidence showing that small, consistent dietary changes and household-level food production significantly improve nutrition outcomes. AI tools make this support scalable, low-cost, and accessible to families with limited digital literacy. Immediate benefits include improved nutrition knowledge, healthier meal preparation, reduced reliance on ultra-processed foods, and increased consumption of fresh produce. Sustainable benefits include ongoing garden production, lower food expenses, stronger food autonomy, and enhanced resilience against food-price fluctuations.

core_fields.title: "Eco Green: Ethiopia's leading organic liquid fertilizer, driving sustainable farming, improving livelihoods & food security"
core_fields.description: Eco Green is a patented organic liquid fertilizer produced through a controlled fermentation process using locally sourced plant and animal waste. It restores soil health, enhances biodiversity, improves water retention, and increases crop yields by 10 20 quintals per hectare, while costing up to 2.7 times less than imported chemical fertilizers. This project seeks USD 195,000 over 30 months to expand production capacity, farmer adoption, strengthen climate resilience, reduce food insecurity and improve rural livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: Eco Green Organic Liquid Fertilizer Producing PLC has developed a patented, fully organic liquid fertilizer that provides an affordable, scientifically proven, and scalable solution to Ethiopia's soil degradation and fertilizer shortage. Ethiopia relies heavily on imported chemical fertilizers whose high cost, foreign exchange demands, and frequent supply delays limit smallholder farmers productivity. Long-term use of these inputs has also contributed to soil acidity and declining yields, making the need for sustainable alternatives urgent and relevant. Eco Green addresses this challenge by converting locally available plant and animal materials into a nutrient-rich liquid fertilizer containing fourteen essential macro and micronutrients, including nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, and boron. Through a controlled fermentation process and foliar application, these nutrients are rapidly absorbed by crops, correcting deficiencies and improving growth more effectively than traditional fertilizers. Field studies show that Eco Green increases wheat and barley yields by three to seven quintals per hectare and potato yields by ten to fifteen quintals per hectare. Farmers also experience cost savings because Eco Green is significantly more affordable than imported fertilizer. The solution delivers immediate results in crop productivity and long-term benefits by restoring soil health, reducing reliance on chemical inputs, and lowering carbon emissions through local production. Eco Green has already reached more than one hundred ninety eight thousand farmers, with plans to expand to 1 million beneficiaries. This innovation strengthens food security, supports climate resilience, restores degraded land, and promotes sustainable rural development across Ethiopia and the wider African region.

core_fields.title: Transforming agricultural by-products into safe and nutritious foods: A community-driven circular model
core_fields.description: We develop and scale a low-cost pH-based detoxification and solar dehydration platform that transforms diverse agricultural by-products, such as bamboo leaves, old leaf tea, lotus root, and citrus peel, into safe, nutritious foods. Working with women and farmer cooperatives, the project strengthens rural livelihoods, reduces food waste and emissions, and expands access to affordable functional foods. The grant consolidates the proven model and equips more cooperatives to adopt the technology through a scalable training toolkit.
core_fields.abstract: Across Viet Nam, large volumes of nutrient-rich agricultural by-products are discarded or burned due to bitterness, toxins, or rapid spoilage. This results in lost nutrition, reduced farmer income, and avoidable emissions. The issue is especially relevant for women- and minority-led cooperatives that lack machinery, face unstable markets, and depend heavily on seasonal crops. Our innovation is a low-cost, science-based circular processing platform that combines: (1) pH-enabled detoxification, which removes bitterness and anti-nutritional factors while preserving proteins, fibers, chlorophyll, and bioactives; (2) solar-energy dehydration, which stabilizes color and nutrients without electricity; and (3) low-carbon value-add technologies. This solution grew from scientific insights into how pH influences protein stability, bitterness pathways, enzymatic activity, and pigment retention in plant tissues. Combined with field experience working directly with rural cooperatives, the approach was designed to be technically robust yet accessible for small producers. These technologies are already successfully transferred to multiple cooperatives. Examples: the bamboo leaf tea for T n Xu n Cooperative (ethnic minority communities at Son La province) or the white dried bamboo shoots and lotus root for N KA Garden Eco-Homes (business run by women at Son La province). Immediate benefits include new income streams for rural producers, reduced waste burning, lower electricity use due to solar-based drying, the removal of chemical preservatives in dried products, and the availability of safe, affordable functional foods for households and schools. Long-term, the model enhances rural livelihoods, promotes gender equity, reduces emissions, conserves local forests, and fosters a scalable circular food system for the Global South.

core_fields.title: REGEN-ED: EDucation on REGENerative agriculture and biodiversity through sustainable nutrition
core_fields.description: At Food Phi, we view biodiversity education and farmer empowerment as foundations of sustainable nutrition. This project integrates both our "SEEDS for Climate Resilience" and "Eat and Greet Biodiversity" programs under the REGEN-ED project. It promotes regenerative wheat sorghum crop rotation to enhance farmer resilience and local sourcing, while educating schoolchildren on biodiversity and emblematic species through CookiMatic products and a dedicated educational app.
core_fields.abstract: We address a key food-system challenge: how to deliver sustainable nutrition while strengthening farmer resilience and biodiversity awareness in the context of climate change? Conventional food systems rely on resource-intensive crops, disconnect consumers from biodiversity loss, and leave farmers exposed to drought and market volatility, particularly in Lebanon and the wider region. Food Phi s innovation responds to these challenges through regenerative nutrition, integrating climate-resilient food production, farmer empowerment, and biodiversity education into a single model. Farmer empowerment is achieved through regenerative agricultural practices, with a focus on wheat sorghum crop rotation to improve soil health, yields, and climate resilience while strengthening local sourcing. The project currently engages three farmers across 8,000 m of agricultural land. A central innovation is CookiMatic, Food Phi s flagship trademark and the first food brand globally to use biodiversity as a high-resolution educational model. Its 3D biodiversity cookie- Lebanon series (also scalable across other countries) - features emblematic species including the Cedar of Lebanon, the striped hyena, the Lebanon cyclamen, and the Asian crimson-winged finch. Each product integrates storytelling, scientific and Latin names, and IUCN Red List status to raise biodiversity awareness through everyday nutrition. The cookies are complemented by an interactive CookiMatic App that educates children and adults on species ecology, ecosystems, food webs, endangerment levels, and conservation actions. Immediate benefits include climate-resilient farmer incomes, engaging biodiversity education for schools and communities, and healthier, low-impact food choices for consumers. Long-term impacts include improved soil health, increased biodiversity awareness, and more resilient local food systems.
