core_fields.title: Transforming Urban Food Waste into Compost and Nutrition Through Decentralized Systems
core_fields.description: Our project scales a decentralized circular food system for dense urban areas. Organic kitchen waste from urban businesses is processed on-site through aerobic digestion, reducing landfill disposal and emissions. The resulting digestate is collected and used for organic vegetable farming at a dedicated farm, producing healthy food for vulnerable communities. Building on a proven pilot, the project demonstrates a practical, affordable, and trusted model for urban waste generators, with replication planned in Jakarta and Bali.
core_fields.abstract: Urban food systems generate large volumes of organic kitchen waste that are often sent to landfills, producing methane emissions, increasing disposal costs, and burdening city infrastructure. At the same time, many urban communities lack access to fresh, nutritious vegetables, while hotels and restaurants struggle to adopt waste solutions that are safe, practical, and acceptable in dense environments such as Jakarta and Bali. This project introduces a decentralised circular food system using aerobic digestion. Organic kitchen waste from hotels is processed on-site or nearby using compact aerobic digester units, converting waste into stabilised digestate. The digestate is collected, cured, and transformed into compost that supports organic vegetable farming at a dedicated urban farm and partner community gardens. Separating waste treatment from food production ensures food safety, operational efficiency, and regulatory clarity while maintaining a local nutrient loop. The innovation lies in applying low-odour, methane-avoiding aerobic digestion in dense urban settings and linking it to compost-based vegetable production rather than animal feed. This approach is grounded in established biological processes: aerobic microbial activity rapidly stabilises organic matter, reduces pathogens, and preserves nutrients, while compost-based farming restores soil health and avoids chemical inputs. Pilot operations have demonstrated technical feasibility, consistent waste reduction, and strong interest from hotel partners. Immediate benefits include reduced landfill waste, lower waste management costs for hotels, and increased availability of fresh vegetables for vulnerable communities. Long-term benefits include improved soil health, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, and scalable urban waste solutions.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Decision Support Enabling Sustainable Resource Use for Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: This project delivers a precision climate-smart advisory system that helps climate-vulnerable smallholder farmers plan and use resources sustainably. By providing hyper-local forecasts and actionable guidance, the platform supports better decisions on planting, inputs, water use, and harvest timing, reducing losses and improving resilience. The solution empowers farmers and communities to manage climate risks, adopt regenerative practices, and strengthen food security while staying within planetary boundaries.
core_fields.abstract: Farmers in the Global South depend on weather information to decide when to plant, apply inputs, manage water and protect their crops. Yet most of them only receive generic regional forecasts from radio or national bulletins that do not reflect local conditions and do not provide practical guidance. As a result, farmers waste resources, face higher losses and remain highly vulnerable to climate variability. Our innovation addresses this challenge by translating complex atmospheric science into simple, hyperlocal forecasts combined with clear advisory messages on crop and resource management. The technology is built on a proprietary modelling system designed for tropical environments and strengthened by a virtual radar approach that reconstructs storm patterns in places where physical radar systems are sparse or unavailable. This allows us to produce accurate and dependable forecasts at the village scale in regions where conventional weather systems do not perform well. To ensure last-mile accessibility, the service is delivered through partnerships with mobile network operators and accessed through SMS and an interactive USSD menu. This gives farmers with basic phones and limited literacy a reliable way to obtain information that is specific to their location rather than broad information meant for large regions. Farmers receive timely guidance on planting, irrigation, fertilizer use, soil protection and harvest planning. This supports more sustainable resource use, reduces waste, strengthens regenerative practices and lowers the risk of crop loss. By making advanced climate science accessible to climate-vulnerable communities, the innovation helps farmers plan better, improve productivity and increase long-term resilience.

core_fields.title: Building circular food systems through local nutrient cycling in Uganda
core_fields.description: Smallholder farmers in the in peri-urban lakeside of Uganda are struggling to maintain yields of cash crops and food staples on degraded, over-mined soils - perpetuating a vicious cycle of synthetic fertilizer mis-use which has degraded Lake Victoria's ecosystem. 300 farmers have adopted artisanal humanure compost in transition to organic farming. This project will scale-up adoption of pelletized bio-fertilizers derived from humanure and organic waste to accelerate value-addition and improve farmer incomes and food security.
core_fields.abstract: GiveLove introduced Container-based Sanitation (CBS) in Uganda in 2016 in collaboration with several NGOs and community-based organizations in Kampala's informal settlements. CBS when combined with composting and skills training initiatives in waste recycling can safely manage sanitation, and transform waste into fertilizer for circular agriculture. In Kampala and Entebbe, only 10% of excreta is safely managed and landfills are at capacity. Thus, there is a huge need and potential for circular nutrient management. Recent studies indicate that nutrients from excreta could replace 50-100% of imported synthetic fertilizers in Africa, enabling Africa to become self-sufficient in food production. Studies show that 95% of vegetables and fruit in Kampala contain unsafe chemical residues. Many farmers are afraid of the health and environmental risks associated with synthetic fertilizer use. Value-addition to humanure fertilizer provides a viable pathway for creating safer, more resilient, and regenerative food systems. GiveLove has developed pelletized humanure fertilizers in collaboration with an informal business. 300+ farmers have adopted the pellets and compost. Our case study data demonstrates that farmers are willing to pay a premium price for the pelletized compost compared to standard compost ( $10 per 10 kg bag vs. $100 per ton). Pelletizing provides numerous benefits to farmers: 1) the products are shelf stable and easy to apply in efficient micro-doses; 2) increases crop yields by 50- 100%; 3) provides an organic alternative to synthetic fertilizers; 4) enables farmers to earn higher prices for organic cash and food crops; 5) protects lakeside watersheds from runoff nutrient pollution

core_fields.title: Smart Agri-Pyramid System: Integrated Urban Micro-Farms for Nutritious Food and Youth Livelihoods
core_fields.description: Agrisiti s Smart Agri-Pyramid System (SAP-Sys) is a compact, modular urban farming unit integrating hydroponics, recirculating aquaculture, and poultry within a low-water, solar-enabled system. The Seed project will deploy three full-production SAP-Sys units in Lagos to generate fresh vegetables, fish, and eggs while training urban youth. Funding will support system optimization, pilot deployment, and rigorous monitoring to validate adoption, productivity, and scalability.
core_fields.abstract: Urban households in Nigeria face rising food costs, limited access to fresh produce and animal protein, and persistent youth unemployment. Most urban agriculture solutions address single commodities, rely on high resource inputs, or lack the human capacity systems required for safe, consistent operation at scale. Agrisiti s Smart Agri-Pyramid System (SAP-Sys) is a modular, space-efficient urban farming unit that integrates hydroponics, recirculating aquaculture, and poultry within a compact footprint of 6-8 m . Each unit can operate either as a full aquaponics system or as a recirculating aquaculture system when plants are not in cycle, providing operational flexibility while maintaining resource efficiency. The system reduces water use by approximately 80% compared to conventional soil-based farming, uses renewable energy for core operations, and incorporates nutrient reuse across subsystems. The innovation extends beyond hardware. Agrisiti integrates a digital learning management system (LMS) that serves as the backbone for deployment and scale. The LMS supports standardized training, operational protocols, food safety guidance, and performance tracking for youth operators and households. All installations are paired with structured, hands-on training delivered onsite and reinforced through the LMS, ensuring consistent system performance and reducing reliance on continuous in-person support. Together, the SAP-Sys and LMS form a replicable deployment model that couples food production infrastructure with skills development, enabling safe operation, livelihood creation, and scalable impact across dense urban environments.

core_fields.abstract: The EcoSyNC platform is a pioneering, digital-first solution designed to resolve the systemic crisis in Kenya's livestock sector, whose viability is compromised by outdated regulations, severe data gaps, and immense economic loss driven by poor animal welfare. Kenya has over 44.6M poultry and produces 8B litres of milk annually, yet its animal products face trade restrictions in high-value markets (EU, US, UK) due to inconsistent adherence to global welfare, hygiene, and traceability requirements. Current certification systems fail to integrate full lifecycle welfare, environmental sustainability, and digital traceability, leaving producers unable to meet export standards and consumers with no transparent assurance of ethical production. The problem is solved by replacing fragmented, opaque systems with a holistic, financially self-sustaining ecosystem. The scientific insight is that improving animal welfare is an economic imperative. EcoSyNC integrates: 1. Creates a transparent data narrative, correcting misinformed policy and satisfying global market demands for verifiable sourcing. 2. Builds smallholder capacity in high-welfare, sustainable, nature-based husbandry, leading to safe and nutritious food. 3. Formalizes a standard, developed with industry/consumer partners, and guarantees certified farmers a price premium, correcting market failure. Sustainable benefits include: 1. Increased incomes for smallholder farmers owing to higher productivity and access to premium international markets 2. Consumers/Communities will access equitable, affordable, trusted and appealing high-quality animal products, and this will mitigate public health risks (zoonoses, AMR) 3. The livestock sector will drive sustainable/regenerative practices, ensuring long-term food security and proving that smallholders can sustainably meet national demand.

core_fields.title: Regenerate the Soil (Regesoil)
core_fields.description: This project addresses the challenges of infertile clay soil, reliance on chemical fertilizers, and the resulting long-term soil degradation in the Nakivale refugee settlements. Through a holistic approach, the project involves producing organic fertilizer from food waste decomposed by worms, carbon sequestration through biochar and the co-creation of micro syntropic agroforest adapted to the local climate in 3 zones, and providing practical and comprehensive training to farmers to grow food in an environmental repairing way.
core_fields.abstract: Nakivale Refugee Settlement hosts around 200,000 people, where most households depend on agriculture for survival. However, farmers face major challenges due to poor soil fertility, as surveys show that much of Nakivale's soil is sandy, sandy-loam, or clay, conditions that make food production difficult without external inputs. At the same time, the settlement produces an estimated between 10-40 tons of waste each day based on Uganda's national average of 0.5 kg per person. Much of this waste remains unmanaged, creating environmental and public-health risks, including contamination of water sources and pest-borne diseases. Our innovation directly addresses both the soil-fertility crisis and the waste-management challenge by engaging youth and farmers in collecting biodegradable waste, especially food scraps, and transforming it through vermicomposting. Worms decompose the waste to produce a nutrient-rich organic fertilizer containing essential elements such as nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium. This fertilizer improves soil structure, increases water-retention capacity, and helps crops tolerate drought. We further enhance the fertilizer by mixing it with biochar, which we produce from agricultural residues such as maize stalks. Biochar provides long-term carbon sequestration, supports nitrogen-fixing microbes, and acts as a catalyst that boosts soil activity. This combined approach offers a low-cost, locally sourced alternative to agro-chemicals, reducing farmers' dependence on expensive external inputs. It also diverts waste from the environment, increases crop productivity, restores degraded soils, and creates income and job opportunities for youth. The result is a sustainable, community-driven solution that improves food security, soil health, and environmental resilience

core_fields.abstract: Rural farmers and food producers often rely on diesel generators due to limited or unreliable grid electricity. This dependence increases operational costs, reduces productivity, and contributes to environmental pollution, while exacerbating local food insecurity. YY ReGen addresses this challenge by deploying the ReGen-R8, a portable, modular solar PV generator offered through an affordable rental and pay-as-you-go model tailored for farmers, food processing units, cold storage facilities, and nurseries. Fully mobile and modular, units can be shifted between locations depending on seasonal or operational needs, ensuring maximum utilization and accessibility. By removing upfront investment barriers, the solution accelerates clean energy adoption across underserved rural areas. Immediate benefits include lower energy costs by up to 50%, reliable power for food production and storage, reduced post-harvest losses, and cleaner, quieter working environments. Importantly, by enabling new agricultural and processing activities, the ReGen-R8 creates job opportunities for youth and women, fostering inclusive rural economic growth. Sustainable long-term impacts include increased resilience of local food systems, higher farm and producer profitability, scalable access to renewable energy, and reduced carbon footprint. By improving productivity, livelihoods, and access to electricity, YY ReGen contributes directly to addressing food insecurity while empowering rural communities and strengthening the overall sustainability of the food value chain.

core_fields.title: Strengthening Drought-Tolerant QDS Production for Smallholder Farmers in Dodoma and Singida Regions-Tanzania
core_fields.description: This project strengthens drought-tolerant seed systems in Dodoma and Singida by empowering smallholder farmers to produce and distribute Quality Declared Seeds (QDS) for sorghum, pigeon pea, and millet. Through training, input support, and improved last-mile distribution, the project increases access to quality seed, enhances climate resilience, reduces counterfeit seed, and boosts farmer incomes improving food security and livelihoods in Tanzania s dryland communities.
core_fields.abstract: The project introduces a community-based model for producing drought-tolerant Quality Declared Seeds (QDS) for sorghum, pigeon pea, and millet crops essential for food security in the dryland regions of Dodoma and Singida. The core innovation lies in shifting seed production from centralized companies to trained smallholder farmers, making high-quality seeds available where they are most needed. The problem addressed is the chronic shortage of affordable, drought-tolerant quality seed, which forces farmers to rely on recycled or counterfeit seeds, resulting in low yields, vulnerability to drought, and persistent food insecurity. This innovation is relevant because climate change continues to intensify droughts in central Tanzania, increasing pressure on households already struggling to produce enough food. The solution integrates scientific seed production protocols, TOSCI-supported QDS certification, and last-mile seed distribution models to ensure availability, accessibility, and traceability of quality seed. Insights from agronomic research show that when farmers use improved drought-tolerant varieties, yields can double or triple even under low-rainfall conditions. By equipping farmers with the skills, foundation seed, and basic tools needed for QDS production, local seed supply becomes reliable, affordable, and climate-resilient. Immediate benefits include improved access to quality seed, higher yields, increased incomes, and reduced dependence on counterfeit and informal seed sources. Sustainable benefits include stronger community seed systems, enhanced climate resilience, reduced environmental degradation through improved crop performance, and long-term food security for households, schools, and rural communities.

core_fields.title: Low-Cost Bio-Nano Micropropagation and Smart Indoor Farming of Disease-Free Cacao Seedlings for Nigerian Farmers
core_fields.description: This is a project developing cost-saving bio-nano methods for the rapid multiplication of disease-free cacao seedlings in tissue culture (micropropagation), in combination with smart indoor farming systems with sensors to ensure that light, water, and nutrients are optimally provided. It reduces propagation costs by 70%, increases yields, and provides disease-free, pest-resistant cacao seedlings; this is ideal for black pod disease prevention and suitable for smallholder farmers in major cacao-producing regions like Nigeria.
core_fields.abstract: The production of cacao is heavily constrained by diseases such as black pod caused by Phytophthora and swollen shoot virus in Nigeria and most countries in West Africa, with estimated annual losses of around 30-40% of total harvests, while the major producers are smallholder farmers with no access to disease-free planting materials. Conventional propagation is time-consuming, expensive, and susceptible to contamination. Our innovation couples low-cost bio-nano micropropagation by using plant-based nanoparticles-from neem or garlic extracts-as antiviral agents in the tissue culture medium with IoT-enabled smart indoor farming. Sensors monitor pH, humidity, light, and nutrients in real time via affordable Arduino/Raspberry Pi set-ups; automated conditions achieve 90% survival rates. This stems from insights in microbial biotech: nanoparticles disrupt pathogen cell walls without harming plant cells, while smart systems mimic optimal tropical microclimates. Farmers get disease-free seedlings 5x faster at 70% lower cost: $0.10/seedling vs. $0.50. Immediate benefits include the farmers producing over 10,000 seedlings per year, increasing yields by 25%; the communities receive stable food or income; and there is a reduction in the use of pesticides within the environment. Sustainable benefits: Can be scaled up for schools for agro-education; producers export at premium price of cacao; society reduces import dependence; ecosystems are conserved through resilient farming.

core_fields.title: Fish for Health and Wealth by enhancing access to climate-smart ponds to Kenya s ASAL communities.
core_fields.description: The project will enable Iviani Farm to scale sustainable fish farming across Kenya s arid and semi-arid lands through training and deployment of smart ponds. We will train 2,000 women and youth, construct 100 smart ponds with water-efficient recirculating systems and an IoT real-time pond management. The project will reduce fish mortality by 25%, increase household incomes by >30%, and enhance access to an affordable source of protein to 15M people in Kenya's ASAL regions.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation deploys 100 smart ponds that combine locally adapted recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) with IoT pond monitoring to cut water use by 75%, reduce fish mortality by 25%, and improve feed conversion by up to 20%. Each smart pond houses 1,000 fish and completes a six-month production cycle without water replacement. Real-time sensors track fish behavior and key water parameters such as pH, temperature, and dissolved oxygen, and use cloud analytics and SMS alerts for prompt corrective action. Hunger and poverty remain persistent challenges in Kenya, particularly in ASAL counties where water scarcity, climate shocks, and limited livelihoods constrain food production. In addition, fish farming is virtually absent in Kenya s ASAL regions because of water scarcity and limited technical capacity. This project solves that problem by marrying a proven closed-loop RAS approach with low-cost IoT for remote management and by training women and youth as trainers of trainers. The novelty lies in adapting RAS to drylands with locally serviceable components and embedding data-driven decision support to make production predictable and low risk. Immediate benefits include two production cycles per year yielding 200,000 fish and a gross revenue potential of KES 100M annually at KES 500 per fish. The project will directly engage 2,000 households and more than 15,000 value-chain participants, increasing incomes, expanding access to nutritious fish, and creating jobs. Sustainable benefits include durable local technical capacity, reduced nutrient discharge, lower land pressure, and a scalable climate-resilient aquaculture model benefiting 15 million people in Kenya's ASAL regions.

core_fields.title: Green Congo-Transforming Organic Waste into Sustainable Agricultural and Energy Solutions
core_fields.description: Green Congo is a social-environmental project that transform urban organic waste into safe compost, bio-fertilizers, biomass pellets, and natural disinfectants in Kinshasa. Its eco-friendly products improve soil health, boost crop yields, and enhance food safety in peri-urban farming zones across Western DRC, while supporting sustainable agriculture, green jobs, and a circular local economy. By collecting and transforming food waste during 24 months, the project will reduce pollution, lower greenhouse-gas emissions, and promote cleaner urban environments.
core_fields.abstract: This project introduces a data-driven initiative that converts urban organic waste into high-value agricultural and clean-energy products, tackling two systemic challenges in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC): unmanaged organic waste and declining soil fertility. Kinshasa, the DRC capital city generates 3,556-8,090 tons per day of organic waste daily, much of which is dumped openly, polluting waterways and emitting methane. Meanwhile, peri-urban farmers in Western DRC pay 80% more for chemical fertilizers, contributing to declining soil health and food insecurity. The project s approach uses scientifically optimized microbial composting and controlled fermentation to convert organic waste into compost, bio-fertilizers (liquid & solid), biomass pellets, and natural disinfectants through its Organic Waste Processing Center in Kinshasa. We will secure feedstock through formal partnerships with markets, enterprises, hotels/restaurants, schools, and municipal authorities, and operate community hubs staffed by trained youth and indigenous groups for decentralized collection and distribution. Products will reach users via a network of agro-dealers and direct sales agents, enabling affordable access specifically within Kinshasa and peri-urban agricultural regions in Western DRC. The project directly improves food safety and nutrition through safe organic fertilizers, school and community garden support, farmer training, and demonstration plots promoting pesticide-free production that advance regenerative practices by diverting over 5,000 tons of organic waste annually, restoring soil carbon, reducing reliance on chemical inputs and lowering household emissions. Long-term benefits include healthier diets, resilient soils, new green jobs per year, reduced emissions, and strengthened local food systems in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

core_fields.title: Harvesting Resilience: Nutrition-Centered Reforestation in Indigenous Maya Communities
core_fields.description: Our project expands Nutrition Forest Corridors in Guatemala s Western Highlands indigenous-led agroforestry systems that increase access to nutritious foods, restore degraded watersheds, and strengthen local livelihoods. By growing women-led nurseries, training smallholder farmers in nutrition-focused agroforestry, and using GIS tools to restore high-risk slopes and spring recharge zones, we create resilient, community-driven food systems. This innovation improves diets, protects ecosystems, and generates sustainable income opportunities while rebuilding ecological function across vulnerable mountain landscapes.
core_fields.abstract: Communities in Guatemala s Western Highlands face declining soil fertility, water scarcity, deforestation, and limited access to nutritious foods. Traditional reforestation programs rarely integrate nutrition, livelihood generation, and watershed restoration into a unified system. Our innovation, Nutrition Forest Corridors, creates community-designed agroforestry systems that restore degraded landscapes while improving food security and climate resilience. The model integrates four complementary components: 1. Nutrition-focused agroforestry: Farmer field schools support families to integrate fruit trees, perennial vegetables, nitrogen-fixing species, coffee/cacao, and native timber into multi-strata systems that enhance diet diversity and regenerate soil and water cycles. 2. Women-led nurseries and microenterprises: Indigenous women cultivate native and fruit seedlings, including nutrient-rich species such as mulberry, supplying the community with climate-resilient planting material while generating income and leadership opportunities. 3. GIS-guided watershed restoration: ArcGIS analysis identifies erosion hotspots, spring recharge zones, and degraded slopes. This guides the establishment of continuous nutrition forest corridors that stabilize soils, protect water sources, and increase biodiversity. 4. Economic feasibility and adoption pathways: National forestry incentives (PINPEP) provide medium-term income, while fruit trees generate early food and cash returns. This dual pathway supports long-term adoption and economic viability. Immediate benefits include improved nutrition, restored soils, and women s economic empowerment. Long-term outcomes include protected watersheds, reduced climate risk, and a scalable, indigenous-led model for regenerative food systems.

core_fields.title: Strengthening the Economic Resilience of Smallholder Farmers Through Digital Finance and Markets
core_fields.description: Smart Mavuno empowers smallholder farmers with insured, collateral-free loans, affordable farm equipment leasing, and a digital marketplace accessible via USSD for non-smartphone users. A solar-powered cold-chain minivan helps reduce post-harvest losses and enables farmers to reach premium buyers. Through climate-smart training, digital credit records, and a pilot insured loan fund, the project strengthens farmer productivity, market access, and income resilience, creating sustainable and inclusive agricultural growth.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Kenya face three major problems: they lose up to 30% of their harvest due to poor storage, earn 30-40% less because middlemen take most of the profit, and over 60% lack access to affordable, insured loans. These challenges trap households in cycles of low income, high risk, and food insecurity, making farming unsustainable. Smart Mavuno solves this by combining finance, technology, and logistics into one integrated solution. Farmers access insured, collateral-free loans through blockchain-backed records, helping them invest in quality seeds, equipment, and storage. The digital marketplace connects farmers directly to buyers, showing real-time prices and ensuring fair payment. A solar-powered cold-chain minivan safely stores produce, reducing post-harvest losses from 30% to under 20%. Digital tools provide agronomic advice and weather alerts, helping farmers make better planting and harvesting decisions. The solution is based on scientific and technical insights showing that finance alone is not enough; farmers also need fair markets, climate-smart storage, and reliable advisory support to increase productivity and income. Immediate benefits: Farmers earn 15-25% more, face less spoilage, and have access to finance and quality inputs. Long-term benefits: Farmers build credit histories, increase productivity, and improve climate resilience. Communities gain more food availability, schools and households get stable supplies, and the environment benefits from reduced food waste and lower emissions. Women and youth are empowered through training and access to credit.Smart Mavuno transforms smallholder farming into profitable, sustainable, and climate-smart livelihoods for rural households.

core_fields.title: Information for Regenerative Practices and Safe Diets: Green Leaf Social Enterprise
core_fields.description: Without relevant timely information, rural farming communities are unable to make informed decisions concerning sustainable practices and safe, healthy diets. Our innovation is a scalable e-extension communication platform that leverages the power of radio and interactive mobile technology to deliver farmer-centered agricultural knowledge at scale across 70% of Uganda reaching over 11 million farmers twice-weekly. The innovation has advanced operating as a social enterprise for sustainability, deepening farmer reach and promoting adoption of regenerative practices.
core_fields.abstract: The gap in advisory extension services severely impacts rural farmers adoption of regenerative agriculture practices. A recent Annual Agriculture survey revealed only 14.3% agricultural households in Uganda received extension services in 2020 and there is low access to agricultural extension services across the country (UBOS, 2020). Face-to-face extension is insufficient and unsustainable with current ratio of extension staff to farmers severely imbalanced at over 1:5,000. Our solution is Green Leaf sustainable dialogue and information sharing platform on regenerative practices. A social enterprise sustained by partnerships with government, technical partners and investors. It harnesses the power of 12 radio stations, reaches 70% of the rural population, and combines with basic mobile phones to bridge the extension gap. Existing solutions from organizations like Farm Africa and M-Omulimisa include equipping extension workers with digital knowledge and tools (apps, smartphones). While this is resourceful, it is limited to agents/farmers with literacy/digital skills and is dependent on access to digital tools and internet data affordability. Limitations of the government-led extension system, coupled with short-term project-based approaches to provision of extension services, prompted innovation of a localized radio-based extension program, set up as a networked platform solving information poverty, targeting rural communities and marginalized groups. The innovation offers an accessible two-way information service that promotes inclusion and multi-stakeholder collaboration in agribusiness from a micro-level. Green Leaf provides critical and quality advisory services twice-weekly to farmers and other rural residents who have limited sources of information on regenerative agriculture and safe diets.

core_fields.title: Rescuing Food and Feeding Communities
core_fields.description: Sharing Excess seeks $250,000 to expand its innovative food rescue operations, addressing food insecurity and food waste. Over two years, the project will scale its technology, including dashboards for tracking and transparency, and increase food access through expanded food rescue routes. This initiative will provide fresh food to over 5 million people, onboard new partners, and improve efficiency. By fostering sustainability and equity, Sharing Excess aims to create lasting community impact and environmental benefits.
core_fields.abstract: Sharing Excess addresses the dual crises of food waste and food insecurity by removing logistical barriers that prevent surplus food from reaching communities in need. In the U.S., nearly 40% of food is wasted annually, generating 8% of global greenhouse gases, while over 47 million Americans face food insecurity, disproportionately impacting low-income, BIPOC, and immigrant communities. This is not a lack of food but a lack of efficient systems to redirect surplus equitably. Since 2018, Sharing Excess has rescued 195 million pounds of surplus food, delivering fresh, nutritious produce to over 5 million people. Our approach operates on three pillars: (1) high-volume food rescue at wholesale markets, intercepting millions of pounds of edible surplus before it reaches landfills; (2) efficient redistribution using a custom technology platform that matches supply with demand and tracks impact in real time; and (3) community-driven design, where local voices guide decisions on what food is needed, when, and where. Community partners distribute this food through choice-based, no-cost programs, prioritizing culturally relevant and nutrient-dense items to ensure equitable access. Immediate benefits include access to fresh produce for over 1 million people annually, cost savings for food providers, and reduced methane emissions. Long-term, our model strengthens the charitable food system, empowers communities, supports sustainable food practices, and is creating replicable solutions nationwide. By combining operational efficiency, data-driven insights, and community-centered design, Sharing Excess transforms surplus into access, delivering measurable social, environmental, and health impact while building a sustainable, equitable food system.

core_fields.title: Generating Field-Based Evidence on Plant-Derived Control of Ripening and Microbial Spoilage
core_fields.description: This project will generate field-based evidence on a plant-derived, non-refrigerated preservation technology that slows ripening and suppresses microbial spoilage in mangoes, bananas, ovacado and oranges. Through pilot deployment with smallholder farmers and traders, the project will measure reductions in post-harvest food loss, preservation of nutritional quality, and user adoption. The results will inform scalable, climate-smart approaches to improving food availability, farmer incomes, and sustainable food systems in the Global South.
core_fields.abstract: Post-harvest food loss is one of the most critical yet overlooked challenges in the Global South, where up to 40 50% of fresh fruits and vegetables spoil before consumption. This loss reduces access to nutritious food, undermines farmer incomes, and wastes scarce natural resources such as water, land, and energy. Cold-chain solutions are often not viable due to high costs, unreliable electricity, and limited infrastructure. This project addresses the problem through Karpoolax, a plant-based, non-refrigerated preservation innovation that slows ripening and suppresses microbial spoilage in fresh produce. The innovation uses biodegradable sachets containing naturally derived plant volatile compounds. When placed inside produce crates or packaging, these compounds act in the surrounding atmosphere to regulate ethylene activity, inhibit spoilage microorganisms, and suppress phospholipase D (PLD), an enzyme that drives cell membrane degradation during ripening and senescence. By reducing PLD activity, the technology helps maintain cellular integrity, firmness, and freshness without direct contact with food. The scientific insight behind this solution comes from plant physiology and post-harvest biology. Plants naturally emit volatile compounds as defense mechanisms and to regulate ripening processes. Research shows that controlling ethylene signaling and PLD activity can significantly delay senescence. This project translates these insights into a controlled-release, field-ready format and generates real-world evidence of effectiveness. Immediate benefits include reduced food spoilage, extended market windows, and improved incomes for smallholder farmers and traders. Consumers gain more reliable access to safe, nutritious produce.

core_fields.title: Meru Poultry Living Lab: Scaling BSF Feed Innovation, Farmer Training, and Safe Market Access
core_fields.description: This project deploys a scalable agri-food living lab that lowers poultry production costs, de-risks smallholder supply, and expands access to safe, affordable protein for mass BoP markets. By commercializing BSF-based feed, upgrading farmer productivity, and anchoring supply to a licensed processor, the model unlocks durable margins, reduces environmental risk, and accelerates market-ready innovation. Integrated research-to-market pathways enable rapid replication, strong unit economics, and measurable social, nutritional, and climate impact.
core_fields.abstract: This innovation strengthens Kenya s poultry value chain by integrating applied research in sustainable feed technologies with practical animal husbandry and inclusive market systems. The approach enhances resilience among rural smallholder farmers while expanding access to safe, nutritious, and affordable poultry products for low-income consumers. Smallholder poultry producers face persistently high feed costs, limited technical training, low-performing breeds, and weak market access constraints that suppress productivity and restrict reliable supply to Base-of-the-Pyramid (BoP) markets. To address these challenges, Meru University of Science and Technology (MUST) and Kulamawe Poultry Industries Ltd (KPI Ltd) are establishing a metro agri-food living lab that enables rapid translation of university research into scalable, field-level solutions. By integrating a licensed private-sector processor, multidisciplinary university departments, organized farmer groups, and end-market actors, the model creates a permanent research-to-field and market feedback loop that accelerates innovation uptake and adaptation. MUST s Sanitation Institute will advance regenerative waste-management solutions by training farmers in Black Soldier Fly (BSF) production and working with the Animal Science Department to develop affordable BSF-based protein concentrates for on-farm feed formulation. This reduces dependence on costly commercial feeds while improving feed efficiency and farm profitability. KPI Ltd will open its Kenya Veterinary Board-licensed slaughterhouse as a practical training hub for food science and animal science students, ensuring academic innovations directly strengthen poultry husbandry, food safety, and processing standards. The Food Science Department will co-develop value-added poultry products such as fortified meats, dried products, and ready-to-cook items while training food vendors in safe handling practices.

core_fields.abstract: VMG s key innovation is an integrated vertical gardening and composting system that creates 36 square-feet of soil with only a 9 sqft footprint. Benefits include: year-round vegetable production[ 4-6 annual harvests], reduced waste, improved nutrition for mothers and children, additional increased income from surplus sales of surplus, lower reliance on synthetic fertilizers, and reduced environmental footprint. The system is highly scalable, low-cost, easy to maintain, and ideal for women, youth, and displaced communities.

core_fields.title: Indigenous Climate-Resilient Food Systems: From Taps to Boreholes, Syntropic Farming, and Community Resilience in Namibia
core_fields.description: In rural Namibia, repeated droughts and climate shocks push Indigenous communities into severe food insecurity and poverty. The Marginalised Mirror pilots a proven climate-resilient food system with 50 Indigenous families using community irrigation. The Seed Grant will expand this to a solar-powered borehole, extending food security benefits to additional villages while also providing clean water. By integrating syntropic agroforestry, water security, and rights-based knowledge-sharing, we demonstrate a scalable, community-owned model that transforms landscapes and lives.
core_fields.abstract: The problem: Namibia is experiencing an agricultural crisis: repeated droughts, below-average rainfall, and El Ni o variability have caused widespread crop failure, livestock deaths, and water shortages, pushing Indigenous communities into severe poverty and malnutrition. Conventional top-down projects fail because they ignore Indigenous knowledge and land rights. The solution: Our innovation is a community-led, work-based place model integrating three core elements: 1. Regenerative syntropic agriculture that plants like a forest, restoring soil, biodiversity and productivity; 2. Sustainable water infrastructure: expanding from a successful tap-fed irrigation pilot (currently serving 50 families) to a solar-powered borehole serving multiple villages with food production and clean water access; 3. Rights-based knowledge-sharing on responsible agriculture, Indigenous land/water rights, and ancestral territories. While individual components exist elsewhere, very few combine them into one integrated, community-designed platform. The key insight: food system transformation must happen in the place where people work every day, aligning Indigenous knowledge with regenerative practices and economic incentives. Benefits: Immediate: improved food access and nutrition, reduced climate-driven crop failure, new income from surplus produce, and water security. Sustainable: restored soils and water cycles, stronger understanding of land rights, increased community pride and confidence, replicable model for other Indigenous territories.

core_fields.title: Traceable Ethiopian Herbal Lactation Tea Improving Maternal Nutrition and Smallholder Farmer Incomes
core_fields.description: Kuri produces an affordable, food-grade herbal lactation tea using locally sourced Ethiopian herbs and standardized processing. It supports postpartum mothers nutrition and hydration while creating reliable demand for smallholder herb farmers through contract sourcing, quality specifications, and batch traceability. By improving consistency and safety versus informal remedies and expensive imports, Kuri strengthens maternal nutrition, rural livelihoods, and a more resilient local food system.
core_fields.abstract: Postpartum mothers in Ethiopia often lack safe, trusted, and affordable nutrition-support options that fit local diets and daily routines, especially working mothers balancing recovery, breastfeeding, and time constraints. In the absence of a standardized lactation product, families frequently rely on informal, home-prepared herbal mixtures with variable quality. At the same time, imported supplements (where available) are often costly and inconsistent, increasing stress and limiting practical support for breastfeeding and maternal nutrition. Kuri addresses this by producing a ready-to-brew, food-grade herbal lactation tea made from Ethiopian herbs such as fenugreek, fennel, nettle, mint, lemongrass, and cinnamon. The innovation is not only the product but the system behind it: contract sourcing from smallholder farmers, clear post-harvest handling standards, batch-level traceability, controlled drying and blending, and hygienic packaging, improving consistency and food safety while keeping the product accessible. The solution emerged from the founders clinical and public health experience and their direct observation of significant breastfeeding challenges among working mothers, informing a practical product designed for trust, convenience, and scale. Kuri is novel in Ethiopia because there is no known locally available, purpose-built lactation tea product in the market. Kuri provides immediate benefits by offering a convenient, culturally familiar tea that supports mothers hydration and dietary intake, with clear preparation and usage guidance through standardized packaging. It delivers sustainable benefits by creating more predictable income for smallholder herb farmers through structured sourcing, generating local jobs in aggregation and processing, and reducing post-harvest losses.

core_fields.title: Pathways for Optimal School Health, Access & Nutrition at SCALE - POSHAN SCALE
core_fields.description: Mandala Foods is a women-powered circular food enterprise that upcycles both surplus and non-marketable Nepali fruits into affordable, nutrient-dense snacks for schoolchildren and low-income families. By connecting farmers, women-led processing, and school meal programs, we reduce food loss, boost rural farm incomes, and deliver reliable nutrition for just 11 cents a child. With WHH support, we will strengthen and scale school partnerships in Nepal, with scalable potential in South Asia.
core_fields.abstract: In Nepal, up to 40% of fruits are lost post-harvest while millions of schoolchildren lack daily access to micronutrient-rich foods. Women remain underpaid in local food economies, and climate change is increasing harvest volatility and waste. Food security has often meant any calories . Our innovation at Mandala Foods shifts attention to nutrient density, daily nutrient needs, and the dignity of income. Mandala Foods is a women-led circular food model that preserves surplus and market-rejected fruits from smallholders using cost-effective technologies like passive Modified Activated Packaging (MAP) bags, upcycles them into shelf-stable, nutrient-dense pur es, spreads, and snack bars, and redistributes them as school snacks. Using energy-efficient processing, strict food-safety protocols, and good manufacturing practices (GMP), we preserve fiber, vitamins, and natural fruit goodness without added sugar. The core scientific and technical insights are: simple, low-energy technologies can safely upcycle fruits into high-value products. nutrient-dense fruit snacks can replace ultra-processed, sugar-rich foods in school markets. Women-run micro-enterprises (Smart Bakery hubs) are effective last-mile delivery systems. Immediate benefits: Farmers receive guaranteed off-take and fair prices. Community women gain paid work, training, and ownership. Children access affordable, nutrient-dense snacks through schools, while households receive nutrition guidance. Sustained benefits: Reduced food loss and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, resilient local fruit value chains, stronger women-led enterprises, and scalable models that can be adapted in South Asia (Bangladesh, India, and beyond) through knowledge transfer and regional sourcing partnerships.

core_fields.title: Turning Waste into Food and Energy: A Bioshikha-Based Circular Food System in Rajbari District
core_fields.description: This project pilots the Bioshikha circular system in Rajbari District, Bangladesh, integrating clean cooking with organic food production. The initiative uses bio-slurry from Bioshikha units as fertilizer to grow safe and nutritious vegetables, while training women and youth in system use, sustainable farming, and food practices. By linking waste-to-energy solutions with local food systems, the project improves household health, food security, and livelihoods in climate-vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation is the Bioshikha circular clean cooking and food production system, which addresses interconnected problems of unsafe cooking practices, organic waste mismanagement, declining soil fertility, and limited access to safe and nutritious food in rural Bangladesh. Many households still rely on biomass cooking, causing indoor air pollution and health risks, while organic waste and animal dung are underutilized and chemical fertilizers degrade soil quality. Bioshikha integrates a household-scale bio-digestion system that converts organic waste into clean cooking energy and produces nutrient-rich bio-slurry as a by-product. Instead of being discarded, this bio-slurry is applied as an organic fertilizer for home gardens and small-scale food production. The scientific insight behind this solution is the well-established process of anaerobic digestion, which safely stabilizes organic matter, reduces pathogens, and enhances nutrient availability for crops. The project solves the problem through piloting Bioshikha units, hands-on training, and community-led adoption, with a strong focus on women and youth. Immediate benefits include reduced indoor air pollution, lower fuel costs, improved soil fertility, and increased access to fresh vegetables. Sustainable benefits include improved household nutrition, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, healthier soils, climate-resilient food production, and strengthened local circular economies. Communities benefit from cleaner environments, enhanced skills, and a scalable model that links clean energy, sustainable agriculture, and food security in an inclusive and environmentally responsible way.

core_fields.title: Agro-Waste to Food Value Intelligence Platform Agro
core_fields.description: The Agro-Waste to Food Value Intelligence Platform is a decision-support system that converts agricultural waste data into actionable intelligence for climate-resilient food systems. By integrating crop residue availability, climate stress, and local value pathways, the platform enables anticipatory actions such as waste diversion, composting, and feedstock optimisation. Led by AUST, the project delivers a scalable, non-extractive intelligence layer that strengthens food security and circular agriculture in Nigeria and beyond.
core_fields.abstract: Innovation Description and Benefits Agricultural systems across Nigeria and much of Africa face a persistent paradox: large volumes of agro-waste coexist with food insecurity, climate stress, and declining soil productivity. The core problem is not the absence of technologies, but the absence of decision-ready intelligence that connects waste availability, climate risk, and feasible food value pathways in time to act. The Agro-Waste to Food Value Intelligence Platform addresses this gap by transforming fragmented data on crop residues, climate and water stress, and local agricultural practices into actionable signals that enable anticipatory, circular responses. Instead of reacting to losses after they occur, the platform supports early decisions such as targeted composting, soil amendment, feedstock diversion, or other locally appropriate waste-to-value actions. The innovation lies in its systems-integration approach. Drawing on insights from climate science, agricultural systems, and decision modelling, the platform integrates existing datasets rather than inventing new hardware or extractive data pipelines. A probabilistic decision logic links agro-waste availability, environmental stress indicators, and context-specific value options, generating simple, actionable guidance for institutions and intermediaries. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, improved soil health, and more efficient use of agricultural residues for farmers and cooperatives. Over time, the platform strengthens climate resilience, supports circular food systems, reduces environmental pollution from unmanaged waste, and enables evidence-based planning by public institutions and development partners. By design, the solution is scalable, non-extractive, and institutionally adoptable, ensuring sustained benefits for communities and the environment.

core_fields.title: Turning Fish Waste into Nutrition: Calcium Innovation for Healthy Children and Sustainable Communities.
core_fields.description: This project addresses child calcium deficiency and fish waste in Northeast Thailand by converting discarded fish bones into safe, calcium-rich powder using GMP-certified, solar-powered processes. Integrated into school meals, the innovation improves nutrition for vulnerable children, reduces greenhouse gas emissions, and creates community micro-enterprises for fishing families. Over 18 months, it will benefit 10,300 people, foster circular food systems, and establish a scalable, replicable model aligned with SDGs on health, sustainability, and economic growth.
core_fields.abstract: This project addresses two urgent challenges in Northeast Thailand (Esan) including severe calcium deficiency among children and significant food waste from freshwater fisheries. Research from Mahidol University, Northeast School Children Study shows schoolchildren in Esan consume only about 130 mg of calcium per day, far below the recommended intake. National nutrition surveys confirm Esan has the highest stunting rate in Thailand (~18 19%), linked to micronutrient deficiencies including calcium and vitamin D. At the same time, communities around Ubolratana Dam in Nong Bua Lamphu and Khon Kaen provinces catch over 350 tons of fish annually, generating 87 122 tons of fish bones and scraps currently discarded as waste. This practice creates environmental burdens and greenhouse gas emissions. The innovation transforms these fish bones into safe, calcium-rich powder using GMP-certified processes, solar-powered drying, and rigorous lab testing for heavy metals and microbial safety. This approach leverages food science and circular economic principles to create a sustainable, affordable nutritional supplement without relying on large-scale factories. Immediate benefits include improved child nutrition through school meals and household diets, reduced organic waste, and new income streams for fishing families via community micro-enterprises. Long-term benefits include healthier growth and learning outcomes for children, reduced greenhouse gas emissions from decomposing fish waste, and a replicable model for other regions. By linking nutrition, sustainability, and livelihoods, this innovation drives systemic change toward equitable and regenerative food systems.

core_fields.title: Digital Climate Smart Seed and Nutrition Hub for Smallholder Farmers in Rwanda
core_fields.description: Agriresearch Unguka Ltd will pilot a 5 hectare Digital Climate Smart Seed and Nutrition Hub that integrates certified seed production of Irish potatoes, wheat and biofortified beans with a 1 hectare dairy unit and the "SmartInput" digital advisory platform. The project will supply traceable, high yielding seed, organic compost and affordable milk to smallholders around Rwerere, improving productivity, soil health and rural nutrition while de-risking a scalable, youth-led regenerative model for Rwanda s seed system.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Rwanda face chronic shortages of certified seed for Irish potatoes, wheat and beans, leading to low yields, seed borne diseases and dependence on informal markets. At the same time, rural households struggle with soil degradation, climate variability and persistent malnutrition, including protein and micronutrient deficiencies. The Digital Climate Smart Seed and Nutrition Hub addresses these interlinked challenges. The project will establish a 5 hectare integrated hub at Rwerere and partner RAB stations that combines certified seed production for potatoes, wheat and biofortified beans on 4 hectares with a 1 hectare dairy unit for organic manure and milk. The SmartInput digital platform will provide end to end traceability, farmer profiling, e ordering and tailored advisory on climate smart practices. This model is novel in Rwanda because it unites seed systems, livestock, digital advisory and nutrition in one regenerative, youth led platform rather than treating them as separate value chains. Existing solutions focus either on standalone seed multiplication, conventional extension, or fragmented dairy services, often without digital traceability or guaranteed market linkages. End users (smallholder farmers, cooperatives, schools and local consumers) benefit from access to disease free, high yielding seed, organic compost, and affordable, safe milk that supports community nutrition. Farmers gain climate smart extension, fair pricing, and buy back contracts that reduce risk and strengthen market inclusion. Over time, the hub is expected to raise yields, stabilize incomes, improve diet quality and reduce environmental pressure through better nutrient management, crop rotation and reduced reliance on synthetic fertilizers.

core_fields.title: Carbon-Financed Agroforestry for Resilient Smallholder Food Systems
core_fields.description: This project works with smallholder farmers in Northern Malawi to turn degraded land into productive, resilient farms. Working with farmers, especially women and youth, we will establish syntropic agroforestry systems that combine food crops, fruit and nut trees, and soil-restoring species. Upfront costs are covered through blended financing, while a digital monitoring system tracks food, income and environmental outcomes to enable sustainable scale.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Malawi depend on land that is increasingly degraded by soil erosion, declining fertility and climate shocks. As a result, food yields are falling, diets are limited, and household incomes are unstable. While agroforestry is widely recognized as a solution, most farmers cannot adopt it because the transition requires upfront cash, labor and technical support that they do not have. Our innovation removes this barrier by combining syntropic agroforestry with blended financing and digital monitoring. Farmers establish diversified systems that integrate food crops with fruit, nut and nitrogen-fixing trees, restoring soil health while producing food and income throughout the year. Upfront costs for seedlings, training and monitoring are covered, allowing farmers to participate without financial risk. The approach is grounded in well-established agroecological science showing that diverse, layered systems improve soil structure, water retention, nutrient cycling and resilience to climate variability. We pair this with practical insight from working alongside farmers and with a digital platform that tracks tree survival, farm practices, food production and income at plot level. This creates transparency, accountability and trust for farmers, communities and funders. Immediate benefits include improved crop yields, early income from short-cycle products such as bananas, mushrooms and honey, and reduced vulnerability to climate shocks. Over time, farmers gain higher-value tree crops, more diverse diets, stable incomes and restored land. Communities benefit from healthier landscapes, increased food availability and local climate mitigation, creating a sustainable pathway for resilient smallholder food systems.

core_fields.title: Strengthening Nutritious Food Systems Through AMCOS Offtaker Partnerships for Improved Household Diets

core_fields.abstract: TAPBDS introduces an innovation that strengthens AMCOS in Katavi, Rukwa, and Tabora to become reliable hubs for producing and supplying safe, nutritious cereal crops. The regions face food shortages, malnutrition and unstable markets because most farmers depend on traditional cash crops like tobacco and cotton, have limited access to improved seeds and lack structured relationships with offtakers. This makes nutritious cereals scarce, unsafe, or unaffordable for households and institutions. The innovation solves this by providing coordinated technical assistance to AMCOS and offtakers/ anchor firms, building their capacity to manage inputs, negotiate structured contracts, ensure grain quality and facilitate stable supply chains. Through these contracts, offtakers are enabled to supply improved and nutricious seeds to farmers via AMCOS, strengthening both sides and creating predictable, transparent market relationships. Insights from TAPBDS s extensive market systems development work show that when farmer organizations are strengthened and linked to reliable buyers(offtakers/anchor firms), adoption of improved seeds increases, yields rise and nutritious food availability expands. Evidence from the Mavuno Millers Limited-AMCOS model further confirms that structured contracting reduces risk and stabilizes grain supply. Through the internvation, TAPBDS also intends to provide technical assistance to the anchor firms in area of finance,budgeting, human resource,contract management and overall compliance. End users benefit immediately and sustainably: farmers achieve higher yields and stable incomes; households and schools access safer, nutritious food; processors receive consistent quality supplies; and communities experience reduced malnutrition, stronger local economies and more climate-smart cereal production. This creates a resilient, nutrition-focused food system with long-term impact.

core_fields.title: Transforming Local Food Systems for Nutrition, Regeneration, and Equitable Market Access in Homabay and Migori
core_fields.description: The project transforms food systems in Homa Bay and Migori Counties by promoting safe, nutrient-rich food production, regenerative farming, and equitable market access. Farmers adopt biofortified crops, climate-smart practices, and improved post-harvest methods, while producer groups link to off-takers through digital platforms and quality-assured supply chains. Nutrition interventions improve dietary diversity. The initiative boosts productivity, reduces food loss, strengthens livelihoods and rural economies, improves health, and builds long-term environmental resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Homa Bay and Migori Counties face interconnected challenges of poor nutrition, declining soil health, climate vulnerability, and limited market access. This project addresses these constraints through three integrated pillars that transform local food systems. First, it strengthens nutrition-sensitive seed systems by expanding access to biofortified, nutrient-dense, and locally preferred crops through reliable last-mile distribution and farmer-managed seed systems, improving availability of safe and nutritious foods. Second, the project promotes regenerative, climate-smart agriculture via community-based champions who equip farmers with practical soil restoration skills, including vermiculture, black soldier fly production, effective microorganisms, biochar, and composting. These practices improve soil health, enhance water-use efficiency, reduce losses and input costs, and build long-term climate resilience. Third, the initiative advances inclusive market innovations by strengthening farmer groups to aggregate produce, improve quality, negotiate better prices, and access transparent markets, supported by flexible credit mechanisms and short-cycle value chains that create opportunities for women, youth, and people with disabilities. The approach is novel in its integration of seed systems, regenerative practices, soil health improvement, and market access into a single, community-led model anchored in agro-dealers and farmer groups. While individual elements exist elsewhere, their coordinated, evidence-based application is new to these counties. Immediate benefits include higher yields, reduced losses, lower costs, and improved access to nutritious foods. Long-term outcomes include healthier soils, resilient production systems, stronger incomes, trusted local markets, and sustained nutrition, environmental, and economic gains for communities.

core_fields.title: Odor-Neutral 20% Soy-Enriched Maize Staple Flour for Better Nutrition
core_fields.description: We will scale a simple hydrothermal soybean pre-treatment that enables odor-neutral soybean flour to be blended into maize flour for 20% soybean-enriched nsima. This solves the main adoption barrier for soy fortification, off-beany flavor, while improving protein and energy density in a familiar staple. Our Malawi studies showed 20% soybean-enriched nsima was acceptable ( >=5/7 on a Hedonic scale ) and not detected by consumers, and a 90-day intervention recorded higher body weight versus
core_fields.abstract: Nsima, a maize-based stiff porridge, is a principal staple across Southern and Eastern Africa, yet it is protein-deficient and many households cannot afford animal-source foods. Adding soy often fails because nsima is expected to be flat, neutral, and flavorless, and small taste deviations are rejected. Common soybean processing for porridges, such as roasting or extrusion, creates flavor compounds that are unsuitable for stiff porridge. Raw maize-soy blends are also impractical because they take longer to cook and still retain beany notes. Beany off-flavors arise largely from lipoxygenase-driven reactions during grinding. Hydrothermal treatment can deactivate lipoxygenase at 80 C or higher before off-flavors form. Our innovation was applying this principle specifically to nsima by developing a hydrothermal pre-treatment and blending approach that produces odor-neutral soybean flour suitable for 20% soybean enrichment in maize flour, without compromising nsima sensory expectations. In Malawi, our study showed 20% soybean-enriched nsima achieved hedonic acceptability scores of at least 5/7 and consumers did not detect soybean inclusion (Kalumbi et al., 2019). In a single-blind 90-day household intervention using soybean-fortified maize flour (1:4 soy:maize, wt/wt), participants recorded 3.7 to 5.2% higher body weight than controls across age groups (Mtimuni et al., 2023). Immediate benefits include a familiar staple with improved nutrient density while maintaining trusted taste, cooking behavior, and household routines at scale. Sustainable benefits include stronger demand for locally produced soybeans for farmers, practical processing compatible with community mills and school feeding supply chains, and scalable nutrition gains for households, schools, and communities.

core_fields.abstract: The NVC Foundation's Mingo Meals Nutrition Program addresses the high prevalence of stunting among children aged 6 months to 5 years in Negros Occidental, a problem linked to inadequate access to nutritious, culturally appropriate food and gaps in health services and caregiver knowledge. The program solves this by providing a holistic, systems-level approach integrating Mingo, a locally manufactured nutrient-rich complementary food made from rice, mongo, and malunggay, with milk and vitamins, growth monitoring, medical check-ups, mothers' classes, quarterly Mingo assemblies, and community pantry support. This solution draws on scientific insights from nutrition and child development research emphasizing the first 1,000 days as critical for growth and cognitive development, and the importance of micronutrient intake for immune function. The combination of nutrient provision, caregiver education, and integrated community services ensures both immediate and long-term impacts. Immediate benefits include improved child growth indicators, enhanced caregiver knowledge, better health monitoring, and access to nutrient-dense food. Sustainable benefits extend to strengthened local food systems through the use of locally sourced ingredients, community capacity building, increased resilience against malnutrition, and a replicable model for other high-risk areas. By combining technical nutrition knowledge with culturally and locally relevant practices, the program not only addresses stunting but also empowers families, reinforces social support networks, and contributes to healthier, more resilient communities.

core_fields.title: Transforming Food and Nutrition through Climate-Smart Agriculture and AI-Enabled Integrity Systems in Bwari Area, Nigeria
core_fields.description: This project will transform the food system in Bwari Area Council of Nigeria's Federal Capital Territory (FCT) by strengthening food safety skills, climate-smart agricultural (CSA) production, and nutrition outcomes for smallholder farmers, especially women and youth. It integrates regenerative agriculture, hygienic processing, and AI-enabled climate and integrity systems to reduce current heavy postharvest losses, adapt to climate shocks, and improve access to safe, nutritious food. Multi-sector partnerships will ensure scalable, transparent, and resilient food system.
core_fields.abstract: The Bwari Food System Innovation addresses declining agricultural productivity, high post-harvest losses, food safety risks, and poor nutrition outcomes driven by climate change, economic instability, and weak coordination across the food value chain. Smallholder farmers, especially women and youth, face unpredictable rainfall, soil degradation, limited access to climate information, unsafe storage and processing practices, and poor market linkages, resulting in food loss, low incomes, and unsafe food for consumers. The innovation integrates climate-smart agriculture (CSA), regenerative production, and AI-enabled integrity and climate information systems into a single, community-anchored solution. Farmers are trained in food safety, regenerative practices, and clean processing while adopting climate-resilient crops, soil restoration techniques, and water-efficient methods. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools translate local weather, satellite, and farm data into simple, actionable advisories for planting, harvesting, storage, and risk prevention. Digital integrity systems improve traceability, reduce post-harvest losses, and strengthen trust across markets. This solution is informed by evidence that regenerative agriculture improves soil health and yields under climate stress, while AI-driven decision support significantly reduces climate risk and food loss when adapted to local contexts. The immediate benefits of the project include improved yields, safer food, reduced losses, and higher incomes for farmers. Schools and communities gain access to more affordable, nutritious food. Long-term benefits include healthier ecosystems, lower emissions, resilient livelihoods, empowered women and youth who acquire better skills of agricultural production, financial literacy, and linkage to finance, improved nutrition outcomes, and a coordinated, transparent food system that can scale across the FCT and beyond.

core_fields.title: Cashew Apples for a Change: A Vertical Integration of A Forgotten By-Product
core_fields.description: Through an ideal innovative food processing, the underutilized cashew apples are proven to bring economic, environmental, and social beneficials for cashew stakeholders and the cashew sub-sector as a whole. This Cashew Apples for a Change: A Vertical Integration of A Forgotten By-Product project is going to shift the focus of stakeholders along the cashew value chain to realize the potentials of this often neglected and forgotten by-product through capacity building, food processing and marketing campaigns.
core_fields.abstract: According to Cambodia National policy for agricultural development 2022- 2030, the cashew production across the country has increased significantly in the last decade. By 2021, the cashew cultivation area had increased to 405,991 hectares and the harvesting area to 275,679 hectares, with an average yield of 1.74 tons per hectare and a total yield of 472,636 tons per year. However, Cambodia s cashew production is still facing many challenges in either production and value-added activities. Most interventions initiated by the government and the development agencies focus heavily on cashew nut value chains, while the cashew apples are often overlooked after they are separated from the nuts during the harvests. Million tons of ripe cashew apples are left to rot each year at the field. This proposed project seeks to vertically integrate cashew apple value chains, aiming at scaling up domestic processing of cashew by-products, specifically from cashew apples, and contributing to reduce million tons of cashew apple waste annually. The processing of cashew apples into vinegar has been proven successful at ECOLAND s facility/lab through established two-stage fermentation technology. ECOLAND is now ready to go on to the next steps with this innovation through a replicated initiative with communities by transferring the processing knowledge to two cashew nut agricultural cooperatives in Kampong Thom province, and supporting them to build processing facilities and commercialize the products to the markets.

core_fields.title: Solar-powered spice processing
core_fields.description: In Ethiopia s spice sector, over 70% of agro-processors rely on firewood and diesel as their primary thermal energy source, generating an estimated 278,000 metric tons of CO₂ annually and causing 25 35% post-harvest losses. Green Scene Energy introduces solar-powered spice processing to replace firewood-based methods, reducing deforestation, emissions, and losses. Clean processing safeguards nutritional quality and food safety while enabling equitable access for farmers through cooperatives, unions and SACCOS to lease systems and connect to markets.
core_fields.abstract: In Ethiopia s spice sector, over 70% of agro-processors rely on firewood and diesel for energy, generating approximately 278,000 metric tons of CO₂ annually, driving deforestation, and causing 25 35% post-harvest losses due-to inefficient drying and storage. These losses reduce product quality and farmer incomes, while rural electrification below 43% limits access to clean processing solutions. Traditional high-carbon processing is therefore environmentally unsustainable and economically restrictive for farmers, cooperatives, and communities. Green Scene Energy introduces solar-powered agro-processing hubs for spices. These decentralized facilities use renewable solar energy for washing, boiling, slicing, drying and milling preserving nutritional quality, ensuring food safety, and enhancing marketable product value. The model enables cooperatives, unions, and SACCOs leveraging Ethiopia s over 92,000 agricultural cooperatives and more than 21,000 SACCOs to lease and give access to energy without upfront costs, including partnerships with MFIs, fostering equitable participation for smallholders and women farmers. The technical insight behind this approach is that controlled, smoke-free solar processing significantly reduces contamination, and spoilage while retaining essential nutrients and volatile compounds. By replacing firewood and diesel, the innovation lowers emissions, mitigates deforestation, and strengthens climate resilience. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, higher-quality spices, faster processing (reducing traditional sun-drying from 20 days to 1 4 days) safer working conditions, lower labor burden and improved economic returns for farmers and producer groups. Sustainable impacts extend to society and the environment through lower CO₂ emissions, preserved natural resources, improved food safety, and the development of a regenerative, resilient, and inclusive spice value chain within planetary boundaries.

core_fields.title: Building Climate-Smart Grain Market Infrastructure for Smallholder-Led Food System Resilience
core_fields.description: The project builds climate-smart grain market infrastructure that enables smallholder farmers to reliably produce, store, finance, and supply staple crops. By deploying pop-up Farmer Service Centers, digital farm and credit scoring tools, and tradeable warehouse receipts, the project reduces post-harvest losses, improves access to finance, and connects farmers to structured grain markets. This strengthens food security, farmer incomes, and resilience across key staple value chains.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers produce most of Africa s staple grains, yet they remain poor because fragmented markets, weak storage, limited access to finance, and high post-harvest losses prevent them from selling reliably or at fair prices. As a result, food availability is unstable, incomes are low, and grain value chains remain inefficient and vulnerable to climate shocks. This problem is highly relevant as population growth, climate stress, and global supply disruptions continue to threaten food security. Our innovation solves this by integrating physical and digital infrastructure into a single, scalable system for grain aggregation and trade. We deploy pop-up Farmer Service Centers that provide standardized aggregation, quality control, and storage close to farmers. These centers are powered by digital tools that register farmers, track volumes, generate farm-level credit scores through YieldMax, and issue tradeable warehouse receipts backed by stored commodities. The solution is informed by proven insights from commodity exchanges, warehouse receipt systems, and climate-smart agriculture: when farmers can store safely, verify quality, and access finance against their produce, they avoid distress sales and supply markets more consistently. Digitizing these processes reduces transaction costs, builds trust, and unlocks working capital across the value chain. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, faster access to finance, better prices for farmers, and a reliable grain supply for buyers. Sustainably, the system strengthens local food availability, increases farmer incomes, enables data-driven decision-making, and builds resilient, transparent grain markets that support long-term food system stability and climate resilience.
