Through sustainable agriculture training, eco-friendly crafts, and planting 10,000+ trees, the project provides income opportunities, enhances nutrition, and revitalizes cultural knowledge, creating a regenerative, resilient, and equitable food system that benefits both communities and the environment.
core_fields.abstract: The project is a pioneering initiative that aims to fight against environmental degradation and hunger in the region of Southwest Cameroon, particularly in the 13 indigenous villages that are impacted the most. The cutting down of trees, depletion of soil, and use of non-environmental friendly farming practices have all contributed to low crop yield, loss of animals and plants, and the local people becoming poorer, as they do not have the necessary skills and access to different sources of income. The project is built around an innovative idea which is an ecosystem restoration alongside development of livelihoods in the village. The project intends to plant over 10,000 trees that will produce both timber and fruits, teach the sustainable practice of agriculture, and eco-friendly crafts to 2,500 individuals, as well as make the use of indigenous knowledge. The project is simultaneously restoring soil and biodiversity through reduced dependency on forest exploitation. Scientific knowledge gained from agroforestry and regenerative land management is used to determine appropriate sites for taking up trees and practicing intercropping, thus assuring both ecological resilience and long-term productivity. The project will provide immediate advantages such as diversified and nutritious food supplies, new sources of income, and better trained youth and women. The eco-sustainable benefits of the project will be the rebirth of forest ecosystems, better soils, strengthened local food systems, and cultural and environmental stewardship for the long term. The communities will own the conservation efforts, thus contributing to the creation of resilient, equitable, and regenerative food systems.

core_fields.title: FARMING FOR MALNUTRITION
core_fields.description: Malnutrition kills over 3 million children yearly in Sub-Saharan Africa, including 63,000 in Tanzania. Climate-driven crop failures deepen nutrient shortages, leaving vulnerable mothers and children without reliable, life-saving food.Farming for Malnutrition empowers climate-vulnerable families to grow their own clinically appropriate, child specific, life-saving nutrients using the AgriSprout Box, a climate adaptation micro-farming tool designed for low rainfall, low-resource settings. We work for the future where Climate Crisis is not Preventing children from being Fed.
core_fields.abstract: Farming for Malnutrition is a community-centered nutrition resilience project designed for the realities of today s climate crisis, where malnutrition is increasingly driven not only by poverty but by collapsing local food systems. The project enables vulnerable households-including those in refugee settlements, indigenous communities, and climate-stricken rural areas-to produce clinically appropriate nutrients for children under five using AgriSprout Box, a climate-adaptation micro-farming technology engineered for low-rainfall and low-resource settings where traditional agriculture can no longer be relied upon. The innovation integrates three scientific pillars: WHO-approved nutrient seed varieties rich in iron, zinc, vitamin A, and essential proteins needed for optimal early childhood development; Low-water, protected cultivation systems that maintain stable growing conditions despite extreme heat, water scarcity, or erratic rainfall; Behavior-change and nutrition support to ensure harvests are translated into improved maternal and child dietary outcomes. Drawing on climate-smart agronomy, micro-environment design, and first-1,000-days nutrition science, the AgriSprout Box reduces water use by up to 80%. This makes it suitable for mobile populations such as refugees, culturally specific diets in indigenous communities, and remote households facing recurrent crop failure. Immediate benefits include predictable access to nutrient-dense foods, reduced dependence on fluctuating markets, and improved dietary diversity for pregnant women and young children. Long-term benefits include strengthened climate resilience, localized nutrition production, community self-reliance, and reduced dependence on emergency feeding programs.

core_fields.abstract: Calcium deficiency remains a major global health concern, contributing to bone disorders, poor growth, and weakened immunity especially in developing regions. Meanwhile millions of tons of eggshells waste are discarded annually, polluting the environment. Our innovation bridges this gap by transforming eggshell waste into a safe, affordable, and bioavailable calcium supplement for human consumption. Using a novel low-energy processing technology, eggshells are sterilized, refined, and converted into nano-calcium powder ensuring high purity and absorption efficiency. The process is sustainable requiring minimal chemicals and producing near to zero waste. The solution is relevant because it tackles two critical challenges simultaneously, nutritional deficiency and environmental pollution. It empowers communities through local sourcing, waste collection, and manufacturing creating green employment opportunities. Scientifically, the innovation leverages the naturally high calcium carbonate content (about 95%) of eggshells, processed into a fine bioavailable form. This ensures both nutritional impact and environmental responsibility. Immediate benefits include; improved calcium intake for consumers, reduced waste for communities, and new income opportunities for producers. Sustainable benefits include; a circular economy model, healthier population, and environment protection through waste reduction and responsible production.

core_fields.title: Improving Smallholder Farmers Access to Finance by Leveraging Production Data
core_fields.description: Smallholder farmers make up 80% of Kenya's farming population, supporting about 9.7 million households that farm to 1 acre. Key value chains such as dairy, horticulture, grains, and poultry drive rural livelihoods but face persistent inefficiencies. Our AI-enabled data management platform uses production data to power credit appraisal and integrate payments, enabling farmers to access finance through partnerships with their buyers. Buyers also use our platform to track produce flows and analyze patterns.
core_fields.abstract: Produce buyers, such as farmer cooperatives and private enterprises, often struggle to track production records from the farmers they source from accurately. This gap exposes them to losses caused by fraud or produce theft, sometimes involving staff or collusion with farmers. To recover these losses, enterprises typically reduce the prices paid to farmers. Meanwhile, farmers lack verifiable financial records, limiting their access to credit. Our web-hosted enterprise platform, supported by mobile applications, enables buyers to accurately track every stage of their operations from produce purchase to processing and sales. The platform also allows enterprises to provide inputs to farmers on credit and automatically recover the value during produce payments. For farmers, the digital records generated through our system create reliable financial histories that commercial lenders can use for credit appraisal. In addition, farmers gain access to a network of peers, extension information, and advisory support that strengthens their productivity and resilience. By serving the needs of produce off-takers, i.e, farmer cooperatives and vertically integrated enterprises alongside those of the smallholder farmers they serve, we have created a thriving ecosystem where each of the key value chain actors in the food production system can flourish. For the buyers, they get certainty that the produce they sourced was accurate, and thus they can confidently calculate their margins. For the farmers, they get to connect to a network of fellow farmers, access essential inputs on credit, and use their production data to access much-needed financing. Ultimately, the cost of food reduces.

core_fields.title: ProteinCore Kenya
core_fields.description: ProteinCore Kenya pioneers a climate-smart bioprocessing model that converts indigenous legumes like pigeon-peas into affordable, fortified plant protein concentrates for food and feed applications. The project pilot s human-grade proteins for plant-based foods, therapeutic and nutrition applications and feed-grade proteins for animals. By building a circular, locally integrated value chain linking farmers, processors and food-innovators, ProteinCore Kenya reduces reliance on imports, strengthens local industries and accelerates Kenya s transition toward a sustainable, nutrition-secure and climate-resilient food -system.
core_fields.abstract: Kenya faces an escalating protein deficit driven by dependence on imported soy and fishmeal, both costly, environmentally intensive and vulnerable to global price shocks. This shortage limits access to affordable, nutritious foods and constrains growth of the future foods industry. ProteinCore Kenya introduces a locally anchored, science-driven innovation that transforms climate-resilient indigenous legumes like cowpeas, pigeon peas and mung beans into high-quality, affordable protein concentrates for both human nutrition and livestock feed. Using low-energy mechanical extraction, green processing technologies and natural fortification, the project produces: 1. Human-grade proteins for plant-based meats, dairy alternatives, therapeutic nutrition and school or community or refugee feeding programs 2. Feed-grade proteins that lower production costs in poultry, aquaculture and dairy systems. This dual-use approach simultaneously strengthens food and feed systems, reduces import dependence, stabilizes protein supply and accelerates Kenya s emerging future-foods sector. By integrating circular economy principles, crop diversification and inclusive processing, ProteinCore Kenya creates new value chains for smallholder farmers, processors, innovators and SMEs. Immediate benefits include more affordable proteins, improved nutrition for vulnerable populations, reduced feed costs for producers, growth of the future food industry and enhanced market opportunities for rural communities. Long-term, the innovation boosts climate resilience, enhances local manufacturing and strengthens national food security. It provides a scalable model for Africa s sustainable protein economy rooted in indigenous crops and low-carbon technologies.

core_fields.title: Strengthening climate-resilient and sustainable food systems through Farmers' Hub Model in Nasarawa state, Nigeria
core_fields.description: Strengthening Climate-Resilient and Sustainable Food Systems through the Farmers Hub Model in Nasarawa State, Nigeria aims to empower 20,000 smallholder farmers with climate-smart innovations that enhance productivity, income, and food security. Through last-mile hubs delivering, ag inputs, regenerative training, mechanization, and market access, FSSS will strengthen local value chains disrupted by conflict and weak infrastructure. Fully aligned with Sowing the Future: Global Food System Challenge, the project champions locally led, climate-resilient food system transformation
core_fields.abstract: The Foundation for Sustainable Smallholder Solutions (FSSS) addresses the vicious cycle of low productivity, poverty, and weak climate resilience among smallholders in Nasarawa State. Farmers struggle with limited access to quality inputs, finance, agronomic knowledge, and fair markets challenges that perpetuate food insecurity and vulnerability to climate shocks. Our Farmers hub innovation breaks this cycle through decentralized, commercially viable one-stop centre that deliver bundled, last-mile services. Each Hub provides: 1. Certified climate-resilient and nutrient-dense seeds and quality inputs to tackle input scarcity. 2. Capacity building on Climate-Smart and Regenerative Agriculture to close knowledge gaps. 3. Inclusive aggregation and market linkages to correct market failures and enhance farmers incomes. Backed by FSSS s data-driven approach, our team conducted food security and nutritional assessments (Food Consumption Score, Household Dietary Diversity Score, MUAC) and on-spot market analyses to identify and tailor interventions. The scientific and operational insight driving this solution is that bundling services and decentralizing delivery through community-based Hubs reduces transaction costs, increases technology adoption, and institutionalizes climate resilience at the grassroots. Through Community-Based Seed Producer Organizations (CBOs), the project delivers locally adapted, certified seeds within a 10 km radius, enhancing affordability and accessibility. FSSS s innovation drives sustainable, inclusive transformation in alignment with Sowing the Future: Global Food System Challenge. Benefits: Farmers: Higher yields, income, and climate resilience; improved access to inputs and food security. Consumers: Stable supply of safe, nutritious, and biofortified foods. Environment: Restored soil health and ecosystems through regenerative practices.

core_fields.title: Scaling Circular Food Waste Transformation to Safe, Affordable and Nutritious Livestock Feed in Uganda
core_fields.description: This project aims to scale our science-proven, renewable-energy-powered bio-refinery that collects, decontaminates and converts urban food waste into high-quality, nutritious, digestible, palatable, and shelf-stable commercial livestock feed. By expanding processing capacity, expanding and digitising waste collection, and strengthening quality control, we advance a circular bioeconomy model that reduces waste, enhances hygiene of waste sourcing areas, promotes food security and supports climate-resilient farming in Uganda.
core_fields.abstract: Uganda s food and livestock systems face three interlinked challenges: poor urban food waste management, high livestock feed costs, and weakly regulated feed supply chains. Kampala, the capital city, generates approximately 786 tons of food waste daily, most of which is landfilled, contributing to public health risks and an estimated 149,554 tCO₂-eq emissions annually. This crisis intensified following the collapse of Kiteezi landfill in August 2024, leaving the city without a functional disposal site. At the same time, livestock feed, accounting for up to 75% of production costs, is increasingly unaffordable and reliant on food crops, such as maize and soy, intensifying food feed competition amid rapidly rising feed demand. Bio-Novedosa addresses these challenges through a science-proven, renewable-energy-powered innovation that upcycles food waste into safe, nutritious, affordable, and shelf-stable livestock feed for poultry, pigs, and crickets. Using a multidisciplinary approach, the process involves structured waste collection, sorting, decontamination, drying, and formulation. Laboratory and pilot data confirm that the resulting feeds meet or exceed commercial safety and nutritional standards, with a verified one-year shelf life. The solution is a testament that nutrient-laden food waste can safely replace conventional feed ingredients when properly treated and standardised. Immediate benefits include lower feed costs for farmers, cleaner urban environments, and new income opportunities, especially for youth and women. Long-term impacts include reduced greenhouse gas emissions, restored nutrient cycles, improved food security, and a scalable circular bioeconomy model for Uganda and beyond.

core_fields.title: "Sweet Printer": a device that transforms children s drawings into sweet, edible creations.

core_fields.abstract: The Sweet Printer is an innovative device that offers both an educational and entertaining experience by combining art, technology, and hands-on creativity. It allows children to turn their own drawings into lollipops, encouraging creative thinking and interest in simple digital technologies. A key part of our innovation is the eco-friendly approach. Our project addresses two major issues: the lack of interactive, creative tools in educational programs and the shortage of safe, eco-friendly confectionery options on the market. Sweet Printer solves both by offering a new educational format and a healthier environment. It is innovative both technically digital 2D printing with edible materials and socially, as children actively participate in creating their own sweets. The result is a sustainable and accessible solution suitable for schools, children s centers, and family events, serving as an example of positive scientific and social impact.

core_fields.title: Pfumvudza/Intwasa: Scaling Climate-Smart Agriculture for Nutrition and Resilience in Zimbabwe
core_fields.description: This project strengthens Zimbabwe s Pfumvudza/Intwasa program by embedding innovations beyond its conservation agriculture baseline. Fertilizer microdosing, jab planters, microbial inoculants, and hermetic storage are bundled with legume-sunflower intercropping, nutrition education, and Village Business Units. Digital dashboards track soil health, adoption, and incomes in real time. These innovations go beyond government s current focus, embedding agroecology, postharvest safety, and market integration to deliver resilience, equity, and nutrition at national scale.
core_fields.abstract: The government s Pfumvudza/Intwasa program has successfully promoted conservation agriculture, but important gaps remain in soil regeneration, postharvest safety, and market access. The innovation addresses these gaps by combining climate-smart farming techniques with digital monitoring and value chain systems. Jab planters ensure precise seed and fertilizer placement, reducing labor by 80 percent for women, youth, and elderly farmers. Fertilizer microdosing increases yields by up to 40 percent while cutting costs and nutrient runoff. Intercropping with legumes and sunflower restores soil fertility, breaks pest cycles, and diversifies household diets. Beyond the baseline, we introduce SIRDC microbial inoculants and organic amendments to enhance nitrogen fixation, phosphorus availability, and soil organic matter. Hermetic PICS bags and solar dryers reduce grain losses by 20 30 percent and eliminate aflatoxin contamination, protecting food safety and market value. Village Business Units add value by milling maize into meal, pressing sunflower into oil, and packaging legumes for markets. Digital dashboards track inputs, soil health, and farmer adoption, enabling adaptive management and transparent evidence for policy. Nutrition and financial literacy education empower households to make healthier food choices. By embedding agroecology, postharvest safety, and market systems into Pfumvudza/Intwasa, the innovation delivers immediate gains in yields (20 40%), nutrition (dietary diversity up 40%), and labor efficiency (80% savings), while building long-term soil health, incomes, and resilience. This positions Pfumvudza/Intwasa as a replicable, scalable model for climate-resilient, nutrition-sensitive agriculture that goes beyond the current government baseline.

core_fields.title: NutriSeed: Growing Nutritious and Locally made Baby Food for Healthy Children and Empowered Farmers
core_fields.description: NutriSeed aims to scale up the production of locally-sourced, nutritious baby food to improve child nutrition in underserved communities in Senegal. By partnering with women-led and smallholders value chains, we reduce food loss, empower farmers, and deliver culturally adapted, affordable products. This project leverages circular, inclusive and locally-based ecosystems to create a replicable, sustainable model that strengthens food systems, promotes healthy growth for children, and supports resilient livelihoods for communities.
core_fields.abstract: NutriSeed addresses the critical challenge of child malnutrition in Senegal, where 1 in 5 children under five is stunted, and West Africa, where 1 in 3 children under five suffers stunting. This is exacerbated by broken local value chains, leading to significant post-harvest losses of nutritious cereals and local crops. At the same time, up to 90% of baby foods are imported, often high in sugar and salt, and not adapted to local tastes, limiting accessibility and cultural acceptance. Our solution is to develop healthy, locally sourced baby food using highly nutritious indigenous ingredients and forgotten such as baobab, moringa, fonio, millet, cowpea, mango, sweet potato, etc... Local women-led groups pre-process the raw cereals, and Le Lionceau transforms them into complementary feeding products, including fruit, vegetable, and meals purees and infant cereals, without any added sugar or salt. This ensures safe, culturally adapted, and affordable products that improve child nutrition while supporting local economies. Immediate benefits include improved child nutrition, increased income for women and farmers, and reduced food waste. Sustainable benefits extend to strengthened local food systems, empowered communities, and a replicable, circular model for nutritious food production. NutriSeed combines nutrition science, food technology, and local knowledge to deliver a scalable, systemic solution addressing both the symptoms and root causes of malnutrition in Senegal.

core_fields.title: Validating Circular Livestock and Food Waste Recovery for Climate-Resilient Food Systems
core_fields.description: LWR s patented system transforms livestock manure and food wastewater into clean water and concentrated natural nutrients that regenerate soils while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Using millions of sensor-generated data points and AI-enhanced optimization, the system improves nutrient efficiency, drought resilience, and farm economics. This project will validate circular nutrient and water recovery across two operating facilities, generating integrated, real-world evidence to support climate-positive, resilient food systems and accelerate adoption across diverse livestock and food-production regions.
core_fields.abstract: LWR s innovation addresses one of the most urgent challenges in global food systems: the growing pressure on water, soil, and climate resilience caused by livestock production. Livestock operations generate large volumes of wastewater rich in nutrients that, when unmanaged, contribute to water scarcity, soil degradation, methane emissions, and rising farm costs. These impacts reduce food security, strain rural communities, and worsen climate and drought vulnerability. Our solution transforms this wastewater into valuable resources through a circular, data-driven nutrient recovery system. Using mechanical separation, smart flocculation, and advanced filtration, enhanced by millions of operational data points and AI-driven optimization, LWR s technology produces clean recycled water, concentrated crop-ready nutrients, and climate-positive inputs such as biochar feedstocks. This replaces costly and environmentally harmful waste handling with a regenerative system that conserves water, improves soil fertility, reduces emissions, and lowers operational costs. The insight behind this solution came from recognizing that manure is not waste, but is a natural nutrient-rich resource containing all nutrients required for crop growth. By combining mechcanical engineering, chemistry, and AI, LWR turns a persistent environmental burden into an engine for climate-positive food production. The benefits are immediate and permanent. Farmers reduce hauling, energy use, and fertilizer purchases; communities gain cleaner water and reduced odor and emissions; consumers benefit from more resilient, drought-adapted food systems; and the environment gains healthier soils, reduced pollution, and lower methane emissions. This innovation helps livestock regions produce food more sustainably and is VERRA validtaed for methane avoidance credits.

core_fields.title: Agrifood Entrepreneurship Center (AEC): Transforming Haiti s Agricultural Sector into an Engine for Inclusive Growth
core_fields.description: Through the Agrifood Entrepreneurship Center, we will deliver improved inputs, enhanced food processing, and regenerative agricultural training, alongside storage and enterprise support that increase yields, reduce post-harvest losses, restore soils, and help farmers adapt to climate stressors. This integrated, equitable model creates a systems-level multiplier effect, expanding access to safe, nutritious foods and catalyzing sustainable transformation across Haiti s food system, with solutions designed for scale and replication in other climate-vulnerable contexts.
core_fields.abstract: Although agriculture is the backbone of Haiti s economy, small farmers struggle to earn a living and domestic production meets only 45% of national food needs. Chronic underinvestment, fragmented supply chains, and poor infrastructure contribute to high post-harvest losses and unreliable access to essential inputs. Heavy reliance on food imports leaves households vulnerable to global market shocks, while nearly half of Haitians face acute food insecurity. Haiti s climate vulnerability further reduces yields and income stability. The AEC addresses these systemic gaps by co-locating four complementary enterprises: a food processing facility, certified seed farm, goat meat production hub, and vocational training program. This integrated model is novel in Haiti and uniquely suited to climate-vulnerable, resource-constrained contexts, combining improved inputs, agriculture training, value-added processing, and enterprise development in one coordinated platform. The scientific and technical foundation comes from a decade of field trials conducted by Zanmi Agrikol and partners, which identified high-performing, climate-resilient seed varieties and goat husbandry techniques, alongside proven regenerative practices that enhance soils, water retention, and pest resilience. The AEC generates immediate and sustained benefits. Farmers gain access to certified, climate-resilient seeds, technical assistance, and stable markets that increase yields and income. Consumers access more nutritious and affordable foods, including black beans and locally processed plantain and yucca products. Women and youth expand their opportunities through skills training and viable agri-enterprises. Environmentally, regenerative practices restore soils, increase biodiversity, reduce emissions, and help farmers adapt to climate stressors. Together, these interventions deliver durable, scalable impact across the food system.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Solutions for Food Sovereignty in Lake Victoria Communities
core_fields.description: In many Lake Victoria fishing communities, small fish such as sardine are traditionally dried on sand or spread over fishing nets a practice that leads to contamination, low quality, and significant post-harvest losses. These challenges have worsened with changing climate conditions, including unpredictable rainfall, strong winds, and prolonged humidity, which make open-air drying unreliable and further threaten food security and livelihoods. This project introduces elevated mesh drying racks as a climate-smart and low-cost solution.
core_fields.abstract: This innovation introduces elevated mesh drying racks as a climate-smart, low-cost solution to improve the drying of small fish such as sardine in local name call (dagaa) in Lake Victoria fishing communities. Currently, most fish are dried on sand or on old fishing nets a practice that leads to contamination, low product quality, and high post-harvest losses. These challenges are worsening as climate change brings unpredictable rainfall, stronger winds, and prolonged humidity, making traditional open-air drying increasingly unreliable. As a result, food safety, incomes, and local livelihoods are at risk. The elevated mesh racks address these problems by keeping fish off the ground, allowing better airflow, and using minimal solar energy to dry fish more quickly and hygienically. The design is simple, affordable, and adaptable to changing weather, making it especially relevant for vulnerable small-scale processors. The solution is informed by practical insights from food safety best practices and post-harvest handling research, which demonstrate that raised drying surfaces significantly reduce contamination and spoilage. Training youth to construct and maintain the racks, and training women processors to use improved drying and handling techniques, further strengthens local ownership and skills. Immediate benefits include cleaner, safer dried fish, reduced losses, and more consistent production. Long-term benefits include increased incomes for processors, improved nutrition for consumers, youth employment, reduced environmental pressure from waste, and stronger community resilience to climate impacts. This innovation directly supports sustainable fish processing, food security, and community-driven adaptation in Lake Victoria communities.

core_fields.title: Transforming Agricultural Waste into Food Sovereignty, Organic Fertilizer and Clean Energy
core_fields.description: Powerstove tackles energy poverty and soil degradation by converting agricultural waste into clean bio-CNG fuel and organic fertilizer, 75% cheaper than NPK alternatives. Our circular economy model boosts smallholder yields by 120%, cuts deforestation, and increases farmer income. With proven pilot results, we seek the Seeding The Future Grand Prize to scale this integrated solution for sustainable, equitable food systems in Nigeria and beyond
core_fields.abstract: Powerstove addresses Nigeria s interconnected crises of energy poverty and agricultural decline. Smallholder farmers struggle with costly, often counterfeit chemical fertilizers which can consume 20% of production costs leading to soil degradation, nutrient deficiencies, and stagnant yields despite high potential. Meanwhile, over 80% of the population relies on biomass fuels, causing deforestation and health issues. Our innovation converts abundant agricultural waste (e.g., rice husks, corn cobs) via proprietary gasification. This process yields both purified, compressed bio-CNG a clean cooking fuel and nutrient-enriched biochar-based organic fertilizer. This circular approach eliminates waste while cutting fertilizer costs by 75% and boosting crop yields by 120%. Immediate and sustainable benefits include: Farmers: Increased income through higher yields and affordable organic inputs. Consumers: Access to clean, affordable cooking energy. Environment: Reduced deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions. Society: Job creation in waste collection and production, improved public health, and greater food sovereignty. By turning waste into energy and fertility, Powerstove builds a resilient, equitable food system while promoting ecological and economic sustainability.

core_fields.title: Advancing equitable access to affordable and safe fish protein for vulnerable households in Africa.
core_fields.description: Our project links smallholder fish production, improved by our simple, offline-first digital tool, AquaSense+, with youth and women-led community point-of-sales kiosks. This drives down costs and post-harvest losses, ensuring traceable, sustainable protein reaches low-income households. We strengthen nutrition resilience by making safe, affordable, nutrient-dense fish accessible to underserved families, especially mothers and children. The Seed Grant will catalyze this scalable model that boosts farmer productivity, enhances cold-chain distribution, and expands equitable access to nutritious food.
core_fields.abstract: Current fragmented systems fail to establish efficient, climate-smart production pathways or connect them to the communities most in need, a gap widening rapidly under climate and urbanization pressures. Our project tackles a critical food systems failure: thousands of smallholder fish farmers produce far below potential, while food-insecure households, especially mothers and children in their first 1,000 days, struggle to access affordable, safe, traceable and nutrient-dense protein. We address this challenge by integrating AquaSense+, an offline-first digital aquaculture productivity tool, with a community-based fish products distribution network. This forms an end-to-end ecosystem where scalable digital efficiency on farms translates into equitable access to safe, traceable fish in underserved communities. Farmers use AquaSense+ to learn better practices, reduce input waste, and improve yields. Through coordinated logistics, they access quality inputs and farm services at lower costs. Our model s novelty lies in connecting this farm-level productivity directly to last-mile nutrition impact, integrating socio-economic transformation and traceable access for vulnerable households. We expand inclusive, traceable access to fish through women- and youth-operated fresh stalls, quick-cook vendors, and kiosks supported by a last-mile cold chain. This ensures safe, nutritious fish reach underserved families at lower prices, stimulating grassroots entrepreneurship and reducing post-harvest losses. Immediate benefits include lower production costs, higher yields, and improved and equitable access to essential protein. Long-term, we deliver stronger child nutrition, resilient local economies, reduced pressure on wild fisheries, and a scalable, climate-smart model for future food systems. The seed grant is catalytic for scaling distribution and accelerating our systemic impact.

core_fields.title: Scaling Regenerative Agriculture Through Seed Ball Innovation in Ethiopia
core_fields.description: Seed Balls Ethiopia is scaling regenerative agriculture by delivering low-cost, climate-resilient seed ball technology that boosts crop germination, restores degraded soils, and reduces input costs for smallholder farmers. Our project empowers women and youth with accessible, sustainable farming tools that increase nutritious food production while rehabilitating landscapes. By combining traditional knowledge with innovative delivery methods, we enable communities to strengthen food security, adapt to climate change, and expand regenerative practices across Ethiopia.
core_fields.abstract: In Ethiopia, over 85% of agricultural land is degraded, reducing yields, threatening food security, and deepening rural poverty. Smallholder farmers reliant on rain-fed agriculture and lacking access to seeds, tools, or irrigation are most affected. Climate change worsens the problem through droughts and soil erosion, making traditional reseeding costly, inefficient, and unreliable. Seed Balls Ethiopia addresses this with a low-cost, regenerative seed ball technology. Seeds are encased in clay, compost, and biochar, protecting them from pests, birds, wind, and drought while improving germination. The mixture enriches soil, retains moisture, and promotes healthy growth requiring no tilling, watering, or tools. This approach blends centuries-old Indigenous practices with modern soil science and is optimized for locally adapted seeds. Immediate benefits include faster, more reliable establishment of crops, trees, and vegetables reducing costs and labor. Communities gain quick access to nutritious foods such as moringa, legumes, and fruit trees, improving diets and household food security. Long-term benefits include restored soils, improved water retention, carbon sequestration, biodiverse agroecosystems, and reduced reliance on chemical inputs. Women and youth are engaged in climate-smart farming and policy dialogues, fostering local stewardship and resilience. To support quality and replication, we use community training hubs and drone-assisted monitoring to track germination and landscape recovery. By turning degraded land into productive, regenerative space with minimal resources, Seed Balls Ethiopia offers a simple, science-based, scalable solution that strengthens food security, empowers communities, and restores ecosystems across Ethiopia.

core_fields.title: Sustainable Rice Production and Solar-Powered Irrigation Initiative
core_fields.description: The Sustainable Rice Production and Solar-Powered Irrigation Initiative aims to improve food security, increase farmers incomes, and promote climate resilience by combining modern rice farming with clean solar-powered irrigation. The project will train and equip smallholder farmers with sustainable agricultural skills and reliable water access, enabling year-round rice production, reduced costs, higher yields, and improved livelihoods in underserved rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder rice farmers in rural communities face persistent challenges of unreliable rainfall, high fuel costs for water pumping, low productivity, and limited access to modern farming skills. These challenges result in low yields, seasonal farming, poverty, and food insecurity. This problem is highly relevant as climate change continues to increase droughts and unpredictable weather, threatening local food supply and rural livelihoods. This project introduces an integrated solar-powered irrigation and sustainable rice production model that enables farmers to access clean, reliable water throughout the year. By replacing fuel-powered pumps with solar systems, farmers can irrigate their fields at low operational cost while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, farmers receive hands-on training in climate-smart rice production, improved seed use, soil health management, and post-harvest best practices. The innovation is grounded in proven renewable energy technology and climate-smart agriculture research, which show that solar irrigation improves water efficiency while sustainable farming increases yield and soil fertility. The combined use of both solutions creates a powerful, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly farming system. Immediate benefits include increased crop yields, lower production costs, year-round farming, and higher farmer incomes. Sustainable long-term benefits include improved food security, youth and women empowerment, reduced environmental pollution, stronger community resilience, and enhanced climate change adaptation.

core_fields.title: Seeding Liberia s Innovative & Regenerative Food Future
core_fields.description: This project integrates regenerative agriculture training, a circular microfinance mechanism, and the activation of two community processing facilities for gari, palm oil, and honey. By empowering 700+ smallholders (mainly women), we aim to increase food production, rural incomes, and soil health. Funding accelerates raw material procurement, utilizes idle processing capacity, and develops markets to ensure long-term food security and economic resilience.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation addresses a critical bottleneck in rural African food systems: increasing agricultural production has limited impact if surplus cannot be absorbed, processed, financed, and commercialized. Many communities face soil degradation, low productivity, post-harvest losses, underutilized processing capacity, and weak access to markets. Our solution integrates three pillars into a single, replicable ecosystem: 1. The Engine (Regenerative Farm School): We train smallholders in regenerative agriculture to boost cassava and palm productivity while restoring soil health and biodiversity. This generates a stable raw-material supply and builds environmental resilience for future ecosystem-service markets. 2. The Enabler (Community Agro-Processing): We activate two existing, fully equipped community facilities to process cassava into gari, palm kernels into oil, and honey. Increased working capital allows these facilities to operate at full capacity, reducing post-harvest losses and creating local employment. 3. The Multiplier (Circular Finance & Market Access): A community microfinance mechanism reinvests revenues from product sales into seasonal crop procurement, creating a revolving fund that multiplies production and incomes. Simultaneously, we professionalize branding and packaging, transitioning from bulk commodities to high-value products for local markets and future export readiness. Sustainable benefits: Farmers gain higher incomes and healthier soils; women access leadership roles and employment; consumers receive reliable, nutritious local foods; and communities strengthen food security. Environmentally, the project improves soil carbon and water efficiency. Together, these elements form a scalable model for a resilient Liberian food system.

core_fields.title: Building Climate-Resilient Local Food Systems in Southwest Sumba
core_fields.description: Southwest Sumba faces persistent food insecurity, with nearly half of households experiencing seasonal hungry periods lasting around three months each year. su-re.co s field analysis indicates this is driven by unstable dryland production, limited access to indigenous nutritious crops, high fuel and fertilizer costs, and monotonous diets. This project scales a proven, integrated food system model developed that restores native crops, applies circular biogas solutions, and strengthens community capacity to improve diet quality, affordability, and resilience
core_fields.abstract: The innovation introduces an integrated, village-level food system model that strengthens food security in dryland contexts by linking indigenous crop restoration, circular waste management, and community capacity building. First, the project restores indigenous, climate-resilient staple crops (Jali, Ganyong, and Uwi) through locally adapted cultivation practices. Evidence from the pilot phase shows these crops are well suited to Southwest Sumba s dryland conditions, requiring less water and fewer external inputs than irrigated rice, consistent with projected longer dry seasons in Sumba, while contributing to improved diet diversity and more stable local food availability. Second, the model applies a circular food energy soil approach by converting livestock manure and agricultural residues into biogas. Su-re.co s biogas systems reduce household reliance on firewood and LPG to around 33% of previous levels, lowering cooking fuel expenses and saving up to two hours per day for women previously spent collecting firewood. The resulting bioslurry functions as a high-quality organic fertilizer, reducing fertilizer expenditure by up to IDR 2 million per household per year while improving soil fertility and moisture retention. Third, the innovation embeds community capacity building through farmer field schools, women s groups, and youth technician training. These platforms act as living laboratories, transferring practical skills in indigenous crop production, biogas operation and maintenance, nutrition practices, and participatory monitoring. By grounding learning in local conditions and linking it to village governance and extension systems, the model ensures long-term adoption, maintenance, and replication.

core_fields.title: Scalable Sustainable Food-System Model for Independent Small Restaurants
core_fields.description: This project creates a scalable, tech-enabled model that transforms small independent restaurants including Asian American, minority-owned, and underserved operators into healthier, low-waste, sustainable food providers. By integrating operational systems, nutrition improvements, and regenerative sourcing partnerships, the innovation expands access to nutritious, affordable, and trusted meals while reducing environmental impact. The result is a sustainable, economically viable food-service model that strengthens community food security and can be replicated across diverse communities.
core_fields.abstract: Small independent restaurants play a critical role in feeding communities but often operate within outdated systems that limit food safety, nutrition, sustainability, and efficiency. Many minority-owned, Asian American, and underserved restaurant operators face additional barriers such as limited access to technology, training, or incentives to adopt healthier and more sustainable practices. This innovation introduces a replicable, data-driven model that modernizes these restaurants into sustainable, low-waste, nutritious community food hubs. The solution integrates operational engineering, nutrition optimization, waste-tracking tools, and regenerative sourcing pathways into a unified platform that can be adopted by restaurants of any background. Insights originate from proven operational improvements such as producing over 500 meals per hour in small spaces, reducing food and packaging waste, and increasing consistency in healthier menu offerings. These early findings show that small operational upgrades can significantly improve nutrition, reduce emissions, and maintain affordability when scaled across thousands of small restaurants. Immediate benefits include improved food safety, standardized workflows, reduced waste, healthier and more appealing menu options, and better margins for restaurant owners. Long-term benefits include strengthened community food security, higher use of regenerative ingredients, lower environmental impact from more efficient kitchens, and expanded access to nutritious meals in neighborhoods where restaurants serve as primary food sources. This model supports consumers, diverse restaurant operators, producers, and the environment by creating a scalable and economically viable pathway for sustainable food-system transformation.

core_fields.title: Green Giraffe Track n Trace Project
core_fields.description: The Trace-n-Grow project expands Green Giraffe s blockchain-enabled track-and-trace system to onboard 5,000 smallholder farmers and 60 field Quality Assurance Agents. The project delivers regenerative agriculture training, climate-smart extension support, and direct market access for nutritious, traceable crops. By combining digital identity, geotagged field logs, and regenerative practices, farmers improve yields, reduce losses, and access premium buyers strengthening food safety, sustainability, and equitable livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers across Zambia and Angola struggle with low productivity, climate shocks, and limited access to markets that demand safe, traceable, and sustainably produced food. Many remain excluded from premium buyers because they cannot meet verification, quality, or sustainability requirements trapping them in low-income cycles. Trace-n-Grow solves this by combining blockchain-enabled traceability, AI-driven agronomy insights, and regenerative agriculture training into one farmer-friendly system. Each farmer receives a digital identity, their fields are geotagged, and trained Quality Assurance Agents validate all farm events planting, inputs, harvest, moisture, quality, and sustainability actions. This ensures trusted, tamper-proof farm records that meet certification and buyer standards. Scientific insights from vegetation indices (NDVI/EVI/NDMI) and soil-health monitoring guide tailored regenerative practices biochar use, crop rotation, mulching, low-tillage, and composting improving nutritional quality while restoring degraded soils. The system also reduces food loss by offering early warnings for pests, drought, and nutrient stress. On the market side, farmers gain access to buyers seeking safe, nutritious, traceable, and climate-positive commodities. Every batch harvested is linked to a QR code showing safety checks, regenerative practices, field history, and post-harvest handling building consumer trust.

core_fields.title: Establishing Laboratory Infrastructure for Quality Spawn Production and Farmer Empowerment
core_fields.description: Parah Enterprises seeks to establish a professional spawn production laboratory to address the critical shortage of quality oyster mushroom spawn in Malawi. Currently producing only 100 kg monthly with basic equipment, the laboratory will increase capacity to 1,000 kg monthly, serving 200+ farmers. This investment will reduce contamination from 15-20% to below 5%, enable training of 250 farmers annually (60% women, 70% youth), create 15 jobs, and strengthen food security through increased mushroom production
core_fields.abstract: The Problem: Spawn is the "seed" for mushroom cultivation, but Malawi has only 2-3 spawn producers, creating severe shortages. Poor-quality spawn causes high contamination rates, leading to farmer crop failures. Only a small percentage of trained farmers continue production due to spawn access problems. The Solution: Establish a professional laboratory with laminar air flow hoods, autoclaves, and incubators. This dramatically increases production capacity and significantly reduces contamination rates. The Science: Contamination occurs when airborne bacteria enter spawn during production. Laminar flow hoods eliminate airborne contaminants through HEPA filtration, while autoclaves sterilize substrates at high temperatures. This proven combination ensures spawn purity and farmer success. Benefits: Farmers: Access to affordable, reliable spawn priced below competitors; dramatically improved success rates Food Security: Substantial increase in nutritious mushroom production; improved protein access for communities Employment: Hundreds of farmers trained annually with focus on women and youth; sustainable monthly income opportunities; multiple direct jobs created Environment: Uses agricultural waste; requires minimal water; enables year-round production Economic Impact: Significant income generation for farmers; reduces dependency on imports

core_fields.title: SUSTAINABLE PASTURE RESTORATION TO IMPROVE LIVESTOCK PRODUCTIVITY AND FOOD SECURITY FOR MAASAI PASTORALISTS IN LONGIDO
core_fields.description: Maasai pastoralists in Matale Ward, Longido District, Tanzania face food insecurity due to declining livestock yields of meat and milk, their primary food source. This project introduces an evidence-based regenerative approach integrating rotational grazing, invasive plant removal, and water-harvesting structures (semi-circular bunds) to restore degraded rangelands. By improving pasture availability and quality, the project will increase livestock productivity, strengthen sustainable household food security, and promote diversification of complementary foods for more nutritious diets.
core_fields.abstract: While the Maasai pastoralists in Matale Ward, Longido District have long relied on open grazing and seasonal migration, they continue to suffer recurring livestock deaths caused by insufficient pastures and water. Climate change has intensified prolonged droughts and high temperatures, accelerating pasture loss. Reports from the Longido Livestock Officer indicate that 39,000 cattle have died due to drought, severely threatening household food security among pastoralists who depend entirely on livestock for nutrition and livelihoods. This project introduces an evidence-based, regenerative grazing innovation that integrates rotational grazing, identification and uprooting of invasive species, community-constructed semi-circular bunds to harvest runoff, and awareness creation on improved livestock feeding. These measures collectively restore degraded rangelands, improve pasture quality and moisture retention, and ultimately enhance the production of nutritious meat and milk while strengthening dietary resilience. In addition, the project will incorporate community trainings on food and nutrition to promote diversification of diets beyond staple livestock products, ensuring improved household nutrition and food security. Given Matale Ward's semi-arid nature, these interventions are supported by research from the Sokoine University of Agriculture showing that rotational grazing and soil-water conservation structures significantly outperform traditional open grazing systems in similar environments. The approach is practical, community-driven, and scalable to other pastoralist communities across northern Tanzania.

Organic surpluses are repurposed to regenerate the soil and feed PNASE livestock (pigs and chickens), creating a sustainable production cycle and reducing waste. Centralised monitoring ensures equitable distribution and efficient planning, guaranteeing that all schools receive fresh, nutritious food. Sustainable Benefits: Institutional strengthening of PNASE, regenerative cultivation practices, preservation of soil biodiversity, reduction of chemicals and greenhouse gas emissions, garden resilience to climate change, greater autonomy for schools, and the promotion of environmental and food education in communities.

core_fields.title: Revolutionising native species aquaculture in Lake Tanganyika through genetic selective breeding
core_fields.description: This project will establish a selective breeding program, by capturing wild native species of Tanganyika tilapia from across Lake Tanganyika and selectively breeding them to improve for growth rate and feed conversion ratio. By repeatedly selecting the best performing fish, we will create native species broodstock that can commercially compete with invasive species, such as the Nile tilapia, and be used to share with other fish farmers on the lake.
core_fields.abstract: Lake Tanganyika is the Earth's largest tropical freshwater lake, home to more than 2,000 species of fish. Yet climate change, illegal gear, and rapid population growth have driven wild-catch landings down sharply over the past two decades. Interest is shifting to farmed fish and regional aquaculture, but there is a major risk that invasive species, and in particular Nile tilapia, will be introduced to other fish farms on the lake. When Nile tilapia escape, they overwhelm native fish, and this has already happened in other major lakes in East Africa. The indigenous Tanganyika tilapia (Oreochromis tanganicae) represents a native species alternative whose population has fallen on the lake through over fishing, but is perfectly suited to Lake Tanganyika's ecosystem. Trials show excellent growth, feed utilisation and strong market acceptance, but decades of selective breeding have given Nile tilapia a head start, meaning Tanganyika tilapia still lags in growth rate and feed conversion efficiency. This project will establish a Genetic Selective Breeding Programme (GSBP) to make Tanganyika tilapia profitable and competitive, especially for smallholder fish farmers. The GSBP will create a fast-growing, disease-resistant strain that directly benefits up to 70,000 future smallholders, adds up to 7% to regional GDP, and doubles total aquaculture output.

core_fields.title: Waste 2 Value through Black Solider Fly (BSF) Waste Bioconversion
core_fields.description: CESDA in partnership with EcoProtein Innovations Limited "Waste2Value project converts degradable waste into high quality protein-rich animal feed (larvae) and nutrient-rich biofertilizer (frass) using the black soldier fly bioconversion technology. Our "Waste 2 Value project empowers smallholder farmers in Nigeria by reducing feed costs by up to 30% and improving crop and livestock yields by at least 20% while helping to cut food waste going to landfills and greenhouse gas emissions.
core_fields.abstract: The Waste2Value project addresses two pressing challenges in Africa's food system, the high cost of animal feed impacting on the price of food and the growing environmental burden of organic waste. Smallholder farmers in Nigeria and across West Africa are burdened with high animal feed prices accounting for between 70% - 85% of production costs with millions of tons of agricultural and food waste pollute the environment and emit greenhouse gases coupled with straining waste management systems. Our proven proprietary biotechnology solution leverages on BSF as a natural bioconversion agent to transform organic waste into two valuable products - larvae, a high-protein insect-based animal feed with 45-55% protein including other essential micro-nutrients and frass, a nutrient-rich organic biofertilizer (NPK: 3:1:1, > 90% organic matter). This circular model approach is novel because it achieves waste reduction, protein production, and fertilizer generation simultaneously which is faster than traditional composting. It also requires minimal land, water and energy making it a highly efficient, nature-based technology. Our approach adapts BSF technology to local contexts using low-cost substrates, indigenous design and community-driven models to make it accessible to small-scale farmers. The benefits are immediate and measurable to farmers by helping to cut feed costs by up to 30% while increasing yields by over 20% and improve soil fertility naturally. Communities gain cleaner environments through waste reduction and consumers access safer, cheaper locally produced animal protein. The project thus contributes directly to Zero Hunger, Climate Action, building a regenerative equitable food future for Africa

core_fields.title: ECO-NutriGuard RapidScan (ENURA): Scientific, Low-Cost Detection of Nutritional and Climate Risks in Roadside Foods.
core_fields.description: In Uganda, millions of low-income people rely on roadside meals cooked under unsafe and smoky conditions. This project introduces a compact, low-cost scientific device that rapidly scans roadside foods and cooking oils for nutritional and climate-related risks. Using simple test strips and a low-cost optical reader, ENURA gives vendors quick, clear safety results. This project will build, test, and refine ENURA with Ugandan vendors, communities, and standards authorities to promote safer, cleaner street-food environments.
core_fields.abstract: In Uganda's towns and cities, many low-income families rely on roadside-cooked foods as their primary daily meals. These foods are often prepared using overheated, repeatedly reused cooking oils and cooked over smoky charcoal or wood fires. Both practices create harmful chemical compounds, elevate smoke exposure, and contribute to poor nutrition and rising climate and health risks. Yet vendors and consumers have no simple way to detect these invisible dangers before the food is eaten. ECO-NutriGuard RapidScan (ENURA) introduces a practical, community-ready solution. ENURA is a small, ultra-low-cost scientific machine that integrates color-changing test strips with a simple optical reader to quickly scan cooking oils and food surfaces for signs of degradation, harmful compounds, and heat-related damage. When a vendor places a drop of oil or a swab onto the strip, the machine reads the resulting color change and gives a clear traffic-light result (safe, caution, unsafe). An additional lightweight indicator helps users understand smoke intensity around cooking areas, linking food safety with climate-related air-quality concerns. ENURA is innovative because it brings food-safety and climate-risk detection directly to Uganda's street level. Unlike laboratory tests or expensive meters, ENURA is designed for affordability, simplicity, and use by vendors, youth assistants, community health workers, and local inspectors. Its scientific foundation builds on proven colorimetric reactions used in low-cost food diagnostics, adapted for real roadside environments. By empowering vendors with simple, evidence-based information, ENURA encourages safer oil-use cycles, cleaner cooking practices, and healthier meals for Ugandans.

core_fields.title: Regenerative "Food is Medicine" System for Urban Community Health
core_fields.description: Our project builds a regenerative "Food is Medicine" system linking DOL's urban farms, Black Farm CSA, and Food Hub to deliver fresh, nutritious produce to medically vulnerable residents in Washington, DC. By integrating regenerative agriculture, nutrition access, and clinical partnerships, we create a scalable model that improves community health, strengthens local farm economies, and transforms urban food systems through sustainable, community-driven supply chains.
core_fields.abstract: Communities in Washington, DC face interconnected challenges of nutrition insecurity, diet-related disease, and limited access to nutritious foods. Although Food is Medicine programs are expanding nationally, most rely on external supply chains that are fragile, carbon-intensive, and disconnected from the communities they aim to serve. This reduces program impact, increases costs, and limits opportunities to build local resilience through food system transformation. Our innovation creates a regenerative, community-focused Food is Medicine system that integrates Dreaming Out Loud s (DOL) urban farms, Black Farm CSA, and Food Hub into a unified supply chain delivering fresh produce to medically vulnerable residents. We will provide Food is Medicine boxes at no expense to 520+ families and thousands of participating individuals. The project will deliver 46,800 pounds of fresh produce across 130 weeks of service, with each weekly box averaging 9 pounds of fruits and vegetables. This approach draws on evidence that produce prescriptions improve dietary intake and chronic disease outcomes, and on research indicating that community-owned supply chains increase resilience and reduce emissions. By coordinating production, aggregation, and delivery across farms and clinical partners, DOL sources from regional farmers and delivers directly to homes referred by healthcare providers. Immediate benefits include consistent access to fresh food, reduced nutrition insecurity, and increased economic opportunity for marginalized farmers. Benefits include improved soil health, reduced food waste, strengthened community resilience, and a replicable model for localizing Food is Medicine programs. This innovation advances healthier families, sustainable food production, and a more equitable food system.

core_fields.title: Farmflex: AI-Driven Hydroponics and Market Access Powered by a Pay-As-You-Grow Model
core_fields.description: Farmflex combines AI-driven hydroponics, IoT monitoring, and a Pay-As-You-Grow model to empower women and youth farmers across Lesotho. The system delivers real-time guidance in Sesotho, boosts yields by up to 500%, and operates on solar-powered, circular economy methods. It strengthens market access by aggregating farmer produce, adding value and then negotiating off-take deals on behalf of the collective farmers. The project creates a scalable, resilient, and climate-smart pathway for nutritious, year-round food production.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Lesotho face declining soil fertility, erratic rainfall, limited access to nutritious food, and weak market connections, resulting in low productivity, food insecurity, and reduced incomes. FarmFlex addresses these challenges by integrating AI-driven hydroponics with IoT monitoring and a Pay-As-You-Grow model, creating a holistic, climate-smart farming system tailored for women and youth farmers. The system provides real-time guidance in Sesotho and English on nutrient management, pest control, and crop scheduling. Scientific insights from controlled-environment agriculture, plant physiology, and data-driven crop management inform the AI recommendations. IoT sensors track water quality, temperature, and nutrient levels, enabling farmers and project managers to make precise, adaptive decisions. Farmers receive hands-on training in solar-powered hydroponics operations, sustainable practices, and circular production, including recycling crop waste into compost for seedling soil. Farmflex also strengthens market access by aggregating produce, adding value, and negotiating off-take deals on behalf of collective farmers. Immediate benefits include higher yields (up to 500%), up to 300% income increase, nutritious produce, and water-efficient cultivation. Long-term benefits include resilient, empowered smallholder communities, expanded farmer networks (0 → 168), replicable climate-smart farming models (now in 10 districts of Lesotho), and environmental sustainability reducing 435kgCO₂/project/year. Schools and communities gain reliable access to fresh vegetables, while society benefits from improved food security and sustainable land use. By combining technology, capacity building, renewable energy, circular economy practices, Pay-As-You-Grow financing, and market integration, Farmflex delivers measurable impact and demonstrates a scalable pathway for sustainable, productive, and resilient smallholder agriculture in Lesotho and beyond.

core_fields.title: Transforming Community Aflatoxin Control Through Integrated Agricultural and Public Health Solutions in Chikhwawa District.
core_fields.description: The project aims to reduce dietary exposure to aflatoxin by at least 30% by the end of July 2026, targeting smallholder farmers, pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, and children under five. This will be achieved through a multifaceted approach that includes training farmers on safe harvesting and storage, raising awareness among mothers and caregivers, empowering farmers with use of biocontrol products (Aflasafe) in Maize and Groundnuts fields, and establishment of community-based Mycotoxin rapid testing hubs.
core_fields.abstract: The core problem being solved is the widespread dietary exposure to Aflatoxin in Malawi, which is confirmed to cause severe public health issues, including low birth weight, smaller brain size, and growth restriction in children. This is highly relevant because it critically undermines child survival, human capital, and Malawi's economic development. The challenge is intensified by the informal food sector, which lacks regulatory oversight. The problem will be solved through the Aflatoxin Shield Initiative, a novel, holistic, and scalable approach. While similar solutions like farmer training and biocontrol exist, our novelty lies in integrating four critical components: comprehensive farmer training on safe post-harvest handling, targeted Antenatal mother education, empowering access to certified biocontrol (Aflasafe), and the introduction of community-based AflaCheck testing hubs. The scientific insight leading to this solution is recognizing the need for an accessible, rapid, and point-of-use screening tool within the informal sector. AflaCheck, which detects total aflatoxins at critical thresholds (10 ppb/20 ppb), provides this technical insight. Its portability and ease of use allow smallholder farmers and vendors to perform immediate, on-site checks, blocking contaminated products from the food chain. The specific and sustainable benefits are widespread: Consumers (mothers and children) gain immediate protection against dietary exposure, leading to enhanced public health outcomes. Producers (smallholder farmers) benefit from practical training and Aflasafe promotion, reducing contamination at the source, which strengthens their compliance with food safety standards. Communities benefit from inclusive outreach, fostering system-wide engagement for sustained aflatoxin risk management.

core_fields.title: Strengthening Micro Agriculture and Kakuma, Kenya s Women s Food Futures
core_fields.description: Kakuma Women s Food Futures strengthens food security for refugee women and girls in Kakuma Refugee Camp, Kenya by piloting a sustainable micro agriculture model supported by simple, introductory digital and solar tools. AgriHope will lead hands-on training in soil health, irrigation, small garden management, and post harvest practices, while Ampere provides basic solar kits and digital resources. core_fields.abstract: Kakuma Women s Food Futures introduces an integrated micro agriculture model that improves food security for refugee women and girls in Kakuma by combining sustainable farming practices with simple, introductory digital and solar tools. Women in Kakuma face chronic food shortages, limited access to land and water, and few opportunities for technical training, The innovation strengthens small scale food production through practical training in soil preparation, composting, water efficient irrigation, seedling management, and post harvest handling. These practices are supported by basic digital skills and low cost solar tools that track planting schedules, map small garden plots, monitor water, and power simple devices in low infrastructure settings. The insight behind this model is that women already engaged in small farming activities can significantly increase yields and resilience when provided with accessible tools, climate smart practices, and foundational technical confidence. Kakuma Women s Food Futures addresses immediate needs by helping women grow more food, reduce loss, and manage scarce water more effectively. It also strengthens long term resilience by building transferable skills in digital literacy, simple circuitry, record keeping, and basic environmental monitoring. As women increase production and diversify crops, households gain more reliable access to nutritious food and new possibilities for micro enterprise. The approach is sustainable because it builds on existing agricultural routines, uses tools designed for low connectivity environments, and reinforces practices that regenerate soil, conserve water, and support climate adaptation. Over time, the model can be extended to additional groups and integrated into broader community food system initiatives.

core_fields.abstract: KIREAP digitalizes and democratizes the Agriculture Value Chain End to End. core_fields.title: Improving Food Security and Environmental Sustainability through Integrated Soil Fertility Management Approach
core_fields.description: The overall objective of the project is to increase food security and environmental sustainability in agricultural systems through capacity building of 5 cooperatives of 4,600 smallholders located in 2 provinces by 2027; by adopting an integrated approach of soil fertility management and the use of quality seeds; hence maximizing agricultural production while minimizing depletion of nutrient reserves and degradation of physical and chemical properties of soils.
core_fields.abstract: Agriculture is the driving engine of growth in Burundi with + 50% of its GDP, and more than 85% active population being smallscale farmers. However, the yields remain very low due to land degradation and post harvest loss, with less than 20% harvest of the seed planted. Over the past two crop seasons, we have experienced a continued increase in rainfall. This has led to flooding and landslides, adversely affecting major food crops like beans and potatoes. Consequently, production losses have been significant. Furthermore, fertilization techniques remain poorly understood. This is largely due to inadequate management of residential and farm waste in the Cr te-Congo Nil region. This area features extensive farmable land on hillsides, which are highly vulnerable to various types of erosion, water runoff, and the leaching of vital minerals. Although Burundi's economy thrives on agriculture, smallholder farmers, who rely heavily on crop production for their income, are among the most affected. Today, Burundi is home to over 150,000 smallholder farmer cooperatives, each consisting of approximately 450 to 460 members. Our main focus is on 5 cooperatives located in the MURAMVYA and MWARO provinces comprising a total of 4,600 members. We aim to provide these cooperatives with essential knowledge and tools to tackle food insecurity. By implementing bio-intensive farming methods, they can achieve high yields in limited spaces while ensuring soil fertility and environmental sustainability. This approach also emphasizes reducing greenhouse gas emissions by recycling agricultural waste as much as possible.

core_fields.title: "Transforming Saline Water into Food Security for Coastal Kenya Communities"
core_fields.description: We will install a 168,000-liter/day water treatment system converting highly saline borehole (13,826 ppm) - almost sea water into safe drinking water for 5,000 people in Mariakani, Kenya. The system enables: (1) free water for 1000 schoolchildren at Missions of Hope International, (2) subsidized irrigation water for 50 smallholder farmers (60% women) producing 15 tons/month vegetables through contract farming, and (3) sustainable operations through mineral byproduct sales creating climate-resilient food security where conventional solutions fail.
core_fields.abstract: The Problem: Coastal Kenya's groundwater is highly saline (8,000-15,000 ppm TDS) making 80% of boreholes unusable for drinking or agriculture despite severe water scarcity. Mariakani's borehole yields 581,000 liters daily but at 13,826 ppm salinity 17 above safe drinking limits. Communities pay KSh 3,000 per 10,000 liters for trucked water while fertile land lies fallow. Traditional reverse osmosis is prohibitively expensive (KSh 150/m ), wastes 50% of water, and requires perpetual donor subsidies. The Innovation: We've developed proprietary modified pumice ion exchange technology 90% cheaper than RO, 100% solar-powered, generating zero waste. The breakthrough: treating volcanic pumice with specific mineral compounds creates ion exchange sites that selectively remove calcium, magnesium, and sodium from saline water. Unlike conventional systems that create toxic brine waste, our cascade regeneration process converts extracted minerals into valuable livestock supplements (28 tons/month calcium carbonate worth $350,000 annually). How It Works: Raw saline water flows through four-stage treatment columns containing 36,500 kg modified pumice, progressively reducing salinity from 13,826 ppm to 800 ppm. Spent media regenerates using seawater plus biochar enhancer restoring capacity while precipitating minerals for commercial sale. Immediate Benefits: 1,000 schoolchildren: Free safe drinking water daily (eliminating waterborne disease risk) 50 smallholder farmers (60% women): Subsidized irrigation enabling year-round vegetable production, tripling household income from KSh 3,000 to KSh 7,500 monthly 4,000 community members: Affordable safe water at KSh 50/m (83% cheaper than trucked water) Sustainable Benefits: Financial self-sufficiency through mineral sales (operational costs covered perpetually) Climate adaptation model replicable across Kenya's 75% arid lands Zero environmental waste complete circular economy

Through training, local cooperatives, and product value addition, women improve their incomes and community resilience. core_fields.abstract: AFY's innovative approach aims to strengthen a sustainable food system by empowering rural women in North and South Kivu through agroecology, simple agricultural technologies, and cooperative models. It addresses the major problem of chronic food insecurity, exacerbated by conflict, low productivity, lack of access to resources, and the economic marginalization of women, who are nevertheless the primary actors in food production. This innovation is relevant because it combines gender equality, food security, and climate resilience three essential issues for rural Congolese communities. The solution relies on disseminating agroecological practices, providing access to improved seeds, introducing appropriate agricultural tools, offering training in food processing and management, and structuring women's cooperatives capable of accessing markets. Knowledge of sustainable agronomy, community nutrition, social economics, and participatory management has guided this integrated approach, which is based on evidence demonstrating that women's economic empowerment directly improves family and community food security. Immediate benefits include increased production, reduced post-harvest losses, improved incomes for women, and greater access to diverse foods. In the long term, users farmers, families, schools, and communities?benefit from a healthier environment, a food system more resilient to climate shocks, a more stable rural economy, and strengthened community cohesion. For society and the environment, this innovation promotes soil restoration, biodiversity conservation, and poverty reduction, contributing to a fairer and more sustainable future.

core_fields.title: Reducing Postharvest Tomato Losses through Edible Coatings from Recycled Snail Shells in Ghana.
core_fields.description: This project addresses Ghana's 40% postharvest tomato losses by developing edible coatings from snail shell waste from the food industry. The natural coatings extends shelf life of tomatoes by creating a protective barrier that reduces moisture loss and microbial growth. This affordable, preservation method specifically benefits smallholder farmers lacking cold chain access. The solution directly addresses food waste, poverty, hunger and sustainability, empowering farmers with an affordable, locally sourced technology to reduce post-harvest losses.
core_fields.abstract: We address the 40% post-harvest loss of Ghana's tomatoes, that is over 100,000 tonnes of tomatoes lost anually ,caused by smallholder farmers' lack of cold storage and the crop's short shelf life. This is critically relevant as it causes severe economic hardship and poverty for farmers, deepens food insecurity and hunger, and contributes to climate change through methane emissions from rotting waste. Solution: We transform local snail shell waste into an edible, chitosan-based coating. Applied by spraying or dipping, it creates a protective barrier that slows respiration, retains moisture, and inhibits microbial growth, extending shelf life by 7-14 days at room temperature. While chitosan coatings are known, our innovation lies in its is novel application in the Ghanaian context: Circular Sourcing: We derive chitosan from a major local waste stream (snail shells), not imported chemicals. Context-Specific Design: We optimize the solution for affordability and room-temperature use by farmers lacking any cold chain. Similar synthetic coatings or expensive cold-chain logistics exist but are inaccessible to smallholders. Scientific basis: The coating s active ingredient is chitosan, a natural biopolymer known for its biocompatibility, biodegradability, and antimicrobial properties. By forming a protective barrier, it effectively reduces moisture loss, moderates gas exchange, and inhibits microbial contamination. Research confirms chitosan extends shelf life of fresh produce. Benefits: Farmers: Immediate 30-40% income increase from reduced losses. Environment: Sustainable waste valorization and reduced methane emissions. Communities: Enhanced food security, stable prices, and local green jobs. Sustainability: Fully biodegradable, non-toxic, locally sourced, and scalable across West Africa's tomato-growing regions
