core_fields.title: The ChurchGate Sweet Potato Initiative
core_fields.description: The ChurchGate Sweet Potato Initiative improves nutrition, incomes, and ecosystem health in rural Abia State by scaling biofortified Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato and restoring nutrient-rich indigenous fruit trees. Through women-led vine multiplication hubs, community agroforestry, and church-based nutrition campaigns, the project strengthens food systems, increases Vitamin A intake, and expands livelihood opportunities for women and youth while enhancing climate resilience and biodiversity
core_fields.abstract: The ChurchGate Sweet Potato Initiative is a community-led solution that brings together nutritious food, trusted local institutions, and climate-smart farming to improve lives in rural Abia State. Many children and mothers still suffer from vitamin A deficiency, even though Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) varieties such as Mother s Delight are available. These varieties are rich in provitamin A, mature quickly, tolerate drought, and are proven to improve nutrition. Yet many families cannot access clean planting materials, lose a large share of their harvest after digging, and lack awareness of OFSP s health benefits. At the same time, indigenous fruit trees-African Breadfruit, Bush Mango, and African Oil Bean, are disappearing due to deforestation and aging mother trees. These culturally important foods support diverse diets and provide vital income for rural women, but they are rarely replanted. Our innovation addresses these challenges through a simple, locally owned approach. Women-led OFSP vine hubs supply reliable planting material, while Farmer Field Schools train women and youth in climate-smart production, value-chain skills, and agroforestry, integrating indigenous fruit trees into sweet potato farms. To reduce post-harvest losses, the project introduces solar-powered sweet potato curing units, extending shelf life and protecting beta-carotene. Churches serve as trusted entry points for training, distribution, and nutrition education, helping families adopt OFSP meals and fruit-based foods they already value. Immediate benefits include improved diets, reduced food losses, and higher incomes, while long-term gains include restored biodiversity, healthier soils, and resilient, community-owned food systems.

core_fields.title: Millet-to-Meal: Digital Group Farming with Guaranteed Buy-Back for School Nutrition
core_fields.description: Nepal s National School Meals Program targets basic education in food-insecure geographically disadvantaged areas, including Madhesh Province. However, the program faces challenges related to limited nutritional diversity, weak local procurement, poor farmer linkages, and supply-chain inefficiencies. At the same time, millet-producing farmers lack reliable market access. This initiative integrates locally produced millets to enhance meal nutrition and farmer incomes, supported by digital monitoring, geospatial tools, and guaranteed produce buy-back to strengthen transparency, planning, and accountability.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation addresses two interconnected challenges: limited nutritional quality and weak local supply chains in the National School Meals Program, and the lack of reliable, remunerative markets for smallholder millet farmers. Schools often struggle to provide diverse, nutritious meals, while millet farmers lack precision agriculture knowledge for optimized yields and face price volatility, low demand, and income insecurity. This disconnect undermines food security, farmer livelihoods, and trust between producers and consumers, including concerns about pesticide use and food safety. The solution integrates locally produced millets into school meals through a digitally enabled, buy-back guaranteed farming and procurement model. Farmers are organized in group farming systems and supported with crop advisories derived from geospatial technologies, remote sensing, and field-level data. These tools enable accurate crop area mapping, yield estimation, and production forecasting, allowing schools and local governments to plan procurement in advance. End-to-end digital monitoring ensures transparency across production, aggregation, and delivery, while a guaranteed buy-back mechanism provides farmers with secure markets and fair prices. The approach builds on scientific insights from crop yield modeling, geospatial analysis, and participatory data collection, combined with nutrition science recognizing millets as climate-resilient, nutrient-rich crops suitable for Nepal s agro-ecological conditions. Immediate benefits include improved meal nutrition for schoolchildren, stable incomes for farmers, and reduced supply-chain risks for schools and municipalities. Long-term impacts include strengthened local food systems, enhanced resilience to climate and market shocks, improved trust between producers and consumers, reduced reliance on imported foods, and positive environmental outcomes through climate-smart, low-input millet cultivation.

core_fields.title: District-Led Integrated Food System Governance Model for Climate-Resilient and Nutrition-Sensitive Development in Cambodia
core_fields.description: Water, land, fisheries, and natural resources are part of the food systems that support the livelihoods of local communities in the Mekong River basin. Currently, the governance of these resources is siloed, sectoral, centralized, and fragmented. The conflicts and weak coordination among these line agencies undermine the connectivity of water, land, and natural resources ecosystems, causing weak governance. This project is promoting the ecosystem-based management of these resources at the district level, regardless administrative boundaries.
core_fields.abstract: Problem Statement & Relevance: Cambodia s food system is fragmented across multiple sectors, including agriculture, water, fisheries, education, health, and environment, which operate independently. Although climate change, water stress, market volatility, and malnutrition directly impact farmers and consumers at the local level, planning and investment decisions are centralized and lack coordination. This fragmentation results in inefficient water use, declining fisheries, unstable farmer incomes, inadequate school nutrition programs, and escalating environmental degradation. The lack of an integrated district-level governance mechanism constrains Cambodia s capacity to develop climate-resilient, inclusive, and sustainable food systems. The Innovative Solution: The proposed model establishes a District Integrated Food System Governance Platform, led by district authorities and comprising line departments, farmer groups, water user communities, fishery organizations, schools, health centers, women s groups, and local markets. This platform facilitates joint planning, data sharing, and coordinated investment across food production, water management, nutrition, and markets. The district serves as the operational hub, aligning national policy objectives with local community needs. Scientific & Technical Foundation: The model is based on food systems science, climate adaptation research, and community-based resource governance. Empirical evidence demonstrates that decentralized, multi-sector coordination enhances climate resilience, improves nutrition outcomes, and strengthens ecosystem protection. The model applies systems thinking at the district level, which is considered the most effective scale for governance. Immediate & Sustainable Benefits: * Farmers & producers: stable water access, diversified production, and reliable local markets. * Consumers & schools: improved food safety and child nutrition through local sourcing. * Communities: stronger climate resilience and livelihood.

core_fields.title: W-COLD- Women-Led Cold Chain Micro-Facility Network
core_fields.description: BASICS proposes a consulting-led model to design and operationalize a Women-Led Cold Chain Micro-Facility Network. SHGs and PGs will manage decentralized 5 MT units, while FPOs operate 10 MT solar-powered facilities to reduce perishables spoilage, stabilize prices, and improve dietary diversity. The project will develop planning tools, business models, institutional procurement linkages, and convergence pathways. Seed Grant support will establish a replicable framework for states to scale women-managed solar cold chain solutions.
core_fields.abstract: Post-harvest losses of perishable fruits, vegetables, milk, eggs, and fish continue to undermine nutrition outcomes, farmer incomes, and food system efficiency. Although cold chain investments have grown, access at the first-mile remains extremely limited, especially for smallholders and women producers. A decentralized network of solar-powered micro-cold rooms (5 MT) managed by Self Help Groups (SHGs) and Producer Groups (PGs) , linked to a centrally operated 10 MT cold storage run by Farmer Producer Organizations (FPO), offers a transformative opportunity to reduce spoilage, and enhance availability of nutrient-rich foods. When supported with district-level planning tools and viable business models, such systems deliver measurable economic and nutritional gains. Such a Micro-Facility Network is a consulting-led solution designed to help State Rural Livelihood Missions (SRLMs), SHGs, PGs, and FPOs plan, manage, and scale decentralized cold chain infrastructure. BASICS brings strong implementation intelligence, drawing from: 1. Its collaboration with CoolCrop in Himachal Pradesh to deploy cold storage and operationalize cooling-as-a-service models for FPOs; and 2. Extensive advisory engagements with National Rural Livelihood Missions (NRLM), and other SRLMs across diverse value chains. Leveraging this experience, BASICS will support two districts in Uttar Pradesh to: Prepare cold chain micro-plans optimized for seasonality, and market demand. Design financially viable cold chain enterprise models. Facilitate partnerships with different value chain partners; Integrate cold chain nodes into SHG, PG/FPO ecosytem The innovation shifts first-mile cold chain ownership to women s collectives, creating a decentralized yet seamlessly connected storage grid that reduces wastage, enhances climate resilience.

core_fields.title: The Community-Based Regenerative Farming Intelligence System for Smallholder Farmers in Kumbungu, Ghana
core_fields.description: The project builds a community-based regenerative farming intelligence system that blends IoT climate data, indigenous knowledge, and agroforestry guidance to support smallholder farmers in Kumbungu, Ghana. Farmers receive real-time insights, localized training, and regenerative practice support that improve yields, restore soil health, and strengthen climate resilience. The system empowers women and youth farmers with accessible, language-friendly tools that reduce losses, enhance food security, and create a scalable model for sustainable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Kumbungu, Ghana face rising climate uncertainty, declining soil health, and frequent crop losses because they lack timely, localized guidance to respond to weather shifts and manage their farms regeneratively. This challenge is urgent because climate impacts in the savannah zone are intensifying, and many farmers depend entirely on rain-fed production for food and income. Our innovation is a community-based regenerative farming intelligence system that blends hyper-local IoT climate data, agroforestry mapping, indigenous knowledge, and simple mobile alerts to help farmers make better decisions each day. Farmers receive real-time information on rainfall changes, soil moisture, pest risks, and tree-crop conditions, combined with tailored regenerative practices that improve yields and restore degraded land. The system also integrates Dagbani voice notes and culturally familiar training methods to ensure accessibility for women and youth farmers who may have limited digital literacy. The underlying insight behind this solution is that climate adaptation becomes effective only when scientific data, local knowledge, and regenerative practices are combined into one practical, easy-to-use system. IoT and remote sensing alone do not change outcomes; community ownership, regenerative design, and daily decision support do. Immediate benefits include reduced crop losses, improved water and soil management, higher survival of tree crops, and increased farmer confidence in planning. Sustainable benefits include restored soil fertility, stronger agroforestry systems, increased household food security, improved incomes, and greater resilience across the community.

core_fields.title: Enhance fresh food availability and prevent spoilage with an innovative, mobile, solar-powered refrigeration system.
core_fields.description: KUYODA will introduce mobile solar-powered refrigeration carts to reduce food spoilage and increase access to fresh, nutritious food in Kyaka Refugee Settlement. Operated by Deaf and disabled youth, the system provides affordable cooling for fruits, vegetables, and other perishable foods, supporting farmers and vendors who struggle with high post-harvest losses. The carts help improve diets for families, including children with disabilities and developmental delays linked to poor nutrition.
core_fields.abstract: In districts such as Kyegegwa, Mubende, and other high-temperature regions, including Kyaka refugees camp and its host communities, fresh food spoils rapidly due to intense heat, long distances to markets, and the absence of affordable cold-chain systems. Farmers, vendors, and families frequently lose fruits, vegetables, milk, and other perishables before they can be consumed or sold. This reduces income, increases food insecurity, and limits access to nutritious diets, especially for children with disabilities or developmental delays linked to poor nutrition. KUYODA's innovation introduces mobile solar-powered refrigeration carts that bring cooling services directly to farms, trading centers, schools, and households. Operated by Deaf and disabled youth, these carts close the critical first-mile and last-mile gaps where spoilage is highest. Mobility ensures that cooling is available anywhere, unlike traditional stationary cold rooms, making it well-suited for dispersed rural and peri-urban communities. The solution uses solar direct-drive refrigeration, high-efficiency insulation, and modular battery storage integrated into a lightweight mobile unit. This scientific and technical design enables continuous cooling without fuel or grid electricity, making the system both climate-friendly and cost-effective. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, increased income for farmers and vendors, safer food handling, and improved diets for families. Schools and community nutrition programs gain access to fresher produce, while Deaf youth gain meaningful employment and leadership roles. Long-term benefits include strengthened local markets, lower carbon emissions, greater resilience to heat, and a more inclusive and sustainable food system that supports both rural communities and expanding urban markets

core_fields.title: Conserving and developing indigenous vegetable and fruit varieties along the value chain in Northwestern, Vietnam
core_fields.description: The project focuses on conserving and developing indigenous vegetable and fruit varieties through value chain approaches. It aims to enhance food security, promote biodiversity, and improve income for local communities. Key activities include researching native varieties, optimizing cultivation practices, and establishing market connections. By integrating health, environmental, and economic perspectives, the project seeks sustainable growth while preserving cultural heritage.
core_fields.abstract: Indigenous vegetables and fruit are an important crop for providing nutrition, improved health and income security to northern mountainous populations. Often considered as underutilized crops, these indigenous and naturalized fruits and vegetables generally harvested from wild populations are easy to grow, often require lower inputs than F1 vegetable varieties, are more adapted to local conditions and environmental stress, and could provide local opportunities for income generation and improving health and nutrition. By strengthening the indigenous vegetables and fruit using a market-first approach to overcome constraints along the value chain leading to improved production practices, supply, postharvest handling, distribution and consumer acceptability of indigenous vegetables and fruit, opportunities for smallholder farmers to become more engaged in the supply chain will emerge. These key ingredients are needed to develop a sustainable and resilient indigenous vegetables and fruit system providing opportunities to smallholders. We suggest that focus is needed first on improving indigenous vegetables and fruit genetic materials, then ensuring systems are put in place for growers to access such materials, coupled with the development of sustainable production and postharvest systems that allow for year-round production as well as seed production/saving techniques. By doing this in parallel and in partnership with industry and the private sector, greater gains can be made in improved market access and building capacity of stakeholders through outreach programs across the indigenous vegetables and fruit value chain while creating awareness of health and nutritional benefits of indigenous vegetables and fruit which further serve to drive market demand

core_fields.title: Biofortified Soya Bean Empowerment Hubs for Women and PWDs in Luuka
core_fields.description: LNFA will establish women and PWD-led Biofortified Soya Empowerment Hubs in Luuka District, Uganda. Using high-iron/zinc soybean varieties, solar-powered processing and guaranteed buy-back with crop insurance, we transform our proven pilot into climate-resilient micro-enterprises producing fortified soya milk and porridge flour. The project reaches 600 vulnerable mothers and PWDs, reduces hidden hunger for 1,000 people, doubles household incomes and prevents post-harvest losses delivering safe, nutritious, affordable food year-round while empowering the most marginalized
core_fields.abstract: In Luuka District, smallholder women, teenage mothers and PWDs grow soya bean, yet hidden hunger affects 42% of children and 35% of women due to low micronutrient intake and seasonal food shortages. Post-harvest losses exceed 30%, and sugarcane monoculture has degraded soils and incomes. Our innovation upgrades LNFA s proven soya bean pilot into women and PWD led Biofortified Soya Bean Empowerment Hubs. We introduce conventionally bred high iron (+80%) and high zinc (+50%) soybean varieties, combine them with solar-powered village level processing units (milk, fortified porridge flour, spices), climate-index insurance, real-time weather alerts and guaranteed fair price buy back. Every product showing farmer story and nutrient content. This solves three interconnected problems; Nutritional: Biofortified soya delivers absorbable iron and zinc directly in daily meals, clinically proven to reduce anemia and stunting. Economic: value addition and reliable markets double women s income (from $250 to less than $600/season). Environmental: solar energy, crop rotation and agroforestry restore soil health and cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Immediate benefits: 600 vulnerable producers (80% women/PWDs) gain resilient income and insurance. 15,000 consumers (especially schoolchildren) access affordable, safe, micronutrient-rich foods year-round. Less than 200 tones of soya beans saved from loss. Long-term benefits: Replicable hub model ends seasonal hunger. Empowers marginalized groups to lead food-system change and regenerates degraded land transforming food security for the entire district.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Agriculture for Women Farmers
core_fields.description: This project empowers women farmers in rural Zambia through solar irrigation, soil restoration and zero-waste food processing. By adding value to surplus such as tomatoes into relish and powder, we reduce post-harvest losses and improve year-round nutrition. Our initiative strengthens women cooperatives, builds regenerative food systems, and expands equitable access to safe, nutritious foods. The result is climate-smart agriculture that increases incomes, enhances food security and supports healthier, more resilient communities.
core_fields.abstract: The Harvest Fund works with women smallholder farmers in Zambia to strengthen climate-smart agriculture, cooperative development, and market access. Through this work, we have identified persistent barriers, climate shocks, declining soil fertility and high post-harvest losses of perishable crops that directly informed the design of this innovation. Women farmers face food insecurity driven by climate variability, degraded soils, and high post-harvest losses, particularly of tomatoes. These challenges are highly relevant as women produce most household food yet remain under-resourced, limiting nutrition outcomes, incomes, and climate resilience. We address this problem through a holistic, women-led innovation integrating solar-powered irrigation, regenerative agriculture, and zero-waste food processing. Solar irrigation enables year-round production without fossil fuels. Regenerative practices including composting, mulching, intercropping, bokashi making and crop rotation restore soil fertility, improve nutrient density, and increase long-term productivity. Surplus tomatoes are processed into shelf-stable relish and powder using locally appropriate technologies, reducing food loss and creating value-added income and this needs scaling for higher impact.. While irrigation, regeneration, or processing exist elsewhere, this innovation is novel in its integrated, cooperative-based approach, linking climate adaptation, nutrition, and circular food systems within women-led structures. It draws on agroecology, renewable energy and food preservation research, showing that addressing soil health, water access and post-harvest management together drives greater resilience and adoption. Immediate benefits include higher yields, reduced losses, improved diets, and new income streams for women farmers. Long-term benefits include healthier soils, lower emissions, stronger cooperatives, and scalable, climate-smart food systems benefiting communities, schools, markets, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Scaling Sustainable Plant-Based Beverages for Better Nutrition in African CommunitiesTo
core_fields.description: Our project expands the production and distribution of nutritious, plant-based hibiscus beverages that provide affordable, healthy alternatives to sugary drinks. By sourcing directly from local farmers, we support regenerative agriculture, reduce waste, and strengthen rural livelihoods. This project will scale a sustainable, youth-led food innovation that improves community nutrition, increases access to safe and appealing beverages, and contributes to an equitable and resilient African food system.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation transforms locally grown hibiscus into nutritious, affordable, and preservative-free beverages that offer a healthier alternative to the high-sugar drinks dominating Nigerian markets. Many communities lack access to safe, natural, and appealing beverages, contributing to rising diet-related health issues. Simultaneously, smallholder farmers struggle to earn stable incomes from these climate-resilient crops due to limited market opportunities. We address both challenges through a scalable, youth-led beverage model that sources raw materials directly from local farmers using sustainable and regenerative practices. Hibiscus are naturally drought-tolerant, require minimal chemical inputs, and thrive in diverse soils making them ideal crops for climate-affected regions. Their high nutritional value, rich fiber content, antioxidants, vitamins, and plant-based profile provided the scientific insight behind selecting them as the foundation of our solution. Our processing method preserves nutrient integrity while ensuring food safety and extending shelf life without additives. We utilize low-waste production, responsible water use, and recyclable packaging. Immediate benefits: 1)Consumers access affordable, nutrient-rich beverages that support healthier diets. 2) Farmers receive better incomes and a reliable market for their crops. 3) Youth and women gain local employment and entrepreneurship opportunities. Sustainable benefits: 1)Strengthened local value chains and reduced dependence on imported, carbon-intensive beverages. 2)Increased cultivation of climate-resilient crops supporting soil health and biodiversity. 3)Long-term availability of safe, appealing, culturally relevant plant-based drinks for schools, communities, and low-income consumers. Our innovation provides a holistic, scalable approach to nutrition, sustainability, climate resilience, and equitable food access.

core_fields.title: Empowering Farmers with Blockchain Traceability to Reduce Loss, Ensure Safety, and Boost Income
core_fields.description: AgTrail is a blockchain-powered traceability and compliance platform enabling smallholder farmers in Nigeria to reduce post-harvest loss, boost income, and access trusted markets. By digitizing production, certification, and supply chain records, AgTrail builds transparency and food safety from farm to fork. With over 5,500 farmers onboarded and 40% traceability achieved, we re now scaling to strengthen food systems across WHH regions and the Global South.
core_fields.abstract: AgTrail is a blockchain-based traceability and compliance platform designed to solve the deep-rooted transparency, trust, and data fragmentation issues in Africa s agricultural value chains. Smallholder farmers, who produce over 80% of Nigeria s food, face exclusion from premium markets due to lack of verifiable records, quality assurance, and post-harvest visibility. As a result, up to 40% of produce is lost post-harvest, and farmers earn significantly below fair market value. AgTrail addresses this by digitizing production, aggregation, processing and certification using a mobile-first interface tailored for rural users. Farmers are onboarded in under 15 minutes via mobile agents, and their data, from planting to processing, is logged onto a blockchain ledger. This enables real-time traceability, risk alerts, and digital certification that buyers, exporters, and regulators can instantly verify. To date, over 5,500 farmers across 10,000+ acres have used AgTrail to boost traceability to 40%, reduce post-harvest losses by 25%, and increase income by up to 40%. Our AI engine supports agribusinesses with insights on compliance and supply chain integrity, while QR codes on products offer consumers verified farm-to-shelf visibility. Designed for low-connectivity regions with a pay-per-trace model, AgTrail scales sustainably. The platform directly benefits farmers, cooperatives, buyers, and consumers, while building a foundation for export readiness, regenerative practices, and safer food systems. AgTrail is a system redesigned for trust, inclusion, and resilience in food systems, starting with Nigeria, and built to scale across WHH countries.

core_fields.title: Upayaku: Regenerating Andean Food Systems through Women's Innovation
core_fields.description: La Divina Papaya drives regenerative food systems in the Ecuadorian Andes through its Upayaku Rural Innovation Hub. We transform native plants and edible flowers into functional foods via women-led biocultural innovation and fair trade. This scalable model empowers producer communities, heals ecosystems, and connects conscious consumers to a new food economy. We seek the Growth Grant to establish Upayaku as a leading demonstration center, proving that ethical value chains can make regenerative agriculture the norm
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation is the Upayaku Rural Innovation Hub, a women-led, place-based model that transforms the systemic undervaluation of Andean agrobiodiversity into a regenerative food economy. The core problem is dual: in Cayambe, Ecuador, land is shifting from food to toxic rose monocultures, eroding ecosystems and livelihoods, while the profound knowledge and nutritional value of native plants and edible flowers (PANC) remain marginalized. We solve this with a technically sophisticated and bioculturally deep first step: regenerative hydrological landscape design. We implement a fusion of advanced earthworks and ancestral Andean water wisdom to restore watershed function and wetland health. This creates a resilient biocultural infrastructure a living system that is both technically viable and culturally rooted. On this restored foundation, we integrate three core elements: 1) Biocultural R&D, where ancestral knowledge meets applied science to prototype functional foods from PANC; 2) A Regenerative Production Network of women farmers cultivating with agroecology; and 3) A Value-Based Market Link that converts conscious demand into equitable income. The key, innovative insight is that true resilience requires a layered approach: first, the technical and ancestral restoration of natural cycles; then, the socio-economic creation of new value from the bottom up. This shifts economic incentives from extraction to regeneration. Immediate benefits: Women producers gain dignified income; consumers access unique, nutritious products; and hectares of land transition to regenerative systems. Sustainable benefits: We build a proven, replicable blueprint that counters agro-industrial expansion, conserves agrobiodiversity, creates a climate-resilient local economy, and reestablishes cultural pride.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Livelihoods for Resilient Rural Communities
core_fields.description: Our project helps smallholder farmers adapt to climate change by providing solar-powered irrigation, clean household energy, and training in climate-smart agriculture. We support communities to participate in high-integrity carbon projects, earn new income, and strengthen resilience through insurance for their crops and livestock from the proceeds of carbon projects. By combining clean energy, carbon markets, and practical farming solutions, the project improves productivity, reduces emissions, and creates long-term livelihood opportunities for rural families.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation combines clean energy, climate-smart agriculture, and community-based carbon projects into one practical solution that directly benefits smallholder farmers. Farmers face three major challenges: unreliable rainfall, rising production costs, and limited access to carbon markets or insurance. These issues reduce yields, increase vulnerability to climate shocks, and prevent rural communities from earning income from activities that protect the environment. Our solution tackles these problems by integrating solar-powered irrigation, homestead solar systems, regenerative agriculture training, and digital carbon monitoring into everyday farm activities. Solar irrigation ensures farmers can grow food year-round without expensive diesel pumps. Training in regenerative agriculture helps restore soils, increase yields, and store carbon. Our Digital MRV system uses mobile tools and geo-mapping to verify these climate benefits accurately, allowing communities to generate high-quality carbon credits. This innovation is based on the insight that carbon projects work best when they are built into activities farmers already value such as irrigation, soil improvement, and reliable energy. By bundling insurance into the program, farmers are also protected from climate risks, ensuring long-term participation and stability. Immediate benefits include increased crop production, lower energy costs, reduced reliance on rain-fed farming, and improved household energy access. Sustainable benefits include healthier soils, higher farm incomes, resilience to drought, and new revenue from carbon credits. Communities gain new skills, reduced environmental impact, and improved living standards. Society and the environment benefit from reduced emissions, better climate resilience, and stronger local economies.

core_fields.title: Biorational Pest Management: Scaling Biopesticide Adoption Through Digital Innovation in Bangladesh
core_fields.description: This project scales the adoption of validated IPM packages and biopesticides among Bangladeshi smallholders. It leverages iFarmer's digital platform to provide integrated access to finance, agri-advisory, awareness building and market linkages, while company supplies proven biopesticides and technical expertise. National partners lead the dissemination of validated IPM strategies and field training, supported by international collaborators for policy and scaling. This holistic public-private partnership will create a scalable model for sustainable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: Bangladeshi smallholder farmers face 30 40% crop losses due to persistent pest pressure, worsened by climate change driven shifts in pest dynamics. Heavy reliance on chemical pesticides leads to resistance, environmental damage, and health risks. Notably, 47% of farmers report pesticide-related penalties each year, highlighting misuse and the absence of safer, accessible alternatives. Solution: We propose an integrated biorational pest management system that combines the company s validated biopesticide formulations with iFarmer s digital agriculture platform. This enables efficient last-mile delivery, structured farmer training, and improved market linkages, ensuring farmers receive both quality inputs and practical knowledge. Novelty: The model leverages a public private partnership approach that embeds sustainable pest management directly into Bangladesh s digital agriculture ecosystem and national extension services. This ensures scalability, long-term commercial viability, and continuity beyond project-based support. Scientific Insight: Field data generated through BWMRI, BARI, and BRRI confirm that biopesticides used within Integrated Pest Management (IPM) frameworks can perform comparably to conventional chemicals while preserving ecological integrity. The proposed formulations specifically target major insect pests in rice, maize, and vegetable systems. Immediate Benefits: Farmers gain access to affordable, effective pest control options that have demonstrated yield improvements of 15 20%. Additional benefits include reduced exposure to harmful chemicals and enhanced market opportunities through iFarmer s established supply chain network. Sustainable Benefits: Lower chemical use reduces environmental contamination, protects aquatic systems, and supports soil biodiversity. Through collaboration with national and international research partners, the farming system becomes more climate-resilient, promoting long-term sustainability across smallholder communities.

core_fields.title: Sustainable aquaculture of cuchia, turtles, snails, crabs, native fish, for enhancing tribal livelihoods in Bangladesh
core_fields.description: This action research enhances tribal livelihoods in six Bangladesh districts through sustainable aquaculture of turtles, snails, crabs, cuchia, and native fish. Pilot seed and breeding units, along with demonstration sites, will be established to evaluate the impacts on income, nutrition, and empowerment. By integrating traditional knowledge, the initiative promotes food security and inclusive growth. Community participation and value addition strengthen resilience, while workshops and documentation ensure replicability, positioning grassroots innovation within the global SDG agenda.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation focuses on introducing sustainable aquaculture practices for cuchia, turtles, snails, crabs, and native fish to strengthen tribal livelihoods in Bangladesh. The problem being addressed is the economic vulnerability and food insecurity of tribal households, who rely heavily on seasonal agriculture and forest resources that are increasingly unstable due to climate change and ecological degradation. This solution is relevant because it diversifies income sources, improves nutrition, and promotes ecological balance. By establishing pilot seed production units for cuchia and breeding centers for endangered turtles, alongside demonstration farms in each district, the project creates practical models that communities can replicate. The scientific insight behind this approach lies in recognizing the ecological compatibility of native species with local water bodies and the potential of integrating traditional knowledge with modern aquaculture techniques. This ensures species survival, reduces environmental stress, and enhances productivity without relying on imported or invasive species. Immediate benefits include: Farmers and households gain new income streams from fish and aquaculture product sales. Communities improve food security and nutrition through accessible protein sources. Schools and youth benefit from skill development and ecological awareness programs. Sustainable benefits include: Environmental preservation through better water resource management and conservation of endangered species. Social empowerment via collective ownership, stronger local institutions, and inclusive participation. Economic resilience through value addition and reduced dependence on fragile agriculture. Overall, the innovation offers a replicable framework for community-driven aquaculture that supports livelihoods, biodiversity, and long-term sustainability.

core_fields.title: Murmushi Nutri-Pap, A Locally Formulated Nutrient-Dense Pap Powder for Combating Child Malnutrition in Northern Nigeria.
core_fields.description: Murmushi Nutri-Pap is an affordable, nutrient-dense pap powder made from 100% localy sourced grains and legumes to combat child malnutrition in Nigeria. MPDF will refine the formula, improve food safety and packaging, and pilot the program with 100 vulnerable households. The project strengthens local food systems, empowers women producers, and provides a culturally familiar, nutritious complementary food that improves child health, reduces dependency on costly imports, and lays the foundation for scalable community-based nutrition solutions.
core_fields.abstract: Murmushi Nutri-Pap is a decentralized, locally manufactured complementary food system that transforms widely available indigenous grains and legumes into a safe, nutrient-dense, and affordable pap powder for young children in Nigeria. The innovation addresses chronic child malnutrition by replacing traditional single-grain pap, which is calorie-dense but nutrient-poor, with a modular, optimized formulation that delivers balanced protein, essential fats, and key micronutrients using culturally familiar foods. The Nutri-Pap formulation combines millet, soybeans, bambara nuts, groundnuts, beans, benniseed, moringa, and other locally sourced ingredients selected for their complementary amino-acid profiles, micronutrient density, and climate resilience. Unlike imported fortified blends, Nutri-Pap is designed for low-resource production environments, using basic processing equipment (roasting, milling, blending, and sealing) and standardized hygiene protocols that can be replicated through women-led cooperatives and community nutrition hubs. The core innovation is not only the product, but the production and delivery model. Nutri-Pap introduces a decentralized nutrition manufacturing approach that shortens supply chains, lowers cost barriers, and embeds food safety and quality control at the community level. This model enables consistent access to nutritious complementary food in underserved and displacement-affected areas where commercial fortified foods are either unavailable or unaffordable. Early prototypes, developed through MPDF s nutrition programming and informed by local health workers and nutritionists, demonstrated high caregiver acceptance and observable improvements in child feeding outcomes. Building on this foundation, the proposed project will refine nutrient ratios, validate safety and nutritional content through laboratory analysis, and standardize production protocols to enable scalable replication.

core_fields.title: Roots of Resilience: Indigenous-Led Food, Water, and Climate Resilience in Colombia s Orinoqu a
core_fields.description: This transformative, indigenous-led model integrates food, water, and climate resilience in the Kanalitojo Indigenous Territory in Vichada, Colombia. Rooted in ancestral agroforestry practices, the project establishes diversified agroecological gardens, sustainable cashew-based production systems, solar-powered water access, associative community models, and local mentoring structures to ensure long-term sustainability. It aims to secure nutritious diets, stable livelihoods, and restored ecosystems for 30 indigenous families, while generating an evidence-based, scalable model for the broader Orinoqu a region.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation is a systems-based, indigenous-led approach that integrates climate-smart food production, water security, and regenerative value chains in Colombia s Orinoqu a region. In the Kanalitojo Indigenous Territory, 30 Saliva, Sikuani, and Amor a families face chronic food insecurity, degradation of moriche palm forest wetlands, and highly volatile incomes.Our model strengthens traditional production systems by transforming them into diversified agroforestry plots that combine ancestral crops, vegetables, small livestock, and cashew trees. These systems are managed through organic fertilization, community seed banks, efficient water use, and soil restoration practices, enabling a transformation of the local food system toward greater resilience and sustainability.Due to climatic seasonality and limited infrastructure, the project installs solar-powered water wells and pressure-compensated irrigation systems for agroecological gardens. This reduces dependence on distant or contaminated water sources and stabilizes food production during dry seasons.On the market side, the project co-designs a fair and tradable cashew value chain through formalized commercial partnerships, while strengthening short food supply chains via local and proximity markets. This enables food exchange and local commercialization, reinforcing resilient and inclusive local food systems.Throughout the process, indigenous knowledge and participatory training methodologies are integrated to co-create curricula, governance rules, and a community-based monitoring system. The result is a replicable, evidence-generating platform that simultaneously improves access to safe and nutritious food, strengthens livelihoods, and conserves critical ecosystems in one of Colombia s most vulnerable frontier regions.

core_fields.title: Integrated Downstream Model For Local Products Innovation, Circular Economy And Empowerment Of Sambeng Kulon Village
core_fields.description: This project implements an Integrated Downstreaming Model for corn and peanuts in Sambeng Kulon Village, Banyumas, to increase farmer income, reduce waste, and strengthen local food systems. Through product innovation, circular economy practices, and farmer institutional empowerment, the project transforms raw commodities into value-added products while utilizing agricultural residues. Over 18 months, the initiative builds sustainable village enterprises, improves nutrition, and delivers a scalable and replicable model for inclusive, climate-smart rural development
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Sambeng Kulon Village primarily sell corn and peanuts as raw commodities, resulting in low and unstable incomes, high post-harvest losses, limited market access, and underutilization of agricultural by-products. This linear production system is increasingly irrelevant in the context of food security challenges, nutrition gaps, youth disengagement from agriculture, and growing demands for sustainable and circular food systems. The proposed Integrated Downstreaming Model for Corn and Peanuts addresses these challenges by transforming raw produce into diversified, value-added food and non-food products (nutritious snacks, fortified flours, peanut-based spreads, corn-based foods, animal feed, compost, and bio-inputs), while embedding product innovation, circular economy principles, and farmer institutional empowerment. The model integrates post-harvest handling, small-scale processing technologies, quality and safety standards, waste-to-resource conversion, and cooperative-based enterprise management at the village level. The novelty lies in its systemic integration: combining multi-product downstreaming, zero-waste utilization of residues (husks, shells, cobs), and strengthened farmer organizations within a single, replicable village ecosystem. Unlike existing solutions that focus only on processing or training, this model links innovation pipelines, local institutions, and markets simultaneously. The approach is informed by scientific insights on agri-food value chain upgrading, nutrition-sensitive agriculture, and circular bioeconomy models adapted to smallholder contexts. Immediate benefits include higher farmer incomes, reduced waste, improved food availability, and new local employment. Sustainable benefits include strengthened village enterprises, improved nutrition for consumers and schools, reduced environmental impact, enhanced resilience of farming communities, and scalable pathways toward inclusive, climate-smart rural development.

core_fields.title: Turning Rice Husk Waste into Soil & Climate Solution (CSV-P Biochar Pilot)
core_fields.description: AgroGreen Dynamics Ltd will run a 6-month pilot in Nasarawa State to convert rice husk waste mostly burned or dumped into high-carbon biochar using a hybrid pyrolysis system. The project will install a medium-scale unit, train 30 farmers (60% women, 40% youth), and establish demonstration plots to improve soil health and raise yields by 25 40%. It will cut open burning, strengthen circularity in the rice value chain, and create a scalable climate-smart model for future growth funding.
core_fields.abstract: Nigeria s rice sector produces millions of tons of rice husk annually, yet most of it is openly burned, releasing harmful smoke, greenhouse gases, and ash that contaminate soil and water. At the same time, smallholder farmers in Nasarawa face declining soil fertility, high fertilizer costs, and low yields. This project addresses both challenges through an innovative, community-scale solution that transforms rice husk waste into climate-smart biochar. AgroGreen s innovation combines a hybrid pyrolysis system locally fabricated with modular imported components for temperature control and emissions safety with a regenerative agronomy model. The system converts rice husk into high-carbon biochar, a scientifically proven soil amendment that improves nutrient retention, enhances microbial activity, increases water-holding capacity, and permanently stores carbon in soils. The scientific insight behind the solution is rooted in pyrolysis chemistry: heating biomass without oxygen stabilizes carbon, creating a porous material that rebuilds degraded soils while reducing emissions by 2.7 3.4 tCO₂e per ton of biochar. Paired with an advanced MRV (Monitoring, Reporting, Verification) framework aligned with VERRA/Gold Standard, the project generates verifiable carbon data essential for future carbon finance. Immediate benefits include cleaner air from reduced burning, new green jobs for youth technicians, improved soil fertility, and 25 40% yield increases on rice, maize, and legumes. Farmers also reduce fertilizer use by 10 25%, lowering production costs. Sustainable benefits extend to long-term carbon sequestration, a circular rice value chain where waste becomes a valuable product, stronger cooperative enterprises, and new opportunities for women and youth in biochar production and regenerative farming.

core_fields.title: Reducing Food Loss through Regenerative Production and Decentralized Cold Storage
core_fields.description: Farm Boksi supports smallholder farmers to improve soil health, increase yields, and reduce losses through regenerative farming training and access to quality inputs. After harvest, farmers aggregate produce with our mobile solar-powered cold storage units, and store them at our cold hub which preserve quality and stabilize prices. Our digital B2B marketplace links them to buyers. We strengthen climate resilience, boosts farmer incomes, and creates a reliable supply of nutritious food for local markets.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Tanzania face declining soil fertility, low productivity, limited access to quality inputs, and significant post-harvest losses caused by poor handling, long transport times, and lack of reliable storage. These challenges reduce farmer incomes, weaken local food supply, and heighten vulnerability to climate shocks. Farm Boksi addresses this through an integrated approach combining regenerative farming practices, mobile and stationary cold storage, and digital market access. The innovation begins with regenerative production. Farmers receive training in soil-building techniques such as composting, mulching, and intercropping, supported by access to appropriate inputs. These practices draw on well-documented scientific evidence showing that healthier soils boost yields, retain moisture, and improve resilience. After harvest, produce is collected through Farm Boksi s two mobile solar-powered cold units, which stabilize perishables at the farmgate and prevent spoilage caused by heat, handling, and transport. The produce is then delivered to our stationed solar-powered cold room, where it is aggregated, graded, and kept in optimal condition. A digital B2B platform connects this high-quality, aggregated produce directly to institutional buyers, retailers, processors, hotels, and schools ensuring better prices and consistent demand. This integrated model reduces losses, increases income, and strengthens local value chains. Immediate benefits include reduced spoilage, improved quality, fairer prices, and lower risk for farmers. Long-term benefits include healthier soils, higher productivity, climate resilience, and a more reliable supply of nutritious food for communities. Environmentally, the model cuts emissions through solar energy and supports more sustainable farming systems.

core_fields.title: Un menage sans Fain (MsF) A household without hunger (MsF)
core_fields.description: The project aims to save the lives of 2,500 displaced households in regions experiencing humanitarian crises and acute food insecurity (Phases 3 and 4) by scaling up the Nafama Garden initiative. The AMSODE approach addresses immediate food needs through a bio-intensive gardening technique using climate- and water-resilient technology that enables families in the Sahel to grow large quantities of food for their own consumption and to generate income and savings.
core_fields.abstract: In a context where more than 792,000 people are facing acute food insecurity in Mali in 2025 (3.10% of the country's total population) are in phase 3 and 26,025 people (0.10%) are in phase 4, the "Un M nage Sans Faim - MsF" project targets 400 vulnerable households in S gou and Kidal, representing 2,400 people: 600 men, 720 women, and 1,080 children. The households affected are facing a decline in production due to insecurity, lack of inputs and difficulties in accessing land and water. The Jardin Nafama approach, developed by AMSODE, provides a sustainable solution by combining sustainable farming and biointensive agriculture. Simple, tailored technological innovations enhance the efficiency of the Nafama Garden through a locally manufactured drip irrigation system (perforated pipes) that reduces watering effort and optimises available water. The approach uses accelerated thermal composters that enable rapid and continuous fertilisation with decomposition in just 2 to 3 weeks. AMSODE provides digital monitoring via a QR code affixed to a stake in each garden. The AMSODE agricultural technician scans the code with a phone and updates the monitoring data (photos, soil condition, production), which also allows for remote advice and improves management and reporting. MsF prevents households from falling back into cyclical need and dependence on humanitarian aid, which can be time-consuming. In just 30 days, households master a technique that they will use throughout their lives, becoming self-sufficient and productive all year round. IDPs become both producers and consumers by using local inputs and technologywithin their reach.

core_fields.title: Planetary Healthy Snack Solutions from Locally Sourced Indigenous Ingredients tamuboost.com
core_fields.description: Tamu Boost is a Kenyan agrifood start-up that reduces food loss and improves nutrition by transforming surplus and indigenous crops into affordable, shelf-stable snacks. Using solar dehydration and light fortification, we create products like fruit strips, fortified mixes, and sweet potato cookies. By sourcing from smallholder farmers and urban markets, we strengthen circular food systems while increasing access to healthy foods for children and low-income communities.
core_fields.abstract: Tamu Boost (tamuboost.com ) addresses two interconnected challenges in Kenya and much of Africa: persistent child malnutrition and high levels of food loss among indigenous and perishable crops. Despite Kenya s rich agricultural diversity, many nutritious foods such as mangoes, pineapples, sweet potatoes, and traditional grains are underutilized or wasted due to poor storage, limited processing options, and weak market access. At the same time, children and low-income households increasingly rely on cheap, ultra-processed snacks that are calorie-dense but micronutrient-poor. Our innovation transforms surplus and locally sourced indigenous crops into affordable, nutrient-dense, shelf-stable snacks using solar dehydration and simple fortification techniques. These low-energy, climate-smart processing methods preserve key micronutrients, extend shelf life, and reduce post-harvest losses without reliance on expensive industrial infrastructure. Products such as fruit clusters, fortified snack mixes, and sweet potato-based snacks are designed to integrate easily into school feeding programs and community food environments. The scientific insight behind Tamu Boost lies in combining dehydration proven to retain nutrients when done at low temperatures with food-to-food fortification and minimal processing. This approach ensures nutritional value while keeping production costs low and accessible. Immediate benefits include improved dietary diversity for children, additional income streams for smallholder farmers, and reduced food waste. Long-term benefits include stronger local food systems, improved community health outcomes, and environmentally sustainable food production that supports resilience across farmers, schools, and communities.

core_fields.title: Agriman Agventures : Circular Nutrition System for Kids
core_fields.description: Children across the Caribbean face limited access to affordable, nutritious snacks, while large volumes of locally grown fruit are lost as waste. WHYFARM is addressing both challenges by transforming surplus mangoes into safe, nutrient-dense snacks for children, produced through youth-led agripreneurship and trusted AGRIman branding. The project creates a circular nutrition system that improves child diets, reduces food waste, and generates youth livelihoods through a scalable, locally rooted model.
core_fields.abstract: Across the Caribbean, children face limited access to affordable, nutritious food, contributing to rising diet-related health risks, while farmers experience income losses due to high levels of fruit waste from seasonal overproduction and cosmetic rejection. Mangoes, despite being nutrient-dense and widely grown, are among the most wasted crops, representing both a nutrition gap and an environmental inefficiency. WHYFARM s innovation is a circular kids nutrition system that transforms surplus mangoes into safe, shelf-stable, nutrient-dense snacks for children, produced through youth-led micro-processing and distributed using the trusted AGRIman brand. The system integrates food science, agripreneurship training, and culturally relevant branding to ensure products are appealing, affordable, and trusted by families and schools. The solution is informed by nutritional science on fruit-based micronutrient delivery, post-harvest loss reduction strategies, and behavioral insights showing that trusted characters and education increase healthy food adoption among children. Simple, low-energy preservation techniques are used to extend shelf life while maintaining nutritional value, making the model feasible in resource-constrained settings. Immediate benefits include improved access to healthy snacks for children, reduced post-harvest losses for farmers, and income-generating opportunities for youth. Long-term benefits include strengthened local food systems, reduced environmental waste, scalable youth-led agribusiness models, and a replicable pathway for improving child nutrition and food security across vulnerable communities.

core_fields.title: Regional Freeze-Drying Hub - Novel Infrastructure to Scale Fresh Food Rescue
core_fields.description: This project launches and scales a regional processing and freeze-drying hub, stabilizing 15,000-150,000 pounds of rescued fresh foods annually. By preserving up to 97% of nutrition and producing shelf-stable, convenient meals, snacks, and ingredients, this novel infrastructure strengthens food recovery programs, reduces spoilage and greenhouse gas emissions, and expands equitable, nutritious food availability. Funding validates replicable, scalable operations and demonstrates measurable impact, creating infrastructure that transforms regional food systems and enables long-term national expansion.
core_fields.abstract: Over 100 billion pounds of fresh food are wasted annually, while 45 million individuals in the U.S. face food insecurity. Fresh food rescue efforts today focus on redistribution of surplus, relying on cold storage, transportation, and immediate handoff. While essential, these models face structural constraints: up to 40% of rescued fresh foods spoil before reaching a plate. Food recovery is hampered by inherent perishability, seasonal supply swings, and limited access to logistics and processing infrastructure. Our innovation is a regional food rescue processing and freeze-drying hub that provides the missing infrastructure layer in food recovery systems. We process surplus and rescued foods for existing food access organizations and local producers, transforming their perishable resources into nutritious, delicious, shelf-stable goods. By stabilizing their foods at peak freshness, our hub enables partners to maximize the impact of their existing resources without the burden of additional infrastructure or complex logistics. Combining coordinated logistics with light processing and freeze-drying, our hub preserves up to 97% of original nutrition, maximizes flavor, and ensures long-term safety without additives, extending shelf life from days to years. Freeze-dried meals and snacks are convenient, requiring minimal preparation. Our approach unlocks healthier, dignified options for individuals with limited kitchen access, mobility challenges, or transportation barriers who otherwise rely on canned or ultra-processed foods. Immediate benefits include reduced food loss and emissions, improved nutritional access, and stronger food networks. Long-term benefits include resilient regional food systems, regenerative supply chains, emergency preparedness, and equitable access to trusted, healthy food.

core_fields.title: Energy to Food: Solar Energy Financing Food Access for Wayuu Communities
core_fields.description: Energy to Food is an integrated model that strengthens food systems in Wayuu communities in La Guajira by linking energy efficiency, food access, and community nutrition. The project will install solar panels at the Food Bank and expand the Food for All program through solidarity stores and community-based animal rearing for household consumption, generating immediate social and nutritional benefits while ensuring long-term environmental and financial sustainability.
core_fields.abstract: The department of La Guajira faces a structural challenge within its food systems. An estimated 52.35% of the population experiences food insecurity, and nearly 49% lives in dispersed rural areas with severe limitations in food access. Wayuu communities, representing approximately 45% of the population, often travel between 1 and 8 hours to purchase food, with transportation costs of up to USD15 per trip, significantly increasing food costs and limiting access to nutritious diets. In response, the Food for All program was launched in 2023 in partnership with La Guajira Food Bank, promoting food access and availability through community-managed solidarity stores and community-based livestock initiatives. A solidarity store is a community-run access point for food and basic goods that operates as a sustainable distribution channel in areas with accessibility barriers. Over the past two years, 22 solidarity stores have been established, benefiting more than 19,800 people and distributing over 94 tons of food. Complementarily, eight Wayuu communities have strengthened household diets through small-scale livestock production, providing more than 3 tons of protein for self-consumption. This new phase, Energy to Food, is a circular model that integrates energy efficiency, food access, and nutrition. Through the installation of solar panels at the Food Bank, the project reduces energy consumption associated with cold storage and freezing systems, avoids approximately 14 tons of CO2emissions annually, and strengthens operational sustainability. In parallel, project resources will support the installation of five additional solidarity stores and the expansion of animal rearing in five Wayuu communities.

core_fields.title: Project BREAD ( Biodiversity Restoration Employing Aerial Drones)
core_fields.description: This project will use drones to restore degraded habitats in buffer zones, conservation areas, and community forests by seeding native fruit plants like Bel, Jamun, Chiuri, figs, guavas, rhino apple, and traditional varieties of bananas. This revives vital food options for wildlife, keeping animals in forests and effectively reducing human-wildlife conflict. Simultaneously, these forests and orchards generate new livelihoods for local people by transforming depleted territories into thriving ecosystems and improved biodiversity.
core_fields.abstract: This project employs Drone technology i.e. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to restore degraded forest food systems. Currently, depleted natural habitats force hungry wildlife like wild boar, monkeys, porcupines, deers to raid agricultural lands, destroying crops and livelihoods. Our innovation addresses this root cause by using drones to precisely disperse seed balls of native, high-nutrition species Bel (Aegle marmelos) sacred in local culture, vital for monkeys and birds ; Jamun (Syzygium cumini) rich fruit for birds, bats, and mammals, Chiuri (Aesandra butyracea) butter tree providing fruit and valuable fat; Amla (Phyllanthus emblica) highly nutritious fruit for people and wildlife, Lapsi (Choerospondias axillaris) beloved sour fruit for local communities, Guava (Psidium guajava) accessible fruit for wildlife and households, Wild figs such as bargad into human-access restricted zones within conservation areas/national park and surrounding buffer zone area where a limited human acitvity are allowed. This precision ecological intervention rebuilds the natural food supply deep within the forest, encouraging animals to remain within park boundaries. The benefits are immediate and sustainable for all end users. For farmers, the restoration of the forest s "living pantry" significantly reduces crop raiding, ensuring safety and protecting yields. For local communities, the project catalyzes a green economy; residents are employed to manufacture seed balls, and eventually, user groups can harvest surplus fruits for high-value products like juices and medicines. Environmentally, this transforms barren wastelands into biodiversity hotspots, stabilizing fragile soils against landslides and sequestering carbon.

core_fields.title: Creating Resilient Rural Communities through Adaptation Strategies and Climate-Smart Agriculture
core_fields.description: The project aims to scale climate-resilient, self-sustaining agricultural model farms to improve food security, diversify livelihoods, and promote environmentally responsible practices. By introducing tunnel farming, rainwater harvesting, organic soil management, kitchen gardening, and apiculture, it enhances productivity and sustainability. Through trainings, demonstrations, and enterprise support, farmers adopt improved practices and generate stable incomes. Building on three years of successful pilots, the project will expand community participation and establish replicable models for broader rural impact.
core_fields.abstract: Pakistan is an agricultural country where 65% of people live in poverty in countryside zones. Agriculture has low yields due to old-fashioned practices, little revenue, and climate induced crises. Majority of the people are facing unstable livelihoods and long-term socioeconomic risk as poverty are on the higher side from 30% to 40%. Through community-led adaptation, the Kafalah Foundation's effort aims to create a climate-smart, village-centric, rural based agricultural livelihood model that would enable them to become self-sufficient. This smart agricultural strategy will provide economic security for marginalized groups. Through the use of science-based instruments, such as tunnel farming, efficient water management, organic composting, bio-fertilizers, apiculture, and kitchen gardening, the idea replaces outdated methods. Farmers may make productive use of barren land through protected cultivation, soil regeneration, and water efficiency. Kafalah's novelty is the integration of such techniques into a community-led strategy that can be replicated throughout Pakistani rural agricultural regions. This structure helps KF increase its influence and provide long-term financial benefits. The approach quickly improves household income, nutrition, farm production, and dependency on aid. Long-term outcomes include diverse livelihoods, a scalable rural development strategy, ecological restoration, community ownership, and climate resilience. The Kafalah Foundation's all-encompassing approach includes reducing poverty cycles, enhancing environmental sustainability, and building economically vibrant, climate-resilient rural communities in Pakistan.

core_fields.title: Ndoto Bora
core_fields.description: We empower smallholder farmers, particularly women, to increase their yields and incomes through regenerative agriculture. We use our proprietary IoT-powered drone technology for precise monitoring and biofertilizer application to enhance soil health, increase farm productivity, and conserve water. We off-take maize produce from farmers and process it into fortified instant meal options, ensuring both farmer profitability and food security for low-income communities.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Tanzania, particularly women, face persistently low maize yields often below 2 tons per acre (compared to a potential 4.5tons/ha), alongside low incomes and significant post-harvest losses that exceeds 35% of total production. These challenges are driven by declining soil health due to nutrient depletion, inefficient water use, and limited access to reliable markets. The widespread reliance on costly synthetic fertilizers further degrades soil quality, strains farmers' finances, and fails to close the yield gap, making this challenge very urgent. We have developed a Precision Regenerative Farming Ecosystem designed to make agriculture a profitable and sustainable economic activity for smallholder farmers. Through our proprietary IoT-powered drone technology, we monitor over 1,200 acres per day, generating real-time insights on crop and soil conditions. This enables precise application of water, biofertilizers, and pest control in line with our regenerative farming model. Combined with natural biofertilizers, our approach restores soil organic matter, improves water retention, and sustainably closes the yield gap. Importantly, we off-take the maize produce from farmers and process it into fortified instant meal products, directly addressing post-harvest losses and market uncertainty. As a result, our farmers have achieved more than double their yields and increased incomes through guaranteed market access. Reductions in post-harvest losses have led to a 115% increase in household income. At the same time, our fortified products improve nutrition and food security for low-income communities. Environmental benefits include water conservation and reduced carbon emissions, while long-term impacts include restored soil biodiversity and improved soil.

core_fields.title: Wasted Avocados to Appealing Nutritious Food: Rural Households as Change Agents Address Stunting in Rwanda
core_fields.description: This project aims to make households active agents of change to end stunting in children under 5 years by utilizing wasted avocados, a rapidly growing crop in Rwanda and India. Stunting rates are very high in some parts of both countries. Rural small-farming households and groups will be trained to use economical home-scale technologies to convert non-marketable avocados into nutritious, delicious and shelf-stable products for children, pregnant and lactating mothers.
core_fields.abstract: The Government of Rwanda s Fifth Strategic Plan for Agriculture Transformation (PSTA5) focusses on nutrition. Stunting in children is a major concern; the country average is 33% with a high 40% in northern Rwanda. The previous policy focused on economic conditions by growing high-value export crops, like avocados, that never reached local nutrition deficient diets. Post-harvest avocado wastage is over 40%. The opportunity lies in converting non-marketable avocados into nutritious food to prevent stunting. While many initiatives are taken by government, private sector and NGOs, the marginalized and rural poor continue to be out of reach. In India, Arunachal Pradesh faces identical problems of stunting and post-harvest avocado wastage. This social innovation project applies a circular-economy approach, making households active agents of change to end stunting in rural poor areas of northern Rwanda and North-East India. Rural small farming households (>90% in agriculture) and groups will be trained to fabricate and use economical home-scale technologies to convert rejected avocados into nutritious, delicious, long shelf-life products for children, pregnant and lactating mothers. The process will create nutrition awareness that is lacking. These villages will become catalysts in influencing other villages through social media. The novelty lies in the sustainable, scalable endogenous approach, not requiring continued intervention. Households and local cooperatives can expand to other high value export crops, and market their surplus for economic sustainability. The solution is guided by existing scientific safe drying and food processing insights/methods ensuring nutrient retention, quality and safety along with fabrication of equipment with local resources.

core_fields.title: Scaling Greenhouse Vegetable Production to Strengthen Community Nutrition in Sierra Leone
core_fields.description: Limited access to nutrient-rich vegetables and income diversification remains a challenge for smallholder farmers in Sierra Leone. FOOP will establish two greenhouses and two outdoor vegetable gardens in Western Rural Area to serve as practical training sites and vegetable production centers. Farmers will be trained in greenhouse and open-field vegetable cultivation and supported with seed packages to establish their own gardens. This project improves household nutrition while generating sustainable income from local market linkages.
core_fields.abstract: Sierra Leone is deficit in vegetable production and relies heavily on neighboring countries to meet national demand. In 2023, only 29% of households had a good quality and quantity of diet (Feed Salone, 2023). Most families own small vegetable gardens for subsistence, with minimal financial return and production spanning for just half the year. There are currently five operational greenhouses in Sierra Leone, but they mainly supply hotels and supermarkets, putting affordable vegetables out of reach for the average household. FOOP addresses this gap at the first mile by combining greenhouses with open-field gardens that serve both as production sites and practical training platforms, increasing local vegetable availability while building farmers skills and income opportunities. The controlled environment shields crops from extreme weather and pests, enabling year-round cultivation and significantly increased yields. By constructing greenhouses near the strategic market hub of Waterloo, FOOP will minimize post-harvest losses in transit and provide reliable market access for farmers. FOOP s greenhouses also double as training centers. Farmers particularly women who often have limited access to inputs, land, and income receive hands-on training to start home gardens, improve nutrition, and earn sustainable livelihoods. By leveraging insights from FOOP s current greenhouse operations and market access in southern Sierra Leone, FOOP is well-positioned to scale its impact in a new district. In the short term, farmers improve household dietary diversity and generate income from surplus vegetable sales. In the long term, farmers gain core skills and market linkages needed to maintain their own vegetable gardens and sell.

core_fields.title: Building Nutritional Security and Decent Livelihoods in Imbabura.
core_fields.description: The proposal aims to ensure nutritious and culturally appropriate food baskets to reduce chronic malnutrition in Imbabura, through improved infrastructure, trained staff, and sustainable supply chains with small agroecological producers. It includes training on nutrition, protection, healthy habits, and responsible consumption, as well as support to create employment opportunities. The project promotes a healthier, more inclusive, and environmentally sustainable territory, reducing waste and fostering responsible practices.
core_fields.abstract: The solution proposed by the BADI FUDELA project is grounded in scientific and technical knowledge from public nutrition, sustainable family farming, food logistics, and circular economy models. Its innovation lies in transforming a traditional food bank into a comprehensive system for nutritional security and local economic development. The Imbabura Food Bank (BADI) currently operates across the province, serving approximately 6,000 users per month, equivalent to 1,500 families. However, food distribution has historically lacked nutritional planning, limiting its effectiveness in addressing chronic malnutrition and food insecurity. The core challenge is the limited access to nutritious foods for vulnerable families, alongside the absence of stable and fair market channels for small local producers. To address this, the project introduces three integrated components: 1. Evidence-based nutritional planning, ensuring balanced and culturally appropriate food baskets tailored to household needs. 2. Circular productive value chains, integrating local producers as fair-trade suppliers. 3. Community strengthening, promoting healthy behaviors, environmentally responsible practices, child protection, and sustainable institutional capacities. The model also incorporates a solidarity exchange mechanism that allows participating producers to receive complementary food baskets in return for their contributions, reinforcing both food security and economic stability. The proposal is grounded in public nutrition, sustainable family farming, food logistics, and circular economy principles. Its immediate and long-term benefits include improved nutritional quality for the 1,500 families served monthly, greater economic opportunities for producers, communities better trained in healthy and environmental practices, and a more inclusive, efficient, and resilient territory in the face of food insecurity.

core_fields.title: Expanding Compost Infrastructure for Regional Sustainability in Antigua Guatemala
core_fields.description: Our project expands a community-centered composting system that in 2.5 years of operation transformed 350T of food scraps and organic materials into high-quality compost for local use. We collect and process waste from homes, businesses, and schools, and return nutrients to the soil while reducing landfill dependency. By strengthening infrastructure, educating the community, and increasing processing capacity, we aim to create a scalable, circular model that improves environmental health and supports long-term sustainability in Guatemala.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation is a community-scale composting system that turns organic waste currently one of the largest and most overlooked contributors to landfill volume into a valuable resource for local soils, farmers, and green spaces. In our region, more than half of household and commercial waste is organic, yet almost all of it is transported to an overflowing, poorly managed landfill where it generates methane and contamination. This problem is urgent: communities face contamination, maxxed out landfill capacity, and declining soil health. We solve this by creating an accessible, inclusive composting model that combines efficient collection, low-tech but refined processing methods, and community education. We use windrow turner and static aeration techniques and monitor net weight, carbon ratio, temperature and humidity. This allows us to accelerate decomposition safely and consistently and produce high-quality compost. Our technical insight comes from understanding that well designed small and mid-scale systems can be both flexible and replicable, filling gaps that municipalities wont due to lack of vision and prioritization of the environment. End users benefit immediately: households and businesses reduce their waste footprint; farmers, gardeners, and schools gain access to nutrient-rich compost that restores soil structure, boosts yields, and eliminates the need for chemical inputs. Communities see cleaner neighborhoods, lower landfill contributions, and increased environmental awareness. The sustainable, long-term benefits include carbon sequestration, healthier soils, reduced methane emissions, and a local circular economy where waste becomes a resource. By integrating science-based composting practices with community participation, our project offers an effective, scalable solution to a growing crisis.
