core_fields.title: Advancing Circularity in Kenya's Agriculture and Food Ecosystem
core_fields.description: The Advancing Circularity in Kenya s Food Ecosystem program strengthens regenerative, low-waste agricultural systems while accelerating circular agri-SME innovation. Through ecosystem convening, capacity-building, and enterprise support, the program connects farmers, cooperatives, SMEs, and financial actors to adopt circular practices that reduce waste, restore ecosystems, and improve incomes. By catalysing collaboration across value chains, the initiative aims to create scalable, community-driven circular models that advance climate resilience and a more sustainable Kenyan food economy.
core_fields.abstract: Kenya's economy is highly dependent on natural resources, with climate-related sectors contributing over 50% of GDP. Agriculture largely rain-fed and non-mechanized employs more than half the labor force, making it highly vulnerable to climate shocks that cost the country an estimated 2.6% of GDP annually. Despite growing awareness, over 70% of Kenyan SMEs fail within their first three years, constrained by limited finance, technical capacity, and fragmented markets. Advancing Circularity in Kenya's Agriculture and Food Ecosystem addresses these challenges by equipping Agri-SMEs to adopt regenerative, low-waste business models that strengthen food security, climate resilience, and rural livelihoods. The project integrates three interlinked components: Ecosystem Activation: Convening producers, processors, policymakers, and investors to co-create circular value chains. A national Circularity Toolkit and open-source case library will share replicable models across five counties. The project will also identify 2-3 solutions in agriculture and food system circularity to be further piloted. Enterprise Support: Provide technical assistance, mentorship, and catalytic mini-grants to +20 Agri-SMEs developing circular innovations from by-product valorization to regenerative inputs and AI-enabled traceability tools. Policy & Market Linkages: Engage National and County governments and sector platforms to embed circular practices within food, nutrition, climate policies and to unlock green finance and inclusive markets. Foster partnerships that improve SME access to green finance and inclusive markets. Catalyze the release of 4 policy briefs. The innovations novelty lies in combining enterprise acceleration with ecosystem coordination and policy mainstreaming moving beyond isolated interventions toward systemic transformation.

core_fields.title: Restoring Landscapes with Smart Productive Forests, mutually beneficial to humans and nature
core_fields.description: Green Intelligence(GI) restores degraded Himalayan landscapes through NBS agroforestry (food system transformation) + digital transformation + blended finance. Agroforestry transforms to resilient land use and provides increased farmers income (fruits). The digitalization through innovative GI farmers app and GI platform enables real-time monitoring, financial incentives and advisory for farmers, and direct (climate/carbon) market access. Blended finance integrates community funds, grants, and carbon credits. This holistic approach enables resilient communities and sustainable food production
core_fields.abstract: The Problem Nepal faces a climate crisis: ranking among the world's top 10 most vulnerable countries, with 80% of the population threatened by landslides, floods, and droughts causing $27.78 million in annual damages. Rural communities lack access to climate finance, technical knowledge, and reliable monitoring systems. As traditional agriculture becomes increasingly unreliable due to climate change, food security and livelihoods for vulnerable households are at critical risk. The Solution Green Intelligence (GI) integrates three essential elements: I. Food System Transformation through nature-based agroforestry that combines productive trees with quick-return crops (ginger, turmeric), leveraging Nepal's existing forest ecosystems and edible forest species to enhance food security; II. Digital Transformation via the Green Intelligence innovative technology, a specifically developed mobile app and platform enabling farmers to digitalize farmers practices for monitor resources (aligned with top tier Gold Standard carbon credit criteria), receive advisory, and access direct financial rewards; and III. Blended Finance mechanisms connecting communities to carbon/climate finance, local government funding, and development aid (for kickstarting and capacity building) making landscape restoration economically viable. Impact & Benefits For farmers, incomes increase 200% within 3-6 years while food security improves through diversified production. Environmentally, the initiative restores 500+ hectares, sequesters 38,000 tons of CO₂, and enhances water retention by 20%. Community-level outcomes include 80% tree survival, green jobs, and increased resilience resulting in reduction in climate disasters. This integrated approach combining food system resilience, technology-enabled monitoring, and innovative financing ensures both economic viability and sustainable landscape restoration across Nepal's vulnerable regions.

core_fields.title: Nutrient Kins: Cocoa-Milk & Veggie Powered Nutrition for Vulnerable Children
core_fields.description: Nutrient Kins is an affordable, shelf-stable nutrition solution for children in low-income and crisis-affected communities. We transform locally grown crops into fortified cocoa-milk drink powder and dried fruit and vegetable boosters, ensuring access to safe, nutritious, and culturally familiar foods. Using solar-powered drying and community-based production, we reduce food waste, support local farmers, and improve child health. This pilot will produce and distribute daily Nutri-Packs to at-risk households, schools, and IDP camps in Nigeria.
core_fields.abstract: Nigeria faces increasing child malnutrition, diet-related illness, and rising food insecurity, especially among displaced and low-income families. Many children consume calorie-heavy but nutrient-poor diets lacking protein, iron, calcium, and vitamins essential for healthy growth. Perishable local fruits and vegetables are also lost to spoilage, contributing to hunger, waste, and reduced farmer income. Nutrient Kins introduces a practical and appealing nutrition innovation: a fortified cocoa-milk drink powder and complementary dried fruit and vegetable boosters preserved using solar drying technology. This approach combines local supply chains, food waste reduction, and nutrition access into a single integrated solution. The drink provides protein, calcium, vitamins, and antioxidants using milk powder, cocoa, moringa, soy protein, and dried fruits for natural sweetness. The booster sachets made from dried carrots, tomatoes, pumpkin, and leafy greens enhance everyday meals like pap, rice, soups, and noodles. Our scientific insight is that children readily consume culturally familiar cocoa drinks, making them an ideal vehicle to deliver micronutrients and fight malnutrition. Solar drying extends shelf life by 6 12 months, while retaining nutritional quality without preservatives or cold storage. Immediate benefits include improved child nutrition, reduced food waste, strengthened food resilience, farmer income support, and youth employment in processing and distribution. Long-term, Nutrient Kins builds sustainable nutritional self-reliance, scalable to schools and humanitarian feeding programs nationwide. This pilot in Benue and Lagos will demonstrate feasibility, taste acceptance, and measurable health outcomes to prepare for broader impact.

core_fields.title: AI-powered smart bin autonomously sorts waste, provides real-time monitoring, ESG analytics, and ad-enabled revenue generation.
core_fields.description: The AI-powered Smart Sort Bin automatically identifies and segregates waste using high-accuracy vision and sensors. It offers real-time monitoring of fill levels, odor, air quality, fire risks, and sends instant alerts. With solar power, Wi-Fi/SIM connectivity, ESG analytics, and a cloud dashboard, it optimizes waste collection and sustainability performance. Its digital advertising display creates added revenue, while user rewards and CO₂ credits encourage responsible waste disposal across public and commercial spaces.
core_fields.abstract: SortyX introduces an AI-powered Smart Sort Bin that solves the long-standing challenge of inefficient waste segregation in cities, campuses, and public spaces. Today, most waste is mixed, manually sorted, and often ends up in landfills due to contamination, lack of monitoring, and absence of real-time data. This leads to environmental pollution, higher municipal costs, and extremely low recycling rates. Our innovation addresses this problem using computer vision, sensors, and cloud intelligence. The Smart Sort Bin automatically identifies waste items and segregates them in less than 0.5 seconds with high accuracy. Scientific insights from image recognition, machine learning, and sensor fusion make this automated sorting possible without human intervention. The system also monitors air quality, odor, fire risk, and fill levels, sending instant alerts to waste-management teams to prevent overflowing bins and hygiene issues. The bin is solar-powered and connected via Wi-Fi/SIM, enabling continuous data flow to a cloud dashboard. Municipal bodies and enterprises receive ESG analytics, recycling metrics, fuel optimization insights, and route-planning support. A built-in digital advertising display generates additional revenue, making the system economically sustainable. Users can earn CO₂ credits and rewards for proper disposal, encouraging community participation. Immediate benefits include cleaner public spaces, reduced labor requirements, and improved safety for sanitation workers. Sustainable benefits include increased recycling rates, reduced landfill load, lower carbon emissions, and stronger circular economy practices. This innovation benefits municipalities, schools, hospitals, airports, corporates, and communities by combining environmental impact with operational efficiency and economic value.

core_fields.title: Scaling Sustainable Food Futures Initiative for Women in Local Rice (SSFF-WILR)
core_fields.description: The Scaling Sustainable Food Futures Initiative for Women in Local Rice (SSFF-WILR) empowers women in three districts of Ghana to strengthen the local rice value chain. By providing training, improved inputs, post-harvest technologies, and market linkages, the project boosts productivity, income, and food security. It promotes sustainable, climate-smart farming and women's leadership, creating a scalable model to transform local rice systems and enhance economic and social impact.
core_fields.abstract: The Scaling Sustainable Food Futures Initiative for Women in Local Rice (SSFF-WILR) addresses the low productivity, post-harvest losses, and limited market access in Ghana's local rice sector, particularly among women farmers. Rice farmers face challenges such as outdated farming techniques, insufficient access to quality seeds and inputs, poor storage facilities, and weak supply chains. These challenges reduce income, threaten food security, and limit women's economic empowerment. SSFF-WILR introduces an integrated, women-led solution to these problems. Through the adoption of climate-smart farming practices, improved rice varieties, affordable post-harvest technologies, and structured market linkages, the initiative increases productivity, reduces losses, and enhances incomes. The innovation is guided by scientific insights from agronomy, post-harvest management, and value chain development, tailored to local environmental and social contexts. Immediate benefits include higher rice yields, better quality produce, and increased incomes for women farmers. Farmers gain knowledge and skills that improve resilience to climate variability and strengthen local food security. Communities benefit from more affordable, locally produced rice, while schools and households enjoy improved nutrition. Long-term, the initiative creates a scalable model for sustainable, women-led rice production, supporting economic empowerment, environmental sustainability, and social equity. By focusing on women as change agents, SSFF-WILR ensures lasting transformation of local rice systems, contributing to broader food system resilience in Ghana.

core_fields.title: Scaling Resilient and Traceable Artisanal Fisheries on Kenya s Northern Coast using Affordable Cold Chain Management
core_fields.description: The project aims to double the share of affordable, sustainably caught, food-safe fish in Kenya s local market to 30% within two years. This project will scale our work to strengthen the artisanal fishing value chain along Kenya s northern coast. Our interventions to reduce go-to-market costs by 17% strengthens community nutrition and livelihoods, improves food safety and quality, boosts fisher incomes, and catalyses a shift to sustainable fishing practices that protect marine ecosystems.
core_fields.abstract: Fishing is the primary source of income for many coastal communities in Kenya. In Lamu, one of the country s most important artisanal fishing hubs and the base of Kumbatia s sourcing, around 70% of households depend on fishing. Yet poverty rates exceed 60%, and most small-scale fishers earn less than $1.90 per day. High input costs, inconsistent quality, and food safety risks limit access to formal markets, trapping fishers in subsistence livelihoods while reducing consumer confidence in local seafood. Over the past five years, Kumbatia has tackled this challenge by becoming the one-stop-shop for artisanal fishers. Our regenerative value chain model is built upon - sushi grade capacity building, sharia-compliant financing for conservation-safe fishing gear and inputs, off-grid cold chain logistics, and industry-best digital sustainability and traceability practices. By unlocking access to premium markets we have delivered 100% traceability while our fishers and dealers earn 87.5% and 300% more than their peers. Kenya s fish markets are dominated by cheap, unsafe, and unsustainably harvested fish, while Kumbatia s responsibly sourced, fairtrade, traceable products remain too costly locally. Our fishers use 4X ice in comparison to peers to maintain quality. Establishing a local ice plant strengthens cold-chain management, cuts costs by 28%, and enables competitive pricing, allowing Kumbatia to expand its domestic market share and scale. Reliable, affordable ice reduces post-harvest losses, improves food safety and boosts fishing livelihoods. The intervention creates local enterprise, promotes uptake of sustainable fishing, protects vital ecosystems, and increases access to affordable, high-quality, environmentally responsible locally sourced protein.

core_fields.title: SWEET: Sustainable Woodlands & Environmental Enterprise for Transform
core_fields.description: SWEET strengthens rural food security and livelihoods by combining modern honey production with regenerative agroforestry in Nimba County, Liberia. The initiative enhances nutrition through the production of safe, affordable honey while increasing crop yields through improved pollination. By restoring degraded land, supporting biodiversity, and creating income opportunities for women and youth, SWEET builds a resilient, community-owned food system that is environmentally sustainable, economically viable, and accessible to all.
core_fields.abstract: The SWEET initiative Sustainable Woodlands & Environmental Enterprise for Transformation introduces a combined honey production and agroforestry system designed to improve food security, restore degraded land, and expand livelihood opportunities for rural families in Nimba County. The project responds to declining crop yields, reduced forest cover, limited income opportunities for women and youth, and the lack of affordable, trusted, nutrient-rich food in local markets. SWEET solves these challenges by integrating three proven approaches: modern beekeeping, regenerative agroforestry, and community-based food processing. Beekeeping provides a reliable source of safe, nutritious honey while improving the pollination of vegetables, fruits, and other crops. Agroforestry restores soil health, increases tree cover, and strengthens farms against climate shocks. A small-scale honey processing unit ensures clean, well-packaged, and traceable products that are affordable and trusted by consumers. The solution is guided by well-established scientific insights on the role of pollinators in boosting crop yields, the ecological benefits of agroforestry in restoring degraded landscapes, and the strong nutritional value of natural honey. By combining these elements into a single model, the project generates both immediate and long-term benefits for rural communities. Farmers gain higher yields and new income streams; women and youth gain practical skills and business opportunities; households gain access to affordable, nutritious honey; and the environment benefits from increased biodiversity and regenerated land. SWEET creates a food system that is healthier, more sustainable, and more inclusive, while remaining fully community-owned through the nonprofit cooperative structure.

core_fields.title: Micro-propagation and delivery system for plantain
core_fields.description: Plant tissue culture technology has demonstrated major impact potential to transform plantation development across the world and can be used to generate millions of plantlets that can spark transformations of our food systems, with a particular focus on addressing planting material shortages among food and plantation crops. This proposal focuses on the production and delivery system for plantain, an important food security crop, export commodity and shade provider in plantation development in Agro-forestry system.
core_fields.abstract: Agricultural is the mainstay of Ghana's economy, yet it faces a number of challenges, notably those linked to modernization which limits large plantation development and returns on investment in the different value chains. Planting material availability in the right quantities at the right time is a major obstacle to agricultural expansion and large-scale plantation development. Leveraging the extensive expertise in tissue culture and biotechnology to provide an avenue for producing plant materials that are of superior economically, environmentally, and socially acceptable. The links between food security, climate change, and technological innovation requires that we proffer science-based solutions that improve food availability, support job creation, and increase communities' power to be more resilient. Between 2007 and 2019, the in vitro laboratory of the Ghana Genebank developed micro-propagation protocols for 6 crop species that contributes to food security in Ghana. (Plantain, Pineapple, Cassava, Cocoyam, Yam and Sweat potato). Though tissue culture is not new in Ghana, its major use in Ghana involved large scale farmer for the introduction of a new pineapple variety. Mainstreaming tissue culture for planting material production could revolutionize agriculture in Ghana. However, the human and infrastructural capacity for handling the technology is lacking. This project seeks to build capacities of fresh graduates, nursery managers and farmers in the production, handling and use tissue culture derived plantain plantlets for tree crop development in Ghana. The initiative seeks to provide the critical delivering mechanism for the deployment of the technology and create jobs by engaging unemployed youth, women and men.

core_fields.title: Building a Resilient Food System for Gorilla Highlands Coffee Farmers
core_fields.description: The Gorilla Highlands Coffee (GHC) Food Systems Project aims to strengthen the sustainability, resilience, and profitability of the coffee-based livelihoods in the Gorilla Highlands region of southwestern Uganda. This region home to endangered mountain gorillas and rich volcanic landscapes relies heavily on smallholder farming, yet farmers face persistent challenges including low productivity, limited market access, inconsistent quality, climate pressures, and insufficient household nutrition. These challenges not only undermine farmer well-being but also increase pressure on fragile conservation
core_fields.abstract: 1. What problem is being solved? Coffee farmers in the Gorilla Highlands rely heavily on a single cash crop coffee for their income. This makes them vulnerable to:Climate change (drought, heavy rainfall, landslides that harm coffee trees),Market fluctuations (falling global coffee prices) Food insecurity during poor coffee seasons, Soil degradation from steep, mountainous land and Limited income diversification, especially for women and smallholder households This combination creates fragile livelihoods and increases poverty and environmental pressure in a region that is ecologically sensitive. 2. Why is this problem relevant? The Gorilla Highlands region is both: an important coffee-growing zone, and a critical biodiversity area near mountain gorilla habitats. If farmers lose income or food security, they may clear forests, overuse land, or abandon sustainable practices. At the same time, climate change is already impacting yields and threatening long-term production. Therefore, strengthening food security and agricultural resilience is essential for:stable farmer incomes, healthier communities, sustainable coffee supply chains, protection of mountain ecosystems 3. What is the solution (the innovation)? The innovation is a Resilient Food System Model built around coffee agroforestry + diversified food production + community support services.It combines: Coffee grown under agroforestry systems,Trees provide shade, protect soil, conserve water, and create microclimates that protect coffee from climate stress How is the problem being solved? The model solves the problem by addressing both economic vulnerability and ecological fragility:Agroforestry stabilizes soil, reduces erosion, improves water retention, and shields crops from climate stress.

core_fields.title: Enhancing Horticultural Food Systems through Smallholder Empowerment
core_fields.description: The initiative employs affordable local materials such as bamboo sticks and shade nets to establish low-cost greenhouses that support dry-season farming in the rural and peri-urban districts. The project enhances year-round food availability and creates income-generation opportunities for women and youth who migrate to the south in search of jobs. This project aims to promote and revitalize food systems in Northern Ghana by empowering smallholder farmers to adopt climate-smart agricultural practices.
core_fields.abstract: Women and youth are the backbone of many rural communities, engaging primarily in agriculture. Despite their contributions, they encounter numerous challenges, including limited access to land and quality inputs, financial constraints, and inadequate irrigation resources. These obstacles, worsened by the climate crisis, hinder their progress, leading to unemployment, food insecurity, hunger, migration, and poverty. For instance, the July-August drought of 2024 caused over 50% food losses, emphasising the urgency of addressing these issues. Smallholder farmers who can produce food during the dry season through irrigation do so in very small quantities, making it difficult to access markets. This project employs an innovative yet simple and affordable approach by constructing low-cost, climate-smart greenhouses using locally available materials such as bamboo frames, neem extract as an organic pesticide, and shade nets. This demonstrates that sustainable food production can be achieved using indigenous knowledge. During the dry season, characterised by extreme heat, poor soil moisture retention, and acute water scarcity, these structures offer a suitable and controllable environment for growing vegetables. This idea is informed by the hydroclimatic nature of Northern Ghana, where the region currently experiences frequent droughts and prolonged dry seasons, erratic rainfall patterns, which significantly affect crop growth, limit food availability, increase the cost of vegetables, and impose a burden on farmers, particularly women and youth. This initiative aims to benefit communities by supporting a sustainable supply of fresh produce while maintaining environmental gains through the use of renewable resources and readily available materials.

core_fields.abstract: This project addresses the thematic area of Agriculture and Food Security, covering four sub- thematic areas: access to quality inputs, access to extension services, market linkages, and reduction of post-harvest loss. The Haor region of Sunamganj faces seasonal livelihoods, frequent floods, limited income opportunities, and inadequate access to agricultural subsidies, quality inputs, and services. The project aims to transform agricultural practices in Sunamganj Sadar, Derai, and Dowarabazar by equipping smallholders especially women, marginalized groups, and ethnic minorities with skills, resources, and technology to optimize land use and strengthen food security. core_fields.title: Transforming Ethiopia's beloved Bulla into a fortified, nutrient-rich solution to fight childhood malnutrition nationwide.
core_fields.description: Gro provides Ethiopian parents with locally made, fortified Bulla that is hygienic, easy to prepare, and trusted like homemade meals. Bulla is a local staple that is carbohydrate-dense but lacks essential nutrients. By enriching this traditional staple with essential nutrients, Gro tackles critical dietary gaps, as 37% of children under five are stunted and 21% are underweight. Our mission is to support healthy growth and development through accessible, nutritious, and culturally familiar.
core_fields.abstract: Gro introduces a fortified version of Bulla, a beloved Ethiopian staple, to address one of the country's most urgent challenges: early-childhood malnutrition. Ethiopia has 17.8 million children under five, yet 37% are stunted, 21% underweight, and 62% face micronutrient deficiencies, largely because families rely on inexpensive, carbohydrate-heavy foods (EDHS 2019). Our research confirms parents understand the problem but lack viable solutions. Across 50 parent interviews, 45 qualitative sessions, and 105 survey responses, caregivers consistently expressed the same tension: while 76% prioritize nutrient-dense foods, 64% struggle with cost, and many distrust highly processed products. This leaves them choosing between trusted but nutritionally incomplete staples or nutritious but distrusted alternatives. Gro bridges this gap by fortifying traditional Bulla with iron, omega-3, and protein, meeting children's recommended daily nutrient needs without altering cultural familiarity. The scientific insight behind this approach comes from medical experts who emphasized that deficiencies in the first 1,000 days have long-term effects on cognitive development, immunity, and growth. By enriching a food families already trust and consume daily, Gro provides a practical, high-impact intervention. The benefits are immediate and lasting: improved nutrient intake, enhanced cognitive and physical development for children, reduced preparation time for caregivers, and an affordable, reliable alternative to costly fortified imports. Long-term, Gro strengthens local food systems, supports local producers, and contributes to lowering national healthcare burdens associated with malnutrition. Gro transforms a traditional staple into a powerful, sustainable solution for healthier Ethiopian children.

core_fields.title: Building Inclusive Millet Food Systems for Nutrition and Equity
core_fields.description: This project strengthens women-led, climate-resilient millet food systems in rural Tamil Nadu by linking sustainable farming with processing and fair markets. It trains small farmers in biodiversity-based agriculture, expands community seed systems and water conservation, supports women-run millet processing enterprises, and builds strong market linkages through an established farmer producer network. The project increases farmer incomes, improves household nutrition, and promotes inclusive, sustainable food systems from production to consumption.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation is a women-led, end-to-end millet food system model that connects climate-smart farming directly to local processing, fair markets, and nutritious consumption. Problem: Small farmers face climate shocks, low incomes, poor market access, and reduced demand for nutritious indigenous crops. Food consumers lack affordable, healthy alternatives, while women farmers remain under-valued in agricultural value chains. These gaps weaken livelihoods, nutrition security, and environmental sustainability. Solution: The project integrates biodiversity-based millet cultivation, community seed conservation, water-smart farming practices, women-run processing units, and farmer producer company marketing networks into a single coordinated system. Farmers receive scientific agro-ecology training (soil health management, mixed cropping, moisture conservation), while women groups manage cleaning, grading, processing, and packaging of millet foods. Products are branded and sold through institutional buyers, retail outlets, and community nutrition programs, ensuring fair prices for farmers and affordable nutritious foods for consumers. Innovation Insight: Research and traditional knowledge show that millets are drought-resilient, nutrient-dense, and suitable for rain-fed systems, yet their potential remains untapped due to fragmented production and weak markets. Integrating women enterprise leadership with FPO-led aggregation creates both social inclusion and economic scale, an approach proven locally but rarely operationalized across entire food systems. Benefits: Farmers: Stable markets, higher incomes (30 40%), reduced crop losses. Women: Enterprise ownership, leadership roles, financial empowerment. Consumers & schools: Access to affordable, healthy millet foods. Environment: Improved soil health, biodiversity restoration, water conservation. Communities: Local jobs, improved nutrition, and stronger climate resilience.

core_fields.title: Modular Solar-powered Food Processing, Packaging and Preservation Hub for Smallholder farmers
core_fields.description: In Northern Nigeria, over 95 percent of households depend on farming, and smallholder farmers produce more than 70 percent of the nation's food, yet remain underpaid and under-rewarded. Over 60 percent of food crops are lost due to poor drying, storage, and unsafe preservation practices using harmful chemicals. This project deploys modular drying, processing, packaging, and preservation hubs to reduce post-harvest losses by 40-50 percent, improve food safety, and increase incomes by 30-50 percent locally.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Nigeria face a serious challenge that affects their income, survival, and socio-economic development. They produce over 90% of the food consumed nationally, yet remain among the poorest due to multiple factors limiting economic growth. A major problem is post-harvest losses, which are a leading cause of food insecurity, as over 60% of crops spoil before reaching consumers. I personally experienced this, losing over 90% of my ginger in 2022 and 60% in 2023, reflecting the pain, economic loss, and lost hope that many farmers endure. Focus group discussions with cooperative members show that over 90% of smallholder farmers face similar challenges annually, with few strategies to address them, driving youth away from agriculture. Another pressing challenge is the lack of proper drying and storage facilities. Most farmers rely on open-sun drying, exposing crops to contamination by wild animals, birds, and rodents, which reduces quality. Storage is often unsafe, with some farmers using harmful chemicals or storing produce in homes, creating high pesticide residues and increasing post-harvest losses. To address this, we are deploying a modular solar-powered hub for drying, processing, preserving, and storing farm produce. Farmers can dry crops in a controlled, hygienic environment, store them chemically-free using supplied hermetic bags, and process produce into market-ready forms, reducing losses and improving income. Our community co-owned, hybrid model ensures sustainability, empowers rural communities, and delivers a scientific, scalable solution that tackles post-harvest losses while promoting food security, safer food, and improved livelihoods.

core_fields.title: Enhancing Crop Yields Through IoT Smart Hives and Precision Pollination
core_fields.description: This project enhances crop yields by deploying IoT-enabled smart hives and precision pollination services to smallholder farmers. Using real-time hive data and AI insights, farmers receive timely guidance to boost pollination efficiency, reduce bee colony losses, and improve productivity. By integrating technology with locally trained field agents especially women the project strengthens food security, promotes climate resilience, and supports sustainable agriculture in underserved communities.
core_fields.abstract: Pollen Patrollers is an Agritech innovation that uses IoT and AI to solve the growing problem of bee colony loss and low crop productivity across Africa. Today, over 40% of global bee colonies and 60% in Africa collapse each year due to climate stress, pests, and poor hive management. This directly harms food security, because bees pollinate more than 80% of the crops we depend on. Farmers face low yields, and beekeepers lose income due to preventable hive deaths. Our solution combines smart hive devices, AI analytics, and precision pollination to protect bees and increase agricultural productivity. The IoT devices monitor hive temperature, humidity, sound, weight, and bee activity in real time. AI models analyze these data points to detect early signs of colony stress, pests, swarming, or hunger, allowing beekeepers to act before a crisis occurs. The same data helps us guide farmers on exactly when and where to place bee colonies for optimal pollination. This approach is based on scientific insights linking micro-climate, hive acoustics, and bee behavior to colony health and pollination efficiency. By translating these signals into simple, actionable messages, the technology makes advanced management accessible even to rural, offline communities through USSD and SMS. Immediate benefits include reduced colony losses, increased honey production, and higher crop yields, often by up to 50%. Long-term benefits include improved household incomes, stronger biodiversity, reduced chemical use, and climate resilience. By combining women's training through #Patrollers4Her, the innovation also delivers social empowerment and inclusive economic growth.

core_fields.title: Harnessing Solar Energy to Enhance Mbilimbili Innovation for Better Food Security-TILIME Project.

Using demonstration sites, the project will introduce pupils to climate-smart agriculture while surrounding farmers equally benefit through participation in trainings and field demonstrations. core_fields.abstract: Malawi's agricultural sector remains overwhelmingly dependent on rain-fed smallholder farming, making it highly vulnerable to climate variability. Around 90-95% of cultivated land is rain-fed, with only about 4% under irrigation (AUDA-NEPAD, 2023). Most smallholder farmers cultivate on tiny plots, with more than 70% having less than one hectare, and together they account for the bulk (75-80%) of the country's food production (Trocaire, 2025). As a result, crop output is susceptible to rainfall patterns and climatic shocks such as droughts or erratic rainfall. Furthermore, soils are being depleted with the use of chemical fertilizers, a lack of crop rotation and a lack of climate-smart methods. All of these factors lead to food insecurity, year in year out. Vulnerability to drought is addressed through small-scale solar irrigation, which, once installed, ensures a constant water supply at no cost. The tiny farming plots of less than one hectare become more productive through frequent cropping using the Mbili-mbili Innovation, which improves production by 37% and the use of locally sourced manure to enrich the soil. Placing the project in a primary school allows pupils to gain supervised practical experience with climate-smart farming methods. They are introduced to these farming techniques at an early stage, which can serve them for a lifetime and ripple through their communities. It will also promote environmental preservation at that tender age. There is an additional advantage for the school: it can use the produce for a school feeding program and generate income to further develop its infrastructure

core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Cold Storage Pods for Rural Farmers (SP-COLD PODS PROJECT )
core_fields.description: The SP-COLD PODS project deploys affordable, solar-powered cold storage pods to rural farming communities to reduce post-harvest losses of fruits and vegetables, improve food quality, and increase farmer income. By providing reliable, off-grid cooling and digital monitoring, the project strengthens climate resilience, enhances access to nutritious foods, and supports women and youth-led agricultural enterprises.
core_fields.abstract: Rural farmers in Nigeria lose up to 40 50% of harvested fruits and vegetables because they lack affordable cold storage. High temperatures, long distances to markets, and reliance on diesel-powered cooling systems make it difficult to preserve produce, leading to income losses, food shortages, and reduced access to nutritious foods in local communities. This challenge is worsening under climate change, which accelerates spoilage and threatens food security. The Solar-Powered Cold Storage Pods (SP-COLD PODS) provide an innovative, climate-smart solution by offering modular, energy-efficient cooling units powered entirely by solar energy. Each pod uses a low-energy refrigeration system, insulated panels, and small battery storage to maintain optimal temperatures for perishable crops. This innovation is built on proven scientific insights showing that maintaining produce at 8 15 C can extend shelf life by 3 7 days, significantly reducing post-harvest losses. Solar refrigeration technology has advanced to become more efficient, affordable, and well-suited to off-grid communities in Africa. Immediate benefits include reduced food spoilage, higher market prices for farmers, improved household income, and better availability of fruits and vegetables for consumers and schools. Over time, the pods support sustainable food systems by lowering emissions, eliminating diesel dependence, empowering women and youth farmers, and strengthening community resilience to climate impacts. This project model is scalable, cost-effective, and designed for long-term sustainability in low-resource settings.

core_fields.title: Circular economy system for the production of an optimized protein for human nutrition
core_fields.description: A cultural heritage of the Sonora state in the north of Mexico is the production of Bacanora, a distilled beverage. We propose to evaluate the viability to clean the residuals from the Bacanora production after reducing its toxic and organic content using a fermentation process to produce an optimized protein for human nutrition.
core_fields.abstract: Distilled beverages are world-widely consumed, yet their production generate a liquid waste referred to as vinasses, that contain large quantities of organic material and secondary alcohols. In Mexico there are different regions that produce distilled beverages with protected designation of origin, that on one side recognizes their cultural heritage but also increases their market size. Treating vinasses increases the sale price and reduces the profit for the producer, which represents a disincentive for the artisan Bacanora's producer, such is the case for most producers in the Sonora state in the north of Mexico where Bacanora is produced. By collaborating with artisan producers of Bacanora, DProtein observed at laboratory scale that a proprietary yeast fermentation process is able to produce large quantities of an optimized protein for human nutrition using vinasses as the fermentation media. DProtein creates proteins with the correct proportion of essential amino acids for human nutrition, and at the same time the proteins's properties are adequate to be used in food production for human consumption (high solubility, high stability, flavorless, non-allergenic). In this project, we propose to scale the production of an optimized protein for human nutrition up to 300 L, using the Bacanora's vinasses as fermentation media, to determine the quality of the vinasses before and after the fermentation process. Since the protein purification involves nanofiltration, we hypothesize the fermentation and downstream processing to obtain the protein would clarify the vinasses allowing its liberation to the environment without any harm to the environment.

core_fields.title: Vermicompost As Growth Substrate For Organic Greenhouse Tomato Production
core_fields.description: This project evaluates vermicompost as a sustainable growth substrate for organic greenhouse tomato production. It investigates vermicompost s physical and nutritional properties, its effects on plant vigor, yield, and fruit quality, and its potential to replace conventional synthetic nutrient media. By integrating eco-friendly nutrient cycling with controlled-environment agriculture, the study aims to enhance productivity, reduce input costs, and promote environmentally responsible tomato cultivation. The findings will guide best practices for growers.
core_fields.abstract: WHAT PROBLEM IS BEING SOLVED Tomato production in Nigeria often faces challenges with low soil nutrient availability, indiscriminate use of expensive non-renewable synthetic fertilizers, poor soil water holding capacity and climatic extremities. These limitations reduce yield, increase production costs, and undermine environmental sustainability. Additionally, farmers lack reliable organic substrate options that simultaneously support plant growth, maintain soil health, and reduce waste. HOW PROBLEM IS BEING SOLVED The project will use vermicompost an organic material produced through the biological activity of earthworms as a primary growth substrate for tomatoes in greenhouse conditions. Vermicompost will be assessed for its physical structure, nutrient availability, microbial activity, water-holding capacity, and compatibility with organic nutrient management. The study will involve comparing vermicompost-based substrates with conventional media to determine their influence on seedling establishment, vegetative growth, flowering, yield performance, and fruit quality. SCIENTIFIC OR TECHNICAL INSIGHT THAT LED TO THIS SOLUTION Vermicompost is scientifically recognized as a biologically active, nutrient-rich material containing plant-growth-promoting microbes, and slow-release nutrients. Research has shown that its porous structure enhances aeration and moisture balance, while its microbial diversity improves nutrient mineralization. These characteristics make it a strong replacement to synthetic nutrient sources, especially in environments where nutrient stability is critical. IMMEDIATE AND SUSTAINABLE BENEFITS TO END USERS Farmers benefit from reduced input costs, higher yields, and access to renewable, local substrate. Communities and schools gain opportunities for low-cost organic gardening. Consumers enjoy safer, chemical-free tomatoes with enhanced nutritional quality, replacing synthetic inputs, promotes waste recycling, and improves soil health.

core_fields.title: SaltiSolve: Nano Tech for Healthier Soil and Better Irrigation Water
core_fields.description: Our innovation transforms irrigation by combining nanobubble technology with tailored gaseous input & filtration medium to reduce soil salinity and improve crop performance. Nanobubbles bind sodium and magnesium ions while boosting dissolved oxygen levels up to 20 mg/L, supporting healthier soil biology, nutrient uptake, and root growth. The system adapts to each farm using crop-specific gases and organic filtration media, restoring soil balance and increasing yields with minimal changes to existing farming practices.
core_fields.abstract: Soil salinity is an escalating challenge worldwide, reducing crop yields, limiting nutrient uptake, and increasing dependence on water, fertilizers, and pesticides. Small- and medium-scale farmers are particularly affected, as they often lack access to expensive soil remediation solutions. Our innovation addresses this at the molecular level. By combining nanobubble technology with a tailored mix of gaseous inputs and organic filtration, we directly reduce soil salinity while enhancing crop growth. Nanobubbles interact with positively charged ions, especially sodium and magnesium the main drivers of salinity helping move them away from plant roots. At the same time, dissolved oxygen levels in water and soil rise up to 20 mg/L, roughly a 280% increase, supporting healthier soil microbiology, improved nutrient uptake, and stronger roots. The system is highly adaptable. Farm-specific gaseous inputs, such as compressed air or oxygen, are paired with organic filtration media optimized for crops like dates, potatoes, and lettuce. It can be retrofitted into existing irrigation systems, restoring soil vitality and boosting yields without altering standard farming practices. Rooted in nanoscience and plant physiology, our technology enhances ion balance, oxygenation, and water and nutrient use efficiency. It works in both soil-based agriculture and hydroponics, delivering immediate productivity gains while building long-term soil resilience, sustainability, and climate adaptation. We are collaborating with the National Agricultural Research Centre (NARC) in Jordan and several agri-business partners to validate and scale this solution for commercial use.

This project addresses a critical - yet overlooked - challenge in Kenya s agriculture ecosystem: the lack of structured, reliable post-harvest systems and market access for smallholder farmers, particularly youth and women. According to FAO, over 40% of grains in Kenya are lost post-harvest, while farmers are often forced to sell immediately at low prices because they lack safe storage. At the same time, only 4% of total loans to the private sector go to agriculture, despite the sector employing 70% of the rural population, leaving farmers without capital to grow their enterprises. This challenge is highly relevant because more than 70% of Kenyan farmers depend on rain-fed agriculture and remain vulnerable to climate and market shocks. Yet cooperatives across the country already own warehouses that, if modernized and digitized, can become powerful engines for local economic transformation. Mavuno Hubs solves this problem by digitizing cooperative warehouses, integrating them with the Warehouse Receipt System (WRS), and linking them directly to banks, buyers, and insurance providers. Through digital inventory tracking, grain quality testing, and mobile-based warehouse receipts, farmers can store grain safely, monitor value, and use their produce as collateral for credit. Solar power ensures reliable operation in off-grid rural areas. By modernizing grain aggregation and trade infrastructure at the community level, the hubs bridges the gap between smallholder farmers and high value markets, reducing post-harvest losses, improving incomes, and enhancing resilience in the face of climate

core_fields.abstract: KIVU AGRO BIO introduces an integrated, eco-industrial model that transforms underused Congolese medicinal plants into affordable, safe and high-value natural health products. The innovation addresses two major challenges in the DRC: limited access to quality, evidence-based natural health solutions, and the underutilization of rich local biodiversity that could improve nutrition, income, and community well-being. Our solution combines local agro-processing, bio-innovation, and circular economy practices to convert leaves, roots, seeds and agricultural by-products into superfoods, herbal teas, therapeutic oils, soaps, and natural supplements. This model is relevant because the DRC imports the majority of its wellness products, making them expensive and inaccessible, while rural producers lack markets for the abundant plant resources they cultivate or collect. The approach is possible thanks to insights drawn from traditional ethnobotanical knowledge, combined with modern food science, drying and extraction techniques, and low-energy processing technologies. By integrating these methods locally, we preserve nutrients, ensure product safety, and reduce post-harvest losses that typically exceed 40% in rural areas. The innovation benefits communities immediately by: Offering affordable natural health products adapted to local needs (malnutrition, anemia, hypertension, malaria prevention, intestinal health). Increasing incomes for smallholder farmers through structured sourcing partnerships and fair purchasing. Creating green jobs, especially for women and youth, across production, processing and distribution. Reducing waste through upcycling of agricultural residues (e.g., citrus peels for soaps). Strengthening local resilience by reducing dependence on imported supplements and pharmaceuticals. Sustainably, the model builds a local bioeconomy, supports responsible harvesting of medicinal plants.

core_fields.title: Scaling the Starter Pump in Kenya: A Breakthrough Irrigation Innovation for the Ultra-Poor
core_fields.description: Under 5% of farmland in sub-Saharan Africa is irrigated, leaving smallholders vulnerable to hunger gaps and climate shocks. KickStart proposes to scale the MoneyMaker Starter Pump, an affordable irrigation technology launched in 2022, across Kenya. With a USD 250,000 Grand Prize, ~1,600 1,700 pumps will support 4,000+ farmers, improving food security, incomes, and climate resilience for ~20,000 people - especially women, youth, and climate-vulnerable smallholder communities, while accelerating adoption of sustainable, market-based irrigation solutions nationwide.
core_fields.abstract: Under 5% of farmland in sub-Saharan Africa is irrigated. There s little food between rainfed harvests and farmers can t adapt to climate change. With irrigation smallholders harvest and sell fruits/vegetables year-round and save crops in droughts. Some ~20% have surface-water or shallow aquifers on their farms; others dig catchment-ponds. Irrigation is profitable, but solar/petrol pumps are expensive and hard to maintain. Even KickStart s popular (>400,000 sold) lowest-cost ($185) treadle-pumps are too costly. An affordable, scalable, easy-to-use solution is needed for vulnerable farmers, facing frequent crop failures and poverty. Designed in 2021, KickStart s MoneyMaker Starter Pump is a breakthrough innovation, engineered for extreme affordability, minimal physical effort, portability, durability, and inclusion of vulnerable and excluded farmers. Weighing just 2.5Kg, it looks like a bicycle pump on a hinged base and is operated with an easy full-body-rocking motion. It pulls water from surface sources, or hand-dug/tube wells up to 6.5m deep and pushes it through a hosepipe to 7.5m above the pump, or 150m on flat ground. Its innovative surge chamber enables single operators to irrigate with sprinklers, and it retails with hosepipes and spares, for ~$80 in Kenya. Farmers can irrigate ~0.5 acre of vegetables in 4-5 hours, feed their communities and earn ~$800/year. It s uniquely accessible to poorest ASAL households, vulnerable women, entrepreneurial youth, the disabled and elderly. KickStart s innovative scaling incorporates; marketing and promotions, private sector retail shops, and dynamic partnerships with NGO/CBOs, agribusinesses, governments to train farmers on pumps, profitable regenerative irrigated-farming, and accessing water sources, inputs and markets.

core_fields.description: P-Vita transforms agricultural waste and algae into low-carbon raw materials using patented, AI-enhanced bioprocessing. core_fields.abstract: P-Vita addresses two critical challenges in the global food system: the high cost of natural raw materials and the environmental damage caused by agricultural waste. In the Middle East and Africa, over 95% of raw materials used in the food, beverage, and pharmaceutical industries are imported, causing unstable supply chains, delays, and high costs. At the same time, millions of tons of agricultural residues especially palm waste are burned or discarded, worsening soil health, air quality, and greenhouse gas emissions. P-Vita solves this by converting agricultural waste into high-value, sustainable raw materials using a patented bioconversion process enhanced by AI and IoT. Our technology transforms palm byproducts into beta-carotene and organic biofertilizers, providing eco-friendly alternatives to chemical inputs. By utilizing regional agricultural waste, we offer a scalable, low-energy solution that reduces both the environmental footprint and reliance on costly imports. Our innovation brings multiple benefits: smallholder farmers gain new income streams by selling waste previously discarded, while food and pharmaceutical manufacturers access affordable, locally sourced, natural raw materials. This reduces their reliance on synthetic chemicals, lowering costs and enhancing supply chain stability. Environmentally, P-Vita s process reduces carbon emissions by up to 58,000 tons annually, prevents pollution from waste burning, and improves soil and water health through sustainable agricultural practices. P-Vita s model supports regenerative agriculture, strengthens local economies, and contributes to a circular food system. Our solution is both scalable and adaptable, enabling the MENA region and beyond to achieve sustainable food production and enhance food security.

core_fields.title: Scaling Assessments on the Footprint Impact Platform
core_fields.description: Developed and tested over five years, Food & Trees for Africa's proprietary Footprint Impact Platform leverages data to enhance decision-making within food security and agroecological projects. With a 92% success rate across 180 small-scale farming and 300 school interventions (2025), Footprint is challenged by a 5,000-project assessment backlog, preventing network growth and funding. A $100,000 grant will increase capacity to rapidly expand Footprints data-set, accelerating high-impact, regenerative food security initiatives in South Africa.
core_fields.abstract: The problem being solved is a fundamental assessment and project selection gap: where donors lack verifiable, granular and relevant data needed to confidently fund and scale effective grassroots food security and climate action projects. This is important for effectively channeling capital towards the most effective and impactful interventions. The core solution is the Footprint Impact Platform , a non-profit-owned digital solution that standardises and quantifies impact using a mobile data collection tool and a scientifically informed scoring model to assess agroecological projects (e.g., organic school gardens), calculating verified impact and Social Return on Investment (SROI). This approach is novel as one of the first non-profit-owned platforms to offer verified, standardized SROI metrics for both social and environmental outcomes, ensuring all data is anchored in direct field verification. While similar donor platforms exist, none offer this level of grassroots, comprehensive and non-profit-controlled impact data. The solution is rooted in FTFA s 30 years of on-the-ground experience and data insight into sustainable community project management. Crucially, the platform s potential is currently challenged by an assessment bottleneck with a gap between beneficiary applications and physical assessments. The grant solves this by rapidly assessing new beneficiaries, preparing them for donor funding. The sustainable benefits, once potential beneficiaries are onboarded is they become known and eligible for grant funding from multiple sources. This includes Communities, Farms, Schools and climate-linked projects. Additionally potential donors can receive custom proposals that individually and precisely fund impact within this data-driven eco-system and build more resilient food and climate systems.

core_fields.title: Pathways Through Which Biogas Improves Livelihoods and Sustainable Food Systems.
core_fields.description: Our project installs community biogas systems in rural Kenya, converting livestock waste into clean cooking fuel and organic fertilizer. This reduces deforestation and indoor air pollution, improving health especially for women while enhancing soil fertility and food security. The initiative empowers households through sustainable energy, lowers farming costs, and promotes a circular economy, directly supporting healthier communities and environmental regeneration.
core_fields.abstract: Our initiative, Pathways Through Which Biogas Improves Livelihoods and Sustainable Food Systems, addresses interconnected challenges of energy poverty, environmental degradation, and food insecurity in rural Kenya. Many households rely on wood fuel, leading to deforestation, indoor air pollution, and significant health risks especially for women and children. Simultaneously, declining soil fertility reduces agricultural productivity, threatening local food security. The project introduces community-scale biogas systems that convert readily available livestock manure and organic waste into clean cooking energy and nutrient-rich bio-slurry fertilizer. This circular solution directly reduces household dependence on firewood, conserving indigenous trees and lowering greenhouse gas emissions. By providing a smoke-free cooking alternative, it significantly decreases respiratory illnesses and reduces the time burden of fuel collection, particularly for women. The bio-slurry byproduct serves as an organic fertilizer, enhancing soil health, reducing reliance on chemical inputs, and increasing crop yields. This improves household nutrition and creates a new income stream through the sale of surplus fertilizer. Our approach integrates principles of environmental science, agricultural extension, and community economics, ensuring the solution is technically sound, culturally appropriate, and economically viable. By installing systems, training users, and establishing local maintenance committees, we empower communities to adopt a sustainable and regenerative practice that strengthens livelihood resilience, improves health, and fosters a healthier environment, directly contributing to SDGs 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7.

core_fields.title: Hedgerows and Compost: The Challenge of Food and Agricultural Self-Sufficiency in Madagascar
core_fields.description: The Hedgerows and Compost project addresses the challenge of agricultural self-sufficiency in Madagascar by breaking dependence on imported fertilizers. Agriculture is neither resilient nor sustainable if it depends on costly inputs that simultaneously deplete our soils. We propose to create a local organic fertilizer production chain using biomass from hedgerows. This innovation makes the most of our resources, creates jobs, keeps wealth in the local economy, and, above all, sustainably regenerates the soil fertility.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation proposes an integrated agroforestry system structured around agriculture for input autonomy: the creation of a green manure and compost production chain based on hedgerows, because a well-nourished plant is productive and more resistant to disease. The regional climate is humid and hot, with rain 10 months out of 12, making it very favorable for biomass production and composting parameters. Input production: Plots are dedicated to growing hedgerows, particularly Tithonia diversifolia and the legume Tephrosia vogelii. Nutritional richness: These plants are transformed into green manure and compost. The compost produced from these high-value agroforestry plants is ultra-rich, containing three times more nitrogen (N), twice as much phosphorus (P), and four times as much potassium (K) as traditional cattle manure, which is a very considerable amount for crops. Progressive independence: After the first year (when cattle manure is needed to establish the hedges), farmers become completely independent in terms of fertilizer within one to two years. Specific benefits For farmers: Total autonomy in terms of inputs, substantial savings, improved yields thanks to compost equivalent to 2 to 6 tons per 150 m of hedgerow. Support, training, and equipment for their involvement in the project through storytelling about their agroforestry system and the results on their products. Soil regeneration through abundant mulching and the addition of organic matter, reactivating microbial life and the mycelium network. This climate-smart system produces organic products while reducing capital flight. Utilization of naturalized exotic plants as sources of concentrated nutrients, exceeding the quality of traditional manure.

core_fields.title: Digitized Multi-Crop Value Chains for Safe, Nutritious, Trusted Food in Nepal
core_fields.description: This project scales an innovative, tech-enabled multi-crop value chain in Nepal, enabling smallholder farmers to produce safe, nutritious, and climate-resilient food while earning higher incomes. Through a tech-and-touch model, farmers adopt regenerative multi-cropping supported by pay-after-harvest access to organic inputs and direct market linkages. Over 18 months, the project will enable end-to-end traceability for 2,500 additional farmers using digital Farmer Cards, expand supply to 100 institutional customers, and catalyze $1 million in follow-on investment.
core_fields.abstract: Nepal is the fourth most vulnerable country to climate change, with smallholder farmers among the most affected. Most rely on mono-cropping systems dependent on chemical inputs, leaving them exposed to food insecurity, price volatility, soil degradation, and climate shocks. At the same time, opaque supply chains and multiple intermediaries prevent fair pricing and trust between farmers and consumers. This project introduces a digitized, multi-crop value chain model that enables farmers to transition to diversified, regenerative production while securing household nutrition and generating income through high-value domestic and international markets. Through a tech-and-touch, vertically integrated approach, the model directly links farmers and buyers, reducing intermediaries to improve affordability for buyers and increase prices received by farmers. Farmers receive training in organic multi-cropping and food safety via a digital platform complemented by local agri-extension officers. Organic inputs are provided through a pay-after-harvest financing model, removing upfront cost barriers. The value chain is digitized using aQysta s GROWN ERP platform and Farmer Cards (NFC) to provide buyers and consumers with verified transparency on product origin, farming practices, volumes, and prices paid. This enables food companies and institutions to confidently source ingredients that are safe, fairly produced, and aligned with sustainability standards. Market linkage follows a B2B model, supplying domestic and international food brands, restaurants, and school canteens and meal programs improving access to affordable, nutritious food and strengthening food security. What makes this solution novel is the integration of agronomy, financing, market linkage, and digitization into a single, market-driven system.

core_fields.title: Mtengo Trace: Offline Toolkit for Safe and Transparent Smallholder Food Systems.
core_fields.description: Mtengo Trace is an offline-first toolkit that empowers smallholder farmers and cooperatives to document production, pesticide use, storage, and handling practices. Using simple paper logbooks, batch labels, and facilitator devices, the system builds trust in informal food markets and aligns with Malawi s food safety policy. With Seed Grant support, Mtengo Trace will scale pilots, train farmers, and deliver safer, traceable food to communities while opening access to structured markets.
core_fields.abstract: Mtengo Trace is a simple but powerful innovation designed to bring food safety and transparency into Malawi s informal agricultural sector. The problem it tackles is clear: smallholder farmers and local processors often lack any system to document how food is grown, handled, or stored. This absence of traceability exposes consumers to contamination risks and locks farmers out of higher‑value markets that demand proof of safe practices. Our solution combines paper logbooks, mobile data forms, and batch labeling into a toolkit that is practical for rural communities with limited digital access. Farmers and processors can record planting, pesticide use, storage, and delivery in ways that are easy to understand and affordable. The scientific insight behind this approach is that traceability does not require complex or costly technology; instead, hybrid systems that blend low‑tech tools with simple digital forms can achieve the same accountability while remaining accessible to users with varying literacy and digital skills. The immediate benefits are safer food and stronger trust between producers and buyers. Farmers gain confidence and market access by proving their handling practices, while consumers, schools, and communities benefit from reduced risks of contamination. Over time, the toolkit supports sustainable change: cooperatives can scale traceability across hundreds of members, policymakers gain reliable data for food safety frameworks, and the environment benefits from better monitoring of pesticide use and storage practices.

core_fields.abstract: Our innovation transforms an extensive green roof, originally designed only for insulation and stormwater management, into a productive urban farm and outdoor classroom. Growing food on a rooftop with just five inches of soil demonstrates a repeatable model for dense cities where land access is limited and the need for local food solutions is urgent. The core problem we address is the lack of access to fresh, affordable produce and meaningful nature experiences in low-income, high-rise communities. Many residents, especially youth, live far from green space and have little opportunity to learn how food is grown. We solve this by using organic growing methods and climate-ready practices that draws on established knowledge in green roof engineering, soil science, and intensive urban agriculture, showing that underused rooftops can become community food assets. Our rooftop farm then becomes a hands-on learning environment where residents, students, and youth gain practical skills in growing, harvesting, and understanding ecological systems. Immediate benefits include increased access to fresh produce, new learning opportunities for schools and families, and a safe, welcoming green space for community connection. Long-term, the model supports climate resilience, reduces urban heat, strengthens local food literacy, and empowers residents with the knowledge to grow food at home, in community gardens, or on other rooftops. By transforming existing infrastructure into productive landscapes, we create sustainable pathways for healthier, greener, and more food-secure cities.

core_fields.title: Seeding Resilience: Conserving Repatriated Heirloom Varieties in a Circular, Regenerative Agroenterprise for Input Independence
core_fields.description: Our Circular Agroenterprise System (CAES) establishes Input Independence in an Integrated Demo Farm. A Community Seed Bank conserves repatriated heirloom seeds, eliminating costly external inputs. Integrated Black Soldier Fly (BSF) larvae composting and Korean Natural Farming (KNF) methods convert waste into zero-cost fertilizer, reducing synthetic inputs by 50%. Revenue from a diversified basket of value-added products and agrotourism provides perpetual funding, transforming the farm into a resilient, equitable, and zero-waste model.
core_fields.abstract: The core problem addressed is Input Dependence, specifically the crippling cost of seeds and synthetic fertilizers that limits farmer profitability and jeopardizes food security in the Philippines. This intervention tackles smallholder vulnerability and environmental damage from chemical inputs. Our innovation is the Circular Agroenterprise System (CAES), a closed-loop model that achieves Input Independence through resource sovereignty, anchored in an Integrated Demo Farm. A Community Seed Bank (CSB) conserves repatriated heirloom seeds, eliminating dependence on F1 hybrid seeds while ensuring access to climate-resilient genetics. For fertilizer production, CAES employs biological pathways Black Soldier Fly (BSF) technology and Korean Natural Farming (KNF) methods to convert organic waste into zero-cost feed and soil amendments. Urban paper waste collected from schools and businesses is co-composted with animal waste to provide carbon-rich substrate, supporting microbial activity, nutrient cycling, and system balance. BSF larvae process appropriate organic fractions, while composted biomass enhances soil fertility, ensuring total waste recovery. Crucially, the Demo Farm functions as a permanent Farmer Training Hub, delivering capacity building in seed banking, BSF/KNF operations, composting, and enterprise management. The scientific insight lies in integrating biological systems to regenerate soil capital, while the economic insight links seed sovereignty and soil health directly to market productivity. Immediate benefits for farmers include zero-cost seed access and a 50% reduction in synthetic input expenses. Long-term benefits include diversified, high-margin farm products and an educational agro-tourism hub. Consumers gain access to nutritious, traceable food, while society benefits from reduced GHG emissions, enhanced agrobiodiversity, and improved community-wide waste management.

core_fields.title: "Youth and Women Agri-food Innovation Pathway for Nutrition and Livelihood Resilience
core_fields.description: BCDA proposes an innovative Skills-to-Enterprise Agri-food Pathway that equips economically excluded women and youth in Batu with practical food-processing, sustainable agriculture, and food-safety skills. The project supports participants to develop nutritious, affordable food products using local crops, reduces waste through value-addition, and provides start-up support for micro-enterprises. By combining training, seed grants, and market linkages, the project strengthens nutrition, increases income, and builds resilient, community-based agri-food systems.
core_fields.abstract: In Batu City and surrounding rural kebeles, women and youth face persistent food insecurity, low income, and limited access to nutritious, affordable foods. Despite the area s rich horticultural production vegetables, fruits, and grains post-harvest loss, poor food-processing skills, and minimal value addition prevent communities from benefiting economically or nutritionally. Farmers lose income, households lack diverse diets, and young people struggle to enter the agrifood economy. BCDA s innovation the Skills-to-Enterprise Agrifood Pathway introduces a community-based model that transforms local crops into safe, nutritious, market-ready foods while creating viable micro-enterprises for women and youth. The solution integrates: (1) low-cost, climate-smart food processing and preservation techniques; (2) nutrition-sensitive product design using local produce; (3) value-addition methods that reduce post-harvest loss; (4) entrepreneurship, digital literacy, and market linkage support; and (5) micro-seed grants enabling start-up agrifood businesses. The idea is based on proven food science principles: dehydration, solar drying, bio-preservation, hygienic handling, and micronutrient retention strategies. These techniques are simple, affordable, and adaptable to local contexts requiring minimal equipment and enabling quick adoption by women and youth. The innovation directly benefits: Consumers: increased access to affordable, safe, nutritious foods. Farmers: reduced spoilage and higher income through reliable demand. Women & Youth: enterprise creation, income security, and empowerment. Communities: stronger local food systems and reduced dependence on imported processed products. Environment: reduced food waste and better use of local resources. By linking practical food-processing skills with enterprise creation, BCDA s innovation creates immediate livelihood gains and long-term food system transformation making nutritious food accessible, sustainable, and community-driven.

core_fields.title: Agroecological and Biotechnology Trails
core_fields.description: The project Agroecological and Biotechnology Trails strengthens Prato Verde s network of community gardens, which currently provides fresh food to over 1,000 people. Through agroecological education and accessible biotechnologies, the program empowers local residents to cultivate healthy produce, improve environmental resilience, and reduce food insecurity in underserved neighborhoods.
core_fields.abstract: The Agroecological and Biotechnology Trails" introduces an innovative approach to addressing food insecurity and environmental degradation in underserved urban areas. Many peripheral communities face food and environmental deserts, where access to healthy food, green spaces, and sustainable agricultural knowledge is extremely limited. This lack of resources directly affects nutrition, local biodiversity, and community resilience. Our solution combines agroecology with low-cost, accessible biotechnologies to strengthen Prato Verde s network of community gardens, which already provides fresh, healthy produce to more than 1,000 people. The project integrates hands-on learning, soil regeneration techniques, composting systems, biofertilizers, and water-efficient cultivation methods. These scientific and technical insights come from established agroecological practices and recent advances in community-scale biotechnology that enhance productivity without harming the environment. By empowering residents with practical skills and scientific understanding, the project transforms community members into active producers rather than passive consumers. This increases food autonomy, strengthens social cohesion, and builds long-term self-sufficiency. Immediate benefits include access to fresh food, lower household food costs, and improved environmental quality in neighborhoods. Sustainable benefits extend to schools, families, and local farmers who gain knowledge, healthier ecosystems, and replicable, low-cost cultivation models. Ultimately, the innovation addresses hunger, climate vulnerability, and lack of opportunities simultaneously creating a scalable, community-driven model that promotes healthier lives and more resilient urban environments.

core_fields.title: Scaling low cost bio-input and solar drier technologies for regenerative food systems and biodiversity conservation.
core_fields.description: Through integrating regenerative agriculture techniques with homemade solar dryer, this project aims to heal the land, strengthen local food systems, and improve community wellbeing by reducing post-harvest losses, increased access to safe food and nutritious food and entrepreneurship. The approach is holistic, community-centered, and designed for long-term environmental and human health impact. Through collaboration, capacity building, and ecological restoration, marginalized Kenyan communities in Machakos and Makueni transition toward healthier soils and sustainable, transformative food futures.
core_fields.abstract: Communities in Machakos and Makueni counties in Kenya face intersecting challenges that range from food safety to post-harvest losses and limited livelihood opportunities and severe environmental degradation. Contamination of vegetables by heavy metals is a key aspect of food quality assurance given the importance of vegetables in the human diet. The use of polluted urban streams water for irrigation contributes significantly to the heavy metal content in soil and then the vegetables, which poses health risks to consumers of the vegetable commodities (Nzeve, 2021). Losses up to 25 percent have been reported in some key staples (ASTGS 2019-2029). The project highlights two innovations interconnecting to support robust regenerative gardens. The first innovation is production of bio-inputs such as biochar at community level. This innovation aims at elimination the heavy dependence on synthetic chemical fertilizers and raw sewage as sources of soil nutrients for continuous access to safe nutritious foods. To enhance access to safe nutritious foods throughout the year by reducing post-harvest losses and support value addition within regenerative agriculture systems, the project also introduces a low cost home-made solar dryer designed with locally available materials. The solar dryer is used to dry farm products helping communities preserve nutritious produce during peak seasons. This innovation aligns with seeding the future s vision and mission by improving access to safe nutritious foods and reduced food losses. Households and institutions can preserve surplus harvests from their regenerative gardens, ensuring year-round access to nutritious food, reducing post-harvest losses and increasing household and institution income.
