core_fields.title: Hybrid Solar Dryer with Eco-friendly Auxiliary Heating for Climate-Resilient Crop Preservation in Nigeria
core_fields.description: Our team has developed a Hybrid Solar Multi-Crop Dryer that combines solar thermal energy, battery-powered Positive Temperature Coefficient (PTC) heating, thermal storage using black stones, and cloud-based IoT monitoring. The system delivers fast, uniform, and hygienic drying for crops despite unpredictable weather. With the Seed Grant, we will optimize the design, pilot in multiple Nigerian farming communities, validate economic and environmental benefits, and build a pathway for scalable local manufacturing and distribution.
core_fields.abstract: Post-harvest losses remain a major threat to food security across tropical and sub-Saharan Africa, where high humidity, fluctuating temperatures, and inconsistent sunlight undermine the performance of traditional solar dryers. These systems often fail during cloudy periods or at night, causing moisture to condense inside the chamber and rewet crops. The result is mold growth, microbial contamination, spoilage, and significant declines in product quality and market value. Previous attempts to add auxiliary heating to solar dryers have been largely ineffective due to inefficient energy use, manual operation, and inability to maintain stable drying conditions. Our Hybrid Solar Dryer offers a reliable, year-round solution by combining solar thermal heating with a battery-powered PTC heater that automatically activates during low-sunlight hours. A microprocessor-controlled feedback loop regulates temperature, humidity, and airflow using real-time sensor data, ensuring consistently optimal drying conditions. A thermal storage bed of black stones absorbs excess heat during peak sunlight and releases it slowly, preventing nighttime condensation and maintaining stable chamber temperatures. The system also integrates a cloud-connected IoT interface that supports remote monitoring, data logging, and crop-specific drying profiles, improving precision and reducing the need for constant supervision. This scientific and technical integration, hybrid energy management, thermal storage, and automated control, creates a continuous, weather-independent drying environment. Immediate benefits include faster, hygienic drying, reduced post-harvest losses, improved product quality, and increased income for farmers and processors. Long-term benefits include enhanced food safety, lower reliance on diesel, greater climate resilience, and strengthened rural value chains through sustainable processing technologies.

core_fields.title: Advancing Food Safety and Health Among Smallholder Farmers, Consumers and Refugee Communities in Uganda
core_fields.description: The project aims to promote an Integrated Aflatoxin Management Innovation (IAM) that combines biological control (using Aflasafe), good agronomic, improved post-harvest and storage practices, testing, and market-based incentives. This will minimize aflatoxin contamination in groundnuts and maize, equitable access and consumption of safer food. The project will improve public health and nutrition, enhance household incomes, and contribute to sustainable production systems and socioeconomic development for smallholder farmers and refugee communities in Uganda
core_fields.abstract: This project addresses a critical challenge in Uganda, the pervasive threat of aflatoxin contamination in groundnuts and maize. Aflatoxins not only compromise food safety but also undermine public health, reduce market access, and perpetuate poverty among vulnerable populations. Smallholder farmers and refugees are disproportionately affected by aflatoxin contamination as they consume what they produce, thus, limiting their ability to achieve food security and sustainable livelihoods. Aflatoxin exposure can lead to severe liver damage, jaundice, and death in extreme cases. Chronic exposure is more insidious, contributing to hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer), immune suppression, and stunted growth in children. To tackle this complex problem, we propose an Integrated Aflatoxin Management (IAM) innovation that combines bio-control, good agronomic practices, improved crop varieties adapted to the target regions, improved post-harvest handling and storage, routine testing, and market-based incentives to reward compliance. By reducing contamination risks at every vulnerable stage of the value chain, the project will ensure production and consumption of safer food, protect human health of vulnerable population and open access to premium markets. It will be possible to source locally produced crops meeting required standards. This project will scale IAM innovations across agricultural schemes of farming communities around refugee settlements and farming communities in Uganda. The anticipated outcomes include improved nutrition, better well-being, higher incomes, and enhanced resilience against food safety risks. Beyond immediate health benefits, this initiative contributes to long-term socioeconomic development and aligns with global priorities for food security, public health, and poverty reduction.

core_fields.title: Scale PURE Agriculture in Malawi
core_fields.description: Wala is scaling climate-resilient solar irrigation for smallholder farmers in Malawi. Through affordable solar water pumping systems, last-mile agent distribution, and a digitally coordinated platform, Wala enables year-round food production, higher incomes, and reduced reliance on fossil fuels. The project will expand distribution capacity and deploy digital tools to reach more farmers, strengthen food security, and build long-term resilience to climate shocks.
core_fields.abstract: Wala s innovation addresses one of the most persistent barriers to food security for smallholder farmers in Malawi: lack of reliable and affordable access to water for agriculture. Most farmers depend on increasingly erratic rainfall, while existing irrigation options diesel pumps, public schemes, or manual methods are either too expensive, inaccessible, or unsustainable. This vulnerability directly drives low productivity, unstable incomes, and climate-related food insecurity. Wala solves this problem through an integrated solar irrigation model that combines appropriate technology, last-mile delivery, financing, and digital coordination. At the core are energy-efficient solar water pumping systems designed for small plots and shallow water sources, enabling farmers to irrigate year-round without fuel costs or carbon emissions. The technology is paired with affordable credit, allowing low-income farmers to overcome high upfront costs. The innovation goes beyond hardware. Wala deploys a decentralized agent network equipped with transport and digital tools to ensure rural accessibility, farmer onboarding, training, and after-sales support. A centralized, AI-enabled digital platform coordinates inventory, customer management, repayments, and impact tracking, improving operational efficiency and scalability. This solution is informed by the insight that technology alone is insufficient; adoption requires trust, proximity, financing, and ongoing support. By integrating these elements, Wala delivers immediate benefits such as increased cropping cycles, higher and more stable incomes, and reduced labor and fuel expenses. Long-term benefits include improved food availability, enhanced climate resilience, job creation in rural areas, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions, contributing to sustainable agricultural systems for communities and the environment.

core_fields.title: Scaling Iron-Rich Millet Whole Yoghurt for Climate-Resilient Dairy Systems among Smallholder Farmers in Uganda
core_fields.description: This project scales an iron-rich millet whole yoghurt developed by Farm Reap to improve nutrition for children and women while strengthening climate-resilient dairy systems in Uganda. By integrating nutrient-dense millet into yoghurt and sourcing milk from smallholder dairy farmers adopting climate-smart, regenerative practices, the innovation improves dietary quality, stabilizes milk supply during dry periods, increases farmer incomes, and expands equitable access to affordable, trusted nutritious food.
core_fields.abstract: In Uganda, approximately 26% of children under five (about 2.4 million) are stunted, while 25% of women of reproductive age are anemic, largely due to inadequate dietary diversity and limited access to nutrient-dense foods (UNICEF, 2025). At the same time, climate variability, especially prolonged dry spells, is increasingly undermining dairy production, reducing milk yields, farmer incomes, and the availability of nutritious foods. These challenges are compounded by high food loss and waste, estimated at 30 50% along Uganda s food supply chain, driven by inefficiencies in production, aggregation, processing, and market access (Mutambuka M & Male D, 2024). This project will scale an integrated nutrition and climate-sensitive food system innovation: iron-rich millet whole yoghurt linked to a climate-smart dairy value chain. The innovation leverages the nutritional complementarity of dairy proteins and micronutrient-rich millet to enhance iron content and dietary diversity in a safe, affordable, and culturally acceptable format. It deliberately aligns milk sourcing with farmers adopting climate-resilient and regenerative practices such as resilient fodder production, improved feeding systems, and water management resulting in more stable milk supply, and minimized post-harvest milk losses. Farm Reap s millet whole yoghurt addresses micronutrient gaps among children and women of reproductive age, as evidenced by product nutritional analysis, while creating reliable market incentives for farmers to adopt sustainable practices. Immediate benefits include improved micronutrient intake, reduced milk wastage, and more stable farmer incomes. Long-term benefits include enhanced climate resilience, lower food loss, improved environmental outcomes, and a scalable model for delivering safe, affordable, and nutritious trusted foods.

core_fields.title: Locally sourced simplified hydroponics for emergency food production in Haiti.
core_fields.description: Haiti faces alarming levels of food insecurity. Access to food production is limited by disappearing arable land. Hydroponics, or the growth of plants in a water-based nutrient solution without the use of soil, offers a solution. However, hydroponics is reliant on expensive imported specialty equipment and supplies. Through collaborative international research, we have developed a protocol for the growth of crops hydroponically in Haiti using only locally sourced materials.
core_fields.abstract: The majority of Haitians face critical food insecurity in an increasing desperate situation, which is classified as alarming by the 2025 Global Hunger Index. Food production is threatened by extreme poverty and a shortage of arable land. Simplified forms of hydroponic agriculture enable affordable food production on nonarable land. Haiti is almost entirely cut off from international trade and so specialty supplies used to construct and run hydroponic agriculture are not available. In response, we endeavored to create a simplified hydroponic system that can be fully locally sourced in Haiti. We have successfully operated electricity-free simplified hydroponic systems constructed from materials available in the central plateau region of Haiti. We have replaced specialty hydroponic substrates with locally sourced gravel and coconut husks. The last piece to a fully sustainable system is a local fertilizer option. We completed a research project to create a protocol for use of corn-based products as organic fertilizer in our systems. Preliminary tests using locally acquired corn have been successful in Haiti. With support from this grant our research teams in Pignon, Haiti and Connecticut, USA will optimize our protocol and supply 100 families with systems for food production. We are positioned for maximum impact because we have an established research team in Haiti that carries out product testing and community outreach with remote technical support from our US-based team. Our research progress and community impact has continued since 2016 despite a deteriorating political situation that has rendered travel between the U.S. and Haiti difficult.

core_fields.title: Nutrient-Infused Compostable Seed Cups for Regenerative Crop Establishment
core_fields.description: Nutrient-Infused Compostable Seed Cups for Regenerative Crop Establishment replace plastic seedling pots with plantable, biodegradable seed cups made from agricultural residues. The cups retain moisture, deliver nutrients, and decompose naturally in soil, improving early crop establishment while reducing plastic pollution. Designed for affordability and local production, the innovation supports smallholder farmers with a low-cost, regenerative tool that enhances soil health and seedling survival.
core_fields.abstract: Plastic seedling cups are widely used in agriculture but create persistent soil pollution, increase transplant shock, and contribute to waste accumulation, especially in smallholder farming systems where plastic recovery is limited. This problem is increasingly relevant as global agriculture seeks solutions that are both productive and environmentally sustainable. This project introduces nutrient-infused, compostable seed cups made from locally sourced agricultural residues such as straw, grass, reeds, or sawdust, bound with natural starch and clay. The cups are designed to be planted directly into the soil, where they gradually decompose. Their fibrous structure retains water around the root zone, reducing moisture stress during early growth, while optional nutrient or microbial additives support healthy seedling development. The solution is informed by scientific insights into soil organic matter, water-holding capacity, and root-zone nutrition, applying circular economy principles to agriculture. By transforming biomass waste into functional planting inputs, the innovation reduces plastic use, improves crop establishment, and enhances soil health. The benefits include lower costs, improved seedling survival, reduced labor, and better moisture retention. Long-term benefits include reduced plastic pollution, improved soil quality, and more resilient, regenerative farming systems for farmers and communities.

core_fields.title: CoolCycle: Climate-Smart Solar Hubs for Cooling, Irrigation and Nutritious Food Access in Nigeria
core_fields.description: CoolCycle deploys solar-powered cold hubs and smart irrigation to transform handling of perishable produce and protein in Nigeria. By boosting yields and harvest cycles, then providing clean, hygienic pre-cooling, storage and handling near farms, abattoirs and markets, CoolCycle tackles post-harvest losses of up to 50%. The project improves access to nutritious food, reduces waste to less than 5% and raises smallholder incomes by 3x through better quality and reliable market access.
core_fields.abstract: CoolCycle is a network of solar-powered farm-to-market hubs that address three linked failures in Nigeria s food system: lack of irrigation, weak cold chains, and dependence on diesel. Today, over 50% of perishables are lost post-harvest, less than 1% of arable land is irrigated, 114 million Nigerians lack adequate cooling, and smallholders sell only about a quarter of what they grow at the right quality and price. Each CoolCycle hub combines: (1) solar irrigation systems that replace small diesel pumps and boost yields and harvest cycles; (2) modular cold rooms and ice plants that keep fresh produce and protein within safe temperatures; and (3) a mobile/USSD and AI layer that lets farmers and traders book irrigation slots and cold space, and connects them to reliable bulk buyers. Under this scale-up project, we will deploy four new hubs adding 65 tonnes of cold capacity plus daily ice production for horticulture and protein storage, alongside 10 solar irrigation systems serving at least 500 smallholders and around 3,500 direct users, with over 30,000 indirect beneficiaries. By providing clean, hygienic pre-cooling, storage and handling close to farms, abattoirs and markets, CoolCycle reduces post-harvest losses of up to 50%, cuts waste to below 5% for users, improves access to safe, nutritious food in urban and peri-urban markets, and can raise smallholder net incomes by up to 3x compared to diesel-based, makeshift and unhygienic practices.

core_fields.title: Circular Upcycling of Rice By-Products to Deliver Affordable Protein and Sustainable Livelihoods
core_fields.description: This project scales a low-cost, community-driven fermentation process that transforms rice bran and husk into safe, nutrient-dense animal feeds, improving the quality and affordability of eggs, milk, fish, and meat for human diets. Adapted from traditional food systems, the approach reduces waste, lowers feed costs, and strengthens rural livelihoods. By empowering farmers, processors, and pastoralists across rice-producing regions, it delivers a scalable, climate-smart, help-for-self-help solution for resilient and equitable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Nigeria and other African rice-producing countries generate millions of tonnes of rice bran and husk annually, much of which is wasted or burned, contributing to environmental pollution and loss of valuable nutrients. At the same time, high feed costs and reliance on maize limit livestock productivity, reducing access to eggs, fish, and milk essential for safe and nutritious diets. Low animal protein intake contributes to chronic and hidden hunger, while scarcity of affordable feed places pressure on grazing lands and weakens rural livelihoods. The core innovation is a low-cost, low-tech, community-controlled fermentation process that converts rice by-products into safe, nutrient-dense animal feed. While fermentation is well established in human foods such as ogi, it is rarely standardized or applied for animal production. By controlling moisture, anaerobic conditions, and fermentation time in simple, food-grade vessels, the process improves feed safety, reduces anti-nutritional factors (25 to 40%), stabilizes rice bran against rancidity, and enhances protein digestibility and micronutrient bioavailability. In poultry and fish, fermented rice bran partially replaces costly maize, reducing feed costs by up to 40% while maintaining productivity. For ruminants, it functions as a low-cost complete feed when combined with molasses, easing grazing pressure. Bioactive compounds and micronutrients are deposited into eggs, milk, and fish improving their nutritional quality. Immediate benefits include reduced feed expenses, new income streams, and improved livestock performance. Sustainable benefits include safer, more nutritious food, reduced waste and environmental pressure, and equitable access to affordable animal protein for households and communities through a scalable, help-for-self-help pathway.

core_fields.title: Distribution the developed mobile low pressure drip installation with photovoltaic panels
core_fields.description: As a result of climate change, there is a shortage of fresh water for drinking and irrigated agriculture. The introduction of mobile low-pressure drip installations with photovoltaic panels on household and dehkan farms, greenhouses and suburban areas located in regions with water and energy shortages will increase crop yields and the financial well-being of the population
core_fields.abstract: Today, water-saving technologies, especially drip irrigation, are being widely implemented in Uzbekistan (more than 35% in 2024). There are more than 4.425 million families (on an area of 1043.7 thousand hectares 692.2 thousand hectares of homesteads and 351.5 thousand hectares of suburban areas, as well as 7,175 thousand hectares of greenhouses) are engaged in agriculture. In fact, homestead landowners account for 84% of potatoes grown in the country, 71% of vegetable products, 55-60% of apples, grapes and fruits, and more than 94% of livestock products. At the same time, the size of household plots can be 0.16-0.50 hectares, and suburban plots up to 0.06 hectares. Currently, Uzbekistan has accelerated the introduction of various types of water-saving technologies, especially drip irrigation systems on large cultivated areas (ω=1.0-100.0 hectares or more). However, due attention is not paid to the installation of a drip irrigation system on small (ω=0.01-1.0 hectares) household and suburban areas, as well as in greenhouses. For drip irrigation of small areas (ω = 0.01-0.5 hectares), the Suvchi research team has developed Mobile drip irrigation installation with photovoltaic system (MDIIPS-2/550-1100), for which a patent was obtained. The installation consists of the following main components: low pressure drip irrigation system, photovoltaic panels, pumping unit, four-wheeled trolley with metal structure, and automated control system. The dissemination of this water-saving technology through demonstrations and trainings among stakeholders will make it possible to develop agriculture more efficiently and reliably in small areas with water and energy shortages

core_fields.title: SMART SOLAR HYBRID FISH DRYERS FOR SAFE, SUSTAINABLE, AND PROFITABLE POST-HARVEST FISHERIES IN KENYA
core_fields.description: This project seeks to deploy Smart Solar Hybrid Fish Dryers in Lake Victoria (Sindo Beach) and Lake Turkana (Kalokol) to reduce post-harvest losses, improve fish safety and quality, and enhance livelihoods for small-scale processors, particularly women. By integrating renewable energy, hygienic design, and skills training, the innovation increases the availability of nutritious fish, strengthens sustainable practices, and boosts economic opportunities within value chains. It supports food security, climate resilience, and inclusive economic growth
core_fields.abstract: Kenya s inland fisheries in particular Lake Victoria and Lake Turkana are vital for national food security, rural livelihoods, and the economy. In 2024, fish from Lake Victoria generated approximately KES 14 billion from 86,394 MT, while Lake Turkana contributed KES 3.3 billion from 17,251 MT (Kenya Fisheries Service, 2024). The main commercial species being omena (Rastrineobola argentea), Nile perch, and tilapia, which support nutrition, employment, and income generation for thousands of households. Fish is a highly nutritious and affordable animal-source food, providing 17% of global animal protein and supporting the livelihoods of 10 12% of the world s population (FAO, 2020; UNCTAD, 2023). Its proteins, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin D, riboflavin, calcium, and minerals make it crucial for healthy diets and reducing malnutrition. In Kenyan riparian counties, fish accounts for up to 75% of animal protein intake, underscoring its importance for food and nutrition security (KMFRI, 2024). Despite its significance, post-harvest losses (PHL) threaten safety, nutrition, and economic returns. Artisanal fishers and small-scale processors, over 78% of the sector, use rudimentary handling and open-air drying on bare ground or old nets, exposing fish to contamination, pests, and spoilage. (KMFRI, 2017 2024). Inefficient drying also contributes to environmental degradation and unsustainable practices. Addressing these losses is critical for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 3 (Good Health), SDG 8 (Decent Work), and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption), by improving food security, nutrition, livelihoods, and resilient fisheries value chains (United Nations, 2023).

core_fields.title: AI-Driven Mobile Solution for Plant Health Diagnosis and Sustainable Input Access for Nigerian Smallholder Farmers.
core_fields.description: AgroMareh is an AI-powered agritech venture utilizing mobile and web apps for smallholder farmers. It offers early crop disease detection via image diagnostics, geolocation insights, and access to a verified marketplace for certified agro-inputs. Our mission is to bring precision agriculture and actionable data to every farmer, building Africa's most trusted digital ecosystem for intelligent crop health management, advancing food security and climate resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Innovation Description (AgroMareh) AgroMareh is an AI-powered mobile platform that helps smallholder farmers identify crop diseases, receive localized farming advice, and connect directly to verified agro-input suppliers all in one app. The innovation tackles a pressing agricultural challenge in Nigeria and Africa: millions of farmers lose up to 40% of yield yearly due to late or wrong diagnosis of crop diseases, use of fake inputs, and limited access to extension services. The relevance lies in improving food security, farmer income, and sustainable agricultural productivity in an era of climate change and rural-urban migration. AgroMareh solves this by using machine learning and computer vision to detect plant health issues from images captured through the farmer s phone. It provides instant, easy-to-understand results in local languages, paired with actionable audio-visual guidance and recommendations on genuine agro-products available from trusted suppliers. This solution draws on insights from field testing and agricultural data science integrating AI diagnostics, geospatial intelligence, and human-centered design. Immediate benefits include early disease detection, reduced crop loss, access to verified inputs, and improved yields. Long-term, AgroMareh promotes climate-smart agriculture, data-driven decision-making, and youth participation in agribusiness. For communities and the environment, it enhances resilience, reduces chemical misuse, and fosters sustainable food systems contributing directly to SDGs 2 (Zero Hunger), 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), and 13 (Climate Action).

core_fields.title: TRANSFORMING LOCAL DIETS FOR SUSTAINABLE FOOD ACCESS THROUGH CIRCULAR PROTEIN SYSTEMS (CPS-DIETS)
core_fields.description: Building on prior research confirming the superior nutritional profile of Black Soldier Fly (BSF) larvae, the CPS-Diets project transforms local agro-processing waste into safe, biofortified BSF protein for human consumption while producing organic fertilizer to enhance soil health. Through food-grade product development, innovative household BSF rearing kits, community training, and market creation, the project improves access to affordable protein, generates farmer income, and strengthens climate-resilient, circular food systems grounded in local culture.
core_fields.abstract: This proposal addresses the dual challenge of malnutrition and inefficient agro-processing waste management prevalent in many Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), including Kenya. Over 10.8 million Kenyans face food insecurity, with children and women disproportionately affected by stunting and micronutrient deficiencies. Conventional livestock systems, although they utilize agro-processing by-products as feed, contribute nearly 30% of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions and cannot sustainably meet rising protein demand. CPS-Diets introduces a scalable Black Soldier Fly (BSF) production system that converts targeted agro-processing waste into nutrient-dense food and agricultural inputs. Building on evidence of superior nutritional quality of Black Soldier Fly larvae (BSFL), the project biofortifies BSFL by formulating substrates from pre-characterized local agroprocessing waste streams, including maize germ, wheat bran, avocado, and banana residues, to enhance key micronutrients such as vitamin A precursors, iron, and zinc. This approach is integrated with participatory development of culturally appropriate food products for vulnerable populations. Coupled with systematic use of frass as organic fertilizer, creating closed-loop system. Scientifically, BSFL rapidly bioconvert organic waste into high-quality, food-grade protein within 10 12 days. Trials conducted at Meru University of Science and Technology (https://sri.must.ac.ke/from-waste-to-health-and-wealth/) show BSFL contain 43 52% high-quality protein, while requiring minimal land, water, and energy. The process generates nutrient-rich frass that improves soil health and crop productivity. Immediate benefits include improved access to fortified foods, reduced organic waste, and improved soil fertility. Systemically, CPS-Diets establishes a resilient, community-led enterprise and a replicable model for circular, climate-resilient food systems that advance nutrition, sustainability, and equitable development.

core_fields.abstract: Small farmers in rural Pakistan depend heavily on diesel-powered tube wells for irrigation. More than 90% of farmers are small-scale, each receiving only 22 minutes of canal water per acre weekly, insufficient for irrigation. This leads to reliance on diesel-powered tube wells, irregular irrigation, crop stress, lower yields, rising production costs, food waste, and the emission of significant greenhouse gases. Diesel engines produce 2.7 kg of CO2 per litre of fuel consumed. This makes the current irrigation system both financially and environmentally unsustainable for farmers who already face climate-related pressures. Our project proposes installing fifteen shared mobile solar-powered irrigation units across five villages. Fifteen mobile solar units will be enough for 650 -750 acres, that will shut down more than 180-200 diesel engines. This innovation builds on a successful pilot in two villages where 3 units shifted 30 farmers from diesel to mobile solar pumping, showed strong results, including sharp reductions in diesel use, more reliable irrigation, approximately 243 tons of CO₂ per year avoided, and visibly healthier crops. Solar panels generate clean electricity to run the pump, while the shared and mobile design allows one system to serve several small farms efficiently, making it affordable and easy to adopt. Immediate benefits include lower irrigation costs, protection from fuel price shocks, consistent water availability, and cleaner air due to reduced emissions, reduced greenhouse gases, and approximately 1,370 1,400 metric tons of CO₂ emissions reduction per year. core_fields.title: Osh-UPCYCLE: Coffee Grounds + Apple Pomace into Safe Functional Snacks for Affordable Nutrition
core_fields.description: We will upcycle two underused local by-products-spent coffee grounds from cafes and apple pomace from juice production-into a shelf-stable food-grade ingredient and 2-3 affordable snack prototypes (cookie, bar, and/or dairy snack). Seed Grant funds will support safety testing, process optimization (drying, milling, stabilization), and pilot sales through partner outlets in Osh and Nookat, creating a scalable circular model for the region
core_fields.abstract: Problem: Cafe coffee grounds and seasonal apple pomace are often discarded, creating disposal costs and environmental burdens, while affordable nutrient-dense snacks remain limited for low-income consumers. Solution: We collect the by-products from two anchor partners, stabilize them (controlled drying/roasting; optional lactic fermentation to improve safety and flavor), mill to a standardized powder, and blend into familiar foods (bread, rolls, cookies, bars, and a dairy snack) using clear quality specifications and HACCP-based controls. Novelty: (1) a dual-stream, year-round supply model (coffee grounds year-round + pomace stored as stabilized powder); (2) a low-cost, SME-ready processing package (batch dryers, small mills, simple QA); and (3) a circular partnership model that turns waste management into a revenue stream for local micro-businesses. Similar solutions exist globally as 'upcycled' ingredients, but they are rarely localized for Central Asia with food-safety validation and a practical replication toolkit. Insight: combining two complementary by-products improves ingredient functionality and balances seasonality, making a more reliable micro-enterprise model. Benefits: reduced organic waste, new local income, and affordable products that can be trusted due to third-party safety tests and transparent labeling.

core_fields.title: From Soil to School: Regenerative Supply Chains for Affordable, Nutritious School Meals
core_fields.description: This project scales affordable, nutritious school meals in Nepal from 2,500 to 50,000 children by strengthening regenerative, nutrition-sensitive supply chains linking local farmers directly to schools. By integrating improved crop varieties, regenerative farming practices, quality assurance, and digital traceability, the project improves nutrient quality at source, increases farmer incomes (15 25%), reduces import dependence, and delivers safe, trusted meals within government price limits, creating a scalable, climate-resilient model for equitable school nutrition.
core_fields.abstract: The project addresses a critical bottleneck in scaling affordable school nutrition in Nepal: the limited availability of consistent, high-quality, nutrient-dense raw materials produced locally. While fortified foods are currently delivered to approximately 2,500 students, expansion to 50,000 students is constrained by variable nutrient quality in local crops, unstable domestic supply, and continued reliance on imported raw materials. These constraints weaken nutrition outcomes, increase costs, and reduce climate and supply-chain resilience. Rather than relying solely on downstream fortification, the innovation embeds nutrition at the production stage through a regenerative, nutrition-sensitive supply chain that directly links farmers to school food manufacturing. The system integrates regenerative soil management, nutrient-dense and climate-resilient National Agricutlure Research Council-developed crop varieties, structured farmer clusters with aggregation and quality assurance, and digital traceability linking farm practices and crop quality to school meal production. The scientific foundation of the innovation is based on evidence that soil health and crop genetics jointly determine micronutrient density, yield stability, and resilience to climate stress. By improving nutrient density before processing, the model reduces dependence on fortification inputs while improving nutritional quality and bioavailability. Immediate benefits include reliable access to safe, affordable meals with verified nutrient composition for schoolchildren; stable markets, improved incomes (15 25%), and reduced input costs for farmers; and predictable supply and policy-aligned procurement for schools. Over time, the model restores soil health, reduces synthetic inputs, lowers import dependence (20 30%), and offers a replicable pathway for transforming school feeding into equitable, climate-resilient food systems.

core_fields.title: Youth Led organic Firming to Promote Food Production and Consumption
core_fields.description: The Youth-Led Organic Farming to Promote Food Production and Consumption project aims to produce chemical-free, nutritious crops through sustainable organic farming. Led by youth at the community level, it promotes safe and healthy food consumption while reducing reliance on harmful agrochemicals. The project seeks to establish resilient, community-based food systems that enhance food security, improve nutrition, support local livelihoods, restore soil health, protect the environment, and revive biodiversity for long-term sustainability.
core_fields.abstract: The Youth-Led Organic Farming to Promote Food Production and Consumption project is an innovative response to the growing problems of chemical-dependent agriculture, unsafe food, declining soil fertility, and loss of biodiversity. In many communities, excessive use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides has reduced nutritional value of food, harmed human health, degraded soil, and increased production costs for small farmers. At the same time, youth unemployment and weak local food systems remain major challenges. This project addresses these problems by engaging young people as leaders and practitioners of organic farming at the community level. Youth are trained in organic cultivation methods such as composting, bio-fertilizers, natural pest management, crop rotation, and seed preservation. These practices are based on proven agroecological and scientific principles that enhance soil microorganisms, improve nutrient cycling, and increase ecosystem resilience without harmful chemicals. The innovation lies in combining youth leadership with community-based organic food systems. By producing chemical-free, nutritious crops locally, the project strengthens food security, promotes healthy consumption, and reduces dependence on external agricultural inputs. Immediate benefits include safer and more nutritious food for consumers, reduced production costs and improved income for farmers, and practical skills and employment opportunities for youth. In the long term, the project improves soil health, restores biodiversity, protects water and ecosystems, supports climate resilience, and builds sustainable, community-owned food systems that benefit society and the environment.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Agroforestry and Cattle-Centered Livestock Systems for Food Security and Green Enterprise Development in Ghana
core_fields.description: This project strengthens food security in Northern Ghana by integrating regenerative agroforestry, composting, and cattle-focused nutrition and animal health, with spillover benefits for small ruminants supporting women and youth. Demonstration plots and digital extension will be used to directly build the capacities of 2,000 farmers and indirectly reach 10,000 more. Local cooperatives will be supported to establish enterprises in compost, fodder, moringa, and livestock value chains, restoring soil fertility, and strengthening livelihoods and climate resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Farming communities in Northern Ghana face interconnected challenges: degraded soils, declining crop yields, chronic dry-season feed shortages, low cattle productivity, and limited availability of safe, affordable animal-source foods. Crop residues, manure, and agroforestry biomass are underutilized, while traditional dairy and meat products suffer from poor hygiene and low market value, constraining nutrition, incomes, and resilience. This innovation introduces a livestock-crop-centered circular food system that converts biomass into three reinforcing outputs: soil fertility (compost), livestock nutrition (fodder), and safe animal-source foods (milk and meat). Rather than treating composting, fodder production, and livestock as separate interventions, the model integrates them into a closed-loop production system. Compost restores soil fertility and increases biomass; biomass feeds cattle; healthier cattle produce manure, milk, and meat; and manure feeds back into compost production. Technically, the solution leverages the synergistic benefits of integrating agroforestry with multipurpose, drought-tolerant trees (moringa and leucaena), Brachiaria/Napier fodder systems, and composting to restore soil fertility, increase biomass for cattle feeding, and protect the environment. These proven regenerative practices are combined with improved cattle nutrition and preventive animal health into a single, community-scale system supported by digital extension. The innovation lies in system integration and operational design, enabling consistent replication rather than one-off pilots. Immediate benefits include improved feed availability, healthier cattle, increased milk and meat supply, and reduced fertilizer costs. Sustainable benefits include improved feed availability, increased availability of diverse nutritious food, and reduced fertilizer costs. Long-term benefits include restored soils, stronger rural enterprises, improved diets, and more resilient, equitable food systems.

core_fields.title: Integrated Mangrove Agro-ecologies for Regenerative Food Security in Ghana Wetlands
core_fields.description: ReDAW s Integrated Mangrove Agro-ecologies (IMA) project combines sustainable aquaculture with mangrove restoration, a model that improves both environmental and socioeconomic outcomes for Ghanaian communities living within the KLRCS. The project is occurring in tandem with Ghana s first Blue Carbon project, demonstrating a more lucrative and resilient aquaculture model for coastal communities to replicate. Over 20 tonnes of tilapia will be produced annually from initial pilots, with expansion plans in place across the region.
core_fields.abstract: The project aims to create environmentally-sustainable, profitable food systems to reduce multidimensional poverty in Ghana s Volta Region, while supporting biodiverse restoration. The Ramsar Site and KBA supports a list of IUCN threatened species, but, without intervention, it will be 90% eutrophied in the near term. Local fisheries have depleted over 60% in the past 20 years, stressing household income and food security, in turn leading to further degradation of the sensitive mangrove ecosystems on which the fisheries and abundant wildlife depend. Some aquaculture systems have been trialled, but they tend to contribute to pollution and have underperformed on yields. Despite these realities, and a national commitment to bolster aquaculture production capacity, sustainable food systems change is underfinanced. Nature-based carbon is a solution to help finance aquaculture with private, international investment. Communities in Ghana are wary, however, of carbon developers who have failed to follow-through on projects and commitments for investments. Agricultural projects in tandem with 40-year carbon projects promise more immediate benefits to communities, addressing the underlying drivers to deforestation and land degradation. Restoration requires community-buy in and training, and the promise of returns from blue carbon combined with immediate returns from IMA and livelihood projects have achieved local commitment. Within 5 years we will have 10 operationalized ponds, producing 50 tonnes of tilapia annually and providing up to 10 jobs. Revenue ($150,000+) is managed by community trust funds that have a mandate to help the community at large by investing in projects that help achieve the SDGs.

core_fields.title: The Nutri-Potato Seed-Farmer Franchise: Circular, Market-Led Model for Climate-Resilient Nutrition in Ethiopia
core_fields.description: We scale a-proven franchise model that empowers smallholders as producers of biofortified potato-seed and potato-ware-table. By integrating aeroponics, circular waste-to-fertilizer systems, digital agronomy, and guaranteed markets, we boost yields by 126%, reduce post-harvest loss by 65%, and deliver essential micronutrients to women and children. Our pilot with 500 farmers validates the model. The $100,000 Growth Grant will catalyze replication across 12 cooperatives, directly benefiting 10,000 households and creating a national blueprint for potato transformation.
core_fields.abstract: The Problems: Ethiopia s potato sector is trapped in entrenched cycles of scarcity and loss. A mere 0.5% of smallholders can obtain certified seed, locking yields at a fraction of the crop's genetic potential. Over one-third of the harvest spoils, degraded soils struggle under climate pressures, and malnutrition silently afflicts half of all women and children. Within fragmented, extractive supply chains, farmers retain less than 15% of the end value, cementing poverty. The Solution: We transform this crisis through a regenerative, market-powered franchise: The Nutri-Potato Seeds and Tables. Aeroponic-hubs multiply disease-free, iron-and-zinc-biofortified minitubers with 90% resource savings. Franchiser s Farmers, women-and-youth-led Agripreneur Networks act-as local seed multipliers and service-hubs. The Sena Farm Assistant, a USSD/SMS platform, provides hyperlocal agronomic guidance and unlocks input-credit via verified practice logs. Solar-powered Mobile-Processing Units salvage culls into Nutri-Potato-Flour for schools, preserve premium-tubers for market, and convert waste into organic-fertilizer via insect bioreactors. Marketing-Linkage Guaranteed forward contracts with schools, retailers, and processors-branded Iron-Potato for Stronger Children ; secure a 30% price premium for farmers. The Novelty: This is Ethiopia s first integrated franchise model for a root crop, uniquely merging farmer ownership, seed-origin biofortification, digital-credit verification, and closed-loop circularity into one self-reinforcing system. The Benefits: A 10-month pilot with 500-farmers validated the outcomes: 128% higher yields, 65% less post-harvest loss, 98% income growth, measurable reductions in child anemia, and visible soil regeneration. The model achieves full economic self-sustainability within 18-months through revenues from seeds, inputs, ware potatoes, and service fees; nourishing resilience from soil-to-society.

core_fields.title: Forest Lab: An Itinerant, Community-Led Food Laboratory for Amazonian Regeneration
core_fields.description: Forest Lab is an itinerant, community-led food laboratory driven by Amazonian Indigenous communities and supported by Fab Lab Peru. The project co-creates regenerative food systems across the Amazon Basin through regenerative gastronomy, community-based agriculture, and hands-on innovation workshops. It strengthens local nutrition, revitalizes ancestral food knowledge, and regenerates relationships between communities and territory, with the Puerto Ocopa community in the Tambo River serving as a learning and replication hub.
core_fields.abstract: ForestLab is an itinerant, community-led innovation that regenerates Amazonian food systems by restoring the relationship between forests, food, culture, and nutrition. The project addresses the erosion of local food systems driven by malnutrition, biodiversity loss, declining use of native plant species many at risk of extinction and growing dependence on external, low-nutrient foods that weaken both health and ecological resilience. The innovation combines ancestral knowledge with regenerative practices and appropriate technologies. Working with Amazonian Indigenous communities, ForestLab identifies and revalorizes native edible and medicinal plant species through the co-creation of culturally rooted food products and regenerative gastronomy experiences. These products increase demand for native species, creating direct incentives for forest conservation and regeneration rather than extraction. Community and family gardens are established as living laboratories where these species are cultivated using regenerative methods such as composting, bio-inputs, seed recovery, and collective stewardship. These gardens improve food access, dietary diversity, and autonomy while strengthening ecological knowledge and intergenerational transmission. Technology plays a supporting and empowering role. Digital tools and artificial intelligence are used to document plant properties, optimize food formulations for precision nutrition, systematize learning, and support communities in developing their own technologies and data systems without replacing ancestral knowledge. This enhances the effectiveness, safety, and nutritional impact of locally produced foods. Immediate benefits include improved nutrition, new livelihood opportunities, and strengthened food sovereignty. Long-term impacts include forest regeneration, protection of threatened species, resilient community-led food systems, and a scalable model for Amazonian river basins, with communities as leaders and FabLab-Peru as technical support

core_fields.title: Sustainable edible insect farming (SEDIF): Nutritional/sensory characterization of Rhynchophorus palmarum bred using agricultural by-products
core_fields.description: Chontacuro (Rhynchophorus palmarum) is an edible insect traditionally consumed by the Amazonians. Its production is sporadic and constrains forest resources. Chontacuro larvae are bred at a small scale in the community of Campo-Cocha, Ecuador. The challenge is to contrast the nutritional value and sensory acceptability of traditionally-bred chontacuro vs alternative-bred using agricultural by-products as a feeding substrate. Through outreach tools, the upcycling prototype model of sustainable production will be disseminated among indigenous communities.
core_fields.abstract: Malnutrition primarily affects Indigenous communities (18), and their traditional diet, linked to local biodiversity, is being gradually displaced (19). The chontacuro (R. palmarum) is one of the emblematic foods of the Amazon region, a symbol of Indigenous identity and cultural continuity. However, its traditional farming depends on palm logging. This production system, while viable on a small scale, can limit forest ecosystems and the possibility of expanding production (6). As a semi-cultivated and unpredictable system, the supply is irregular and does not respond to growing demand, generating risks of scarcity and hindering its stable incorporation into the local diet and potential value chains (20). A sustainable alternative is the use of locally available agricultural byproducts and their integration into the chontacuro's diet, contributing to the transformation of waste into biomass of high nutritional value (as depicted in other insect production models). This approach would not only lead to a reduction in agricultural waste and production costs, but also to a more sustainable and continuous farming method, capable of supplying both local communities and nearby markets (12,14). The challenge is to contribute to the development of more sustainable models for insect production and consumption with the potential for scalability and replicability, seeking to impact environmental sustainability, biodiversity conservation, and the strengthening of local food culture. This includes nutritional and sensory evaluation, social and cultural acceptance of the chontacuro and derived products in the Amazonian Campo-Cocha community and other communities, generating positive impacts on food security, local income, cultural resilience, and sustainability.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Kitchen Gardens for Food Security and Livelihoods in Bahawalpur District, South Punjab
core_fields.description: Help in Need (HIN) proposes a 12-month initiative in District Bahawalpur, South Punjab to improve household nutrition and resilience through climate-smart kitchen gardening. The project will equip vulnerable families particularly women-headed households with starter kits, hands-on training, and continuous technical support to grow diverse vegetables at home. By improving food access, reducing household expenses, and enabling income from surplus produce, the project promotes sustainable, nutrition-sensitive livelihoods and community self-reliance.
core_fields.abstract: Households in Bahawalpur District, South Punjab face persistent food insecurity due to limited income opportunities, high food prices, climate variability, water scarcity, and increasing pressure on household resources. Women-headed and low-income families are particularly affected, often lacking the space, skills, and inputs needed to grow nutritious food at home. This project addresses these challenges by introducing climate-smart, space-efficient household kitchen gardens, enabling vulnerable families to grow fresh vegetables year-round, improve nutrition, and generate supplementary income. The innovation applies scientifically proven micro-gardening techniques, including container-based cultivation, vertical gardening, organic soil enrichment, and water-efficient irrigation methods suited to arid and semi-arid conditions. These approaches allow households with small courtyards or limited water access to sustainably produce food. The model is novel locally because it integrates climate-smart production, nutrition-sensitive crop selection, basic enterprise skills for selling surplus produce, and community-led peer learning groups to support long-term adoption. While informal kitchen gardening exists, it is rarely implemented as a structured, technically guided, climate-resilient livelihood model. Insights from agronomy, nutrition science, and small-scale irrigation research inform crop choices, soil mixes, and water-saving techniques. The benefits are immediate and sustainable. Households gain access to fresh vegetables, reduce food expenditures, and diversify diets. Surplus produce generates additional income, particularly empowering women and youth. Environmentally, the project encourages organic inputs, water conservation, biodiversity, and lower carbon footprints. Socially, it strengthens household resilience, community cohesion, and local food systems. This integrated approach offers a replicable, scalable solution to enhance food security, nutrition, and livelihoods in vulnerable communities of Bahawalpur.

Nutrition education and knowledge A multi-dimensional strategy that combines practical skills building coupled with behavior change communication to overcome cultural barriers to healthy eating will be implemented to sustainable household nutrition enhancement. EcoLiving promotes long-term sustainability by connecting local producers to their communities, improving food system resilience, and fostering economic stability through a community-based model. core_fields.title: Kamnie Farm: Heliculture for Rural Food Systems
core_fields.description: BoldStep Initiative will establish a small snail-farming demo and training centre in rural Siaya to improve food security, incomes, and soil health. Over 15 months, it will build pens, stock breeding snails, and train at least 120 youth and women, giving 50 starter kits to launch micro farms. Households will gain affordable, high-protein food, new income from snail sales, and organic fertilizer. The project will document a toolkit for scaling heliculture across rural Kenya.
core_fields.abstract: This project will introduce smallscale snail farming (heliculture) as a simple, climate-smart way to turn local crop leftovers into nutritious food, income and organic fertilizer for rural communities in Siaya, Kenya. The main problem it tackles is protein and micronutrient deficiency in households that rely heavily on maize and cassava, combined with limited livelihood options for youth and women and degrading soils. These challenges are highly relevant as climate change makes rainfed crops less reliable and conventional livestock more expensive to keep. The innovation lies in adapting proven heliculture practices and science on snail nutrition, reproduction and housing into a lowcost package that can fit small homesteads. Snails are biologically efficient, they convert vegetable scraps, leaves and peels into high protein, low fat meat and nutrient rich manure, using little land and water. Technical insights from existing African heliculture farms and practical manuals guide stocking density, humidity control, feeding mixes and simple, hygienic processing methods, making it feasible for first-time farmers. The problem is solved through a working demo farm and living classroom that trains youth and women to build pens, manage snails, process them safely, and use the manure on vegetables. Immediate benefits include access to affordable animal-source protein, additional cash income from snail sales, and better crop yields from organic fertilizer. Over time, communities gain a diversified, climate-resilient livelihood, schools and local institutions can source healthy protein locally, and the environment benefits from reduced waste, improved soil health and more circular, regenerative food production.

core_fields.title: Producing and Conserving Rabbit Urine Liquid Fertiliser to Improve Maize Yields for Cameroonian women Farmers
core_fields.description: This project aims to produce and conserve liquid natural fertiliser from rabbit urine to improve maize yields for women farmers in Cameroon. It will train women in safe collection, processing, and application of the fertiliser, establish demonstration plots, and monitor soil health and crop performance. The project promotes low-cost, sustainable agriculture, increases food production, and strengthens women s livelihoods while protecting the environment.
core_fields.abstract: This project introduces an innovative, low-cost, and environmentally friendly solution to declining soil fertility and low maize yields faced by women farmers in Cameroon. The problem being addressed is the high cost and environmental impact of chemical fertilisers, which are often inaccessible to smallholder farmers and can degrade soil health over time. At the same time, organic waste such as rabbit urine is largely underutilized despite its high nutrient content. The innovation lies in the production and conservation of liquid fertiliser from rabbit urine, a natural source rich in nitrogen and micronutrients essential for maize growth. Scientific and agroecological knowledge shows that animal urine, when properly collected, diluted, and applied, can significantly enhance plant growth while improving soil microbial activity. This project applies that insight through simple, safe processing and storage techniques suitable for rural communities. The solution involves training women farmers to collect rabbit urine hygienically, ferment and conserve it, and apply it correctly to maize fields. Demonstration plots will showcase results and encourage adoption. Immediate benefits include improved maize growth, reduced production costs, and increased household food security. Long-term benefits include healthier soils, reduced chemical pollution, climate-friendly farming practices, women s economic empowerment, and a scalable model for sustainable agriculture that benefits communities and the environment.

core_fields.title: Expansion of an Innovative Agro-processing Solution through its brand Aifa Foods
core_fields.description: Yarashoo Agro Industry is expanding its value-added processing of locally sourced fruits and vegetables to reduce Ethiopia's high post-harvest losses and improve food security. By integrating cold-chain logistics and scaling production of dried fruits, frozen vegetables, and other nutritious products, the initiative will stabilize markets, increase farmer incomes, and create jobs for women and youth. The project strengthens sustainable supply chains while unlocking local and international market opportunities for high-quality, climate-resilient food products.
core_fields.abstract: Yarashoo Agro Industry introduces an integrated agro-processing and cold-chain innovation that directly tackles one of Ethiopia's most persistent challenges: post-harvest losses of up to 33% for fruits and vegetables. The innovation combines value-addition processing, direct farmer sourcing, and cold-chain logistics, creating a system that preserves product quality, reduces waste, and opens new markets. Yarashoo's model is built on technical insights from dehydration and food-grade processing, enabling the production of dried fruits, frozen vegetables, chili sauces, and other value-added products using dryers, freezers, packaging machinery, and quality-control equipment. Cold-chain infrastructure, including refrigerated transport and cold storage, further ensures perishable produce maintains freshness from farm to factory and into distribution channels, significantly reducing spoilage and enabling year-round supply. This is complemented by training programs that equip 200 smallholder farmers with improved post-harvest handling, storage, and quality management practices, strengthening the entire supply chain and improving farmer productivity. The solution delivers immediate benefits, including reduced waste, higher-quality food products, stable markets for farmers, and better prices. It also creates 100 jobs prioritizing women and youth, in processing, packaging, and logistics. Long-term, the innovation transforms local agricultural systems by increasing farmer incomes by 30%, enabling export-ready production, supporting food security through extended shelf life, and positioning Ethiopia as a competitive player in the global agro-processing market. Communities benefit from sustainable economic growth, enhanced skills, reduced losses, and greater access to nutritious, affordable products.

core_fields.title: Scaling Community-Owned Circular Protein Hubs Using Black Soldier Fly
core_fields.description: Entojutu operates a community-led Black Soldier Fly model that converts organic waste into affordable animal feed and organic fertilizer, improving farmer incomes while reducing waste and emissions. Entojutu has trained 6,200 farmers, processed 8,200 kg of organic waste, and achieved an average 40% reduction in feed costs across pilot communities in Nigeria, Kenya, and Uganda. This Growth Grant will enable Entojutu to scale proven community hubs, strengthen feed safety systems, and reach 5,000 more people.
core_fields.abstract: Across rural Africa, food systems face linked challenges: high livestock feed costs, unmanaged organic waste, low farmer incomes, and environmental degradation. Organic waste is commonly dumped or burned, releasing methane, while livestock producers depend on feed ingredients such as fishmeal and soy linked to overfishing and deforestation. These pressures increase food costs, emissions, and vulnerability for smallholder farmers. Entojutu responds with a decentralized, community-owned circular protein system using Black Soldier Fly (Hermetia illucens). Local women and youth collect food and agricultural waste that would otherwise go to landfills or open dumping sites. BSF larvae biologically convert this waste into high-protein animal feed and organic fertilizer, replacing a significant share of conventional feed ingredients. The solution is grounded in established entomological science: BSF larvae efficiently transform organic waste into protein using minimal land and water while reducing methane emissions from waste decomposition. By substituting fishmeal and soy-based feeds, the model reduces pressure on overharvested fisheries and lowers demand for deforestation-linked soy production. Entojutu s innovation lies in adapting this science into a community-led system designed for rural and informal contexts. Hubs are co-created with community leaders and women s groups and supported by training, feed safety standards, waste sourcing agreements, and market linkages. Immediate benefits include lower feed costs, higher farmer incomes, and new livelihoods for women and youth. Environmentally, the model diverts waste from landfills, cuts methane emissions, reduces pressure on marine and forest ecosystems, and supports regenerative, climate-positive food systems owned by local communities.

core_fields.title: AgriRisk AI: Voice-Based Climate Intelligence for Vulnerable Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: AgriRisk AI is a conversational, chatbot-style platform and an agriculture-focused extension of RiskAI that delivers real-time, localized climate and crop advisories in local languages Nepali and Maithali of Dhanusha district. Targeting low-literacy, marginalized farmers in Charnath, Janakhandi, and Sahidnagar municipalities of Dhanusha District under Welthungerhilfe's (WHH) CS4FS project, the initiative integrates multilingual AI guidance with an extension-worker-led delivery model, ensuring accurate, trusted, and widely adopted climate-smart knowledge for approximately 1,500 smallholder farmers.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Nepal face increasing climate risks, including drought, floods, and pest outbreaks that destabilize agriculture and livelihoods (FAO, 2024; Inside Story, CDKN; Koshi River Basin study). Despite national climate-smart agriculture policies, local implementation remains weak, with gaps in extension services and localized information dissemination (UNDP report). Many existing digital platforms rely on text interfaces that exclude low-literacy and marginalized farmers, especially women (Southasia Institute survey; IFPRI analysis). Existing digital agriculture platforms rely heavily on text-based interfaces and generic advisories, excluding women, older farmers, and marginalized groups who depend on voice communication and trusted intermediaries. AgriRisk AI addresses this gap through a voice-enabled, AI-driven agricultural risk intelligence platform designed for low-literacy environments. Built as an agriculture-focused extension of the existing RiskAI platform, it integrates climate and weather data, crop-soil-pest information, local farming practices, seasonal trends, and policy frameworks to generate timely, localized advisories. The innovation lies in combining multilingual voice delivery, including Maithili the primary language spoken in Dhanusha with a highly automated, simplified user experience. Integrating Maithili ensures that farmers who are low-literacy or do not read Nepali can fully understand and act on advisories, increasing trust, relevance, and adoption of climate-smart practices. Farmers receive voice alerts and advisories, while extension workers and CBOs act as trained intermediaries, further strengthening accessibility and adoption. Immediate benefits include improved access to climate-smart advisories, reduced crop losses, and increased inclusion of women and low-literacy farmers. Long-term benefits include strengthened extension systems, improved local policy integration, and more resilient, sustainable agri-food systems.

core_fields.title: Post-Harvest Drying of Fruits and Vegetables for Improved Nutrition and Farmer Incomes
core_fields.description: This project reduces post-harvest losses of fruits and vegetables by converting surplus produce into nutritious, shelf-stable dried foods through post-harvest drying. By creating a reliable market for surplus harvests, the project improves smallholder farmer incomes while increasing access to affordable, nutrient-dense foods. The approach strengthens local value chains, reduces food waste, and contributes to more resilient and sustainable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: In Western Kenya, particularly in Nyamira, Kisii, Siaya, and Migori counties, smallholder farmers face high post-harvest losses of fruits and vegetables due to short shelf life, seasonal market gluts, and limited access to affordable preservation options. Crops such as bananas, mangoes, sweet potatoes, pumpkins, pineapples and leafy vegetables often spoil within days during peak harvest periods. As a result, farmers are forced to sell at very low prices or discard produce entirely, leading to income instability and reduced availability of nutritious foods. This project addresses the problem by applying post-harvest drying to surplus fruits and vegetables sourced from smallholder farmers in these counties. Drying preserves fresh produce at peak quality and converts it into safe, shelf-stable foods that can be stored and sold over several months. This allows surplus harvests to be absorbed into a structured value chain rather than wasted. The solution builds on practical experience working with farmer groups in Western Kenya and on proven food preservation practices suited to local conditions. Drying is a low-cost, energy-efficient method that does not rely on cold storage or complex infrastructure. Through controlled drying, proper handling, and basic quality checks, the project ensures food safety and consistent product quality that meets market requirements. In the short term, farmers benefit from a reliable market for surplus produce and more stable incomes, while consumers gain access to affordable, nutrient-dense dried foods. Over time, the project contributes to reduced food waste, stronger local value chains, and more resilient food systems in Western Kenya.

core_fields.title: EquipHer Agri Transforming the Lives of Women Farmers in Bangladesh [
core_fields.description: Heifer International s EquipHer Agri project in Bangladesh addresses women's marginalization and the heavy manual labor they perform by establishing a women-led sharing economy. It enables 470 women owners to buy and rent out vital, accessible farm machinery (e.g., reducing 8-hour tasks to just 1 hour). This boosts their income, transforms them into service providers, and grants over 11,000 other women access to time-saving technology, supporting sustainable economic growth and social empowerment.
core_fields.abstract: The pervasive problem we address is the systemic exclusion of rural women from asset ownership and the crippling inefficiency of manual labor, which traps families below the Living Income Benchmark. The solution is based on the insight that time is wealth and that it accelerates change by transforming labor. This is achieved through the EquipHer Agri initiative, a highly novel women-led sharing economy in which 470 women entrepreneurs are enabled to purchase machinery through 40% co-investment from group savings. Central to this project model is the role of Women s Cooperatives and Self-Help groups. They are not only the source of co-investment funds but also provide a space to share knowledge, offer support, and build social capital and confidence. Heifer has been highly successful in achieving impact goals by focusing on these groups in projects worldwide. This model provides immediate and specific benefits, drastically reducing labor time (e.g., 8-hour chore becomes 1 hour) while securing a rental income stream for the owner. While comparable to the collective approach of the Self-Employed Women s Association (SEWA) Farm Tool Libraries in India, EquipHer is distinct in prioritizing individual ownership and entrepreneurship to maximize women's social and economic control. This ensures sustainable benefits, accelerating family income growth (from BDT 183 to BDT 454) and securing equitable access for over 11,000 women, a change amplified by Heifer s "Passing on the Gift " principle.

core_fields.title: Sustainable Production of Circular Fiber Packaging to Reduce Food Loss and Plastic Waste
core_fields.description: This project converts waste paper into durable, biodegradable molded-fiber trays for eggs, fruits, and food transport. By replacing plastic packaging and improving protection during handling and distribution, the trays reduce post-harvest food losses, lower packaging costs for farmers and retailers, and support circular, climate-smart food systems. The solution is locally manufactured, scalable, and designed to strengthen food supply chains in emerging market
core_fields.abstract: Food systems in many low- and middle-income countries experience significant losses not because food is unavailable, but because it is poorly protected during transport, storage, and distribution. Eggs, fruits, and fresh produce are especially vulnerable to breakage, bruising, and spoilage due to inadequate or expensive packaging. At the same time, plastic food trays are costly, environmentally harmful, and increasingly restricted, while large volumes of recyclable paper waste remain underutilized. This innovation addresses both challenges by transforming waste paper into molded-fiber food trays specifically designed to protect eggs, fruits, and packaged foods throughout the supply chain. The trays are engineered to absorb shock, distribute weight evenly, and allow airflow, significantly reducing damage during handling and transport. Unlike plastic alternatives, they are biodegradable, recyclable, and affordable for farmers and food distributors. The solution is enabled by proven fiber-molding technology that converts recycled paper into strong, form-fitting trays using pulping, vacuum molding, and controlled drying. Scientific insight into fiber structure and compression strength informed the tray design, ensuring durability while maintaining low material use and cost. The modular nature of the molds allows rapid adaptation for different food products and market needs. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, lower packaging costs, and improved food quality reaching consumers. Over time, the solution supports smallholder farmers, creates local manufacturing jobs, reduces plastic pollution, and strengthens circular food systems. It links waste recovery with food protection, the innovation delivers both food security and environmental impact in a scalable, sustainable way

core_fields.title: Akatale On Cloud: Circular AI Solutions for Nutritious, Regenerative, and Inclusive Food Systems
core_fields.description: Akatale On Cloud delivers a circular, AI powered solution that converts organic waste into affordable bio-fertilizers and animal feeds, provides real-time farm guidance through the Agro-Brain platform, and connects smallholder farmers to training, inputs, and reliable markets via local hubs and a Ready Market Model, improving soil health, boosting yields, reducing food waste, and increasing access to nutritious, affordable food for vulnerable communities in Africa.
core_fields.abstract: Akatale On Cloud addresses a major food system challenge in Uganda, declining soil fertility, high food losses, and limited access to affordable, nutritious food for smallholder farmers and vulnerable communities. Over 65% of farmland is degraded, fertilizer costs are rising, and up to 40% of food is lost due to weak production and market systems. These challenges reduce yields, incomes, and food availability while increasing environmental damage. Our innovation combines circular bioproduction, artificial intelligence, and inclusive market systems into one integrated solution. Organic waste is converted into climate smart bio-fertilizers and nutritious animal feeds, restoring soil health and reducing pollution. The Agro-Brain platform analyzes soil, crop, and weather data to provide real time, practical guidance that helps farmers use inputs efficiently and increase productivity. Akatale Hubs deliver training and local access to inputs, while the Ready Market Model connects farmers to reliable buyers, reducing losses and improving incomes. Our solution is based on proven scientific data insights, regenerating soils with organic amendments improves nutrient use efficiency, water retention, and yields, while data driven advisory reduces fertilizer misuse and risk. By linking production, knowledge, and markets, Akatale creates immediate benefits such as higher yields, lower input costs, and better market prices for farmers. Sustainably, it improves soil health, reduces waste and emissions, strengthens local food supply, and expands access to affordable, nutritious food for communities, contributing to a resilient and equitable food system.

core_fields.title: Bioleft: Scaling Open-Source Agroecological Tomato Value Chains
core_fields.description: This project scales existing farmer-led, agroecological tomato breeding into a sustainable food value chain. Building on Bioleft s open-source tomato varieties, we will ensure seed availability through decentralized multiplication, support a network of tomato producers, and create value-added products such as pur e and dehydrated tomatoes. With the Bioleft platform and product label, quality assurance, and direct links with consumers and chefs, the project strengthens farmer incomes, food trust, and biodiversity while offering healthier, locally produced foods.
core_fields.abstract: Most tomato cultivars available today are hybrids bred primarily for yield. As a result, farmers must buy expensive seeds every year and rely on agrochemicals to achieve yields high enough to recover those costs. Bioleft has been addressing this challenge by developing open-pollinated, open-source tomato varieties selected for flavor and suitability for low-input agroecological farming. To date, Bioleft has developed three such varieties. However, farmers growing Bioleft varieties operate in markets that prioritize uniformity and shelf life leaving them with limited commercial opportunities. At the same time, consumers increasingly seek sustainably produced food but remain disconnected from how crops are developed. This project addresses that problem by integrating our existing participatory plant breeding and open-source seed licensing activities, with food commercialization into a coherent model. We will extend Bioleft s digital seed catalogue to include a new section for value-added tomato products, enabling producers to sell pur e and dehydrated tomatoes directly through the platform. These products will be dentified with a new Bioleft label, which provides information on the seed variety, seed breeders, agroecological producer, and food processer, , ensuring traceability from open-source seed to sustainable food The project helps farmers and breeder-farmers to earn a living from open, just, and sustainable agricultural innovations, while offering consumers nutritious, traceable food. The idea is entirely novel in South America (one similar initiative exists in Berlin, selling bread made with open-source wheat). Our proposal for an integrated value chain is grounded in scientific evidence and field experience, delivering resilient seeds and fairer incomes.
