core_fields.title: Integrated Agroecology Innovation for Sustainable, Healthy Livelihoods and Regenerative Food Systems
core_fields.description: TAFIKA Horticultural Enterprise and Services delivers an integrated agroecology innovation that improves nutrition, restores ecosystems, and strengthens livelihoods for smallholder farmers in Malawi. The project combines grafted, early-maturing fruit trees for agroforestry practice, biochar-enriched organic fertilizer, livestock pass-on programs, and low-cost solar drying in order to increase access to nutritious food, reduce post-harvest losses, regenerate soils, and build equitable, climate-resilient food systems.
core_fields.abstract: TAFIKA Horticultural Enterprise and Services addresses interconnected challenges faced by smallholder farmers in Malawi, including poor soil fertility, limited access to nutritious foods, high post-harvest losses, and low, climate-vulnerable incomes. These challenges reduce food availability, affordability, and diet quality, while contributing to land degradation and environmental stress. The problem is highly relevant in Malawi, where agriculture underpins livelihoods and nutrition for most rural households. The innovation is an integrated agroecology model that combines four mutually reinforcing solutions. First, we produce and supply grafted, early-maturing fruit tree seedlings for agroforestry systems, enabling farmers to access nutritious fruits and income sooner while improving biodiversity and microclimates. Secondly, we produce biochar-enriched organic fertilizer using agricultural residues, which restores soil organic matter, improves water retention, and reduces dependence on chemical fertilizers. Thirdly, livestock pass-on programs increase access to animal-source protein while supplying manure for organic fertilizer production. Finally, we train communities to build and use low-cost solar dryers from locally available materials to preserve fruits and indigenous vegetables, and this helps to reduce food loss and enables availability of value-added products such as dried mango, tomatoes, indigenous leafy vegetables and edible mushrooms. This solution is informed by scientific evidence on agroforestry, soil carbon management, circular nutrient systems, and solar drying for food preservation. Immediate benefits include increased food availability, improved diets, reduced post-harvest losses, and higher household incomes. Sustainable benefits include healthier soils, lower emissions, enhanced climate resilience, and equitable, regenerative food systems that benefit farmers, consumers, communities, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Soil First: Turning Coastal Biomass into Farm Resilience
core_fields.description: This project delivers an 18-month, multi-farm demonstration in Barbados to validate Red Diamond Compost s locally produced biostimulants derived from sargassum and other biomass. Seed Grant funds will support field deployment, monitoring, and independent testing to generate a clear evidence base and standardized application protocols, enabling rapid adoption and replication across small-island and climate-vulnerable farming systems.
core_fields.abstract: Small-island food systems face degraded soils, rising input costs, and heavy dependence on imported fertilizers, while simultaneously managing increasing volumes of organic waste such as sargassum seaweed. These pressures reduce farm profitability, weaken local food supply, and increase climate vulnerability. Red Diamond Compost addresses this challenge by converting locally available biomass, especially sargassum and nutrient-dense tropical plants, into biologically active biostimulants that support soil function, nutrient-use efficiency, and crop performance under stress. Unlike imported inputs, these products are designed for local conditions, local economics, and farmer usability. The proposed Seed Grant project focuses on field validation and demonstration, not product invention. We will implement standardized applications across 3 5 farms, paired with baseline, midline, and endline soil and crop assessments. Independent laboratory testing and structured field observations will translate biological signals into outcomes that farmers and stakeholders can trust. Project execution and learning will be supported by Red Diamond s internal Diamond Matrix (DMX) system, which documents inputs, application protocols, observations, and results across sites. DMX ensures consistency, disciplined learning, and replicability without adding operational burden for farmers. By integrating local waste conversion, on-farm validation, and standardized deployment, this project delivers a practical pathway for regenerative adoption in food-import-dependent regions.

core_fields.title: Turning Food Waste into Nutrition and Regenerative Livelihoods
core_fields.description: We work to reduce food that would otherwise go to waste by operating a community agro-processing hub that converts surplus produce into nutritious foods, including RUTF. The organization trains youth and farmers in agro-processing and offers shared, pay-as-you-use processing space that enables micro-entrepreneurship. By turning food loss into nutrition, income, and soil regeneration, the project strengthens food security, livelihoods, and resilience in vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: we address the growing contradiction in food systems where hunger&malnutrition coexist with large-scale food waste. Climate change is disrupting growing seasons, increasing crop gluts in some periods and shortages in others. In Kenya, one in every four children suffers from malnutrition, yet up to 40% of horticultural produce is lost post-harvest due to limited processing capacity&poor coordination. The value of wasted food is equivalent to what is needed to feed starving populations. The innovation combines community agro-processing hub with simple digital coordination to recover surplus and near-end-life produce and convert it into nutritious foods, including dried products and Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF). Youth and smallholder farmers are trained in agro-processing and access shared processing facilities through a pay-as-you-use model, enabling micro-entrepreneurship without high capital barriers. Our WhatsApp-based chatbot helps aggregates surplus produce from farmers, coordinates processing schedules, shares basic quality guidance, and connects processors to buyers and humanitarian partners. This low-cost technology improves efficiency, reduces spoilage, and works effectively in low-connectivity contexts. The solution is informed by the insight that food waste, nutrition, and livelihoods must be addressed together. Processing stabilizes food supply across seasons, while circular use of unsalvageable produce as organic fertilizer restores soils. To date, the model engages 18,743 smallholder farmers, trains 831 women and youth annually, reduces 1,092 tons of food waste per year, reaches 250,000 families, supports 1,881 mothers with therapeutic food, and increases farmer incomes by 60 80%. Immediate benefits include improved nutrition$ income s. longterm include resilient food systems, reduced emissions, and restored farmlands

core_fields.title: Waste into Wealth: Regenerative Granulated Organic Fertilizer for Pest Control and Africa s Sustainable Food Future
core_fields.description: BIO PLANET TMC is scaling Africa s first pest-control granulated organic fertilizer, produced from recycled biodegradable waste to regenerate degraded soils in agriculture, boost crop healthier yields by up to 45%, combat hunger, minimize post-harvest losses and reduce pest attacks by 65%. By expanding access for women and indigenous farmers across Benin and West Africa, we aim to restore over 500,000 hectares of degraded farmland by 2030, advancing food security, climate resilience, and sustainable rural livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: Across Benin and West Africa, millions of smallholder farmers, mainly indigenous women growers face declining soil fertility, pest pressures, and reduced yields due to dependence on chemical inputs, and climate stress. Smallholders, who produce up to 90% of the region s food, are trapped in a cycle of low productivity and poverty. The lack of quality and affordable organic alternatives has left over 200 million farmers vulnerable, while 30 million children remain at risk of malnutrition and hunger, according to UNICEF. We have developed a certified pest-control organic fertilizer in granulated form from biodegradable waste that regenerates soil while protecting crops naturally. The granules blend pest-repelling plant extracts, beneficial microorganisms, and nutrient-rich organic matter into one regenerative product, replacing synthetic fertilizers while restoring soil biodiversity, and productivity. Grounded in proven scientific insights from soil microbiology and ecological pest management, validated through laboratory analyses and farmer field trials, our innovation harnesses the synergy between organic carbon, beneficial microbes, and bioactive compounds to strengthen plant immunity and enhance natural pest resistance. To date, over 130 tons have been supplied to 1,500 farmers, paired with sustainable farming training, regenerating 1,200 hectares of degraded farmland. Farmers have reported yield increases of up to 45%, pest reductions of up to 65%, and income growth averaging 35%, improving food security and air quality for 150,000 people in Benin. By 2030, BIO PLANET TMC aims to reach 10 million people with cleaner air and healthier food and help 5 million children escape malnutrition across West Africa.

Rooted in indigenous practices, it offers a sustainable, locally adapted solution for resilient food systems. Problem and Relevance: District Charsadda poor women farmers face multiple problems of food insecurity with declining soil fertility due to dependence on chemical fertilizers, pest attacks, heavy pre- and post-harvest losses from hailstorms, excessive floods, lack of awareness, extreme cold weather, linked with climate change. Solution and Approach: FRD s model integrating nature-based solutions with tunnel farming utilizing bamboo structure, uses organic rice straws to improve soil health and moisture, and introduces jute rope netting for vertical vegetable growing. Anti-insect nets protect crops from pest attacks naturally, reducing dependence on chemical pesticides. These nature-based solutions create a protected, low-cost, and organic farming system that increases productivity and resilience to climate stress. Scientific and Technical Insight: The model applies simple principles of regenerative agriculture and natural balance by using organic materials to restore soil, conserve water, and manage pests without chemicals and environmentally friendly. Immediate and Sustainable Benefits: Farmers can grow more vegetables on small plots, spend less on input, and face fewer crop losses. It also reduces carbon emissions by over 50% through renewable energy and minimized waste. Immediate benefits include higher incomes, improved market access, and reduced post-harvest losses. Sustainable benefits extend to enhanced food security, climate resilience, and ecosystem protection. By integrating renewable energy, shared logistics, and data-driven insights, GreenBox creates a scalable, climate-smart solution that empowers communities, strengthens local economies, and contributes to a sustainable, equitable food system.

Immediate benefits Rapid establishment of productive plots, increased fresh vegetable supply, reduced household water use, and short income generation cycles for youth. core_fields.title: Eggs for Life: Women-Led Regenerative Agriculture for Climate-Resilient Livelihoods in Kenya s Drylands
core_fields.description: Driving food system transformation in Kenya s drylands, Eggs for Life utilizes the innovative WYETU Model to empower women to integrate regenerative poultry and horticulture enterprises, creating a circular economy producing eggs, sunflower oil, and vegetables year-round. This holistic approach restores soil biodiversity, enhances community nutrition, fosters climate resilience, and promotes inclusive markets, ensuring access to affordable, healthy diets for vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: Eggs for Life targets the critical nexus of malnutrition, youth unemployment, and environmental degradation in Kenya s arid and semi-arid lands. Specifically, we address the 35% of women and young mothers (18 34) who are unemployed and disconnected from sustainable agriculture. The Solution: We utilize a circular poultry horticulture system anchored in the government-recognized Community Unit Model. leveraging existing social structures for rapid adoption and product aggregation. We empower women to formulate affordable feed using drought-resistant crops (sunflower, sorghum, cowpeas) and agricultural by-products, processed via solar-powered systems and oil pressing systems. Poultry manure fertilizes the soil, while crop residues feed the birds, effectively closing the nutrient loop. Scientific Insight: The innovation is built on scientific principles of soil crop livestock integration and nutrient cycling. Validated through participatory research with university partners, our MSc-level field data confirmed that localized, regenerative feed formulations significantly lower input costs while maintaining high egg productivity and soil health. Benefits: Immediate: Farmers will see a 25% reduction in production costs and new income streams from eggs, sunflower oil, and vegetables amplified by collective marketing efforts. Households gain access to affordable, nutritious food ("an egg a day"). Sustainable: Regenerative practices like legume intercropping and mulching restore soil fertility and water retention. The model reduces food waste and builds a climate-resilient, low-carbon, youth-led local food system.

core_fields.title: Balancing food security and nutrition under climate change for smallholder farmers in Uganda (YAMS-NUTS-TREES)
core_fields.description: Accelerated tree planting and management is achieved where food is accrued especially for smallholder farmers (SHF) who own very small spaces for food production. SHF make up to 70% of the food producers in Uganda. Yams (Dioscorea species) and Oyster nuts (Telfairia pedate) are shade tolerant crops and require trees to optimally yield, and could stimulate tree management on farm. YAMS-NUTS-TREES will support SHF to optimise space by concurrently growing quality yams, nuts and trees.
core_fields.abstract: Food insecurity and malnutrition in Uganda remain high, where an estimated 4-5 million people are vulnerable, especially in the North and Eastern, including refugee hosting areas (FAO, 2024). This is exacerbated by the reduced land for farming and climate change, where increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events have threatened sustainable food production especially among smallholder farmers who mostly depend on rain-fed agriculture. Agroforestry-the mixing of trees with crops and animals has been viewed as a space-sensible, nature-based, low cost solution. Agroforestry has been promoted as a green strategy for working towards better food security, climate change adaptation and mitigation, and livelihood resilience in the country. Accelerated tree planting and management is optimised where food is accrued from the trees, especially for smallholder farmers who own very small spaces for production. The nutritious yams (wild; yellow and aerial [Dioscorea spp), and Oyster nuts (Telfairia pedate) are shade tolerant food crops and require trees to optimally yield, and could be an affordable driver to tree management. They are hardy, easy-to-grow crops, and able to thrive under extreme climates. These yams and nuts are not popular due to limited knowledge and germplasm. YAMS-NUTS-TREES project will characterize, select, multiply, promote and distribute quality yam and nut, along with tree germplasm for enhanced planting in agroforestry, which will promote tree planting. Using participatory innovative approaches, especially involving women, youth in refugee areas, the project will design value-addition activities for the yams, nuts and trees to reduce food loss and improve system profitability.

core_fields.title: A Low-Cost Soil Testing and Advisory Service for Smallholder Farmers in Rwanda.
core_fields.description: SOILSENSE Ltd provides affordable, on-site soil testing and clear, practical recommendations to help Rwanda s smallholder farmers start making informed fertilizer decisions. Using trained youth agents and portable testing kits, we test soils, making the service accessible to farmers who can t reach traditional labs. Our goal: help farmers improve yields, save money, and protect their soil. We are currently piloting the service and seeking support to refine our model and build a basic digital advisory platform.
core_fields.abstract: SOILSENSE introduces an affordable, field-based soil testing and advisory service designed specifically for Rwanda s smallholder farmers. The core problem we address is that most farmers apply fertilizers without knowing what their soils actually needs. This leads to environmental degradation and financial losses. Existing soil testing services are far away, expensive, or deliver results farmers cannot interpret making them inaccessible to rural communities. Our innovation solves this by bringing soil intelligence directly to the farm. Trained youth agents use portable testing kits to analyze key soil parameters including pH, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and organic matter. Results are then translated and simple, conservation, practical recommendations that farmers can easily understand and implement are provided. The solution is grounded in insights from conservation agriculture and the increasing availability of reliable, low-cost field diagnostic tools. These tools allow us to provide timely soil data without the need for expensive laboratory infrastructure. Combining scientific testing with personalized advisory creates a service that is both technically sound and farmer friendly. Immediate benefits include improved fertilizer efficiency, reduced input costs, and better crop performance. Farmers can avoid overuse of fertilizers while ensuring their crops receive exactly what they need. Sustainable long-term benefits include healthier soils, increased food production, improved household incomes, and climate-resilient farming practices. By training youth especially women to deliver the service, SOILSENSE also creates rural employment and strengthens community-based extension networks. This innovation supports farmers, communities, and the environment while building a more sustainable and data-driven agriculture sector.

core_fields.title: Kubikira munhu wese kwakachena,
core_fields.description: The project seeks to scale up our business activities by selling approximately 2400 biodigesters, which would total over 6000 clean cooking services between 2023 and 202
core_fields.abstract: Energy poverty has been a major challenge in Zimbabwe with more 70 % of the population living in rural areas without access to clean energy. The rural populace depends mostly on fossil fuels in the form of firewood, charcoal, and other crop residues for cooking. The burning of fossil fuels emits GHG gases into the atmosphere which causes global warming and climate change at large. Using fossil fuels further causes massive deforestation at the same time exposes the end users to serious health risks due to indoor pollution from the burning of fossil fuels. Despite the majority being off the grid, those who are connected to the national electricity grid are continuously disrupted by load shedding which has a bearing effect on production and operations. We install both fixed dome and portable biodigesters converting organic waste into biogas, a clean and renewable fuel source which can be used for cooking, heating, cooling and even generating electricity. They also come with an agricultural solution in the form of organic fertilizer rich in nutrients thereby enhancing agricultural yields whilst at the same time cutting down costs for chemical fertilizers. We help communities and institutions transition from traditional energy sources to cleaner and more sustainable alternatives. Our technology promotes waste management and provides a readily available fuel source for cooking, heating, cooling or even lighting. We help farmers minimise food loss along the value chain through biogas powered freezers. With access to cooling farmers are guaranteed minimum post-harvest losses.

core_fields.title: Production of Ready-to-Use Food from Edible Seeds, Cereals, and Legume Grains.
core_fields.description: This project encompasses the full cycle of food crops including edible seeds such as pumpkin and sunflower, along with cereals like maize, and legume crops such as soybeans utilization: food crops growing (cultivation and harvest), food crops milling (processing the grains into flour or meal), and creating ready-to-use food (formulating the milled product into easily consumed, often fortified, food items). The goal is a vertically integrated process from farm to consumer for nutrition or market.
core_fields.abstract: The use of maize, soybeans, pumpkin seeds, and sunflower seeds as fundamental food crops for the project addresses food insecurity, malnutrition, and limited economic opportunities in agricultural areas. The project is relevant because it tackles the lack of a reliable, high-quality, and nutritious food source derived from staple crops. By integrating growing, processing, and food formulation, it ensures nutritional value is preserved and creates a stable market for farmers. The problem is solved through vertical integration (farm-to-table approach). Growing: Promoting improved varieties and sustainable farming practices. Milling: Using modern, efficient, and hygienic milling techniques to produce high-quality flour. Ready-To-Use Food (RTUF): Formulating the milled food crops into fortified, easily-prepared, and often shelf-stable food products (e.g., specialised porridge, complementary foods). The novelty lies in project context-specific design, focusing on local varieties, adding nutrients for local shortages, and building a sustainable, locally owned value chain to minimise post-harvest loss. Similar solutions exist globally, primarily as commercial food processing plants or government/NGO food aid programs. The solution is driven by scientific insight into local nutritional needs/gaps for the targeted population. Technical insight uses small-scale milling and food science for safe, appealing, and ready-to-use products. Economic/social insight creates local employment and a stable procurement market for farmers, ensuring project sustainability. Consumers immediately gain nutritious, ready-to-use food and reduced malnutrition. Farmers secure a guaranteed market and stable income for sustainable practices. Schools get reliable feed sources, and producers create local jobs. Society benefits from a stronger local economy and lower environmental impact.

core_fields.title: Nutrition For All
core_fields.description: Nutrishell Eco-Cycle turns discarded eggshells into safe, affordable calcium powder to fight malnutrition and reduce waste. The project improves community health by providing low-cost nutrition for families, children, and the elderly while creating local jobs. By transforming waste into a valuable resource, Nutrishell promotes environmental sustainability, economic empowerment, and better nutrition helping build healthier, cleaner, and more resilient communities across Kenya and beyond
core_fields.abstract: Nutrishell Eco-Cycle is an innovation that turns waste eggshells into a safe, affordable, and eco-friendly calcium powder. The main problem it solves is calcium deficiency and food waste. Every year, tons of eggshells are thrown away, polluting the environment, while millions of people especially children and the elderly lack enough calcium in their diet due to the high cost of supplements. This issue affects health, food security, and the environment. Nutrishell solves this by collecting used eggshells, sterilizing them through heat treatment to kill bacteria, and grinding them into a fine, tasteless powder that can be added to common foods like porridge or smoothies. The process follows food safety standards set by the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) and uses simple but effective scientific methods based on the fact that eggshells are 95% calcium carbonate, a natural and safe mineral for human consumption. The benefits are immediate and long-term. Consumers get an affordable, nutritious product that improves bone health and prevents diseases like osteoporosis. Farmers and waste collectors gain income through the eggshell collection chain. Schools and hospitals can include the powder in feeding programs to improve nutrition. Environmentally, the project reduces waste and promotes a circular economy where nothing goes unused. Overall, Nutrishell Eco-Cycle is a sustainable innovation that combines science, community action, and environmental care to improve health, create jobs, and build a cleaner, more self-reliant society.

core_fields.title: SOLAR CARGO QUEENS: Women-Led Green Mobility to Reduce Post-Harvest Food Loss
core_fields.description: SOLAR CARGO QUEENS is a women-led project in rural C te d Ivoire that aims to tackle post-harvest food loss caused by poor mobility. Our ambition is to establish a solar charging hub and operate electric cargo bicycles to help women farmers move produce quickly from farms to markets, reducing spoilage, increasing incomes, and cutting emissions through clean, reliable rural logistics.
core_fields.abstract: In many rural communities in C te d Ivoire, food is lost not because farmers fail to grow it, but because they cannot move it in time. Smallholder farmers most being women harvest produce in scattered plots, often far from roads or markets. Transport is expensive, unreliable, and physically demanding. As a result, crops spoil, incomes shrink, and families remain trapped in a cycle of low returns and food insecurity. This problem is both economic and environmental: wasted food also means wasted labor, energy, and emissions. Solar Cargo Queens tackles this gap at its source rural mobility. We introduce a women-led, solar-powered transport service built for off-grid villages and entrusted to a local farmers cooperative for management. Each station combines a simple solar charging hub with electric-cargo bicycles operated by trained local women. These riders collect produce directly from farms and move it quickly to aggregation points or weekly markets, cutting hours sometimes days out of the journey from harvest to sale. What makes this approach new is not the bike alone, but the system around it. Cargo bikes exist, but they are rarely adapted for rural African terrain, off-grid energy, or cooperative use by women farmers. This solution grew from years of field experience in post-harvest loss and from recent advances in solar affordability that now make clean rural transport viable. The impact is immediate: less spoilage, lighter workloads, and higher incomes for women farmers. Over time, communities gain more reliable food supply, reduced fuel use, and a practical, replicable model for climate-smart rural logistics.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Dehydration and Nutrition Value Addition to Reduce Food Losses for Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: This project scales clean-energy Dehydration-as-a-Service and nutrition value addition to reduce food losses, improve food safety, and strengthen climate resilience for smallholder farmers. BioAfriq Energy s hybrid solar-biomass hubs deliver affordable, all-weather dehydration and food-safety testing for drought-resilient crops. Farmers then access a guaranteed market pathway through Taliana, BioAfriq s nutrition division, which purchases dried crops and processes them into nutritious flour blends. The model increases incomes, regenerates soils, and expands access to safe, nutritious foods.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers growing drought-resilient crops such as cassava, sorghum, and pearl millet lose up to 60% of their harvest due to slow, weather-dependent sun drying that exposes food to moisture, pests, dust, and microbial contamination. This leads to high levels of mold, yeast, and aflatoxins, limiting market access, reducing incomes, and posing serious public-health risks. Communities also lack affordable, nutritious foods processed under safe conditions. BioAfriq Energy solves these challenges through a clean-energy, climate-smart innovation: patented hybrid solar-biomass dehydrators equipped with IoT temperature and humidity control. These systems enable fast, uniform, all-weather dehydration using solar energy and recycled agricultural biomass. Each Dehydration Hub provides affordable Dehydration-as-a-Service at USD 0.20/kg and onsite food-safety testing for moisture, mold, yeast, and aflatoxins. This eliminates contamination risks and extends shelf-life, significantly reducing food losses. The scientific insight driving this solution is that the timeliness and control of drying not just the crop variety determine food safety. Controlled dehydration prevents microbial growth, avoids aflatoxin formation, and protects nutritional quality while enabling climate-resilient crops to reach their full market potential. Once dried, farmers access a guaranteed market pathway through Taliana, BioAfriq s nutrition division, which purchases the safely dried crops and processes them into nutritious flour blends sold in retail and bulk formats. This provides stable demand, improved income, and safe, affordable, nutritious foods for consumers. Sustainably, the system regenerates soils through biomass-to-ash recycling, lowers emissions, prevents methane from spoilage, creates rural jobs, and strengthens climate resilience for smallholder communities.

core_fields.title: Biodegradable Nanotechnology Solution for Fruit and Vegetable Preservation to Empower Smallholder Farmers in Africa.
core_fields.description: Freza Nanotech makes biodegradable sachets, bags, and stickers using nanotechnology to keep fruits and vegetables fresh for 14 to 30 days, cutting spoilage by 80%. We work with smallholder farmers, most of whom are women, across Uganda and plan to expand to Kenya, Zimbabwe, and the UAE. We have supported over 90 vendors and 300 farmers, and have received $181,000 in grants and awards. Each sachet costs just $0.15 and helps prevent methane emissions.
core_fields.abstract: More than 40% of fruits and vegetables in sub-Saharan Africa are lost before reaching consumers, leading to food insecurity for over 146 million people, worsening farmer poverty, and contributing to 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions as methane from decomposing produce. Smallholder farmers, especially in West Nile, Uganda, often lose 30-50% of their harvest due to a lack of affordable preservation, forcing them to sell at reduced prices. Freza's patent-pending biodegradable sachets, coated bags, and stickers use electrospinning nanotechnology to protect fruit membranes, slowing decay and extending shelf life by 14-30 days with or without refrigeration or chemicals. This innovation addresses spoilage at the molecular level, offering a safer alternative to banned chemical preservatives or expensive cold storage. Immediate benefits include over 30% income increases for farmers, economic empowerment for women, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, improved nutrition, and new export opportunities, as shown in a UAE supermarket experimental pilot. At $0.15 per sachet with 60% profit margins, Freza solution is commercially viable and accessible, making advanced preservation possible for rural farmers while combating food insecurity and environmental harm across the region.

core_fields.title: Seed to Post harvest: Climate-Smart Vegetable Systems for Healthy, Affordable Food
core_fields.description: Seed to Post harvest is an end-to-end, climate-smart vegetable production and post-harvest system that improves farmer productivity, reduces food loss, and delivers safe, nutritious vegetables to consumers. By combining tested seedlings, regenerative farming practices, efficient irrigation, farmer training, tool access, and cold storage, the project strengthens the entire vegetable value chain while improving incomes, reducing chemical misuse, and making healthy food more affordable and trusted.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder vegetable farmers face declining yields, high input costs, excessive chemical use, and post-harvest losses of up to 50%. These challenges limit farmer income, increase food waste, and reduce access to safe, nutritious vegetables for consumers. The problem is especially relevant as climate stress, soil degradation, and food price volatility threaten local food systems. Our innovation solves this by integrating the full vegetable value chain from seed selection to post-harvest into one practical, scalable system. Farmers begin with high-quality, resilient seedlings that have been tested on our model farm for pest and disease tolerance. We then support them with proper farm setup, efficient irrigation systems, and regenerative production practices that reduce chemical application while maintaining strong yields. Farmers also access rented tools, technical consulting, and hands-on training, lowering production barriers and improving consistency. To address food loss and affordability, the project integrates a solar-powered cold storage facility that extends shelf life, preserves nutritional quality, and allows farmers to sell at better prices instead of distress sales. Vegetables are sold to health-conscious households, schools, and businesses that value food safety and traceability. This solution is informed by agronomic trials, climate-smart agriculture principles, and on-farm experience showing that strong seedlings, efficient water use, and reduced chemical dependence significantly improve outcomes. Immediate benefits include higher yields, reduced waste, safer food, and increased farmer income. Long-term benefits include healthier soils, lower emissions, resilient food systems, and more equitable access to affordable, nutritious vegetables for communities.

core_fields.title: Integrated livelihoods and conservation enhancement project (Ukulima bora Mazingira bora project)
core_fields.description: Ukulima bora Mazimgira project is an livelihoods and conservation solution, targeting to transform the socio- economic standards of 500 youth and women indegineous farmers within the Chyulu and Tsavo border areas, through supporting adoption of integrated technologies in apiculture , SME irrigation, dryland aquaculture and organic waste management practices. The project will establish integrated, nature positive practices involving RAS Aquaculture, honey production, value addition, fruit aggregation and processing of local fertilizers from organic waste matter.
core_fields.abstract: Chyulu Development Foundation has existed within the targeted communities, supporting locally led and collaborative conservation efforts. Although these efforts have brought immense success in terms of mindset change and increasing green cover, the communities have bee found to undergo rapid shifts from the original condition of depending on natural forests and poaching as their prime source of livelihood. The speedy transition has left households grappling with means to find alternative survival means, worsened by the climate crisis, policy shifts and leading to instances of hunger, mulnourishment and diminishing community dietary quality . In order to address these extremes, our team of experts undertook a baseline research(2023), to come up with alternative ways of locally-led solutions to the challenges of poor feeding and low climate resilience adaptation, which threatens to push the communities back to deforestation, poaching and worsen the already imbalanced dietaries. The research activity identified sustainable apiculture, dryland aquaculture, crop/ fruit farming and sustainable waste management as the most potential means to supporting the indegineous communities that are yet to recover from the just ended human- wlidlife conflict and socio- economic marginalization. The research also found farmers with untapped potential in their abilities to produce and earn from their shallow wells, which are common assets within the targeted ecosystem area. Designed from the basis of baseline reports and stakeholders inclusion, the proposed project will introduce 500 farmers who own and use shallow wells, into RAS aquculture model of farming for Tilapia and Mudfish production, and support fish consumption locally.

core_fields.title: Clean Seed, Healthy Harvests: Scaling Virus-Free Potato Production for Improved Nutrition in Zimbabwe
core_fields.description: The project aims to enhance virus-free seed potato production using an aeroponics system. Building on existing institutional capacity, it employs a three-stage approach: (i) tissue culture for clean plantlet generation, (ii) aeroponics for rapid multiplication of mini-tubers, and (iii) regenerative field cultivation. The certified seed potatoes will be distributed to farmers in rehabilitated irrigation schemes for large-scale production and improved yield quality.
core_fields.abstract: The objective of this innovation is to establish an integrated three-stage system for virus-free seed potato production combining tissue culture, aeroponics, and regenerative agriculture. This approach enhances productivity, sustainability, and resilience within Zimbabwe s potato value chain.In the first stage, tissue culture techniques are employed to generate pathogen-free plantlets from elite potato varieties. Through meristem culture and in-vitro propagation, the system enables the mass multiplication of genetically uniform, disease-free stock, ensuring high-quality planting material and reducing reliance on imported seed.The second stage utilizes the aeroponics system, where plantlets are grown in a controlled, soilless environment with nutrients delivered directly to the roots as a fine mist. This method enhances nutrient uptake efficiency, reduces water use by up to 90%, and eliminates soil-borne diseases. The result is the rapid and cost-effective production of high-quality mini-tubers with minimal environmental impact, exemplifying precision agriculture.The third stage, based on regenerative agriculture principles, involves the field multiplication of mini-tubers under practices that rebuild soil organic matter, enhance microbial activity, and promote biodiversity. This ensures long-term soil fertility and ecosystem health, enabling sustainable production cycles. Collectively, this innovation improves seed quality, increases potato yields, and reduces production costs. Farmers benefit through higher profitability and resilience, while consumers gain access to affordable, nutrient-rich potatoes. Environmentally, the system minimizes chemical inputs, optimizes resource use, and supports climate-smart agriculture positioning it as a scalable model for sustainable food systems in Zimbabwe.

core_fields.title: Our Food-Climate-Smart School & Community Nutrition Ecosystems for Amajuba Youths

The project combines school food gardens, community nutrition hubs, and youth-led food entrepreneurship to reduce hunger, strengthen local food systems, and build climate resilience. By empowering women and youth with nutrition and agro-innovation skills, it creates sustainable, equitable food environments that support healthier learning and thriving communities.
core_fields.abstract: Across the Amajuba District, about 70 percent of many children and families in rural areas and poor urban face food insecurity, poor nutrition, and limited access to affordable, safe, nutritious foods. Low agricultural productivity and learning barriers is largely contributing to hunger. Our Food addresses this by creating a climate-smart, community-driven nutrition ecosystem that improves both food access and long-term resilience. The innovation combines three proven solutions into one integrated model: Climate-Smart School Food Gardens: indigenous local crops, and water-harvesting systems, schools produce fresh vegetables year-round, despite climate shocks. Community Nutrition Hubs: Women and youth process garden produce into nutritious, low-cost foods (soups, dried vegetables, fortified snacks) while receiving training in food safety, nutrition, and entrepreneurship. Nutrition Education & Digital Monitoring: Learners use simple digital tools to track plant growth and learn nutrition science, food safety, and climate resilience. This solution is grounded in insights from nutrition science (the importance of consistent access to micronutrients), climate-smart agriculture research, and evidence showing that community-led food systems improve both health and local economies. Immediate benefits include more nutritious meals in schools, reduced hunger, lower food costs, and improved child learning and wellbeing. Sustainable benefits include climate-resilient food production, income opportunities for women and youth, stronger local food markets, and reduced environmental impact through regenerative practices and reduced food waste. core_fields.title: Strengthening Food Security and Nutrition Through Scalable Climate-Smart Agri-Intelligence.
core_fields.description: Bakhabar Kissan's project scales a Climate-Smart Food Security and Nutrition Intelligence Platform integrating digital advisories, GIS crop analytics, agri-centers, and financial inclusion. Proven with 1,500 farmers in Sargodha achieving 20 to 25% rice yield gains, the project will expand to 20,000 farmers within 24 months through enhanced profiling, refined GIS, improved data quality, and platform upgrades. The scalable model advances safe nutrition, regenerative agriculture, and equitable access to trusted food systems across Pakistan.
core_fields.abstract: Bakhabar Kissan (BKK) presents a Climate-Smart Food Security and Nutrition Intelligence Platform, combining digital advisory, GIS crop analytics, agri-centers, verified input supply chains, and financial inclusion. This phygital agriculture ecosystem tackles key issues in Pakistan, such as low dietary diversity, unsafe inputs, soil degradation, food loss, and climate shocks. National assessments highlight fragmented data, weak extension systems, and limited traceability as significant barriers to a resilient, nutrition-secure food system. BKK started with providing timely, actionable knowledge delivered through SMS, IVR, and call centers, overcoming literacy and smartphone barriers. BKK expanded into GIS mapping, crop intelligence, soil analysis, and climate alerts, establishing agri-centers for support and market linkages. This trust allowed for piloting credit, insurance, and digital wallets, aligning the value chain. Currently, 1.7 million farmers use BKK services. AI/ML models for crop identification, stress detection, nutrient planning, and climate-risk alerts, combined with GPS digitization and soil analytics, enhance precision regenerative agriculture. Immediate benefits include higher yields, safer inputs, and reduced losses, while long-term advantages are healthier soils, resilient incomes, and stronger markets. In Sargodha, of approximately 300,000 8-acre farmers, 1,500 end-to-end users report rice yield increases of 20 to 25%. Collectively, this translates into PKR 360-420 million in additional annual profit across the current 1,500 farmers. Scaling this proven model to 20,000 farmers through enhanced profiling, refined GIS capabilities, improved data quality, and upgraded BKK platforms under the Growth Grant unlocks PKR 4.8-5.6 billion annually, positioning Sargodha as a demonstration for scalable national food system innovation, nutrition, sustainability, and equity.

core_fields.title: A water Kiosk at School - Integrated Aquaponics
core_fields.description: In drought prone Ildamat ward, Kajiado county, Kenya, we're piloting an integrated aquaponics system within our proven Water Kiosk at School model. At ACK Oloosuyian Education Centre, this student-led initiative will provide clean water, fresh food, and income to support school meals and infrastructure. Serving 345 students and 10,500 community members who walk 14+ km for unsafe water, the project addresses water insecurity, malnutrition, gender inequality, and school absenteeism through a sustainable, community driven solution.
core_fields.abstract: The ACK Oloosuyian Education Centre and surrounding Ildamat ward in Kajiado County, Kenya, face a critical water crisis. Over 10,500 residents, including 345 students, walk more than 14 kilometers to collect water from unsafe sources shared with livestock and wildlife. This leads to waterborne diseases, poor sanitation, and school absenteeism especially among girls. Our innovation integrates aquaponic farming into the proven Water Kiosk at School model, creating a student managed, school based social enterprise. The system recycles nutrient rich water from fish tanks to grow vegetables, maximizing water use in a drought prone region. It combines smart water metering, mobile payments, and remote monitoring to ensure efficiency and transparency. This solution emerged from the need to address interconnected challenges: water scarcity, food insecurity, poor nutrition, and lack of sustainable school funding with a single, scalable model. Immediate benefits include: - Clean, affordable water access - Nutritious school meals from fresh fish and vegetables - Reduced absenteeism, especially among girls - Income generation to support school operations Sustainable benefits include: - Youth empowerment through hands on training in agriculture, entrepreneurship, and water management. - Strengthened local food systems and climate resilience - Improved public health and sanitation - Reduced plastic waste and pressure on natural water sources This holistic, community driven approach transforms schools into hubs of sustainability, education, and development benefiting students, families, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Advancing Climate-Resilient Maize for Smallholder farmers in Ghana.
core_fields.description: The project has two components, stress resilience and nutritional improvement in maize, to enhance food security and improve livelihoods. The project will evaluate elite white and yellow maize hybrids for superior yield and climate resilience under drought and low soil fertility conditions and profile the nutrient composition of promising maize hybrids. Through participatory trials with smallholder farmers, the project will generate agronomic and nutritional data, validate farmer-preferred varieties, and establish a foundation for varietal release.
core_fields.abstract: In Africa, the consequence of climate change is reported as very alarming because its agricultural system is predominantly rain-fed (African Development Bank, 2023), with Ghana not being an exception. Ghana's average annual temperature has risen by 0.21 C and is projected to increase by 1.7 C by 2030, while rainfall has declined across all regions over four decades (Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation, 2013). These shifts, including low soil fertility, have made crop production unstable, with maize, the most cultivated crop in Ghana, at risk. Farmers frequently experience total crop loss due to these stresses, that is, drought and low soil fertility, which are the key abiotic stresses of maize. Most maize varieties cultivated are nutrient poor and poorly adapted to stressful environments. This dual challenge threatens household nutrition and food security. The project introduces a two-track breeding and evaluation innovation where elite yellow hybrids will be profiled for provitamin A, lysine, and tryptophan content while evaluating performance under drought and low-nitrogen stress, and elite white hybrids will be evaluated for yield stability and tolerance to drought and low-nitrogen conditions, with the aim of identifying climate-resilient varieties for smallholder farmers in Ghana. Using elite hybrids from the WACCI maize breeding programme, the project integrates field trials, nutrient assays/profiling, and participatory farmer field evaluations. Farmers benefit from resilient, low-input varieties; consumers gain access to nutritious maize; and communities strengthen food security under a changing climate. Essentially the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and communities, especially in rural Ghana, are improved.

core_fields.title: Circular Food hub: integrated apiculture, aquaculture and youth Micro-entreprenureship
core_fields.description: An integrated, sustainable enterprise designed to improve nutritional security, create youth livelihoods, and demonstrate a working circular economy model in agriculture. The business combines high-demand aquaculture, apiculture (Honey), and horticulture (Organic Vegetables). The core innovation is the symbiotic integration: fish wastewater feeds the vegetables, and bees boost pollination. Commercial distribution is driven by a unique "Youth Micro-Franchise" model, overcoming youth capital barriers by supplying products on credit to business oriented women and youth
core_fields.abstract: In Kalungu District, high fish prices and seasonal vegetable scarcity create food security gaps, while youth unemployment remains critical. NG FORAYS LTD introduces a Circular Food Hub innovation that integrates three mutually beneficial value chains: aquaculture, horticulture (organic vegetables), and apiculture (honey). The innovation lies in the closed-loop system: we utilize nutrient-rich wastewater from fish ponds to irrigate and naturally fertilize our organic vegetable gardens.This eliminates costly chemical fertilizers, prevents waterway pollution, and ensures continuous, year-round production of safe and nutritious vegetables for consumption, addressing seasonal scarcity. Simultaneously, the strategic integration of 40 beehives ensures high pollination rates, boosting crop yields by 30-40%, and provides a high-margin product (honey) which has a variety of health benefits when consumed. Socially, we employ a unique "Youth Micro-Franchise" model. We empower aspiring youth entrepreneurs by supplying them with our fresh produce on credit, eliminating the barrier of startup capital. They retail the products and repay us, establishing a robust, self-sustaining distribution network. This system delivers affordable and safe food, lowers environmental impact, and creates immediate economic pathways for marginalized youth.

core_fields.title: WISE - Whey Integration for Sustainable Economies
core_fields.description: Lebanon discards 450-900 tonnes of acidic whey each year, polluting waterways and wasting valuable nutrients. WISE introduces a new technique that transforms this whey into Kishk, a nutritious, shelf-stable staple central to Lebanon's food security. This is achieved through two pillars: deploying this new technique through women-led cooperatives and enabling its adoption through consumer awareness, traceability, market partnerships, and policy alignment. WISE reduces environmental harm, strengthens rural livelihoods, and expands access to affordable, nutritious food.
core_fields.abstract: Lebanon's dairy sector generates large volumes of acidic whey, a nutrient-rich but high-Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) by-product of strained yogurt that most small and medium dairies dispose of directly into wastewater systems. This creates environmental pollution, financial burdens, and a lost economic resource. Simultaneously, rural cooperatives- particularly women-led ones- face rising production costs, limited product diversification, and constrained market access. These challenges create a dual gap in environmental management and rural livelihoods. WISE introduces a scientifically validated method that upcycles acidic whey into Kishk, a nutritious, shelf-stable cereal-dairy powder central to Lebanese food security. The process includes controlled whey concentration, standardized blending with bulgur, managed fermentation, and hygienic drying. It was validated through laboratory experiments on 33 samples that confirmed safe titratable acidity, water activity, and sensory equivalence to traditional Kishk. Pilots with 3 women-led cooperatives further demonstrated the method's practicality, with teams successfully applying SOPs, maintaining batch records, and passing key safety parameters using simple kettles, mixers, and dehydrators. The innovation addresses the environmental challenge by upcycling a high-BOD waste stream, reducing pollution and lowering disposal costs for dairies. It simultaneously strengthens rural livelihoods by providing women-led cooperatives with a low-cost input and a profitable, culturally trusted product with strong market demand. Immediate and sustainable benefits include: -Consumers: affordable, nutritious, culturally familiar food. -Cooperatives: new income streams, strengthened skills, and increased economic resilience. -Dairies: reduced disposal costs and environmental liabilities through steady whey offtake. -Environment: reduced organic load in waterways and a scalable circular-economy solution.

core_fields.title: Smart Organics for Precision Farming With Compost Manure
core_fields.description: Solafam is a climate smart agribusiness supporting smallholder farmers with affordable organic compost guided by farm sensors and LYN AI. We convert manure into high quality compost and use simple sensors to guide farmers on the right quantity and timing of application. We have successfully piloted this model and are now ready to scale helping farmers improve soil health and grow stronger crops at a quarter of the cost of synthetic fertilizers.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation brings affordable compost manure and low cost farm sensors to help smallholder farmers improve soil fertility in a reliable way. Many farmers cannot afford synthetic fertilizers and the soil in their gardens is getting weaker every season. This creates low yields, poor food quality and high production costs that keep families in poverty. Our approach solves this by giving farmers a clean soil booster at a price they can manage and guide them with AI on how to use it in the right amount and at the right time. We compost organic waste into tested rich manure then sell it at a quarter of the price of synthetic fertilizers. We deploy simple sensors in the gardens that read soil moisture and soil nutrients. These sensors send signals to LYN AI which tells the farmer how much compost to apply for each crop. This makes application more accurate which reduces waste and helps the soil recover naturally. The idea came from noticing that farmers want natural fertilizers but they are not sure how to use them well. The scientific insight behind our approach is that soil responds better when organic matter is applied based on real soil needs. The sensors make this possible and LYN AI makes the guidance simple for any farmer to follow. We have a very deep understanding of farmer needs because solafam has piloted this project and scaled others like solar powered cold storage and irrigation in rural communities.

core_fields.title: Transforming Ugandan food systems through sustainable, enzyme-enhanced plant-based milk alternatives for healthier communities
core_fields.description: Aviyo develops affordable, nutritious plant-based milks tailored for East African supply chains. Using food-grade enzymes (proteases for soy, amylases for oats) we transform local crops into products with improved flavor, digestibility, and ambient shelf stability (6 12 months). This allows distribution into rural and peri-urban markets without cold chain dependence. Our model integrates smallholder farmers through contract-sourcing, uses by-products (okara) for animal feed, and prioritizes low-impact aseptic packaging. The result: healthier, affordable diets; reduced food loss;
core_fields.abstract: Millions of lactose‑intolerant and hypertensive patients lack affordable, nutritious alternatives to dairy milk. Current plant‑based options are costly, poorly fortified, or have short shelf lives, while dairy production contributes significantly to carbon emissions, worsening climate change. Our innovation develops enzyme‑enhanced plant‑based milk from soybeans, oats, and blends. By applying food‑grade proteases and amylase enzymes, the products achieve superior digestibility, taste, and nutritional value. Renewable‑energy‑powered processing units ensure sustainability, while advanced machinery and eco‑friendly packaging extend shelf life and reduce food waste. This solution emerged from scientific insights into enzymatic hydrolysis, which improves protein bioavailability and carbohydrate breakdown, making plant milks more suitable for sensitive consumers. Early pitching and consumer testing have confirmed strong demand, with positive feedback and willingness to purchase. Immediate benefits include safe, affordable nutrition for lactose‑intolerant individuals, hypertensive patients, and communities seeking animal‑free options. Schools and households gain access to shelf‑stable products that reduce spoilage and costs. Producers benefit from reliable processing systems and market entry, while society gains market and reduced emissions and improved dietary diversity. Sustainable benefits include strengthened local food systems, reduced reliance on imports, and climate‑smart nutrition solutions that empower communities across Uganda and, eventually, East Africa.

core_fields.title: Strengthening the food system to end child and maternal malnutrition in Maiduguri, Nigeria's Borno State
core_fields.description: EVC, in collaboration with Brimarg, aim at rebuilding Maiduguri s food system: empowering local farmers to produce more and better in a climate-resilient way; processing foods into nutrient-dense flours for malnutrition management; employing vulnerable people with fair contracts and education for children; distributing Tom-Brown to malnutrition programs and NGOs facing pipeline ruptures; making appropriate, affordable complementary foods available for all children 6 23 months to prevent malnutrition; and supporting humanitarian response by replicating this model.
core_fields.abstract: EVC, in collaboration with Brimarg, tackles high child/maternal malnutrition, vulnerable women s economic exclusion, and a fractured food system by rebuilding it on four pillars: climate-resilient production through farmer associations that increase quantity and diversity; safe transformation of local crops into nutrient-dense Tom Brown; equitable distribution to malnutrition programs and NGOs facing pipeline ruptures while supplying markets with age-specific complementary foods for children 6 23 months to also prevent malnutrition; and fair employment for vulnerable women with schooling support. Our evidence-based approach aligns with FAO and WFP strategies to expand culturally accepted, locally sourced porridges like Tom-Brown in nutritional programs in northeast Nigeria. The missing link is pioneer, consistent production near the point of care. EVC, in collaboration with Brimarg, fills this gap through a 'mission-locked social business' that turns global guidance into reliable, program-ready supply at scale. Relevance is acute. Nigeria bears one of the world s highest undernutrition burdens. Funding cuts and repeated stock-outs have depressed nutrition programs' coverage, and UNICEF/WFP projections indicate that in 2026 imported nutrition supplies may cover ≤40% of needs, leaving children and women untreated unless reliable local supply is in place. Beside many immediate benefits, the Sustainable and longer-term benefits are: farmer associations producing more and more diverse crops (including fruit trees) with higher resilience to shocks; markets stocked with appropriate, affordable baby foods that support healthy growth and development; reduced food insecurity through local availability; and a scalable, solar powered, documentable model that other states can replicate to stabilize the wider humanitarian nutrition response elsewhere.

core_fields.title: Automating Farm-to-Fork Market Access to Boost Rural Farmers Income and Ensure Nutri-Safe Food Supply
core_fields.description: Over the years, Farmatago has operated a nutri-safe food supply process from farm to fork. To streamline this, we built an agritech innovation called MAKET, a platform with Its model which automates market access and ensures nutritious, and appealing food supply to consumers. The MAKET model expands consumers access to safe, nutritious and appealing food, reduces post-harvest loss, and increases farmer income. Integrating technology, value-added processing, and rural farmer empowerment for a sustainable agri-food system.
core_fields.abstract: Over 70% of Nigerian consumers lack access to safe, nutritious food due to poor handling, the absence of processing and sorting hubs, and the lack of an automated, traceable marketplace. Simultaneously, up to 50% of perishable produce is lost annually, while farmers earn low income because of intermediaries, delayed offtake, and limited market information. The MAKET Model addresses these challenges by combining digital innovation, community-based processing, and a traceable supply process to create a seamless farm-to-fork system for nutri-safe food supply. How it works: 1. Farmer's Signaling: Farmers signal produce availability via USSD, web, or adaptive solar-powered chillers, The MAKET platform's AI instantly process this alert and updates it to a central dashboard. Produce is aggregated and then transported to processing hubs. 2. Community Processing Hubs: Community-based hubs recieves the produce hygienically sort, lab-test, package, and process value-added foods while training rural women in post-harvest management and processing. 3. Consumer Access: Consumers order verified nutri-safe produce through the MAKET marketplace, with real-time visibility and delivery tracking. Leveraging AI-driven demand matching, climate-resilient storage, digital traceability, and value-added processing, MAKET delivers immediate benefits: safe, nutritious, traceable food for consumers, higher income for farmers, and reduced post-harvest losses. Key Benefits: 1.For Farmers: Instant market access, demand-driven harvesting, faster offtake, increased income, and full traceability to build trust with buyers. 2. For Consumers & Buyers: Real-time availability, seamless ordering, and verified nutri-safe food with origin and harvest-date transparency. This dual-sided value proposition creates a fully integrated system that benefits farmers, consumers, and the community.

core_fields.title: A Blueprint for Transforming School Feeding in Africa
core_fields.description: This project will enhance school feeding by improving meal nutritional value through nutrient-dense enhancements that support learning and growth, strengthening supply chains with aggregators and smallholder farmers by creating stable and reliable markets for local farmers, and improving operational efficiency by reducing food waste. Built on a proven model serving over 600,000 learners daily in Kenya, it offers a scalable blueprint for school feeding across Africa.
core_fields.abstract: Food4Education aims to scale the delivery of daily school meals by addressing three interconnected challenges that affect children's cognitive development and learning: nutrient-poor diets, unstable and costly supply chains, and avoidable food waste. 1 in 3 children under 5 in Africa experience severe food poverty, making them up to 50% more likely to suffer from life-threatening malnutrition. At the same time, smallholder farmers, who produce more than 70% of domestic food, face unpredictable markets, and kitchens often lack the simple planning tools needed to minimise waste and keep meal costs affordable. Our solution integrates three practical innovations into one delivery system: nutrient-dense meal enhancements, a reliable, environmentally conscious farmer supply chain, and low-cost tools that reduce food waste. We will increase the nutritional value of meals by exploring nutritional enhancements such as soy flour for added protein, healthy fats, and essential vitamins; milk for calcium and B12 in porridge; and fortified cooking oil for vitamins A and E to support immunity and cell health. To diversify nutrients, we will also explore adding locally sourced kale, rich in iron, vitamin C, and fibre. To reduce food waste and improve efficiency, we will use waste monitoring tools for kitchen planning, inventory management, and daily meal tracking. Built on learnings from delivering 600,000+ meals daily across 13 counties, this integrated model delivers immediate benefits, better nutrition for learners, stable markets for farmers, more efficient kitchens and long-term gains for communities, education systems, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Locally Made Iodine solution: Promoting Human Health Through Productivity and Accessibility of Safe, Nutritious Food.
core_fields.description: The traditional ways of making aqueous iodine have issues such as needing iodine crystals and their solubility. This new method offers an efficient way to produce a pure iodine solution that is cost-effective. It can be used in food, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals as a sanitizer and for fortification, promoting sustainable chemical manufacturing in Malawi.
core_fields.abstract: The main issue with conventional iodine solution is its solubility problems. Pure aqueous iodine are nearly impossible to prepare. Iodine solution which are formulated by dissolving iodine crystals and potassium iodide in water or alcohol, contains significant levels of other elements like iodide (I-) and triiodide (I3- , leading to irritation, staining, and unpleasant smell. Conversely aqueous iodine with little or no other iodine elements is less irritating, odorless. The irritating and toxic nature of conventional formulated products limits their usability, particularly in long-term wound management and consumer-friendly applications During the COVID-19 pandemic, some potential consumers avoided alcohol-based sanitizers due to odor and safety concerns. Investigating alternatives led to the realization that pure iodine does not cause the irritation linked to iodinated commercial products. action. These innovative products shall have specific benefits for diverse sectors like healthcare, agriculture, and research. In medicine, this iodine solution enhances wound care and infection control, helping to prevent antibiotic resistance. In agriculture, it promises improved crop yields and plant stress and climate change effects resilience, contributing to better agricultural practices. The iodine solution also offers nutritional enrichment through biofortification, enhancing livestock health and productivity and supporting safer veterinary practices. In academic and research contexts it as a reagent for various experiments, showcasing its versatility and broad applicability in enhancing health, food security, and educational outcomes. Therefor the adoption of this innovative iodine stands to transform practical uses across multiple fields.

core_fields.title: Scaling Healthy Diets: A School-Based Ultra Processed Food (UPF) Screening Tool for Adolescents in Pakistan
core_fields.description: In this project, a culturally appropriate UPF screening questionnaire (UPF-SQ) will be integrated into schools in Karachi. After the validation, it will be incorporated for periodic screening of adolescents dietary intake and provide real-time advice to students, teachers and their parents about their consumption and long-term impact. This project will collaborate between education, health, and food environment stakeholders, including canteens and vendors, for primordial prevention of obesity and non-communicable diseases, benefiting adolescent health.
core_fields.abstract: Pakistan is facing a classic nutritional transition. The daily intake of adolescents in Pakistan included sweets (47.8%), bakery items (25%), and sugar-sweetened beverages (85%) (Sheikh et al., Appetite, 2024). Adolescents prefer the intake of highly processed and ultra-processed foods (UPF) that are high in sugar, fat, sodium, and additives over traditional home-cooked food. Although a recent Lancet series emphasized UPF and its association with non-communicable diseases (NCDs) that can be mitigated by preserving cultural food traditions, Pakistan has limited data on the magnitude and health impacts of UPF consumption. National nutrition surveys mainly focus on undernutrition and the dietary intake of essential vitamins and minerals. The Dietary Quality Questionnaire (DQQ) for Pakistan is available, but it does not screen for UPF consumption. Although the Nova UPF screener developed by Brazil has been validated culturally by many countries, including India but not in Pakistan. This innovation fills a significant gap by developing the first culturally validated Nova-based UPF screening tool designed specifically for this demographic through a multi-phase approach: Preparation & item development, adaptation & pilot testing, validation & main data collection and analysis, integration & dissemination. and can be digitized in the future with automated reporting and a sustainable monitoring dashboard that allows schools and policymakers to continuously track UPF risk trends over time, ensuring long-term impact and integration into routine school health systems. The project will enhance adolescent nutrition awareness, equip schools for monitoring, inform policy, and support a lower-waste, less processed food environment.

core_fields.title: Improving nutrition quality of school meals while promoting sustainable production of biofortified crops.
core_fields.description: The project will refine and scale composite flour product options developed using Vitamin A rich maize, High Iron beans and Orange sweet potatoes. Products will be refined through sensory evaluation and investigating their efficiency in delivering micronutrients in school meals. Schools, communities and millers will be empowered to produce the biofortified crops and products by applying regenerative climate smart agriculture practices as well as the use of recommended post-harvest storage and processing practices.
core_fields.abstract: The innovations are nutrient dense composite flours made from biofortified crops which not only contain proteins and carbohydrates but also micronutrients ; vitamin A, Iron and Zinc. Vitamin A and Zinc boost immunity while iron is important for cognitive function and productivity, which are key to child growth and development. The biofortified composite flours will be produced and made available at about the same cost as the regular flours, yet they will provide significantly more micronutrients and better acceptability. This is relevant given the low nutrient density of school meals and high malnutrition rates in school children. Building capacity of the different food system actors will ensure continuous supply of the crops while applying climate smart practices to increase productivity. Vulnerable groups in the targeted communities will benefit nutritionally as they consume the composite flours and economically as producing households will have increased trade and marketing opportunities of the different biofortified crops. The school-going children will be the main target consumer segment. Households in the targeted communities will be empowered with appropriate skills to produce and conduct appropriate post handling practices thus increasing marketable volumes of the crops. There will better diet, increased attendance and retention of school children, increased capacity schools and communities to produce the crops and increased incomes. The practice and adoption of regenerative climate smart agriculture principles will mitigate effects of climate change. Thus, this intervention will not only increase access to nutritious food, mitigate food loss and waste but also entrench sustainable food production.

core_fields.title: Ikolomani Land Rebirth: Hydroponics for Women and Indigenous Foods
core_fields.description: The Ikolomani Land Rebirth project restores degraded land along River Isiukhu by converting abandoned gold-mining pits into women-led hydroponic farming units. Using soil-free systems, women cultivate nutritious indigenous crops such as vegetables, millet, and sorghum that are disappearing due to pollution and climate stress. By merging modern hydroponics with traditional seed knowledge, the project strengthens food security, empowers women excluded from land ownership, and regenerates damaged landscapes in Ikolomani.
core_fields.abstract: Decades of artisanal gold mining in Ikolomani have left deep pits, polluted soils, and severely degraded land along River Isiukhu. These conditions make traditional farming nearly impossible, while cultural norms prevent women from owning or accessing land, deepening food insecurity. The innovation responds to these intertwined challenges through a simple, science-informed idea: repurposing abandoned mining pits into productive hydroponic farming hubs for women. Hydroponics eliminates the need for fertile soil, allowing clean, controlled crop production in areas where the land has been rendered unusable. This technical insight growing plants in nutrient-enriched water rather than contaminated soil creates an immediate pathway to restore food production in a polluted landscape. The project integrates this technology with cultural and ecological knowledge by focusing on indigenous crops such as vegetables, millet, and sorghum, which hold nutritional value and are becoming endangered as soils degrade. The innovation lies in merging land reclamation, gender inclusion, and indigenous seed preservation into one solution. By leasing and rehabilitating these pits, women gain safe, accessible growing spaces and new economic opportunities. The community benefits from increased availability of local, nutritious foods, while the landscape heals through the clearing, draining, and management of previously hazardous sites. Immediate benefits include clean food production, new livelihood spaces for women, and reduced safety risks around open pits. Long-term benefits include revived indigenous seed varieties, improved nutrition, restored land, and a more resilient, community-led food system that blends science with culture to safeguard Ikolomani s future.

core_fields.abstract: TEKA-NA is a first-of-its-kind, locally produced textured vegetable protein (TVP) designed for low-income markets and rooted in smallholder agriculture. It tackles interconnected challenges related to Seeding The Future s mission: persistent protein malnutrition, unstable farmer livelihoods, and the expansion of unsustainable protein production in Africa. Animal-sourced proteins are unaffordable and often unsafe since refrigeration and phytosanitary systems are limited. Beans are accessible but require long cook times and significant fuel. *Livelihoods: Smallholders farm tiny, degraded plots and earn low, volatile returns from staple crops, with few opportunities to enter higher-value markets or diversify into more profitable crops. *Sustainability: As protein demand rises in Africa, resource-intensive industrial livestock is spreading. Meanwhile, smallholders lack incentives to adopt regenerative practices or shift away from maize monocropping. Wageningen University developed a custom prototype that cooks quickly, integrates into local dishes, and is produced via dry extrusion. Energy efficient and made without solvents, it is a safe, shelf-stable, low-cost protein. SYSTEMIC BENEFITS: TEKA-NA builds an inclusive, climate-positive value chain that links smallholder legume production, regenerative farming, local processing, and nutrition. Water harvesting systems, grey-water reuse, and mobile drip kits will help farmers maintain production even during dry spells. This challenge is highly relevant as millions of smallholders in Africa struggle to adopt modern, climate-smart, and profitable agriculture. The solution combines practical training, advisory services, digital tools, and market linkages. Farmers receive hands-on guidance on improved seeds, soil health, irrigation, pest management, and value addition. Digital platforms provide real-time advisory, weather alerts, and market information, enabling data-driven decisions. The approach is informed by insights from agricultural research, extension best practices, and agribusiness models that integrate technology and training with community-led solutions. Communities benefit from increased availability of safe, nutritious, and affordable food, while society gains from improved food security and environmental sustainability through regenerative practices. By bridging knowledge gaps and fostering innovation, this hub transforms agriculture from subsistence-based to technology-driven, profitable, and sustainable, creating long-term impact for farmers, consumers, and the environment.
