core_fields.title: Empowering farmers by rejuvenating degraded farmlands through long-term agroforestry model implementation.
core_fields.description: AGRO RANGERS addresses severe soil degradation and climate change, and heavy chemical use in farming, which traps small and marginal farmers in cycles of low yield, high input costs, debt, and a path to suicide. We aim to transition 100 farmers and 100 acres of land from 20 drought villages to regenerative agroforestry models, which restore soil health, improve climate resilience, and create diversified long-term income streams for small and marginal farmers in rural India.
core_fields.abstract: Soil degradation and climate change are destroying the livelihoods of small and marginal farmers in India. The farming community is important for producing food for the global population. We have created farmer-centric innovative agroforestry models, using deep traditional knowledge while using the latest technology and research. We are solving the problem of soil degradation due to long-term use of chemicals in farming. This weakens the soil, reduces farm yield, increases farming input costs, and pushes small and marginal farmers into debt and suicide in rural India. In our state, Maharashtra, sadly, 200+ farmers commit suicide every month due to debt and poverty. Our own research in the farming community of testing over 5000 soil samples has shown that carbon content in soil is alarmingly low. The carbon content of soil is crucial for sustainable food production. AGRO RANGERS helps small and marginal farmers transform their degraded land through regenerative agroforestry models. This model combines trees, crops, and solid restoration practices on the same land. Over the last 7 years, we have developed multiple agroforestry models which are customised to land type and weather conditions in our part of rural India. Our solutions are based on scientific evidence that demonstrates that improved soil carbon content and farmlands become climate resilient. Immediate and sustained benefits to small and marginal farmers are increased soil carbon, improved crop quality, lower input costs, stable income, healthier and chemical-free food, restored farmlands, improved water quality, and strong resilience for farmers and rural communities.

core_fields.title: The SOWETO project - Sustainable Organic Wellbeing and Economic Transformation Opportunities
core_fields.description: SoliDrip aims to establish five new organic farms in schools' courtyards across Soweto township in Johannesburg, building on our successful two-year pilot at Faranani Primary School. Using SoliDrip s autonomous irrigation technology, we demonstrate advanced cultivation techniques. Together with our local partners, Siyosile Indlala, we developed methodologies and a comprehensive training program in sustainable organic agriculture and urban farm business management. We work together to empower participating smallholder farmers to build self-sustaining and profitable farming businesses.
core_fields.abstract: SoliDrip s patented and field-proven irrigation technology operates either by gravity from a simple water tank (no need for a high tank elevation) or, when connected to a water grid, through a SoliDrip proprietary low-pressure regulator, delivering precise irrigation exactly where and when plants need it, without pumps, electricity, or digital control systems. Its unique design enables differential irrigation along a single irrigation line, delivering optimal irrigation to each plant based on its specific needs, microclimate, and growth stage. This makes SoliDrip ideally suited for polyculture farming, where multiple crops grow side by side, as well as for both in-ground cultivation and detached substrate systems such as planters, raised beds, and vertical farming structures. SoliDrip provides low-volume, plant-driven irrigation that improves plant health and yields while reducing water consumption by up to 60% and ultimately eliminating losses from leaks, runoff, and over-irrigation. The system is modular, flexible, and easy to install, requiring minimal technical training, making it accessible to smallholder farmers, schools, and community-based growing initiatives operating under resource constraints. By eliminating the high pressure and infrastructure requirements of conventional drip systems, SoliDrip enables cultivation in locations previously considered too resource-constrained or spatially limited for efficient agriculture, such as rooftops and built urban desert environments. In the short term, SoliDrip improves water efficiency, reduces human intervention, and eliminates irrigation errors, freeing farmers and farm workers to focus on higher-value agricultural tasks. Over time, it supports climate-resilient food systems, improved livelihoods, and scalable food production that respects planetary boundaries and local realities.

core_fields.title: Nourish & Flourish: A Sustainable, Equitable Community Food System for Vulnerable Households.
core_fields.description: Nourish & Flourish will strengthen UAA s existing food support infrastructure and build a sustainable, culturally anchored, low-waste community food system supporting 100 vulnerable households per week.
core_fields.abstract: Nourish & Flourish introduces an innovative, low-waste community food system that ensures vulnerable households especially migrant and NRPF families can reliably access nutritious, culturally appropriate food. The problem it solves is twofold: rising food poverty and high levels of avoidable food waste caused by manual stock tracking, inconsistent supply, and limited storage insights. These issues contribute to hunger, inefficiency, and unnecessary pressure on landfill systems. The solution combines digital innovation, sustainable practices and culturally competent support. A new inventory system uses simple technology to monitor expiry dates, track stock movement and identify surplus before it spoils. This reduces waste at source and enables redistribution to households or partner organisations. Improved transport routing lowers emissions, while reusable packaging minimises waste. Nutrition guidance and low-waste cooking workshops empower families to make healthier and more sustainable choices at home. The innovation is guided by practical insight from UAA s frontline work and partnerships with health, local government and community providers. We recognized that food support systems fail when they lack data, cultural relevance and environmental responsibility so our model integrates all three. Immediate benefits include reliable access to nutritious food for 100 households per week, reduced waste, improved efficiency, and better wellbeing support. Sustainable long-term benefits include stronger household resilience, improved public health, a circular community food system with lower environmental impact, and a scalable model that can support other multicultural communities, producers and local growers. The project strengthens both people and the planet.

core_fields.title: Solar Learning Farms: School-Based Climate-Smart Irrigation and Nutrition Model for Zambia
core_fields.description: The project establishes school solar learning farms where each school features a solar-powered water system with dual lines for drinking water and irrigation. Schools develop gardens, orchards, and climate-smart demonstration plots. Teachers and pupils gain practical skills in irrigation, agroecology, nutrition, and small-scale agribusiness. The school becomes a hub for improved diets, hands-on learning, and community replication. The project will be centred on the Central and Lusaka provinces of Zambia.
core_fields.abstract: Many rural schools lack safe drinking water, reliable irrigation, and practical learning environments for agriculture. This limits attendance, weakens nutrition outcomes, and leaves young people without marketable skills. The innovation introduces a school solar learning farm, a combined water-energy-agriculture platform that turns schools into functional production and training hubs. Each school features a borehole powered by solar energy, a low-pressure drip irrigation network, and designated areas for vegetables, fruits, and climate-smart demonstration plots. A dedicated drinking-water line ensures safe water access for pupils throughout the day. The model functions as a practical cycle in which pupils apply skills directly in school gardens, harvests contribute to daily meals, and families adapt similar practices based on what is demonstrated at the school. The model is built on insights from groundwater mapping, solar pumping efficiency, and agroecological methods that reduce input costs and increase year-round productivity. Teachers are trained to run the gardens as learning laboratories, supported by simple monitoring tools and structured curriculum. Immediate benefits include improved hydration, better diets, reduced absenteeism, and hands-on agricultural education. Over time, schools become centres of climate-resilient food production, influencing community practices and strengthening local food systems. The environmental footprint is low, as solar energy replaces fuel-based systems, and drip irrigation significantly reduces water use. The approach responds to water scarcity, nutrition gaps, and limited practical education by introducing a single system that links water access, food production, and learning within existing school structures.

core_fields.title: Producing low-GI rice to reduce diabetes risk and increase farmers income and value.
core_fields.description: Rice is the main carbohydrate source in Indonesia, yet its high glycemic index increases the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other non-communicable diseases. To address this issue, we developed low-glycemic rice varieties, including antioxidant and parboiled rice. These healthier products also provide direct benefits for farmers by increasing the added value of their harvested grain, enabling higher income and supporting the long-term sustainability of farming communities in meaningful ways for their families locally.
core_fields.abstract: This project focuses on the innovation of developing Low Glycemic Index (LGI) Rice, starting with environmentally friendly cultivation practices and followed by a modern parboiling process, including soaking, steaming, and drying. This innovation transforms conventional rice typically high in glycemic index into healthier LGI rice. The primary issue addressed is the high prevalence of diabetes in Indonesia, affecting 21.8% of the population, placing the country fourth in the world. Diabetes is the root cause of many chronic diseases and the third leading cause of death in Indonesia. Considering that rice is the staple food for most Indonesians, providing low-GI rice is highly relevant for reducing daily spikes in blood glucose and improving public health. The technical insight behind the solution is the understanding of the Glycemic Index (GI) as an indicator of how quickly carbohydrates are absorbed. Through parboiling technology, the starch structure in rice is modified, resulting in a significantly lower GI. The benefits of this project are direct and sustainable for multiple groups. For consumers, it provides healthier rice suitable for people with diabetes. For farmers, the project offers guidance on environmentally friendly cultivation, improves product quality, adds value to their harvest, and creates opportunities to increase income. Farmer cooperatives are strengthened through business training, branding and packaging development, processing SOPs, and marketing plans. Additionally, the project promotes sustainable agriculture, gender inclusion, youth participation, and compliance with food safety certification. Overall, the LGI rice innovation enhances public health, supports farmer welfare, and contributes to long-term environmental sustainability.

core_fields.title: Scaling Safe Organic Fertilizer Production for Smallholder Farmers (SafeFert Africa)
core_fields.description: SafeFert Africa will develop and field-validate a low-cost and efficient, locally fabricated solar chamber that thermally-treats poultry and cattle manure, aiming to sustain >55 C to reduce E. coli/coliform risks by >90% within 72 hours. Over 6 8 months, we will use desk review and farmer inputs to refine design-requirements, run simulations to optimize materials and thickness, and test prototype performance at two urban-farms across feedstock types and loading conditions. Outputs include validated design-specification and performance-evidence scale-up.
core_fields.abstract: SafeFert tackles a major driver of vegetable contamination in Ghana s urban and peri-urban farming systems: the widespread use of pathogen-rich, untreated manure. This matters because most smallholders in Sub-Saharan Africa (80 90%) depend on organic fertilizers, yet only 30 40% treat them properly, allowing E. coli/coliforms to persist from farm to market and undermining food safety, yields, and consumer confidence (FAO, 2023; World Bank, 2022). Untreated manure can also contribute to wider public-health risks, including antibiotic-resistance pathways (Marti et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019). The innovation is a low-cost and efficient, locally fabricable solar thermal sanitization chamber (e.g., plywood with biogas-grade plastic glazing) that passively captures heat and uses temperature probes to verify performance. Under this Seed Grant, we will optimize the chamber design, material type and thickness, geometry, loading depth/volume, and moisture conditions. We will combine desk research and farmer inputs, run process design simulations parameters of the chamber, to predict heat retention and climate sensitivity. We will then validate prototypes performances at two farm sites using the feedstock (poultry manure, cattle dung, and co-amendments usually adopted), tracking temperature profiles, moisture/evaporation, and microbial reduction across Day 1 3+. The technical insight is that contamination risk concentrates at the growing stage, making pathogen reduction at cultivation a high-leverage control point (Amoah et al., 2007; Natvig et al., 2002; Essilfie et al., 2023; Appau & Ofori, 2024). Benefits include safer organic fertiliser, lower contamination risks for consumers/schools, improved farm productivity, reduced environmental pathogen loading, and a validated design/SOP package for future scale.

core_fields.title: KisanMitra
core_fields.description: KisanMitra is an AI-driven circular food economy platform that links restaurants, composters, and farmers. It diverts food waste from landfills into compost, restores soil health, reduces farm input costs, and improves farmer incomes through collective selling and AI-guided pricing. By integrating logistics, pricing intelligence, and traceability, KisanMitra transforms waste into value while strengthening sustainable food systems. Additionally, it fuels a more nutritious and organic produce from farm to plate.
core_fields.abstract: Food systems are highly fragmented. Restaurants discard 7 to 10 percent of raw materials, while farmers face declining soil health, rising fertilizer costs, and weak bargaining power. This leads to environmental harm, food loss, and unstable farmer incomes. KisanMitra solves this by creating an AI-enabled, closed-loop coordination platform that links food waste generators, composters, and farmers. The platform dynamically routes organic waste to composting partners, matches compost output with farm soil needs, and forms farmer cooperatives for bulk selling and shared resources. AI models analyze cost price, domestic and export markets, logistics, and intermediary margins to recommend optimal selling prices for crops. The innovation is novel in its full-cycle integration. Unlike existing solutions that address waste management, composting, or farm marketplaces in isolation, KisanMitra connects all stages from crop to consumption to compost. Scientific insights from soil regeneration research, waste stream analytics, and market price modeling informed the system design. Immediate benefits include reduced disposal costs for restaurants, steady raw material supply for composters, subsidized organic compost for farmers, and improved crop quality. Long-term benefits include soil carbon restoration, reduced chemical fertilizer dependency, lower methane emissions, higher farmer profitability, and transparent, trusted food supply chains for consumers and institutions.

core_fields.title: A Community Hub Model for Climate-Resilient Food Systems
core_fields.description: We are piloting a community university Food Systems Hub in Nairobi, Kenya, that connects graduate research directly to community-defined food system challenges. We support applied field research and co-design climate-resilient, regenerative agricultural solutions with a rural community. The hub functions as a new operational model that reduces graduate dropout, strengthens local food production and climate adaptation, and produces a practical framework that can be replicated across similar contexts.
core_fields.abstract: In many agricultural universities, graduate research never reaches the field. Students drop out because they cannot afford fieldwork, and communities rarely benefit from the knowledge produced on campus. At the same time, rural farmers face climate stress, declining soil health, and unstable food production, even though they hold strong traditional and local knowledge about their land and crops. We are addressing the gap between universities and the local food systems they are meant to support. Our innovation is the establishment of hubs that bring academic research and traditional knowledge into the same space. Anchored at Kenyatta University, the hub supports graduate students to work directly with a rural community on locally defined food system challenges. What makes this model new is that it treats fieldwork as shared infrastructure, not an individual academic cost, and positions communities as co-creators rather than research subjects. We provide basic field support and structure the research process around co-design, where scientific methods and community knowledge guide solutions together. This approach is informed by practical experience showing that food system solutions are more effective when communities are not treated as beneficiaries, but as knowledge holders. The hub removes the financial barrier to fieldwork while ensuring research responds to real needs. Immediate benefits include improved, locally adapted farming practices that support climate resilience, stronger trust and uptake among farmers, and increased graduate completion. Over time, the hub produces a simple, documented model that other universities and communities can adapt to strengthen local food systems in similar contexts.

Unlike stand-alone agronomic interventions, NAHC-STIP integrates cooperative-led aggregation, quality assurance, and traceable market access for food and botanical products, ensuring reliable demand, fair pricing, and reduced exposure to single-crop failure. Women and youth benefit through targeted participation in food, botanical, and value-addition enterprises. core_fields.title: Surveillance and sustainable management of Fusarium diseases in staple crops.
core_fields.description: SporeSmart is a climate-smart agriculture project that helps farmers detect fungal crop diseases early using field-based spore collection and laboratory data analysis. Timely alerts delivered through agricultural extension services enable targeted treatment, reduced pesticide use and improved yields. The project also trials a bio-pesticide as an alternative to chemicals, supporting healthier soils, biodiversity, climate resilience and food security for smallholder farmers in Ghana with potential to scale across West Africa.
core_fields.abstract: SporeSmart addresses a growing challenge in agriculture: rising crop losses from fungal diseases driven by climate change, yet most farmers lack early warning systems. Consequently, diseases are often detected only after visible damage occurs, causing severe yield losses, excessive pesticide use, higher production costs and risks to food safety from, for instance, mycotoxins that can enter the food chain. The project focus is on Fusarium which alone causes billions in global crop losses. In Ghana, maize, legumes and staple crops are highly vulnerable, with maize losses estimated at 700,000 tons annually, equivalent to USD 175 million. While farmers urgently need earlier and more accurate detection tools, current solutions are reactive, slow and heavily reliant on chemical fungicides. Manual spore identification remains costly, labour-intensive and error-prone. SporeSmart solves this problem through early detection and prevention. The innovation uses simple, field-based spore collection devices to monitor airborne fungal spores before disease symptoms appear in crops. Collected samples are laboratory analysed to identify spore type and density, when combined with weather and agronomic data and an AI model, currently in development, this has the potential to predict outbreak risk. Farmers will receive timely alerts through extension services, enabling early, targeted action. In parallel, SporeSmart is trialling a bio-based pesticide to support safer early treatment. The solution is grounded in plant pathology and climate science. Immediate benefits include reduced crop losses, lower pesticide costs and improved yields. Long-term benefits extend to safer food, healthier soils, protected biodiversity, cleaner water and stronger climate resilience.

core_fields.title: AI-Powered One-Photo Child Growth Screening and Personalized Nutrition Action Plans
core_fields.description: MAAP (Malnutrition Assessment and Action Plan) is a smartphone-based platform that turns a single child photo and basic details into reliable growth measures, flags stunting/underweight/wasting risk, and generates practical, locally relevant diet and referral guidance. Designed for frontline workers and caregivers in low-resource settings, it reduces reliance on equipment, improves data quality, and helps programs target nutrition support earlier turning screenings into timely action.
core_fields.abstract: MAAP solves a critical last-mile nutrition problem: in many low-resource settings, child growth screening is infrequent, equipment-dependent, error-prone, and often does not translate into timely diet action. As a result, stunting/underweight/wasting can go undetected until it becomes severe, while nutrition support and counselling remain generic rather than targeted. Our innovation is a smartphone-based, AI-powered nutrition assessment and action platform. Using a single child photo plus basic inputs (age/sex and minimal context), MAAP estimates growth measures, calculates WHO-style growth indicators, flags malnutrition risk, and instantly generates practical, locally appropriate diet guidance and referral prompts for caregivers and frontline workers. The system also supports structured digital records and geo-tagged data capture to improve trust, reduce manual errors, and strengthen follow-up. The key technical insight is that computer vision and machine learning can extract reliable anthropometric cues from everyday smartphone images, enabling screening without specialized hardware when paired with guided capture workflows and quality checks. By combining measurement with decision support, MAAP turns screening into action. Immediate benefits include faster screening, earlier risk detection, individualized counselling, and clearer referral pathways. Sustainable benefits include improved adherence to nutrition plans, better targeting of supplementary nutrition resources, more consistent follow-ups, and stronger community trust helping schools, communities, and public programs deliver safer, more nutritious diets more effectively.

core_fields.title: CefDol for Degraded Soil Restoration: A Nature-Based Engineering Approach to Climate-Resilient Agriculture
core_fields.description: TerraParc Solutions LLC develops climate-smart materials derived from geoparticulates and waste biomass for restoring severely degraded soils. Its flagship product, CefDol, fabricated from coffee husk cellulose and natural dolomite, delivers a multifunctional system that reduces soil acidity while enhancing water retention, structural stability, and soil organic carbon. This proposed project will advance CefDol to pilot scale, validate its performance through collaborative field trials, and establish commercialization pathways for real-world agricultural deployment.
core_fields.abstract: CefDol, cellulose fiber/dolomite particle cluster, is a novel, nature-based, climate-smart soil regeneration technology developed by TerraParc Solutions. It is composed of self-assembled clusters formed from waste biomass-derived cellulose fibers and micronized dolomite. Unlike conventional soil inputs, CefDol functions as a physicochemical soil-architecture intervention, designed to modify soil structure rather than simply supply nutrients. By controlling particle size, swelling behavior, surface chemistry, and cellulose-clay interfacial interactions, CefDol forms stable organic-inorganic networks within the soil matrix. These networks deliver controlled calcium and magnesium release, reduce soil acidity, enhance water retention, improve aggregate stability, supply soil organic carbon, and increase nutrient mobility. In parallel, CefDol supports soil carbon stabilization and enhanced mineral weathering, contributing to climate mitigation. Designed to be tunable to different soil types, and manufactured from locally available, low-cost materials, this multifunctional solution enables scalable soil restoration pathways, particularly relevant for degraded and acidic soils in vulnerable smallholder farming systems. Guided by a nature-to-nature ethos, CefDol supports climate resilience, food security, and environmental stewardship - merging sustainable innovation with precision engineering to deliver all-in-one sustainable solutions. The preliminary experimental evidences showed that CefDol has key product features including: adjusting soil pH, improving water-retention capacity, enhancing soil microstructure and aggregate stability, supplying calcium, magnesium and soil organic matter while enhancing nutrient mobility, and boosting carbon sequestration pathways relevant to carbon markets.

core_fields.title: Advancing a Low-Tech Modular System for Neighbourhood Self-Harvest Food Hubs
core_fields.description: Our project advances a modular, low-tech system that produces living greens directly inside neighbourhood markets. Building on a successful prototype, we will refine the retail-scale design, environmental controls, materials, and operating protocols to create a manufacturable, scalable model for self-harvest food access. This phase focuses on engineering, materials testing, and small-batch fabrication to validate performance and prepare the system for replication in affordable, walkable urban food hubs, strengthening local food autonomy.
core_fields.abstract: Urban food systems face converging pressures: soil degradation, loss of arable land, long-distance supply chains, rising energy costs, and increasingly unaffordable fresh produce. Most cities rely on greens grown thousands of kilometers away, requiring transport, refrigeration, and packaging that drive emissions and inflate retail prices. At the same time, many vertical farming solutions remain too high-tech, energy-intensive, and capital-intensive to serve small neighbourhood markets. Our innovation addresses these challenges through a modular, low-tech farming system that places production directly inside the retail unit, eliminating transport and cold-chain costs while offering living greens at significantly lower prices. Using simple hydroponic principles, low-energy lighting schedules, optimized airflow and irrigation, and standardized operating protocols, the system reliably produces high yields in compact spaces without soil, pesticides, or long-distance inputs. A key advancement is its design for self-harvest and community interaction: the system invites users to pick living greens at peak freshness, strengthening their connection to food while reducing waste and improving nutritional quality. This approach emerged from a technical insight validated through our Seed Grant work: urban food resilience can be achieved through simplified, resource-efficient systems rather than complex automation and high-tech, capital-intensive models. By designing for manufacturability, low energy use, easy maintenance, and direct public interaction, we created a system suitable for widespread deployment in everyday retail environments. Immediate benefits include lower prices, fresher produce, reduced waste, and community engagement. Long-term benefits include reduced GHG emissions, food access and affordability, and scalable decentralized urban food hubs.

core_fields.title: Scaling conversion of municipal market food waste into organic fertilizer and animal protein in Nairobi
core_fields.description: The project aims to enhance collection of food waste from Municipal markets and hotels around the Nairobi metropolitan area ,converting it into organic fertilizer and animal feed protein using the black soldier flies. The Organic Fertilizer is sold through a network of women lead farmers aims to regenerate degraded soils and promote health food production in rural Kenya while the black soldier fly larvae provides affordable and sustainable protein for poultry and pigs farmers
core_fields.abstract: This addresses the growing problem of food waste and soil degradation in Kenya. Large amounts of organic waste from municipal markets and hotels in the Nairobi metropolitan area are dumped in landfills and dumpsites, causing environmental pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, while farmers face declining soil fertility and high costs of animal feed. The project solves these challenges by mobilizing youths and women to collect the food waste and converting it into valuable products using Black Soldier Fly (BSF) technology. The waste is fed to BSF larvae, which naturally and efficiently break it down. The process produces two key outputs: nutrient-rich organic fertilizer which is granulated to enhance adoption and high-protein BSF larvae for animal feed. The scientific insight behind this solution is the unique ability of Black Soldier Fly larvae to rapidly convert organic waste into biomass and organic soil amendments with minimal water, land, and energy use. This nature-based solution creates a circular economy where waste becomes a resource. Immediate benefits include reduced waste going to landfills, employment for youths and women, lower feed costs for poultry and pig farmers, and increased availability of organic fertilizer. Long-term benefits include improved soil health, higher and safer food production, reduced reliance on chemical fertilizers, and increased climate resilience. Selling fertilizer through women-led farmer networks strengthens rural livelihoods, promotes inclusive economic growth, and empowers women. Overall, the innovation improves environmental health, food security, and incomes for farmers and communities while supporting sustainable urban and rural systems.

core_fields.title: Wawee Valley Food Jungle:A scalable, nutrition-driven regenerative food system.
core_fields.description: This project will scale the Wawee Valley Food Jungle, a systems-level food innovation that links regenerative, no-burn farming with nutrition-driven product development and inclusive markets. Over 18 months, 150 smallholder farmers will transition from climate-vulnerable monocropping to diversified agroecological systems, delivering 70 100% income gains, improved soil and biodiversity, and expanded access to nutritious foods. By converting underutilized crops into scalable, market-ready products, the project demonstrates how regenerative agriculture can drive equitable, climate-resilient food-system transformation.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in upland face persistent challenges of low and unstable incomes, degraded soils, and limited access to nutritious food markets. Climate-vulnerable monocropping systems are increasingly exposed to climate shocks, rising input costs, and price volatility, while nutrient-dense and diverse crops are often undervalued or excluded from formal value chains. These interconnected challenges undermine food security, farmer livelihoods, and environmental sustainability. WVFJ addresses these challenges through an integrated, regenerative food-system model that links ecological restoration, nutrition, and inclusive market access. At the farm level, monocropping is replaced with diversified agroecological systems that regenerate soil health and improve climate resilience. On-farm trials, continuous monitoring, and adaptive management are used to optimize yields and plant nutrition while reducing reliance on external inputs, enabling more stable and higher farmer incomes. Unlike many regenerative agriculture initiatives that focus primarily on production, the Food Jungle embeds nutrition-driven product development and commercialization directly into the farming system. Nutrient-dense and underutilized crops are transformed into safe, high-quality food and wellness products through partnerships with universities and technical experts, reducing food loss and retaining more value at the farmer level. One example is Emerald Latte, a functional, plant-based beverage developed from chia leaves, currently in its final research phase. The model s novelty lies in its systems-level integration of regenerative farming, nutrition science, and inclusive markets into a single, scalable approach. Designed for replication across similar smallholder contexts, WVFJ delivers immediate and sustained benefits for farmers, consumers, and the environment, demonstrating how regenerative agriculture can drive equitable climate-resilient system.

core_fields.title: Catalysing climate adaptation in drylands.
core_fields.description: NARA creates vertically integrated supply chains from regenerative community-led farm cooperatives all the way to local and regional markets for crops and carbon credits. Through partnerships with communities in drylands, the company restores thousands of hectares of drylands while building resilient local businesses across the agri-value chain. Approaches like agro-forestry and pasture management are supported through the sale of carbon credits that facilitate funding to address climate challenges in drylands.
core_fields.abstract: Drylands are underdeveloped and overlooked in the context of building resilient agri-value chains. Making up over a third of African and global landscapes, these environments often face the brunt of climate breakdowns and food insecurity. By restoring these rangelands, and building agro-forestry cooperatives, communities are able to mitigate these risks while building holistic livelihoods in agriculture. NARA Climate designs these technical approaches and supply-chain innovations in a place-based approach, spending years with local partners like WFP and Welt Hunger Hilfe in places like Turkana in Kenya. At its core, the blue-print involves the identification of how people, planet and profit intersect. NARA's recent drylands model is a testament of how resilient and community-led initiatives can make rapid progress in addressing the most pressing needs in drylands, in particular drought, food security and youth employment opportunities. The introduction of carbon crediting to finance restoration and agriculture is a key innovation that has unlocked significant capital to restore landscapes and allow locally-led initiatives to develop their own operations and routes to market, especially in places like Turkana county that are often overlooked in the development of large-scale regenerative projects.

core_fields.title: Circular Farming for Improved Nutrition: Communal Gardens for Land-Insecure Households
core_fields.description: This project scales a circular farming model by creating communal rented plots with integrated gardens, chicken coops and composting. These hubs supply fresh ingredients for "pangan sehat" (healthy foods) packages for land-insecure poor households, delivered through our community network and posyandu. By replacing ultra-processed posyandu snacks with vegetables, eggs and other minimally processed foods, we aim to improve diets for at least 100 vulnerable households and build a replicable regenerative micro food system.
core_fields.abstract: In peri-urban Indonesia many pre-prosperous households, including pregnant women and young children, still lack affordable vegetables and animal-source foods. Most rent or share housing and cannot control land, so home-garden programs mainly benefit landowners, and gardens vanish when families move. Existing urban gardening initiatives often stop at production and lack a reliable market, while newer community-supported agriculture (CSA)-style farms, where consumers prepay for vegetable boxes, mostly serve better-off households in big cities, not land-insecure families. Our innovation, Circular Farming for Improved Nutrition, builds on our work since 2023 to provide "pangan sehat" (healthy foods) packages for children, elderly people, and pregnant women. These packages contain bundles of fresh vegetables, eggs, and sometimes meat. They are assembled from communal garden harvests, donations, and foods we still need to buy. We distribute them through our own community network and during routine sessions at government health posts (posyandu), reaching priority groups regularly. With the Seed Grant, we will establish and expand circular farming hubs on rented communal plots, managed by women's farmer groups and local residents, using composted household organic waste and chicken manure to grow vegetables and eggs. This will allow most pangan sehat packages to be supplied directly from community production, reduce dependence on personal funds, and provide a stable supply of diverse, familiar foods. core_fields.title: God's sustenance: fortified rice that nourishes the body and hope.
core_fields.description: Sustenance of God: Fortified Rice That Nourishes the Body and Hope is a social initiative that improves nutrition and food security in vulnerable communities through the production and distribution of rice enriched with 12 essential micronutrients. It aims to reduce malnutrition, anemia, and other nutritional deficiencies in children, pregnant women, the elderly, and low-income families by strengthening their diets without altering traditional habits.
core_fields.abstract: The Sustenance of God: Fortified Rice project addresses a critical problem: malnutrition and anemia, which affect millions of people, especially children, pregnant women, and families living in poverty. These deficiencies limit cognitive development, reduce productivity, and increase the risk of disease, making their resolution key to improving public health and social well-being. The solution involves producing and distributing rice fortified with 12 essential micronutrients (iron, zinc, calcium, vitamins A, B12, B9, and D, folic acid, among others). This innovation allows people to receive vital nutrients without altering their eating habits, as rice is the most consumed food in the target communities. The proposal is innovative because it combines advanced fortification technology, nutritional education, and community distribution through parishes, schools, and local organizations. While other fortified foods exist, this project stands out for its accessible, culturally appropriate, and low-cost approach, tailored to vulnerable populations. The solution is based on scientific evidence regarding food fortification, bioabsorption studies, extrusion technologies, and global policies to combat malnutrition promoted by the WHO and FAO. The benefits are immediate and sustainable: Rapid improvement in the nutritional status of children and adults. Reduction in anemia and increased energy, concentration, and school performance. Decrease in diseases associated with micronutrient deficiencies. Affordable access (with social support) to an essential and healthy food. Community strengthening, local employment, and solidarity-based distribution chains. In the long term, it contributes to human development, productivity, and food resilience in the region. This project is not about providing assistance.

core_fields.title: Seeding Food Sovereignty: Women-Led Opportunity Crop Hubs for Dzaleka Refugees
core_fields.description: Dzaleka's 56,000 refugees face catastrophic malnutrition 89% cannot afford nutritious food, children suffer 37% stunting, pregnant women 68% anemia. MAGUFINA will establish three Opportunity Crop Hubs where 90 women cultivate, process, and market nutrient-dense traditional crops using solar drying and milling. Women will produce shelf-stable nutritious foods, generate income, and deliver nutrition education. This will increase dietary diversity by 65%, create US$40 monthly household income, and transforms 600 families from food dependency to food sovereignty.
core_fields.abstract: Dzaleka Camp's 56,000 refugees face catastrophic food insecurity. Malawi has Africa's third-highest diet unaffordability rate at 42% (FAO, 2024), but Dzaleka exceeds 89% (UNHCR, 2024). Since December 2024, refugees receive zero food assistance previously only US$5 monthly. Child stunting reaches 37% versus 28% nationally. Women and children eat once daily 92% maize with minimal micronutrients causing anemia in 68% of pregnant women (Dzaleka Health Center, 2024). Over three years, MAGUFINA established four community gardens serving 800 families, increasing vegetable consumption by 23%. However, assessments revealed critical gaps: refugees lacked knowledge of nutrient-dense crops, could not preserve harvests (losing 40% annually to spoilage), and had no income from production. In Dzaleka Camp, Welthungerhilfe operates therapeutic feeding programs treating acute malnutrition but does not build sustainable food production or processing capacity treating symptoms rather than root causes. In 2024 community consultations, 347 women requested integrated training in growing, processing, and selling nutritious foods to achieve food independence. Our innovation establishes "Opportunity Crop Hubs" addressing these gaps through four components. First, women will cultivate amaranth, moringa, and African millets containing 3-5 times more iron, calcium, and protein than maize (WHH Research, 2023). Second, cooperatives will use solar dryers and hand-mills to process crops into shelf-stable porridge flours, eliminating losses. Third, women will sell products at camp markets with sliding-scale pricing, making nutrition affordable while generating income. Fourth, nutrition education will teach families to prepare these foods. Our Nkhotakota pilot increased dietary diversity by 68% and generated US$45 monthly income within 12 months.

core_fields.description: WellSprout is developing affordable, mushroom-based plant foods that improve nutrition, reduce environmental impact, and increase access to healthy diets. By transforming locally grown mushrooms into snacks, seasonings, and beverages, the project addresses rising diet-related diseases, food loss, and limited availability of nutritious plant-based foods. The innovation combines food science and culinary design to deliver safe, appealing, and sustainable products that benefit consumers, farmers, and communities.
core_fields.abstract: WellSprout addresses the growing challenge of poor nutrition, environmental strain from food systems, and limited access to affordable, healthy foods. In many low- and middle-income communities, nutritious diets are unaffordable or unavailable, while smallholder farmers face post-harvest losses and unstable markets. The innovation centers on value-added mushroom-based foods, including snacks, condiments, and beverages, designed using food science, nutrition, and culinary innovation. Mushrooms were selected based on scientific evidence showing they are nutrient-dense, rich in protein, fiber, and micronutrients, while requiring significantly less land, water, and energy than animal-based foods. Using dehydration and formulation techniques, WellSprout extends shelf life, reduces food loss, and ensures food safety and quality. Products are designed to be culturally familiar, appealing, and affordable, increasing adoption of healthier diets. Immediate benefits include access to nutritious plant-based foods for consumers, stable market opportunities for local mushroom farmers, and reduced post-harvest losses. Over time, the innovation supports healthier communities, improved livelihoods, and more sustainable food systems. By integrating nutrition, sustainability, and equity, WellSprout delivers a scalable solution aligned with global food system transformation.

core_fields.title: Prosopis
core_fields.description: In arid Marsabit, Prosopis juliflora, an invasive species, degrades ecosystems and livelihoods. NaPO transforms this challenge into opportunity by converting Prosopis into a regenerative value chain. Using our UN-recognized RAMAT restoration approach, we remove Prosopis to restore landscapes, process it into organic compost for community nurseries, and train women to produce essential oils and natural products through a Best Practice Centre. The project restores ecosystems, improves food security, and creates women-led, climate-resilient livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: In Marsabit s arid landscapes, Prosopis juliflora is a highly invasive species that degrades soils, displaces native vegetation, reduces grazing land, and undermines food security and livelihoods. NaPO s innovation transforms this environmental threat into a regenerative, community-led economic value chain. Using NaPO s RAMAT restoration approach, recognized under the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, Prosopis is systematically removed from degraded sites. The harvested biomass is converted into organic compost that restores soil fertility in community-managed nurseries producing indigenous, drought-resilient crops. This directly supports food production, ecosystem recovery, and climate adaptation. Beyond restoration, the innovation creates women-led green enterprises by training communities to process Prosopis into essential oils, soaps, and natural products through a Best Practice Centre (BPC). The BPC provides skills development, quality control, and branding support, enabling access to local markets and sustainable income generation in an arid zone with limited livelihood options. The solution is based on scientific evidence that invasive biomass can be safely repurposed to improve soils, enhance carbon retention, and reduce further ecosystem degradation. Immediate benefits include land restoration, improved soil health, and income generation for women. Long-term benefits include enhanced food security, biodiversity recovery, reduced land degradation, and a scalable model for invasive species management and regenerative livelihoods across dryland regions.

core_fields.title: Scaling Healthier, Low-Carbon Diets Through Digital Grocery Ecosystems
core_fields.description: CarbonTrac uses AI to help people make healthier, low-carbon food choices while they shop online. By adding real-time nutrition and carbon scoring into supermarket loyalty apps, we guide shoppers toward better options without extra effort or cost. Our system identifies nutrient gaps, reduces ultra-processed foods, and lowers the climate impact of grocery baskets through personalised swaps. CarbonTrac turns everyday shopping into a simple way to improve health and protect the planet.
core_fields.abstract: CarbonTrac is an AI-powered nutrition and sustainability engine that helps people make healthier and lower-carbon food choices directly while shopping online. The problem we address is simple but widespread: consumers want to eat well and reduce their environmental impact, but grocery platforms provide no guidance. As a result, diets are increasingly high in ultra-processed foods, nutrient deficiencies are common, and food consumption drives 34% of global emissions. CarbonTrac solves this by embedding real-time nutrition and carbon scoring into supermarket loyalty apps, no downloads or behaviour change required. Our 7-layer nutrition system analyses allergens, UPF scores, glycaemic load, nutrient density, and micro-macro profiles, while our carbon engine evaluates the full footprint of each product. The system then recommends affordable, easy swaps that improve both health and environmental impact, such as shifting from high- to lower-emission proteins or choosing fibre-rich alternatives. The insight behind CarbonTrac is that the online grocery ecosystem, worth $943B and rapidly growing, is the largest underused lever for improving public health and reducing food emissions. By acting at the exact moment of purchase, we remove complexity and make better choices effortless. Immediate benefits for consumers include a more balanced nutrient intake, reduced UPF consumption, fewer glycaemic spikes, and accessible nutrition guidance. For retailers, CarbonTrac improved profits, strengthens loyalty, and supports sustainability goals. For society and the environment, CarbonTrac drives lower food-related emissions and accelerates demand for healthier, more sustainable products. CarbonTrac turns everyday grocery shopping into a simple, scalable pathway toward healthier people and a healthier planet.

core_fields.abstract: Children and youth with disabilities in Tanzania face persistent barriers to nutrition, learning, and inclusion. Many come from families with limited agricultural knowledge, weak food security, and social stigma, which together restrict opportunities for healthy growth, participation, and future livelihoods. School feeding programs rarely integrate disability inclusion or hands-on food production, leaving a gap in both nutrition and skills development The innovation lies in combining disability-inclusive training, climate-smart agriculture, and school nutrition improvement into a single, scalable system designed specifically for youth with cognitive challenges. Unlike traditional school gardens or vocational programs, Gabriella s model integrates occupational therapy methods, adaptive tools, and structured routines to ensure that learners with cognitive disabilities can participate meaningfully and master real farming skills. The approach transforms the garden into a functional learning laboratory, where youth learn through multisensory, hands-on activities that match their developmental strengths economic pathway. Youth not only grow food for school meals but also generate surplus produce that becomes a micro-enterprise opportunity. This connects agriculture skills to actual income something rarely available in disability programs. community replication. Gabriella serves as a demonstration hub where schools, local leaders, and parents can learn how to create their own inclusive gardens. This makes the model low-cost, community-owned, and easily adoptable, even in rural settings. stigma-breaking mechanism. When youth with cognitive challenges successfully grow food, contribute to household security, and earn income, community attitudes shift from pity to respect. This positions agriculture not just as skill but as a vehicle for inclusion, dignity, and societal change

core_fields.title: Regenerative Rural Futures: Youth-Led Transition to Resilient Food Systems in Colombia
core_fields.description: Regenerative Rural Futures (RRF) empowers 100 rural youth in Colombia to lead the transition to resilient food systems. Through community biofactories, regenerative demonstration plots, technical training, and the RegeneraHub platform, the project reduces agrochemical use by up to 60%, restores soil health, and strengthens local economies. RRF combines ecological restoration with social inclusion, creating national impact by replicating regenerative practices in 100 rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: Rural territories in Colombia face soil degradation, biodiversity loss, and economic vulnerability due to decades of extractive agriculture and heavy agrochemical dependence. Regenerative Rural Futures (RRF) addresses this by introducing a regenerative paradigm that restores ecological vitality while strengthening rural economies. The innovation combines community biofactories, regenerative demonstration plots, and a digital platform (RegeneraHub) with a comprehensive training program for 100 rural youth. Biofactories produce biofertilizers and biostimulants, reducing agrochemical use by 40 60% and restoring soil health. Demonstration plots showcase diversified agroecological systems that enhance biodiversity and climate resilience. RegeneraHub connects youth, systematizes soil and productivity data, and ensures scalability. This solution is grounded in scientific evidence on regenerative agriculture s ability to improve soil organic matter, reduce external inputs, and increase functional biodiversity. By integrating ecological restoration with social inclusion, RRF creates immediate benefits lower production costs, healthier food, and improved food security and long-term impacts, including climate resilience, rural entrepreneurship, and national replication across 100 communities. For farmers and communities, RRF means autonomy, reduced costs, and sustainable livelihoods. For consumers and society, it delivers nutritious food and mitigates environmental degradation. Ultimately, RRF transforms rural youth into leaders of a regenerative future.

core_fields.title: Imitating Nature: Living Soils for Sustainable Abundance in Tropical Agroforestry Food Production Ecosystems of Bolivia
core_fields.description: The project addresses low productivity in organically certified systems by regenerating degraded soils using biologically based, sustainable practices. Compost, compost tea, cover crops, biological pest control, and circular resource use rebuild the soil food web, improve nutrient availability, and enhance climate resilience. The approach increases yields and nutrient density while maintaining organic certification, improving farmer profitability, reducing emissions, and supporting healthier, more resilient local food systems.
core_fields.abstract: We are tackling the challenge of an organically certified food system where plants show nutrient deficiencies, yields reach only 40% of potential, and farmers lack sustainable alternatives to increase production without compromising certification. This is highly relevant because low soil productivity drives rural poverty, raises food costs, reduces nutritional quality, and leaves producers vulnerable to climate variability, particularly droughts linked to El Ni o events. Our innovation restores soil health through sustainable regenerative practices, including thermophilic bio-complete amendments (compost and compost tea), cover crops, circular economics and biological pest control. All solutions are natural, use locally available ingredients, and fully comply with organic certification standards, ensuring that productivity gains do not compromise certification. This approach boosts nutrient density, raises farmer profits through higher yields and lower input costs, improves food accessibility, and captures carbon, generating environmental benefits. We will also conduct research to reduce food waste and extend shelf life. The solution is inspired by natural ecosystems. In living soils, plants obtain nutrients from a functioning soil food web. Forests, for example, maintain productivity year after year without plowing, fertilizers, pesticides, or irrigation. Our approach replicates these self-sustaining mechanisms in agricultural systems. Immediate and sustainable benefits include safer, healthier, and more nutritious local food at lower cost; higher profits and resilient production systems for farmers; hands-on learning for schools; stronger, drought-resilient communities; improved public health; reduced poverty; more stable food supply; and a healthier environment through lower greenhouse gas emissions and soils transformed into carbon sinks.

core_fields.title: Strengthening Indigenous Protein for Food and Nutrition Security in Central Africa, Building on Ghanaian Innovation
core_fields.description: Legendary Foods has developed a scalable insect-farming and processing system in Ghana for West and Central Africa, upcycling agricultural waste into a culturally desired source of protein, healthy fats, iron, and zinc. We are establishing a farm in Brazzaville to supply the DRC and Congo, combining proven farming technology with innovative processing to produce a shelf-stable dried palm larva product. Naturally nutrient-dense and fortifiable, it can be cost-competitive with staple starches and improve nutrition security.
core_fields.abstract: Legendary Foods addresses a critical food and nutrition security challenge in West and Central Africa: strong demand for affordable protein and micronutrients alongside reliance on seasonal, informal, and imported foods. Palm larva is a widely consumed and culturally valued indigenous food with high consumer acceptance and existing market demand. However, supply is seasonal, often unsafe, and increasingly linked to deforestation as wild palm trees are cut down to harvest larvae. Prices can exceed USD 30 per kilogram, limiting access for many households. The core insight behind this solution is that palm larva already provides protein, healthy fats, iron, and zinc and is widely consumed; the challenge is not acceptance, but unsafe, seasonal, and environmentally damaging supply. Insect farming offers a resource-efficient alternative, converting agricultural waste into nutrient-dense food with minimal land, water, and emissions. Legendary Foods has developed a scalable insect-farming system in Ghana and is now establishing a farm site in Brazzaville to adapt this technology to Central African conditions. Innovative processing converts fresh palm larva into safe, dried products similar to traditional dried fish and seafood, enabling year-round availability, improved food safety, more stable pricing, and optional micronutrient fortification. Immediate benefits include improved access to affordable, nutrient-dense foods, local job creation, reduced food waste, and lower pressure on forests. This approach supports schools, communities, and local producers while offering a replicable, low-cost model for improving nutrition security across Central Africa.

By providing low-cost, sustainable alternatives to chemical inputs, ROOTs build resilience, restores dignity, and creates safe, viable agricultural pathways for the most vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: The ROOTs Project introduces a community-led, climate-smart agroecology model that responds to food insecurity, climate shocks, and insecurity in Borno State conditions that make traditional farming unsafe, costly, or inaccessible, especially for women, youth, and persons with disabilities (PWDs). The problem is highly relevant: recurrent flooding, insecurity (including attacks and kidnappings on farmlands), rising costs of chemical fertilizers, and limited access to land have pushed many households out of food production. As a result, communities remain dependent on food aid with limited pathways to sustainable livelihoods. ROOTs address this gap through low-cost, locally adaptable innovations such as backyard farming, sack and vertical farming, compost-based soil enrichment, and waste-to-value practices. These methods enable food production in small, secure spaces using organic inputs, reducing dependence on expensive and environmentally harmful chemicals. The approach is supported by hands-on training, distribution of basic farming inputs (vegetable seeds, watering cans, compost tools), and the formation of peer learning groups to encourage knowledge sharing and long-term adoption. The solution is informed by agroecological principles, urban agriculture research, and practical experience in insecure and resource-constrained environments, including IDP camps and urban settlements. Demonstrations conducted with the Borno State Agency for the Great Green Wall showed strong community interest and viability of sack and vertical farming systems. Immediate benefits include improved household nutrition, reduced food costs, and safer income-generating opportunities. Long-term benefits include climate resilience, environmental restoration, reduced waste, and inclusive livelihoods, contributing to sustainable food systems and dignity for marginalized populations in Borno State.

core_fields.title: Enhancing Maternal Nutrition: Germinated Porridges with Safe, Sustainable Processing and Storage
core_fields.description: The goal of the project is to formulate nutrient dense porridges from germinated haricot beans, teff, and barley to improve maternal health in Ethiopia as eating porridge is a common practice. It enhances nutrient bioavailability, ensures microbial safety, reduces food waste, and extends shelf life. The innovation supports pregnant and lactating women via antenatal care, trains youth and women's cooperatives for scalable, eco-friendly production, contributing to improved nutrition, food security, and improved pregnancy outcome
core_fields.abstract: Maternal malnutrition affects 42-44% of pregnant women in rural Ethiopia, largely due to diets dominated by grains and deficient in essential nutrients like iron, protein, and fiber (1-3). Rural women are 2.6 times more vulnerable because of food insecurity and limited access to nutrient-dense foods, a challenge that persists despite ongoing interventions (6). These deficiencies contribute significantly to poor birth outcomes and increased child morbidity and mortality (4,5). This project addresses the problem by developing nutrient-rich porridges formulated from germinated haricot beans, teff, and barley, optimized to enhance nutrient bioavailability. The formulation demonstrated increased levels of key nutrients, including iron, zinc, calcium, and protein, while significantly reducing antinutritional factors (7). To ensure product safety and longevity, the blanched and dried product undergoes solar drying and hermetic storage, extending shelf life and reducing post-harvest losses. Product acceptability and scalability will be evaluated among pregnant and lactating women, alongside targeted training to promote sustained adoption and local production. The product undergoes validated germination, blanching, solar drying, and hermetic storage to ensure microbial safety and quality preservation. Health awareness and distribution will be integrated into antenatal care services, while youth and women's cooperatives are trained to scale production locally. This innovation is distinct from commercial products through its use of local germination to improve mineral absorption and hermetic packaging for preservation. It provides a culturally acceptable, WHO-aligned nutrient-dense food for pregnant and lactating women, contributing to reduced under-five mortality, improved food security, and reduced food waste in rural Ethiopia, nationwide impact.

core_fields.title: Microbial seed-applied solutions to enhance crop establishment and reduce chemical inputs.
core_fields.description: This project develops a microbial seed-coating probiotic that improves seed germination, early root system development, and protection against soil-borne stress. Acting at the most vulnerable stage of crop production, the solution reduces establishment failure and dependence on chemical seed treatments. Laboratory germination, root development, and biosafety data support feasibility. The technology offers a scalable, low-cost approach to strengthen sustainable and resilient food production systems globally.
core_fields.abstract: Poor seed germination and weak early crop establishment are major contributors to yield loss, input inefficiency, and production risk, particularly under variable soil and climate conditions. Farmers often rely on chemical seed treatments to manage early stress and disease, increasing costs and environmental burden while offering limited resilience under real-world conditions. This project addresses this problem by developing ProbiRoot , a microbial seed-coating probiotic that acts at the earliest stage of crop production. ProbiRoot uses selected beneficial microorganisms applied directly to seeds to improve germination consistency, stimulate early root system development, and protect germinating seeds against soil-borne biological stress. The innovation is based on the insight that small biological interventions at the seed stage can have disproportionate downstream impacts on crop performance. Laboratory germination assays demonstrated that selected microbial strains enhance radicle development and root system architecture without phytotoxic effects. The strains also exhibit complementary probiotic traits, including phytohormone modulation, stress mitigation, nutrient mobilisation, and antimicrobial activity, enabling both growth promotion and protection. By focusing on seed application, ProbiRoot is designed to be low-dose, scalable, and compatible with existing seed treatment practices. Immediate benefits include improved crop establishment, reduced early seedling failure, and lower reliance on chemical seed dressings. Over the long term, the technology supports more sustainable and resilient food production by reducing input dependency, improving resource use efficiency, and strengthening soil-friendly agricultural practices. This approach offers value to farmers, food producers, and food systems seeking affordable, biologically based solutions.

core_fields.title: Bishopstowe Agroecological Living Lab: A Circular Bioeconomy Model for Nutritious, Regenerative, and Equitable Food Systems
core_fields.description: The Bishopstowe Agroecological Living integrate proven agroecological and circular bioeconomy components into a single, community-owned food system that regenerates soil, reduces waste, improves nutrition, and creates inclusive livelihoods for women and youth. The innovation lies in unifying validated elements to regenerate soil, reduce waste, improve diets, and create women- and youth-led livelihoods. The Living Lab will demonstrate and scale this model to >25 hubs, reaching >5,000 households in seven years.
core_fields.abstract: Context South African communities face challenges due to fragile food systems, characterised by soil degradation, high food prices, low dietary diversity, obesity and undernutrition, food loss, unmanaged organic waste, and high unemployment rates among youth and women. These challenges compromise nutrition, agricultural productivity, and exacerbate environmental and economic vulnerability. Approach The Bishopstowe Agroecological Living Lab integrates agroecology, biobased soil amendments, biofeeds, climate-resilient indigenous crops and livestock, small-scale aquaculture, post-harvest handling, renewable energy agro-processing, and food waste valorisation into a circular, community-owned food system that regenerates soils, improves diets, reduces losses, and creates livelihoods. Novelty While each component has been validated individually, the innovation is novel in its systems integration, linking nutrient cycles, food production, renewable energy processing, market access, and nutrition behaviour change into one unified model designed for replication. Alternative solutions Individual practices, such as composting, BSFL, and agroecology, exist, but no integrated, circular, nutrition-sensitive model of this scope operates in the South African context. Technical feasibility Insights from UKZN, RUNRES, and global circular bioeconomy research show that combining biological waste valorisation, regenerative agriculture, and indigenous food systems delivers synergistic improvements in soil health, nutrition, and livelihoods. Immediate outcomes: Reduced food loss and spoilage, increased availability of affordable and nutrient-dense foods, lower input costs for farmers, improved household dietary diversity, and early income opportunities for women and youths. Long-term outcomes: Regenerated soils and reduced environmental waste, reduced malnutrition, renewable-energy-driven local value chains, climate-resilient food production, sustainable, and inclusive livelihoods across replicated hubs.

core_fields.title: RNA-based pest Biocontrol to Enable Sustainable and Nutritious Production in Latin America
core_fields.description: Current production relies heavily on chemical pesticides, increasing environmental harm, health risks, and costs. APOLO Biotech develops sprayable, GMO-free RNA solutions that target fungal pathogens without affecting beneficial organisms or leaving toxic residues. This project scales field-stable, sequence-specific dsRNA to protect high-value fruits and vegetables. By replacing chemical inputs with RNA-based products, it enables safer, more nutritious, and sustainable food production while accelerating real-world adoption.
core_fields.abstract: In the context of global warming, the emergence and spread of new crop pests are intensifying. As a result, the use of agrochemicals continues to rise, further contributing to pollution and accelerating climate change. Alongside herbicides and fertilizers, synthetic pesticides remain among the most harmful inputs, impacting ecosystems as well as the health of farmers, nearby communities, and consumers. Among our key developments, we have validated a highly specific double-stranded RNA molecule targeting Botrytis cinerea, a destructive fungal pathogen responsible for significant losses in key crops such as tomato, lettuce, strawberry, grapevine and blueberry. We have also designed another dsRNA specifically aimed at protecting banana crops from Black Sigatoka, a devastating fungal disease responsible for severe yield losses. Current control relies on fungicide applied between 15 and 50 times per year, which is close to being banned in Europe due to its toxicity. This situation is particularly critical in Central American countries, where major banana-producing regions lie in close proximity to populated areas, heightening exposure risks. Our stabilized dsRNAs act as exogenous precursors that trigger precise, crop-specific defenses against targeted pathogens. By leveraging these highly selective tools, we enable farmers to protect their crops more effectively, improve yields, and safeguard environmental and human health while significantly reducing the ecological footprint associated with conventional agricultural practices. APOLO Biotech is pioneering a new era in agriculture, where innovation and sustainability converge to secure the future of global food production.

core_fields.title: Climate-Resilient Organic Poultry Feed Using Black Soldier Fly and Soya Beans
core_fields.description: The project develops organic poultry feed using Black Soldier Fly larvae and soya beans to reduce feed costs, improve poultry productivity, and promote climate-resilient food systems. By converting organic waste into high-protein feed, it lowers environmental impact, supports sustainable protein use, and creates income opportunities for smallholder farmers, youth, and women. The initiative combines innovation, training, and scalable production to enhance livelihoods, nutrition, and local food system sustainability.
core_fields.abstract: he project introduces an organic poultry feed formulated from Black Soldier Fly (BSF) larvae and soya beans, providing a sustainable, nutritious, and climate-resilient alternative to conventional protein feeds. Smallholder poultry farmers face high feed costs, dependence on environmentally harmful fishmeal and imported soybean meal, and limited access to locally available, safe feed. These challenges reduce productivity, incomes, and food security while contributing to environmental degradation. The innovation addresses these problems by recycling organic waste into BSF larvae, which, when combined with locally sourced soya beans, creates an affordable, balanced, and environmentally friendly feed. BSF larvae efficiently convert food and agricultural waste into biomass, requiring minimal land, water, and energy, while producing significantly lower greenhouse gas emissions. Scientific insights into insect protein efficiency, amino acid composition, and sustainable feed formulation informed this solution. Immediate benefits include reducing feed costs by at least 30%, improving poultry growth, egg production, and household income, and creating employment opportunities for youth and women in BSF farming and feed production. Communities benefit from reduced organic waste and environmental pollution. Sustainable, long-term benefits include enhanced local food system resilience, circular economy adoption, conservation of conventional protein sources, and improved nutrition and livelihoods. By combining scientific innovation with social and environmental impact, this project delivers a scalable solution that supports healthier diets, sustainable agriculture, and climate-resilient food systems. core_fields.title: Early crop pests and pathogens detection solar-powered AI technology.
core_fields.description: Every year, 43% of global crop production is lost to pests and plant diseases, with Africa alone losing over 56% of its produce. Meanwhile, agriculture contributes approximately 24% of GHG emissions annually. To address these issues, FarmerLifeline developed proprietary solar-powered AI devices equipped with camera scanners that detect crop pests and diseases in real time. Farmers receive instant text notifications with tailored recommendations for fertilizers and pesticides, enabling them to take swift action.
core_fields.abstract: Globally, pests and diseases destroy 43% of crop production annually, costing over USD 220billion enough to feed 1.5billion people. In Africa alone, losses reach 47% of total crop output. Climate change is expanding pest habitats, intensifying crop damage, and threatening SDG#1(No Poverty) and #2(Zero Hunger). Meanwhile, the global agricultural sector emits approximately 9.8billion tonnes of greenhouse gases annually 24% of total global emissions and is projected to rise above 38% by 2036, potentially surpassing emissions from burning of fossil fuels for electricity and transportation sector. Farmer Lifeline developed proprietary solar-powered autonomous agricultural AI-devices that are permanently installed in the farmers' fields, equipped with AI-camera scanners that continuously scan crops in the farm, and utilizes Machine Learning and AI algorithms to detect any crop pests or pathogens. Farmers are then promptly notified via text messages in their local language with recommendations of carbon-negative fertilizers and environmentally-friendly pesticides. These recommendations reduce the use of harmful, emission-intensive chemicals and contribute to the reduction of overall GHG emissions in the agricultural sector. The devices also integrate an Early Warning API, satellite data and GenAI-powered predictive analytics to provide early warnings of extreme weather events such as floods, heatwaves, and droughts as well as climate-driven pest and disease outbreaks. This proactive system empowers farmers in underserved, climate-vulnerable communities to anticipate risks, make informed planting and harvesting decisions. The AI devices have been deployed across more than 5,900 farms, benefiting 23,970 marginalized small-scale farmers in Kenya, 65% of them being women. 1. core_fields.title: Promotion of Dried Foods for Advanced Nutrition (PODFAN)
core_fields.description: Rural markets face poor hygiene and unsafe food handling, increasing food safety risks and post-harvest losses, especially during periods of market glut. Fresh produce is highly seasonal and perishable, leading to waste and income losses. Although dried and minimally processed foods are more stable and sustainable, they remain underutilised. To address this, the PODFAN project is creating demand for nutritious, shelf-stable dried foods by increasing their appeal, trust, and acceptance among low-income consumers.
core_fields.abstract: Nigeria s food system faces a fundamental disconnect: nutritious foods are produced, yet up to 45% are lost due to poor handling, unsafe market practices, and weak demand for stable food options (FAO, 2021). Low-income households are disproportionately affected, cultural misconceptions, limited awareness, poor access, and low consumer trust limit the adoption of safe, nutritious foods, undermining diets, incomes, and food security. This project utilizes a market-driven, nutrition-led innovation that positions dried, minimally processed foods, like dried tomatoes, dried okra, and dried fish, as affordable, safe, and desirable everyday foods. With long shelf life and year-round availability, these products reduce post-harvest losses, improve food safety, and ensure consistent access to nutritious foods for low-income consumers. The innovation combines value addition with social and behaviour change communication (SBCC) to shift food handling practices, challenge cultural norms, and build trust and sustained demand for shelf-stable nutritious foods. The approach is guided by scientific evidence from the Nutritional Value Score (2025), which ranks these dried foods highly for nutrient density and essential dietary value. Food safety and market hygiene research in Nigeria, alongside UNICEF (2021) findings on malnutrition, highlight how poor handling and limited access drive nutrition challenges. Proper handling and minimal processing preserve nutrients, extend shelf life, and reduce environmental impact. The innovation delivers immediate and long-term benefits, low-income consumers get access to safe, nutritious foods, women producers and retailers reduce losses, increase sales, stabilise incomes, farmers and communities retain more value while cutting waste, strengthening resilient, inclusive, and nutrition-secure food systems.
