core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Food Hubs for Nutritious and Sustainable Rural Food Systems
core_fields.description: Agro-Product establishes solar-powered food hubs that enable smallholder farmers to transform local crops into nutritious, affordable and shelf-stable foods. By reducing post-harvest losses, promoting regenerative farming and empowering women s cooperatives, the project creates sustainable rural food systems. This innovation combines clean energy, food fortification and community entrepreneurship to ensure equitable access to healthy diets while strengthening local livelihoods and protecting the environment.
core_fields.abstract: In many rural areas of Chad, smallholder farmers lose up to 40% of their harvests due to lack of processing, poor storage and limited market access. At the same time, communities face widespread malnutrition and limited access to safe and affordable food. Agro-Product addresses these twin challenges through an innovative, solar-powered food processing model that transforms perishable local crops into nutritious and shelf-stable products such as fortified flours, fruit snacks and instant porridges. Our solution integrates clean energy technology, food fortification science and community entrepreneurship. Solar dryers and milling units reduce post-harvest losses, while fortification with key micronutrients (iron, vitamin A, and protein) improves dietary diversity. Farmers are trained in regenerative practices that restore soil health and increase productivity. Women s cooperatives manage local processing hubs, ensuring equitable participation and income generation. This approach is grounded in applied agricultural and food technology research showing that low-temperature solar drying preserves nutrients and prevents contamination, while local fortification can cost-effectively reduce malnutrition. Immediate benefits include reduced food waste, higher farmer incomes and improved nutrition for families. Over the long term, Agro-Product builds sustainable, low-carbon food systems that strengthen rural economies, empower women and youth and help communities adapt to climate change therefore turning local harvests into a foundation for food security and resilience.

core_fields.title: 50% Surplus: from waste to nutrition and flavour
core_fields.description: 50% Surplus transforms food that would otherwise go to waste; starting with okara, the nutrient-rich pulp from soy milk and tofu, into affordable, nutritious and delicious products. By turning surplus into high-value ingredients like okara flour and artisanal foods, the project reduces waste, improves nutrition, and supports a circular, zero-waste food system in the Global South.
core_fields.abstract: South Africa wastes 10 million tonnes of food every year. At the same time, low-income households, and institutional settings like schools and clinics, lack access to affordable, nutritious foods. A large portion of this waste comes from by-products like okara, the fibre- and protein-rich pulp left over from making soy milk and tofu. Although widely used in Asia, in South Africa okara typically ends up as animal feed or is discarded. Our innovation lies in processing okara into a shelf-stable flour suitable for baked goods, porridges, bars, wraps, and more. But the real breakthrough is introducing and championing the idea in South Africa that healthy, nutritious foods can be made with at least 50% rescued ingredients. Okara is only the starting point, the model is scalable to multiple surplus streams, turning waste into nutrition and flavour. Through product development, early prototypes already include wraps, crackers, bread, seasoning mixes, and bars. In addition to retail, applications range from school and hospital nutrition programmes to meal replacements and baby food enrichment. Based on our experience, a key part of the innovation also lies in strong partnerships. We are in discussions with a local university to formalise collaboration and have begun scouting potential commercial partners.

core_fields.title: Growing Futures: Scaling Coastal Organic Farms for Women and Youth Empowerment
core_fields.description: This project expands a five-acre coastal organic farm to 20 acres, empowering 100 women and youth with sustainable farming skills. It produces safe, nutritious food for schools and communities, strengthens local food security, promotes environmental sustainability, and ensures equitable access to healthy, affordable food, while fostering income generation and self-sufficiency for participants.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation expands a five-acre coastal organic farm into a 20-acre model farm, empowering 100 women and youth with practical skills in sustainable organic agriculture, nutrition-sensitive food production, and entrepreneurship. It addresses critical challenges in food systems: limited access to safe, nutritious food, unsustainable farming practices, and economic marginalization of women and youth. The project introduces innovative technologies to maximize productivity and sustainability, including a solar-powered irrigation system, greenhouses, and a nursery for high-quality seedlings. Organic waste is converted into compost to enrich soil, creating a closed-loop, regenerative system. Participants receive hands-on training in these technologies, alongside mentorship and market linkages, enabling them to become self-sufficient and economically empowered. Scientific insights guiding this approach show that solar irrigation, greenhouse cultivation, and compost-based soil enrichment significantly improve yields, nutritional quality, and resilience to climate variability. Integrating technology with community-based training ensures the innovation is scalable, sustainable, and replicable across coastal regions. Immediate benefits include improved food security, income generation, and skills development for women and youth, while communities gain access to affordable, safe, and nutritious food. Long-term benefits include a resilient local food system, sustainable agricultural practices, and empowerment of marginalized groups, fostering environmental stewardship, healthier diets, and stronger livelihoods. This project demonstrates how technology-driven organic agriculture can transform local food systems, providing a scalable model for nutrition, sustainability, and economic empowerment in Tanzania.

core_fields.title: Fruit Rescue: Scaling-up a Sustainable Practice for Preventing Food Loss in France and Croatia
core_fields.description: This project transfers a proven PoPEx sustainable practice of collecting and using unharvested fruit to NGOs in France and Croatia. It aims to adapt this initiative regionally/locally to (1) reduce food loss and waste and (2) raise awareness about affordable and nutrition food in surrounding. By training and engaging local NGOs in harvesting, processing, and donating unharvested fruit in cooperation with local stakeholders, we can save tonnes of accessible, nutritious, and chemical-free fruit from decay.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation of our project lies in transforming unharvested fruits (potentially wasted food) into a practical educational and community model. Rural areas in Croatia and France face a significant problem: more than 30% of fruit remains unpicked due to a lack of labour or organisation. This leads to economic loss, unnecessary food waste, and increased GHG emissions as fruit decomposes. Our solution adapts and transfers a proven good-practice model developed by the PoPEx NGO, which organises communities and volunteers to harvest and systematically distribute local fruit. Their long-standing experience, combined with practical insights into community engagement and circular-economy principles, shows that even small initiatives can save large quantities of fruit(up to now 3 tonnes). This project aims to spread and implement this model among rural NGOs through hands-on learning, structured training materials, and local pilot activities. Scientific insights show that young people learn best through experience and that practical sustainability education significantly improves environmental awareness, decision-making skills, and community responsibility. Immediate benefits include: Private fruit owners-access to labour for harvesting and agreed share of the picked fruit; NGOs-new regenerative model, vocational knowledge, and revenue from agreed share of the collected fruit; Local communities-stronger cooperation and improved resilience, less GHG emissions; Pickers (students, volunteers, citizens)-health benefits and free access to the share of the fruit, with possibilities for processing in schools and The environment-reduced food waste and lower GHG emissions. Long-term benefits: establishing a sustainable, regenerative model, raising environmental awareness of stakeholders, and reducing food loss, waste and GHG emissions.

core_fields.title: Scaling protein production through Vertical-Lake and its hub-and-spoke ecosystem for Sustainable Food and Equitable Livelihoods
core_fields.description: Vertical Lake is a unique modular lake-in-the-sky aquaculture system that stacks fish tanks vertically, producing traceable, organic fish while turning 100% fish waste into organic fertiliser and collagen products. This Growth Grant will fund four Mini-Vertical Lake pilots in Kenyan communities, growing our Hub-and-spoke ecosystem, validating technical performance, community operations and buy-back markets for fish and waste, and building the evidence and partnerships needed to scale a climate-resilient, circular protein and soil-health crop solution.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation tackles three linked problems in East African food systems: low access to affordable animal protein, soil degradation driven by synthetic fertilisers, and water and land scarcity in rapidly urbanising areas. Conventional fish farming uses large ponds, high water and chemical/antibiotic inputs, and often releases polluted effluent. Existing aquaculture systems are mostly horizontal, capital-intensive and not circular. Our insight was to redesign aquaculture as a modular, low-footprint, even community-scale infrastructure that mimics a healthy river lake ecosystem, can run off-grid and generates multiple revenue streams (fish, fertiliser, collagen). Our Earthshot Prize nominated Vertical Lake, now commercial in Nairobi, is a lake-in-the-sky : vertically stacked, gravity-fed fish tank system powered by renewable energy and cleaned by proprietary microbial biofilters. The system reuses ~98% of water and converts all fish waste into organic biofertiliser, collagen products for chronic wounds and biodegradable plastics, creating a zero-discharge, zero-synthetic-input loop that produces organic tilapia and regenerative plant nutrition from the same litre of water. We have now created a Mini-Vertical Lake (MVL) deployable in underserved communities, forming a hub-and-spoke ecosystem where communities operate/benefit from these units and sell surplus fish and waste back to Vertical Lake through a buy-back scheme. End users benefit equitably: low-income households gain affordable, safe, antibiotic-free, organic fish; smallholder farmers access local organic fertiliser that improves yields and soil health, minimising synthetic fertiliser use; youth operators earn livelihoods managing MVLs; and cities gain a replicable model for climate-resilient, circular protein and crop nutrition production close to markets.

core_fields.title: Strengthening Indigenous Crops Value Chain for Nutritious School Meals and Regenerative Futures in Nepal.
core_fields.description: Sarvaguna will scale a regenerative, indigenous-crop value chain that links more than 1000 smallholder farmers in Nepal with 15000+ nutritious school meals daily for children. The project does this by building farmer networks, creating sustainable supply chains, and innovating processing and recipes suitable for the taste and nutritional requirements of children. It provides affordable, healthy meals through HACCP standard kitchens and menu R&D, increasing farmer incomes while accelerating Nepal's transition to sustainable, equitable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: School meals in Nepal are highly dependent on refined and imported processed foods. On the other hand, indigenous crops like millets, sorghum, local legumes etc. possess nutrient-dense, climate-resilient, and culturally rooted characteristics but are on a decline due to weak markets, low incentives to farmers, and limited product innovation. Sarvaguna brings about a system-shifting approach that connects regenerative farmers with institutions where mass of people consume food daily and transforms indigenous crops into nutritious, child-friendly meals through processing, product development, and menu innovation. Our model brings together three innovations: i) Regenerative farmer networks: We organise and train smallholders, especially women, to produce indigenous crops; we guarantee offtake and fair prices. ii) Processing & Product Innovation: Small-scale and cold-pressed milling and central processing facility convert raw indigenous crops into school-meal-ready ingredients: multigrain flours for baking, noodles, porridges etc. The nutrition and culinary teams co-develop recipes aligned with children's taste preferences. iii) Nutritious meals at scale: Sarvaguna, through a HACCP-standard central kitchen and satellite/franchise school canteens, delivers affordable and nutritious meals daily by the thousands. This creates stable demand, reduces reliance on foods with nutritional voids, while unlocking long-term markets for local farmers. Our innovation has impacts on: 1) students through improved nutrition and eating habits, 2) farmers through assured income and regenerative farming practices, 3) communities through local value addition and jobs, and 4) the environment through diversified cropping and reduced food miles. It is scientifically rooted in nutrition research on the ground, evidence from local diets, and proven operational success.

core_fields.title: Healthy Plates for Seniors: A Community Food Security Initiative
core_fields.description: Healthy Plates for Seniors is a community-based food security initiative supporting vulnerable older adults facing hunger and isolation. The project provides consistent access to nutritious food, culturally appropriate meals, and essential nutritional education. Using a tech-enabled distribution system and community engagement, we identify high-need seniors, deliver tailored food support, and monitor wellbeing. Our goal is to reduce food insecurity, improve health outcomes, and ensure older adults live with dignity and connection.
core_fields.abstract: Healthy Plates for Seniors addresses the growing challenge of food insecurity among vulnerable older adults who face limited mobility, poor nutrition, rising living costs, and social isolation. Many seniors struggle to access or prepare nutritious meals, leading to worsening health outcomes and preventable hospital admissions. This problem is especially relevant in underserved communities where older adults are disproportionately affected by poverty and lack of support. Our innovation combines community-based food support with a tech-enabled identification, monitoring, and distribution system. Using simple digital tools and data insights, we map high-need households, assess nutritional gaps, and coordinate culturally appropriate food delivery through local volunteers and partners. The solution integrates three components: nutritious food packs, tailored nutritional education for seniors, and wellbeing monitoring to track improvements in diet, health, and social connection. The scientific insight behind this approach is the strong link between malnutrition, ageing, and long-term health decline. By providing targeted nutrition and consistent support, we reduce risks of illness, strengthen immune function, and improve quality of life. Technically, the project leverages digital data collection, community mapping, and a lightweight beneficiary-tracking system to ensure efficiency and transparency. Immediate benefits include increased access to healthy food, reduced hunger, improved daily energy, and stronger social ties. Sustainable benefits include long-term health improvements, reduced healthcare strain, empowered communities, and a scalable model that can be replicated across low-resource settings. Ultimately, the innovation ensures older adults receive the right food, at the right time, in a dignified, culturally relevant way.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Opuntia Feed and School Water-Harvesting Gardens for Resilient Dryland Food Systems
core_fields.description: This project transforms Laikipia's invasive Opuntia stricta into safe, nutritious livestock pellets and establishes rainwater-harvesting vegetable gardens in dryland schools. By restoring rangelands, reducing drought-related livestock losses, and providing children with fresh, healthy meals, the initiative strengthens food security and nutrition. Women and youth gain new livelihoods through harvesting, pellet production, and gardening, creating a scalable, community-led model that enhances resilience, promotes climate adaptation, and builds sustainable, integrated food systems in arid regions.
core_fields.abstract: Laikipia North faces a severe food and livelihood crisis driven by invasive Opuntia stricta and chronic water scarcity. The cactus has overtaken grazing lands, injuring livestock and reducing pasture, which undermines pastoral incomes and increases household vulnerability. At the same time, many dryland schools lack access to fresh vegetables, leaving children with nutritionally poor meals that affect growth, learning, and attendance. This project delivers an integrated, climate-smart solution to these linked challenges. The first component transforms harvested Opuntia into safe, nutrient-rich feed pellets for small ruminants. This ensures livestock survival during drought, improves milk and meat production, and creates a new income stream for pastoral families. Women and youth are trained in harvesting, de-spinning, processing, quality control, and market development. After harvesting Opuntia, degraded rangelands are restored using indigenous grasses and shrubs to enhance biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. The second component establishes water-harvesting micro-catchments, sunken beds, zai pits, and bunds in five dryland schools. These structures capture and retain scarce rainfall, enabling the continuous production of leafy vegetables for school meals. Children gain access to nutritious, locally grown food that improves health, classroom performance, and attendance, while households rely on Opuntia pellets to reduce migration for pasture. Scientific insights guide every step, from fodder nutrient analysis to soil-water conservation design. The project delivers immediate benefits, reliable livestock feed, improved nutrition, and new livelihood opportunities while creating long-term impacts through restored rangelands, resilient school gardens, and a scalable model for food security and climate adaptation in arid communities.

core_fields.title: Agroecological Adaptation Laboratories (AeD-LABs)
core_fields.description: Smallholders, representing 82% of farmers, are producing 75% of global food. They face daily climate impacts and urgently need scalable, farmer-led solutions. AeD-LABs supports them, especially women and young people, to test, validate, and share agroecological innovations through field labs, universities, and the farmbetter platform. With the Growth Grant, AeD-LABs will scale to 37 innovations, train a total of 40 farmer advisors, reach 2,000 smallholders, and secure sustainable financing for the long-term adoption.
core_fields.abstract: Farming families who rely on agroecology avoid intensive agricultural practices, which enhance deforestation, biodiversity loss, soil erosion, water pollution and increase vulnerability to climate change. Agroecological innovations, such as diverse seeds, soil regeneration, organic fertilization, landscaping, water management and microclimate creation, strengthen resilience, food security and farm-level autonomy. However, these local solutions rarely move beyond their community, limiting their potential impact. AeD-LABs addresses this gap through a farmer-led research and scaling model. AeD-LABs picks up farmer innovations in agroecology, researches them systematically and shares them widely, incl. via the farmbetter app. Communities with similar ecosystems and situations can apply the solutions and make them evolve. The farmers who invent a practice, steer the process: the intellectual property remains theirs, and they choose whether and how to share their innovation further. farmbetter provides the digital platform and app for farmer innovation. WOCAT provides data on the app regarding existing adaptation and sustainable land management practices. The Growth Grant will allow to promote innovation further: Several universities in Colombia & Ecuador will support the farmers in their research and document the progress of the innovations, starting in 2026. Through rural facilitators, AeD-LABs will reach more farmers, incl. working with other civil society organizations, cooperatives, extension agents and connecting with ongoing initiatives. Sustained financing, e.g. via consumers, will be explored.

core_fields.title: Making crops defend themselves against pests with natural elicitor compounds
core_fields.description: We restores crops natural ability to defend themselves by biomimicking wild plants. Instead of killing pests or genetically modifying crops, we target the interaction between plants and insects, re-activating defenses that modern varieties no longer express. Our solution are foliar sprays based on natural elicitor compounds that penetrate through stomata, activating plant defenses and boosting physiological responses that increase tolerance to herbivory; inducing semiochemicals that repel the pest and attract natural enemies.
core_fields.abstract: Pests are rapidly developing resistance to existing insecticides, while climate change is allowing tropical pests to expand into temperate regions. At the same time, decades of domestication have weakened natural plant defenses, making modern crops increasingly vulnerable and dependent on synthetic pesticides. This creates escalating costs for farmers, environmental degradation, and declining sustainability in food production. Semion addresses this challenge by restoring the natural defensive capacity of plants. Instead of killing pests or genetically modifying crops, we identify which innate defense pathways fail to activate during attack and use foliar sprays composed of safe, natural compounds to switch them back on. Once activated, these pathways trigger plants to emit volatile signals that repel pests, attract natural enemies, and improve resistance to diseases transmitted by insects. Our team chemical ecologists, plant biologists, entomologists, and agronomists draws inspiration from how non-domesticated plants use odor-mediated communication to defend themselves. Our first product targets the corn leafhopper, a major pest across the Americas that drives heavy insecticide use, particularly in South America. Field trials demonstrate that our approach can replace insecticides, increase beneficial insect biodiversity, and improve yield. The active compounds are biodegradable, food-grade molecules already used in perfumery, with no known harm to people or the environment. Because the defense pathway we activate is universal across plant species, our platform can be extended to numerous crops and pests. This positions Semion to deliver a scalable, sustainable alternative to chemical pesticides, improving farmer profitability, environmental health, and the resilience of global agriculture.

core_fields.abstract: Smartel delivers portable IoT-smart hydroponic systems designed to transform food production in cities and peri-urban areas. Using a combination of environmental sensors, organic nutrient solutions, and green energy, our systems automatically detect plant defects, trigger risk alerts, and allow remote control of the growing environment. This precision ensures consistent, high-quality yields with minimal resource use. We address a critical intersection of challenges: shrinking arable land, water scarcity, urban food deserts, and rising climate volatility. Conventional soil farming is increasingly unreliable, while current hydroponic solutions remain costly, energy-intensive, and inaccessible to small growers. Smartel s innovation emerged from insights in plant physiology, IoT engineering, and data-driven agriculture, enabling a solution that is affordable, modular, and optimized for constrained spaces. Our systems use 90% less water, 100% organic nutrients, and recycled single-use plastics, making them both environmentally regenerative and circular by design. By producing food locally, users reduce post-harvest losses, logistics emissions, and dietary deficiencies, particularly among children and low-income households. Immediate benefits include access to fresh vegetables year-round, improved nutrition, reduced costs, and increased farmer income. Long-term benefits include measurable reductions in carbon emissions (1.2 tons CO₂ saved annually per unit), water conservation, resilience against climate shocks, and decentralized food security for vulnerable communities. By integrating technology, sustainability, and community empowerment, Smartel redefines food production as a tool for equity, health, and climate resilience.

core_fields.title: Scaling Low-Cost Farming Technologies for Resilient Food Systems in DRC
core_fields.description: In North Kivu, DRC, where 72% live below $1.90/day and 25% face acute hunger, CODESPA will expand a completed, proven model that helps the poorest farmers grow more food and earn more income using four simple, low-cost technologies: donkeys, $4 tools, organic compost, and family gardens. Delivered through local sellers and savings groups, the model increased incomes by 439% and yields by 451%. This grant will scale it to thousands more farming families.
core_fields.abstract: In North Kivu, DRC, conflict and poverty have decimated rural food systems, leaving farmers without tools, transport, or the basic materials they need to grow food or earn an income. CODESPA s Rural M4P (Making Markets Work for the Poor) model rebuilds local food systems by developing both supply and demand for four regenerative, low-cost innovations, each designed to be Adequate, Affordable, Accessible, and Adaptable: -Donkeys to support field work and transport across mountainous terrain -Specialized tilling and weeding tools that double crop yields -Organic fertilizer made from household and market waste that increases yields up to 50 percent -Family vegetable gardens that provide food security and agroecological training Technologies are sold at market price through 95 trained local sellers, whose incomes increase by 11 percent. Demand is built through 11 savings and credit groups, awareness campaigns, and 888 installed gardens. Savings groups recycle capital, financing future purchases and local lending. From 2017 to 2020, the completed pilot reached 888 farmers (625 women), increasing farming income by 439 percent and production by 451 percent. Soils were restored without chemical fertilizer, and families consumed vegetables grown in their own gardens. The model is fully operational without ongoing donor funding. Its innovation lies in bundling simple, regenerative tools into a self-sustaining local system led by rural entrepreneurs, supported by communities, and designed for scale.

core_fields.abstract: Our innovation integrates honey traceability, localized early-warning systems, regenerative agroforestry, and carbon-credit incentives into one climate-smart platform that protects farmers, restores ecosystems, and builds trusted food supply chains. Smallholder farmers in East Africa face a triple challenge : Climate extremes that destroy hives, crops, and incomes, Market exclusion, especially in honey, where lack of traceability has led to EU rejections since 2011, and Low income and limited resilience, with 97% lacking climate insurance. Communities need solutions that improve livelihoods while regenerating land and restoring trust in food systems. Early-warning alerts use satellite and weather-station data to warn farmers five days before heatwaves, storms, or pests. Scientific insights: The solution was shaped by evidence that: Hive traceability reduces fraud and enables safe, premium honey markets. Agroforestry increases yields by 40 65% while sequestering carbon. Predictive climate analytics reduce losses by up to 30%. Smart-contract insurance unlocks instant financial protection. Benefits: Farmers earn up to 45% higher income, gain climate insurance, and access premium markets, Consumers receive safe, transparent, contaminant-free honey, Communities benefit from restored ecosystems and resilient livelihoods and Environment gains long-term carbon sequestration and regenerative land use.

core_fields.title: E-Chautari Community Hubs: Scaling Digital-Physical Services for Nutrition-Sensitive, Climate-Resilient Farming in Nepal
core_fields.description: E-Chautari Community Hubs strengthen Nepal's vegetable farmers and enterprises through a digital-physical, multi-sectoral partnership based model. GeoKrishi delivers climate-smart, nutrition-sensitive services and post-harvest support, while local facilitators provide field-ready solutions. Aadyanta Advisory coordinates private sector, cooperatives, and government. This Growth Grant will help transition GeoKrishi, Nepal's leading AgTech platform, into a private-sector-driven enterprise, using traceable data and sustainable business models to boost productivity, resilience, nutrition, and inclusive, financially viable rural food systems at scale.
core_fields.abstract: Rural-based farmers and enterprises in Nepal face low productivity, fragmented supply chains, limited adoption of climate-smart practices, and restricted market and finance access. Public extension reaches only 1/4 farmers, and Nepal's 51 Agriculture Knowledge Centres (1:1,500 ratio) are under-resourced. Farmers also grapple with degraded soil, unsafe chemical use, pests, climate shocks, high production costs, and low digital and financial literacy, trapping them in low-income cycles, limiting year-round nutritious food access, and weakening rural food system resilience. GeoKrishi has piloted an innovative digital-physical service model through E-Chautari hubs, local cooperatives, and government structures, delivering climate-smart, nutrition-sensitive services. The E-Chautari Community Hub system rests on three pillars. The service pillar offers on-the-ground guidance via hub facilitators, translating digital advisories into locally tailored practices. The technology pillar delivers climate-smart, nutrition-sensitive advisories, market and post-harvest information, financial tools, geotagged recommendations, traceability, and tele-agriculture linking farmers to experts nationwide. The business model pillar strengthens cooperatives, engages private-sector actors, coordinates inputs, and connects farmers to reliable markets. This integrated system is unique in combining digital precision, physical facilitation, and multi-stakeholder collaboration. Scientifically, it enhances yields, soil health, and climate-smart practice adoption; technically, it enables real-time advisory, traceability, and financial management; socially and economically, it builds cooperative networks, community trust, and equitable market access. Previously largely grant-supported, the next step is refining and de-risking the model to enable private-sector-driven scaling. Expected outcomes include higher productivity and income, improved access to nutritious vegetables, wider adoption of climate-smart practices, and stronger, more resilient, inclusive agricultural systems.

core_fields.title: Enhancing Centas Plus: A Sustainable, Natural Sanitizer to Improve Fresh Produce Safety, Quality, and Accessibility
core_fields.description: Centas Plus is a natural food sanitizer and preservative derived from Centella asiatica, known for its strong antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. Preliminary laboratory studies show that Centas Plus effectively inhibits major foodborne pathogens by disrupting microbial cell membranes and increase fresh produce shelf life. This Seed Grant project aims to advance Centas Plus from concept to scalable, explore more potential of this prototype for communities use.
core_fields.abstract: Centas Plus is a natural, plant-based food sanitizer and preservative developed from Centella asiatica, a traditional Malaysian herb known for its strong antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. This innovation addresses a major global challenge including contamination of fresh produce by harmful foodborne pathogens that cause thousands of illnesses every year, especially in households, schools, markets, and small food businesses where safe and effective sanitizing methods may be limited or unaffordable. Globally, 1.3 billion tonnes of food are wasted each year, with fresh produce contributing a major portion while Malaysia generates over 17,000 tonnes of food waste daily, and an estimated 45% of this is fresh produce such as vegetables and tropical fruits. Therefore, Centas Plus offers a safe, sustainable solution by using bioactive compounds in C. asiatica that naturally inhibit microbial growth. Scientific analysis shows that these compounds disrupt bacterial cell membranes, causing leakage of cellular contents and rapid cell death. This allows Centas Plus to effectively reduce pathogens on fruits and vegetables without the need for harsh chemicals. The formulation is biodegradable, non-toxic, and made from locally available plants, supporting regenerative and eco-friendly food systems. The immediate benefits include safer fresh produce, longer shelf life, reduced food waste, and greater confidence in food safety for consumers, farmers, schools, and communities. Over the long term, the innovation will help build a more resilient and regenerative food system by strengthening supply chains, reducing environmental impacts and ensuring that nutritious, affordable, and sustainably produced fresh foods remain accessible to all communities.

core_fields.title: Low-Carbon Rice Systems Enabled by Digital MRV and Farmer-Led Adoption
core_fields.description: This project pilots a Low-Carbon Rice System that enables irrigator associations adopt and document Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) and other low-emission practices. Using sensors, satellite and drone data, and a digital-based Measurement, Reporting, Verification (MRV) platform (Digisaka), the project supports carbon accounting and the branding of Low Carbon Rice product. The pilot will demonstrate environmental benefits, farmer livelihood potential through carbon markets, and a scalable pathway for climate-smart rice systems in the Philippines.
core_fields.abstract: Rice farming is a major contributor to methane emissions, driven by continuous flooding, inefficient fertilizer use, and post-harvest straw burning. These practices accelerate climate change, degrade soil and water systems, and expose farmers to rising input costs and climate risks. At the same time, farmers lack practical pathways to adopt low-emission practices that are measurable, trusted, and economically rewarding. Our innovation addresses this gap through a Low-Carbon Rice System that enables the adoption and verification of Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) and other climate-smart practices across diverse irrigation contexts. The system combines field-level water and environmental sensors, drone observations, and satellite-based remote sensing with a mobile and web platform (Digisaka) to monitor irrigation regimes, crop conditions, residue management, and emissions proxies in near-real to real time. This integrated approach makes low-emission rice production both operationally feasible and scientifically measurable. The solution is grounded in advances in agronomy and remote sensing, recognizing that AWD adoption fails when farmers and irrigation managers lack reliable monitoring and coordination tools. The system enables farmers, irrigators, and local governments to coordinate water management while generating credible evidence for carbon accounting frameworks such as the Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM). Immediate benefits include reduced water use, lower methane emissions, avoided straw burning, and improved input efficiency. Sustainable benefits include new livelihood opportunities for farmer cooperatives through carbon credits, strengthened trust in sustainably produced rice, improved irrigation governance, and scalable pathways for low-carbon rice systems that stay within planetary boundaries while supporting affordable and resilient food production.

core_fields.title: FishChain: Safe, nutritious, and equitable fish through sustainable EcoHealth innovation
core_fields.description: FishChain project involves application of a science-driven EcoHealth approach to improve fish safety, nutrition, and equity in Kenya's inland food systems. It leverages on molecular and microbial risk research at Kibabii University and community biosurveillance by EcoHealth CBO. It deploys rapid assays and toxin screening across cage farms and informal markets. The support will help validate the toolkit, generate baseline contamination data, and establish a scalable model for safe fish systems serving low-income communities.
core_fields.abstract: This innovation involves development of an EcoHealth fish value chain toolkit that integrates microbial science, community participation, and regenerative food system practices. It targets Kenya s inland fish value chains, which currently face increasing contamination from pathogens, algal toxins, and deteriorating fishing water quality (Wasonga 2023). Fish vendors and low-income consumers are disproportionately affected by these risks. Yet there are no rapid diagnostics, context-appropriate hygiene tools, and transparent market information that these stakeholders can rely on. Our innovation introduces: Rapid Microbial and Toxin Testing Tools:- Low-cost, field-ready assays will be developed and deployed to detect microbial contamination and toxin hotspots in cage farms and markets. This enables generation of real-time, actionable biosurveillance data that could support safer harvest and handling decisions. Community-centered safe-handling toolkit:- The fishing communities, particularly the market women, are disproportionately affected, and therefore, the project will design protocols with women vendors, cage farmers, and youth groups. This helps improve hygiene, water use, cross-contamination control, and waste management in informal markets. Micro-traceability and regenerative practice integration:- Involves creation of vendor logbooks, simple origin labels, and QR identifiers. These tools will help in guiding cage siting, ecological stress reduction, as well as adoption of regenerative aquaculture practices, thereby improving transparency and rebuilding consumer trust. Immediate benefits include a reduction in contamination, a more nutritious fish, improved vendor income, and strengthened consumer confidence. In the long term, the community actors will be empowered, with better climate-resilient, regenerative fish systems and scalable pathways for equitable and safer food access across East Africa.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Food Futures: Ensuring Equitable Access to Nutritious and Sustainable Diets for All.
core_fields.description: This project advances regenerative, sustainable, and human-centred food system innovations to ensure equitable access to safe, nutritious, and appealing food. By integrating climate-smart practices, water-efficient cultivation, and reduced post-harvest losses, it minimises water use and enhances resource efficiency. core_fields.abstract: 1. Innovation and Its Benefits This project introduces Nanak Kheti, a regenerative, water-efficient agricultural technology improving soil health, crop yield, and nutritional quality. It ensures sustainable production of safe, nutritious food, reducing water use by 40% and food loss by 20-25%. The innovation empowers farmers and strengthens local food systems by using scalable, human-centred approaches that are adaptable across diverse contexts, promoting climate-resilient and sustainable livelihoods. 2. Problem Being Solved and Relevance Traditional farming overuses water, degrades soil, limits root growth, reduces productivity, and restricts access to nutritious food. These challenges are severe in water-scarce and climate-stressed regions. Unsustainable practices threaten food security, farmer income, and ecosystem health, demanding immediate innovative solutions. 3. How the Problem is Being Solved In Nanak Kheti, fields are pulled 3 feet deep, and crops are planted in 1-foot-high pits. Tractor tracks form irrigation channels (nalis) delivering water 3 feet deep, promoting deeper roots. This improves nutrient uptake, strengthens plants, increases water efficiency, and provides biomass for livestock. Yield increases by 20-30%, and soil fertility and resilience improve. 4. Scientific and Technical Insight Based on soil hydrology, plant physiology, and regenerative agriculture, deep soil pulling and structured pits optimise water distribution, reduce evaporation, and enhance root growth. Integrating traditional knowledge with mechanisation makes the approach scalable, adaptable, and climate-smart. 5. core_fields.title: Chew me cup
core_fields.description: Reearth Uganda Ecovative Solutions is a youth-led startup creating edible, biodegradable cups from surplus fruits to fight plastic pollution, food waste, post-harvest losses, and food insecurity. Our nutritious, chemical-free Chew Me Cups offer a sustainable alternative to single-use plastic while providing farmers with a market for excess produce. Currently in product development, we aim to scale production and seek support to advance this eco-smart, locally driven solution for cleaner environments and stronger food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Reearth Uganda Ecovative Solutions is pioneering the Chew Me Cup, an edible, biodegradable cup made from surplus fruits that would otherwise be lost post-harvest. Our innovation addresses two urgent challenges: plastic pollution and food waste, both of which heavily impact Uganda's environment, farmers, and communities. Uganda experiences high post-harvest losses due to limited storage, transportation, and market access, causing nutritious fruits to go to waste and contributing to food insecurity. At the same time, single-use plastic cups continue to pollute ecosystems, block drainage systems, and harm human and environmental health. The Chew Me Cup solves both problems by upcycling surplus fruits into a functional, safe, and nutritious product that replaces plastic disposables. Using food science, dehydration techniques, and natural binding processes, we transform fruits into a heat-resistant, chemical-free cup that leaves behind zero waste. This approach is grounded in the scientific principles of moisture reduction and natural polymer stability, enabling durability without synthetic additives. Immediate benefits include: Farmers gain a stable, value-added market for excess produce, reducing financial loss. Consumers access a safe, eco-friendly, and edible alternative to plastic. Schools, cafes, and events reduce waste generation and improve sustainability practices. Long-term and sustainable benefits include: Reduced plastic pollution and improved environmental health. Lower food waste and strengthened local food systems. Increased income opportunities for youth and farmers through local production. Greater adoption of circular economy models in Uganda. Reearth's innovation demonstrates how everyday products can be reimagined to protect the planet while supporting communities.

core_fields.title: We develop scalable deep-substrate insect technology producing affordable protein and organic fertilizer from organic waste.
core_fields.description: Intrasect develops a scalable deep-substrate insect-rearing technology that converts organic waste into affordable protein and high-quality organic fertilizer. By simplifying infrastructure and increasing production density, our system enables significantly higher efficiency and lower costs than conventional insect-farming methods. The technology supports sustainable food and feed systems while reducing waste and environmental impact.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation addresses a fundamental inefficiency in todayâ€™s food system: we produce protein in ways that waste land, energy, and nutrients, while enormous quantities of edible organic material are discarded, and millions of people face food insecurity. Current protein sources, such as fishmeal and soy, are environmentally costly, and existing insect-farming systems are too expensive and complex to scale to a meaningful level. We solve this by introducing a new deep-substrate insect bioconversion system. Instead of raising insects in thousands of shallow trays that require constant handling and expensive automation, our method allows larvae to grow in substrate layers over one meter deep. Our simple proprietary approach ensures oxygen, temperature, and moisture remain evenly distributed throughout the material, enabling healthy larval growth at much higher densities. Immediate benefits include lower-cost, locally produced protein for aquaculture and livestock feed, reducing dependence on fishmeal and soy. Farmers and fertilizer users worldwide gain access to nutrient-rich organic fertilizer that improves soil health. Waste producers reduce disposal costs and emissions. At scale, the system cuts greenhouse gases, reduces pressure on land and oceans, and enables circular, resilient food systems that benefit communities, producers, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Integrated Food & Environmental Ento-based Development (I-FEED)
core_fields.description: Farm Uganda Farmers Group Limited s Integrated Food & Environmental Ento-based Development (I-FEED) project strengthens nutrition, sustainability, and livelihoods for over 3,000 smallholder farmers and refugee households. I-FEED fortifies cassava and maize flours with protein-rich crickets while converting cassava peels and maize bran into affordable animal feed using Black Soldier Fly Larvae. This circular, insect-powered model boosts food security, reduces waste, empowers women farmers, and creates scalable, climate-smart opportunities across Uganda s rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: The Integrated Food & Environmental Ento-based Development (I-FEED) innovation addresses malnutrition, low protein intake, rising food prices, and the high cost of animal feed affecting smallholder farmers and refugee households in Uganda. Cassava and maize core staples consumed daily are energy-rich but protein-poor, contributing to micronutrient deficiencies, especially among women and children. At the same time, large volumes of cassava peels and maize bran go under-utilized, while livestock farmers struggle with expensive conventional feeds. I-FEED solves these challenges through a circular, insect-powered model. First, Farm Uganda fortifies its existing cassava and maize flour with nutrient-dense crickets, significantly boosting protein content, essential amino acids, iron, and zinc without changing taste or affordability. Second, the project converts cassava peels and maize bran into high-quality, low-cost animal feed using Black Soldier Fly Larvae (BSFL), which efficiently transform organic by-products into protein-rich larvae and organic fertilizer. The scientific foundation of I-FEED lies in proven entomology and food science research showing insects superior feed conversion efficiency, low environmental footprint, and high nutritional density. Unlike traditional livestock, insects require minimal land, water, and inputs making them ideal for sustainable food systems in the Global South. End users benefit immediately and sustainably: Households, schools, and hospitals gain access to affordable, protein-enriched flours that improve diets. Farmers and feed manufacturers access cheaper, reliable BSFL-based animal feed. Rural women and refugees gain new income opportunities through insect farming. The environment benefits from reduced waste, lower emissions, and regenerative nutrient cycling. I-FEED creates a scalable pathway to healthier diets, stronger livelihoods, and climate-smart

core_fields.abstract: The Moroccan national water situation remains critical, given that agriculture alone consumes over 70% of water resources. Furthermore, thecountry and the continent suffers from recurring droughts, depletion of groundwater, and water losses estimated at over 30% due to inefficient irrigation systems. This scarcity, combined with inefficient management and a lack of field data, leads to systemic waste and major economic risks that threaten food security and rural livelihoods. RayAI introduces a hybrid ML/AI framework that delivers actionable insights for smallholders and largeholders without heavy hardware costs, bridging the gap between data and field-level decisions, via combined data, AI analytics, and local calibration to optimize irrigation and measure verified water savings. RayAI is an algorithmic ML models based on ingested multi-source DATAS ( satellite NDVI/LAI + Meteo-stations + SOIL+CROPS) to produce weekly/daily irrigation recommendations with mm of water needed, timing, and alerts to avoid over-watering and to improve water-use-efficiency , with a clear goal to make farmers reduce irrigation by 20 25%, increase yields by 15% and generate new income from verified water savings. Since rayAI will help to verify the quantity of water SAVED via Volumetric Water Benefit Accounting (VWBA) methodology and independent audit, and works with ESG BUYERS companies like Cococola, Nestl ,Danone, OCP, Unliver..etc. In addition, we provide to the farmers community an ISA Agreement program that allows farmers especially smallholders to benefit from regular free/lowcost monitoring and maintenance of their irrigation systems by approved third parties.

core_fields.title: Regenerating Kenya s Croplands to Strengthen Food Security and Farmer Livelihoods
core_fields.description: Boomitra s Kenya Croplands project enables smallholder farmers to turn regenerative practices into verified soil carbon credits removing carbon from the atmosphere while restoring degraded soils. Designed specifically for the Global South, it supports plots as small as one acre and aligns with Kenya s climate-smart agriculture goals. Using AI- and satellite-based measurement, the project produces high-integrity credits that channel climate finance to farmers, improve yields, build resilience to drought, and strengthen food security in vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Kenya face declining soil fertility, erratic rainfall, and rising input costs that reduce yields and farmers incomes while threatening food security. Over 30% of Kenya s agricultural soils are degraded, and about 75% of smallholders live on less than $5 per day, limiting their ability to invest in soil health. Boomitra s Kenya Croplands project supports farmers to transition to regenerative practices reduced tillage, residue retention, crop diversification, and cover crops working with implementation partners including the Farm to Market Alliance (FtMA), the Kenya Organic Agriculture Network (KOAN), the World Food Programme, and Food Security for Peace and Nutrition. Boomitra uses AI and satellite-based remote sensing to measure changes in soil organic carbon on plots as small as one acre. This replaces costly field sampling, making rigorous measurement affordable across smallholder landscapes. Verified carbon gains are converted into high-integrity soil carbon credits, creating an income stream alongside yield benefits. In the first crediting period, 987 farmers restored 44,673 acres and removed 88,294 tonnes of CO2, with potential to deliver US$728,426 in farmer income. The project has expanded to 3,730 farmers across 68,000 acres. Participants report an 8.5% increase in yields and a 20% reduction in chemical fertilizer use, with 100% observing improved soil health. Most soil carbon programs are built for large farms in the Global North. Boomitra s innovation combining satellite-based MRV, AI, and community-led extension with Kenyan partners brings high-integrity carbon finance to smallholders, delivering benefits for farmers, communities, and the environment.

core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Mini Processing Units for Climate-Smart Dagaa & Senene Production
core_fields.description: Our project deploys smart solar-powered mini processors on Lake Victoria islands to eliminate the 40 50% post-harvest losses in dagaa and improve safe, sustainable harvesting of senene. By replacing fuel-based drying and insect-catching systems with clean, rapid, weather-independent technology, we increase incomes for 5,000+ fishers and harvesters, deliver affordable protein to low-income families, and accelerate a climate-resilient blue-and-green economy.
core_fields.abstract: East Africa relies heavily on small fish (dagaa) and edible insects (senene) as affordable protein sources. Yet traditional practices, sun drying, fuel-based lighting, smoky insect-catching, and open-air processing, cause 40 50% post-harvest losses, contamination, inconsistent quality, and significant climate and health risks. These inefficiencies trap small producers in poverty and limit access to nutritious foods for millions of households, especially children. Our innovation is the Solar-Powered Mini Processing Unit (SMPU), a compact, climate-smart system combining: Solar-powered insect-catching lights that eliminate kerosene, generators, and smoke; IoT-enabled rapid dryers that reduce drying time from 1 3 days to 5 hours, independent of weather; Integrated frying stations for value-added ready-to-eat products; and Sensors and SMS alerts that monitor temperature, humidity, load, and energy use. This system is based on applied engineering research in solar dehydration, IoT sensing, and controlled-environment processing, technologies already validated in pilot deployments within our network. It directly tackles malnutrition, food contamination, and waste while reducing carbon emissions and improving revenue stability for small producers. Immediate benefits include: Higher incomes for 5,000 fishers and insect harvesters; Drastic reduction of post-harvest losses; Safer, traceable, hygienic protein for consumers; Lower environmental footprint by replacing fossil fuels with solar; Affordable, accessible protein for low-income families. Sustainable long-term benefits include scalable climate-resilient processing hubs, regional market expansion, empowered women and youth vendors, and a reliable protein supply chain across Tanzania, Rwanda, and DR

core_fields.title: RED DE ALIMENTACI N, INNOVACI N Y SOBERAN A - RAIS
core_fields.description: RAIS is a food intelligence ecosystem that strengthens capacities to understand and transform the food system in Cali, Colombia. It combines a collaborative digital learning platform, open territorial data, and a community of practice that connects schools, gardeners, entrepreneurs, youth, institutions, and citizens. RAIS promotes regenerative practices, informed decision-making, and participatory food governance, enabling sustainable, scalable, and community-led change through shared knowledge, collective action, and locally driven innovation.
core_fields.abstract: Cali s food system faces structural failures that limit its ability to ensure healthy, sustainable, and equitable diets. Limited access to reliable information, weak coordination among key actors, and low citizen participation in food governance deepen territorial inequities: 54% of residents faces food insecurity; the city produces only 1% of the food it consumes; 54% of adults are overweight or obese; and 1,650 tons of food are wasted daily. At the same time, Cali hosts a diverse ecosystem of positive initiatives, including community gardens, schools engaged in food education, youth leadership, sustainable micro-enterprises, communities with traditional knowledge, and local food policies. However, the absence of a shared space to learn, access trustworthy data, coordinate actions, and make these efforts visible limits their collective impact. RAIS proposes creating a collective food intelligence ecosystem to accelerate food system transformation through three interconnected components: (1) inclusive learning pathways for teachers, students, and citizens, linking nutrition, climate, agroecology, circular economy, and public policy; (2) a territorial food intelligence system that maps community gardens, sustainable businesses, and regenerative practices, democratizing data for decision-making; and (3) a community of practice that enables co-creation, collaboration and participation in food governance. By enabling local actors to generate data, share stories, and make practices visible, RAIS reshapes food narratives, reframing food as an act of health, justice, and territorial care. Grounded in global evidence and local experience (HLPE 2024; IPES-Food 2023; Urban Futures Cali), RAIS connects existing initiatives into a scalable, community-led ecosystem for long-term cultural and systemic change.

core_fields.title: Climate-Resilient Nutrition-Sensitive Agriculture for Most Vulnerable Families in the Coastal Sundarbans
core_fields.description: This project enhances climate resilience and nutrition security for most vulnerable poor households in the coastal Sundarbans by promoting nutrition-sensitive agriculture, diversified and ecological livelihoods, and women-led community governance. It strengthens adaptive farming systems through salt-tolerant crops, nutrition gardens, integrated farming, and water-smart solutions. Women, landless families, and marginalized groups receive productive assets, skills, and market access to improve food diversity, income stability, and resilience to recurrent climate shocks such as cyclones and salinity intrusion.
core_fields.abstract: Communities in the Sundarbans face severe climate impacts cyclones, tidal floods, salinity intrusion that have collapsed agricultural livelihoods and deepened poverty and malnutrition. Agriculture has become uncertain, forcing families into precarious wage labour and climate-sensitive fishing reducing access to nutritious food. Women and children bear the worst nutritional burden, with high stunting and anaemia levels. This project introduces nutrition-sensitive and climate-adaptive farming systems that reconnect food production with nutritional wellbeing while reducing climate vulnerability. Innovations include promotion of: □ Salt- and flood-tolerant crops, neglected and underutilized indigenous varieties □ Household & community nutrition gardens (including floating models) for year-round micronutrient supply □ Integrated Farming Systems (IFS) combining crops, livestock, fish, and poultry for diet diversity and income stability □ Diversify livelihood through livestock management and aquaculture □ Low-cost ecological practices composting, biofertilizers, IPM reducing input costs □ Water-smart technologies rainwater harvesting, pond desalinization, micro-irrigation □ Women-led enterprises and value addition (solar drying, pickles, puffed rice) The solution is grounded in agroecology, local knowledge, and climate science, with community seed banks and farm schools ensuring continuous innovation. Strong governance through SHGs and youth groups empowers women to lead local food and climate strategies. Benefits More diverse and nutritious household diets Improved Resilience, Risks distributed Reduced crop losses and growing season extension Improved soil, water, and ecosystem health Stronger community leadership This approach delivers nutrition access and long-term resilience for the region s most vulnerable families.

core_fields.title: From Seed to Sustainability: Millet-Based Pathways for Nutrition, Equity, and Climate Resilience in 4 districts.
core_fields.description: This project advances millet-based innovations to deliver safe, nutritious diets, regenerative farming practices, and reduced food loss across 8 blocks in 4 Districts of Odisha. By combining farmer training, community nutrition programs, and affordable processing solutions, it strengthens resilience and equity in food systems. Over 2 years, the initiative will empower communities with trusted, appealing, and accessible foods while restoring ecosystems and ensuring sustainable livelihoods within planetary boundaries.
core_fields.abstract: This project harnesses millet-centered innovations to address two urgent challenges: widespread malnutrition and unsustainable farming practices. By aligning with SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 3 (Good Health), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption & Production), and SDG 13 (Climate Action), it positions millets as a cornerstone of resilient food systems. Millets are nutrient-rich and climate-resilient, yet remain underutilized due to limited consumer awareness, inadequate processing infrastructure, and weak market linkages. Our solution integrates nutrition, regenerative agriculture, and food waste reduction. Farmers will adopt soil-restoring practices supported by seed varieties and soil health kits, while communities gain access to small-scale processing units and solar drying technologies that reduce post-harvest losses by up to 25%. Packaging innovations and consumer surveys ensure millet products are affordable, appealing, and trusted. The immediate impact includes healthier diets, reduced food waste, and 15 20% higher farmer incomes. Schools and communities benefit from reliable access to safe, nutritious foods, while producers strengthen market confidence through transparent labeling and safety standards. Long-term, regenerative practices restore ecosystems, diversify diets, and embed resilience into local economies. By combining nutrition, sustainability, and equity, this innovation empowers farmers, consumers, and communities to thrive within planetary boundaries. It demonstrates how millet-based pathways can transform local food systems, reduce environmental footprints, and create scalable models of inclusive growth.

core_fields.title: Sundry: Using Solar-powered Technology to Reduce Post- Harvest Losses of Perishable farm Produce
core_fields.description: Sundry is a school-led project that uses solar-powered dryers to reduce post-harvest losses of perishable crops like tomatoes and okra in Bauchi State, Nigeria. Coordinated by Gwani Ibrahim DanHajja Academy, the project provides farmers with safe, hygienic drying facilities while engaging students in climate-smart agriculture and agribusiness. This improves food quality, increases farmers income, and builds youth-led, sustainable food systems.
core_fields.abstract: The Sundry Project addresses a major Challenge of Post-harvest loss of perishable farm produce such as tomatoes and okra. This loss is estimated at about 46% in Nigeria, and is exacerbated by lack electricity, storage, and safe processing facilities, they are often forced to sell produce at very low prices or dry it openly in the field. Open-air drying exposes food to dust, insects, moisture, and direct sunlight, leading to spoilage, poor quality, and health risks. Our innovation is a solar powered, enclosed drying system that allows fresh produce to be dried in a clean, protected, and controlled environment using renewable energy. The dryers are built with locally available materials and do not rely on grid electricity, making them practical and affordable for rural communities. The solution is coordinated through Gwani Ibrahim DanHajja Academy, where students help operate and manage the dryers while learning about climate-smart agriculture and agribusiness. The scientific insight behind this solution is simple but powerful: controlled low-temperature drying using solar heat preserves food quality, extends shelf life, and prevents microbial growth caused by moisture. Enclosing the drying process improves hygiene and consistency compared to traditional methods. Immediately, farmers benefit from reduced post-harvest losses, better-quality dried produce, and higher income through value addition and off-season sales. Students gain practical skills and real-world learning. In the long term, communities benefit from improved food security, reduced waste, lower environmental impact, and a scalable, school-led model that strengthens local resilience and sustainable development.

core_fields.title: Catalyzing Antibiotic-Free Food Systems through Women and Youth-led Community-based Agro Hubs with Black-Soldier-Fly and Vermicomposting
core_fields.description: Ecohub-Solutions tackles a critical, underfunded global food challenge on antibiotic contamination in food-feed-value-chain. Antibiotic-laden animal feeds contaminate food, while overuse of chemical fertilizers and degraded-soils reduce productivity. Ecohub-Solutions tackles this through circular bio-upcycling system that produces Black-Soldier-Fly feed, BSF-frass, and vermicompost; providing affordable, antibiotic-free and chemical-free inputs. Women-and-youth-led agro-hubs generate income, promote safe feed adoption, and regenerate soils; delivering safer, nutrient-rich foods, higher crop-yield- creating scalable, low-cost, community-driven solutions for resilient, sustainable, and equitable food-systems.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation creates community-based agro hubs where women and youth convert the highly abundant, locally available agricultural residue and food waste into antibiotic free Black-Soldier-Fly larvae-feed and high-quality organic-fertilizers. It addresses major problems of dependence on antibiotics-laced feeds, degraded soils from overuse of synthetic fertilizers, organic waste being underutilized; leading to environmental pollution, greenhouse-gas emissions, and lost nutrients. Communities face unsafe animal-based foods, low crop-yields, and rising input costs, while women and youth struggle to access sustainable livelihood opportunities; issues that are particularly harmful to smallholder-farmers and low-income communities. The solution uses proven scientific insights from entomology, circular bioeconomy, animal nutrition, and soil health. BSF naturally breaks down organic-waste while producing a highly nutritious, antibiotic-free protein source for poultry, fish, cattle and pigs. Vermicomposting transforms remaining residues into nutrient-rich organic-fertilizer that restores soil health and boosts crop productivity. Community-centered hubs help ensure local ownership, cost-effectiveness, consistent supply, and hands-on green-skills. Technically, the system requires low water, minimal land, simple equipment, short-production-cycles, making it affordable, feasible and scalable. Environmentally, it cuts greenhouse-gas emissions, reduces chemical-runoff, and enhances soil-biodiversity. Socially, it empowers women and youth through green-skills, agripreneurship, and income opportunities. Immediate benefits include cheaper, safer livestock-feed; improved animal-health; reduced antibiotic residues in eggs, meat, milk and fish, and higher crop yields. Long-term benefits include resilient, regenerative food systems; cleaner environments; and sustained community livelihoods. For consumers, it means safer foods with fewer antibiotic residues. For society, it strengthens One Health outcomes by linking environmental-protection, animal-welfare, and human-nutrition into a single, sustainable solution.

core_fields.title: Transforming Macadamia Value Chains Through Affordable Grafted Seedlings and Regenerative Agricultural Practices.
core_fields.description: Our project revolutionizes macadamia farming by providing affordable grafted seedlings to smallholder farmers in Kenya. We offer comprehensive end-to-end services including seedling production, farmer training, crop aggregation, and processing into healthy snacks, oil, and butter. By promoting regenerative agricultural practices and biodiversity conservation, we create a sustainable value chain that enhances nutrition, reduces food waste, and ensures equitable access to profitable farming opportunities while protecting planetary boundaries.
core_fields.abstract: The Problem: Kenyan smallholder farmers lose 30% of their macadamia harvest to post-harvest waste and receive only 25% of market value due to exploitative middlemen. Traditional seedlings take 7-8 years to mature, limiting profitability and food security for over 10,000 small-holder farming households. Our Solution: We provide grafted macadamia seedlings that mature in 3-4 years and yield 90% more nuts per tree. Our end-to-end model integrates seedling production, farmer training, crop aggregation, and processing into healthy snacks, oil, and butter. Quantified Benefits: -Farmers: 60% income increase; harvest 50kg vs. 15kg per tree annually. -Food Waste: Reduced from 35% to under 5% through local processing. -Nutrition: Over 10,000 consumers access affordable protein and healthy fats. -Environment: 260 hectares planted which equals to 1,250 tons carbon; sequestered yearly. -Jobs: Over 150 processing and distribution jobs created per facility. -Timeline: Farmers earn returns in 4 years vs. 8 years. Our integrated approach transforms macadamia farming from subsistence to prosperity while regenerating ecosystems.

core_fields.title: Demonstration Farm: Responding to Drought , Maintaining Production of Nutritious Crops in rural Kisarawe District
core_fields.description: Smallholder farmers in Kisarawe District rely solely on unpredictable seasonal rainfall, making food production highly vulnerable to drought and climate variability. This demonstration farm introduces rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation to strengthen year-round production of nutritious, high-value crops. The project equips farmers with practical skills, improves food security, and builds long-term climate resilience through sustainable water management technologies.
core_fields.abstract: This project introduces a combined rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation model uniquely suited for drought-prone rural Tanzania. By addressing the critical challenge of unreliable water access, it provides farmers with a sustainable, climate-resilient alternative to rain-fed agriculture. Drip irrigation delivers water directly to plant roots, significantly reducing evaporation, runoff, and nutrient loss while improving yields and crop quality. When paired with rainwater harvesting (an underutilized but highly feasible technology in Kisarawe), the system creates a reliable water reserve even during long dry seasons. This reduces dependence on erratic rainfall, ensures continuous production, and stabilizes nutrition and household income. The innovation draws on established agronomic evidence showing that drip irrigation can dramatically increase productivity while lowering labor and input costs. However, adoption remains low in Tanzania due to lack of training, demonstrations, and upfront investment. This project fills that gap by establishing a hands-on learning site where farmers can observe, practice, and adopt water-efficient horticulture techniques. Immediate benefits include improved yields, reduced water waste, and enhanced food security. Long-term benefits include climate adaptation, environmental conservation, and strengthened community capacity to implement regenerative agricultural practices. This innovation enables smallholder farmers to shift from vulnerable subsistence production to sustainable, market-responsive agriculture.

core_fields.title: Turning Githurai Market Waste into Regenerative Inputs for Urban Farmers
core_fields.description: Ecofarm Organics turns daily heaps of unsorted food waste from Kiambu's Githurai Market and urban farmers waste into affordable organic fertilizers for low-income urban farmers, schools, and households. With a practical 6-Stage Farming Cycle and hands-on training, we will close the loop between markets and farms, boosting yields, cutting chemical dependence, and creating dignified green jobs for women and youth while reducing landfill waste and greenhouse gas emissions.
core_fields.abstract: Across major cities in Kenya, urban markets and farms generate tons of organic waste spoiled produce and manure that often decomposes in open dumps, near rivers and drains, releasing methane, contaminating water, and attracting pests. Githurai Market, which serves over 100,000 urban dwellers, produces more than 50 tons of food waste daily, 80% of it organic, yet the county manages only about 15 tons. Urban and peri-urban farmers simultaneously struggle with depleted soils, high fertilizer prices, and harmful pesticides, and face the stigma of irrigating with polluted river water, which undermines trust in their vegetables. Ecofarm Organics closes the food and farm waste loops with a circular, community-owned waste-to-soil system. We collect and sort organic waste from Githurai Market and urban farms, then transform it into compost, fortified biofertilizers, foliar sprays, and biopesticides, cutting greenhouse gas emissions from a landfill 35 kilometres away. With the Seed Grant, we will restore 100 acres near water bodies by applying 1,600 bags of compost plus 850 litres of foliar sprays, soil conditioner, and biopesticide, while training 200 farmers to make and use their own biological inputs. Our innovation uses simple biological processes composting, carbonizing, microbial brews, and botanically based pest control powered by materials already in communities hands. Immediate benefits include affordable, safer inputs, cleaner markets and waterways, and improved reputation for farmers. Long-term, we reduce dependence on imported chemicals, protect aquatic ecosystems, create dignified green jobs for women and youth, and build a replicable model for regenerative, circular food systems in African cities and settlements.

core_fields.title: Climate Smart Sesame for Nutrition, Equity, and Resilience in Zimbabwe
core_fields.description: Zimbabwe s reliance on imported sesame undermines food security and market growth. This project establishes climate-smart seed systems, multiplying 12 tons of foundation seed across 20 irrigated plots. At 3 5 kg/ha, this catalyzes >100 tons of certified seed, enough to plant 20,000+ hectares nationally within the project cycle. Twenty Village Business Units with hermetic storage and solar cleaning cut losses by 25%. Digital extension reaches 10,000 farmers, embedding nutrition, equity, and resilience in national transformation.
core_fields.abstract: Zimbabwe imports most of its sesame despite strong domestic demand and export potential. Farmers face three critical gaps: lack of certified seed, high postharvest losses, and limited value-added processing. This project addresses these gaps by scaling farmer-led seed systems and establishing decentralized sesame hubs that integrate seed multiplication, postharvest safety, and market linkages. Fifty Village-Based Advisors will multiply 12 tons of foundation seed across 20 irrigated demonstration plots, ensuring varietal purity, resilience, and data-verified performance. Through certified seed multiplication, this starter stock catalyzes over 100 tons of certified seed, enough to plant 20,000+ hectares at a recommended seed rate of 3 5 kg/ha. Twenty Village Business Units will be equipped with hermetic storage and solar cleaning technologies, reducing postharvest losses by 25% and minimizing aflatoxin risk through improved drying, segregation, and quality control. Digital extension platforms will deliver agronomic advisories, pest alerts, and market information to at least 10,000 farmers, prioritizing women and youth inclusion. Beyond seed and storage, sesame hubs will diversify products: cold-pressed oil for premium markets, flour and protein concentrates for bakeries and plant-based foods, and by-products repurposed for livestock feed and bioenergy, embedding food safety, nutrition, and circular economy principles. Immediate benefits include higher yields, safer grain, reduced losses, and lower import dependence. Sustainable impacts encompass stronger food security, inclusive market participation, healthier communities, and environmental gains, positioning sesame as a pillar of Zimbabwe s climate-resilient, nutrition-sensitive, and equitable food systems.

core_fields.title: From Desert to Dose: Solar-Automated, Organically Cultivated Moringa Value Chain for Anemia Control
core_fields.description: Desert to Dose transforms Tharparkar s indigenous Moringa trees into safe, affordable iron tablets using a solar-powered, contamination-free farm-to-tablet system. By integrating regenerative Moringa Sorghum cultivation with a GMP-aligned solar processing hub, we produce single-origin, SGS-verified tablets that improve anemia outcomes. A cross-subsidy model premium exports funding free supply creates sustainability while delivering Green Prescriptions to 1,000 vulnerable women.
core_fields.abstract: Pakistan faces a widespread anemia crisis affecting nearly half of women. Imported iron supplements remain expensive, poorly tolerated, and often inaccessible in rural regions. Open-air herbal drying introduces microbial and heavy-metal contamination, while synthetic binders reduce safety and traceability. Tharparkar s indigenous Moringa naturally rich in plant-based ferritin is underutilized due to inconsistent processing and lack of standardization. Our innovation introduces Sindh s first closed-loop, single-origin, solar-powered therapeutic production system. Moringa and Sorghum (binder source) are intercropped on saline, degraded soils using regenerative methods that improve organic matter and biodiversity. Sorghum starch is extracted onsite to create a natural binder, enabling excipient-free, traceable tablets. A 50 kW solar automation hub powers controlled-environment dryers, solar-ozone sterilization, micronization mills, and a precision tablet press. Solar-ozone drying preserves >95% micronutrient integrity while achieving a 3-log microbial reduction without chemicals. Batch-level SGS testing confirms purity and heavy-metal safety, enabling compliance with Organic, HACCP, and DRAP standards. Key innovations: A contamination-free process from leaf to tablet Sorghum-derived natural binder eliminating synthetic excipients Solar energy reducing operating costs and emissions Regenerative saline agriculture restoring degraded land This integrated system improves women s nutrition, strengthens local livelihoods, and establishes Pakistan s first scalable model for certified, single-origin therapeutic botanicals.
