core_fields.title: Scaling Hair-Based Mulch and Fertilizer to Regenerate Drought-Affected Farmlands
core_fields.description: Our project helps farmers facing severe drought regenerate their soils, save water, and improve crop productivity using hair-based mulch and fertilizer. We will distribute 8,800 Agropelo mats and 2,200 liters of Fertipelo to 220 farmers, preserving soil moisture, reducing irrigation demand, and restoring nutrient cycles. With training and field support, farmers will adopt a regenerative, low-cost solution that boosts yields while transforming discarded hair into a climate-positive agricultural input.
core_fields.abstract: According to the World Health Organization, by 2025 half of the world s population will live in water-scarce regions. In Chile, this crisis is already severe: 104 municipalities face prolonged drought, and more than 12 million hectares are at high risk of desertification. As soils dry out and irrigation becomes insufficient, farmers, especially smallholders, experience declining yields, rising production costs, and increasing dependence on synthetic fertilizers that further degrade fragile soils. There is an urgent need for affordable, regenerative tools that help farmers adapt to water scarcity. Our innovation transforms discarded human hair, an abundant, locally available waste, into regenerative agricultural inputs that directly address drought, soil degradation, and farmer vulnerability. We convert hair into two circular products: Agropelo, a hair-based mulch that forms a dense, breathable barrier over the soil, reducing direct evaporation by 71% and lowering irrigation requirements by up to 48%. It also suppresses weeds, stabilizes soil temperatures, protects roots, slows erosion, and gradually releases organic nitrogen and carbon as it decomposes over 3 5 years. Fertipelo, a liquid biofertilizer created through alkaline hydrolysis, delivers organic nitrogen, organic matter and micronutrients while enhancing microbial activity, without contaminating water sources or leaching into waterways. Together, these inputs immediately improve soil moisture, plant vigor, and crop quality. Over time, they rebuild soil organic matter, strengthen root systems, reduce dependence on synthetic fertilizers, regenerate soil and increase resilience to climate-driven drought, while diverting hair waste from landfills and transforming it into a scalable, climate-positive solution for farmers facing water scarcity.

core_fields.title: Smart Aquaponics & Digitized Solar Drying Hubs for Resilient Food Systems in Sierra Leone
core_fields.description: Advocate Plus proposes Smart Aquaponics & Digitized Solar Drying Hubs to boost food security, nutrition, and climate resilience. The project integrates water-efficient aquaponics with solar-powered, sensor-monitored drying to reduce post-harvest losses and produce safe, nutrient-dense foods year-round. Over 12 months, five hubs will train 1,250 women and youth, create microenterprises, cut food waste by 60%, and provide affordable fish and vegetables to more than 5,000 people across rural communities.
core_fields.abstract: Rural communities face chronic food insecurity driven by low agricultural productivity, rising input costs, post-harvest losses exceeding 40%, and limited access to affordable, nutritious food. Traditional farming depends heavily on rainfall, uses degraded soils, and offers limited income opportunities for women and youth. Furthermore, fresh fish and vegetables often spoil within days due to inadequate preservation and unreliable electricity. This innovation solves these challenges by integrating two complementary solutions: 1. Smart Aquaponics Farming - a water-efficient, closed-loop system where fish farming (aquaculture) and soil-less vegetable production (hydroponics) operate together. Fish waste fertilizes the plants; the plants clean the water. 2. Digitized Solar Drying Hubs - solar-powered dehydrators equipped with sensors that monitor temperature, humidity, and airflow to ensure safe, hygienic drying of fish and vegetables. Why this matters: Aquaponics increases yields 3-5 while using 90% less water, making it ideal for climate-stressed communities. Digital solar drying reduces spoilage, increases shelf life and ensures food safety without chemicals or refrigeration. Aquaponics harnesses natural nitrogen cycling principles and recirculating aquaculture technology. Solar dryers apply controlled-environment drying and thermodynamic airflow principles to retain nutrients while preventing microbial growth. Digital sensors ensure consistency, safety, and efficiency in both systems. Immediate and long-term benefits: Farmers: Higher yields, reduced input costs, new income streams Consumers & schools: Year-round access to affordable, nutrient-dense foods. Women & youth: Skills training and microenterprise opportunities. Environment: Lower water usage, reduced chemical fertilizer pollution, and minimized food waste. Communities: Stronger food security, improved

core_fields.title: AI-Driven Soil Intelligence With Minimal Sensors: A Drone-Based Solution for Affordable Farm Diagnostics
core_fields.description: This project develops and validates an affordable soil intelligence system that minimizes sensor use while delivering high-resolution fertility diagnostics for smallholder farmers. By integrating sparse in-situ soil parameter measurements such as pH and EC, with drone imagery through AI-based data fusion, the system generates continuous soil maps for targeted fertilizer management. This approach addresses Ghana s yield gaps by reducing input waste, improving decision-making, and enabling cost-effective, scalable soil diagnostics for resource-constrained farming systems.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Ghana face persistent yield gaps due in part to limited access to reliable, spatially explicit soil fertility information. Conventional soil surveys typically rely on high-density sampling, often requiring dozens or hundreds of measurements per field to capture spatial variability. This makes them costly, labor-intensive, and impractical for smallholder farming systems. While remote sensing provides continuous spatial coverage, it cannot directly quantify key soil parameters such as pH and electrical conductivity (EC). This project introduces an innovation that bridges this gap by integrating a minimal number of ground-based measurements with drone-derived spatial data through AI-driven data fusion. Strategically placed in-situ probes serve as anchor points, while multispectral drone imagery captures spatial patterns. Machine-learning models, including supervised regression and geostatistical interpolation, learn relationships between soil properties and remotely sensed indicators. Rather than attempting to measure soil conditions everywhere, the system extrapolates limited ground truth across entire fields, producing continuous, high-resolution soil fertility maps while requiring an order of magnitude fewer sensors than conventional approaches. In addition to technical accuracy, the project explicitly evaluates cost-effectiveness by comparing performance under different sensor densities. Scientific studies in Ghana show that spatial variability in soil fertility is a major contributor to yield gaps in staple crops. This innovation operationalizes those findings by offering a scalable, evidence-based alternative to high-density soil surveys.In the short term, the solution improves fertilizer targeting and reduces input waste. In the long term, it supports sustained soil health, lower production costs, improved yields, and climate resilience for smallholder farmers.

core_fields.title: Field Validation of Solar-Powered Pest Traps to Reduce Pesticide Use, Boost Smallholder Productivity in Ethiopia
core_fields.description: Arba Minch University has developed a functional prototype of a solar-powered pest trap designed to reduce insect pest pressure and pesticide dependence. With external funding, the Renewable Energy Centre will refine the prototype and conduct structured field validation in Lante village, including pilot deployment, farmer training, and preparation of local-language manuals. Building on the Centre s experience in rural renewable energy systems, the project aims to demonstrate performance, adoption potential, and scalability for smallholder agriculture.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Ethiopia experience significant crop losses due to insect pests and often rely heavily on chemical pesticides, which increase production costs, degrade soil health, and pose risks to human and environmental wellbeing. This innovation addresses these challenges through a low-cost, solar-powered pest trap developed at Arba Minch University to support non-chemical pest management in rural farming systems. The device uses a photovoltaic panel to power a violet-wavelength LED light that attracts targeted nocturnal insect pests during evening hours. Attracted insects are guided into a simple oil water collection chamber, where they are trapped without the use of chemical pesticides. The system operates autonomously and off-grid, making it suitable for remote areas with limited or no access to electricity. The solution is grounded in scientific insights on insect phototaxis and the effectiveness of specific light wavelengths (approximately 315 400 nm) for attracting key agricultural pest groups. A functional prototype has been developed and will be further refined in the laboratory with support from the award funding to improve durability, energy efficiency, and field performance. The project then focuses on structured field validation and performance evaluation under smallholder farming conditions. In addition to the technology, the project includes farmer training on correct device use, basic maintenance, and awareness of organic and integrated pest management practices to support effective adoption. Immediate benefits include reduced pesticide use, lower input costs, and safer working conditions for farmers. Over time, the innovation contributes to improved soil health, reduced environmental contamination, increased crop productivity, and enhanced resilience.

core_fields.title: Biofortified rice and wheat for nutrition security (BRAWN)
core_fields.description: This project tackles zinc and iron deficiencies in rural Bangladesh. It promotes biofortified rice and wheat, addressing low farmer awareness, value-chain gaps, and weak market demand. QR-code digital passports ensure traceability, seed authenticity, and consumer awareness. A central data system and QR-enabled booths provide verified seed info, agronomy guidance, nutrition details, and purchase locations. The project leverages iFarmer s platform, Dotlines Social s IT support, and national partners for farmer mobilization and seed supply.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: Bangladesh faces a major public-health challenge due to widespread micronutrient deficiencies, zinc and iron, among women and young children due to heavy reliance on polished rice, with minimal consumption of animal-source or zinc-rich foods. Zinc-biofortified rice and wheat can provide up to 40% of daily zinc requirements, adoption is limited due to low farmer awareness, mixing of biofortified and conventional grains, and insufficient consumer trust. Solution: The project introduces a QR-based digital traceability system to ensure seed traceability, authenticity, and nutritional assurance. A central data repository captures farmer, seeds, and crop information, while digital booths at agro-dealer shops provide easy QR access. Farmers receive seed authentication, localized agronomy advice, and harvest/post-harvest guidance to help them grow pure, high-quality biofortified grain. Consumers receive clear information on zinc and iron benefits, variety verification, recipes, and a map of reliable purchase points. Novelty: This approach integrates digital traceability, nutritional verification, and user education across the value chain. It protects grain identity from seed to consumer, ensuring reliable nutrient delivery and strengthening markets. Scientific Insight: National research institutes developed biofortified rice and wheat varieties with proven nutritional benefits. Pairing these with digital traceability preserves nutrient integrity, maintains seed purity, and supports informed use linking biological effectiveness with practical, scalable value-chain solutions. Immediate Benefits: Seed, grain quality, supply chains improved, better consumer trust premium pricing for farmers and millers. Sustainable Benefits: Reductions in zinc and iron deficiencies, reliable biofortified markets, improved public health, and meaningful contributions toward Zero Hunger and nutrition-focused sustainable development goals.

core_fields.title: Seeding Climate-Smart, Nutrition-Rich Rice Systems at Scale
core_fields.description: This project integrates high-protein biofortified rice (CR Dhan 310) with a climate-smart, low-emission rice production system across 50,000 hectares in Odisha. The combined innovation improves nutrient density by 40-60%, raises yields by 15-20%, and reduces ~114,000 tCO2e annually while saving water and lowering production costs. It strengthens farmer incomes and builds equitable, community-led seed and grain value chains through FPOs and women-led SHGs.
core_fields.abstract: Rice is the staple food for millions in India, yet current systems face two linked challenges: low nutritional quality and high environmental impact. Most widely grown varieties contain only 6 7% protein, contributing to dietary gaps, while conventional flooded rice generates high methane emissions and strains water resources. These challenges disproportionately affect smallholders, women, and low-income households who rely heavily on rice for both calories and income. The innovation integrates a breakthrough biofortified variety - CR Dhan 310, containing 10-11% protein, with a proven climate-smart cultivation system. CR Dhan 310 delivers 40 60% higher protein and 15-20% yield gains while maintaining desirable grain quality and consumer acceptance, directly improving nutrient density per hectare for rice-dependent communities. This package will be integrated within the FAIR CARBON PROGRAMME FOR RICE FARMERS registered under Gold Standard (https://registry.goldstandard.org/projects/details/4606 ). Connecting CR Dhan 310 with an existing carbon-certified rice program strengthens scientific and operational rigor by leveraging established digital MRV systems, farmer logbooks, and remote sensing tools to quantify water savings and methane reductions. Immediate benefits include improved household nutrition, reduced irrigation and energy costs, higher farmer incomes (10,000 12,000/acre), and strong consumer acceptance of taste and satiety. Long-term benefits include ~114,000 tCO2e avoided annually at 50,000 hectares, enhanced climate resilience, significant water conservation, and livelihood opportunities through FPO and women-led SHG seed and grain enterprises. Together, this integrated innovation offers a scalable pathway to transition rice systems toward higher nutritional value, lower emissions, and more equitable socioeconomic outcomes for farmers, consumers, and communities.

core_fields.title: NutriSpread Uganda: Sustainable High-Protein Peanut Solutions for Food & Nutrition Security
core_fields.description: We aim to contribute to food and nutrition security in Uganda by producing an affordable, high-calorie, high-protein peanut spread made from locally sourced peanuts. Distributed in low-cost sachets, the product will rapidly expand access to nutritious supplements for schools and low-income communities. The project strengthens farmer livelihoods through sustainable production and postharvest training, reduces aflatoxin risks, and promotes a climate-smart, locally driven nutrition solution that enhances community wellbeing and resilience.
core_fields.abstract: Uganda continues to experience significant gaps in food and nutrition security, particularly among school-aged children and low-income households who lack regular access to affordable, protein-rich foods. Existing peanut-based therapeutic products though highly effective are imported, costly, and restricted to health facilities. Their limited availability has contributed to black-market diversion, further reducing access for vulnerable communities. This reveals a substantial unmet need for legitimate, affordable, community-level nutrition solutions. Our innovation introduces a locally produced, high-calorie, high-protein peanut spread, packaged in low-cost 30 g sachets specifically designed for preventive and supplementary nutrition. Leveraging scientific evidence that energy-dense peanut pastes reliably improve weight gain and nutrition status, we formulated a simpler, non-therapeutic version using locally sourced peanuts, whey protein, and glucose syrup dramatically reducing cost while maintaining nutritional impact. The solution addresses the problem through a systems-strengthening approach: Localizing production to reduce reliance on imports and improve affordability Partnering with smallholder farmers and training them in aflatoxin control and sustainable postharvest handling Deploying youth and women as last-mile distributors to ensure equitable, community-wide access Integrating climate-smart and circular practices to reduce waste and environmental impact Immediate benefits include increased access to affordable protein supplements for schools and low-income households, safer peanut supply chains, and improved community nutrition. Long-term, sustainable benefits include enhanced farmer incomes, strengthened local value chains, youth employment, reduced aflatoxin contamination, and a resilient, community-driven model for nutrition security

core_fields.title: Community-Led Nutri Green Innovation for Safe, Sustainable and Equitable Food Systems in Northern Sri Lanka
core_fields.description: Communities in Northern Sri Lanka continue to face the lasting effects of conflict, climate shocks and economic instability, leading to poor nutrition, degraded soils and reduced resilience. This project introduces the NutriGreen Innovation Model, integrating climate-smart nutrition gardens, biofortified crops and community nutrition hubs; regenerative farming and food-waste reduction; and equitable food access through inclusive distribution, fair market linkages and women-led micro-enterprises to ensure safe diets, sustainable practices and affordable, trusted food systems
core_fields.abstract: Northern Sri Lanka continues to struggle with food insecurity driven by climate shocks, economic instability, degraded soils, and rising food prices. Many families especially resettled, women-headed, and low-income households cannot access affordable, nutritious food. Children and women face high rates of malnutrition, while unsustainable farming and chemical fertilizer dependency have reduced soil fertility. At the same time, 20 30% of local produce is lost due to food waste and weak value chains. These challenges demand an integrated, community-driven, and affordable innovation. The NutriGreen Innovation Model offers a practical solution by combining scientific insights from nutrition science, regenerative agriculture, and inclusive market systems. The approach recognizes that food insecurity is not only a production problem but a nutritional, environmental, and equity problem. The innovation solves these challenges through three integrated components: 1. Nutrition Innovation: Biofortified vegetables, drought-resistant crops, and climate-smart garden kits ensure families grow and consume safer, more nutritious food. Community Nutrition Hubs train households in child nutrition and healthy food preparation. 2. Regenerative Agriculture Innovation: Soil restoration using compost, microbial inputs, mulching, and natural pest management improves fertility while reducing chemical dependency. Food waste-to-value groups convert household waste into compost and feed, cutting losses and reducing environmental harm. 3. Equity & Access Innovation: Women-led micro-enterprises produce affordable nutrient mixes and safe foods, while community markets create fair value chains and provide low-cost options for consumers. Immediate benefits include improved household diets, reduced food costs, better soil health, and income for women. Long-term benefits include resilient climate-smart farming, reduced waste, stronger local markets,

core_fields.title: AtoANI Produce-to-Demand Regenerative Farming with Carbon-Financed Food Systems
core_fields.description: This project introduces a produce-to-demand farming model that helps smallholder farmers grow only what the market needs, reducing food waste and improving incomes. Using data on soil, climate, and demand, farmers adopt regenerative practices that restore soil health and cut reliance on synthetic inputs. The project links sustainable production to buyers and carbon finance, enabling farmers to earn from both food sales and verified soil carbon sequestration creating a climate-smart, equitable, and scalable food system.
core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in the Global South often overproduce without knowing real market demand, leading to high food waste, unstable prices, low incomes, and environmental damage from excessive chemical inputs. At the same time, consumers and food businesses struggle to access affordable, trusted, and sustainably produced food. This disconnect across the food system drives food loss, farmer poverty, and ecosystem degradation, making it a critical challenge to solve. The innovation addresses this gap through a produce-to-demand farming model that aligns what farmers grow with what buyers actually need. Using data on soil conditions, climate, and market demand, farmers receive clear guidance on what crops to plant, how much land to use, and when to harvest. This prevents overproduction before it happens, rather than managing waste after the fact. Regenerative farming practices are integrated to restore soil health, reduce dependence on synthetic fertilizers, and improve long-term productivity. The solution is grounded in agricultural science, digital soil mapping, and data analytics, combined with practical farmer knowledge. Scientific insights on soil carbon, cropsoil compatibility, and regenerative agriculture informed the system, while real-world pilots validated its feasibility and accuracy. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, more stable incomes for farmers, and reliable access to affordable, traceable food for consumers and institutions such as schools and food businesses. Over time, the model improves soil fertility, enhances climate resilience, reduces greenhouse gas emissions, and enables carbon finance to flow directly to farmers, creating a sustainable, equitable, and scalable food system that benefits people and the planet.

core_fields.title: Adaptive Crop Management for Climate-Resilient Agricultural Production
core_fields.description: This project extends an operational agronomy decision platform into additional crops and regions, focusing on production systems in Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and European supply chains. The work concentrates on adapting and validating dynamic fertilization, irrigation, and crop management protocols under variable climate conditions and regenerative management practices. By standardizing agronomic decision-making at scale, the project reduces input waste, improves yield stability, and supports more resilient food production systems.
core_fields.abstract: Agricultural production is increasingly challenged by climate variability, rising input costs, and inconsistent agronomic decision-making. In many farming systems, recommendations for fertilization, irrigation, and crop protection are made independently, using fixed plans or generic guidelines that do not adapt to changing conditions. This often results in poorly timed interventions, unnecessary input use, yield variability, and increased environmental pressure. These challenges are particularly acute in regions with limited access to experienced agronomists and in supply chains that require consistent and sustainable production. The innovation addresses this problem through an adaptive agronomy decision system that translates agronomic knowledge and field data into dynamic, field-specific management protocols. Rather than prescribing fixed inputs or products, the system works with locally available resources, including the fertilizers, pesticides, water sources, and agronomic practices already used by farmers. Recommendations are continuously adjusted based on crop development, soil conditions, weather, and field observations, allowing the system to adapt to local agronomic and regulatory contexts. A key technical insight behind the solution is that agronomic decisions are interdependent. Irrigation affects nutrient availability and disease pressure; fertilization influences crop vigor and susceptibility to pests; crop protection decisions depend on both water and nutrient status. The system therefore manages fertilization, irrigation, and crop protection together, accounting for their cross-effects rather than treating them as isolated actions. The platform does not require dedicated hardware, making it scalable and deployable in both high-tech and resource-constrained environments. Immediate benefits include improved timing of interventions, reduced input waste, and more consistent crop performance.

core_fields.title: Bacillus Starter Cultures for Sustainable, Safe Iru Production in Nigeria
core_fields.description: This project aims to create safe and sustainable Bacillus starter cultures for making Iru (fermented locust beans). We will also standardize how it is produced, make it the best it can be, and package it properly. By making Iru safer, more consistent, better tasting, and longer-lasting, we'll help producers give healthy, ready-to-eat Iru to homes and businesses in Nigeria. The project uses microbiology, fermentation improvements, and simple packaging to keep consumers safe, lower food risks,
core_fields.abstract: Iru is usually fermented spontaneously using whatever microbes happen to be around, which can make it unsafe, inconsistent, and not last very long. This can cause food safety issues, financial losses for producers, and limit Iru s potential as good food. We plan to find safe and effective Bacillus species from traditional Iru and turn them into starter cultures for controlled fermentation. Using standard ways to identify microbes, we'll select types that make Iru safer, taste better, more nutritious, and better overall. We'll then package them in a way that's easy for small businesses to use. Simple, cheap packaging for both the starter and the final product will make it last longer and be sold in more places. The idea is based on the fact that certain Bacillus types can make Iru better and can be used as starters, just like in yoghurt and cheese. We will play around with how warm it is, how acidic it is, and how much starter to use to get the best results. This will result in safer, more consistent Iru for consumers, with a better taste and longer shelf-life. Small producers will make more money because less of their product will spoil, and the quality will be better. In the future, this project will help with food safety, nutrition, and the growth of local businesses, allowing schools, canteens, and communities to have access to good Iru while also cutting down on waste and promoting the use of locust beans in a sustainable way.

core_fields.title: Track Seeds: Integrated Viability Tracking & Smart Seed Counting Platform
core_fields.description: Track Seed is a portable device and AI app that helps farmers and seed banks instantly count seeds and predict their germination rates. By combining these two vital insights into one affordable tool, it eliminates guesswork, reduces seed waste, and improves crop yields. Our solution empowers sustainable growing and equitable access to reliable seeds for resilient food systems.
core_fields.abstract: The Problem & Relevance: Farmers and seed companies globally face two fundamental, wasteful inefficiencies: not knowing how many seeds they have (leading to poor planning) and not knowing how many will germinate (leading to over-planting or crop failure). This uncertainty wastes a critical input, reduces yields, increases costs, and discourages the use of diverse, climate-adaptive seed varieties. It is a systemic barrier to sustainable and equitable food production. The Solution & Insight: Track Seed solves this by merging seed counting and non-destructive viability assessment into a single, user-friendly platform. The technical insight is that computer vision and machine learning can accurately classify, count, and by analyzing seed morphology a predict germination. Our innovation packages this lab-grade analysis into a low-cost, field-ready device and mobile app. Immediate & Sustainable Benefits: For Farmers & Growers: Immediate benefits include precise planting, reduced seed purchase costs by 20-30%, and higher germination success. Sustainably, this increases food production per seed, improves income stability, and encourages biodiversity by making local seed varieties a reliable, data-backed choice. For Seed Banks & Communities: They can instantly inventory stocks and certify seed viability, building trust in community seed-sharing networks. This preserves genetic diversity and ensures equitable access to high-quality, affordable seeds. For the Environment: The solution promotes regenerative practices by drastically reducing seed waste (a form of agricultural loss) and the associated waste of water, land, and energy from failed plantings. By optimizing input use, it helps keep food systems within planetary boundaries.

core_fields.title: Democratizing Precision Agriculture: Women-Led, Solar-Powered Community Aeroponics for Replicable, Data-Driven Food Production in Rural Lebanon
core_fields.description: This project aims to democratize precision agriculture in rural Lebanon by upgrading Human Link s pilot indoor aeroponic farm in Lebanon s Bekaa Valley into a solar-powered, multi-crop training and innovation hub. We will optimize the system (solar, water treatment, sensors), develop and validate protocols for traditional Lebanese herbs, leafy greens, and vegetables, finalize bilingual SOPs, and train around 25 local women and small producers, supported by a practical replication kit for low-cost aeroponic micro-farms.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation resides in adapting a technology usually found in high-tech greenhouses into a low-resource, easy-to-run, solar-powered indoor aeroponic hub that grows herbs, greens, and vegetables, and pairing it with a complete package of SOPs, training, and simple data tools that build local skills and make precision agriculture accessible to women and smallholders in rural Lebanon. Lebanon s economic, energy, and climate crises undermine food security, especially in rural Bekaa, with importantly limited and increasingly expensive agricultural lands making conventional soil farming difficult and risky. Under these conditions, open-field agriculture struggles to provide affordable, nutritious food year-round. Human Link established the only vertical indoor aeroponic farm in Lebanon to introduce a different approach: vertical soilless crop production where plants grow vertically with their roots suspended in air and irrigated with a nutrient solution, saving space and using up to 95% (based on our numbers) less water than soil farming with faster growth, cleaner production, and more consistent yields. We have already piloted this system using basil, documented problems and translated lessons into practical operating procedures and troubleshooting guides. This pilot demonstrated that aeroponics can operate in fragile settings and produce high-quality herbs. We seek to upgrade this pilot into a solar-powered, multi-crop precision farming and training hub. Immediate benefits include better local access to fresh, pesticide-free produce and practical skills for participating women and smallholders. The combination of optimized technology and structured SOPs, training, and a farmer-friendly replication kit creates a scalable precision agriculture model that other rural communities can adopt.

core_fields.title: People of eThekwini Woza Nathi (isiZulu term meaning come with us )
core_fields.description: Building on five years of learning and success in developing a farmer innovation precinct at Inchanga Agroecology Hub in eThekwini, this project scales an embedded approach to climate-resilient food production through three interconnected strategies: establishing inclusive multi-actor governance embedded in municipal structures; consolidating agroecological practices under the Participatory Guarantee Scheme (PGS) across multiple hubs and farmer networks; and connecting smallholder producers to Early Childhood Development centres (ECDs) as sustainable markets for nutritious, locally-grown food.
core_fields.abstract: Urban food insecurity and environmental degradation are a persistent feature of eThekwini s peri urban areas. After the five-year Woza Nami pilot at Inchanga Agroecology Hub, scaling faces three barriers: governance weighted toward field staff without senior authorisation; tenuous municipal commitment to agroecological principles and local knowledge systems; and weak smallholder market access with underdeveloped food safety systems for ecological production. There is clear evidence of success, with innovation centred on embedding governance mechanisms through a three-pronged approach: Structured multi-actor governance integrating government and civil society as long-term coordination body, activating eThekwini's 2026 food strategy framework, Consolidating and testing a locally adapted innovation in agroecological practices based on five core principles (biological soil fertility, pest management, polycultures, saved seed systems, water conservation) and enabling access to sustainable OPV seed and seedlings through municipal hubs and PGS networks, preserving indigenous and heirloom crop varieties and concession planting adoption. Linking farmers to ECDs as sustainable markets through PGS, addressing seed financing challenges. Evidence for these solutions emerges from research by Stellenbosch University, Medical Research Council, Seriti Institute, and Southern Africa Food Lab, plus insights from the Erasmus Institute, ICLEI, and the pilot at Inchanga. Evidence shows phased adoption of core practices works better than introducing all HLPE 13 agroecology principles simultaneously for resource-poor producers. Embedded municipal governance mechanism enables lasting food system transformation; increased volume and diversity of climate-resilient production; farmer income growth from healthy food sales; improved nutritional access for vulnerable communities; and demonstrated pathways for scaling agroecological transitions.

core_fields.title: Meat & Milk for Safe and Nutritious Diet Project (M2 Project)
core_fields.description: The M2 Project is aimed at improving access to safe, nutritious milk and meat in Ntoroko District. The project will support small-scale livestock farmers to ensure sustainable livestock production, digital market access, and compliance with sanitary and phytosanitary standards. Through a digital ordering and delivery mobile app, the project will enhance access to safe milk and meat products, reduce post-harvest losses, improve food safety, and expand dignified economic opportunities for youth and women pastoralists.
core_fields.abstract: Animal-source foods such as milk and meat contribute 33% of global high-quality protein and 17% of dietary calories, and essential micronutrients (FAO, 2025). In Ntoroko District, among Batuku pastoralist communities, climate stress, livestock disease outbreaks, weak market linkages, and poor food safety practices limit the availability of safe and nutritious animal-source foods, thereby reducing incomes for small-scale livestock farmers. Milk and meat are largely traded informally, even across borders into the DRC, without observing sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) controls, hence increasing health risks to consumers (UNBS, 2023). Evidence shows that healthy livestock, proper milk and meat handling, and transparent value chains are critical for food safety and resilient livelihoods (FAO, 2023; ILRI, 2021). The M2 Project introduces an innovation strategy that integrates climate-smart livestock production, food safety assurance, and digital market access. The project will pilot women and youth-managed milk and meat aggregation points in urban and peri-urban areas, where products will undergo quality checks before they are sold to consumers through a simple digital ordering and doorstep delivery mobile application (M2 Market App). The project will leverage the widespread smartphone and internet access to implement the digital app and reduce market inefficiencies and losses during milk and meat handling. Immediate benefits included increased access to safer milk and meat, reduced losses and improved incomes for livestock farmers, and dignified employment opportunities for youth and women pastoralists. Over time, the pilot will strengthen food safety culture, build consumer trust, and generate scalable evidence for climate-resilient, nutritious animal-source food systems

core_fields.title: Adolescents at the table: Co-creating healthier food environments in rural Vietnam
core_fields.description: This project implements a co-created, community-led intervention in rural northern Vietnam to improve adolescent food environments by increasing access to nutritious foods, promoting healthy diets, discouraging unhealthy options, and supporting sustainable practices. Adolescents, parents, schools, vendors, and authorities co-developed actions and will co-implement them at school, household, and community levels. Grounded in local realities, it strengthens multi-level, multi-sector capacity, fosters system-oriented solutions for healthier diets, and generates evidence for equitable, and sustainable food-system transformation.
core_fields.abstract: The food environment is the interface between food systems and people s diets, the settings where food is accessed and the characteristics of that food, its price, marketing, distribution and consumption. Vietnamese adolescents navigate complex food environments offering various foods, increasingly promoting ultra-processed and low-nutrient quality foods, with limited access to affordable, safe, and nutritious options. Adolescence is a critical period for shaping dietary habits, autonomy, and decision-making, with long-term consequences for health and productivity. Yet adolescents perspectives and agency are rarely incorporated into food-system interventions. Co-creation approaches can generate practical insights for problem definition, produce grounded solutions addressing stakeholder realities and enable broader policy and system change. Drawing on prior participatory research using co-created videos documenting adolescents perceptions and interactions within their food environments, community action plans were co-designed with adolescents, parents, school staff, local vendors and authorities. This process prioritised challenges and opportunities, proposing locally relevant actions. We intend to co-implement these co-designed food environment interventions in rural northern Vietnam to improve adolescents access to and consumption of healthy diets. Co-designed actions focus on increasing availability of fruits, vegetables and other nutritious foods; improving diversity and quality of meals, while discouraging unhealthy options; and strengthening positive food messaging in schools and communities. By combining adolescent agency with coordinated action among community and institutional actors, and leveraging system-level linkages across sectors, the project will strengthen capacities, align with institutional processes, and foster equitable, locally driven, and sustainable food-system transformation, with potential for adaptation and scaling to other contexts.

core_fields.title: Promoting Food Security and Environmental Protection through Establishment of an Indigenous-led Bioinput Training Center
core_fields.description: As part of the Sustainable Family Agriculture program coordinated by TWP and Utz Che', the project will expand knowledge and application of bioinputs ("bioinsumos") through establishment of a community-owned bioinsumos factory with Utz Che's agroecology training center, La Pecesita. By facilitating production of natural alternatives to chemical inputs, and creating a central space for workshops and classes, the project will improve food security and protect ecosystems amongst Guatemala's Indigenous communities within Utz Che's network.
core_fields.abstract: Guatemala is one of the lowest-income countries in the Americas, with nearly half of households facing moderate to severe food insecurity. The rural and Indigenous communities in which we work are particularly vulnerable, and often depend on household-level production for their subsistence and income. Increasingly, these communities have come to rely on chemical fertilizers and pesticides to produce sufficient food for their families, but these chemicals are costly to their income, health, and local environments. In cooperation with our local partner, Utz Che', our innovation focuses on the expanded knowledge, infrastructure, and application of "bioinsumos" (bioinputs) natural fertilizers and pesticides made from locally-sourced materials through our community-based Sustainable Family Agriculture (AFS) program. Engaging farmer-to-farmer learning, revitalization of heirloom species, and agroecology practices, AFS improves local food security through integration of Mayan ancestral knowledge and scientific innovation. Made from locally available materials, including manure, plants, and microorganisms collected from forest soils, variants of bioinsumos have been used by Indigenous communities in the region for generations, but this knowledge has largely been lost amidst social and political upheaval. Now, this ancestral practice is being revived through collaboration between rural communities and agricultural engineers, biologists, and soil scientists. Ultimately, bioinsumos boost soil fertility and crop yields, reduce family expenses, and prevent contamination in local ecosystems. The communities in which bioinsumos are being piloted have already observed increased yields and reduced pests and disease in beans, corn, coffee, and avocado, which promote household-level food security and increased income.

core_fields.title: Scaling Traditional Maize-Sorghum Mixtures for Climate Resilience, Soil Health, and Nutrition
core_fields.description: This project revives disappearing maize-sorghum mixed cropping through farmer trials and seed multiplication. Targeting 200+ smallholders, it demonstrates the agronomic, nutritional, and economic benefits of these systems. The goal is to improve dietary diversity, soil health, and climate resilience in drought-prone Ethiopia, creating a scalable, low-input model for similar regions.
core_fields.abstract: The Innovation is Reviving a Traditional Solution for Modern Challenges Problem: In Ethiopia's South Wollo zone, climate shocks and the promotion of maize monocultures are eroding traditional, resilient farming. This leads to fragile food systems, soil degradation, and hidden hunger due to poor dietary diversity. Relevance: This threatens the food security and nutrition of smallholder farmers, especially women and children, in a region highly vulnerable to drought. The Solution: We are reviving and scientifically optimizing the traditional practice of intercropping maize with sorghum in the same field. This leverages ancient farmer wisdom with modern validation. Key Insight: Scientific research confirms that mixing these crops creates a synergistic system. The tall maize and deep-rooted sorghum use light, water, and nutrients more efficiently together than alone. Sorghum's drought tolerance acts as a crop insurance, while its grains are richer in essential proteins and minerals like iron and zinc. Benefits: For Farmers: Immediate increased climate resilience and more stable yields. Sustainable improved soil health and reduced need for costly inputs. For Families & Communities: Direct improved nutrition from a more diverse harvest. Long-term strengthened local seed systems and knowledge sovereignty. For the Environment: Enhanced biodiversity in fields, reduced soil erosion, and a lower environmental footprint. This project turns proven local knowledge into a scalable, science-backed model for climate adaptation and nutrition security.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Cold Storage for Reducing Food Loss In Rural Communities
core_fields.description: This project delivers affordable, climate-smart refrigeration to off-grid communities, enabling smallholder farmers and rural market women to preserve fresh produce, fruits, and livestock products for up to 10 days, rather than 2. core_fields.abstract: Project Title Climate-Smart Cold Storage for Reducing Food Loss In Rural Communities Project Summary This project deploys affordable, solar-powered cold storage systems to reduce post-harvest food losses in off-grid and underserved communities. By extending the shelf life of vegetables, fruits, and livestock products, the solution improves farmer incomes, stabilizes food supply chains, and lowers emissions associated with food waste. The project supports climate resilience, food security, and inclusive economic growth in line with global food system transformation goals. Innovation Description, Relevance, and Benefits Post-harvest food loss remains one of the most critical challenges in global food systems, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, where up to 40% of perishable produce is lost due to a lack of cold storage, unreliable power, and fragmented market access. This undermines farmer livelihoods, increases food insecurity, and contributes significantly to avoidable carbon emissions. This project addresses the problem through Coola, a climate-smart refrigeration system designed specifically for off-grid and low-income communities. Coola combines solar energy with passive thermal storage (ice-as-battery, latent heat systems) to maintain stable cold temperatures even during power interruptions, eliminating dependence on diesel generators or grid electricity. The system is further enhanced by an antibacterial self-cleaning interior coating that improves food safety and reduces contamination risks. Coola is deployed using inclusive business models: pay-to-own and pay-per-use storage, which remove upfront cost barriers and align with the cash-flow realities of smallholder farmers and rural market women. This ensures adoption, scalability, and long-term sustainability.

core_fields.title: Biological Nanotechnology for Sustainable Agriculture and more nutritious foods
core_fields.description: This project develops innovative, sustainable bio-nanotechnology for agriculture using biogenic selenium nanoparticles, selenized bacteria, and plant growth-promoting microbes. These next-generation bioinputs boost yields, reduce agrochemicals and carbon footprint, enhance climate resilience, and improve soil quality. Additionally, our technology improves food nutritional quality through crop biofortification. Scaled at laboratory scale and tested in multiple crops, our technology offers multiple benefits and strengthens sustainability without complicating the field management and at low cost.
core_fields.abstract: Agriculture faces a critical challenge: producing more food while reducing the dependence on agrochemicals that harm soils, and human health. Current solutions are insufficient, agrochemicals degrade land over time, and existing biofertilizers often show inconsistent performance in real-field conditions. A sustainable, effective alternative is urgently needed. We solve this problem by combining plant growth-promoting (PGP) bacteria with nanotechnology to create next-generation bionanofertilizers. Using bacteria, we produce non-toxic biogenic selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) and selenized bacteria, along with PGP microbes from non-conventional genera. This platform is novel and merges microbiology and nanotechnology into a single, low cost, solution that increases nutrient efficiency and yields, enhances plant resilience, and improves soil health. Bio-synthesized SeNPs are rare and not commercially available at scale. Our approach is differentiated by its safety, stability, scalability, and proven field results in multiple high-value crops. Selenium (Se) is an essential micronutrient in the human diet, yet global intake levels remain below the recommended daily allowance. Selenium deficiency affects over one billion people worldwide and are linked to neurodegenerative and thyroid disorders, cancer, and infertility. Our technology enhances selenium and micronutrient uptake, as well as increased antioxidant levels in plants. This biofortification of crops offers an additional benefit to consumers, improving overall human health. Benefits -yield, reduced nitrogen use (150 300 kg/ha), and lower costs. -more nutritious foods enriched in selenium and micronutrients. -reduced pollution, improved soil fertility, and lower carbon footprint. -healthier diets and sustainable food systems. This innovation delivers immediate impact and long-term sustainability.

core_fields.title: Integrated Aquaculture and Insect-Based Feed Systems for Sustainable Local Food Production
core_fields.description: This project pilots an integrated food system combining multi-trophic aquaculture with insect-based feed production to deliver affordable, nutritious protein while restoring aquatic ecosystems. Fish and freshwater prawns are produced alongside vermiculture, black soldier fly, and local fly larvae to reduce feed costs and waste. Open-access training notes and videos will equip smallholder farmers, youth, and women to adopt and scale this regenerative, community-driven model.
core_fields.abstract: Small-scale aquaculture in Nigeria and similar contexts faces high feed costs, environmental degradation, and limited access to affordable protein, leading to low productivity and food insecurity. Conventional aquaculture depends on imported fishmeal, which is expensive, environmentally damaging, and vulnerable to supply shocks. At the same time, organic waste and nutrient pollution from farming systems remain underutilized. This innovation integrates Integrated Multi-Trophic Aquaculture (IMTA) with insect-based feed production to create a low-cost, circular food system. Fish and freshwater prawns are co-cultured with nutrient-cycling organisms, while black soldier fly larvae, vermiculture, and locally available fly larvae convert organic waste into high-protein feed. Waste from one component becomes input for another, reducing costs and environmental impact. The solution is grounded in ecological principles of nutrient recycling and trophic efficiency, supported by scientific evidence that insects can safely replace a significant portion of fishmeal, while IMTA improves water quality and system resilience. This combined approach maximizes resource efficiency using locally available materials and simple technologies suitable for smallholders. Immediate benefits include reduced feed costs, higher farmer income, improved water quality, and increased availability of affordable animal protein. Sustainable benefits include lower environmental pollution, reduced pressure on wild fisheries, climate-resilient food production, youth and women employment opportunities, and scalable open-access knowledge for communities, schools, and producers.

core_fields.title: Solar-Powered Modular Cold Room for Smallholder Produce Preservation.
core_fields.description: Our Modular solar-powered cold room reduces post-harvest losses by up to 40% for Ugandan smallholders. Using locally fabricated steel frames, high-efficiency PV panels, and battery-free refrigeration, each unit stores 5 tons of produce at 4oC. Pilot trials show 30% higher market price and 25% increased farmer incomes. We aim to deploy 50 units within two years, scaling through partnerships with cooperatives and impact investors, delivering climate-smart, profitable storage solutions across the region.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation is a modular, solar-powered cold-room that keeps fresh products at 4oC for up to 14 days without grid electricity. In Uganda, 30-40% of harvested fruits and vegetables spoil before reaching market, eroding farmer incomes and food security. The cold room tackles this loss by providing affordable, on-site storage that can be assembled in one day using locally sourced steel and fabricated panels. The design build s on two key insights (1) high-efficiency photovoltaic panels that generate enough power to compact refrigeration unit even in cloudy conditions, and (2) a battery-free system that reduces phase-change material (PCM) for thermal storage eliminates costly batteries and maintenance. Our engineers adapted a small-scale vapor-compression cycle and integrated PCM capsules that absorb excess solar energy during the day and release it at night, ensuring continuous cooling. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest waste (up to 40% less spoilage), higher market prices for farmers (average 25% increase), and reliable supply for schools, community kitchens. Sustainable benefits are low carbon emissions from reduced food loss, empowerment of youth-led agribusinesses, and scalable deployment through cooperatives, creating a resilient, climate-smart food system for Uganda and beyond.

core_fields.title: Sustainable Mountain Tea: A Climate-Resilient Food System Innovation in Albania
core_fields.description: This project introduces a climate-resilient mountain food system based on the sustainable cultivation of Mountain Tea (Sideritis raeseri) in Albania. By shifting from unsustainable wild harvesting to controlled cultivation, improved post-harvest processing, and traceable value chains, the project enhances food safety, nutrition, and rural livelihoods while conserving biodiversity. The planning grant will generate a scalable model for resilient, biodiversity-positive food systems in mountain regions.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation addresses a growing food system challenge: how to protect biodiversity-based traditional foods while meeting rising demand for safe, nutritious, and sustainable products. In the Gramos Mountains of Albania, Mountain Tea (Sideritis raeseri) a widely consumed, caffeine-free herbal food is increasingly overharvested from the wild due to poverty, climate stress, and informal markets. This threatens fragile alpine ecosystems while limiting income opportunities and food safety. The project introduces a cultivation-for-conservation food system model that replaces destructive wild harvesting with controlled, climate-resilient cultivation. The solution integrates scientific and practical innovations: conservation genetics to identify locally adapted plant material; nursery-based propagation to ensure consistent, traceable supply; Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) to improve food safety and quality; and low-cost solar drying technologies to reduce post-harvest losses and energy use. These components are combined into a single, inclusive value chain linked to fair, transparent markets. The approach is grounded in scientific insights showing that Mountain Tea is well adapted to harsh, low-input mountain conditions and responds positively to cultivation and post-harvest improvements. By aligning biodiversity conservation with economic incentives, the model transforms farmers and collectors into long-term stewards of the resource. Immediate benefits include safer, higher-quality food for consumers; more stable incomes and new roles for farmers, women, and youth; and reduced pressure on wild populations. In the long term, the innovation delivers a scalable blueprint for resilient mountain food systems that support nutrition, livelihoods, and ecosystem health.

core_fields.title: DIG scales Indigenous Farmer Field Schools to build resilient, community-led food systems in Western Kenya
core_fields.description: DIG Kenya will expand its Indigenous Farmer Field Schools (IFFS) to revive nutrient-dense indigenous crops, strengthen seed systems, and catalyze new market opportunities in Homa Bay & Kisumu, Western Kenya. Farmers will test traditional varieties, build seed-saving banks, and convert surplus into early food enterprises that spark broader market development. To complement IFFS s, DIG will engage in public outreach activities including radio and television broadcasting and local cooking demonstrations to further promote the indigenous foods.
core_fields.abstract: DIG Kenya s innovation adapts its globally recognized Farmer Field School model to intentionally preserve, grow, and commercialize indigenous foods, resulting in an Indigenous Farmer Field School (IFFS) approach designed for scale. This innovation emerges at a critical moment, as traditional species and local varieties rapidly disappear across Kenya due to hybrid seed expansion, climate pressures, and declining intergenerational knowledge. Unlike conventional agricultural training programs focused on production techniques, IFFS integrates indigenous seed saving, agroecology, market development, and farmer-to-farmer exchange into a single, community-driven framework. The innovation will train 400 farmers to identify culturally significant crops and conduct experimental trials that build a library of best practices testing resilience to drought, flooding, and pests. These trials generate guidance on optimal planting, harvesting, preparation, and seed-saving. Through DIG s self-scaling model, practices are then adopted by an additional 1,600 farmers, as each DIG-trained farmer trains an average of four others in their community. As a result, indigenous foods become integrated into 1,800 farmers fields and micro-enterprises, benefitting up to 10,800 people (average household size is 6). Once production is strengthened, the IFFS supports farmers to introduce their products into local markets. Public outreach, including cooking demonstrations, radio features, and television programs, builds community awareness and stimulates demand for indigenous vegetables. By pairing increased supply with targeted consumer engagement, the model establishes a reinforcing system that supports farmers success and expands market access. By combining scalable farmer-led production with demand creation strategies, DIG s IFFS model strengthens indigenous food systems across Homa Bay and Kisumu.

core_fields.title: Turning Organic Waste into Regenerative Fertilizer for Smallholder Farmers
core_fields.description: This project establishes a decentralized, community-led Trico-compost production system in rural Bangladesh to reduce chemical fertilizer dependency and create income for poor households. core_fields.abstract: Smallholder farmers in Bangladesh rely heavily on chemical fertilizers and pesticides due to land scarcity and yield pressure, resulting in degraded soils, rising input costs, health risks, and environmental damage. Rather than centralized factory production, the innovation lies in the inclusive system design: households are trained, guided, and quality-monitored; the compost is purchased directly, packaged, and distributed to local markets. Immediate benefits include reduced fertilizer costs for farmers, improved soil fertility, and new income streams for poor households. Long-term benefits include healthier food production, reduced chemical runoff, improved soil carbon, waste recycling, and stronger local food system resilience. The model is scalable, environmentally regenerative, and easily replicable across rural contexts.

core_fields.title: The Agrinexus hub initiative
core_fields.description: The Agrinexus hub initiative is an integrated, community-level service model that empowers smallholder farmers to store and trade their produce, basing on 3 strategic pillars. 1 Robust infrastructure (modern storage hubs in farming communities where farmers access a range of services and products including inputs, safe storage, processing and market linkages).2 Digital tools (We leverage technology and use smart platforms to manage, track, and engage different actors) & 3.Flexible finance through the warehouse receipt system.
core_fields.abstract: Farmers across sub-Saharan Africa commonly suffer post‑harvest losses of 20 40%. In Uganda, the loss is estimated between 4 to 5 million USD annually due to poor post harvest handling and lack of storage which forces them to sell their produce immediately at low prices. These losses combined with poor-quality inputs and weak access to reliable markets erode farmer incomes, compromise food quality, threaten regional food supply, and entrench cycles of poverty. The initiative addresses these challenges in our 3 strategic pillars that fuse into one farmer-centric solution. Farmers safely store their harvest in our warehouses, track inventory, access industry updates via digital platforms and access cash advances to cover urgent needs, eliminating the pressure to sell early. This enables them to wait for better market prices, make informed decisions, and maximize profits. Schools and institutional buyers benefit from a reliable, predictable supply of quality produce, while communities gain from stabilized food availability and strengthened local markets. While some storage and credit programs exist, none provide this holistic, end-to-end approach, giving farmers full control over their produce and market timing. We developed this model over time after witnessing the challenges that farmers were facing even as we engaged with them as traders. Our turning point was when we saw a farmer who had sold her produce for 2 subsequent seasons to cover a debt from a money lender and the seasons hadn t even started. This excessive exploitation & our knowledge of market dynamics spanning 7 years led us here.

core_fields.title: Banana Climate-Smart Resilience Through Data-Driven Adaptation Technologies for Banana Sustainable Production in Tiko, Cameroon
core_fields.description: Banana plantations in Cameroon are vulnerable to climate change shocks like rising temperatures, declining rainfall and recurrent droughts. These stressors have resulted in yield declined below 41.9t/ha/yr far below global average (100t/ha/yr) threatening livelihoods of over 20,000 workers and national food security. We propose innovative banana climate-smart system combining field sensors, SIMBA-based crop modelling, and farmer-led adaptation training to limit climate change shocks and optimize input use thus building climate-resilient, sustainable and nutritious banana system.
core_fields.abstract: Banana production in Tiko, Cameroon is increasingly threatened by climate change shocks like erratic rainfall, prolonged droughts, rising temperatures and climate-driven disease outbreaks. These stressors have led to declining yields, inefficient use of water and fertilizers, income instability for farming households and risks to national food security. Despite banana being a cornerstone of livelihoods and nutrition, farmers currently lack real-time data and decision tools to respond effectively to climate shocks. This innovation addresses the problem by deploying a data-driven climate-smart banana resilience system that integrates low-cost soil moisture sensors, micro-weather stations, crop simulation model (SIMBA), and timeseries-based yield forecasting. Real-time field data are translated into practical guidance for irrigation scheduling, fertilizer optimization, varietal selection, and adaptive practices like cover cropping and biostimulant use. Farmer training hubs ensure that digital insights are converted into on-farm action. The solution is novel in its holistic integration of digital sensing, crop modelling, time series analytics, and community-led capacity building within a single banana production system, an approach not currently applied in Cameroon s banana sector. While isolated tools exist (like sensors or advisory services), this innovation uniquely combines them into a locally adapted, scalable climate-smart platform. The approach is informed by advances in crop modelling, climate analytics, and precision agriculture, tailored to data-scarce tropical systems. Immediate benefits include reduced water and fertilizer waste, improved yields, and better climate risk anticipation. Long-term, the innovation strengthens farmer resilience, lowers environmental impacts, enhances food system sustainability and provides a scalable model for banana-growing communities across Sub-Saharan Africa.

core_fields.title: Colombia as a Living Lab: Farmer Leadership and AI to Scale Regenerative Agriculture
core_fields.description: Agent Tierra is an AI-powered agronomic advisor designed to support farmer decision-making. The project will expand Rare s proven farmer-led extension model by training, certifying, and activating new farmer multipliers whose leadership generates the social proof essential for widespread adoption of regenerative practices. Agent Tierra amplifies their impact through personalized guidance. This human-centered, AI-enabled system accelerates behavior change, strengthens food-system resilience, and positions Colombia as a national living laboratory demonstrating how responsible technology elevates farmer leadership.
core_fields.abstract: Agent Tierra is an AI-powered agronomic advisor that delivers real-time, personalized guidance to smallholder farmers through a low-connectivity, WhatsApp-based interface. While the technology is robust, the true barrier to scale is behavioral. Farmers adopt new practices when they see trusted peers succeed, not when a digital tool alone recommends a change. This project addresses that challenge by expanding Colombia s network of Profes: skilled farmer-leaders who model regenerative practices, host hands-on workshops, lead farm tours, and integrate Agent Tierra as a complementary support tool. Profes remain the primary agents of change. Agent Tierra reinforces, extends, and personalizes their guidance while ensuring that human leadership stays central. The innovation lies in this hybrid human AI architecture: - Profes create trust, relevance, and cultural legitimacy. - Agent Tierra provides continuous, tailored guidance aligned with farmer needs. - Farmers experience a model where technology enhances human agency rather than displacing it. This combination makes regenerative agriculture visible, credible, and attainable. Scaling the Profes network across Colombia will generate rigorous evidence on how AI can responsibly accelerate farmer-led transformation. The approach is designed for replication across diverse crops, climates, and sociocultural contexts, offering a paradigm shift for countries seeking equitable, human-centered digital agriculture solutions. Colombia becomes a living laboratory demonstrating that the future of agriculture depends on empowered farmers supported by responsible technology, not on technology acting in isolation.

core_fields.title: Digimama Ecosystem
core_fields.description: Soko Kijiji is transforming Kenya s urban fresh food system by connecting smallholder farmers, women traders and consumers through a trusted digital marketplace. We deliver safe, affordable and nutritious produce while reducing food loss across the value chain. Integrated into our operations is a surplus redistribution arm that rescues edible, unsold food and redistributes it to informal settlements. This model improves diets, cuts waste and expands equitable access to quality food.
core_fields.abstract: The DigiMama ecosystem is Soko Kijiji s integrated innovation designed to fix three interconnected failures in urban fresh food systems: unsafe food, high food loss, and the economic exclusion of women traders. The problem is relevant because women dominate informal fresh produce markets in Kenya, yet operate with little data, no demand visibility, high spoilage and low margins. At the same time, cities experience daily food waste alongside persistent food insecurity. DigiMama solves this by combining technology, logistics and social infrastructure into one system. Women traders are onboarded onto a digital platform that aggregates demand, forecasts volumes and coordinates sourcing directly from farmers and aggregators. Produce is quality-checked, handled through fewer touchpoints and delivered using reusable packaging, improving food safety and freshness while reducing waste. A key insight behind DigiMama is that waste is not a supply problem but a coordination problem. When traders see demand in advance and have guaranteed offtake, overbuying drops. When surplus still occurs, it is captured through Soko Kijiji s surplus redistribution arm and redirected to informal settlements through trusted community partners. Immediate benefits include higher and more stable incomes for women traders, safer food for consumers and reduced post-harvest losses. Long-term benefits include improved urban nutrition, lower environmental impact, stronger local food economies and a scalable model for inclusive, low-waste city food systems.

core_fields.title: Women-Led Climate-Smart Livestock Recovery for Food and Income Resilience in Berahle District, Afar
core_fields.description: Roots for Humanity's project improves food security and incomes in earthquake-hit pastoralist communities in Berahle, Afar, using a women-led, climate-smart livestock recovery strategy. Over the course of six months, it directly supports 40 women-headed households through livestock restocking, trains and certifies 15 Community Animal Health Workers (10 women and 5 men), and provides climate-smart livestock feeding and income-generation training to 30 community members, establishing a sustainable, locally managed system for resilient pastoral livelihoods.
core_fields.abstract: Innovation Description and Benefits Pastoralist communities in Berahle District, Afar, lost their primary food and income source when the 2025 earthquake killed livestock and collapsed local animal health services. Traditional responses focus on one-time livestock replacement, which often fails because animals die from disease, poor feeding, or lack of follow-up care leaving households dependent on aid. This project introduces a women-led, climate-smart livestock recovery model that shifts recovery from short-term asset replacement to long-term, community-managed resilience. Instead of large-scale restocking, the project combines targeted livestock restocking for 40 women-headed households with the training and certification of 15 Community Animal Health Workers (10 women, 5 men) and climate-smart feeding and income training for 30 community members. The solution is based on well-established evidence that livestock survival and productivity in drylands depend more on local veterinary access, preventive care, and feed management than on animal numbers alone. By training women as CAHWs and equipping them with veterinary kits and a revolving micro-fund, the project creates a permanent, locally available animal health service. Climate-smart feeding and fodder management reduce drought risk, improve milk production, and protect grazing land. Immediate benefits include restored access to milk and income, reduced livestock mortality, affordable veterinary care, and new paid roles for women. Sustainable benefits include women s economic empowerment, improved household nutrition, climate-resilient livestock systems, reduced environmental pressure, and a scalable recovery model owned and managed by the community long after the project ends.

core_fields.title: Scaling Nature-Based Solutions for Safe, Sustainable, and Affordable Citrus in Nepal
core_fields.description: Nepal s citrus system is collapsing due to pests, degraded soils, and heavy pesticide use, which threatens nutrition, farmer livelihoods, and consumer trust. This project introduces an integrated food-system solution that combines Area-Wide pest control, regenerative Tricho-Vermicompost, and emerging biological control into a scalable, community-led model. It produces safer and more nutritious citrus, reduces chemical dependence, strengthens local bio-input markets, improves affordability and reliability, and aligns with Nepal s food and agriculture policy frameworks.
core_fields.abstract: This project scales a municipality-led Citrus Resilience Package, a replicable operating model to stabilise citrus production and food safety. Rather than isolated farm-level interventions, the model aligns municipal coordination, farmer practices, and local input supply to address mobile pests, soil degradation, and excessive pesticide reliance across citrus-growing areas. Nepal s citrus system faces severe pest pressure, soil degradation, poor planting materials, and weak management. These issues cause 30-70% productivity and postharvest losses, volatile supply, heavy pesticide dependence, and rising imports. With 94% of farmers relying on chemicals, production costs, health risks, and environmental damage are increasing while consumer trust in fruit safety declines. The innovation addresses these challenges through an integrated, nature-based, systems-level model that strengthens the citrus value chain. It combines three scientifically proven components: 1.Area-Wide Control Programs (AWCP) that coordinate municipal-level suppression of mobile pests. Government pilots reduced Chinese citrus fruit fly infestation from 56.7% to below 5%. 2.Parasitoid-based biological control, widely validated internationally but not yet available in Nepal, to sustainably suppress citrus psyllid and fruit-piercing moths. 3.Tricho-Vermicompost (TVC), which iDE s research shows improves soil microbial health, reduces root diseases, and increases yields. This combination is novel because these components, each effective alone, have never been integrated into a unified, municipality-led citrus resilience model in Nepal. The model delivers lasting benefits by reducing losses and chemical costs, improving soil health, restoring consumer trust in citrus safety, strengthening municipal monitoring and early warning systems, and enabling circular bio-input markets that support affordable, nutritious citrus for households and schools.

core_fields.title: Comprehensive agricultural intelligence platform
core_fields.description: Cultiflow bridges Ghana's $117 billion agricultural financing gap while building Africa's first comprehensive agricultural intelligence database. Our AI platform analyzes real-time market demand, connects smallholder farmers with guaranteed buyers before planting, and enables diaspora investors to fund farms starting at just $45. Through quality inputs, smart storage, and market linkages, farmers achieve 40% yield increases and 30-52% income gains. By democratizing both agricultural investment and market data, we transform subsistence farming into profitable, data-driven agribusiness.
core_fields.abstract: The Problem: Sub-Saharan Africa faces a $117 billion agricultural financing gap, with 97% of smallholder farmers excluded from formal credit and forced into predatory loans at 50-100% interest. Simultaneously, farmers operate blind to market demand. Ghana loses $1.9 billion in food waste annually while importing $3.25 billion in food it could grow locally. Why It Matters: This information asymmetry traps 100 million West African farming families in poverty while compromising regional food security. Banks can't assess farm creditworthiness without data; farmers can't optimize production without market intelligence. Our Solution: Cultiflow builds Africa's first comprehensive agricultural intelligence platform while democratizing investment through crowdfarming. Our AI analyzes real-time data from 10 field officers to predict demand 3-6 months ahead, telling farmers what to grow before planting. Meanwhile, everyday investors fund farms starting at $45 via mobile money, with IoT sensors monitoring crops and smart contracts ensuring transparent returns of 12-25%. Scientific Insight: Research proves that combining quality inputs with market access increases yields 40-250% and farmer incomes 30-52%. By solving both capital AND information gaps simultaneously, we create a data-generating investment platform that becomes smarter with every harvest. Immediate Benefits: Farmers: Guaranteed buyers, 40% yield increases, no collateral required Investors: Accessible agricultural investment with transparent returns Consumers: 20% lower prices through reduced waste Sustainable Impact: Environmental: 4,200 tonnes CO2; sequestered, 40% water savings Systemic: Continental agricultural database enabling evidence-based policy Social: Youth employment in digital agriculture, women's economic empowerment

core_fields.description: Introduction of sustainable beekeeping to improve livelihoods, preserve agricultural practices and combat biodiversity loss through carbon sequestration
core_fields.abstract: Zimbabwe is facing a multi-faceted crisis driven by deforestation, which disproportionately impacts vulnerable rural communities. The unsustainable exploitation of forest resources, primarily for firewood and agricultural expansion, has led to severe environmental degradation, economic hardship, and social vulnerability.  Environmental Degradation: The annual loss of approximately 300,000 hectares of forest has resulted in a significant loss of biodiversity, including the decline of critical indigenous tree species like Brachystegia spiciformis (Msasa). This leads to increased soil erosion, diminishing agricultural productivity, and contributing to climate change.Economic Hardship: In many rural areas, limited income-generating opportunities trap communities in a cycle of poverty, forcing a continued reliance on diminishing natural resources.  Social Vulnerability: The burden of deforestation often falls heavily on women, who are traditionally responsible for collecting firewood. As forests dwindle, they must travel greater distances, increasing their labour and exposing them to safety risks. Project Activities  Community Mobilization, Stakeholder meetings and Participant Selection: Engage with community leaders to introduce the project and collaboratively select 40 motivated households to participate.  Comprehensive Training Workshops: Deliver a series of hands-on training modules covering bee biology, modern hive management, honey harvesting, and quality control.  Conservation Education: Conduct local workshops on the impact of deforestation, sustainable forest management, and fire prevention.  Equipment Distribution: Procure and distribute starter kits to all 40 participating households.  Agroforestry Promotion: Distribute bee-friendly indigenous tree seedlings to participants to plant, enhancing local flora. Monitoring and Support: Conduct regular follow-up visits to provide technical support and mentorship
