core_fields.title: Extraction of Yam (Dioscoreae rotundata) Starch for potential food applications.
core_fields.description: This project addresses challenges of post-harvest losses of nutritious white yam (Dioscorea rotundata) by small-holder farmers. By transforming this underutilized crop into a valuable, food-grade starch we bridge a critical knowledge gap concerning its industrial application. This innovation directly tackles food waste, creates new income for small-holder farmers, and delivers simultaneous impact in Zimbabwe and beyond by providing the data needed to commercialize yam starch as a sustainable, gluten-free ingredient.
core_fields.abstract: Problem: White yam, a staple in Sub-Saharan Africa, suffers 25-40% post-harvest losses due to lack of processing markets, undermining food security and farmer livelihoods. A significant knowledge gap exists regarding the optimized extraction and functional properties of D. rotundata starch. Solution: A novel, integrated extraction process was developed , based on established protocols to extract high-purity (>90%), functionally-superior starch from freshly harvested yams, creating an immediate offtake market that eliminates loss. Novelty: While starch extraction is known, a dedicated, commercially-optimized process for D. rotundata is novel. Our research systematically fills the identified gap by characterizing its precise physicochemical properties such as amylose content (22-30%), gelatinization temperature (64-75 C), and pasting behavior for optimal food applications, leading to protectable IP. Existing Solutions: Conventional starches (corn, cassava) dominate. Yam starch is underutilized due to a lack of commercial-scale process knowledge and application data. We provide both the optimized process and the application-specific functionality data. Scientific Insight: The core insight is that valorization through targeted, science-led processing is the most effective PHL intervention. By applying food engineering principles to fully characterize and optimize yam starch, we transform a waste-prone crop into a sought-after industrial ingredient with unique functional benefits (e.g., high gel strength, freeze-thaw stability). Benefits: Farmers gain stable income. Food Manufacturers access a new, sustainable, functional ingredient. Society benefits from reduced waste, enhanced food security, income generation and job creation. The Environment benefits from a circular model that utilizes >95% of the tuber and reduces GHG emissions from decomposing waste.

core_fields.title: "From Waste to Worth: Developing Edible Cutlery for Climate Action and Nutrition Security"
core_fields.description: This project validates the feasibility of transforming agricultural food waste- jackfruit seeds, banana peels, dessicated coconut into nutrient-fortified, edible cutlery. Building on Ecolery's initial prototypes, we will refine the formulas to include proteins and essential micronutrients, testing shelf-life and stability for climate-vulnerable regions. We will conduct a pilot distribution in a flood-affected/coastal area to assess durability, nutritional impact, and consumer acceptance. This project establishes a scalable model addressing plastic pollution, malnutrition, and circular economy practices.
core_fields.abstract: The intersecting crises of plastic pollution and malnutrition create a critical need for integrated solutions in Bangladesh. Annually, 87,000 tons of single-use plastics are discarded, with 96% originating from food and personal care items that clog drainage systems and poison aquatic ecosystems. Simultaneously, nearly 20% of households in flood-prone districts like Kurigram suffer from chronic food insecurity, exacerbated by climate disasters that disrupt supply chains. Agricultural waste offers an untapped resource to address both issues; Bangladesh produces 1.8 million tons of jackfruit annually, yet nearly 500,000 tons are wasted, discarding valuable protein and fiber sources. Our innovation operationalizes a circular economy model by transforming this massive volume of agricultural byproduct, specifically jackfruit seeds, banana peels, and desiccated coconut etc. into biodegradable, edible cutlery. Unlike bioplastics that require industrial composting, our cutlery relies on the natural binding properties of jackfruit seed flour, which contains 13-15% protein and essential minerals. Through a specialized baking process, we fortify this matrix with additional plant-based proteins and micronutrients without compromising its load-bearing durability. This solution delivers immediate dual benefits: it replaces toxic single-use plastics with a fully biodegradable alternative (decomposes within days) and provides a shelf-stable, nutritious food source for climate-vulnerable populations. For farmers, this valorizes zero-value waste into income; for flood-affected communities in countries like Bangladesh, it offers accessible nutrition during crises. By reducing production energy by approximately 22% compared to plastic manufacturing, we establish a scalable, sustainable pathway to combat environmental degradation while enhancing food security.

core_fields.title: Wheat Biofortification 2.0: Reducing Phytic Acid for Improved Mineral Nutrition
core_fields.description: Wheat Biofortification 2.0 aims to significantly improve iron and zinc absorption in wheat-consuming populations by reducing grain phytic acid through advanced breeding. This project strengthens the nutritional impact of existing biofortified wheat by targeting the primary inhibitor of mineral absorption, ultimately improving dietary quality and public health across Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
core_fields.abstract: Micronutrient deficiencies affect nearly one-third of the global population, with iron deficiency remaining a major public health burden, especially among women and children in low-income countries. Wheat is a core staple for hundreds of millions, yet its nutritional impact is limited because phytic acid concentrated in the aleurone where most minerals are stored strongly inhibits iron and zinc absorption. This is especially problematic when wheat is consumed as whole grain or high-extraction flour. Wheat Biofortification 2.0 introduces a next-generation strategy centered on reducing grain phytic acid (PA) to unlock the nutritional potential of biofortified wheat. This approach is grounded in CIMMYT s recent advances in phytic acid phenotyping, genetics, germplasm screening, and monitoring of mineral content. Low-phytic-acid (LPA) germplasm has been identified and widely documented, and LPA trait introgression into elite, high-zinc germplasm is already underway. This innovation addresses the fundamental issue that has historically limited the impact of biofortification: higher mineral content does not necessarily translate into improved human nutrition unless bioavailability increases. Reducing PA increases the absorption of iron, zinc, calcium, and magnesium, offering immediate and sustained benefits for wheat-dependent households. Benefits of this project include (1) Greater mineral absorption and improved nutritional status; (2) Enhanced impact of zinc-biofortified germplasm; (3) Reduced need for costly fortification or supplementation and (4) Lower environmental phosphorus load from undigested phytate. This is a sustainable, food-system-aligned innovation that can meaningfully reduce hidden hunger at scale.

core_fields.title: Advancing Resilient Indigenous Poultry Value Chain Through a Community-Based Infrastructure and Sustainable Insect- Derived Feeds
core_fields.description: Feasts Consultants International is implementing a farmer-centered initiative to strengthen the indigenous poultry value chain in rural Uganda. The project combines improved hatchability, affordable protein-rich feeds, and hands-on training in poultry management, hygiene, and value addition. Using a community-based learning hub, farmers, especially women and youth, access quality chicks through a revolving system, reduce feed costs, and link to local markets. Over 18 months, the project will improve nutrition, incomes, food safety, and environmental sustainability.
core_fields.abstract: The innovation promotes production, productivity, and commercialization of indigenous poultry breeds by addressing critical challenges faced by smallholder farmers: Low productivity (hatchability), high production costs, limited technical support, and weak market access. Although indigenous chickens are resilient, easy to rear, and highly valued for taste and nutritional quality, many farmers rely on poor feeding practices, resulting in slow growth, low yields, and reduced turnover. This project introduces a self-sustaining, low-cost poultry production model using locally adaptable, evidence-based technologies. A demonstration center with a common-user facility will be established, equipped with solar-powered-automated incubators, mini-slaughter facility, and vacuum sealer. Controlled incubation increases hatchability by 90% compared to natural brooding (40%), enabling continuous chicks production. To sustain the local chicken value-chain, a revolving system will enable farmers to sell eggs to the center for incubation and access chicks affordably. Hens purchased from farmers will undergo light value addition and vacuum packaging for higher returns. A Black Soldier Fly (BSF) rearing unit will convert wastes generated into high-protein larvae (60% crude protein)-comparable to fishmeal-offering a low-cost feed alternative (cutting feed costs by 40%). By-products will be used in backyard-gardens established under the project, enhancing food availability. Farmers will receive training in poultry management, feed formulation, biosecurity, and vertical poultry housing to optimize limited land. A resident veterinary officer will offer routine inspections/vaccination and extension support. This initiative enhances food and nutrition security, increases household incomes, reduces waste, and creates employment. Efficient-resource use, renewable-energy, and market linkages strengthens resilience and sustainability within Uganda s food system.

core_fields.title: Farmer-Owned Micro-Ecosystems for Seed Saving through Seed Library Boxes
core_fields.description: GSS strengthens climate-vulnerable food systems in the Philippines by equipping smallholder farmers with education and training that preserve biodiversity and expand access to nutritious food. GSS distributes sustainable, climate-resilient home seed library boxes that are proven to safeguard seeds during typhoons, floods, and earthquakes. Combined with GSS s Seed Inventory Tracking System, farmers gain the data and skills to understand and manage seed quality, secure local seed stocks, and rapidly recover food systems after climate events.
core_fields.abstract: The Philippines is ranked the most disaster-prone country in the world according to the 2025 World Risk Index. This marks the fourth consecutive year that the Philippines has been ranked first, and the 21st consecutive year ranked within the top ten. Since January 2025, the Philippines has experienced 21 typhoons, widespread flooding, and multiple earthquakes that have destroyed homes, infrastructure, and crops. The Philippines unique geography, densely populated coastlines, environmental degradation, social inequities, and lacking infrastructure amplify the impacts of these disasters. The Philippines is also the most food-insecure country in Asia. Forty-four percent of the population cannot afford a healthy diet, and 33% are moderately or severely food insecure. After disasters, farmers must recover and replant, oftentimes needing to purchase seeds. Frequent and severe natural disasters will continue to affect crops, irrigation, food supply chains, and market prices. Ancestral wisdom of the Philippines and indigenous peoples has always included seed saving as a sustainable solution, but this wisdom has been consistently undermined by limited resources, industrialized farming practices, and a lack of access to open-pollinated heirloom seeds. Global Seed Savers (GSS) addresses this by distributing seed library boxes that safeguard heirloom seeds through natural disasters. GSS is the only organization providing free home seed library boxes across the Philippines. In addition, GSS s Seed Inventory Tracking System provides a method for recording the quality and quantity of seed varieties so that farmers understand their own local seed stock to recover quickly after a climate event.

core_fields.title: PoshTara: Community-Led Fortified, Affordable, Trusted Snacks for Healthy Rural Bihar
core_fields.description: This project enhances equitable access to safe, nutritious, and affordable snacks in rural Bihar by transforming women-led Self Help Group (SHG) food production units into sustainable micro-enterprises. Operating under the PoshTara brand, SHGs will produce fortified, culturally relevant snacks as healthier alternatives to ultra-processed foods. The Grant will expand production capacity, promote green practices, and build a scalable, community-driven model to strengthen local food systems and replicate success across SHG-run units.
core_fields.abstract: Rural India faces rising ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption, with 9.6% of rural food budgets spent on low-nutrient snacks driving anemia, overweight, and NCD risks. Affordable, appealing alternatives are urgently needed to combat micronutrient deficiencies while matching convenience and taste. Our innovation offers a community-led solution by transforming women-run self-help group (SHG) food production units, which currently supply Take-Home Rations for Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS), into sustainable micro-enterprises that produce fortified healthier snacks for the open market. Under the PoshTara brand, these units will make millet-based snacks fortified with iron and folic acid, designed through a human-centered process to match local taste preferences and cultural habits while providing healthier options than competing products in the market. This approach ensures trust, acceptability, and consistent demand. What makes this model novel is its combination of product and process innovation. Product innovation includes nutrition-by-design formulations produced through environmentally responsible sourcing of ingredients that follow national food safety and fortification guidelines and remain at low cost due to decentralized production and local sourcing. Process innovation includes participatory product development with SHG women and the introduction of energy-efficient equipment, low-water processing, and structured waste management systems. The model builds on proven feasibility. The intervention production unit has been operational for over a decade, reaching thousands of beneficiaries through ICDS. This will help establish a scalable and replicable model for SHG-based nutritious open-market enterprises across Bihar and beyond and will continue to improve upon recipe formulations as taste preferences shift towards healthier options.

core_fields.title: Elzian Agro Precision Agriculture Demonstration Sites
core_fields.description: At our demonstration site, farmers explore customized web and mobile applications designed for small-scale farms while observing IoT-based systems that optimize water resource management to increase crop yields. They learn to use precise water flow and usage data for environmental monitoring in agricultural and industrial contexts. The site showcases an integrated decision-support system combining high-precision weather and soil monitoring, adaptive irrigation, and precision agriculture solutions to improve water efficiency, crop productivity, and produce quality.
core_fields.abstract: Through research engaging over 60,000 farmers, we found key challenges faced by small-scale farmers, including limited access to water, difficulties in measuring and maintaining water quality, absence of real-time monitoring for critical system parameters, lack of technical knowledge and ongoing support, and inefficient use of water, nutrients, and energy, all of which hinder the sustainability and productivity of hydroponic and aquaponic farming systems. After reaching thousands of farmers, we found that the best way to approach and raise awareness regarding precision agricultural practices is through live demonstrations. Our overall/integrated solution is to develop a well-equipped demonstration site with our integrated solutions, invite marginalized farmers and facilitate them with knowledge transition on-site. This project equips marginalized farmers with sustainable solutions for long-term environmental and economic benefits. ⦿#1. Replacing synthetic nitrogen fertilizers with Azolla significantly lowers nitrous oxide emissions. Precision irrigation reduces water pumping energy use, cutting overall emissions. Studies show biofertilizers can replace up to 50% of chemical fertilizers, reducing emissions accordingly. ⦿#2. Our IoT-based precision irrigation optimizes water use, crucial for arid regions. It has been shown to improve efficiency by up to 95%, cut irrigation costs by 20%, and boost yields by 7%. ⦿#3. Regenerative practices, including vermicomposting and analog forestry, increase microbial activity, improve soil fertility, and restore native plant species, contributing to ecosystem resilience. ⦿#4. Data-driven decision-making helps farmers manage pests, optimize irrigation, and adapt to climate variability. Precision agriculture enhances resilience to extreme weather, minimizing losses.

core_fields.title: Vegie Cooler-Box Project- Cold storage for all
core_fields.description: We provide affordable and reliable solar-powered cold-storage solutions for small holder farmers and vegetable vendors. The Vegie Cooler-Box is an off-grid, user-affordable, solar powered cold room that increases the shelf life of fruits and vegetables from 2 to 21 days. By renting out cold storage space, the Vegie Cooler-Box is more than a storage provider we are a climate-smart, customer-first cold chain partner helping people protect what they produce, reduce waste, and grow sustainably
core_fields.abstract: In developing countries, 45% of fresh produce food spoils mainly due to lack of cold storage. 470 million small farmers to lose 25% of their annual income. Perishable food especially fresh fruits and vegetables start to deteriorate as soon as they are harvested because they are cut-off from their source of water and nutrition. They lose weight, texture, flavour, nutritional value and appeal. When most farmers and vendors at the market place fail to sell their vegetables on the second day after harvesting, on the third day they are forced to sell at ridiculously low price to clear stock or eventually throw-away. However, with our innovation, we make cold-storage services more accessible and affordable for vegetable smallholder farmers and vendors. Adding-on, shelf life is increased from 2 to 21 days for most fruits and vegetables. Whilst our competitors are selling cold rooms, smallholder farmers and vendors hardly can afford these infrastructure as it is too expensive making them almost totally excluded from the cold chain. However, with our solution, farmer do not have to own the infrastructure but rather rent space only for the specific time they need the service. Adding on to the cold room, we have other supporting services for our target clients. We intend to have a mobile application for the ease of doing business with us. Through our vegetable market aggregation center that is next to the cold room, we offer market linkage solutions.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Farming and Nutrition Improvement for Ecologically Vulnerable Communities in Northern Ghana
core_fields.description: We aim to enhance food security in Northern Ghana by expanding regenerative agriculture, agroecologically diversified food production in schools and communities to improve nutrition. We will scale up to additional 1000 smallholder farmers, establish 10 more school gardens and improve diet diversity for 500 children in the Savelugu district and initiate the same in the Mion and West Gonja Districts. Outputs include soil restoration practices, diversifying diets, and sustainable local food systems.
core_fields.abstract: Northern Ghana experiences climatic variabilities resulting in declining soil fertility, erratic rainfall, high temperatures, and declining nutritional food sources. FAO studies show an estimated 60%-70% of cultivated lands in Northern Ghana are severely degraded due to unsustainable land use practices causing Studies on environmental variability and nutrition show the dwindling nutritional food sources and rising food insecurity. This project introduces a regenerative farming model that restores soils, stabilizes crop production, and introduces healthy diets for households and school children. Techniques include organic farm practices; intercropping, zero/minimum tillage, composting, mulching, drought-tolerant seed use, and water-saving strategies that rely on local materials. The innovation draws on agroecology, climate-resilient farming science, school nutrition research, and behavioral approaches to food choices. Pilot demonstration farms established by RAINS with support from Brandeis in communities and school gardens show measurable improvements in yield stability, crop diversity, and household diets. Our pilot shows that farmers adopt regenerative practices when benefits are visible and input costs are lower. Immediate benefits include healthier soils, lower production costs, and access to drought-tolerant seeds and crops, as high-quality nutritious foods. Long-term benefits include increased biodiversity, improved resilience to climate stress, livelihood sustainability, and access to nutritious and high-quality meals at school. The training, research partnership, and community-led approach make the model durable and scalable across districts and eventually nationwide.

core_fields.title: Edible Cities
core_fields.description: Edible Cities is a regeneration initiative that reimagines overlooked urban spaces, like hospitals, schools, prisons, and public spaces, as living and productive ecosystems. By combining vertical farming with permaculture, agroforestry and composting, regenerative food production emerges where least expected, increasing accessibility to healthy food while adopting regenerative practices. It provides a replicable model for cities to be more biodiverse, equitable, and climate-resilient, demonstrating how food systems can advance the SDGs and redefine public space.
core_fields.abstract: Edible Cities addresses critical urban challenges, including the ecological impact of food systems, social inequalities, and unsustainable diets. As cities rely on long food chains that have environmentally detrimental effects and have limit access to fresh, healthy food, particularly for vulnerable populations, the need for inclusive and sustainable practices is urgent. The project transforms underused urban spaces into multifunctional ecosystems, combining outdoor vertical farming, permaculture, composting, and agroforestry with education and community participation. Residents grow food locally while learning practical skills, strengthening social cohesion, and improving food literacy. Its novelty lies in using outdoor vertical farming as a community-centered system rather than a high-tech, closed solution. While community gardens and vertical farms exist, Edible Cities is distinctive in combining sustainable production, social programs, and environmental benefits in scalable urban models. The approach aims to build on agroecology, food sovereignty, and circular economy principles, recognizing that resilient food systems must restore ecosystems and empower communities simultaneously. Immediate benefits include access to fresh, healthy food, skill-building, therapeutic and educational outcomes, and stronger social networks. Sustainable advantages include reduced food insecurity, urban cooling, biodiversity enhancement, carbon sequestration, climate adaptation, and the demonstration of scalable, resilient urban agriculture models that serve consumers, communities, schools, and residents.

core_fields.title: Expanding Safi's Reach to Climate-Displaced Populations in Rwanda
core_fields.description: Building on a successful 60-device pilot from Seeding the Future s Seed Grant, this project will optimize and scale our proven milk pasteurization control unit for climate-displaced dairy farmers in Rwanda. Safi will redesign its device to reduce unit costs by up to 40%, manufacture 500 units locally, and deploy them through trusted partners using a pay-as-you-pasteurize model. The approach enables safe milk, higher farmer incomes, and cost recovery, demonstrating economic feasibility and impact at scale.
core_fields.abstract: East Africa has the highest global incidence of milk-borne disease. Alarmingly, 30% of deaths in children under 5. This is due to a lack of access to safe and quality milk, with up to 90% of milk in East Africa being sold raw by small scale milk sellers in the unregulated, informal market. The challenges of the current dairy supply chain are burdened by many factors but most importantly the lack of adequate traceability and tools to ensure safety. At Safi, we have patented the world's first, small-scale pasteurization control unit targeted towards small-scale dairy farmers and vendors. The device kills milk-borne diseases all while retaining the key nutrients of milk. It is affordable, powered by renewable energy sources, and allows farmers to easily pasteurize their differentiating daily yields. To address inadequate traceability, at the core of the product is a digital tracking system that remotely records milk pasteurization data and centralizes production information for regulators and governments. The Safi solution ensures that the ability to pasteurize milk is democratized to smallholder farmers who supply up to 90% of milk sold in these markets. This allows farmers to earn more money per litre of milk, and also makes pasteurized milk more accessible and affordable to the general public. Safi is also looking to collaborate with the One Cup, One Child initiative in Rwanda to get a cup of safe milk in the hands of every school child in Rwanda. Therefore, Safi provides clear benefits to farmers, consumers and their communities.

core_fields.title: Leveraging Soil Intelligence for Regenerative & Equitable Food Systems Transformation in Vulnerable Agro-Ecological Regions
core_fields.description: AI-based soil intelligence is translated into an decision support system for farmer decision-making, risk reduction, and market access, enabling systemic regenerative change in staple crop production. Through agri-living labs and communities of practice, small-scale rice farmers use measurable soil and climate insights to reduce inputs, stabilise yields, and strengthen resilience under climate pressure. The unique value lies in connecting data, regenerative practices, and economic incentives into a single, scalable model that strengthens food systems from
core_fields.abstract: In the Global South, limited access to insurance, finance, and reliable data means that a single drought or flood can translate directly into income loss and food insecurity. As rice is a staple food for millions, this vulnerability for rice farmers threatens both livelihoods and nutrition at scale. In this project, CinSOIL aims to address this challenge by delivering soil intelligence as an integrated decision, risk, and market-access system for small-scale rice farming. Using high-resolution satellite data and AI-driven soil modeling, CinSOIL monitors soil moisture, soil condition, and soil carbon trends. Soil carbon serves as the operational backbone, linking soil fertility, climate resilience, and long-term productivity. These insights are translated into simple, actionable guidance that helps farmers reduce fertilizer use, manage water more efficiently, and optimize scarce human labor without compromising yields. The scientific insight behind this solution is that soil carbon and soil condition are central indicators connecting productivity, resilience, and climate risk. By making these indicators scalable and affordable, CinSOIL also enables objective, data-driven risk assessment, forming the basis for faster and more accessible parametric insurance where traditional mechanisms fail. Unlike conventional agronomic or carbon tools, CinSOIL combines soil intelligence with communities of practice and living labs, embedding training and peer learning to ensure adoption. Immediate benefits include lower input and labor costs and improved risk management for farmers. Long-term benefits include regenerated soils, resilient livelihoods, traceable production for regulated markets, and a more secure, nutritious rice supply for communities and consumers.

core_fields.title: Healthy food environments: advancing the guarantee of the human right to adequate food and nutrition.
core_fields.description: This project strengthens territorial networks and empowers families, schools, and communities to create healthier food environments for children. Red PaPaz will scale a behavior-change model that promotes real, nutritious and local food and supports school shops through a simple and practical profitability model that prioritizes healthy options. Through training, community engagement, and evidence-based strategies, the initiative aims to reduce barriers to healthy eating, improve children s nutrition, and contribute towards the guarantee of the rigth.
core_fields.abstract: This project addresses a critical structural determinant of malnutrition in Colombia: the configuration of school and community food environments that systematically favor ultra-processed products due to asymmetric information, regulatory gaps, and distorted price signals. These environments generate a persistent mismatch between children s nutritional needs and the foods that are most accessible, affordable, and socially normalized, contributing to early metabolic dysregulation and long-term inequities that impede progress toward adequate food and nutrition. The proposed intervention constitutes a systemic approach to food environment transformation, combining territorial governance mechanisms, socio-behavioral change methodologies, and an evidence-based economic model that optimizes the financial feasibility of healthy school stores. The core innovation lies in integrating behavioral insights such as choice architecture and habitual cue disruption with market-level adjustments that realign incentives for vendors. The goal is to increase the relative availability, visibility, and economic attractiveness of local and minimally processed foods. This includes training in basic financial literacy and differential profitability analysis, empowering vendors to make healthy options both viable and competitive. This design is informed by empirical diagnostics. Unlike existing interventions that typically isolate nutrition education or regulatory compliance, this model operates across multiple causal nodes simultaneously: social norms, vendor decision matrices, institutional policies, and localized supply chains. As a result, the solution produces synergistic effects. Immediate benefits include measurable improvements in children s exposure to nutrient-dense foods and reduced reliance on ultra-processed alternatives. Long-term benefits comprise reduced risk trajectories for chronic disease and reinforcement of local food cultures.

core_fields.title: Upcycling crop residues into Compostable Foam Packaging for Circular Food Systems
core_fields.description: We convert agricultural waste that farmers and agribusinesses pay to have removed into high-performance, compostable foam packaging that replaces polystyrene. Our dual revenue system combining waste collection and material production enables cost-effective, biodegradable packaging compatible with existing manufacturing. We are initially deploying in high-impact markets such as biotech packaging and are working to scale into food packaging to support a circular and resilient global food system.
core_fields.abstract: Polystyrene foam is widely used across food and protective packaging, yet it is petroleum-based, non-biodegradable, and difficult to recycle. At the same time, millions of tons of agricultural residues such as corn stalks, sugarcane bagasse and other crop byproducts are burned, landfilled, or require costly removal, creating emissions and economic burdens for farmers. These two challenges exist side-by-side but are rarely addressed together. Our innovation converts agricultural waste that farmers and agribusinesses pay to have removed into high-performance, compostable foam packaging that replaces polystyrene. We extract and process cellulose from crop residues and engineer it into lightweight, shock-absorbing foams. Through a dual revenue system that combines waste collection with material production, we lower feedstock costs while delivering a biodegradable material compatible with existing manufacturing infrastructure. The key scientific insight behind this solution is that cellulose fibers from agricultural waste, when properly extracted and structured, can replicate the mechanical properties of conventional foam without petroleum inputs. By designing the material to integrate into current equipment, we reduce adoption risk and enable scalable manufacturing. Immediate benefits include reduced disposal costs and emissions for farmers, compostable packaging for consumers and institutions, and lower plastic pollution for communities. Long-term, this approach reduces reliance on fossil-based materials and enables a circular food system where agricultural byproducts are transformed into essential, sustainable packaging at scale.

core_fields.title: Women-Led Food Preservation and Value Addition for Resilient Sahelian Food Systems
core_fields.description: This project aims to scale women-led, climate-resilient food preservation solutions in the Sahel to reduce post-harvest losses, improve food safety, and increase incomes. By deploying decentralized preservation units, providing technical training, and strengthening market linkages, the initiative empowers women entrepreneurs to transform local crops into higher-value products, contributing to food security, climate resilience, and inclusive economic growth across Mali and neighboring Sahelian countries.
core_fields.abstract: Post-harvest losses remain one of the most critical barriers to food security and farmer incomes in the Sahel, with up to 30 50% of fruits and crops lost due to inadequate preservation, limited processing infrastructure, and poor market access. Women, who play a central role in production and transformation, are disproportionately affected by these constraints. This project introduces an integrated, women-led food preservation and value-addition model that combines climate-smart preservation technologies (solar drying, low-energy processing, improved storage), technical training, and structured market linkages. The innovation lies not in a single technology, but in a scalable system that aligns preservation methods with local crops, women s cooperatives, and market demand. Scientific and technical insights on post-harvest physiology, food safety, and shelf-life extension inform the selection of appropriate technologies that are affordable, energy-efficient, and adaptable to Sahelian conditions. These solutions are complemented by quality control protocols and business coaching, enabling women entrepreneurs to move from informal processing to market-ready production. Immediate benefits include reduced food losses, increased shelf life, improved food safety, and higher, more stable incomes for women producers. Sustainable benefits include strengthened local food systems, reduced environmental waste, improved nutrition, job creation, and increased resilience to climate and market shocks. The model is designed for replication across regions, contributing to long-term food security, climate adaptation, and women s economic leadership in the Sahel.

core_fields.title: Regenerative Proteins (REPRO): Community Enterprise Development for Sustainable Supply Chains and Climate Transition Mechanisms.
core_fields.description: REPRO develops community-based regenerative plant protein systems to reduce climate vulnerability, chemical dependency, and protein insecurity in Thailand. The project strengthens farmer networks to produce, process, and distribute local plant proteins through regenerative agriculture, community enterprises, and a digital traceability platform. By linking household consumption, community markets, and external demand, REPRO builds resilient supply chains, increases farmer income, and enables safe, trusted, and low-carbon protein access for consumers.
core_fields.abstract: Thailand s food and agricultural system faces deep structural vulnerability. Farmers bear high production costs and climate risks, while rising temperatures intensify pests in legume crops due to weakened farm ecosystems. This drives farmers toward chemical-intensive monocultures for animal feed, increasing dependency on external inputs and imported protein. At the same time, Thailand experiences protein insecurity, relying heavily on soybean imports. The root cause lies in one-dimensional state promotion that prioritizes short-term cultivation targets without long-term output management, market design, or transition support. REPRO addresses this challenge by increasing plant-based protein consumption and reducing livestock-oriented agriculture, establishing a more resilient and sustainable food system. The initiative strengthens farmer networks to produce local plant protein across three levels: (1) household consumption, (2) community consumption, and (3) external markets, supported by three core pillars. 1. Climate-Resilient Protein Production REPRO promotes regenerative agriculture to enhance soil health, stabilize yields, and build resilience against climate volatility. Secure and safe yields form the foundation of long-term food system security. 2. Community Economic Value Creation Farmer groups are elevated into a community enterprise model that integrates cooperative structures with value-added processing. Local financial mechanisms support farmers during transition, while the REPRO Traceability Platform ensures safe, transparent plant-protein products for consumers. 3.Transition to Plant-Based Protein Shifting from animal to plant-based protein reduces pressure on land and water, restores biodiversity, lowers greenhouse gas emissions and cuts chemical fertilizer use through nitrogen-fixing legumes. A 50:50 shift in Thailand could reduce CO₂ emissions by 9.35 million tons, within safer climate limits.

core_fields.title: Circular Solutions for Clean Energy, Fertile Soils, and Green Livelihoods
core_fields.description: This project introduces a community circular food system in Kabale District that transforms organic market waste into bio-compost and clean biogas. Youth and women groups will collect and process waste, supplying compost to smallholder farmers practising climate-smart and regenerative farming. The model reduces pollution, restores soil fertility, lowers fertiliser costs, and creates green jobs helping communities achieve cleaner markets, improved harvests, and greater food security through sustainable and inclusive local innovation.
core_fields.abstract: Our innovation introduces a community-driven circular food system that converts organic market waste into bio-compost and clean energy, linking urban waste recovery with rural soil regeneration in Kabale because according tothe studies by the Kabale Municipal Environment Office (2024) estimate that nearly 82% of total waste generated in the town is organic, yet less than 8% is reused or recycled. Much of it banana peelings, vegetable leftovers, and spoiled fruits from Central and Mwanjari markets is dumped in open pits or burned, producing greenhouse gases and contaminating water channels that feed Lake Bunyonyi. At the same time, the Kabale District Agricultural Production Report (2023) shows that soil organic matter has fallen below 2.5%, and yields of beans and Irish potatoes have declined by more than 30% over the past five years. The high cost of chemical fertilizer now above UGX 200,000 per 50-kg bag has pushed smallholder farmers to abandon its use altogether. This imbalance, where nutrients are lost in towns while soils in villages continue to degrade, defines a broken local food system that urgently needs a circular solution. Our innovation addresses this gap through youth- and women-led cooperatives that collect and process organic waste into bio-compost and biogas. The compost improves soil fertility and yields, while biogas provides clean cooking energy, reducing reliance on firewood. This practical approach cuts methane emissions, creates green jobs, and strengthens food security fully aligning with the Global Food System Challenge vision of sustainable, inclusive, and regenerative food systems.

core_fields.title: Climate-Smart Solar Micro-Irrigation for Food Security in Somalia s Flood and Drought-Vulnerable Regions
core_fields.description: MEAL is introducing solar-powered micro-irrigation systems across Somalia s flood- and drought-vulnerable regions to stabilize food production, reduce climate shocks, and improve nutrition for women, youth, and smallholder farmers. By combining solar pumps, drip irrigation, climate-resilient crops, and community water governance, the project enables year-round cultivation while strengthening resilience to riverine floods and prolonged droughts. This innovation enhances food security, lowers irrigation costs, and ensures equitable resource access for highly vulnerable communities.
core_fields.abstract: Communities in Lower Shabelle, Gedo, and Bakool face extreme climate stress, characterized by recurrent droughts, erratic rainfall, and destructive riverine floods. Traditional irrigation methods surface canals and diesel pumps no longer provide reliable water access. Diesel costs are prohibitive, water losses are high, and marginalized groups especially women, youth, and minority farmers struggle to access productive land and irrigation systems. MEAL s innovation integrates solar-powered micro-irrigation with community-led water governance to transform food production in fragile environments. Solar pumps replace diesel engines, providing continuous, low-cost water access while greatly reducing emissions. Drip irrigation technology cuts water use by up to 60% and improves crop survival during drought. Climate-smart packages including drought-tolerant seeds, soil regeneration techniques, and flood-adaptive cropping models enable farmers to grow food more consistently despite seasonal shocks. Water governance committees ensure fair distribution across groups, reducing conflict risks and supporting women and youth cooperatives. The innovation was developed through field-based assessments, scientific insights on water efficiency, and lessons from regenerative agriculture. Its benefits are immediate higher yields, lower costs, restored soil health, improved diets and long-term reduced vulnerability, climate-resilient livelihoods, and strengthened social cohesion. With strong potential for scale across East Africa s arid and semi-arid regions, this model offers a transformative pathway for sustainable food systems in fragile, climate-affected settings.

core_fields.title: Biochar-Integrated Agroecological Hubs for Nutrition and Climate Resilience in Smallholder Farming Systems
core_fields.description: PAFID s Biochar-Integrated Agroecological Hubs introduce a circular food system innovation that transforms farm waste into biochar to regenerate degraded soils and enhance nutrient-dense crops. Led by youth and women, each hub integrates biofortified staples, low-cost regenerative practices, and digital agronomy. By restoring soil health, reducing food loss, and improving equitable access to safe, affordable diets, this model offers a scalable pathway to resilient local food economies across Kenya s arid landscapes.
core_fields.abstract: In Kenya s arid smallholder regions, such as Tharaka Nithi County, farmers face a triple crisis: severely degraded soils, nutrient-poor harvests, and recurrent droughts that lead to hunger, child stunting, and crop failure. With annual rainfall often below 750 mm and soils stripped of organic matter, conventional inputs are no longer effective or affordable. PAFID s Biochar-Integrated Agroecological Hubs offer a circular, science-based solution that transforms abundant farm residues into biochar a carbon-rich amendment proven to increase water retention, enhance soil structure, and boost nutrient bioavailability. Scientific studies indicate that biochar can raise yields by 20 50% while sequestering long-term carbon, enhancing both productivity and sustainability. Each hub is managed by trained Climate-Smart Agriculture champions (Farmer Service Centres) and equipped with low-cost pyrolysis units and solar-powered tools. Farmers are trained to integrate biochar within conservation agriculture systems and cultivate nutrient-dense crops such as high-iron beans, zinc-rich sorghum, millet, and orange-fleshed sweet potatoes. AI-enabled agronomic advisories personalize soil and crop recommendations, making regenerative practices accessible even to remote farmers. This innovation goes beyond technology it builds community-owned green enterprises. Hubs generate revenue through packaged biochar, soil advisory services, and sales of biofortified crops and tree seedlings. This ensures financial sustainability while creating dignified livelihoods for rural youth and women. By restoring soil life, reducing food loss, and improving access to safe, nutritious, and affordable foods, this model delivers immediate food security and long-term climate resilience. It is scalable across dryland food systems in Kenya and beyond, redefining how communities nourish both people and the planet.

core_fields.title: Greenhouse Aeroponic and Hydroponic Vertical Tower Growing - strawberries, lettuce, and herbs farm development.
core_fields.description: VertiGenix will commission a 150 m greenhouse with 100 aeroponic/hydroponic vertical towers to grow pesticide-free greens and herbs using ~90% less water. The 12 14-week pilot will validate yield, water intensity, food-safety, and traceability, train a first cohort, and produce a public M&E brief. Results de-risk our larger, three-greenhouse roll-out now raising $850k pre-seed and create a replicable model for water-stressed communities.
core_fields.abstract: Innovation: VertiGenix deploys greenhouse aeroponic & hydroponic vertical towers that use natural sunlight (no LEDs) and closed-loop fertigation. Roots are periodically misted or fed in a recirculating system, delivering oxygen-rich nutrients with ~90% less water and far higher plant density than open-field farming. Integrated QA/traceability logs each batch from seedling to dispatch; operations run on low power with on-site solar. Problem & relevance: Water-stressed regions face volatile supply, pesticide exposure, and long, costly cold chains. Schools, markets, and households need safe, affordable produce year-round. Traditional methods can t guarantee volume, quality, or resource efficiency as climate variability intensifies. How it solves this: Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA) stabilizes temperature, airflow, and irrigation. Vertical towers multiply yield per m while minimizing land disturbance. Closed-loop fertigation slashes water/fertilizer use and eliminates runoff. Pesticide-free protocols and hygiene/IPM SOPs lift food safety and nutrition. Digital monitoring ensures transparency for buyers and regulators. Scientific/technical insight: Combining greenhouse CEA with root-zone aeration (aeroponics) or recirculating hydroponics accelerates growth, improves nutrient uptake, and reduces disease pressure. Using sunlight instead of artificial lighting cuts energy intensity and operating costs, making the model financially and environmentally viable in Southern Africa. Immediate & sustainable benefits: Consumers/schools: fresher, safer produce at stable prices. Farmers/communities: jobs, training, and a replicable, water-smart model. Producers: predictable yields, lower inputs, and traceable quality. Environment: reduced water withdrawal, no pesticide runoff, smaller land footprint, and lower transport emissions via local supply.

core_fields.abstract: The SABAWON Rooftop Circular Food System is an innovative urban farming model that converts unused rooftops into productive, self-sustaining micro-farms. It integrates four interconnected components like poultry, fish, hydroponic vegetables, and biochar composting powered by solar energy and designed as a closed-loop, zero-waste system. The innovation addresses critical urban challenges in Pakistan, including food insecurity, water scarcity, and high input costs. Rapid urbanization has reduced farmland, while rising food prices have made nutritious food inaccessible for many families. The SABAWON system recycles more than 90% of its water and nutrients: poultry manure fertilizes a fish pond, nutrient-rich fish water feeds hydroponic plants, and organic waste is converted into biochar compost to rejuvenate soil in kitchen gardens. This idea evolved from practical livestock management and research in climate-smart agriculture. It demonstrates that even a small 5-Marla rooftop ( 1,250 sq. ft.) can provide year-round eggs, fish, and vegetables without harmful chemicals or antibiotics. Immediate benefits include improved family nutrition, food cost savings, and income generation from surplus produce. Sustainable benefits extend to women empowerment through household micro-enterprises, reduced food waste, lower carbon emissions, improved soil fertility, and stronger community resilience to climate change. By promoting AMR-safe, water-efficient, and renewable-energy-based production, this system contributes directly to healthier urban food systems and a more sustainable environment.

core_fields.abstract: Problem Solved and Relevance The primary problem is the link between poverty, unemployment, and re-victimization among female survivors of human trafficking and gender-based violence (GBV). Without reliable income, survivors remain vulnerable to exploitation. This intersects with the national challenge of post-harvest loss and food insecurity for the urban poor, as raw cassava a vital staple spoils rapidly. The innovation is highly relevant because it addresses the root cause (economic vulnerability) of exploitation while improving the local food system's efficiency. Solution and Insight The problem is solved by establishing a secure cassava value chain run by Survivors Network (SN) Cameroon. This involves: 1. Value-Added Processing: Improve on our processing facility to process the roots into stable, marketable products like gari, flour, and starch. The scientific/technical insight is the focus on value-chain optimization for a highly perishable staple crop. Cassava is a resilient, high-carbohydrate crop, but its rapid decay post-harvest necessitates immediate processing. By investing in processing equipment, the project stabilizes the food supply, shifts the economic activity from subsistence farming (low profit) to agro-industrial processing (high profit), and unlocks the crop's immense market potential. Specific Benefits Immediate Benefit: Immediate Employment, Safe, Affordable Food and Reduced Waste Sustainable Benefit: Economic Resilience, Food Security and Empowerment Model

core_fields.title: Seeds of Tomorrow: Reviving Indigenous Crops for Nutrition and Soil Regeneration in Gushegu, Northern Ghana.
core_fields.description: Seeds of Tomorrow revives indigenous, drought-tolerant crops such as millet, sorghum, and Bambara beans to combat malnutrition and soil degradation in Gushegu, Northern Ghana. Through community seed banks and farmer field schools, youth and women farmers adopt regenerative farming methods that restore soil health, improve nutrition, and strengthen local food sovereignty creating a sustainable, equitable food system rooted in traditional knowledge and climate resilience.
core_fields.abstract: In Gushegu, Northern Ghana, climate change, soil degradation, and the disappearance of indigenous crops have deepened malnutrition and rural poverty. Farmers increasingly rely on imported hybrid seeds and chemical fertilizers that damage soil health and reduce crop diversity. Seeds of Tomorrow tackles this problem by restoring traditional, drought-tolerant crops such as millet, sorghum, and Bambara beans nutrient-rich foods adapted to local conditions and cultural diets. The innovation centers on establishing community seed banks and farmer field schools that teach regenerative farming techniques like composting, intercropping, and mulching. These practices rebuild soil fertility, reduce input costs, and enhance climate resilience. Through participatory seed selection and exchange, farmers preserve genetic diversity and ensure year-round access to trusted, affordable seeds. The scientific and technical foundation lies in agroecology and soil microbiology, which show that organic matter restoration and diverse cropping systems improve both yields and ecosystem stability. By blending these principles with indigenous knowledge, the project creates a sustainable, evidence-based model of food production. The immediate benefits include improved harvests, reduced dependency on expensive inputs, and greater household food security. Over time, Seeds of Tomorrow strengthens community nutrition, restores degraded land, and empowers women and youth farmers to lead local food system transformation. This innovation reconnects people to their traditional crops and landscapes while contributing to global goals on hunger, climate action, and sustainable agriculture.

core_fields.title: Waste-to-Feed Innovation for Sustainable and Inclusive Food Systems in Nigeria
core_fields.description: AMAS GOLDEN TOWER LTD transforms agricultural waste such as maize cobs and soybean husks into affordable, high-quality livestock feed. This circular model reduces farming costs, minimizes environmental pollution, and creates income opportunities for rural farmers. By integrating digital tools for waste collection and farmer engagement, the project promotes sustainable food production, land restoration, and inclusive growth across Nigeria s agricultural communities
core_fields.abstract: The innovation addresses a critical challenge in Nigeria s agriculture sector the high cost of livestock feed and the environmental damage from burning agricultural waste. Feed expenses consume up to 70% of production costs for smallholder farmers, forcing many out of business. Simultaneously, tons of maize cobs, husks, and crop residues are burned after harvest, releasing carbon emissions, degrading soil, and reducing biodiversity. Our solution transforms this waste into affordable, nutrient-rich livestock feed through a circular and climate-smart model. We collect agricultural residues from farmers, process them using locally fabricated machines, and produce quality feed that is 25 45% cheaper than conventional products. Farmers who once burned waste now earn income by supplying it, creating a sustainable incentive loop. This idea was born from years of field research and community engagement, where we observed the strong correlation between waste mismanagement, farmer poverty, and food insecurity. Scientifically, the process uses feed formulation and bioconversion techniques to ensure high nutritional value and digestibility. Immediate benefits include lower production costs, increased farmer income, and reduced pollution. Long-term, the model contributes to land restoration, climate change mitigation, and circular economy growth. Communities gain cleaner environments, youth access green jobs, and livestock producers achieve greater profitability all reinforcing a more resilient and inclusive food system.

core_fields.abstract: Malawi s food systems are threatened by declining soil fertility, erratic rainfall, and dependence on monocropping, challenges that leave rural households vulnerable to hunger and income instability. In Mchinji, PPI introduces a regenerative farming innovation that transforms smallholder farms into climate-smart model villages through an integrated system of permaculture, agroforestry, and food forests. The solution transforms smallholder plots into climate-smart, diversified production systems while reducing food loss and waste through value addition. At its core, is the innovative food preservation producing Drief Fruits and Vegetable Products. Using low-cost solar drying technology, farmers convert surplus harvests into nutritious, shelf-stable products that are hygienically packaged, branded, and marketed, ensuring year-round access to food and new income streams. The model restores 500 hectares of degraded land (home-based food forests, rainfed cropland, and individual forest reserves). Adopting a multilayered ecosystem design, farmers cultivate diverse mix of crops across root, ground cover, shrub, understory, and canopy layers, including cassava, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, moringa, mango, avocado; nitrogen-fixing species like gliricidia and fish beans. Cover crops like cowpeas, jack beans, and mulberry enhance soil aeration, drainage, and fertility while reducing erosion. Builds on over 10-years of applied research at PPI s demonstration school and training centre. Farmers receive intensive hands-on training, starter resources, continuous mentorship delivered through lead-farmer clusters and community facilitators. Immediate benefits include reduced post-harvest losses, improved nutrition, and increased household income. Long-term outcomes include soil conservation, carbon sequestration, biodiversity recovery, and resilient livelihoods, offering a scalable, community-driven pathway toward safe, nutritious, equitable food systems in Malawi.

core_fields.title: Decentralized, Plant-Based Water Purification for Safe Drinking and Sustainable Agriculture
core_fields.description: Blue Filter provides clean and affordable drinking water using a plant-based, zero-electricity purification technology designed for rural and crisis-affected communities. By removing harmful nitrates and microplastics from household and agricultural water sources, the system improves health, food security, and climate resilience. Low-cost manufacturing and decentralized deployment make Blue Filter scalable and equitable. This project will expand pilots, accelerate certification, and build manufacturing pathways to bring safe water and stronger livelihoods to vulnerable families.
core_fields.abstract: Nitrate contamination and microplastic pollution threaten the health and food systems of millions who rely on groundwater especially in agricultural and conflict-affected regions. High nitrate exposure can cause severe health conditions, including blue baby syndrome and increased long-term cancer risk. Existing treatment systems often require electricity, high pressure, and chemicals, making them expensive and inaccessible for low-income or off-grid communities. Blue Filter introduces a novel, plant-based bio-adsorbent material that selectively removes nitrates without generating toxic brine. A second polishing layer enhances safety by capturing microplastics, strengthening both water quality and consumer trust. The system operates entirely without electricity and can be rapidly deployed into homes, farms, schools, and emergency relief sites. The innovation is based on breakthroughs in natural polymer adsorption and decentralized system design. Components can be locally manufactured using sustainable agricultural byproducts, reducing carbon footprint and improving supply-chain resilience. Cartridges are modular and low-maintenance, lowering both cost and operational burden. Immediate benefits include improved access to safe drinking water, reduced disease risks, and healthier crops irrigated with cleaner groundwater. In the long term, Blue Filter strengthens food security, reduces environmental pollution, and enables more sustainable agriculture. By prioritizing affordability and dignity, Blue Filter empowers vulnerable communities to protect their health and resilience even when infrastructure fails.

core_fields.title: Rongbient Biotech
core_fields.description: Rongbient produces scalable macroalgae-based biomaterials, beginning with a next-generation aquaculture feed additive through a patent-pending process. We revolutionizes aquaculture with a circular seaweed ecosystem. We deploy seaweed bio-filters in non-industrial shrimp farms to purify water and double farmer income. This harvested seaweed is fermented into a feed supplement for industrial farms that boosts shrimp immunity and replaces antibiotics. Our solution increases survival rates to 90%, significantly reduces carbon emissions, and ensures sustainable food security.
core_fields.abstract: Feed and additives make up more than half of the cost and emissions of global animal farming, representing a six hundred billion dollar market and roughly four gigatons of annual emissions. Shrimp farming in Asia Pacific is one of the most problematic segments. Rongbient Biotech addresses the critical challenges of high disease rates, financial instability for farmers, and environmental pollution in the shrimp farming industry. Our innovation is a circular, dual-model ecosystem. First, we deploy a seaweed bio-filtration system in non-industrialized farms. This co-culture model uses seaweed to filter wastewater and provide natural food for shrimp. Second, we harvest this seaweed and apply proprietary lactic acid fermentation (using Lactobacillus Plantarum) to convert it into a nutrient-rich feed supplement for industrialized farms. This solution stems from the scientific insight that fermenting specific seaweed species boosts bioavailability of key nutrients like beta-glucans and proteins, significantly enhancing shrimp immunity. Furthermore, we identified that replacing just 5% of conventional feed creates high adoption because it requires no extra effort or investment from farmers. Immediate and Sustainable Benefits: Farmers: Non-industrial farmers can double their annual income through seaweed sales and increased shrimp production. Industrial farmers see shrimp survival rates rise from 67% to up to 90% while completely eliminating the need for antibiotics. Environment: The system sequesters up to 10 tons of CO2 per hectare annually and purifies wastewater, mitigating the industry's heavy carbon footprint.

core_fields.abstract: CLIC TERRA addresses the growing problem of waste and soil degradation by transforming human hair waste from hair salons into a natural agricultural mulch. Today, millions of kilograms of hair are incinerated or landfilled, releasing CO₂ and microtoxins. At the same time, farmers face rising water costs, declining soil fertility, and dependence on plastics and chemical inputs. The innovation is based on a simple biological insight: human hair naturally retains water and nutrients, contains nitrogen, and biodegrades slowly. By processing and shaping hair into a clean, safe mulch layer, CLIC TERRA helps soil hold moisture for longer, protects crops from weeds, and restores organic matter to the land without pesticides or plastic films. The solution is implemented through a local circular economy model. Hair salons pay for waste collection, reducing disposal impact. Farmers purchase an effective, regenerative mulch that reduces water usage by over 50% per hectare, improves soil health, and avoids 6.3 tCO₂e per tonne of material used. The system is transparent and verifiable through blockchain traceability, and environmental performance is monitored using sensor data and AI analysis. Immediate benefits to farmers include: Lower water and input costs Improved soil quality and yields No need for plastic mulching or herbicides Long-term benefits to communities and society include: Reduced waste to landfill Decreased agricultural emissions Stronger local value chains and green jobs CLIC TERRA is a practical, scalable solution that regenerates both soil and community economies.

Parents gain agricultural skills and income opportunities, while schools achieve partial self-sufficiency in feeding programs. Over the long term, the innovation strengthens community resilience, environmental stewardship, and local economic development, creating a replicable model that can be scaled across regions. By linking education, nutrition, and sustainable agriculture, FSSA transforms schools into centers of innovation, empowerment, and lasting social impact.

core_fields.title: Youth-Led Climate-Smart Agriculture for Resilient Food Systems in Kenya
core_fields.description: This initiative empowers 500 marginalized rural NEET youth in Nyandarua and Nakuru to lead a circular, climate-smart agriculture transformation. By converting nutrient-rich lake silt and farm byproducts into low-cost organic fertilizer, youth enterprises will restore degraded soils, increase yields by 30%, and reduce fertilizer costs by 40%. Through CSA training, mentorship, and market access, the project strengthens 1,500 smallholder farmers livelihoods while advancing food security, climate resilience, and equitable green employment across the region.
core_fields.abstract: Kenya s food system faces a dual challenge of declining soil fertility and persistent youth unemployment. Over 40% of arable land is degraded due to erosion, nutrient depletion, and excessive chemical fertilizer use (FAO, 2023), while nearly 70% of rural youth, especially those Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET), remain excluded from meaningful livelihoods (World Bank, 2022). This project offers a transformative, youth-led solution that turns environmental waste into opportunity through circular, climate-smart agriculture. By converting nutrient-rich lake silt and agricultural byproducts, materials often discarded and polluting waterways, into affordable organic fertilizer, the initiative regenerates soil health, restores productivity, and reduces greenhouse gas emissions. Lake silt contains vital nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, proven to enhance crop yields by up to 30% (KALRO, 2022). Through CAP YEI s proven Basic Employability Skills Training (BEST) model, 500 marginalized NEET youth (ages 18 35) from Nyandarua and Nakuru counties will receive comprehensive training in climate-smart agribusiness, biofertilizer production, regenerative farming, digital, and life skills. They will form green microenterprises serving 1,500 smallholder farmers and act as champions of sustainable food systems. The project promotes a circular economy, turning waste into value, while enhancing ecosystem restoration and livelihood resilience. Strategic partnerships with research institutions, private agritech actors, and government agencies will advance policy integration, market access, and carbon credit innovation. By reducing fertilizer costs by 40%, boosting yields, and generating dignified green jobs, the initiative empowers excluded youth to drive Kenya s transition toward regenerative, inclusive, and climate-smart food systems.

core_fields.abstract: Every year, Sierra Leone generates thousands of tons of cassava peels from flour and garri production. At the same time, smallholder livestock farmers face high feed costs, and many rely on roaming animals feeding on people's crops. Our innovation addresses both environmental and social challenges by converting cassava peels into safe, nutritious, and affordable animal feed. Using simple drying, milling, and blending processes, we transform waste into a value-added product that improves livestock nutrition and reduces feeding costs by up to 40% compared to imported or commercial feed. This approach is informed by circular agriculture and feed science, which show that properly processed cassava peels are a rich source of carbohydrates and suitable for livestock diets. By combining practical processing techniques with quality control, we ensure the feed is safe, palatable, and reliable for small-scale farmers. Immediate benefits include reduced feeding costs, fewer conflicts over crops, less cassava waste, and improved income for farmers. Sustainable benefits include lower greenhouse gas emissions, reduced pressure on land, stronger livestock systems, enhanced food security, and opportunities for youth and women to engage in feed production. Communities benefit from a cleaner environment and reduced overgrazing, while society gains a replicable model for turning agricultural by-products into high-value, climate-smart solutions

core_fields.abstract: The Empowering Rural Communities through Sustainable Food Practices project introduces an innovative, community-led food systems model that integrates regenerative agriculture, nutrition education, and local enterprise development to tackle food insecurity and environmental degradation in Eastern Uganda. Rural households in this region face declining agricultural productivity, poor diets, and income instability largely due to unsustainable farming practices, limited access to agronomic knowledge, and climate-related shocks. This innovation applies a participatory approach that empowers youth and women as key agents of transformation. It promotes climate-smart practices such as organic composting, intercropping, agroforestry, and crop diversification techniques proven to restore soil fertility, conserve water, and increase yields. Through demonstration gardens and farmer field schools, communities gain practical skills to sustainably produce safe and nutritious foods. Complementary training in nutrition, post-harvest handling, and value addition ensures that increased production translates into better diets and improved household incomes. The scientific and technical foundation of the innovation draws from agroecological research and local knowledge systems that emphasize biodiversity, soil regeneration, and closed-loop food production. By combining these with digital learning and community cooperatives, the project creates inclusive, replicable pathways for scaling sustainable food systems. Immediate benefits include enhanced food availability, improved nutrition, and strengthened household resilience. In the long term, the project fosters self-reliant rural economies, reduces environmental degradation, and contributes to national goals of sustainable agriculture, gender equality, and climate adaptation ultimately building healthier communities and ecosystems across Uganda

core_fields.title: Land for Life in the Central American rain forest
core_fields.description: After decades of R&D in rain forests, Inga Foundation (IF) knows of no other approach that is, not only, capable of providing food-security to subsistence farming families, but also of regenerating the fertility of land degraded by many decades of slash-and-burn (s-b). Over 600 families have abandoned s-b in favour of sparing existing vegetation and nurturing the re-greening of previously derelict land. This is a new Green Revolution in land-use, replacing desolation with productive agroforest.
core_fields.abstract: The underlying concept of IF's Program is based on reverse engineering from nature and not from conventional agricultural knowledge current in the mid-1980s. The Green Revolution in agriculture of the 1960-70s took existing systems and accelerated their performance with a package of agro-chemicals, "improved" crop varieties, etc. It is widely seen to have failed in rain forest environments. The only model of sustainability available then was the rain forest itself: how the forest rooting system and its symbiont organisms respond to the deeply-weathered and leached Latosols that are typical of their environment. A Cambridge pilot study (1986-88) clearly identified the key nutrient failure that drives shifting agriculture in this context; and it established that physical protection of the upper soil layers is crucial, together with high inputs of organic matter to sustain the soil microbial population. These characteristics are reflected in the mulching technique of alley-cropping with legume tree species; supplemented with rock phosphate. Later Cambridge University trials (1988-2002) proved the system conclusively using trees of the genus Inga as alley species. This is the innovation: lessons learned from the rain forest itself are used to simulate its functioning for subsistence agriculture. The system has proved itself highly sustainable over many decades of use; and, moreover, is the only system known to us as capable of this. IF further discovered that the system, supplemented by Rock P, Dolomitic Lime and other minerals is unique in enabling the restoration of soils previously degraded by decades of slash-and-burn.

core_fields.title: Blended Finance Model for Circular WASH-Agro Resilience in Indigenous Communities to Overcome Hunger-Transform Lives
core_fields.description: Blended financial instrument for circular economy WASH-agroecology model in indigenous communities, La Guajira, Colombia. Addresses child malnutrition and climate-driven water crisis by providing access to safe water through reverse osmosis treatment using solar energy, IoT sensors, ecological latrines, and regenerative gardens. Benefits: Reduces diarrheal diseases -50%, increases carbon +2 t/ha, improves incomes COP$4-6M/month for 4,000 people in Year 1, scalable to 40,000 people in 3 years. Aligned with WHH: healthy diets, sustainability, and equitable access.
core_fields.abstract: Integrally combats water scarcity, deficient sanitation, food insecurity, weak financing, and sustainability in indigenous communities of La Guajira, Colombia. The problem solved is the WASH-agroecology crisis in indigenous communities, exacerbated by climate change, causing multidimensional poverty (50-60% rural, DANE 2025), gender inequality, chronic malnutrition (30% in children under 5 years), and 55 child deaths in 2025 (Defensor a del Pueblo de Colombia). It is relevant in LAC, where 27.4% of the poor face droughts (MPI 2025). The solution integrates reverse osmosis, solar energy (72-hour tests) with predictive IoT sensors, ecological latrines (waste reuse into biofertilizers), and agroecological and regenerative gardens, operated by indigenous community organizations (OCSAS). It is novel due to hybrid fusion: scientific insights (hydrology, >84% chloride reduction) and ancestral knowledge of indigenous peoples (traditional wells), differentiating from assistentialist solutions (government water trucks cost USD$13/m vs. USD$2/m in our model). Similar solutions exist, but lack sustainability, resilience, and indigenous community governance. Immediate and sustainable benefits: elevates quality of life with safe and sustainable access (60 L/day/person, 90% households), eliminates open defecation, reduces sexual violence against women and girls due to open defecation, reduces Diarrheal Diseases -50%, gardens +40% increase healthy diets and nutritious foods; Community: gender equity (more free time for women), decreases school absenteeism, increases incomes +20%; improves soils and environment: +2 t/ha carbon, regenerated soils, boosts community resilience. Pilots already tested in other communities of La Guajira: 5K benefited, validate adoption >85%.
